Unit 1: Health, Wellbeing and Sport Students will explore how physical activity, physical health and mental wellbeing contribute to a healthy lifestyle and improved quality of life. They will investigate the benefits of sport, examine factors influencing health, and consider strategies to maintain and enhance overall wellbeing.

Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory in all sizes Issue 6: Unit 1 (GLH changed) Unit 2: Fitness Testing Students will develop the knowledge and practical skills to conduct safe, inclusive fitness testing and health screening using traditional, modern and technology-enabled methods, interpret results against international standards, and provide evidence-based recommendations for health and performance. Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory from Extended Certificate upwards Optional in Certificate Issue 6: Unit 28 (renumbered) Unit 3: Sports Injuries Management

This unit equips students with the knowledge and practical skills to understand, prevent, assess and manage common sports injuries. Students will explore injury mechanisms, risk factors and treatment strategies, to support safe and effective return to sport. Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory from Foundation Diploma upwards Issue 6: Unit 25 (renumbered) Unit 4: Sports Psychology Students will develop an understanding of the psychological factors that influence sports performance and plan psychological techniques to enhance performance. This unit builds knowledge and practice relevant to coaching, performance analysis and sports science pathways.

Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory from Diploma upwards Issue 6: Unit 27 (renumbered) Unit 5: Anatomy and Physiology in Sport This unit explores the structure and function of key body systems and how they respond to sport and exercise. Students will develop knowledge of the musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory and nervous systems, and their responses and adaptations to physical activity. Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory from Diploma upwards Issue 6: Unit 24 (retitled) Unit 6: Nutrition for Physical Performance

Students explore the importance of nutrition and hydration in supporting health, recovery, and performance in sport and physical activity. They will develop knowledge and practical skills that prepare them for progression into sport, fitness and health-related study or employment. Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory in Extended Diploma Optional in Diploma Issue 6: Unit 26 (renumbered) Unit 7: Careers in Sport

Students will be introduced to different career opportunities in the global sports sector and the skills required to succeed in them. They will develop employability and digital skills, while exploring how to prepare for, and access, a wide range of sport-related roles and progress within them. Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory in Extended Diploma Issue 6: Unit 2 (retitled) Unit 8: Sports Research Methods Students will develop knowledge and understanding of research methods used in sport, including types of research, data collection techniques, and principles of validity, reliability and ethics. Pearson Set Assignment 60 GLH Mandatory in Extended Diploma New in Issue 3 Units 9 to 11

Internally assessed core units Set and assessed by the centre. Mandatory in the Extended Diploma, and in some smaller sizes. Unit 9: Practical Sports Performance This unit develops students’ practical skills and understanding of performance in selected sports through active participation and analysis. Students will explore techniques, tactics and strategies to improve their own performance, and demonstrate competence in competitive situations. Internally assessed 60 GLH Mandatory from Extended Certificate upwards Issue 6: Unit 35 (renumbered) Unit 10: Sports Coaching and Leadership

This unit focuses on the principles and practices of sports coaching and leadership, equipping students to plan, deliver and evaluate sessions across various sport settings. Emphasis is placed on safety, inclusion, motivation, progression, and adapting coaching styles to enhance performance and participation. Students will plan, carry out and present a small-scale research project in a sports context, developing practical investigation and analytical skills. This unit will provide students with skills that transfer well to a sector which is increasingly reliant on innovation via evidence- based practice. Learn: Unit 1 Health, Wellbeing and Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 1 › Learn Unit 1 60 GLH Student learning Health, Wellbeing and Sport This unit is about the difference that physical activity, sport and healthy habits make to people. You will look at the activities people take part in and why, the physical and mental health they bring, how to measure your own health, and how to recognise and support wellbeing. Overview

This unit is about the difference that physical activity, sport and healthy habits make to people. You will look at the activities people take part in and why, the physical and mental health they bring, how to measure your own health, and how to recognise and support wellbeing. Presentation A1 Types of active pursuits

Physical activity covers any movement that uses energy. A sport is a competitive activity with rules and organisation, such as netball or football. Physical recreation is activity done for enjoyment and health, such as cycling to work or a Sunday swim. Outdoor activity takes place in natural settings and often has an adventurous element, such as climbing or kayaking. Physical education is planned learning in school that builds skill and understanding. Physical fitness activity is training designed to improve a particular component of fitness, such as a spin class or a circuit.

Being able to name each type with a real example is the first step. Examiners and assessors expect you to see that these types overlap: a school football team is both sport and physical education. A2 Categories of participants

People take part in physical activity for different reasons and at different stages of life. Children and young people often take part in school sport and clubs. Adults may join clubs or fitness classes to manage work-life balance. Older adults may focus on balance, strength and social contact. People with disabilities may need adapted equipment, rules or facilities. Describing categories helps you tailor provision: a provider that knows its participants can plan sessions they will return to. A3 Benefits of participating

Benefits fall into three groups. Physical benefits include a stronger heart and lungs, healthier body weight and stronger bones and muscles. Mental benefits include better mood, lower stress and higher self-esteem, particularly when a person achieves a goal. Social benefits include making friends, belonging to a team and reduced loneliness. Strong answers connect each benefit to a specific group: for example, a teenager who joins a team may gain both social belonging and self-confidence. A4 Reasons for providing physical activity and sport

Providers such as councils, schools, clubs and private gyms offer activity for different reasons. They may want to improve public health, build community cohesion, reduce anti-social behaviour, develop talent, create jobs or simply make money. Understanding the reason behind a provider helps you judge whether its activities are well designed for the people it wants to reach. A5 Methods of engaging more participants

Providers use several methods to attract people who are not yet active: free taster sessions, flexible timings for people who work, outreach in community spaces, activities that fit the interests of a group, and clear information in the languages people use. The strongest approach usually combines methods, because different people are put off for different reasons. B1 Definition of physical health

Physical health is the condition of the body and its systems. It includes cardiovascular fitness, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility, body composition and the absence of disease or injury that limits everyday life. Physical health is not only about being able to lift heavy weights; a person who runs a marathon but has high blood pressure may not be in good physical health. B2 Factors affecting physical health

Several factors affect physical health: how active a person is, what they eat and drink, how much they sleep, whether they smoke or drink alcohol, their genetics, their age and their environment. You need to explain how these factors interact. For example, low activity combined with a high-calorie diet increases the risk of excess body fat, which in turn raises the risk of heart disease. B3 Health monitoring tests

Health monitoring tests give a snapshot of physical health. Common tests include resting heart rate, blood pressure, peak flow (a measure of lung function), waist-to-hip ratio and body mass index. Each test measures something different and each has limits. A single reading can be affected by stress, caffeine or the time of day, so repeated measurements give a more reliable picture. B4 Benchmarks of good physical health

A result means little on its own. Benchmarks give it meaning by comparing it with a standard: national guidelines for blood pressure or body mass index, or normative data for a population of the same age and sex. When you analyse your own health, state the benchmark you used, say whether you are above, within or below it, and explain what that means in practice. C1 Definition of mental health and social wellbeing

Mental health is a state of wellbeing in which a person can cope with normal stress, work productively and contribute to their community. Social wellbeing is the quality of a person's relationships and their sense of belonging. Both are positive states that can change over time, not only the absence of illness. C2 Factors affecting mental health and social wellbeing Factors include relationships, work or study pressure, sleep, physical activity, money, bereavement, discrimination and access to support. Sport can improve mental health through exercise, routine and social contact, but it can also cause stress if the pressure to win is intense or if a person is injured.

C3 Signs and symptoms of poor mental health Signs include a persistent low mood, loss of interest in things a person used to enjoy, withdrawal from friends, changes in sleep or appetite, irritability, difficulty concentrating and physical symptoms without a clear cause. Recognising these signs early allows a person to get support. A coach or teacher who notices a change should respond sensitively and refer the person to appropriate help. C4 Assessing wellbeing

Wellbeing can be assessed with structured questionnaires and by reflecting on your own patterns: sleep, energy, mood, relationships and motivation. The method you choose should be clear, the questions should be fair, and your conclusions should follow from the answers. Be honest about limits, such as a questionnaire completed on a bad day. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the different types of physical activities and their benefits. Your answer should include: Name at least three types of activity, such as sport, physical recreation and physical fitness activity.

Link each type to a benefit: physical, mental or social. Use a real example for each type. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the reasons for providing different physical activities in a local area and recommend effective ways of engaging more participants. Your answer should include: Give at least two reasons a provider offers activity, such as public health or community cohesion. Evaluate the reasons by weighing strengths and limitations. Recommend specific methods, such as taster sessions and flexible timings, and justify them for a named group. Key terms Physical recreation Activity done for enjoyment and health in leisure time.

Normative data Results from a comparison group that show what is typical for that group. Social wellbeing The quality of a person's relationships and sense of belonging. Peak flow A measure of how quickly a person can breathe out, used as an indicator of lung function. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name and give examples of the five types of physical activity. I can explain benefits in the physical, mental and social groups, and link them to a specific person. I can explain the difference between physical health and mental wellbeing.

I can state a benchmark and say whether a result is above, within or below it. Learn: Unit 2 Fitness Testing | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 2 › Learn Unit 2 60 GLH Student learning Fitness Testing Fitness testing is about collecting reliable information and using it well. In this unit you will learn which tests measure which components of fitness, how to screen a client before testing, how to run tests safely, and how to analyse and explain results so that the person being tested knows what to do next. Overview

Fitness testing is about collecting reliable information and using it well. In this unit you will learn which tests measure which components of fitness, how to screen a client before testing, how to run tests safely, and how to analyse and explain results so that the person being tested knows what to do next. Presentation A1 Fitness tests for different components of fitness

Each component of fitness needs a test that matches it. Sit and reach measures flexibility of the lower back and hamstrings. Grip dynamometry measures hand strength. The multi-stage fitness test (bleep test) and the step test estimate aerobic endurance. Sprint tests measure speed, and vertical jump and the Wingate test measure power. The one-minute press-up or sit-up measures muscular endurance. Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) estimates body composition.

Laboratory-based tests, such as a treadmill test with gas analysis, give precise results but need equipment and expertise. Field-based tests, such as the bleep test, are practical for groups. Your task is to choose the test that fits the purpose and the setting. A2 Advantages and disadvantages of tests

Judge each test by four qualities. Validity asks whether the test measures what it claims. Reliability asks whether the test gives consistent results when repeated. Practicality asks whether the test is affordable, quick and safe in the setting. Cultural adaptability and accessibility ask whether the test suits people from different backgrounds and abilities. A strong evaluation names one advantage and one disadvantage for each quality. B1 Health screening procedures

Before a client is tested, you need to know their health history and any reasons they should not take part in a particular test. Screening uses a questionnaire such as PAR-Q, a conversation about past injuries and medication, and observation. You must explain the purpose of screening, gain informed consent, keep information confidential and refer the client to a medical professional when a concern is raised. B2 Health monitoring tests

Health monitoring tests include resting heart rate, blood pressure, peak flow, waist-to-hip ratio and body mass index. Before recording a reading, make sure the client is rested and in the correct position, and repeat readings when a result seems unusual. Record each value with its unit and date. B3 Fitness tests Choose a fitness test for each component you need to measure. Explain the protocol: the starting position, the instructions to the client, the number of trials and how the result is recorded. A test is only useful if it is carried out the same way each time. B4 Administering tests and screening

Safety comes first. Complete a pre-test check, warm the client up, follow the protocol exactly, watch for warning signs such as chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness, and know the reasons to stop a test. Record what happened, including any test that was stopped and why. C1 Analysing results against normative data A result is more useful when you compare it with a standard. Normative data show how a result compares with a population of the same age and sex, with sports performers or with elite athletes. State the comparison group, say whether the result is above, at or below it, and explain what the difference means for the client's health or performance.

C2 Feedback and recommendations Feedback should be clear, honest and encouraging. Start with strengths, then explain areas for improvement in plain language, then give one or two specific recommendations the client can act on, such as a twice-weekly strength session or a sleep review. Refer the client to a professional when a result needs medical attention. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Justify the selection of fitness tests, commenting on suitability, reliability, validity and practicality for a 16-year-old netball player.

Your answer should include: Choose a test that suits netball, such as the multi-stage fitness test for aerobic endurance. Comment on reliability: the same protocol and pacing must be used each time. Comment on practicality: several players can be tested together, but supervision is needed. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the health screening questionnaire, health monitoring tests and fitness test results for a client, and recommend lifestyle improvements. Your answer should include: Evaluate the questionnaire: useful for spotting risk, but it relies on honest answers. Evaluate a single reading: affected by stress or caffeine, so repeat readings are better.

Recommend specific changes linked to a weaker result, and say how progress will be checked. Key terms Validity The extent to which a test measures what it is intended to measure. Reliability The consistency of a test: similar results when repeated under the same conditions. Informed consent Agreement to take part, given once the client understands the purpose and risks. Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) A method of estimating body composition by sending a small electrical current through the body. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can match each fitness test to the component of fitness it measures.

I can explain validity, reliability and practicality with a specific example. I can describe the screening steps and explain when a client should be referred. I can compare a result with normative data and give a specific recommendation. Learn: Unit 3 Sports Injuries Management | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 3 › Learn Unit 3 60 GLH Student learning Sports Injuries Management Sports injuries are a normal part of sport. In this unit you will learn what the common injuries are, how they happen, how the body heals, what risk factors make injury more likely, how to prevent injury, and how to plan initial and post-injury treatment. Overview Sports injuries are a normal part of sport. In this unit you will learn what the common injuries are, how they happen, how the body heals, what risk factors make injury more likely, how to prevent injury, and how to plan initial and post-injury treatment.

Presentation A1 Types of sports injuries Injuries are grouped by the tissue they affect. Hard tissue injuries include fractures (a break in bone) and dislocations (a bone moved out of its joint). Soft tissue injuries include sprains (ligament damage), strains (muscle or tendon damage) and contusions (bruises). Overuse injuries include tendinopathies and shin splints, which develop from repeated stress. Head and neurological injuries include concussion. Joint injuries include meniscal tears and osteoarthritis. Learning these groups helps you choose the right treatment. A2 Mechanisms of sports injuries

Injuries have different mechanisms. An acute injury happens suddenly, such as a sprained ankle from a landing. A chronic injury develops over time. A traumatic injury comes from a single force, such as a collision. An overuse injury comes from repeated loading without enough recovery. Intrinsic and extrinsic causes can combine: an athlete with a weak hip may be more likely to develop an injury when playing on a hard surface. A3 Physiological responses to injury

After an injury, the body heals in three phases. In the inflammatory phase (about the first four days), swelling, heat, redness and pain appear as the body removes damaged tissue. In the tissue formation phase (about day four to day 24), new tissue and blood vessels form. In the maturation phase (three weeks to a year), collagen fibres reorganise and the tissue strengthens. Knowing these phases tells you what treatment and loading are appropriate at each stage. A4 Psychological responses to injury

An injured athlete may feel denial, anger, frustration, anxiety, low mood or, eventually, acceptance. These responses affect how well the athlete follows a rehabilitation programme and how quickly they return. Social effects are also important: losing a team role or training with friends can affect identity and wellbeing. Good support includes clear communication, realistic goals and regular contact. B1 Extrinsic risk factors

Extrinsic factors come from outside the athlete. They include coaching (the volume and intensity of training), technique, the environment (weather, surface and lighting), clothing and footwear, and safety hazards such as unprotected equipment. Each can be changed by a coach or organisation, which makes extrinsic factors a priority for prevention. B2 Intrinsic risk factors

Intrinsic factors come from the athlete. They include training effects such as muscle imbalance or fatigue, and individual variables such as age, fitness, injury history, sleep and nutrition. An athlete with a previous ankle injury, for example, has a higher risk of re-injury, which should be considered when planning training. B3 Preventative measures Prevention combines several steps: a proper warm-up, progressive training, strength and balance work, good technique, suitable footwear and equipment, a safe environment, and a plan for recovery. Staff roles matter: a coach who sets a safe training load and a first-aider who is trained and available both reduce risk.

C1 Initial treatment of a sports injury Initial treatment follows a set order. Use SALTAPS to assess the injury: Stop, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement, and Strength testing. Use PRICED for the first treatment: Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, and Diagnosis by a professional. Always refer to a qualified professional when a serious injury is suspected, such as a head injury or a suspected fracture. C2 Post-injury treatment

After the initial phase, treatment depends on the injury and the healing stage. Options include taping and bandaging for support, immobilisation for a fracture, cryotherapy (cold) in the early stage, thermal treatment later, and specialist equipment such as TENS (electrical stimulation) for pain relief. Rehabilitation should progress from gentle movement to strengthening and then to sport-specific work, with each step matched to the healing phase. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the physiological responses to common sporting injuries.

Your answer should include: Describe the inflammatory phase: swelling, heat, redness and pain as damaged tissue is removed. Describe the tissue formation phase: new tissue and blood vessels form. Describe the maturation phase: collagen reorganises and the tissue strengthens. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the prevention, initial and post-injury treatment for two common sports injuries, justifying the choices of treatment. Your answer should include: Choose two injuries, such as a hamstring strain and an ankle sprain. Explain prevention for each, linked to risk factors. Explain initial treatment using PRICED, and post-injury treatment matched to the healing phase.

Justify each choice by the stage of healing. Key terms Contusion A bruise: a soft tissue injury caused by a direct blow. Tendinopathy Pain and dysfunction in a tendon, often caused by overuse. Proprioception The body's sense of its position and movement, often reduced after a sprain. Collagen A protein that gives tissue its strength, reorganised during the maturation phase of healing. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name the main groups of sports injuries and give an example of each. I can explain the three phases of healing and what treatment suits each phase.

I can explain extrinsic and intrinsic risk factors, with an example of each. I can use SALTAPS and PRICED correctly, and say when to refer to a professional. Learn: Unit 4 Sports Psychology | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 4 › Learn Unit 4 60 GLH Student learning Sports Psychology Why do some athletes thrive under pressure while others struggle? This unit explores the psychology behind performance: personality and motivation, stress, anxiety and arousal, how teams work, and how psychological skills are planned and judged. Overview Why do some athletes thrive under pressure while others struggle? This unit explores the psychology behind performance: personality and motivation, stress, anxiety and arousal, how teams work, and how psychological skills are planned and judged. Presentation A1 Personality

Personality is a consistent pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Three approaches explain how it affects performance. Trait theory says personality is stable across situations. The situational approach says behaviour depends mainly on the environment. The interactional approach combines both: a trait such as competitiveness shows more in some situations than others. Type A performers are competitive and time-urgent, which can drive motivation but also raise stress. Type B performers are more relaxed, which can reduce stress but may limit drive in a high-pressure contest. A2 Motivation

Motivation is the drive to start and keep going. Intrinsic motivation comes from enjoyment and satisfaction. Extrinsic motivation comes from rewards such as medals, praise or money. Achievement motivation depends on whether a person hopes for success or fears failure. Attribution theory explains how a performer explains a result: attributing success to effort and failure to a changeable cause helps keep motivation high. Consider how a performer's type of motivation affects their persistence in training. B1 Stress

Stress is the response to demands that exceed a person's ability to cope. A performer may feel stress from a difficult opponent, a selection decision or a poor result. Stress produces physical changes, such as a faster heart rate and tense muscles, and mental changes, such as poor concentration. The key distinction is between demands and the response: the same demand can cause stress in one performer and a useful challenge in another. B2 Anxiety

Anxiety is a state of worry and fear about an outcome. Cognitive anxiety is the mental side: worry, negative thoughts and self-doubt. Somatic anxiety is the physical side: sweating, a racing heart and muscle tension. Each can be measured, and each affects performance differently. Cognitive anxiety usually reduces performance, while some somatic arousal can help a performer feel ready. B3 Arousal

Arousal is the level of physical and mental activation. The inverted-U hypothesis proposes that performance improves as arousal rises to an optimal level, then declines. Under-aroused performers lack focus; over-aroused performers narrow their attention and make errors. Catastrophe theory adds that, when cognitive anxiety is high, performance can fall sharply once arousal passes the optimal point. The optimal level varies: fine, precise skills usually need lower arousal than strong, simple skills. B4 Team dynamics

Teams develop over time. Tuckman's stages describe forming, storming, norming and performing. Task cohesion is the shared commitment to a common goal; social cohesion is the friendship and trust between members. Leadership styles shape the team, from directive to participative. Two problems often appear in groups: the Ringelmann effect , where individual effort falls as group size grows, and social loafing , where people contribute less when their individual effort is hard to see. C1 Assessment

Before planning a training programme, assess the performer. Performance profiling rates a performer's psychological strengths and weaknesses. Questionnaires can measure anxiety, motivation or self-confidence. A good assessment explains what was measured, why, and what it means for the performer, so that the programme targets real needs. C2 Planning A psychological skills programme usually lasts four to six weeks. Set SMART aims: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Plan the sequence of sessions so that each technique builds on the last, and schedule how and when the performer will practise. C3 Psychological skills and techniques

The main techniques are goal setting (process, performance and outcome goals), arousal regulation (breathing and relaxation to lower arousal, or activation to raise it), imagery (mental rehearsal of a skill or situation), confidence building (positive self-talk and reviewing successes) and concentration training (focusing on a cue and recovering focus after a distraction). Choose each technique because the performer needs it. D1 Overview of psychological techniques

Each technique aims at a psychological need. Goal setting directs effort, arousal regulation manages anxiety and stress, imagery rehearses skills and builds confidence, and concentration training keeps attention on what matters. A programme works best when its techniques support one another. D2 Evaluating effectiveness Judge a programme using several types of evidence: performance results, changes in psychological measures, the performer's own report, and observation of behaviour in training and competition. One result is rarely enough. Note whether the effect lasted, and whether it applies to every performer in the same way. D3 Modern influences

Modern performers are shaped by social media, pressure from sponsors and the media, and sports science tools such as performance data and wearables. These can support psychological skills, for example by showing progress, but they can also add pressure and self-comparison. Consider both sides when you evaluate. D4 Making recommendations Recommendations should follow from the evidence. A good recommendation names the change, explains why the evidence supports it, says how it would be measured and when it will be reviewed. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1

Explain personality and its effect on sports performance. Your answer should include: Define personality as a consistent pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Explain trait, situational or interactional views, using one of them clearly. Link a personality type to a named effect on performance, such as stress or drive. 6 marks Practice 2 Analyse how stress, anxiety and arousal theories affect performance. Your answer should include: Explain the inverted-U hypothesis and the effect of under- and over-arousal. Explain the difference between cognitive and somatic anxiety. Explain catastrophe theory and why the performance can fall sharply.

Make a judgement about which measure a coach should monitor and why. Key terms Personality A consistent pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviours that influences performance. Inverted-U hypothesis The idea that performance improves with arousal up to an optimal level, then declines. Social loafing Reduced individual effort in a group, where each person's contribution is hard to see. Performance profiling A structured assessment of a performer's psychological strengths and weaknesses. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain trait, situational and interactional views of personality.

I can explain the difference between stress, anxiety and arousal. I can explain the inverted-U hypothesis and catastrophe theory. I can plan a psychological skills programme with SMART aims and justified techniques. Learn: Unit 5 Anatomy and Physiology in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 5 › Learn Unit 5 60 GLH Student learning Anatomy and Physiology in Sport Every movement, breath and sprint depends on the body's systems working together. This unit explains how the musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory and nervous systems are built, what they do, and how they respond to exercise in the short term and adapt over the long term. Overview

Every movement, breath and sprint depends on the body's systems working together. This unit explains how the musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory and nervous systems are built, what they do, and how they respond to exercise in the short term and adapt over the long term. Presentation A1 Structure and function of the skeletal system

The skeleton provides support, protects organs, allows movement and produces blood cells. The axial skeleton is the skull, spine and ribcage. The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and the girdles that join them. Bones are living tissue that adapt to load. Joints connect bones; synovial joints, such as the hip, knee and shoulder, are freely movable and contain synovial fluid that lubricates them. A2 Structure and function of the muscular system

Skeletal muscle produces movement by contracting. Each muscle contains muscle fibres, and each fibre is made of myofibrils containing actin and myosin, which slide over each other. Three fibre types suit different activities: slow oxidative (type I) for endurance, fast oxidative glycolytic (type IIa) for mixed activity, and fast glycolytic (type IIx) for short, powerful efforts. A3 Musculoskeletal response to exercise

In the short term, exercise increases blood flow to muscles and bones and raises their temperature, which makes them more flexible. Synovial fluid production increases. In the long term, regular loading produces adaptations: muscles hypertrophy (grow), tendons and ligaments become stronger, and bone density increases. The adaptations match the type of loading: resistance training builds muscle and bone strength. B1 Cardiovascular structure

The heart has four chambers. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body and the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and the left ventricle pumps it to the body. Valves (the tricuspid, bicuspid, pulmonary and aortic) prevent backflow. Blood is made of plasma, red blood cells that carry oxygen, white blood cells that defend the body, and platelets that help clotting. B2 Respiratory structure

Air enters through the nose and mouth, passes through the trachea and bronchi, and reaches the alveoli. The alveoli are tiny air sacs surrounded by capillaries, where gases are exchanged. The diaphragm and intercostal muscles drive breathing. B3 Functions of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems Together, the two systems deliver oxygen and nutrients to the muscles and remove carbon dioxide and waste. The heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins. The lungs exchange gases, using diffusion: oxygen moves from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out, because each gas moves down its partial pressure gradient.

B4 Cardiovascular and respiratory responses to exercise During exercise, heart rate and stroke volume increase, so cardiac output rises. Breathing rate and tidal volume increase, so minute ventilation rises. Blood is redistributed towards working muscles. Long-term training produces adaptations: a larger stroke volume, a lower resting heart rate, more capillaries around muscle fibres (capillarisation) and a higher VO₂ max. C1 Structure of the nervous system

The nervous system has two main parts. The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system carries messages to and from the rest of the body. Its somatic part controls voluntary movement; its autonomic part controls involuntary functions such as heart rate. C2 Function of the nervous system Nerve cells (neurons) carry electrical impulses. A motor unit is one motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it controls. When an impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction , a chemical messenger is released, which triggers contraction. The nervous system also controls balance and coordination, using sensory information from the muscles and joints.

C3 Nervous system response to exercise Exercise increases the speed and accuracy of nerve signals and improves the recruitment of motor units, so movements become more coordinated. Sensory feedback from the muscles and joints improves with training, which improves balance and reaction time. The sympathetic nervous system raises heart rate and breathing before and during exercise. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the roles of different types of joints and muscle fibre types in sporting movements.

Your answer should include: Identify the joint type and why it suits the movement, for example a ball-and-socket joint for many planes of movement. Explain a fibre type and its use, for example type IIx for short, powerful efforts. Link the structure to the function in a named sport. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the significance of cardiovascular and respiratory responses and adaptations to different types of exercise. Your answer should include: Describe the short-term responses: heart rate, stroke volume and breathing. Describe the long-term adaptations of endurance training and say why each one helps. Compare the adaptations of resistance training.

Judge the significance of each adaptation for the activity. Key terms Stroke volume The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle in one heartbeat. Capillarisation An increase in the number of capillaries around muscle fibres, which improves oxygen delivery. Motor unit A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it controls. VO₂ max The maximum rate at which the body can take in and use oxygen during exercise. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name the bones and joints of the axial and appendicular skeleton. I can trace the path of blood through the heart and of air to the alveoli.

I can explain a short-term response and a long-term adaptation for one system. I can explain how a nerve impulse leads to muscle contraction. Learn: Unit 6 Nutrition for Physical Performance | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 6 › Learn Unit 6 60 GLH Student learning Nutrition for Physical Performance What an athlete eats and drinks affects how they train, recover and perform. This unit covers nutrients, hydration and digestion, energy balance, safe and ethical use of supplements, and how to plan a personalised diet and hydration strategy for a chosen sport. Overview

What an athlete eats and drinks affects how they train, recover and perform. This unit covers nutrients, hydration and digestion, energy balance, safe and ethical use of supplements, and how to plan a personalised diet and hydration strategy for a chosen sport. Presentation A1 Nutrition

Food provides macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats) and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals). Carbohydrate is the main fuel for high-intensity exercise and is stored as glycogen in muscle and liver. Protein supports repair and adaptation. Fats provide a large energy store for low-intensity, long-duration activity. Vitamins and minerals support many processes, such as iron in oxygen transport and calcium in bone health. A2 Hydration

Water is needed for temperature control, blood volume and metabolism. Sweat losses increase during exercise and in heat, so fluid needs vary. Dehydration of even 2% of body mass can reduce performance. Athletes plan fluid intake before, during and after activity, and sports drinks can supply fluid and carbohydrate or electrolytes, depending on the demands of the activity. A3 Diet A diet plan combines food groups in the right proportions for the athlete's goals and activity. Athletes often need more carbohydrate on heavy training days and more protein for recovery. A balanced diet also provides fibre, vitamins and minerals, and fits the athlete's preferences, culture and budget. A4 Digestion

Digestion breaks food into small molecules that can be absorbed. It begins in the mouth, continues in the stomach and small intestine, where most absorption happens, and ends in the large intestine, where water is absorbed. Timing matters: eating a large meal too close to training can cause discomfort, while a light carbohydrate snack can provide energy. B1 Energy concepts Energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (kJ). Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy used at complete rest to maintain basic functions. It depends on age, sex, body size and body composition. Total energy use adds the energy of activity, digestion and adaptation to the BMR. B2 Energy balance

Energy balance is the relationship between energy taken in and energy used. Intake greater than use leads to weight gain; use greater than intake leads to weight loss. Athletes in different sports have different needs: an endurance runner may need more energy than a golfer, and a weightlifter may need more protein than an endurance athlete. B3 Measuring energy intake and use Energy intake can be recorded with a food diary or a nutrition app, and energy use estimated with activity logs or wearable devices. Each method has limits: diaries rely on accurate recording, and wearables may not measure every activity accurately. Use the same method over time so that changes can be compared.

C1 Safe use of supplements Supplements are products taken to support diet or performance, such as protein powder, creatine, vitamins and minerals. Some are safe and useful when prescribed or recommended; others carry risks. Athletes should check the label, follow the dose and seek advice from a qualified professional before starting any supplement. C2 Risk of misuse

Supplements can be contaminated, mislabelled or counterfeit. Some contain prohibited substances, and an athlete who takes them can be banned even by accident. Misuse can also cause harm to health, such as liver or kidney damage from excessive doses. Third-party testing schemes that check products for contamination reduce this risk. C3 Ethical considerations Ethics in sports nutrition cover fair play (not using substances that give an unfair advantage), athlete welfare (not harming health to win), and respect for an athlete's cultural and personal food choices. Coaches and practitioners have a duty of care to give accurate advice and to refer athletes to qualified professionals. D1 Activities

Different activities place different demands on the body. Aerobic activities such as distance running use fat and carbohydrate for long periods. Anaerobic and strength activities depend more on carbohydrate and protein. Weight-category sports and sports with long breaks may need specific timing of meals. Describe the demands of your chosen activity before you plan. D2 Planning diets

A personalised plan begins with an assessment of the athlete: body mass, activity level, goals, preferences and any health needs. The plan sets targets for energy, carbohydrate, protein, fats, fluid and key micronutrients, then translates them into meals, snacks and drinks across the week. Review the plan regularly and adjust it using the athlete's training, performance and body-mass data. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Produce a basic two-week diet and hydration plan for a selected sports performer, based on an initial assessment.

Your answer should include: State the assessment you used: body mass, activity and goals. Set energy and fluid targets with units, and include carbohydrate and protein. Show meals or snacks across the two weeks, and explain the timing around training. 6 marks Practice 2 Justify the effectiveness of a two-week diet and hydration plan, using evidence-based reasoning. Your answer should include: Link each element of the plan to the assessment. Explain the evidence for carbohydrate timing and fluid replacement in the chosen activity. Identify a limitation, such as a missing nutrient or a blood test that is needed, and recommend how to address it. Key terms

Basal metabolic rate (BMR) The energy the body uses at complete rest to maintain basic functions. Hypohydration A state in which the body has lost more fluid than it has taken in. Isotonic drink A sports drink with a similar concentration of solutes to the body, used to replace fluid and some energy. Third-party testing Independent checking of a supplement for contamination and for what its label states. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name the macronutrients and micronutrients and give a role for each. I can explain the stages of digestion and where most absorption happens.

I can calculate energy balance using kcal or kJ and explain BMR. I can plan a diet and hydration strategy linked to a named assessment. Learn: Unit 7 Careers in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 7 › Learn Unit 7 60 GLH Student learning Careers in Sport Sport offers careers in coaching, fitness, sports science, development and leisure management. This unit shows you how those careers work, what employers look for, and how to apply for a role. You will analyse a job, audit your own skills, apply for and prepare for an interview, and build a personal career plan. Overview

Sport offers careers in coaching, fitness, sports science, development and leisure management. This unit shows you how those careers work, what employers look for, and how to apply for a role. You will analyse a job, audit your own skills, apply for and prepare for an interview, and build a personal career plan. Presentation A1 Types of careers in sport

The sports industry includes coaching and teaching, fitness and personal training, sports development, sports science, officiating, event management and leisure management. Each role needs different skills and qualifications. Coaching is delivered in schools, clubs and performance centres. Sports development works with communities to increase participation. Sports science supports performers with testing, analysis and rehabilitation. A2 Career pathways and progression

Most people enter sport through volunteering, a part-time role or an entry-level qualification, then progress as they gain experience and further qualifications. A coach may start as a volunteer assistant, earn a recognised coaching award, become a lead coach and later move into management. Identify the steps a pathway requires and how long each one usually takes. A3 Employment types and opportunities

Employment can be full-time, part-time, self-employed, seasonal or on a zero-hours contract. Each has advantages and drawbacks. Self-employment gives flexibility but no guaranteed income. Seasonal work, such as summer camps, gives short-term income. Consider how a type of employment affects a person's finances, stability and development. A4 Safeguarding and professional standards

Anyone working with children or vulnerable adults has a duty to safeguard them: protecting them from harm, abuse, neglect and exploitation. This means following policy, recognising signs of abuse, reporting concerns to the designated person and keeping appropriate boundaries. Safeguarding is a condition of most sport jobs. A5 Health and safety in sport careers Professionals have a duty of care to keep participants and themselves safe. This involves risk assessment, checking equipment, following emergency procedures and keeping accurate records. Health and safety is part of every sport career, not an extra task. A6 Professional standards and ethics

Professional standards include honesty, confidentiality, respect for participants, fair treatment and keeping skills up to date through continuing professional development (CPD). Ethics means doing the right thing even when no one is watching. A coach who manipulates results or ignores safety breaks professional standards, and can lose their job or qualification. B1 Job role analysis Read a job description and person specification closely. The job description lists the duties; the person specification lists the qualifications, skills and experience an employer needs. Sort each requirement into essential and desirable, and decide which ones you already meet. B2 Personal skills audit

An audit lists your skills, qualifications and experience, and gives evidence for each one. Be specific: "I led a team of six volunteers at a junior football session" is stronger than "I am a team player". Match your audit to the person specification to find gaps, then plan how to fill them. B3 Application process A strong application shows, rather than tells. Use the person specification as a checklist and give a short example for each requirement, using the STAR format: situation, task, action and result. Keep the layout clear and the language simple. B4 Interview preparation

Prepare for common questions, such as "Tell me about a time you handled a difficult participant". Use STAR to structure answers. Research the organisation, prepare two or three questions to ask, and practise answering aloud. Reflect afterwards on what went well and what you would change. C1 Goal-setting A career plan begins with clear goals. Use SMART goals: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. A short-term goal might be completing a coaching award within six months. A long-term goal might be leading a development programme in five years. C2 Action planning

For each goal, list the actions needed, the resources required, the people who can help and the date each action will be completed. A plan with actions and dates is far more likely to succeed than a list of wishes. C3 Reviewing and updating plans Review your plan regularly, perhaps every three months. Check progress against each goal, record what you achieved, and update the plan when roles, qualifications or opportunities change. A plan that never changes is probably no longer useful. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1

Explain different careers and progression pathways in the sports industry. Your answer should include: Name two or three careers in sport, such as coaching and fitness. Describe a progression route for one career, including qualifications. Explain how the pathway changes with experience. 6 marks Practice 2 Analyse a recruitment process for a chosen sport job, and evaluate how effective it is at identifying suitable candidates. Your answer should include: Analyse the job description and person specification. Explain how the application and interview test the requirements. Evaluate the process, with a strength and a limitation, and make a judgement. Key terms

Person specification The qualifications, skills and experience an employer requires from a candidate. Continuing professional development (CPD) Ongoing learning that keeps a professional up to date. Safeguarding Protecting children and vulnerable adults from harm, abuse, neglect or exploitation. STAR A structure for interview answers: situation, task, action and result. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can describe at least three careers in sport and how each progresses. I can match a personal skills audit to a person specification. I can write SMART goals and a dated action plan.

I can explain safeguarding and why it matters in sport careers. Learn: Unit 8 Sports Research Methods | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 8 › Learn Unit 8 60 GLH Student learning Sports Research Methods Research is how sport builds knowledge. A coach who changes training because of a study, or a physiotherapist who chooses a treatment from evidence, is applying research. This unit teaches you how research is designed, how it is judged for validity, reliability and ethics, and how data is analysed and presented. Overview

Research is how sport builds knowledge. A coach who changes training because of a study, or a physiotherapist who chooses a treatment from evidence, is applying research. This unit teaches you how research is designed, how it is judged for validity, reliability and ethics, and how data is analysed and presented. Presentation A1 Purpose of research Research in sport aims to improve performance and training, inform policy, support evidence-based decisions, evaluate interventions such as injury prevention, and add to knowledge. A research question should be clear, focused and answerable with the methods available. A2 Benefits of research

Research benefits athletes through safer and more effective training, benefits coaches by showing what works, and benefits participants and governing bodies through better policy. Give a real example of research changing practice, and explain the change in terms of performance, health or participation. B1 Research approaches

Qualitative research gathers rich, descriptive data, through interviews, focus groups and observation. Quantitative research gathers numerical data, through surveys, performance tests and physiological measures. Mixed methods combine both to give breadth and depth. A deductive approach starts with a theory and tests it; an inductive approach starts with observations and builds a theory from them. B2 Research designs

An experimental design manipulates a variable to test cause and effect. A descriptive design describes what exists. A correlational design measures the relationship between two variables, but cannot show cause. A case study examines one person or group in depth. A longitudinal design follows the same people over time; a cross-sectional design looks at different people at one time. Choose the design that fits your question. B3 Literature review

A literature review summarises and evaluates existing research on a topic. It shows what is already known, where the gaps are and how your research fits. Use reliable sources such as peer-reviewed journals, textbooks and official guidance, and reference every source you use. C1 Validity and reliability Construct validity asks whether a test measures the concept it claims to measure. External validity asks whether the results can be generalised to other people or settings. Reliability asks whether results are consistent: test-retest reliability compares repeated tests over time, and inter-rater reliability compares the scores of different observers. C2 Ethics

Ethical research protects participants. The main principles are informed consent (participants understand the purpose and risks), confidentiality (data is kept private), the right to withdraw at any time, and honesty in reporting results. Ethical approval is usually needed before data is collected. D1 Data types Data are either qualitative (words, themes) or quantitative (numbers). Numerical data are measured on four scales: nominal (categories with no order, such as position played), ordinal (ordered categories, such as a ranking), interval (equal intervals with no true zero, such as temperature in Celsius) and ratio (equal intervals with a true zero, such as sprint time).

D2 Basic analysis techniques Descriptive statistics summarise data: the mean (average), the median (middle value), the mode (most common value), the range (the spread from lowest to highest) and the standard deviation (how far values typically sit from the mean). Use standard deviation to show how variable the data are, not just the average. For qualitative data, thematic analysis codes responses and groups them into themes. D3 Presenting findings

Present findings so the reader cannot misread them. Label every axis, give units, show the spread of the data as well as the average, and choose a chart that suits the data: a bar chart for categories, a scatter plot for two numerical variables, a line graph for change over time. Write a short summary that states the key finding in plain words. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Compare the strengths and limitations of different research methods and designs, using examples from sport. Your answer should include: Compare a qualitative and a quantitative method with a sport example.

State a strength and a limitation for each. Explain when mixed methods would be the better choice. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the effectiveness of different data presentation methods in communicating findings to different audiences. Your answer should include: Choose two presentation methods, such as a chart and a table. Explain which suits a coach and which suits a sports scientist. Explain how each shows variation, and judge which is most effective for each audience. Key terms Construct validity Whether a test measures the concept it claims to measure. Test-retest reliability The consistency of results when the same test is repeated over time.

Standard deviation A measure of how spread out the data are around the mean. Thematic analysis A method of coding qualitative data to find repeated patterns and themes. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods with sport examples. I can identify the design that fits a research question. I can explain validity, reliability and ethical principles. I can calculate and interpret a mean and standard deviation, and present them clearly. Back to ← Unit 8 overview Back to All BTEC units → Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Learn: Unit 9 Practical Sports Performance | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 9 › Learn Unit 9 60 GLH Student learning Practical Sports Performance Performance in sport comes from technique, tactics, decision-making and applying them under pressure. In this unit you will understand the technical and tactical demands of one sport, practise skills in drills, perform in competitive situations, and review your own performance to plan improvement. Overview

Performance in sport comes from technique, tactics, decision-making and applying them under pressure. In this unit you will understand the technical and tactical demands of one sport, practise skills in drills, perform in competitive situations, and review your own performance to plan improvement. Presentation A1 Technical demands

Every sport has core technical skills, such as passing, shooting, defending, footwork and striking. Each skill needs particular components of fitness and coordination. For example, a netball shot needs accuracy, balance and a quick release, and the body must be able to repeat it under fatigue. Identify the technical skills in your chosen sport and the fitness each one depends on. A2 Tactical demands

Tactics are the plans and decisions that shape play. Key principles include creating and dictating space in attack, covering space and pressing in defence, and the transition between attacking and defending when possession changes. Analyse the opponents' strengths and weaknesses and explain how you would exploit them. B1 Skill development Skills develop through drills, moving from isolated practice to small-sided and then full-sided games. Use feedback from a coach, a partner or video to refine technique. Each step should add a decision or a pressure so the skill transfers to the game. B2 Tactical application

Apply tactics in small-sided games and scenarios. Take on roles, such as attacker or defender, and communicate clearly with teammates. Tactical awareness is shown by choosing the right option at the right time, not by performing the most difficult skill. C1 Rules and regulations Know the rules of your sport and apply them correctly in play. Rules govern fouls, scoring, time, equipment and the roles of officials. A player who understands a rule can use it tactically, for example by choosing when to take a stoppage or a free kick. C2 Competitive performance

In competition, skills and tactics must work under pressure. Show good decision-making, technique at speed and communication with teammates. Judge your performance by its effect on the team, not only by your individual touches or points. D1 Performance analysis Review your performance with evidence: video, feedback from a coach or teammate, and your own notes. Identify two or three clear strengths and areas for improvement. Explain how each affects overall performance, and link each weakness to a specific moment in a game. D2 Action planning

An action plan turns weaknesses into targets. For each area for improvement, set a specific target, name the drills or practice you will use, say how often you will practise, and set a date to review progress. Measurable targets, such as "complete 8 out of 10 accurate passes in a drill", show clearly whether you are improving. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain how technical skills and tactical demands influence performance in a selected sport. Your answer should include: Name a technical skill and explain its demands. Name a tactical principle and explain how it affects the skill.

Link both to performance in a specific situation. 6 marks Practice 2 Analyse your own performance in a selected sport and produce a detailed action plan for improvement. Your answer should include: Use evidence, such as video or feedback, to identify two strengths and two areas for improvement. Explain how each area affects overall performance. Set measurable targets, with drills, frequency and review dates. Key terms Transition The change between attacking and defending when possession is won or lost. Small-sided game A game with fewer players on each side, used to increase the number of decisions made.

Opponent analysis Identifying an opponent's strengths and weaknesses to plan tactics against them. Action plan A written plan with specific targets, actions and review dates. Learn: Unit 10 Sports Coaching and Leadership | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 10 › Learn Unit 10 60 GLH Student learning Sports Coaching and Leadership Coaching is more than knowing the skill. A good coach plans a session, communicates clearly, keeps people safe, adapts to the group and reflects on what worked. In this unit you will learn the roles and responsibilities of a coach, compare coaching styles, plan and deliver your own session, and reflect on how it went. Overview

Coaching is more than knowing the skill. A good coach plans a session, communicates clearly, keeps people safe, adapts to the group and reflects on what worked. In this unit you will learn the roles and responsibilities of a coach, compare coaching styles, plan and deliver your own session, and reflect on how it went. Presentation A1 Roles of sports coaches and leaders

A coach or leader takes on several roles at once. As an instructor , you teach skills and tactics. As a motivator , you build confidence and commitment. As a role model , you show the behaviour you expect. As a planner and organiser , you prepare sessions and manage resources. As a mentor , you support a participant's long-term development. A2 Responsibilities Coaches are responsible for the safety of participants: safeguarding them from harm, running risk assessments, checking equipment and following emergency procedures. They must also be inclusive, treating everyone fairly, and act professionally, including keeping information confidential. A3 Skills

Effective coaches communicate clearly, adapt their approach to different people, organise sessions efficiently, observe performance accurately and give feedback that people can use. Leadership is a skill too: setting a clear direction, making decisions and supporting others to take responsibility. B1 Coaching styles

A coach chooses a style to suit the situation. An autocratic style gives clear instructions and makes decisions for the group. It suits beginners and safety-critical activities. A democratic style involves participants in decisions. It builds ownership and suits groups that are developing tactical awareness. Other styles include guided discovery, where participants find solutions with questions. B2 Leadership styles

Leadership styles describe how a leader directs a team. A directive leader sets the direction and expects compliance. A participative leader works with the team to shape goals. A transformational leader inspires people to exceed expectations. Each style affects how the team responds, and the best leaders adapt. B3 Impact on performance and participation A coaching style affects both how well people perform and whether they keep coming back. A style that is too controlling may reduce motivation and enjoyment, leading to drop-out. A style that is too loose may leave beginners unsafe or unclear. Judge a style by its effect on both performance and participation. C1 Planning

A session plan states the objectives, the structure, the timings and the equipment. Build the session from a warm-up, through a main activity that develops the objectives, to a cool-down and time for feedback. Plan adaptations in advance, so you can respond if the group finds something too easy or too hard. C2 Delivery Deliver the session with clear instructions, demonstrations and positive feedback. Keep the group moving, check understanding and watch for safety. Use questions to involve participants and praise specific actions rather than general effort. C3 Integrating coaching principles

Apply coaching principles across the session: progression from simple to complex, specificity of practice, feedback that is timely and useful, and safe, inclusive practice. A session that follows these principles is more likely to produce lasting improvement. D1 Review methods Review your session with evidence: feedback from participants, your own observations, a video or a checklist. Ask what worked, what did not, and why. Ask participants what they enjoyed and what they found hard. D2 Evaluation

Evaluate your planning and delivery against your objectives. Did the participants achieve the objectives? What was the impact of your coaching style? Weigh the strengths and limitations and reach a clear judgement. D3 Action planning Turn each area for improvement into a specific action: a change to your planning, a new technique for giving feedback, or a qualification to pursue. Set a date to review the change in your next session. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the roles and responsibilities of sports coaches and leaders.

Your answer should include: Name two or three roles, such as instructor and motivator. Explain a responsibility, such as safeguarding or health and safety. Give an example of a role in practice. 6 marks Practice 2 Analyse the suitability of different coaching and leadership styles for different situations and participants. Your answer should include: Describe an autocratic and a democratic style. Match each style to a situation, such as beginners or a mixed-ability group. Explain the effect of each style on performance and participation, and reach a judgement. Key terms Mentor A coach or leader who supports a participant's personal development and progression.

Democratic style A coaching approach in which participants share in decisions. Feedforward Advice given to help a participant improve their next attempt. Continuing professional development (CPD) Ongoing learning that keeps a coach up to date. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name the main roles of a coach and their responsibilities. I can match a coaching style to a situation and explain its effect. I can plan a session with objectives, timings and adaptations. I can review a session using evidence and set an action plan. Back to ← Unit 10 overview Back to All BTEC units →

Learn: Unit 11 Sports Research Project | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 11 › Learn Unit 11 60 GLH Student learning Sports Research Project A research project turns a question into evidence. You will choose a topic, write a testable hypothesis, plan and carry out ethical data collection, analyse what you find, draw valid conclusions, and present the project and evaluate it honestly. Overview A research project turns a question into evidence. You will choose a topic, write a testable hypothesis, plan and carry out ethical data collection, analyse what you find, draw valid conclusions, and present the project and evaluate it honestly. Presentation

A1 Selecting a research project Choose a topic that is linked to sport, is feasible within your time and resources, and can be tested with the methods you have. Examples include the effect of a warm-up on sprint performance, or the barriers to female participation in football. A narrow topic is easier to research well than a broad one. A2 Defining the research hypothesis A hypothesis is a clear, testable prediction about the relationship between variables. It states the independent variable (what you change), the dependent variable (what you measure) and the expected direction of the effect. Write the hypothesis before you choose your methods, so that every method serves it.

A3 Project planning Plan the timeline, the resources, the participants and the risks. Break the project into stages: literature review, ethics approval, data collection, analysis, writing up and presentation. Build in time for things that go wrong. A4 Ethical considerations Participants must give informed consent, understanding the purpose, procedures and risks. Their data must be kept confidential and anonymised. They must be free to withdraw at any time. Any project involving physical testing must have a risk assessment and supervision. Ethics approval from your teacher or centre is needed before data collection begins. B1 Data collection

Collect data with methods that suit your hypothesis: fitness tests and questionnaires for quantitative data, or interviews and observation for qualitative data. Record each measurement with a date, the condition and any unusual event. Repeat measurements to check consistency. B2 Professional practice Carry out the project professionally: be punctual, respect participants, keep accurate records, and follow the agreed protocol. If something goes wrong, record it and explain how it affected the data. C1 Data analysis

For numerical data, calculate the mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation, and display the data in clear charts. For qualitative data, code the responses and group them into themes. Look for outliers, and decide whether they should be removed, with a reason. C2 Drawing conclusions State whether the data supports or rejects your hypothesis, and give the evidence. Explain the limitations, such as a small sample or a single test session. Keep conclusions within what the data can support: a correlation does not prove cause. D1 Presentation formats

Present your findings as a written report, a poster, or a presentation, depending on the requirements. Use clear headings, labelled charts and a plain summary of the key finding. Write for the reader, not for yourself. D2 Evaluation Evaluate the project itself, not just the results. Name one strength and one limitation of your methods, and one of your data. For each limitation, suggest a specific improvement for a future study, and explain how it would change the results. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1

Discuss the ethical issues in research and describe how to fulfil ethical responsibilities within a project. Your answer should include: Name two ethical issues, such as consent and confidentiality. Describe how you would address each one in practice. Explain how a risk assessment protects participants. 6 marks Practice 2 Analyse data from a project and draw a justified conclusion about the hypothesis. Your answer should include: State the key result with its mean and spread. Say whether the hypothesis was supported, with evidence. Explain a limitation and what it means for the conclusion. Key terms Hypothesis A clear, testable prediction about the relationship between variables.

Informed consent Agreement to take part, given once the participant understands the purpose, procedures and rights. Outlier A data point that differs markedly from the rest of the data. Limitation A weakness in the design, data or analysis that reduces the strength of the conclusions. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can write a testable hypothesis with an independent and a dependent variable. I can explain informed consent, confidentiality and the right to withdraw. I can analyse data and say whether it supports the hypothesis. I can evaluate my project and suggest a specific improvement.
