Learn: Unit 12 Business in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 12 › Learn Unit 12 60 GLH Student learning Business in Sport Sports and active leisure businesses depend on customer trust. They must follow the law, behave ethically, serve customers well, use technology to improve their service, and market themselves effectively. This unit introduces the business side of the industry. Overview Sports and active leisure businesses depend on customer trust. They must follow the law, behave ethically, serve customers well, use technology to improve their service, and market themselves effectively. This unit introduces the business side of the industry. Presentation

A1 Business-related legislation for sports and active leisure Businesses must follow legislation that affects their work. Data protection rules govern how customer information is collected and stored. Consumer protection rules require honest pricing and fair terms. Advertising rules require claims to be truthful. Health and safety law requires a safe environment. Accessibility rules require reasonable access for disabled customers. A2 Ethical business practices

Ethical practice goes beyond the law. It includes transparency about prices and terms, fair treatment of staff and suppliers, sustainability in operations, and inclusion of different customers. Ethical choices build trust and protect the business's reputation. A3 Professional behaviours when dealing with customers Staff should be polite, reliable and respectful, handle complaints calmly and keep customer information confidential. Safeguarding applies in every customer contact, especially with children. Professional behaviour makes customers feel valued and more likely to return. B1 Advances in technology for sports and active leisure

Technology shapes customer experience: online booking, connected fitness apps, wearable devices, digital memberships, online classes and virtual tours. Each tool can collect data that helps the business understand its customers. B2 Customer service strategies A customer service strategy sets out how the business will meet customer needs. It defines the standards staff must meet, how feedback is collected and how complaints are resolved. The strategy should link to the business's aims, such as retaining members or growing sales. B3 Advances in customer service skills

Customer service now uses digital channels as well as face-to-face contact. Staff need to respond to messages quickly, use data to personalise service and recognise when a customer needs support. B4 The use of customer service skills Apply customer service skills in practice: greet the customer, listen to the need, offer a solution and follow up. Use technology to make this faster and more personal, while keeping the human contact that customers value. C1 Producing a business plan

A business plan describes the business, its market, its services, its operations and its financial position. It explains how the business will succeed and what risks it faces. A plan should be realistic and supported by evidence. C2 Finance and accounting for business planning Financial planning includes start-up costs, running costs, income forecasts, cash flow and break-even point. A cash flow forecast shows whether the business has enough money at each point in time. Check that forecasts agree with the rest of the plan. C3 Using IT for business planning

Spreadsheets, booking systems, customer databases and social media tools support planning and management. Choose tools that suit the size of the business and protect customer data. C4 Market tactics, strategies and research Market research shows who your customers are, what they need and what competitors offer. Use this to choose a target market, set prices and decide how to reach customers. A strategy links the target market to the services and the channels you will use. C5 Developing a marketing plan

A marketing plan sets objectives, the target market, the marketing mix (product, price, place and promotion), the channels and a budget. Each tactic should have a measurable target, such as a number of bookings in a set period. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the importance of legislation, ethics and professional behaviours for a selected sports or active leisure business. Your answer should include: Name one law and explain what the business must do because of it. Explain an ethical principle, such as transparency. Explain how professional behaviour protects the business.

6 marks Practice 2 Produce a marketing plan for a selected business that aligns to its aims and target market. Your answer should include: Identify the target market from research. Set a clear objective linked to the business aims. Choose tactics and channels, each with a measurable target. Key terms Target market The group of customers a business aims to attract and serve. Retention A business's ability to keep its customers over time. Break-even point The level of sales at which income equals costs. Marketing mix The product, price, place and promotion decisions that together make up a marketing plan. Check your understanding

Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain the main laws that affect sports and leisure businesses. I can describe a customer service strategy and link it to business aims. I can explain the elements of a business plan and a cash flow forecast. I can produce a marketing plan with a target market and measurable tactics. Learn: Unit 13 Fitness Training | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 13 › Learn Unit 13 60 GLH Student learning Fitness Training Fitness training is the planned improvement of the body's ability to meet a particular demand. Good programmes are built on principles such as specificity, overload and progression, and they are shaped around the individual. In this unit you will design, carry out and review a programme for a real person. Overview

Fitness training is the planned improvement of the body's ability to meet a particular demand. Good programmes are built on principles such as specificity, overload and progression, and they are shaped around the individual. In this unit you will design, carry out and review a programme for a real person. Presentation A1 Principles of fitness training

The main principles are specificity (training should match the demands of the goal), progressive overload (gradually increasing the load), progression (moving from easier to harder exercises), reversibility (adaptations are lost when training stops), individuality (people respond differently), variation (changing the programme to keep it effective) and recovery (time for the body to adapt). A2 Components of fitness

Health-related components are cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. Skill-related components are speed, power, agility, balance, coordination and reaction time. Each component needs a different training approach and a different test to measure it. A3 Methods of training

Continuous training is steady exercise over a long period, which develops aerobic endurance. Fartlek mixes steady and faster efforts. Interval training alternates work and recovery. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) uses short, intense efforts. Resistance training uses weights or bodyweight to build strength and endurance. Choose each method for the component it develops. A4 Health and safety considerations Check the client before training, warm up correctly, use equipment safely, and monitor for warning signs. Know when to stop an exercise and when to refer the client to a medical professional. B1 Client consultation

Find out the client's goals, health history, current activity and preferences. Ask about injuries, medication and any reason to modify exercise. Record the information and agree the goals with the client. B2 Programme design Design the programme around the client's goals and needs. Choose methods, exercises, sets, repetitions, intensity and frequency. Show how the programme progresses over the weeks and build in recovery. B3 Resources and logistics Plan the equipment, facilities, timings and costs the programme needs. Check that the client can access the resources, and adapt the plan if they cannot. C1 Delivery of sessions

Deliver sessions with clear instructions, correct technique and safe supervision. Watch the client's technique and give specific feedback. Keep a record of each session. C2 Monitoring Monitor the client's response using heart rate, perceived exertion, technique and feedback. Monitoring tells you whether the load is right: too little and progress stalls, too much and injury or fatigue follows. C3 Adaptions Adapt the programme when monitoring shows a need: change the load, the exercise or the recovery. Record each adaptation and why you made it, so that you can evaluate its effect later. D1 Evaluation methods

Evaluate the programme by comparing outcomes with the original goals. Use test results, monitoring data and the client's feedback. Look at what worked and what did not, and why. D2 Recommendations Make recommendations that follow directly from the evidence: a change to the load, a new method, or a longer recovery. Say how the change will be measured and when you will review it. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Justify the design of a fitness training programme with reference to the principles of training. Your answer should include: Name two principles, such as specificity and progression.

Apply each principle to a specific part of the programme. Explain how recovery is built in. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the effectiveness of adaptations made during the programme and recommend the next steps. Your answer should include: Describe the monitoring data and what it showed. Explain the adaptation made and its effect. Evaluate the effect, identify a limitation and recommend the next step. Key terms Specificity Training that matches the demands of the sport or fitness goal. Progressive overload Gradually increasing the demands of training so the body continues to adapt. Fartlek training Continuous training with varied pace, mixing steady running with faster efforts.

Perceived exertion How hard an exercise feels to the person doing it, often rated on a scale. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain the principles of training with an example for each. I can match a training method to the component of fitness it develops. I can design a programme around a client's goals and progression. I can monitor and adapt a programme and evaluate its effect. Learn: Unit 14 Sports Performance Analysis | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 14 › Learn Unit 14 60 GLH Student learning Sports Performance Analysis Performance analysis turns observation into evidence. Coaches and analysts use statistics, video and profiling to see what happened in a performance, compare it with a standard, and decide what to change. In this unit you will learn the methods and technologies, set performance standards, carry out an analysis, and give feedback based on data. Overview

Performance analysis turns observation into evidence. Coaches and analysts use statistics, video and profiling to see what happened in a performance, compare it with a standard, and decide what to change. In this unit you will learn the methods and technologies, set performance standards, carry out an analysis, and give feedback based on data. Presentation A1 Methods of performance analysis Common methods include match statistics, notational analysis (recording events such as passes and shots), live analysis, isolated skill analysis and video analysis. Some systems use automated tracking. Choose a method for its purpose, and consider its practicality: cost, time and expertise.

A2 Performance profiling A performance profile combines physical, technical, tactical and psychological information about a performer. It shows strengths and weaknesses across these areas, and helps set priorities for training. B1 Performance models and benchmarks A benchmark is a standard for comparison: the average of an elite group, a governing body standard or a relevant dataset. Choose a benchmark that matches the performer's level and conditions, and state its limits. B2 Protocols and equipment Use a clear protocol: define each event you will record, use the same definitions each time, and test the equipment before the session. Consistent protocols make the data reliable.

C1 Carrying out a sports performance analysis Observe or record the performer, collect the data using your protocol, and check it for errors. Note the context: the score, the opposition and any unusual conditions. C2 Collating and presenting analysis results Present results in formats that suit the audience: a summary for a performer, a detailed chart for a coach. Use charts, tables and heat maps where they show patterns clearly, and label everything. D1 Reviewing collected analysis data Review the data to find patterns: where successful actions happen, what leads to them, and what the opponent does. Compare the data with the benchmark and explain the differences.

D2 Providing feedback to a sports performer or team Give feedback that is specific, based on data and focused on the next action. Link each point to a piece of evidence, and set SMART goals the performer can measure. Feedback should build confidence as well as correct errors. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Analyse the relevance and practicality of different methods and technologies for performance analysis. Your answer should include: Name two methods, such as notational analysis and video analysis. Explain the relevance of each to a named sport.

Judge practicality, considering cost and expertise. 6 marks Practice 2 Provide evidence-based feedback to a performer, with recommendations for improvement. Your answer should include: Identify a pattern in the data. Link it to a specific recommendation. Set a measurable goal and a review date. Key terms Notational analysis The systematic recording of events in a performance to find patterns. Heat map A visual display showing where events or movement happened on a pitch or court. Benchmark A standard used to judge performance, such as the average of an elite group. SMART goal A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Check your understanding

Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name and compare the main methods of performance analysis. I can choose a benchmark and explain its limits. I can present analysis data in a format that suits the audience. I can give feedback based on evidence and set measurable goals. Learn: Unit 15 Rules, Regulations and Officiating in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 15 › Learn Unit 15 60 GLH Student learning Rules, Regulations and Officiating in Sport Officials make the rules work. A referee, umpire or line judge applies rules in real time, keeps the game flowing and deals with pressure. In this unit you will learn the rules and the roles of officials, the skills of officiating, and how to assess your own performance and improve it. Overview

Officials make the rules work. A referee, umpire or line judge applies rules in real time, keeps the game flowing and deals with pressure. In this unit you will learn the rules and the roles of officials, the skills of officiating, and how to assess your own performance and improve it. Presentation A1 Rules and regulations Learn the rules and competition regulations of your chosen sport, including the playing area, equipment, scoring and conduct. Rules are set and maintained by the governing body, and they change over time. Use the current version when you explain or apply a rule. A2 Roles of the officials

Different sports have different officials: referees, umpires, line judges, timekeepers and, in some sports, video assistant referees. Each role has defined responsibilities for decisions, signals and communication. A3 Responsibilities and professionalism of officials Officials must be impartial, consistent and fair. They must keep their own fitness and knowledge up to date, manage conflict calmly, and follow health and safety rules. Professionalism means making decisions with confidence and accepting that some decisions will be questioned. B1 Applying rules and regulations

Recognise infringements, decide on the sanction and apply it consistently. Manage the flow of play, deal with dissent and unsporting behaviour, and communicate through clear signals and words. The aim is a fair game that players understand. B2 Analysing officials' performance Officials are assessed through observation, video review and feedback. An assessor checks each decision against the rules, the positioning of the official and the clarity of signals. Use the same criteria each time to make the assessment fair. C1 Practical officiating

Prepare before the game: check equipment, the playing area and any safety requirements. Officiate the match, applying the rules consistently and maintaining control. Communicate decisions clearly to players and spectators. C2 Review own performance Review your officiating using video and feedback from a supervisor. Identify decisions that were late, unclear or inconsistent, and link each to a cause, such as positioning. D1 Assessment methods Use at least two methods to assess your officiating, such as video and feedback. Two methods give a more reliable picture than one, and they highlight different things: video shows decisions, feedback shows communication.

D2 Identifying strengths and weaknesses List your strengths and areas for improvement. Be specific: "my signal for a foul was unclear from distance" is more useful than "my communication needs work". D3 Improvement strategies For each weakness, set a strategy: a change in positioning, a practice of a signal, or a review of a rule. Make it specific, measurable and linked to a decision you made. D4 Monitoring progress Check your progress in the next match. Review the video, record the decisions and compare them with your targets. Repeat the review until the weakness is no longer a problem. Practice

Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the key rules, regulations and roles of officials in a selected sport. Your answer should include: Name two officials and their roles. Explain a rule and the decision that applies it. Explain the responsibility all officials share, such as fairness and safety. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate your own officiating using two assessment methods and recommend strategies for improvement. Your answer should include: Use video and feedback as two methods of assessment. Identify a specific weakness, linked to a decision.

Recommend a strategy and say how you will monitor progress. Key terms Infringement A breach of the rules, which the official must recognise and penalise. Sanction A penalty or warning given for an infringement. Game management Maintaining the flow of play while enforcing the rules fairly. Governing body The organisation that sets and maintains the rules of a sport. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain the rules and the roles of the officials in my chosen sport. I can apply a rule to a situation and explain my decision. I can assess my own officiating with two methods.

I can set a specific improvement strategy and monitor it. Learn: Unit 16 Organising Events in Sport and Physical Activities | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 16 › Learn Unit 16 60 GLH Student learning Organising Events in Sport and Physical Activities Every sports event, from a school sports day to a charity run, needs careful organisation. Aims, audiences, venues, budgets, risks and roles must fit together. In this unit you will plan, promote, deliver and evaluate an event, and reflect on your own contribution. Overview

Every sports event, from a school sports day to a charity run, needs careful organisation. Aims, audiences, venues, budgets, risks and roles must fit together. In this unit you will plan, promote, deliver and evaluate an event, and reflect on your own contribution. Presentation A1 Types and purposes of events Events include competitive events, recreational events, educational events, hybrid events that combine in-person and online participation, and inclusive events designed for particular groups. Each has a purpose, such as fundraising, health promotion, social inclusion or community celebration. A2 Event considerations

Consider the target audience, the venue, legal requirements, sustainability and technology. Safe routes and accessible toilets matter for many events. Data protection applies when you collect personal information through registration. A3 Roles and responsibilities An event team includes an event manager, a health and safety officer, a finance lead, a registration lead, marshals and volunteers. Each role has clear responsibilities and a named contact. B1 Planning requirements

Set SMART aims, such as reaching 200 participants and raising £1,500. Build an event plan with a timeline, a budget (including a contingency), resources and a risk assessment. Every part of the plan should link back to the aims. B2 Promotion strategies Promote the event to the target audience through the channels they use: social media, local press, posters, schools and clubs. Make the message clear: what, when, where, who and how much. Measure which channel brings people in. C1 Implementation On the day, check the venue, the equipment and the staffing before participants arrive. Follow the plan, but be ready to change it when conditions change. Keep records of what happened.

C2 Leadership and problem-solving Lead the team calmly and communicate clearly. When something goes wrong, identify the problem, decide on a response quickly and tell the people affected. Good problem-solving protects participants and the reputation of the event. D1 Event evaluation Evaluate the event against its aims, using evidence: attendance, feedback, income and costs. State whether each aim was met, and explain why or why not. D2 Personal reflection Reflect on your own contribution: which role you carried out, what you did well and what you would change. Link each point to a specific moment or decision, and suggest a clear improvement for future events. Practice

Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Describe key considerations for organising an event. Target audience The group of people an event is designed for. Contingency Money or time set aside to deal with problems that were not planned for. Risk assessment A structured review of hazards, who could be harmed, and the controls that reduce the risk. Stakeholder Anyone with an interest in or influence on an event. Learn: Unit 17 Sports Tourism | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 17 › Learn Unit 17 60 GLH Student learning Sports Tourism Sports tourism brings people to places for sport, and sport to places for tourism. It can bring jobs and income, but also crowds and environmental pressure. In this unit you will explore its types and impacts, the role of innovation and sustainability, and how to plan a sports tourism enterprise. Overview

Sports tourism brings people to places for sport, and sport to places for tourism. It can bring jobs and income, but also crowds and environmental pressure. In this unit you will explore its types and impacts, the role of innovation and sustainability, and how to plan a sports tourism enterprise. Presentation A1 Types of sports tourism Sports tourism includes spectator-based tourism (travelling to watch events), participation-based tourism (travelling to take part, such as a cycling tour or a surf holiday) and virtual tourism (experiencing sport remotely). A2 Sports tourism businesses

Businesses that serve sports tourists include transport, accommodation, guides, coaching, equipment hire and food services. Each relies on visitors, so its success depends on the events and attractions around it. A3 Impacts of sports tourism Economic impacts include income and jobs, and the multiplier effect , where spending is re-spent in other local businesses. Social impacts include community pride, but also noise and overcrowding. Environmental impacts include carbon emissions from travel and pressure on natural sites. Judge each impact with evidence, and balance positive with negative. B1 Innovation in sports tourism

New technology adds value: augmented reality tours, digital guides, online booking and personalised training data. Innovation should improve the experience or the business, not just be novel. B2 Sustainability and ethical practices Sustainable practice reduces environmental impact and supports local communities. Examples include eco-certification, carbon offsetting, local sourcing and fair pay for local workers. Sustainability also helps the business appeal to customers who value responsible travel. C1 Market research

Market research shows who the customers are, what they want and how much they will pay. Use surveys, booking data, tourism statistics and competitor information to test whether demand exists. C2 Enterprise opportunities Identify opportunities where demand is growing and the business can compete. Consider the season, the location and the customer groups you can reach. C3 Enterprise requirements Identify the resources needed: staff, qualifications, equipment, insurance, permits, premises and finance. Check that you can meet each requirement before you commit. D1 Components of the plan

An enterprise plan includes the business idea, the market research, the services, the target customers, the operations, the financial forecast and the risks. Each part should link to the evidence. D2 Presenting the plan Present the plan clearly, with visuals that show the key points. Use the market evidence to justify each decision, and label any assumptions. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the economic, social and environmental impacts of sports tourism. Your answer should include: Give one economic impact, such as jobs or spending. Give one social and one environmental impact.

Use an example from a named event or place. 6 marks Practice 2 Justify the feasibility of a sports tourism enterprise and recommend strategies that improve its long-term viability. Your answer should include: Use market evidence to justify demand. Explain the resources needed and whether they are available. Recommend an innovation or sustainability strategy and explain its benefit. Key terms Multiplier effect Money spent by tourists being spent again in other businesses, increasing its total impact. Eco-certification Formal recognition that a business meets environmental standards. Feasibility Whether an enterprise can realistically succeed, given its market, resources and finances.

Carbon offsetting Paying for an action, such as tree planting, that reduces emissions elsewhere to balance those produced. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name the three types of sports tourism and give an example of each. I can explain economic, social and environmental impacts with evidence. I can use market research to judge whether an enterprise is feasible. I can explain how innovation and sustainability add value. Learn: Unit 18 Ethical Issues and Performance Aids in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 18 › Learn Unit 18 60 GLH Student learning Ethical Issues and Performance Aids in Sport Sport depends on trust: that competitors play by the rules, that officials are fair and that athletes are not harmed. In this unit you will explore ethical values in sport, the issues that challenge them, the use of performance aids, and the role of organisations in upholding ethical standards. Overview

Sport depends on trust: that competitors play by the rules, that officials are fair and that athletes are not harmed. In this unit you will explore ethical values in sport, the issues that challenge them, the use of performance aids, and the role of organisations in upholding ethical standards. Presentation A1 Ethical values in sport Core values include fair play, integrity, respect, responsibility, and care for mental health and the environment. Each value can be tested by a real situation. For example, fair play is tested when a player is tempted to take advantage of a referee's mistake. A2 Emerging ethical issues

Current issues include commercial sponsorship that conflicts with health, athlete activism, the use of technology in officiating, online abuse of athletes, sustainability and equality. Consider how each issue affects athletes, fans and organisations. B1 Types of performance aids Performance aids include legal aids such as sports drinks and some supplements, and substances or methods that are prohibited. Each is intended to improve performance, and each has different levels of regulation and risk. B2 Impact of performance aids on fairness and health

Judge each aid by three questions: what is the intended benefit, what is the health risk, and is it regulated? An aid that gives an unfair advantage or harms health is an ethical problem, even if it is not against the rules in every setting. B3 Regulation and monitoring Governing bodies publish lists of prohibited substances and methods, test athletes and apply sanctions. Testing protects fairness and health. Explain the role of monitoring and the limits of it, such as the cost of testing. C1 Key organisations Governing bodies, clubs, schools and event organisers all have a role in promoting ethical values. Each sets codes of conduct and responds to breaches. C2 Organisational strategies

Organisations use codes of conduct, education, monitoring and sanctions. Evaluate each strategy by whether it changes behaviour, not just whether it exists. C3 Challenges Organisations face challenges such as limited budgets, global competition, online behaviour that is hard to police and pressure to win. A strategy must be realistic for the organisation to succeed. D1 Strategies for individual athletes Individuals can uphold ethical values through honest behaviour, respect for opponents and officials, asking for help when under pressure, and reporting concerns. D2 Organisational strategies

Organisations can run education programmes, clear reporting routes, fair selection, and visible sanctions. Recommend the strategy that fits the setting and explain how its impact would be measured. D3 Event-level strategies Events can use codes of conduct for spectators, stewarding, anti-abuse policies and clear rules for officials. These protect participants and the public. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain key ethical issues in sport. Your answer should include: Name one issue, such as sponsorship or online abuse. Explain how it affects athletes or organisations.

Link it to a value, such as fair play or respect. 6 marks Practice 2 Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of performance aids for athletes and organisations. Your answer should include: Give an advantage and a disadvantage for athletes. Explain the role of regulation. Give an advantage and a disadvantage for organisations, and make a judgement. Key terms Integrity Honesty and consistency in performance and in decisions, free from corruption. Gamesmanship Using legal but dishonourable tactics to gain an advantage. Code of conduct A set of standards that describes the behaviour expected of members of an organisation.

Athlete activism The use of sport as a platform to raise social or political issues. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain core ethical values with a real example. I can evaluate a performance aid by its benefit, health risk and regulation. I can describe how an organisation promotes ethical behaviour. I can recommend a feasible strategy and say how to measure it. Learn: Unit 20 Instructing Circuit Exercise Sessions | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 20 › Learn Unit 20 60 GLH Student learning Instructing Circuit Exercise Sessions Circuit training is an efficient way to train several components of fitness in one session. It can be adapted for almost any group, but only if the session is planned around the participants, designed to be safe and adjusted as it runs. In this unit you will prepare participants, plan and deliver a session, and review it. Overview

Circuit training is an efficient way to train several components of fitness in one session. It can be adapted for almost any group, but only if the session is planned around the participants, designed to be safe and adjusted as it runs. In this unit you will prepare participants, plan and deliver a session, and review it. Presentation A1 Principles and benefits of circuit training A circuit moves participants through a series of stations, each with an exercise. Circuits can develop endurance, strength and coordination together. Types include bodyweight, resistance, HIIT and sport-specific circuits. A2 Preparing participants for circuit sessions

Screen participants with a readiness questionnaire such as PAR-Q. If a participant reports a health condition, refer them to a medical professional before they start. Prepare them physically and mentally, and explain what to expect. A3 Health and safety considerations Check the environment, the equipment and the participants before the session. Use a warm-up, explain how to use each station safely, and know the emergency procedures. B1 Planning considerations Plan the session around the participants' fitness, goals and abilities. Use the FITT principle (frequency, intensity, time and type) and progressive overload. Plan adaptations for participants who need an easier or harder version.

B2 Session structure A session includes a warm-up, the main circuit and a cool-down. Sequence the stations so that one muscle group is not fatigued by the one before it. Plan the timings, the rest periods and the number of rounds. B3 Documentation Record your session plan: the stations, the equipment, the timings, the adaptations and the safety checks. A written plan allows you to evaluate the session afterwards. C1 Instruction skills Give clear, brief instructions, demonstrate each exercise with correct technique and check the participants' form. Use positive, specific feedback. C2 Motivation and engagement

Keep participants motivated with clear goals, positive feedback and variety. Adjust the pace and the music or language to the group. C3 Adaptions and inclusive practice Adapt exercises for different abilities and needs, and make sure each participant can take part fully. Change the session when the group needs it. D1 Participant feedback Collect feedback from participants during and after the session. Ask what they found hard, what they enjoyed and what they would change. D2 Self-evaluation Evaluate your own delivery: your instructions, your technique demonstrations, your adaptations and your timing. Use participant feedback and your own observations as evidence.

D3 Action planning for improvement Turn each area for improvement into a specific action, and plan how you will check it in your next session. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the benefits of circuit training and the key considerations for participant readiness. Your answer should include: Name two benefits of circuit training. Explain the readiness check and when to refer. Explain the purpose of a warm-up. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the suitability of a planned circuit session and recommend improvements.

Your answer should include: Justify the choice of stations and the adaptations. Evaluate the session with participant feedback as evidence. Recommend a specific change to the timings or the instructions, and explain why. Key terms PAR-Q Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire: a screening tool used to identify any need for medical advice. Progression A harder version of an exercise, used when a participant can perform the easier version well. Regression An easier version of an exercise, used to make it suitable for a participant. FITT principle Frequency, intensity, time and type: the four variables used to plan exercise. Check your understanding

Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can explain the readiness screening and when to refer a participant. I can plan a circuit using the FITT principle and progressive overload. I can deliver instructions and adapt the session safely. I can evaluate my delivery using participant feedback. Learn: Unit 21 Influence of Technology in Sport and Physical Activities | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 21 › Learn Unit 21 60 GLH Student learning Influence of Technology in Sport and Physical Activities Technology has changed almost every part of sport: the equipment, the measurement of performance, the facilities and the experience of watching and taking part. In this unit you will survey the main technologies, explain how they are used, examine the risks and ethics, and develop a strategy for introducing technology. Overview

Technology has changed almost every part of sport: the equipment, the measurement of performance, the facilities and the experience of watching and taking part. In this unit you will survey the main technologies, explain how they are used, examine the risks and ethics, and develop a strategy for introducing technology. Presentation A1 Types of technology Main categories include smart clothing, sport-specific equipment with sensors, assistive and adaptive technology, personal wearables and apps, simulated facilities, immersive technology such as virtual reality, and officiating technology such as electronic line calling. A2 How technology is used

Technology is used to analyse performance (motion capture, video), track fitness (wearables), design programmes (apps), and support officiating and the viewing experience. Each use needs an expert to interpret the data. B1 Improving performance Technology improves performance by giving objective feedback. Video analysis shows technique visually. Sensors give precise numbers on speed, load and recovery. Compare two technologies using the same measure of improvement. B2 Improving experience

Technology can improve the experience of participants and spectators: better information, instant replays, booking and personalised training. The experience is only improved if the technology is easy to use and inclusive. C1 Issues and risks Risks include cost, reliance on technology, unfair advantage, digital exclusion and failure of equipment. Name a specific risk and explain how it could affect a decision about using the technology. C2 Ethical and legal considerations Data collected by technology is personal and must be protected. Consent, data protection law and the fairness of technology in competition all matter. Explain how these would shape a decision.

C3 Sustainability, safety and governance Consider the environmental cost of equipment, the safety of users and who is responsible for decisions made using technology. Good governance means clear rules about how the technology is used and who decides. D1 Strategy development Develop a strategy for introducing technology: the purpose, the chosen technology, the cost, the people involved and the expected impact. Justify each choice with evidence. D2 Implementation and change management Plan how the technology will be introduced: a pilot, training for users, a timeline and a way to deal with resistance. Consider how the change will affect people. D3 Presentation, evaluation and review

Present the strategy clearly, covering performance, experience, ethics, inclusion and sustainability. Plan how you will review its impact. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain how different technologies are applied in sport and physical activity. Your answer should include: Name two technologies and what each measures or changes. Give a specific sporting example for each. Explain the expert input needed to interpret the data. 6 marks Practice 2 Present a strategy to implement technology, covering performance, experience, ethics and sustainability.

Your answer should include: Justify the choice of technology. Address cost, inclusion and data protection. Explain how the impact will be reviewed. Key terms Motion capture A technique for recording movement, often using markers or cameras, to analyse technique. Wearable technology Devices worn on the body that record data such as heart rate or distance. Digital divide The gap between people who can access technology and those who cannot. Data privacy The protection of personal information collected through technology. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit.

I can name the main types of sports technology and what each one measures. I can compare two technologies on the same measure. I can identify a risk and explain how it would affect a decision. I can develop a strategy that covers cost, inclusion and sustainability. Learn: Unit 22 Inclusive Coaching | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 22 › Learn Unit 22 60 GLH Student learning Inclusive Coaching Some people take part in sport far less than others, often for reasons unrelated to ability: cost, culture, disability, language, safety or not feeling welcome. Inclusive coaching removes these barriers. In this unit you will learn the groups who need extra support, the principles of inclusive coaching, the barriers to participation, and how to plan, deliver and evaluate an inclusive session. Overview

Some people take part in sport far less than others, often for reasons unrelated to ability: cost, culture, disability, language, safety or not feeling welcome. Inclusive coaching removes these barriers. In this unit you will learn the groups who need extra support, the principles of inclusive coaching, the barriers to participation, and how to plan, deliver and evaluate an inclusive session. Presentation A1 Target groups for inclusive coaching

Groups with lower participation include women and girls, young people, older adults, disabled people, carers, neurodiverse people, LGBTQ+ people, refugees, people from lower-income backgrounds and people who speak other languages. Their needs differ, so avoid treating any group as one uniform audience. A2 Principles of inclusive coaching Equity means fair access, which can require different support for different people. Cultural sensitivity means respecting different beliefs and practices. Safeguarding applies to everyone. Universal Design for Learning plans for different ways of taking part from the start. A3 Providers and organisations promoting inclusion

Public providers such as councils, private providers such as gyms, and voluntary organisations such as clubs and charities all promote inclusion. Governing bodies set standards and pathways for their sports. B1 Barriers to participation Barriers include cost, transport, cultural expectations, lack of role models, poor facilities, lack of confidence and feeling unsafe. Identify the barriers for a specific group before you plan. B2 Strategies to overcome barriers Strategies include free taster sessions, flexible timings, culturally appropriate clothing, role models from the group, adapted equipment and a welcoming environment. Compare strategies on how well they work for different groups.

C1 Planning considerations Plan an inclusive session for a chosen group: the objectives, the activities, the adaptations and the environment. Explain how each element meets a need of the group. C2 Adaptions for inclusion Adapt the rules, equipment, space, instructions and pace so that everyone can take part. Adaptation should keep the challenge appropriate, not reduce it for everyone. C3 Delivery skills Deliver the session with clear, simple instructions, demonstrations, visual cues where needed and warm, respectful interaction. Check that each participant understands and feels included. C4 Evaluation

Evaluate the session with feedback from participants and your own observations. Identify what worked, what did not, and an alternative approach you could use next time. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain target groups and principles of inclusive coaching. Your answer should include: Name a target group and its barriers. Explain one principle, such as equity. Explain how the principle changes the planning for the group. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the planning and delivery of an inclusive session, with alternative approaches.

Your answer should include: Describe a strength of the session and the evidence for it. Describe a limitation. Suggest an alternative approach and explain its benefit. Key terms Equity Fairness of access, so that each person gets the support they need to take part. Universal Design for Learning (UDL) An approach that plans for multiple ways of engaging, presenting and expressing learning. Neurodiversity The natural variation in how people think and learn, including conditions such as autism, ADHD and dyslexia. National Governing Body (NGB) The organisation that sets the rules, standards and pathways for a sport. Check your understanding

Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit. I can name target groups and the barriers they face. I can explain the principles of inclusive coaching. I can plan and adapt a session for a chosen group. I can evaluate a session and suggest an alternative approach. Learn: Unit 23 Enhanced Exercise and Fitness Training | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 23 › Learn Unit 23 60 GLH Student learning Enhanced Exercise and Fitness Training A gym instructor helps clients use equipment safely and effectively, and supports them in building a healthier lifestyle. That work begins with building a working relationship, understanding the client's needs and screening for health concerns. In this unit you will learn screening, the safe use of equipment, the needs of different populations, and how to deliver and review a gym-based session. Overview

A gym instructor helps clients use equipment safely and effectively, and supports them in building a healthier lifestyle. That work begins with building a working relationship, understanding the client's needs and screening for health concerns. In this unit you will learn screening, the safe use of equipment, the needs of different populations, and how to deliver and review a gym-based session. Presentation A1 Forming working relationships with clients Build trust through active listening, clear communication and respect. Agree goals with the client and explain what they can expect. A good relationship keeps clients engaged and returning. A2 Client screening processes

Screening includes a conversation about health history, a readiness questionnaire such as PAR-Q or PAR-Q+, and observation. Interpret the results to make lifestyle recommendations, and refer clients to a medical professional when a concern is raised. B1 Health and safety in an exercise environment Keep the gym clean and safe. Carry out risk assessments, check equipment before use, know the emergency procedures and record accidents. Supervise clients and make sure they use equipment correctly. B2 Types of exercise and exercise equipment

Cardiovascular equipment (treadmills, bikes, rowers), fixed resistance machines, free weights, functional equipment and flexibility exercises each have specific uses. Demonstrate correct technique and posture for each. C1 Antenatal and postnatal women Exercise needs change in pregnancy and after childbirth. Activities involving lying flat on the back after the first trimester, contact or a risk of falling or abdominal trauma may need changing. Clients should check with a medical professional before starting or changing a programme. C2 The older adult

Older adults benefit from balance, strength and flexibility work. Adjust intensity to health status, use joint-friendly exercises and allow longer recovery. Refer when a health condition is identified. C3 Adolescents Young people need age-appropriate training that focuses on technique and enjoyment. Avoid maximal loading and build progression gradually. Follow the guidance on safe training for young people. C4 People with disabilities Adapt exercises for the client's abilities and needs, using alternative equipment or positions where needed. Work with the client and, where appropriate, their medical or support team. D1 Instructing a gym-based exercise session

Plan the session around the client's goals and screening. Demonstrate each exercise, check the technique and adjust the load. Keep the session safe and motivating. D2 Reviewing own performance in providing gym-based sessions Review your delivery with evidence: the client's technique, their response and your own observations. Identify one strength and one area for improvement, and recommend a specific change for the next session. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain the contraindications and exercise requirements for antenatal and postnatal women.

Your answer should include: Name one exercise to avoid after the first trimester and explain the reason. Explain the need for medical advice before starting. Describe an adaptation that keeps the client safe. 6 marks Practice 2 Evaluate the delivery of a gym-based session and suggest adaptations for a client from a specific population. Your answer should include: Describe a strength of the session with evidence. Describe an area for improvement. Suggest an adaptation for an older adult and explain why. Key terms PAR-Q Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire: a screening tool used to identify any need for medical advice.

Contraindication A condition that makes an exercise unsafe or unsuitable for a particular client. Sedentary A lifestyle with little physical activity. Antenatal and postnatal Before and after childbirth. Exercise needs change in both periods. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Learn: Unit 24 Personal Training Methods and Programming | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 24 › Learn Unit 24 60 GLH Student learning Personal Training Methods and Programming A personal trainer designs and delivers a programme around one person: their health, goals, habits and reasons for change. In this unit you will learn the biomechanics that affect exercise, how to support long-term change, how to screen for health conditions, and how to plan, deliver and review personal training sessions. Overview

A personal trainer designs and delivers a programme around one person: their health, goals, habits and reasons for change. In this unit you will learn the biomechanics that affect exercise, how to support long-term change, how to screen for health conditions, and how to plan, deliver and review personal training sessions. Presentation A1 Biomechanics in personal training

Levers, gravity, centre of gravity, momentum, force and kinetic chains all affect how an exercise loads the body. Posture matters: a client who sits for long periods may develop a forward-flexed posture, which exercises can help correct. Lever length changes the load: moving a weight further from the joint increases the demand on the muscle. A2 Strategies to encourage long-term positive lifestyle change Use models such as the stages of change and motivational interviewing to match your support to the client's readiness. Set realistic goals, agree small steps and review progress regularly. Celebrate progress to build confidence. A3 Health conditions and client screening methods

Screen for health conditions before training. Use a questionnaire, a conversation and, where needed, referral. Do not give clinical advice: refer any concern to a medical professional. B1 Personal training methods for cardiovascular fitness Cardiovascular training can be continuous, interval or circuit-based. Choose the method and intensity to suit the client's goal, and progress the duration and intensity gradually. B2 Personal training methods for muscular strength Strength training uses heavier loads with fewer repetitions and longer rest. Use progressive overload, correct technique and rest between sessions. B3 Personal training methods for muscular endurance

Muscular endurance training uses lighter loads with more repetitions and shorter rest. It suits clients who need to sustain effort over time. B4 Personal training methods for flexibility Flexibility training uses static stretching, dynamic movements and mobility work. Include it regularly, and match the type to the session's purpose. B5 Personal training methods for functional exercise Functional exercise develops movement patterns used in daily life or sport: squatting, lifting, pushing, pulling and balancing. Progress from simple to complex movements. C1 Planning a personal training session

Plan each session around the client's goals, screening results and progress. Include a warm-up, the main work and a cool-down, with clear progressions. C2 Instructing a personal training session Demonstrate each exercise, check technique and give specific feedback. Adapt the session as the client responds, and keep it motivating. C3 Reviewing own performance in providing personal training Review your delivery with evidence: the client's technique, your instructions and any problems. Identify a strength and an improvement, and suggest a specific change. C4 Reviewing the client's performance and fitness level

Compare the client's performance and fitness with the start of the programme. Use repeated tests and the client's own report. Modify the programme in response to what the review shows. Practice Write or say your answer before you open the points. Use the points to check what you covered, not to copy. 3 marks Practice 1 Explain biomechanics in personal training. Your answer should include: Name a biomechanical principle, such as lever length or centre of gravity. Explain how it changes the choice of exercise for a named client. Give a specific example. 6 marks Practice 2 Produce a safe, progressive personal training programme for a client, with a review point.

Your answer should include: Base the programme on the client's goals and screening. Show progression across the weeks, with sets, repetitions, load and frequency. Set a review point and explain what would change the programme. Key terms Lever A rigid bar that turns about a fixed point, the fulcrum, to move a load. Kinetic chain A linked series of body segments moving together. Stages of change A model describing the stages a person goes through when changing behaviour. Progressive overload Gradually increasing the demands of training so the client continues to adapt. Check your understanding Tick each statement you can do confidently. Any you cannot tick are the parts to revisit.

I can explain biomechanical principles and how they change exercise choice. I can match a training method to a client's goal. I can plan and review a personal training session with progression. I can review a client's progress and modify the programme. Qualification overview This page is based on the Pearson BTEC International Level 3 Qualifications in Sport specification, Issue 3 (October 2026). First teaching is from September 2026, and first certification is from 2028. The qualification replaces the Pearson BTEC International Level 3 in Sport (2020), and Pearson's transition guide sets out the differences between the two.

Every unit is at Level 3 and worth 60 guided learning hours (GLH). The size of a qualification therefore depends on the number of units a student completes. The structures are designed so that a student who starts on a smaller size can progress to a larger one. A centre must be approved by Pearson before it assesses. Units are assessed in one of two ways:

Pearson Set Assignment Briefs (PSABs) are set by Pearson and marked by the centre. Units 1 to 8 are assessed this way. Pearson releases PSABs annually for each assessment window, and centres must use the PSAB specified for the relevant series. Centre-set assignments are used for units 9 to 24. Centres can set their own assignments or use an Authorised Assignment Brief (AAB) provided by Pearson and approved by Pearson Standards Verifiers. Pearson Set Assignment units Two set assignments are available for each series. The advised period for each is: Unit Title Advised period 1 Health, Wellbeing and Sport 20 hours 2 Fitness Testing 20 hours 3 Sports Injuries Management 20 hours

4 Sports Psychology 20 hours 5 Anatomy and Physiology in Sport 12 hours 6 Nutrition for Physical Performance 12 hours 7 Careers in Sport 20 hours 8 Sports Research Methods 10 hours Resubmissions and retakes A student who has not achieved their expected level of performance may be allowed one resubmission of improved evidence for each assignment, if the Lead Internal Verifier authorises it. An authorised resubmission must be completed within 15 working days of the student receiving the assessment result. Feedback may only clarify where the expected level was not achieved. Students must not be given specific guidance on how to improve the work, or solutions to the tasks.

If the pass criteria are still not met after a resubmission, the Lead Internal Verifier may authorise one retake in exceptional circumstances. The retake deadline must fall within the same academic year. Grading Each unit is graded Distinction (D), Merit (M), Pass (P) or Unclassified (U). Unit grades convert to points, and the points are added up to give the qualification grade. Pearson keeps them under review and publishes the current table on its website. Awarding rules Students must complete all units in a valid combination and have an outcome (D, M, P or U) for each. Every mandatory unit must be achieved at Pass or above. The total points must reach the threshold for a grade. Students below the Pass threshold are recorded as Unclassified and are not certificated.

A student who does not meet the requirements for their size may be awarded a smaller qualification in the suite, if they have achieved a valid combination of units for it. Entry and planning There are no formal entry requirements, but centres must recruit students who have a reasonable expectation of success. Students are expected to hold qualifications at or equivalent to Level 2, such as five international GCSEs at good grades and/or a BTEC Level 2 qualification. Students studying in English are recommended to have at least CEFR Level B2 or Pearson Global Scale of English 51. Pearson provides the following support:

Unit 1: Health, Wellbeing and Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 1 Unit 1 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Health, Wellbeing and Sport Students will explore how physical activity, physical health and mental wellbeing contribute to a healthy lifestyle and improved quality of life. They will investigate the benefits of sport, examine factors influencing health, and consider strategies to maintain and enhance overall wellbeing. Cover this Unit Unit 1: Health, Wellbeing and Sport Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

This unit asks students to look at health and wellbeing as a whole: the body, the mind, and the people around them. It starts with why physical activity and sport matter to individuals and communities, and then moves to how a person's physical health and mental wellbeing can be measured, understood and improved. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment, so the teacher's job is to build the evidence base that the set assignment needs: clear definitions, local examples, and the ability to assess and reflect on a real person's health, usually the student's own. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes

Mandatory all sizes Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Examine the importance of physical activity and sport Students learn the main types of activity (sport, physical recreation, outdoor activity, physical education and physical fitness), the groups of people who take part, and the benefits to physical, mental and social health. They then consider why providers offer activity, for example to support health agendas, community cohesion, crime reduction and employment, and what methods can bring more people in. Strong responses Uses named local examples, links each benefit to a specific group of participants, and does not just list activities.

Learning aim B: Investigate the importance of physical health Students define physical health, identify the factors that affect it, and learn to use national benchmarks and health monitoring tests. They apply these to their own health, comparing results with normative data to identify strengths and areas for improvement. Strong responses Explains the test results in plain language, compares them to a benchmark, and names a realistic area to improve. Learning aim C: Explore the impact of mental health and social wellbeing

Students define mental health and social wellbeing, consider the factors that affect them, and recognise the signs and symptoms of poor mental health. They use appropriate methods to assess their own mental health and analyse their strengths and areas for improvement. Strong responses Separates mental health from social wellbeing, uses recognised signs of poor mental health, and uses an assessment method that is described and justified. Sample responses show the standard expected at each level. They are examples, not model answers to copy. Pass A.P1 Explain the different types of physical activities and their benefits. Netball is a competitive sport that needs skill and tactics. Cycling to work is physical recreation, done for enjoyment and health. Kayaking is an outdoor activity with an adventurous element. Spin classes are physical fitness activity that improves cardiovascular fitness. Each type brings benefits: physical benefits such as better heart health, mental benefits such as improved self-esteem, and social benefits such as reduced loneliness through group participation. Distinction A.D1

Evaluate the reasons for providing different physical activities in a local area and recommend effective ways of engaging more participants. Providers in a local area offer activities for health, social and economic reasons. A free weekly walking group supports health and reduces isolation, but it may not reach people who want competitive activity. A community sports club supports cohesion, but its cost can exclude low-income families. The strongest approach is a mix: free taster sessions in the community centre, flexible timings for working adults, and outreach to groups at risk of social isolation. Teaching and assessment tips

Tips Use the five types of activity in A1 as a checklist. Students who name all five with examples cover the Pass criterion in full. Keep benefits linked to people. "Improves self-esteem" becomes stronger when it says who, such as a teenager who joins a team. For the health assessment, students should explain what each test measures and what the benchmark means before they analyse their own result. Distinction answers weigh reasons against each other. Ask students to say what works, what does not, and what they would change. Common mistakes Listing activities without explaining their benefits or the people who take part.

Quoting benchmark numbers without saying whether a result is a strength or a weakness. Describing mental wellbeing as the absence of illness, rather than a positive state that can change. Assessment approach This unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment Brief (PSAB). Centres must use the PSAB specified for the relevant assessment series without alteration or contextualisation. Two PSABs are available for each series, with an advised period of 20 hours. Full information on assessment, resubmissions and retakes is in the BTEC Teacher Hub . Key terms Physical recreation Activity done in leisure time for enjoyment and wellbeing, such as walking or cycling.

Normative data Results from a large group that show what is typical for that group, used as a benchmark. Social wellbeing The quality of a person's relationships and sense of belonging. Signs and symptoms of poor mental health Observable or felt indicators, such as persistent low mood, withdrawal or loss of interest. Unit 2: Fitness Testing | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 2 Unit 2 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Fitness Testing Students will develop the knowledge and practical skills to conduct safe, inclusive fitness testing and health screening using traditional, modern and technology-enabled methods, interpret results against international standards, and provide evidence-based recommendations for health and performance. Cover this Unit Unit 2: Fitness Testing Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Fitness testing is about collecting reliable information on a person and using it well. A test only has value if it measures what it claims to measure, is repeatable, is practical for the setting, and suits the person being tested. This unit asks students to choose and carry out tests safely, and then interpret the results with care. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Students need to show that they can screen a client before testing, administer several fitness tests safely, and give feedback that is honest, clear and encouraging. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes

Mandatory Extended Certificate and above Optional Certificate Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Explore a range of laboratory-based and field-based fitness tests Students learn which tests measure which component of fitness: sit and reach for flexibility, grip dynamometer for strength, the multi-stage fitness test or step test for aerobic endurance, sprint tests for speed, vertical jump and the Wingate test for power, one-minute press-up and sit-up for muscular endurance, and Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis for body composition. They then compare the tests on validity, reliability, practicality, cultural adaptability and accessibility.

Strong responses Matches each test to a component of fitness, and judges each test against the same criteria rather than in general terms. Learning aim B: Apply health screening techniques and fitness tests for a specified purpose Students prepare a health screening questionnaire, consult with the client, obtain informed consent and deal with medical history such as injury, heart disease or pregnancy. They then carry out health monitoring tests (resting heart rate, blood pressure, peak flow, waist-to-hip ratio, body mass index) and selected fitness tests, following pre-test checks, the correct protocol, safety rules and reasons for stopping a test.

Strong responses Checks the client before testing, follows the protocol exactly, and records results accurately with a clear reason for any test that is stopped. Learning aim C: Analyse the results of fitness tests and health screening techniques for a specified purpose Students compare results with normative data for the general population, for sports performers and for elite athletes. They then give feedback in a way that is clear, respectful and motivating, explaining strengths and areas for improvement, and make recommendations on lifestyle, exercise, diet, or referral to a professional where needed.

Strong responses Says what a result means for that person, not just what the number is, and ends with recommendations the client can act on. Worked examples Sample responses show the standard expected at each level. They are examples, not model answers to copy. Merit B.M3 Justify the selection of fitness tests commenting on suitability, reliability, validity and practicality.

For a 16-year-old netball player, the multi-stage fitness test is suitable because it measures aerobic endurance through a continuous, sport-related task. It is reliable when the same protocol and pacing are used each time. It is valid for estimating aerobic capacity but needs a suitable space and a timing system. It is practical for a group, so several players can be tested in one session, although it needs supervision. Distinction BC.D2 Evaluate the health screening questionnaires, health monitoring tests and fitness test results and provide recommendations for lifestyle improvement.

The questionnaire is useful for spotting risk factors, but it relies on honest answers, so a follow-up discussion is needed. Resting heart rate and blood pressure give quick information on health, but a single reading can be affected by stress or caffeine, so repeated readings are better. The fitness results show a good aerobic score but a weak score on grip strength. The recommendation is a twice-weekly strength session, a sleep review and a repeat of the screening in eight weeks. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Make students name the component of fitness before they name the test. A test is only as good as its match to the component.

For validity, reliability and practicality, give one specific example for each. "Reliable because it uses the same protocol" is stronger than "reliable". Safety is assessed as well as accuracy. Students should show pre-test checks, a sequence of tests, and a clear reason for stopping. Feedback is marked on how it is said. Positive language, confidentiality and a next step are all part of the criteria. Common mistakes Choosing a test that does not match the component of fitness being measured. Treating a single test result as a diagnosis rather than an indicator. Giving feedback that lists numbers without explaining the implications for the client. Assessment approach

This unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment Brief (PSAB). Centres must use the PSAB specified for the relevant assessment series without alteration or contextualisation. Two PSABs are available for each series, with an advised period of 20 hours. Full information on assessment, resubmissions and retakes is in the BTEC Teacher Hub . Key terms Validity The extent to which a test measures what it is intended to measure. Reliability The consistency of a test: similar results when repeated under the same conditions. Informed consent The client's agreement to take part, given after being told what the testing involves and any risks.

Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) A method of estimating body composition by passing a small electrical current through the body. Unit 3: Sports Injuries Management | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 3 Unit 3 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Sports Injuries Management This unit equips students with the knowledge and practical skills to understand, prevent, assess and manage common sports injuries. Students will explore injury mechanisms, risk factors and treatment strategies, to support safe and effective return to sport. Cover this Unit Unit 3: Sports Injuries Management Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Sports injuries are a normal part of sport, and the way they are understood, treated and prevented makes a real difference to the athlete. This unit follows an injury through its causes, the body's response to it, and the steps that lead to safe recovery, while also looking at how an athlete feels about the injury. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Students need accurate terms, a clear understanding of how tissue heals, and the ability to justify treatment and prevention decisions for specific injuries. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes Mandatory Foundation Diploma and above Learning aims explained

Learning aim A: Understand the types and causes of, and responses to, common sports injuries Students learn the main types of injury: hard tissue (fractures, dislocations), soft tissue (sprains, strains, contusions), overuse (tendinopathies, shin splints), head and neurological (concussion) and joint-related injuries. They examine how injuries happen, including acute and chronic, traumatic and overuse, and intrinsic and extrinsic causes. They then study the three phases of tissue healing and the psychological responses an athlete may show. Strong responses Describes what happens in each healing phase and links the psychological response to the stage of recovery.

Learning aim B: Explore risk factors for the management and prevention of common sporting injuries Students separate extrinsic risk factors (coaching, technique, environment, clothing and footwear, safety hazards) from intrinsic ones (training effects such as muscle imbalance, and individual variables such as age, fitness, injury history and sleep). They then assess preventative measures, including the roles of staff, equipment checks and environmental conditions. Strong responses Explains how each risk factor increases or reduces injury, and gives a practical prevention step for it. Learning aim C: Develop treatment and rehabilitation programmes for common sports injuries

Students learn the initial response, using the SALTAPS and PRICED frameworks and first aid priorities, and then post-injury treatment such as taping, bandaging, immobilisation, cryotherapy, thermal treatment and specialist equipment. They use this knowledge to plan treatment for two common injuries. Strong responses Sequences initial and post-injury treatment logically, and explains why each step suits that injury. After an injury the body goes through three phases. In the inflammatory phase (roughly the first four days), swelling, heat, redness and pain appear as white blood cells remove debris. In the tissue formation phase (about day four to day 24), new tissue and blood vessels form and the wound begins to close. In the maturation phase (three weeks to a year), collagen fibres reorganise and the scar tissue strengthens, which restores the tissue's strength. Distinction BC.D2 Evaluate the prevention, methods, initial and post treatment for two common sports injuries, justifying the choices of treatments.

For a hamstring strain, prevention focuses on warm-up and fitness, which reduce the chance of overload. Initial treatment uses PRICED, which limits swelling in the first phase. Post-injury treatment uses progressive loading, because the tissue must regain strength during maturation. For an ankle sprain, bracing and taping give support early, but a balance programme is needed later because proprioception is often reduced. The choices are justified because each reflects the healing phase the athlete is in. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Use the three healing phases as a timeline. Students should be able to say what happens and roughly when for each phase.

Learn the difference between extrinsic and intrinsic risk factors, and give one example of each. For treatment, always link the method to the phase of healing. A cold pack suits the early phase; heat and loading suit later stages. Name the professional roles and the reporting steps. Accident reporting and calling qualified help are part of the content. Common mistakes Describing treatment methods without saying why they suit a particular injury or stage. Mixing up acute and chronic injuries, or traumatic and overuse mechanisms. Omitting the psychological response, which is assessed as a separate criterion. Assessment approach

This unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment Brief (PSAB). Centres must use the PSAB specified for the relevant assessment series without alteration or contextualisation. Two PSABs are available for each series, with an advised period of 20 hours. Full information on assessment, resubmissions and retakes is in the BTEC Teacher Hub . Key terms Contusion A bruise: a soft tissue injury caused by a direct blow. Tendinopathy Pain and dysfunction in a tendon, often from overuse. SALTAPS A framework for assessing an injury: Stop, Ask, Look, Touch, Active, Passive, Strength. PRICED The initial treatment framework: Protect, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation, and Diagnosis by a professional.

Proprioception The body's sense of its position and movement, which is often reduced after a sprain.
