Unit 4: Sports Psychology | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 4 Unit 4 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Sports Psychology Students will develop an understanding of the psychological factors that influence sports performance and plan psychological techniques to enhance performance. This unit builds knowledge and practice relevant to coaching, performance analysis and sports science pathways. Cover this Unit Unit 4: Sports Psychology Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Why do some athletes thrive under pressure while others struggle? This unit looks at the psychology behind performance: personality and motivation, the stress and anxiety that come with competition, arousal, how teams function, and how psychological skills can be planned and evaluated. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Students need to explain psychological ideas accurately, apply them to a performer, plan a skills programme, and judge whether that programme worked. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes Mandatory Diploma and above Learning aims explained

Learning aim A: Explore the effect of personality and motivation on sports performance Students define personality and learn the main theories: trait, situational and interactional approaches. They consider personality types (type A and type B), how personality may affect performance in individual and team sports, and modern profiling tools. They then cover motivation, the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and achievement motivation and attribution theories. Strong responses Uses a theory to explain a specific performer, and links motivation type to persistence and effort.

Learning aim B: Analyse the relationship between stress, anxiety, arousal and team dynamics in sports Students distinguish stress, which is the response to demands that exceed a person's ability to cope, from anxiety, which is a state linked to fear and worry. They look at the causes and symptoms of each, the inverted-U hypothesis and catastrophe theory, and how arousal can be regulated. They also study team dynamics: Tuckman's stages, task and social cohesion, leadership styles, and the Ringelmann effect and social loafing. Strong responses Connects a symptom or theory to its effect on performance, and applies team concepts to a real team.

Learning aim C: Plan a psychological skills training programme Students assess a performer's psychological strengths and weaknesses, using tools such as performance profiling and questionnaires. They then set SMART aims and plan a programme of four to six weeks, with sessions and techniques suited to the performer's needs, including goal setting, arousal control, imagery and confidence building. Strong responses Justifies each technique by the performer's needs, and schedules the programme across weeks with clear progression. Learning aim D: Evaluate the effectiveness of psychological techniques in improving performance

Students describe the main techniques (goal setting, arousal regulation, imagery, confidence building and concentration) and learn how to judge whether they work. They consider performance outcomes, psychological indicators, athlete feedback, the difference between short-term and long-term effects, and individual differences. Strong responses Judges effectiveness using more than one type of evidence, and recognises that results differ between individuals. Worked examples Sample responses show the standard expected at each level. They are examples, not model answers to copy. Pass A.P1 Explain personality and its effect on sports performance.

Personality is a consistent pattern of thoughts, feelings and behaviour. Trait theory says these patterns are stable, so a performer may stay calm across different situations. The situational approach says behaviour depends on the environment, and the interactional approach combines both. A type A performer is competitive and time-urgent, which can help motivation but may increase stress. A type B performer is more relaxed, which can reduce stress but may limit drive in a highly competitive setting. Merit B.M2 Analyse how stress, anxiety and arousal theories affect performance.

The inverted-U hypothesis says performance improves as arousal rises to an optimal point, then declines. A performer who is under-aroused may lack focus, and one who is over-aroused may narrow attention and make errors under pressure. Catastrophe theory adds that, once a performer is over-aroused and cognitive anxiety is high, performance can fall sharply rather than gradually. This means a coach should measure both arousal and anxiety, not just one of them. Distinction CD.D3 Justify the design and evaluate the effectiveness of the psychological skills training programme, supported by evidence and recommendations for improvement.

The programme targets the performer's main need, which is anxiety before penalties. Its design is justified by the link between arousal control and performance. Its effectiveness is judged on three types of evidence: penalty success rate, self-reported anxiety before each session, and the performer's own view of the breathing routine. The results show a gain in success rate after week three but no gain in anxiety scores. The recommendation is to add cognitive restructuring in weeks three to five, because the anxiety is driven by negative self-talk. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Name the theory and then apply it to a named performer. A theory on its own does not earn a Pass.

For stress and anxiety, keep them separate: stress is a response to demands, and anxiety is a state of worry and fear. Students often blur them. For the programme, make sure each technique is justified by the performer's need, not chosen from a list. Use at least two kinds of evidence when judging effectiveness, such as performance data and the performer's own report. Common mistakes Describing personality types without connecting them to performance. Listing psychological techniques without a plan for when and how often they are used. Judging effectiveness from one result, or from the performer's feelings alone. Assessment approach

Two PSABs are available for each series, with an advised period of 20 hours. Full information on assessment, resubmissions and retakes is in the BTEC Teacher Hub . Inverted-U hypothesis The idea that performance improves with arousal up to an optimal level, then declines. Task cohesion The shared commitment of team members to achieving a common goal.

Social loafing Reduced individual effort when working in a group, where contribution is hard to identify. Performance profiling A structured assessment of a performer's psychological strengths and weaknesses. Unit 5: Anatomy and Physiology in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 5 Unit 5 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Anatomy and Physiology in Sport This unit explores the structure and function of key body systems and how they respond to sport and exercise. Students will develop knowledge of the musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory and nervous systems, and their responses and adaptations to physical activity. Cover this Unit Unit 5: Anatomy and Physiology in Sport Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Every movement, every breath and every sprint depends on the body's systems working together. This unit explains the structure and function of the musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, respiratory and nervous systems, and then shows how each responds to exercise in the short term and adapts over the long term. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Students need accurate anatomy and physiology, and the ability to explain how a system responds to training, not just describe it. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes Mandatory Diploma and above Learning aims explained

Learning aim A: Examine the structure and function of the musculoskeletal system and its response to exercise Students learn the axial and appendicular skeleton, the types of bone and joint, and the main muscle groups. They study the three muscle fibre types (type I, type IIa and type IIx). They then cover the short-term responses of the musculoskeletal system, such as increased blood supply and synovial fluid, and the long-term adaptations, such as hypertrophy, stronger tendons and denser bone. Strong responses Links a joint type or fibre type to the movements it supports, and explains an adaptation using the process behind it.

Learning aim B: Examine the structure and function of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems and their responses to exercise Students learn the chambers, valves and major vessels of the heart, the components of blood, and the structures of the respiratory tract. They study the functions of both systems, including gas exchange and lung volumes. They then look at short-term responses, such as higher heart rate and stroke volume, and long-term adaptations, such as cardiac hypertrophy, increased VO₂ max and lower resting heart rate. Strong responses Traces the route of oxygen from the air to the muscle, and explains each response in terms of what the body needs.

Learning aim C: Examine the structure and function of the nervous system and its role in sport Students learn the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), the peripheral nervous system (somatic and autonomic) and the motor unit and neuromuscular junction. They study the role of the nervous system in movement, coordination and balance, and its short-term and long-term responses to exercise, such as faster nerve impulses and more efficient motor unit recruitment. Strong responses Explains how the nervous system controls a specific movement, from the signal to the muscle contraction. Learning aims and key content Aim Learning aim Key content

They are examples, not model answers to copy. Pass A.P2 Explain the roles of different types of joints and muscle fibre types in sporting movements.

The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, which is multi-axial, so it allows the wide range of movement needed in a kick or a lunge. The knee is a hinge joint, which allows flexion and extension in one plane and supports running. A marathon runner relies mainly on type I (slow oxidative) fibres, which resist fatigue over long periods. A 100 m sprinter relies more on type IIx (fast glycolytic) fibres, which produce high force quickly but fatigue rapidly. Distinction B.D2 Evaluate the significance of cardiovascular and respiratory responses and adaptations to different types of exercise.

Endurance training increases stroke volume and capillarisation, so more oxygen reaches the working muscle at a given workload. This lowers resting heart rate and improves VO₂ max, which is a key indicator of aerobic fitness. Resistance training produces less change in these measures, so its cardiovascular benefit is smaller, though it may still reduce resting blood pressure. The significance is that the adaptations match the demands of the activity: aerobic training for a marathon runner, and different adaptations for a power athlete. Teaching and assessment tips

Tips Use labelled diagrams for the heart and the respiratory tract. Examiners look for the correct sequence of chambers and valves. For each adaptation, say why it happens: capillarisation increases oxygen delivery to the muscle, for example. Keep the three fibre types consistent: slow oxidative (type I), fast oxidative glycolytic (type IIa) and fast glycolytic (type IIx). When analysing, compare the short-term response with the long-term adaptation for the same system. Common mistakes Listing bones and muscles without linking them to a movement. Describing an adaptation without explaining the mechanism.

Confusing the order of blood flow through the heart, for example placing the valves in the wrong position. Assessment approach This unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment Brief (PSAB). Capillarisation An increase in the number of capillaries supplying a muscle, which improves oxygen delivery.

Motor unit A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it controls. Hypertrophy An increase in the size of a muscle or organ in response to training. VO₂ max The maximum rate at which the body can take in and use oxygen during exercise. Checklist Use this checklist to confirm that each criterion has been covered in teaching and assessment. Unit 6: Nutrition for Physical Performance | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 6 Unit 6 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Nutrition for Physical Performance Students explore the importance of nutrition and hydration in supporting health, recovery, and performance in sport and physical activity. They will develop knowledge and practical skills that prepare them for progression into sport, fitness and health-related study or employment. Cover this Unit Unit 6: Nutrition for Physical Performance Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

What an athlete eats and drinks affects how they train, recover and perform. This unit covers the principles behind sports nutrition: nutrients, hydration, digestion, energy balance, supplements, and how to build a personalised diet and hydration plan for a particular sport or activity. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Students need to describe nutrition accurately, judge the safety and ethics of supplements, and produce a two-week plan that is based on assessment and can be justified. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes Mandatory Extended Diploma and above Optional Diploma Learning aims explained

Learning aim A: Explore the principles of nutrition, hydration and digestion in relation to physical performance Students study the macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats), micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) and fibre, and the signs of different hydration states. They also learn the structure and function of the digestive system, and how a balanced diet supports health and performance. Strong responses Explains how a nutrient or hydration state affects a specific activity, and traces digestion from ingestion to absorption. Learning aim B: Investigate energy intake, expenditure and balance for different sports and activities

Students learn how energy is measured in kilocalories and kilojoules, and where it comes from. They study basal metabolic rate and the factors that affect it, such as age, gender, temperature, altitude and activity. They then learn how to measure energy intake and use, through food diaries, activity logs and wearable technology. Strong responses Compares energy needs between two activities using the same measures, and explains the balance behind any change in body mass. Learning aim C: Examine safe and ethical practices in sports nutrition

Students study the common supplements (vitamins, minerals, protein, carbohydrate, creatine and others) and the risks of misuse, including contamination, counterfeit products and prohibited substances. They consider fair play, the value of third-party tested products, and the cultural and ethical choices athletes make about food. Strong responses Gives a practical safety step for a supplement, and explains why it reduces a specific risk. Learning aim D: Create a personalised diet and hydration plan for a selected sport or activity

Students consider the demands of a chosen activity (aerobic, anaerobic, strength, flexibility, weight category) and the timing of nutrition around training and competition. They assess the performer's needs, including weight gain or loss, and plan a diet using food groups, supplements and sources, with attention to availability, sustainability and cultural choices. Strong responses Bases every part of the plan on an assessment of the performer, and checks it against the demands of the activity. Pass D.P5 Produce a basic two-week diet and hydration plan for a selected sports performer, based on an initial assessment. The performer is a 17-year-old middle-distance runner training five times a week. The assessment shows a body mass index in the healthy range and a low fruit and vegetable intake. Day one includes porridge with banana before training, a rice and chicken meal after, and water throughout. Hydration is set at about two litres a day, with extra fluid before, during and after sessions. Over the two weeks, the plan adds more vegetables and a recovery drink after long runs. Distinction CD.D2

Justify the effectiveness of a two-week diet and hydration plan for a selected sports performer, providing evidence-based reasoning. The plan is effective because each element responds to the assessment. Complex carbohydrates in the morning meal supply energy for a long run, which the evidence supports for endurance performance. The increase in vegetables improves micronutrient intake, which the assessment showed was low. Fluid timing is based on sweat loss during training, and a recovery drink after long runs supports glycogen replacement. The main limitation is that the plan does not yet account for the performer's iron status, so a blood test would be recommended.

Teaching and assessment tips Tips For a diet plan, base each meal and fluid target on the assessment. A plan without an assessment cannot reach the higher criteria. Use the correct units: kilocalories or kilojoules for energy, and litres for fluid intake. For supplements, always name the risk (contamination, counterfeit products or prohibited substances) and the safe practice that reduces it. Check the plan against the activity. A marathon runner, a weightlifter and a basketball player need different plans. Common mistakes Describing macronutrients without linking them to the activity in question. Producing a plan with no reference to the initial assessment.

Recommending a supplement without mentioning its safety or legal status. Assessment approach This unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment Brief (PSAB). Hypohydration A state where the body has lost more fluid than it has taken in, reducing its water content.

Isotonic drink A sports drink with a similar concentration of solutes to the body, used to replace fluid and some energy. They will develop employability and digital skills, while exploring how to prepare for, and access, a wide range of sport-related roles and progress within them. Sport offers a wide range of careers, from coaching and fitness to sports science, development and leisure management. This unit helps students understand those careers, how people progress through them, and the professional standards that employers expect, including safeguarding and health and safety. Students also learn how recruitment works in practice. They analyse a job role, audit their own skills, apply for and interview for that role, and build a personal career plan. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes Mandatory Extended Diploma and above

Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Investigate careers and pathways in the sports industry Students explore the range of roles in sport, including coaching, teaching, fitness, sports development, sports science and leisure management. They study routes into those roles, from entry-level jobs to qualifications and continuing professional development, and the employment types on offer. They also cover safeguarding, health and safety, and professional standards, which apply across all of these careers. Strong responses Compares two pathways on entry requirements, progression and employment type, and explains how safeguarding or professional standards affect the role.

Learning aim B: Explore recruitment processes for a selected job role in sport Students analyse a job description and person specification to understand the duties, qualifications and skills a role needs. They complete a personal skills audit, then apply for and attend an interview for the chosen role. They reflect on how well the recruitment process worked and how ready they are for the role. Strong responses Matches their own evidence directly to the person specification, and reflects honestly on gaps and how to close them. Learning aim C: Develop and review a personal career plan for progression in sport

Students write a personal career plan with short-, medium- and long-term goals. They explain how each goal supports progression towards their chosen career, and evaluate which planning strategies are most likely to support long-term progression. Strong responses Sets goals that are specific and dated, and explains why each step moves the student closer to the chosen role. Pass A.P1 Explain different careers and progression pathways in the sports industry.

A sports coach can start at grassroots level, for example volunteering at a local club, and progress to a paid role with a national governing body after gaining a recognised coaching qualification. A fitness instructor may begin with a Level 2 gym qualification and then become a personal trainer, adding specialist qualifications as they progress. Each route needs a different qualification, and each leads to different types of employment. Merit B.M3 Analyse recruitment processes, making links to their effectiveness in chosen career pathways.

The job description for a sports development officer asks for experience of community projects and a relevant qualification. A strong application shows evidence of project work, linked to the community outcomes the role needs. The interview then tests the same skills through a scenario question. This process is effective because it checks both the qualifications and the practical skills the role requires, which matters for a job that depends on working with communities. Distinction C.D3 Evaluate how career planning strategies can support long-term progression.

A career plan that sets short-term goals, such as completing a coaching award within six months, gives a clear first step. Medium-term goals, such as gaining experience with a team, build the evidence employers look for. Long-term goals, such as leading a development programme, give direction. The strategy works best when reviewed regularly, because roles and qualifications change. Its main limitation is that a plan can become rigid, so it should be adjusted when new opportunities arise. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Use job descriptions and person specifications as the basis for the skills audit. Every point in the audit should map to something in the specification.

For safeguarding and health and safety, name the principle and the professional responsibility that goes with it, such as reporting a concern. For the career plan, make each goal specific and dated. "Get a coaching qualification by March" is far stronger than "improve my coaching". Use real pathways from the country where the student is studying, and say where the examples come from. Common mistakes Listing careers without explaining the qualifications or progression routes they need. Writing a skills audit that does not link to the role's person specification. Setting goals that are general or impossible to measure, so progress cannot be checked. Assessment approach

This unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment Brief (PSAB). Centres must use the PSAB specified for the relevant assessment series without alteration or contextualisation. Two PSABs are available for each series, with an advised period of 20 hours. Full information on assessment, resubmissions and retakes is in the BTEC Teacher Hub . Key terms Person specification The qualities, skills and experience an employer requires from a candidate. Continuing Professional Development (CPD) Ongoing learning that keeps a professional up to date in their role. Unit 8: Sports Research Methods | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 8 Unit 8 60 GLH Pearson Set Assignment Sports Research Methods Students will develop knowledge and understanding of research methods used in sport, including types of research, data collection techniques, and principles of validity, reliability and ethics. Cover this Unit Unit 8: Sports Research Methods Overview

Research is how sport develops its knowledge. A coach who changes training because of a study, or a physiotherapist who uses evidence to choose a rehabilitation approach, is applying research. This unit teaches students how research is designed, how it is judged, and how its data is analysed and presented. The unit is assessed through a Pearson Set Assignment. Students need to describe methods accurately, judge how valid, reliable and ethical a study is, and analyse and present data in a way that another person can understand. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Pearson Set Assignment Status Sizes Mandatory Extended Diploma and above Learning aims explained

Learning aim A: Understand the purpose and importance of research in sport Students learn why research is carried out in sport: to improve performance and training, inform policy, support evidence-based decisions, evaluate interventions such as injury prevention, and contribute to knowledge. They consider the benefits to athlete health, new training methods, sports technology, participation and funding. Strong responses Gives a real example of research changing practice, and explains the change in terms of performance, participation or policy. Learning aim B: Explore different types of research methods and designs used in sport

Students compare qualitative research (interviews, focus groups, observations) with quantitative research (surveys, performance tests, physiological measures), and mixed methods that combine both. They learn about deductive and inductive reasoning, the main designs (experimental, descriptive, correlational, case study, longitudinal and cross-sectional), and how to carry out a literature review. Strong responses Chooses a design that fits the research question, and explains its strengths and limitations with a sport example. Learning aim C: Understand principles of validity, reliability and ethics in sports research

Students distinguish construct validity (does the test measure what it claims?) from external validity (can results be generalised?). They study test-retest and inter-rater reliability, and the ethical principles of informed consent, confidentiality, the right to withdraw, and integrity in reporting data. Strong responses Explains how a weakness in validity or reliability would change the conclusions of a specific study. Learning aim D: Understand how data is analysed and presented in sports research

Students learn the difference between qualitative and quantitative data, and the four scales of measurement: nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio. They use descriptive statistics (mean, median, mode, range, standard deviation), inferential ideas such as correlation and significance, and thematic analysis for qualitative data. They then present findings in tables, charts and a structured report. Strong responses Matches the analysis technique to the type of data, and presents results so the reader cannot misread them. Merit B.M2 Compare the strengths and limitations of different research methods and designs, using examples from sport.

A qualitative interview study on why young footballers leave the sport can explain motives in depth, but its findings may not apply to all players. A quantitative survey of 500 players can show how common each reason is, but it cannot explain why the reason matters to the individual. A mixed methods study combines both, giving breadth from the survey and depth from interviews, though it takes more time and resources. Merit C.M3 Analyse the impact of validity, reliability and ethics on the quality and credibility of research findings, using examples from sport.

If a study uses a fitness test with low test-retest reliability, the same athletes may score differently on different days, and any improvement reported could be noise rather than real change. If informed consent is not obtained, the research is unethical, and the findings may be rejected by a journal, which reduces their credibility. Both issues undermine trust in the conclusions, however well the data is analysed. Distinction CD.D2 Evaluate the effectiveness of different data presentation methods in communicating findings clearly for different audiences within sporting settings.

A bar chart comparing sprint times between two training groups is clear for coaches, who can see the difference quickly. The same data in a table gives the exact values, which a sports scientist may prefer. A short summary with one key chart suits athletes who need the outcome without the detail. The most effective presentation matches the audience, and each version should show the variation, such as standard deviation, so differences are not overstated. Teaching and assessment tips Tips When describing a design, always state the cause-and-effect claim it can and cannot support. An experiment can show cause; a correlational study cannot.

For reliability and validity, give one specific example from sport for each. Name the test and say what would make it less reliable. Match the analysis to the data: means and standard deviations for interval data, thematic coding for interview transcripts. When presenting data, label axes, give units, and show the spread of the data as well as the average. Common mistakes Calling a study valid or reliable without explaining what makes it so. Using correlation to claim that one variable causes another. Presenting an average without its spread, which can make small differences look meaningful. Assessment approach

Key terms Construct validity Whether a test measures the concept it claims to measure. Test-retest reliability The consistency of results when the same test is repeated over time. Informed consent Participants' agreement to take part, given once they understand the purpose and the risks.

Standard deviation A measure of how spread out the data is around the mean. Thematic analysis A method of coding qualitative data to find repeated patterns and themes. Unit 9: Practical Sports Performance | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 9 Unit 9 60 GLH Internally assessed Practical Sports Performance This unit develops students’ practical skills and understanding of performance in selected sports through active participation and analysis. Students will explore techniques, tactics and strategies to improve their own performance, and demonstrate competence in competitive situations. Cover this Unit Unit 9: Practical Sports Performance Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Performance in sport comes from the combination of technique, tactics, decision-making and the ability to apply them under pressure. This unit focuses on a selected sport, asking students to understand its technical and tactical demands, practise skills in drills, and perform in competitive situations with the rules applied correctly. Students also review their own performance honestly and produce an action plan. The unit is assessed through internal assessment, using the Authorised Assignment Brief or a centre-set assignment. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes

Mandatory Extended Certificate and above Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Understand the technical and tactical demands of selected sports Students identify the core technical skills in a sport, such as passing, shooting, defending and footwork, and the components of fitness each one needs. They study the tactical demands: principles of attack and defence, transition strategies, decision-making under pressure, and how opponents can be analysed and exploited. Strong responses Explains how a technical skill and a tactical principle work together in the chosen sport, rather than treating them separately. Learning aim B: Demonstrate skills and tactics in drills for a selected sport

Students progress through drills, from isolated practice to semi-opposed, fully opposed and conditioned games. They refine technique using feedback and video, apply tactics in small-sided games and scenarios, and take on roles such as defender or attacker, with leadership in communication. Strong responses Shows improvement across drills, and responds to feedback with a specific change in technique or decision-making. Learning aim C: Demonstrate effective performance in competitive situations

Students take part in competitive situations, showing skills and tactics under match conditions. They apply the rules of the sport correctly, understand the roles of officials and the time restrictions that affect play, and see how the rules shape tactics. Strong responses Uses skills and tactics at the right moment in the game, and applies the rules correctly under pressure. Learning aim D: Review own performance to identify strengths and areas for improvement

Students review their own performance using evidence such as video, feedback and their own observations. They identify clear strengths and areas for improvement, explain how these affect overall performance, and produce a detailed action plan for improvement. Strong responses Uses evidence from the performance rather than general impressions, and sets an action plan with measurable next steps. In netball, a shooter needs accurate technique, but her success depends on the timing of her movement into space. If the defender is close and the team's tactic is to move the ball quickly, the shooter must receive and shoot in one fluid action. The technical skill of a fast release is therefore only effective if the tactical demand of creating space has been met. Distinction D.D3 Analyse own performance in a selected sport and produce a detailed action plan for improvement.

Video analysis shows that my passing is accurate on the first pass but my decision to pass late reduces attacking options. Feedback from the coach confirms that I wait too long when I have a numerical advantage. The action plan has three parts: two passing drills twice a week with a time limit, one small-sided game each week where I must choose a pass within two seconds, and a video review after four weeks to check whether my decisions have become faster. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Link skills to tactics. Students who describe a pass without its tactical purpose will not reach the higher bands.

For review, use evidence: a clip, a score, or a comment from the coach. General comments about "playing well" do not earn marks. Show the rules in action during competitive play, not just in a written list. For the action plan, set measurable targets with dates so progress can be checked. Common mistakes Describing the drill without showing the skill being developed in it. Reviewing performance in general terms, without evidence. Writing an action plan that is vague, such as "work harder on defending". Assessment approach

Unit 10: Sports Coaching and Leadership | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 10 Unit 10 60 GLH Internally assessed Sports Coaching and Leadership This unit focuses on the principles and practices of sports coaching and leadership, equipping students to plan, deliver and evaluate sessions across various sport settings. Emphasis is placed on safety, inclusion, motivation, progression, and adapting coaching styles to enhance performance and participation. Cover this Unit Unit 10: Sports Coaching and Leadership Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Coaching is about more than knowing the skill. A good coach or leader plans a session, communicates clearly, keeps people safe, adapts to the group and reflects on what worked. This unit develops those roles and skills, looks at how different leadership styles affect performance and participation, and asks students to plan and deliver a session of their own. The unit is assessed through internal assessment. Students need to explain the roles and skills of a coach, judge which style suits a situation, deliver a session that is safe and inclusive, and reflect honestly on their own performance. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Mandatory Foundation Diploma and above Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Understand the roles, responsibilities and skills of sports coaches and leaders Students learn the roles a coach or leader takes on: instructor, motivator, role model, planner and organiser, and mentor. They study the responsibilities that go with them, including safeguarding, health and safety, inclusive practice and professional conduct. They also develop the skills that make a coach effective, such as communication, organisation, adaptability and leadership.

Strong responses Links a role to the responsibility and skill it needs, and gives an example of the role in practice. Learning aim B: Explore coaching and leadership styles and their impact on performance and participation Students compare coaching styles, such as autocratic, democratic and other approaches, and consider the characteristics of each. They look at how a style affects performance and whether participants keep coming back, and which style suits which situation, such as beginners, safety-critical activity or a mixed-ability group. Strong responses Chooses a style for a named situation and explains its effect on both performance and participation.

Learning aim C: Plan and deliver a sports coaching or leadership session Students plan a session for an individual or group, with clear objectives, a structure that moves from warm-up to main activity to cool-down, and time for feedback. They then deliver it safely, using clear communication, and adapt activities when the group or conditions change. Strong responses Has a plan that matches the group, and changes the activity sensibly when something does not work. Learning aim D: Reflect on own coaching or leadership performance

Students review their own planning and delivery, using feedback from others as well as their own observations. They identify strengths and areas for improvement and produce a detailed action plan for their future development as a coach or leader. Strong responses Uses feedback from participants or observers as evidence, and sets an action plan with specific next steps. A coach is an instructor, teaching technical and tactical skills and demonstrating correct technique for safety and performance. They are also a motivator, using positive reinforcement to build confidence. A coach is responsible for safeguarding, which means recognising signs of abuse and reporting concerns, and for health and safety, which means risk assessing the session and checking equipment before it starts. Merit B.M2 Analyse the suitability of different coaching and leadership styles for different situations and participants.

An autocratic style suits a group of beginners on a safety-critical activity, such as gymnastics, because the coach needs to make decisions quickly and maintain control. The same style with an experienced group may reduce creativity and motivation. A democratic style suits a mixed-ability group that is developing tactical awareness, because players can contribute ideas and feel more involved, which supports continued participation. Distinction C.D3 Deliver an engaging and inclusive session that meets planned objectives and adapt activities effectively to meet participants' needs.

The session was planned around passing for a mixed-ability netball group. When two players found the original drill too fast, I slowed the pace and added a no-defence option. When the group became bored, I introduced a scoring game that rewarded accurate passing rather than speed. Every participant had a clear role, and the objective of improving passing accuracy was met. The adaptations were made calmly and kept everyone involved. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Link each role to the skill that delivers it. Being a motivator, for example, depends on the use of specific praise. For styles, say which one you used and why it suits the group. A description of a style alone is not an analysis.

In delivery, plan a warm-up, a main activity and a cool-down with timings, and build in time for feedback. For reflection, use at least one piece of feedback from another person, and turn each area for improvement into a specific action. Planning a session with no timings or adaptations, so it cannot respond when things change. Assessment approach

Unit 11: Sports Research Project | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 11 Unit 11 60 GLH Internally assessed Sports Research Project Students will plan, carry out and present a small-scale research project in a sports context, developing practical investigation and analytical skills. This unit will provide students with skills that transfer well to a sector which is increasingly reliant on innovation via evidence- based practice. Cover this Unit Unit 11: Sports Research Project Overview

A research project turns a question into evidence. This unit takes students through the whole process: choosing a topic, planning a hypothesis and methods, collecting ethical data, analysing it, drawing conclusions and presenting the findings. Each stage matters, because the conclusions can only be as strong as the plan and the data behind them. The unit is assessed through internal assessment. Students need a clear research plan, data that is collected carefully and ethically, conclusions linked to the hypothesis, and an honest evaluation of the project's limitations. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Mandatory Extended Diploma and above Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Plan a sports research project with clear aims and methodology Students choose a topic linked to sport, such as the effect of warm-up on sprint performance or barriers to female participation in football. They write a hypothesis that is clear and testable, and check it is achievable in terms of time, resources and participants. They then plan the timeline, resources and risks, and consider ethics, including informed consent, confidentiality and approval.

Strong responses Writes a hypothesis that can be tested with the planned methods, and plans for a problem before it happens. Learning aim B: Carry out the research project and collect data Students collect data using methods that suit their hypothesis, such as fitness tests and questionnaires for quantitative work, or interviews and observations for qualitative work. They keep records accurately, manage time, and maintain ethical standards throughout, including the right of participants to withdraw. Strong responses Checks accuracy during collection, and explains how the data reflects a systematic approach. Learning aim C: Analyse data and draw valid conclusions

Students analyse quantitative data with the mean, median, mode and standard deviation, and display it in charts. Qualitative data is coded and summarised into themes. They then judge whether the data supports or rejects the hypothesis, consider limitations such as outliers and sample size, and draw conclusions that the evidence can support. Strong responses States whether the hypothesis was supported, and explains the evidence and its limitations. Learning aim D: Present findings and evaluate the research process

Students present their findings using appropriate methods, such as a report, tables or charts. They describe the strengths and weaknesses of the project, and evaluate the limitations, suggesting how a future study could be improved. Strong responses Evaluates the project itself, not just the results, and suggests specific changes for a future study. Participants must give informed consent, which means they understand the purpose, procedures and their right to withdraw. Pass C.P5 Explain how the data collected relates to the project hypothesis.

My hypothesis was that a 10-minute dynamic warm-up would improve 30 m sprint time compared with a 5-minute warm-up. The mean sprint time after the longer warm-up was 0.12 seconds faster, which supports the hypothesis. The data shows the same direction in all participants, but the sample was small, so the result is indicative rather than conclusive. Distinction CD.D2 Analyse data and make well-justified conclusions.

The mean difference supports the hypothesis, but the standard deviation of the 10-minute group is larger, so the effect varies between individuals. One outlier, who was injured during the second trial, was removed, which changes the result slightly. The conclusion is that the longer warm-up may improve sprint times, but a larger sample with controlled conditions would be needed before this could be generalised. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Write the hypothesis first and check that every method and analysis serves it. Methods that do not connect to the hypothesis add length without value.

Record data as it is collected, with a date, condition and notes on anything unusual. Unrecorded data is hard to defend. In conclusions, say whether the hypothesis was supported, then give the evidence, then state the limitation. For evaluation, name one limitation of the method and one of the data, and say how each would be fixed next time. Common mistakes Writing a hypothesis that cannot be tested with the methods chosen. Drawing a conclusion that goes beyond the sample, such as generalising from ten participants. Describing the strengths of the project without evaluating its weaknesses. Assessment approach

Qualitative coding Labelling responses with codes so that repeated ideas can be grouped into themes. Sports and active leisure businesses run on customer trust. This unit introduces the business side of the industry, from legislation and professional conduct to customer service technology and business planning. The unit is assessed through internal assessment. Students need to explain how a real or chosen business operates within the law, use technology to serve customers, and produce business and marketing plans that are realistic and justified. Unit 13: Fitness Training | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 13 Unit 13 60 GLH Internally assessed Fitness Training This unit explores the principles and methods of fitness training, and their application in designing and delivering effective fitness programmes. Students will develop practical skills in designing, implementing and evaluating fitness training programmes. Cover this Unit Unit 13: Fitness Training Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Fitness training is the planned improvement of the body's ability to meet a particular demand. Good programmes are built on established principles, such as specificity, overload and progression, and they are shaped around the components of fitness that matter for the individual. This unit asks students to explain those principles, design a programme for a real person, carry it out, and judge whether it worked. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to explain the principles and methods accurately, justify their programme design, monitor the individual during training, and review the outcome honestly. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Optional all sizes Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Explore the principles and methods of fitness training

Students learn the principles of training: specificity, overload, progression, reversibility, individuality, variation, recovery and adaptation. They study the health-related components of fitness (cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength and endurance, flexibility and body composition) and the skill-related components (speed, power, agility, balance, coordination and reaction time), with a test for each. They then learn the main training methods, including continuous, fartlek and interval training, HIIT and resistance training. Strong responses Links each training method to the component of fitness it develops, and uses a test to show how that component is measured.

Learning aim B: Design a fitness training programme to meet individual needs Students assess an individual's needs and goals, then design a programme that matches them. They select methods and set the training load, and justify each choice with reference to the principles of training, such as progressing the load gradually and building in recovery. Strong responses Explains why each element of the programme suits this individual, rather than describing a generic plan. Learning aim C: Implement and monitor a fitness training programme

Students carry out the programme safely and effectively, monitoring the individual's response to training. When the monitoring data or the individual's feedback shows a problem, they adapt the programme and evaluate whether the changes worked. Strong responses Uses monitoring data, such as heart rate or perceived exertion, to decide an adaptation, and records the effect of that change. Learning aim D: Review the effectiveness of a fitness training programme Students review the outcomes of the programme against its goals, analyse its strengths and areas for improvement, and make justified recommendations for future improvements.

Strong responses Compares outcomes with the original goals, and recommends changes that follow directly from the evidence. They are examples, not model answers to copy. Pass A.P2 Describe methods of fitness training for different components of fitness. Continuous training, such as a steady 30-minute run, develops cardiovascular endurance. Interval training, such as 30-second efforts with recovery, develops aerobic and anaerobic capacity together. Resistance training, such as a 1RM-based squat programme, develops muscular strength. Sprint interval training develops speed and power, because each sprint is short and maximal. Merit B.M2

Justify the design of a fitness training programme with reference to the principles of training. The programme for a 17-year-old footballer applies specificity by using sprint intervals, since the sport needs repeated speed. It applies progression by adding one set each week for three weeks, then holding the load. Recovery is built in with two rest days, which allows adaptation and reduces injury risk. Variation is used by alternating the sprint work with agility drills, which keeps the programme engaging. Distinction C.D2 Evaluate the effectiveness of adaptations made during implementation of the fitness training programme.

In week three, heart rate data showed the athlete was reaching maximum effort in the first set, so the recovery between sprints was extended from 30 to 60 seconds. The result was a steadier sprint time across sets, which shows the adaptation worked. However, the rest change also lowered the training stress, so the next phase needs to increase load in another way, such as a reduction in rest time from a later point in the programme. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Name the principle before you apply it. "Progression" needs a specific example of how the load increases.

Every method should be matched to a component of fitness. If a method cannot be linked to a component, it should not be in the programme. Use monitoring data to justify each adaptation. A change made without data is harder to defend. For review, compare results with the original goals, not with general fitness improvements. Common mistakes Designing a programme that is generic rather than tailored to the individual. Describing training methods without linking them to the components of fitness they develop. Making changes during the programme without recording why, so the effect cannot be evaluated. Assessment approach

Progressive overload Gradually increasing the demands of training so the body continues to adapt. Fartlek training Continuous training with varied pace, mixing steady running with faster efforts.

Reversibility The loss of training adaptations when training stops or reduces. 1RM The maximum weight a person can lift once with correct technique. Unit 14: Sports Performance Analysis | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 14 Unit 14 60 GLH Internally assessed Sports Performance Analysis Students will develop the knowledge and practical skills to analyse sports performance using methods, technology and ethical practices. They will learn to collect, interpret and present performance analysis data to support sports performance or team development. Cover this Unit Unit 14: Sports Performance Analysis Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Performance analysis turns observation into evidence. Coaches and analysts use statistics, video and profiling to see what happened in a performance, compare it with a standard, and decide what to change. This unit introduces the methods and technologies used, the standards that make comparison meaningful, and the practical and ethical issues involved. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to choose appropriate methods, collect and present analysis data, and give feedback that is evidence-based and linked to clear goals. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes

Optional all sizes Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Examine methods and technologies for analysing sports performance Students study the main methods: match statistics, notational analysis, live analysis, isolated skill analysis and video analysis, including AI-assisted tracking. They consider the practicality of each, such as cost and expertise, and the ethical requirements, including consent and data privacy. They also learn how performance profiles combine physical, technical, tactical and psychological information. Strong responses Chooses a method for a specific situation and explains its practicality and ethical requirements.

Learning aim B: Explore performance standards for comparative performance analysis Students identify benchmarks for comparison, such as governing body standards, open performance datasets and the characteristics of elite performers. They consider how to adjust benchmarks for climate, altitude and playing conditions, and assess the validity and reliability of the model they choose. Strong responses Justifies a benchmark and explains how conditions might change what counts as a good performance. Learning aim C: Carry out and present a sports performance analysis

Students observe or record a performer, collect data using appropriate tools, and present it in more than one format, such as charts, heat maps or a profile. They then evaluate the analysis and justify recommendations. Strong responses Presents data in formats that suit the audience, and explains what each format shows. Learning aim D: Review analysis data and provide evidence-based feedback to improve performance Students feed the analysis back to the performer or team, identifying strengths and weaknesses from the data and setting SMART goals. The feedback must be clear, specific and supported by the evidence.

Strong responses Links each point of feedback to a specific piece of data, and sets goals that can be measured. Worked examples Sample responses show the standard expected at each level. They are examples, not model answers to copy. Merit A.M1 Analyse the relevance and practicality of different methods and technologies for sports performance analysis.

Notational analysis is practical for a coach with limited budget, because it needs only a pen, a template and a stopwatch. It shows the pattern of passing and shot positions, which is relevant to tactical decisions. AI-assisted video tracking gives more detail, including player speed and distance, but it needs expensive equipment and technical expertise, so it is less practical for a small club. Merit B.M2 Analyse the suitability of models for comparative performance analysis for a selected sport, considering validity and reliability.

Comparing a club player with the average of a professional league is valid only if the two groups play similar competition levels and in similar conditions. An open dataset for the professional league is reliable because it is recorded consistently, but a small amateur sample may give unreliable averages. A better model uses the performance of a comparison group at the same level, adjusted for playing conditions such as heat. Distinction CD.D3 Provide comprehensive feedback and justify recommendations for improvement.

The analysis shows that the team's successful attacks come mainly down the left, because the right-sided winger receives the ball late. The data supports a change: move the winger earlier into the lane, which the heat map shows is open. The goal is to increase right-side possessions in the final third from 18 per match to 25 over four matches, which can be measured in the next analysis. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Name the method, say what it measures, and say when it is practical. A method with no practicality judgement will not reach the higher criteria. For benchmarks, state what the comparison group is and whether it is valid for the performer being analysed.

Feedback should link each point to a piece of data, and each goal should be SMART. When presenting data, choose the format for the audience. A coach needs a different summary from a performer. Giving feedback that is general, such as "improve your passing", without data or a measurable goal. Assessment approach

Unit 15: Rules, Regulations and Officiating in Sport | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 15 Unit 15 60 GLH Internally assessed Rules, Regulations and Officiating in Sport Students will explore the rules and regulations of a selected sport, and develop the skills needed to apply them while officiating. Cover this Unit Unit 15: Rules, Regulations and Officiating in Sport Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Officials make the rules work. A referee, umpire or line judge applies rules in real time, keeps the game flowing, and deals with the pressure of decisions that players, coaches and spectators may question. This unit explores the rules, the roles of officials, and the skills of officiating, and gives students the chance to officiate and evaluate their own performance. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to explain the rules and the role of officials accurately, observe and assess officiating, officiate in a competitive situation, and review their own performance with evidence. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Optional all sizes Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Understand the rules, regulations and roles of officials in sport Students learn the rules and competition regulations for a selected sport, including playing area, equipment and scoring. They study the roles of officials, such as referee, umpire, line judge, timekeeper and video assistant, and the responsibilities that go with them, including fairness, health and safety, and professional conduct. They consider how technology such as goal-line technology and video review has changed officiating.

Strong responses Explains a rule and the official's decision that applies it, and considers how the rule has changed over time. Learning aim B: Explore the application of rules and regulations in officiating Students learn how officials recognise infringements and apply sanctions, manage the flow of play, deal with dissent and unsporting behaviour, and communicate clearly through signals and words. They also study the observation and assessment methods used to judge officiating. Strong responses Applies a rule to a specific situation and explains the decision in a way players can understand. Learning aim C: Undertake the role of an official in a competitive situation

Students prepare for officiating, check equipment and the playing area, and then officiate in a competitive situation. They apply the rules consistently, communicate clearly and maintain control of the game. Strong responses Makes consistent decisions and communicates them clearly, with control maintained throughout. Learning aim D: Review and evaluate own officiating performance Students review their own officiating using two assessment methods, such as video and feedback from a supervisor. Every sports event, from a school sports day to a charity run, needs careful organisation. Aims, audiences, venues, budgets, risks and roles all have to fit together. This unit introduces the types and purposes of events, the considerations that shape them, and the planning, promotion and delivery of an event that the student runs. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to explain the considerations for an event, produce a realistic plan and promotional campaign, contribute to delivery in a defined role, and evaluate the event and their own contribution. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Optional all sizes Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Explore considerations for organising sports and physical activity events Students learn the types of event (competitive, recreational, educational, hybrid and inclusive) and their purposes, such as fundraising, health promotion, social inclusion and sustainability. They study the considerations for organising an event: the target audience, venue, legal and ethical matters, sustainability and technology. They also learn the roles within an event team, from event manager to health and safety officer.

Strong responses Matches the event type and purpose to the audience, and shows how venue or legal considerations shape the plan. Learning aim B: Plan and promote a sports or physical activity event Students set SMART aims for the event, identify the target audience and produce an event plan with timelines, resources, budgets and a risk assessment. They then create promotional materials and a campaign that link to the aims and the audience. Strong responses Shows how each part of the plan, including the promotion, responds to the aims and the audience. Learning aim C: Deliver a planned sports or physical activity event

Students take on an allocated role and contribute to the delivery of the event. They take responsibility for key decisions where appropriate, and show teamwork and communication under the pressure of the live event. Strong responses Carries out the allocated role reliably, and makes sound decisions when the plan needs to change. Learning aim D: Review the effectiveness of the event and own performance Students evaluate the success of the event against its aims and their own contribution, and suggest improvements for future events. The evaluation should be based on evidence, such as attendance, feedback and budget outcomes.

Strong responses Judges success against the original aims, using evidence, and makes specific recommendations for the next event. Describe key considerations for organising events. An outdoor charity fun run needs a venue with safe routes and accessible toilets, so that participants with mobility needs can take part. The target audience of families and older adults means the route should be short and flat. Registrations collect personal data, so the organiser must follow data protection rules and keep the information secure. A risk assessment covers weather and first aid cover, and a plan for waste reduction supports sustainability. Merit B.M2 Produce a detailed and realistic event plan with timelines and budgets.

A community sports day is planned over ten weeks. Week one sets the aims, including 200 participants and £1,500 raised for a local charity. Weeks two to four cover venue booking, volunteer recruitment and risk assessment. The budget allocates 40 per cent to equipment, 25 per cent to marketing and 20 per cent to first aid and insurance, with a 15 per cent contingency. The timeline ends with a debrief one week after the event, so the outcomes can be measured against the aims. Distinction CD.D3 Evaluate the overall success of the sports or physical activity event and own performance, providing well-justified recommendations for future events.

The event reached 180 of the 200 planned participants, which was below target, but raised £1,700 against a £1,500 goal. Feedback showed the route was popular, but the start time clashed with a local football match. My role as registration lead ran smoothly, though the digital form caused delays for some older participants. Recommendations are to hold the event on a different date, offer a paper form, and set a target for volunteer training so the team is more confident on the day. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Set SMART aims before planning anything else. Every later decision should link back to them.

For the budget and timeline, use realistic figures and show a contingency. A plan with no contingency is weaker. For delivery and review, use evidence such as attendance, feedback and finances, rather than general impressions. Name the role you carried out and say how it contributed. Individual contribution is assessed separately from the event. Common mistakes Setting aims that cannot be measured, so success cannot be judged. Producing a plan without a risk assessment or contingency. Describing the event in general terms without explaining the student's own contribution. Assessment approach

Sports tourism brings people to places for sport, and sport to places for tourism. It can bring jobs, income and pride to a region, and it can also bring crowds, pressure on natural resources and environmental damage. This unit explores the types of sports tourism and their impacts, how innovation and sustainability are changing the sector, and how to plan a sports tourism enterprise. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to describe and evaluate the impacts of sports tourism, explain how innovation and sustainability add value, and produce an enterprise plan that is justified by market evidence and presented professionally. They study the businesses that serve sports tourists, from transport and accommodation to coaching and equipment hire. They also examine the economic, social and environmental impacts, both positive and negative, at local, national and international levels.

Strong responses Balances the positive and negative impacts of a named event or destination, using evidence. Pass A.P2 Explain the economic, social and environmental impacts of sports tourism.

A major international football tournament can boost local income, because visitors spend on hotels, food and transport. It creates jobs in hospitality and event management. Socially, it can build community pride, but it can also bring noise and overcrowding in residential areas. Environmentally, travel and energy use produce carbon emissions, though a venue built to green standards can reduce the long-term impact. Merit B.M2 Explain how innovation and sustainability enhance the value, and appeal of, sports tourism enterprises.

A surf school that offers an augmented reality video of each lesson gives customers a clear record of their progress, which increases the value of the course and encourages repeat bookings. Offering eco-certified accommodation and a carbon offset for travel appeals to customers who want a responsible holiday. Both measures help the business stand out, and both can be promoted to a growing group of customers who value sustainability. Distinction BC.D2 Justify the feasibility of the proposed enterprise, and recommend innovative and sustainable strategies that improve success and long-term viability.

A guided cycling tour of a regional coastline is feasible because local hotels report high demand for activity-based packages, and the regional tourist board predicts growth in visitors who want active holidays. The enterprise can start small with two guides and a fleet of hired bikes, so the financial risk is limited. To improve viability, the tour should use electric bikes to widen participation, and a booking app that offers carbon-neutral options. These strategies respond directly to the market evidence. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Name the type of sports tourism before you describe its impacts. Spectator, participation and virtual tourism have different effects.

Use both positive and negative impacts. A one-sided account will not reach the higher criteria. For feasibility, show the market evidence first, then the conclusion. A judgement without evidence is weak. Use real local data where possible, and label any assumptions in the plan. Cover this Unit Unit 18: Ethical Issues and Performance Aids in Sport Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Sport depends on trust: that competitors play by the rules, that officials are fair, and that athletes are not harmed. This unit looks at the ethical values that protect that trust, the issues that challenge it, and the performance aids that raise questions about fairness and health. It then asks what organisations and individuals can do to uphold ethical standards. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to explain values and issues accurately, evaluate the ethical implications of performance aids, explain the role of organisations, and recommend realistic strategies. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Optional Diploma, Extended Diploma Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Explore ethical values and issues in modern sport Students learn the core values of sport: fair play, integrity, respect, responsibility, digital ethics, mental health responsibility and environmental responsibility. They then examine emerging issues, such as commercial sponsorship, athlete activism, the use of technology in officiating, online abuse, sustainability and equality. Strong responses Connects a value to a specific issue, and explains how the issue affects athletes and organisations.

Learning aim B: Examine the use of performance aids and their impact on fairness and health Students study the types of performance aids, including legal aids such as nutritional supplements and sports drinks, and aids that are prohibited. Sponsorship is an ethical issue when a club accepts money from a company whose products may harm health, such as fast food. The club must balance the income that supports its teams with its responsibility to young members. Online abuse is another issue: athletes receive harassment on social media, which affects their mental health and can deter participation. Organisations must decide how far they are responsible for protecting athletes from this. Merit B.M2

Analyse the advantages and disadvantages of performance aids for athletes and organisations. Some legal performance aids, such as sports drinks, can help athletes maintain hydration during prolonged activity, which supports safety and performance. However, the marketing of some supplements can encourage athletes to rely on products rather than training, and products may be contaminated or mislabelled. For organisations, a clear regulated list of permitted aids protects fairness, but enforcing it requires testing, which has a cost. A club could introduce a short induction course on online conduct for all junior members and parents. This is feasible because it needs a few hours of staff time and no equipment. Its impact may be limited unless it is repeated and linked to a clear reporting route. Combining the course with a visible reporting system gives both education and a response, which is more likely to change behaviour. Unit 20: Instructing Circuit Exercise Sessions | BTEC Sport | Simply Sport Science Home › BTEC Sport › Unit 20 Unit 20 60 GLH Internally assessed Instructing Circuit Exercise Sessions This unit develops the knowledge and practical skills required to plan, deliver and review safe and effective circuit exercise sessions for groups. Students will explore methods to motivate participants, adapt exercises, and ensure health and safety throughout the session. Cover this Unit Unit 20: Instructing Circuit Exercise Sessions Study notes and slide presentation → Overview

Circuit training is one of the most efficient ways to train several components of fitness in one session. It can be adapted for almost any group, from beginners to experienced athletes, but only if the session is planned around the participants, designed to be safe, and adjusted as it runs. This unit introduces the principles of circuit training and asks students to plan, deliver and review a session. The unit is internally assessed. Students need to explain the benefits and preparation required, plan a safe session, deliver it with clear technique and communication, and review both the participants' performance and their own delivery. Unit at a glance Guided learning hours 60 GLH

How the unit is assessed Internal assessment, centre-set or Authorised Assignment Brief Status Sizes Optional Extended Certificate, Foundation Diploma, Diploma, Extended Diploma Learning aims explained Learning aim A: Understand the principles of circuit training and participant preparation Students learn what circuit training develops, the types of circuit (bodyweight, resistance, HIIT and sport-specific), and how a class is structured into warm-up, main circuit and cool-down. They study how to prepare participants: screening with a readiness questionnaire such as PAR-Q, identifying contraindications and referring when needed, and preparing the participant physically and mentally.

Strong responses Uses screening results to decide which exercises suit a participant and which need an alternative. Learning aim B: Plan safe and effective circuit exercise sessions Students plan a session using the principles of fitness, such as the FITT principle and progressive overload, and the participant factors that affect it, such as fitness level, age and health conditions. They design the circuit: the number of stations, equipment, sequence to avoid overloading one muscle group, and adaptations for different abilities. Strong responses Explains how the station order and the adaptations keep the session safe and effective for this group.

Learning aim C: Deliver and adapt circuit exercise sessions Students set up the session and check the equipment before it starts. They deliver it with correct technique and clear communication, monitor participants, and adapt the session through progressions, regressions and motivation as it runs. Strong responses Makes a sensible adaptation during the session and explains why it was needed. Learning aim D: Review participant performance and evaluate own delivery of circuit sessions

Students review how the participants performed and how well they delivered the session. They identify strengths and areas for improvement, make detailed recommendations for future planning, and justify those recommendations with participant feedback and professional standards. Strong responses Uses participant feedback and observations as evidence, and links each recommendation to a specific part of the session. Pass A.P1 Explain the benefits of circuit training and key considerations for participant readiness. Circuit training improves cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength and endurance in one session, which makes it time-efficient. Before the session, a PAR-Q questionnaire is used to identify any health condition that might need a medical referral. A participant who reports a recent injury is given lower-impact alternatives. A gradual warm-up raises heart rate and mobility before the main circuit begins. Merit B.M2

Justify the choice of exercises and adaptations in the planned circuit session. The circuit alternates upper-body and lower-body stations to avoid fatiguing the same muscle group in succession. Press-ups are replaced by wall press-ups for participants who cannot yet lower their body with control. A skipping station is set at a lower intensity for the older participants. Each choice keeps the circuit within the group's ability while still developing strength and endurance. Distinction BC.D2 Evaluate the suitability of the planned session, and the effectiveness of delivery methods and adaptations, providing evidence-based recommendations for improvement.

The session suited the group, with most participants completing every station. The timing of 40 seconds work and 20 seconds rest was too demanding for two participants, who needed longer recovery, so the rest period should be adjusted for those participants. The adaptations worked, but the verbal cues were too quick for some, so slower, clearer instructions with a demonstration should be used next time. Both changes are supported by the participant feedback collected at the end. Teaching and assessment tips Tips Use the FITT principle when you explain your session plan. It gives a clear, professional structure.

For each participant, name one adaptation and say why it suits them. A general statement about adapting is not enough. Check the environment before the session, and do dynamic risk assessment during it. Mention both in your plan and your review. Use feedback from participants in your review, and turn it into a specific change for the next session. Common mistakes Designing a circuit without checking the station order for muscle balance. Adapting exercises without saying who the adaptation is for. Reviewing the session without any participant feedback or evidence. Assessment approach
