Joints, Movements and Muscles | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 1 › Topic 1 Topic 1 Theme 1 · Applied anatomy and physiology AS Level 8386 Joints, Movements and Muscles How the skeleton, joints and muscles produce movement, and how to analyse a movement in full. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview Every movement in sport happens at a joint , where two or more bones meet. Most of the joints you need for Cambridge AS Level are synovial joints , which have a fluid-filled capsule that lets the bones move freely. The type of joint determines which movements are possible and how far they can go.

Movement is produced by skeletal muscles that pull on bones across joints. Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs or groups: one muscle produces the movement, another opposes or controls it, and others stabilise the bones around the joint. Learning to name these roles precisely is central to this topic. Specification content covered in this topic 1.1 Joints and movements Stability and range of movement 1.2 Functions of muscles 1.3 Types of muscle contraction 1.4 Muscle fibre types 1.5 Movement analysis of actions Key Terms Synovial joint A freely movable joint with a fluid-filled capsule, such as the shoulder, elbow or knee.

Agonist The muscle that produces a movement (the prime mover). Antagonist The muscle that opposes an agonist, relaxing to allow a movement or controlling it. Fixator A muscle that stabilises the bone at the origin of an agonist, so that the agonist acts efficiently. Concentric contraction The muscle shortens while it produces force. Eccentric contraction The muscle lengthens while it produces force, usually to control a movement. Isometric contraction The muscle produces force without changing length. Presentations 1.1 Synovial Joints 1.2 Movement Types and Agonist Muscles 1.3 Muscle Roles and Contraction Types 1.4 Muscle Fibre Types 1.5 Movement Analysis of Sporting Actions Deep Dive

1.1 Joints and movements The synovial joints you need to know, and the bones that articulate at each, are shown below. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint; the elbow and knee are hinge joints; the wrist is condyloid; the radioulnar joint is a pivot; the hip is ball-and-socket; and the ankle is a hinge. Joint Type of synovial joint Articulating bones Shoulder Ball and socket Humerus and scapula Elbow Hinge Humerus, radius and ulna Wrist Condyloid Radius and carpals Radioulnar Pivot Radius and ulna Hip Ball and socket Femur and pelvis Knee Hinge Femur and tibia Ankle Hinge Tibia, fibula and talus Stability and range of movement

A ball-and-socket joint (shoulder, hip) is multi-axial , so it allows movement in many planes and has the greatest range of movement. The shoulder has the greatest range of any joint in the body, but is the least stable, because its shallow socket and looser ligaments allow the head of the humerus to move a long way. The hip has a deeper socket and strong ligaments, so it sacrifices some range for stability.

A hinge joint (elbow, knee, ankle) is uniaxial : it moves in one plane, flexing and extending. Its shape and strong ligaments make it very stable in that plane, but it cannot rotate. A condyloid joint (wrist) allows movement in two planes, and a pivot joint (radioulnar) allows rotation only. The movements at each joint, and the main agonist for each, are summarised in the table below. The agonist is the muscle named in the specification for that movement, so learn them as pairs. Joint Movement Main agonist Shoulder Flexion Anterior deltoid Shoulder Extension Posterior deltoid Shoulder Abduction Medial deltoid Shoulder Adduction Latissimus dorsi Shoulder Horizontal flexion Pectoralis major

Shoulder Horizontal extension Posterior deltoid Elbow Flexion Biceps brachii Elbow Extension Triceps brachii Wrist Flexion Wrist flexors Wrist Extension Wrist extensors Radioulnar Pronation Pronator teres Radioulnar Supination Supinator Hip Flexion Iliopsoas Hip Extension Gluteus maximus Hip Abduction Gluteus medius Hip Adduction Adductor longus Knee Flexion Biceps femoris Knee Extension Rectus femoris Ankle Dorsiflexion Tibialis anterior Ankle Plantar flexion Gastrocnemius 1.2 Functions of muscles Agonists produce the movement. During a bicep curl, the biceps brachii is the agonist for elbow flexion.

Antagonists oppose the agonist. The triceps brachii is the antagonist during the bicep curl: it must relax to let the elbow bend, and it controls the movement when the arm is lowered. Fixators stabilise the bone at the origin of the agonist. During a bicep curl, muscles around the shoulder fix the upper arm so that the biceps can pull the forearm efficiently, rather than moving the shoulder. 1.3 Types of muscle contraction Concentric contraction is when the muscle shortens while it produces force, for example the biceps lifting a dumbbell upwards.

Eccentric contraction is when the muscle lengthens while it produces force. During eccentric contraction the agonist is controlling a movement that is different from the one named for it in section 1.1. When the arm is lowered slowly in a bicep curl, the biceps is working eccentrically to control elbow extension , even though it is a flexor. Concentric and eccentric are the two types of isotonic contraction, because the muscle changes length while producing force. Isometric contraction produces force without any change in length, for example holding a wall sit or a plank. 1.4 Muscle fibre types

Slow oxidative (SO, type I) fibres contract slowly, produce low force and are highly resistant to fatigue. They have many mitochondria and rich blood supply, and rely on aerobic respiration. They suit long, low-intensity activity such as marathon running. Fast oxidative glycolytic (FOG, type IIa) fibres contract quickly and produce more force than SO fibres. They can use both aerobic and anaerobic pathways, and are fairly resistant to fatigue. They suit activities that combine endurance with bursts of effort, such as middle-distance running or a rugby forward sustaining high-intensity work.

Fast glycolytic (FG, type IIx) fibres contract very quickly and produce the greatest force, but fatigue rapidly. They rely mainly on anaerobic glycolysis. They suit short, explosive activity such as a 100 m sprint or a weightlifting clean. Use examples whenever you explain fibre types, and link structure to function: many mitochondria and myoglobin support aerobic work; fast contraction and rapid fatigue reflect the anaerobic fibre’s structure and fuel supply. 1.5 Movement analysis of actions The specification asks you to analyse an action in a fixed order. Use this sequence every time: Identify the joint . State the type of joint and the articulating bones . State the type of movement .

Identify the working (agonist) muscle , and the antagonist and fixators where relevant. State the type of muscle contraction . Worked example, bicep curl (lifting phase): the joint is the elbow; it is a hinge joint formed by the humerus, radius and ulna; the movement is flexion; the agonist is the biceps brachii; the antagonist is the triceps brachii; fixators stabilise the upper arm; and the contraction is concentric. Exam Tips Exam tip Name muscles from the specification list and use the agonist for each movement exactly as given in section 1.1.3. Examiners mark the named muscle.

Exam tip Keep movement and contraction separate. "Eccentric" describes how the muscle is working, not which way the limb moves. Exam tip When asked to analyse, follow the five-step sequence in 1.5 and label each step. This is much easier to mark than a paragraph. Exam tip Compare joints using both stability and range. Ball-and-socket joints give range; hinge joints give stability in one plane. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Identify the type of synovial joint at the knee and name the bones that articulate there. 2 marks Answer Model answer Hinge joint. Femur and tibia.

2 Explain why the shoulder has a greater range of movement than the elbow. 3 marks Answer Model answer The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, which is multi-axial and allows movement in many planes. The elbow is a hinge joint, which is uniaxial and moves in one plane only. Therefore the shoulder can move through a much greater range, at the cost of stability. 3 During the lowering phase of a bicep curl, the biceps brachii is working eccentrically. Explain what it is controlling. 2 marks Answer Model answer It is controlling elbow extension, a movement in the opposite direction to its usual action of elbow flexion.

The muscle lengthens while producing force, so the arm is lowered in a controlled way. 4 Describe the structure and function of fast glycolytic (type IIx) muscle fibres and give one sporting example of their use. 3 marks Answer Model answer Structure: large fibres with few mitochondria and a low capillary supply, but large stores of PCr and glycogen. Fast contraction, high force production and rapid fatigue, because they are adapted for anaerobic glycolysis. Use of the fibres is shown by a sprint, such as the 100 m. 5 Analyse the action of elbow flexion during a bicep curl, using the five-step method. 4 marks Answer Model answer

Joint: elbow; hinge joint, articulating bones humerus, radius and ulna. Movement: flexion; agonist biceps brachii. Antagonist triceps brachii; fixators stabilise the upper arm. Contraction type is concentric as the biceps shortens while lifting. Ethics and Deviance | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 3 › Topic 10 Topic 10 Theme 3 · Sociocultural issues and technology AS Level 8386 Ethics and Deviance Performance-enhancing drugs, violence and competition manipulation: their causes, consequences and the strategies used to reduce them. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Ethics and deviance examine behaviour that breaks the rules or the spirit of sport. This topic covers three areas: the use of prohibited performance-enhancing drugs, violence by performers and spectators, and competition manipulation. For each, you need to explain the causes , the consequences for the individual, the sport and society, and the strategies used to reduce the problem, which you must evaluate. Specification content covered in this topic 10.1 Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) 10.2 Violence 10.3 Competition manipulation Key Terms Performance-enhancing drug (PED) A substance or method, prohibited by sporting bodies, used to improve performance.

Violence Physical or verbal aggression that causes harm, by performers or spectators. Competition manipulation Cheating by performers, coaches or officials that affects the outcome of a match or event. Match-fixing An arrangement to determine the result of a match in advance. Tanking Deliberately losing a match. Presentations 10.1 Performance Enhancing Drugs 10.2 Violence in Sport 10.3 Competition Manipulation Deep Dive 10.1 Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs)

Performers use prohibited PEDs for several reasons, which you should explain using the specific causes in the specification: pressure to win ; to increase fitness such as strength or endurance; to reduce weight or body fat ; to speed up recovery after training or injury; to increase the intensity of training ; to reduce the effects of fatigue ; to increase concentration ; to participate despite injury or to mask pain ; to hide the presence of other drugs ; and because of a belief that others are using them .

The consequences are health risks and damage to the performer, the loss of fair competition and public trust in the sport, and the influence on young people who see role models using drugs. Strategies to reduce use include testing, sanctions, education and anti-doping programmes. Evaluate each: testing is effective at detection but can be avoided by new drugs; education can change attitudes but takes time; sanctions deter but cannot remove the pressure to win. 10.2 Violence

Violence can be caused by performers (for example through frustration, pressure to win, or a belief that aggression is part of the game) and by spectators at the event (for example through rivalry, alcohol, or group identity). Explain the cause for each group. The consequences are injury and legal action for the individual, damage to the reputation and finances of the sport, and public disorder and cost to society. Strategies to prevent violence include sanctions for performers, education, stewarding and ticketing, segregation of rival supporters, and CCTV. Evaluate each one: stewarding and CCTV can deter, but they cannot change the attitudes that cause violence.

10.3 Competition manipulation Competition manipulation is cheating by performers, coaches or officials that affects the outcome of a match or event, and removes the unpredictability that makes competition valuable. The forms are betting (wagers linked to the result), match-fixing (an arrangement to fix the result), insider information (using private knowledge to gain an advantage), and tanking (deliberately losing a match).

Strategies to reduce manipulation include monitoring of betting patterns, sanctions, education for performers and officials, and integrity units within sporting bodies. Evaluate each by considering how easily it can be avoided and how much it protects the unpredictability of the sport. Exam Tips Exam tip For causes, name the specific reason from the list and explain how it leads to the behaviour. Do not list causes without explaining them. Exam tip For consequences, name the group affected (the individual, the sport or society) for each consequence. Exam tip For evaluation of strategies, weigh what the strategy achieves against what it cannot change, and reach a judgement.

Exam tip Use the exact terms for forms of competition manipulation: match-fixing, tanking, insider information and betting. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Explain two reasons why a performer might use a prohibited performance-enhancing drug. 4 marks Answer Model answer To increase fitness, such as strength or endurance, to gain an advantage. To speed up recovery after injury, so that the performer can return to competition sooner. Pressure to win is a motivation, as the performer feels they must succeed. Each reason is explained in terms of the advantage it gives the performer.

2 Explain the consequences of the use of prohibited PEDs for society. 3 marks Answer Model answer Young people may copy the behaviour of role models who use drugs, because they admire them. Public trust in sport and its values is damaged. Health services may face costs from the health problems caused by drug use. 3 Explain how tanking affects the unpredictability of competition. 3 marks Answer Model answer Tanking is deliberately losing a match, so the outcome is decided before the match is played. This removes the unpredictability of the contest, which is one of the values that makes competition valuable. Spectators and sponsors lose confidence in the result.

4 Evaluate the use of sanctions as a strategy to prevent violence by spectators. 4 marks Answer Model answer Sanctions such as bans and fines deter spectators who want to avoid the penalty. They are effective where the spectator can be identified, through CCTV and ticketing. However, sanctions only act after violence has occurred and do not change the attitudes that cause it. Sanctions are therefore most effective when combined with education and stewarding. Commercialisation and the Media | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 3 › Topic 11 Topic 11 Theme 3 · Sociocultural issues and technology AS Level 8386 Commercialisation and the Media How growth in media interest, sponsorship and professionalism have changed sport, and who benefits and who loses. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Commercialisation is the process by which sport has become a business, driven by media coverage, advertising and sponsorship. This topic asks you to explain the factors that led to commercialisation, describe the golden triangle that links sponsors, the media and sport, and evaluate commercialisation for each group affected. Specification content covered in this topic Factors leading to commercialisation The golden triangle Evaluating commercialisation Key Terms Commercialisation The process by which sport is organised and funded for commercial profit. Sponsorship Financial or other support from a business, in return for publicity and association with the sport or event.

Golden triangle The relationship between sponsors or business, the media and sport, each of which depends on the others. Primary spectator A person who watches the event in person. Secondary spectator A remote audience who watches through the media. Presentation Evaluating Commercialisation for Stakeholders Deep Dive Factors leading to commercialisation

Sport has been commercialised because of growth in media interest , which has increased the value of broadcasting rights; growth in public interest and spectatorism , which increases the audience a sponsor can reach; professionalism , which has made performers paid employees; advertising , which pays for coverage and events; and sponsorship , which gives businesses access to the audience in return for funding. Explain each factor and link it to the effect it has on sport, rather than listing them. The golden triangle

The golden triangle describes the relationship between sponsorship and business , the media and sport . Sport provides the events and the audience; the media broadcast them and deliver the audience to sponsors; sponsors fund the sport and the media coverage. Each part depends on the others, and each can influence the others, for example by changing the timing of events to suit broadcasters. Evaluating commercialisation Commercialisation affects different groups in different ways, and your evaluation should consider each: The performer or team : higher pay and profile, but more pressure, less control over schedules and greater exposure to criticism.

The sponsor or business : wider exposure and brand value, but cost and the risk of association with negative events. The event or sport : funding, growth and professional standards, but changes to rules, timing and the character of the sport to suit broadcasters. Primary spectators (at the event) : better facilities and entertainment, but higher ticket prices and a less intimate atmosphere. Secondary spectators (remote audience) : access to events they could not otherwise see, but a viewing experience shaped by commentary and advertising. Reach a judgement that considers which group gains most, and which bears the greatest cost. Exam Tips

Exam tip Name each of the five factors, and explain the effect on sport in one sentence each. Exam tip When you describe the golden triangle, show that each part depends on the other two, and give one example of influence in each direction. Exam tip Evaluate commercialisation for each of the five groups, and end with a judgement about which group gains most. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Explain how sponsorship has contributed to the commercialisation of sport. 3 marks Answer Model answer Sponsors provide money for events and performers, in return for publicity. This allows sport to become more professional and better funded.

Sport in turn gives sponsors an audience and an association with success. 2 Explain what is meant by the golden triangle. 3 marks Answer Model answer The golden triangle is the relationship between sponsors or business, the media and sport. Each depends on the others: sport provides the events, the media broadcast them, and sponsors fund both. Each can influence the others, for example by changing event timing. 3 Evaluate the effect of commercialisation on primary spectators. 4 marks Answer Model answer Benefit: better facilities, entertainment and services at the event. Limitation: higher ticket prices can exclude some people.

Limitation: scheduling for broadcasters can change the event and the atmosphere. Judgement: the benefits depend on whether the price and experience are accessible to the wider audience. The Use of Technology | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 3 › Topic 12 Topic 12 Theme 3 · Sociocultural issues and technology AS Level 8386 The Use of Technology The technology used in sport, from equipment and clothing to cameras and software, and the advantages and disadvantages it brings to each group. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Technology is used throughout sport: in equipment, clothing, footwear, surfaces, facilities, cameras and software. Each example can improve performance, safety or the spectator’s experience, but each also brings disadvantages. This topic asks you to explain examples of technology, and to evaluate its advantages and disadvantages for performers, sponsors, the event, and both types of spectator. Specification content covered in this topic 12.1 Examples of technology in sport 12.2 Evaluating technology Key Terms Force plate A measuring device that records the forces a performer applies to the ground.

Photo-finish A camera system that records the moment of finishing, used to decide close results. Motion tracking Software that records the movement of players or performers over time. Compression wear Tight-fitting clothing that is claimed to improve circulation and recovery. All-weather pitch A synthetic playing surface that can be used in all conditions. Presentations 12 Technology in Sport 12b Evaluating Technology in Sport Deep Dive 12.1 Examples of technology in sport Technology in sport includes: Equipment , such as tennis rackets and force plates. Clothing , such as compression wear. Footwear , such as running shoes. Surfaces , such as all-weather pitches.

Facilities , such as sport-specific venues and wind tunnels. Cameras , such as photo-finish and video replay. Software , such as biomechanical analysis and motion tracking of players. For each example, explain how it is used and what it measures or changes, using a sporting example. 12.2 Evaluating technology Technology has advantages and disadvantages for each group. Evaluate each in turn: The performer, team or coach : objective data and better feedback, but cost, dependence on equipment and access inequality between teams. The sponsor : visibility through branded equipment and technology, but cost and risk if the technology fails.

The event, sport or official : fairer decisions through review, but slower play and disputes about how the technology is used. Primary spectators (at the event) : better information and replays, but possible disruption and delays. Secondary spectators (remote audience) : clearer coverage and analysis, but the risk that the viewing experience is shaped by the technology. Make a judgement about which group benefits most, and whether the benefits outweigh the disadvantages in the context given. Exam Tips Exam tip Name the category of technology (equipment, clothing, footwear, surfaces, facilities, cameras or software), then give a specific example and explain its use.

Exam tip For evaluation, give one advantage and one disadvantage for the group named in the question, and reach a judgement. Exam tip Use the five groups in 12.2 to organise your evaluation, and do not confuse primary and secondary spectators. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Explain how a force plate can be used in the analysis of a sprint start. 3 marks Answer Model answer A force plate records the forces the performer applies to the ground. This data shows the force, its direction and how it changes through the start. It can be used to identify weaknesses and to plan training.

2 Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of photo-finish cameras for officials. 3 marks Answer Model answer Advantage: the photo-finish gives an objective decision in close results. The image can be reviewed, so finishes too close for the human eye to separate can be decided. Disadvantage: the technology can take time, which delays the official result and can disrupt the event. 3 Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of motion tracking software for a coach. 4 marks Answer Model answer Advantage: objective data on player movement can inform tactics and training. Advantage: data can be used to track improvement over time.

Disadvantage: the software is expensive, so it may be available only to well-funded teams. Disadvantage: coaches may rely on data over observation and experience. Biomechanics | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 1 › Topic 2 Topic 2 Theme 1 · Applied anatomy and physiology AS Level 8386 Biomechanics Linear and angular motion, forces, flight and stability, described with the quantities and equations the specification requires. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview Biomechanics applies the principles of physics to human movement. In this topic you describe how bodies move in a straight or curved line, the forces that cause and change that movement, the way rotating bodies behave, the paths that objects follow when they are projected, and what makes a body stable.

You need to describe, calculate and compare quantities, and draw and interpret graphs. Always state units, and be precise about whether a quantity is a scalar or a vector. Specification content covered in this topic 2.1 Linear motion 2.2 Newton’s laws of motion 2.3 Angular motion 2.4 Parabolic and non-parabolic flight 2.5 Properties of bodies and objects Key Terms Linear motion Movement in a straight or curved line where every part of the body moves the same distance, in the same direction, in the same time. Scalar quantity A quantity with magnitude only, such as distance or speed. Vector quantity A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement or velocity.

Momentum The product of mass and velocity (p = mv). Angular momentum The product of moment of inertia and angular velocity. Moment of inertia The resistance of a body to angular acceleration, which depends on its mass and how that mass is distributed from the axis of rotation. Centre of mass The point at which the mass of a body is considered to be concentrated. Base of support The area beneath a body that is enclosed by the points of contact with the surface. Presentations 2.1 Linear Motion 2.2 Newton's Laws of Motion 2.3 Angular Motion 2.4 Projectile Flight 2.5 Centre of Mass and Stability Deep Dive 2.1 Linear motion

A body is in linear motion when all its parts move the same distance, in the same direction, over the same time. This is caused by an external force that passes through the centre of mass. Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors. Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish, with direction. Speed is distance divided by time. Velocity is displacement divided by time. Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by time. Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity.

On a distance–time graph , the gradient gives speed. On a displacement–time graph , the gradient gives velocity. On a velocity–time graph , the gradient gives acceleration, and the area under the line gives displacement. Sketch a graph with labelled axes and units before you interpret it. 2.2 Newton’s laws of motion Force is a push or pull that can change the motion of a body. Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass. Inertia is a body’s resistance to change in motion, and depends on its mass.

The forces acting in physical activity include gravitational force (weight), air resistance, friction, the reaction force from the ground, and the muscular (action) force. Forces can be balanced, producing no change in motion, or unbalanced, producing acceleration. Newton’s first law (law of inertia): a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless an unbalanced force acts on it. A sprinter stays still in the blocks until a force from the blocks overcomes their inertia. Newton’s second law (law of acceleration): acceleration is proportional to the unbalanced force and inversely proportional to mass (F = ma). Increasing the force a sprinter applies to the blocks increases their acceleration.

Newton’s third law (law of reaction): for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. A sprinter pushes backwards on the blocks, and the blocks push forwards on the sprinter with an equal force. 2.3 Angular motion Angular motion is movement of a body in a circular path about an axis of rotation. It is caused by a force that acts outside the centre of mass, which produces a turning effect. Three quantities describe it: angular momentum , moment of inertia and angular velocity . They are linked by the equation angular momentum = moment of inertia × angular velocity (L = Iω).

The moment of inertia depends on the mass of the body and the distribution of that mass from the axis of rotation. Mass further from the axis gives a larger moment of inertia. The conservation of angular momentum means that, with no external torque, angular momentum stays constant. A diver or gymnast who pulls their limbs in reduces their moment of inertia, so their angular velocity increases to keep angular momentum constant. When they extend their body, the moment of inertia rises and the rotation slows. Sketch graphs of all three quantities to show this relationship. 2.4 Parabolic and non-parabolic flight

Once released, a projectile has a horizontal and a vertical component of motion. The horizontal velocity stays roughly constant, while the vertical velocity changes under gravity. Sketch both components when you draw a flight path. A shot put follows an approximately parabolic flight path, because it is dense and compact, so air resistance has little effect on it. A badminton shuttlecock has a large surface area for its mass, so air resistance has a major effect; its flight is non-parabolic , with a steep descent.

The horizontal displacement of a projectile depends on the height of release , the speed of release and the angle of release . When a projectile lands lower than it was released, the angle that gives maximum horizontal distance is less than 45°, and it falls further as the release height rises. 2.5 Properties of bodies and objects The centre of mass is the point where the body’s mass is concentrated. Its position depends on the body’s shape and how its mass is distributed, and it moves when the body changes posture.

Stability is greater when the area of the base of support is large, when the centre of mass is low , when the line of gravity falls within the base of support , and when the mass of the body is greater. A wide stance in a rugby scrum and a low crouch in a goalkeeper’s stance both apply these principles. Exam Tips Exam tip State the equation before you substitute, show the units, and give the answer with its unit. Method marks are often awarded for the correct equation. Exam tip Be strict about scalars and vectors. Speed is not velocity, and distance is not displacement.

Exam tip For angular momentum, link the moment of inertia to the position of mass. "Tucking reduces the moment of inertia, so angular velocity increases" is the full chain. Exam tip When explaining stability, name each factor from 2.5.2 and say which way it changes stability. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 A 90 kg player is moving at 6 m/s. Calculate the momentum of the player. 2 marks Answer Model answer Momentum = mass × velocity = 90 kg × 6 m/s. = 540 kg m/s. 2 Explain why a diver rotates faster when they tuck than when they extend their body. 3 marks Answer Model answer

Tucking brings the mass closer to the axis of rotation, which reduces the moment of inertia. Angular momentum is conserved, so when the moment of inertia falls the angular velocity increases. Extending the body does the reverse, slowing the rotation. 3 Explain why the flight path of a shot put is parabolic, but the flight path of a badminton shuttlecock is not. 3 marks Answer Model answer The shot put is dense and compact, so air resistance has little effect on its flight. The shuttlecock has a large surface area for its mass, so air resistance is significant and changes its path. Its descent is therefore steeper and not parabolic.

4 Explain two factors that make a rugby player less likely to be knocked over. 3 marks Answer Model answer A wider base of support, because the line of gravity is more likely to fall within it. A lower centre of mass, which makes the body more stable. A greater body mass gives more inertia, so more force is needed to change the player's state of motion. 5 A sprinter pushes backwards against the blocks. Using Newton’s third law, explain how this produces forward motion. 2 marks Answer Model answer For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The blocks push the sprinter forwards with a force equal to the force the sprinter applies backwards.

The Cardiovascular System | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 1 › Topic 3 Topic 3 Theme 1 · Applied anatomy and physiology AS Level 8386 The Cardiovascular System Heart structure, the conduction system, cardiac output and how the circulation redistributes blood during exercise. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

The cardiovascular system transports oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones and heat around the body. The heart is a double pump: the right side sends blood to the lungs, and the left side sends blood to the rest of the body. Understanding its structure, its electrical control, and how it responds to exercise is central to this topic. You need to know typical values for heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output at rest and during exercise for both an untrained individual and a trained athlete. These values are given in the specification and examiners expect you to use them. Specification content covered in this topic 3.1 Structure and function of the heart

3.2 The conduction system and the cardiac cycle 3.3 Factors affecting cardiac output Starling’s law and the control of heart rate Responses to exercise Long-term training 3.4 Function of the vascular system Key Terms Cardiac output The volume of blood pumped by the heart each minute (heart rate × stroke volume). Stroke volume The volume of blood ejected from the left ventricle in one contraction. Sinoatrial node (SAN) The heart’s natural pacemaker, in the right atrium, which initiates each heartbeat. Atrioventricular node (AVN) The node that delays the impulse before it passes to the ventricles. Venous return The flow of blood back to the heart through the veins.

Vascular shunt The redistribution of blood flow, away from inactive tissues and towards working muscles, during exercise. Presentations 3.1 Heart Structure and Blood Flow 3.2 Conduction System and Cardiac Cycle 3.3 Cardiac Output: Values, Equations and Responses 3.4 Venous Return and Vascular Shunt Deep Dive 3.1 Structure and function of the heart The heart has four chambers. The atria receive blood and the ventricles pump it out. The septum separates the left and right sides. The myocardium is the muscular wall, and it is thickest in the left ventricle, which pumps blood around the whole body.

Four valves prevent backflow. The bicuspid (mitral) valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle; the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and right ventricle; and the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves guard the exits of the two ventricles. Follow the pathway of blood through the heart: the vena cava brings deoxygenated blood into the right atrium; it passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, then through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, through the bicuspid valve to the left ventricle, and out through the aortic valve into the aorta .

3.2 The conduction system and the cardiac cycle The impulse starts in the sinoatrial node (SAN) in the right atrium. The wave of excitation spreads across both atria, causing atrial systole (contraction). The impulse reaches the atrioventricular node (AVN) , which delays it briefly, so that the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract. The impulse then passes down the bundle of His and along the Purkyne tissue , which spreads it through the ventricle walls, causing ventricular systole to begin at the base of the heart and move upwards. Between beats the heart is in diastole , when the chambers fill.

The link between conduction and the cycle is timing: the SAN sets the rate, the wave spreads through the atria, the AVN introduces the delay, and the Purkyne tissue triggers ventricular contraction. 3.3 Factors affecting cardiac output Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume: cardiac output (l/min) = heart rate (beats/min) × stroke volume (l) . Use this equation to calculate any one value if you know the other two, and remember to convert millilitres to litres. The typical values in the table below are those given in the specification. Use them when you describe or compare the two groups. Quantity Rest Sub-maximal Maximal Untrained individual

Heart rate (beats/min) 60–80 100–130 220 minus age Stroke volume (ml) 60–80 100–120 100–120 Cardiac output (l/min) 4.8–6.4 10–15 20–30 Trained athlete Heart rate (beats/min) 30–70 95–120 220 minus age Stroke volume (ml) 80–120 160–200 160–200 Cardiac output (l/min) 4.8–6.4 15–20 30–40 Starling’s law and the control of heart rate Starling’s law states that the more the ventricle is stretched by venous return, the greater the force of its contraction and the larger the stroke volume. Exercise increases venous return, so the heart fills more and ejects more with each beat.

Heart rate is controlled by the cardiac control centre in the medulla. Neural control comes from baroreceptors (blood pressure), chemoreceptors (blood CO₂ and pH) and mechanoreceptors (movement of limbs and joints). The sympathetic nervous system speeds the heart up, and the parasympathetic system slows it. Hormonal control is by adrenaline, which increases heart rate and contractility. Intrinsic control is by stretch of the myocardium and by temperature. Responses to exercise

At rest, heart rate and stroke volume are low and parasympathetic activity dominates. Immediately before exercise, heart rate rises even before movement starts, because of adrenaline and the sympathetic nervous system: this is the anticipatory rise . During exercise, heart rate rises with intensity, and stroke volume rises up to a point and then levels off. Cardiac output therefore increases as intensity rises. During recovery, heart rate falls quickly at first, then more slowly, as parasympathetic activity returns.

Sketch heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output against time on the same axis, and label rest, pre-exercise, exercise and recovery. Use the typical values from the table to show scale. Long-term training Regular endurance training produces physiological changes in the heart. A trained athlete has a larger stroke volume at rest and during exercise, so they can achieve the same cardiac output with a lower heart rate. This gives a lower resting heart rate and a higher maximum stroke volume. 3.4 Function of the vascular system

Venous return depends on several mechanisms: the skeletal muscle pump squeezes veins as muscles contract; valves prevent backflow; the respiratory pump uses pressure changes during breathing; gravity works against return from the legs; smooth muscle (venous tone) narrows the veins; and cardiac suction draws blood in during diastole.

During exercise, cardiac output is redistributed by the vascular shunt mechanism. The sympathetic nervous system causes vasoconstriction in arterioles supplying inactive tissue, such as the gut and kidneys, while vasodilation in the arterioles of working muscles increases their blood flow. Precapillary sphincters control flow into capillary beds, and the vasomotor control centre coordinates the response, using information from receptors. During recovery, blood flow returns to the tissues that were inactive, and the skeletal muscle pump continues to help venous return. Exam Tips

Exam tip Use the heart pathway in 3.1 as a checklist: start at the vena cava and follow every valve and vessel in order. Exam tip When asked to explain the conduction system, name each structure and say what happens there: the SAN initiates, the AVN delays, and the Purkyne tissue triggers ventricular contraction. Exam tip Use values from the tables when you compare. Quote the number, the unit and the group (trained or untrained) together. Exam tip For vascular shunt, name the nervous mechanism, the vessel and the tissue. A complete answer says that vasoconstriction happens in inactive tissue and vasodilation in working muscle. Practice Questions

Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Calculate the cardiac output of a person with a heart rate of 150 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 120 ml. 2 marks Answer Model answer Stroke volume = 120 ml = 0.12 l. Cardiac output = 150 × 0.12 = 18 l/min. 2 Describe the pathway of an electrical impulse through the heart, from the start of one heartbeat to ventricular contraction. 4 marks Answer Model answer The impulse starts at the sinoatrial node in the right atrium. It spreads across both atria, causing atrial systole. It reaches the atrioventricular node, which delays it.

It passes down the bundle of His and the Purkyne tissue, causing ventricular systole from the base upwards. 3 Explain how Starling’s law explains the increase in stroke volume during exercise. 3 marks Answer Model answer Exercise increases venous return, so the ventricle fills with more blood. The greater stretch of the myocardium produces a stronger contraction. Therefore stroke volume increases. 4 Explain how blood flow is redistributed during exercise. 4 marks Answer Model answer The sympathetic nervous system causes vasoconstriction in arterioles supplying inactive tissue, such as the gut. Vasodilation occurs in the arterioles supplying working muscles.

Precapillary sphincters open in the active muscles to increase blood flow. This increases blood supply to the muscles that need oxygen. 5 Compare the resting heart rate and stroke volume of an untrained individual and a trained athlete. 3 marks Answer Model answer The untrained individual has a resting heart rate of 60–80 beats per minute, compared with 30–70 for the trained athlete. The trained athlete has a larger resting stroke volume, 80–120 ml, compared with 60–80 ml for the untrained individual. This is because training increases the stroke volume, so the same cardiac output needs fewer beats. Previous topic ← Topic 2: Biomechanics Next topic Topic 4: The Respiratory System →

The Respiratory System | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 1 › Topic 4 Topic 4 Theme 1 · Applied anatomy and physiology AS Level 8386 The Respiratory System The mechanics of breathing, the control of ventilation, and how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged at the lungs and muscles. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

The respiratory system brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. During exercise, the demand for oxygen rises sharply, and breathing changes in rate and depth to meet it. This topic covers the muscles that drive breathing, the lung volumes that describe it, how breathing is controlled, and how gases are exchanged. You need to use equations and interpret spirometer traces to calculate lung volumes and ventilation, so practise reading a trace as well as learning the definitions. Specification content covered in this topic 4.1 Mechanics and regulation of breathing Lung volumes Regulation of breathing Long-term training 4.2 Gaseous exchange and respiration Key Terms

Tidal volume The volume of air breathed in or out in one normal breath. Breathing rate The number of breaths taken per minute. Minute ventilation The total volume of air moved into or out of the lungs in one minute (breathing rate × tidal volume). Vital capacity The maximum volume of air that can be breathed out after a maximum inhalation. Partial pressure The pressure exerted by one gas in a mixture, which drives diffusion from high to low. Myoglobin A protein in muscle that stores oxygen and helps move it within the muscle cell. Presentations 4.1 Mechanics of Breathing 4.2 Gaseous Exchange and Diffusion Gradients Deep Dive 4.1 Mechanics and regulation of breathing

Inspiration is active. The diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostals lift the ribs, increasing the volume of the thorax. During exercise, the sternocleidomastoids , scalenes and pectoralis minor act as accessory muscles to raise the chest further. Expiration is passive at rest, as the elastic lungs recoil. During exercise and recovery it becomes active: the internal intercostals pull the ribs down, and rectus abdominis compresses the abdomen to push the diaphragm up. Quantity Rest Sub-maximal Maximal Untrained individual Breathing rate (breaths/min) 12–15 20–25 40–50 Tidal volume (l) 0.5 1.5–2.0 2.0–3.0 Minute ventilation (l/min) 6.0–7.5 30–50 80–150 Trained athlete

Breathing rate (breaths/min) 10–12 15–20 50–60 Tidal volume (l) 0.5 2.0–2.5 3.0–4.0 Minute ventilation (l/min) 5.0–6.0 30–50 150–200 Lung volumes Tidal volume is the volume in one normal breath. Inspiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be inhaled after a normal breath. Expiratory reserve volume is the extra air that can be exhaled after a normal breath. Residual volume is the air remaining in the lungs after maximum exhalation. Vital capacity is the sum of tidal, inspiratory reserve and expiratory reserve volumes. Total lung volume is vital capacity plus residual volume. Minute ventilation is breathing rate multiplied by tidal volume.

Sketch a spirometer trace, label each volume, and use the equations to calculate values from the trace. Show units (litres, and litres per minute for minute ventilation). Regulation of breathing The respiratory control centre in the medulla sets the rate and depth of breathing. Chemoreceptors detect changes in blood carbon dioxide and pH, which are the most important stimulus during exercise. Thermoreceptors respond to temperature, and mechanoreceptors and stretch receptors in the lungs and joints provide feedback on movement and lung inflation.

The Hering–Breuer reflex stops over-inflation of the lungs: stretch receptors signal the medulla to end inspiration. Adrenaline increases breathing rate and depth, and the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems adjust breathing during exercise and recovery. Describe the response of each quantity in 4.1.3 before exercise, during exercise of different intensities and during recovery. Breathing rate and tidal volume both rise with intensity, which is why minute ventilation rises so steeply at maximal effort. Long-term training

Regular training improves the breathing response: a trained athlete breathes at a lower rate at rest and during sub-maximal exercise, and achieves a larger tidal volume, so minute ventilation at maximal intensity is higher. Compare the two groups using the table in section 4.1. 4.2 Gaseous exchange and respiration Gas exchange depends on partial pressures . In the alveoli , the partial pressure of oxygen is high and that of carbon dioxide is low, so oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Oxygen then binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells, which carry it through the blood capillaries .

At the muscles the situation is reversed. Muscle uses oxygen, so its partial pressure is low, and carbon dioxide is produced, so its partial pressure is high. Oxygen diffuses from the blood into the muscle, and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Myoglobin stores oxygen within the muscle fibre and helps move it to the mitochondria. The diffusion gradient is what drives exchange at both sites. Anything that increases the gradient, such as more active muscle or a greater ventilation at the lungs, increases the rate of exchange. Exam Tips Exam tip Name the accessory muscles of inspiration and say when they are used (exercise). Examiners mark the named muscles.

Exam tip For spirometer questions, define each volume first, then calculate. Vital capacity = tidal + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve. Exam tip In gas exchange, always state which way each gas diffuses and why: it always moves down its partial pressure gradient. Exam tip Minute ventilation questions often combine two quantities. Calculate breathing rate × tidal volume and state the unit, litres per minute. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Calculate the minute ventilation of an athlete with a breathing rate of 40 breaths per minute and a tidal volume of 2.0 litres. 2 marks Answer Model answer

Minute ventilation = breathing rate × tidal volume = 40 × 2.0. = 80 litres per minute. 2 Explain the role of the diaphragm during inspiration at rest. 2 marks Answer Model answer The diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the thorax. This lowers the pressure in the lungs, so air flows in. 3 Explain how the Hering–Breuer reflex protects the lungs. 3 marks Answer Model answer Stretch receptors in the lungs detect inflation. They send signals to the medulla, which ends inspiration. This prevents over-inflation of the lungs. 4 Explain why oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood. 3 marks Answer Model answer

The partial pressure of oxygen is higher in the alveoli than in the blood. Oxygen therefore diffuses down its partial pressure gradient, from high to low. It then binds to haemoglobin for transport. 5 Describe how the expiratory muscles act during exercise. 3 marks Answer Model answer Expiration becomes active during exercise. The internal intercostals pull the ribs down. Rectus abdominis compresses the abdomen, pushing the diaphragm up. Skill and Ability | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 2 › Topic 5 Topic 5 Theme 2 · Skill, learning and practice AS Level 8386 Skill and Ability How skills are classified along six continua, and what abilities are and how they underpin skilled performance. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Before you can explain how a skill is learned, you need to describe what the skill is. Skills are classified using continua : each is a scale between two extremes, and a skill is placed on each scale to show where it sits. Classification is the first step in deciding how to teach a skill and which practice methods will suit it. Skill is linked to ability , which is the underlying capacity a performer brings to a task. Abilities are innate, underpinning and enduring, and they shape how easily a person acquires new skills. Specification content covered in this topic 5.1 Classification of skills 5.2 Abilities Key Terms

Fine skill A skill that depends mainly on small, precise muscle movements, such as a golf putt. Gross skill A skill that depends mainly on large muscle groups, such as a sprint start. Open skill A skill performed in an unpredictable environment that changes, such as tackling in rugby. Closed skill A skill performed in a predictable environment, with no outside influence, such as a free throw. Discrete skill A skill with a clear beginning and end, such as a penalty kick. Ability A relatively stable, innate capacity that underpins the learning of skills. Presentations 5.1 Classification of Skills 5.2 Abilities Deep Dive 5.1 Classification of skills

Skills are placed on six continua. Each continuum describes a different feature of the skill, so a single skill can sit at different points on each one: Muscular involvement : fine (small, precise movements) to gross (large movements of major muscle groups). Environmental influence : open (the environment changes and must be read) to closed (the environment is predictable). Continuity : discrete (clear start and finish) to serial (discrete actions linked in sequence) to continuous (no clear start or finish, such as swimming). Pacing : externally paced (timed by the environment, such as a return of serve) to internally paced (timed by the performer, such as a golf swing).

Difficulty : basic (simple, few components) to complex (many components that must be coordinated). Organisation : high organisation (a sequence of closely linked components that must follow a precise order) to low organisation (components that can be performed in a looser order). To justify a classification, place the skill on each continuum and give a reason from the activity itself. For example, a netball shot from a set position is fine (precise finger and wrist control), closed (the defence is not moving), discrete, internally paced, and of moderate organisation. 5.2 Abilities An ability is a relatively stable, underlying capacity. The specification describes three characteristics:

Innate : abilities are partly inherited, so performers start with different levels of each ability. Underpinning : abilities form the base on which skills are built. For example, hand–eye coordination underpins many ball skills. Enduring : abilities change slowly and are relatively stable across a person’s life, so they are not easily altered by a short period of practice. Distinguish clearly between an ability and a skill. A skill is learned and specific to a task; an ability is a general capacity that supports many skills. A performer may have a high level of reaction ability but a low level of skill in a particular sport, because they have not yet learned the specific movement patterns.

Exam Tips Exam tip Use all six continua when you justify a classification. Examiners reward a complete justification, not a single continuum. Exam tip Give a reason for each placement that refers to the activity: "closed, because the environment is predictable" is a complete point. Exam tip Keep ability and skill separate in your answer, and use "underpinning" to show how the two are linked. Exam tip Use a sporting example for every continuum you describe, and make sure it fits the continuum you are describing. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it.

1 Classify a basketball free throw on the continua of muscular involvement, environmental influence and pacing. Justify each classification. 3 marks Answer Model answer Muscular involvement: fine, because the shot depends on precise hand and wrist control. Environmental influence: closed, because the shooter is not reacting to a changing environment. Pacing: internally paced, because the shooter decides when to start the shot. 2 Explain what is meant by an ability, and explain how an ability differs from a skill. 3 marks Answer Model answer An ability is a relatively stable, underlying capacity that supports the learning of many skills. A skill is learned and specific to a particular task.

For example, reaction ability is general, while the technique used in a specific sport is a learned skill. 3 Explain why a tennis rally is classified as open rather than closed. 2 marks Answer Model answer The environment is constantly changing, because the opponent’s shots vary in speed, direction and placement. The performer must read and respond to these changes. Theories of Learning | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 2 › Topic 6 Topic 6 Theme 2 · Skill, learning and practice AS Level 8386 Theories of Learning Motor programmes, operant conditioning, cognitive (Gestalt) theory, Bandura’s observational learning and Schmidt’s schema theory. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Learning theories explain how skills are acquired and what conditions help or hinder that process. Some theories focus on the stimulus and response (behaviourist theories such as operant conditioning). Others focus on how the learner thinks (cognitive theories such as Gestalt). Bandura’s theory explains learning through observation . Schmidt explains how a performer builds a general rule for producing movement. For every theory, you must explain it with examples, evaluate its strengths and limitations, and link it to practical teaching. Specification content covered in this topic 6.1 Motor programmes 6.2 Theories related to the learning of motor skills 6.3 Schmidt’s schema theory Key Terms

Motor programme A set of subroutines, stored in memory, that is completed in the correct order to produce a movement. Operant conditioning Learning through the consequences of behaviour: behaviour that is reinforced is repeated, and behaviour that is punished is less likely to be repeated. Reinforcement Any consequence that strengthens the stimulus–response bond. Positive reinforcement adds a reward; negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant. Gestalt theory A cognitive theory that learning involves perceiving the whole pattern, and that understanding comes through insight. Observational learning Learning by watching a model and copying their behaviour.

Schema A generalised rule, built from experience, that is used to produce a movement and to evaluate its outcome. Presentations 6.1 Motor Programmes and Subroutines 6.2a Operant Conditioning and Reinforcement 6.2b Cognitive and Observational Learning Theories 6.3 Schmidt's Schema Theory Deep Dive 6.1 Motor programmes A motor programme is a generalised series of movements, made up of subroutines , that is completed in the correct order. It is a set of nerve impulses sent to the muscles to produce the movement. For example, a golf swing has a motor programme with subroutines such as the backswing, the downswing and the follow-through.

Motor programmes are created through practice, stored in memory, and initiated when the performer decides to act. Once initiated, the programme runs without the need for conscious control of each part, which is why skilled performers do not have to think about each step. 6.2 Theories related to the learning of motor skills

Operant conditioning (behaviourist) theory explains learning through the stimulus–response bond. A learner tries responses by trial and error . The response that is followed by a reward is strengthened, and those followed by punishment are weakened. A teacher can shape behaviour by reinforcing successive approximations to the target skill, and can modify the environment to make the correct response more likely.

The stimulus–response bond is strengthened by positive reinforcement (rewarding a correct response), and by negative reinforcement (removing something unpleasant after a correct response). It is weakened by punishment . Evaluation: the theory is objective and easy to apply, and it explains how habits form. However, it gives little attention to the learner’s thinking, it does not explain how new complex skills are understood at once, and punishment has ethical limits in teaching.

Cognitive (Gestalt) theory proposes that learners perceive the whole task and its structure, rather than building a skill from separate responses. Learning often happens through insight : a sudden understanding of how the parts fit together. This supports whole practice , so that the learner sees the complete skill. Evaluation: the theory explains insight and the value of seeing the whole skill, but insight is hard to observe and test, and it gives less practical guidance on how to structure practice.

Bandura’s observational learning theory proposes that learners acquire behaviour by watching a model. Four processes are needed: attention to the model’s behaviour; retention of what was observed (often through rehearsal or imagery); motor reproduction , which is the physical ability to copy the action; and motivation to perform the behaviour, which is strongly affected by whether the model is admired and whether the behaviour is rewarded. Evaluation: the theory explains why coaches and senior players influence younger performers, and it has strong relevance to teaching. However, observation alone cannot teach a skill that the learner cannot physically reproduce, and it does not account for the learner’s own practice.

6.3 Schmidt’s schema theory Schmidt’s schema theory proposes that, through practice, performers build a schema : a generalised rule that modifies a motor programme so that it can be used in different situations. Two types of schema are described: Recall schema : the rule used to produce a movement, based on the conditions present and the response needed. Recognition schema : the rule used to judge the outcome of a movement, by comparing the sensory information from it with what was expected.

Schema rules are built from four pieces of knowledge: initial conditions (the situation before the movement), response specifications (the movement required), sensory consequences (what the performer feels during the movement), and response outcomes (the result). Practice with varied conditions builds stronger schemas, so a performer can throw a ball to different distances and still produce the correct action. Teachers can use schema theory by varying practice and asking learners to judge outcomes. Exam Tips Exam tip Name each theory and state its key idea in one sentence before you give an example. Examiners look for the core concept first.

Exam tip For evaluation, give one strength and one limitation, and link each to the learning situation in the question. Exam tip Use the correct terms for the stimulus–response bond and for each type of reinforcement. "Reward" alone is not precise enough for negative reinforcement. Exam tip For Bandura, list the four processes in order and give a sporting example of one of them. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Describe what is meant by a motor programme. 2 marks Answer Model answer A generalised series of movements made up of subroutines. Completed in the correct order, as a set of nerve impulses to the muscles.

2 A coach praises a player each time they hit the target. Explain this using operant conditioning. 3 marks Answer Model answer Praise is positive reinforcement, which strengthens the stimulus–response bond. The correct response is therefore more likely to be repeated. Trial and error and shaping are used as the player moves towards the target skill. 3 Explain how Bandura’s observational learning theory explains a young footballer copying the celebrations of a professional. 3 marks Answer Model answer Attention: the footballer watches the professional closely. Retention: they remember the behaviour, often by rehearsing it mentally.

Motivation: the behaviour is admired and rewarded, so the footballer wants to copy it. 4 Explain the difference between a recall schema and a recognition schema. 2 marks Answer Model answer A recall schema is the rule used to produce a movement, given the conditions and the response required. A recognition schema is the rule used to judge the outcome by comparing sensory information with what was expected. Information Processing | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 2 › Topic 7 Topic 7 Theme 2 · Skill, learning and practice AS Level 8386 Information Processing How a performer receives, decides upon and responds to information, how feedback and memory work, and what determines response time. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Information processing describes the performer as a system that takes in information, decides what to do with it, produces a response and uses feedback to improve. Each stage can be explained, and each stage can break down. Many questions in this topic ask you to explain the stage at which a performer’s response fails, and what would improve it. Response time is central to skilled performance. It is the total time from the presentation of a stimulus to the completion of a movement, and it is shaped by reaction time, movement time and the number of choices available. Specification content covered in this topic 7.1 Theory of information processing 7.2 Feedback 7.3 Memory 7.4 Response time

Key Terms Perception Interpreting sensory information so that it has meaning. Intrinsic feedback Information the performer receives from their own senses during a movement. Extrinsic feedback Information from outside the performer, such as a coach’s comment or a video. Selective attention The filtering of sensory information so that only the most relevant information enters short-term memory. Reaction time The time from the presentation of a stimulus to the start of the movement. Movement time The time from the start of the movement to its completion. Hick’s law The principle that reaction time increases as the number of stimulus–response choices increases. Presentations

7.1 Information Processing Model 7.2 Feedback for Skill Development 7.3 Memory and Selective Attention 7.4 Response Time, Reaction Time and Deception Deep Dive 7.1 Theory of information processing The model moves through the following stages. Display is the environment that provides information. Sensory information is detected by the sense organs . Perception gives that information meaning. Decision making selects the response. The effector mechanism (the muscles) produces the response . Feedback returns information about the response to the start of the process, so the performer can adjust the next response.

Explain the model as a loop rather than a line: feedback feeds back into perception and decision making, which is why practice improves performance. 7.2 Feedback Feedback is important because it allows error correction , it supports motivation and it helps the learner understand the skill. Feedback has several types, and each is described in pairs: Intrinsic feedback comes from the performer’s own senses; extrinsic feedback comes from outside, such as a coach or video. Terminal feedback is given after the movement; concurrent feedback is given during it. Positive feedback reinforces what is correct; negative feedback identifies an error to correct.

Knowledge of performance describes how the movement was made; knowledge of results describes the outcome . When you evaluate feedback, consider the stage of learning. Beginners rely on extrinsic feedback and benefit from knowledge of performance, while experienced performers use intrinsic feedback to refine their skill. 7.3 Memory

Memory has three stores. The short-term sensory store holds a large amount of information for a very brief time, and selective attention filters it so that only the relevant information passes on. Short-term memory holds a small amount of information for a limited time, unless it is rehearsed. Long-term memory has a large capacity and holds information for a long time.

Strategies to improve storage in long-term memory include rehearsal (repeated practice), chunking (grouping information into meaningful units, such as a sequence of moves as one pattern), meaningful links (connecting new information with what is already known), and imagery (visualising the skill). Each strategy makes information easier to retrieve when it is needed. 7.4 Response time Response time is the total time from the presentation of a stimulus to the completion of the movement. It equals reaction time plus movement time . Use the equation: response time = reaction time + movement time.

Reaction time is affected by the type of response. Simple reaction time is a single stimulus with a single response, such as a sprint start. Choice reaction time involves more than one stimulus and response, and is longer. Hick’s law states that reaction time increases as the number of choices increases. The psychological refractory period is the delay that occurs when a second stimulus arrives before the first response is completed. The single-channel hypothesis proposes that the brain can process only one stimulus at a time, which causes the refractory period.

A short response time is valuable in skilled performance because it gives the performer more time to act. Performers can deceive opponents with feints and disguised movements, which delay the opponent’s decision and make the response slower. Strategies to improve response time include reducing the number of choices through practice, using anticipation and visual cues, and practising under realistic pressure. Exam Tips Exam tip Name the stage of information processing where a problem occurs. Describe a failure of perception differently from a failure of decision making. Exam tip For feedback questions, name the type and give one reason it suits the performer’s stage of learning.

Exam tip Use response time = reaction time + movement time in calculations, and state the unit (seconds). Exam tip For Hick’s law, say that reaction time increases with the number of choices, and link this to a practical example such as a goalkeeper facing several shooting options. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State the stages of the information processing model in the order they occur. 3 marks Answer Model answer Display, then sensory information detected by the sense organs. Perception, then decision making. Effector mechanism producing the response, with feedback returning to the start.

2 Explain the difference between knowledge of performance and knowledge of results, and give an example of each. 3 marks Answer Model answer Knowledge of performance describes how the movement was made, for example the position of the elbow. Knowledge of results describes the outcome, for example whether the shot went in. Example: a coach’s comment on technique versus the scoreline. 3 A goalkeeper has four possible shooting options to respond to. Explain how Hick’s law applies. 2 marks Answer Model answer Reaction time increases as the number of stimulus–response choices increases. With four options, the goalkeeper’s decision takes longer than with one, so the response is slower.

4 Explain why a player might use a feint before passing the ball. 3 marks Answer Model answer The feint is a deception that disguises the intended action. It delays the opponent’s decision making, so the opponent’s response is slower. The attacking player therefore has more time to make the pass. Practice and Learning | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 2 › Topic 8 Topic 8 Theme 2 · Skill, learning and practice AS Level 8386 Practice and Learning Types of practice, types of guidance, the stages of learning, transfer of learning and motivation. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

How a skill is practised has a major effect on how well it is learned. A coach must choose the type of practice, the type of guidance and the feedback that suit the learner’s stage of learning, and must also consider how the skill will transfer to other situations. This topic asks you to explain each approach and to evaluate its advantages and disadvantages. Motivation links the whole topic, because learners who are motivated practise more and learn more effectively. Specification content covered in this topic 8.1 Types of practice 8.2 Types of guidance 8.3 Stages of learning 8.4 Transfer of learning 8.5 Motivation Key Terms Whole practice The skill is practised as a complete action.

Massed practice Repeated practice with little or no rest between attempts. Distributed practice Practice spread out, with rest periods between attempts or sessions. Positive transfer Learning one skill helps the learning of another. Negative transfer Learning one skill hinders the learning of another. Intrinsic motivation Motivation that comes from within the performer, such as enjoyment. Extrinsic motivation Motivation from outside the performer, through tangible rewards (such as medals) or intangible rewards (such as praise). Presentations 8.1 Types of Practice 8.2 Types of Guidance 8.3 Stages of Learning 8.4 Transfer of Learning 8.5 Motivation in Learning Deep Dive 8.1 Types of practice

Whole practice performs the skill as one action. It suits skills that are continuous or have high organisation, because the parts cannot easily be separated. It can be overwhelming for complex skills, because the learner must attend to everything at once. Part practice breaks the skill into parts and practises each separately. It suits skills that are serial or have low organisation. Parts may be practised out of context, so the skill may not come together at the end. Whole–part–whole practice combines both: the whole skill is performed, then the difficult part is practised, then the whole skill is performed again. It gives the learner a sense of the whole, and targets the difficult part.

Progressive part practice starts with one part and adds the next part in sequence, until the whole skill is built up. It suits serial skills with high organisation. Massed practice has short rest periods; distributed practice has longer rests between attempts or sessions. Massed practice gives more repetitions in less time, but can cause fatigue and lower retention. Distributed practice usually gives better retention and long-term learning. Fixed practice uses the same conditions each time, which helps the learner build a consistent movement pattern. Varied practice changes the conditions, which helps the learner adapt and supports transfer to new situations.

Evaluate each type by giving one advantage and one disadvantage, and by stating the type of skill and the stage of learning for which it suits best. 8.2 Types of guidance Visual guidance uses demonstrations, video or images to show the skill. It is effective for beginners, but a learner may copy the surface of the movement without understanding its key features. Verbal guidance uses instructions, cues and feedback given in words. It helps the learner understand the purpose of the movement, but it can overload a learner in the early stages of learning.

Manual guidance involves the teacher physically moving or supporting the learner. It gives the learner a feel for the correct movement, but it can make the learner dependent on support and may not transfer when the support is removed. Mechanical guidance uses equipment to support or direct the movement, such as a harness or a floating board. It reduces risk and allows the learner to attempt the movement, but the learner may depend on the equipment. Evaluate guidance by stating the advantage for the learner and the risk of over-reliance. 8.3 Stages of learning

Learners move through three stages, which Fitts and Posner described. In the cognitive stage, the learner understands what the skill involves, makes many errors and relies on verbal and visual guidance and on whole or part practice. In the associative stage, errors reduce and the learner refines the movement, using knowledge of performance to correct it. In the autonomous stage, the skill becomes automatic, so attention can be given to other things such as tactics, and the performer uses intrinsic feedback.

When you evaluate the use of feedback, practice or guidance at each stage, link the choice to the learner’s needs. For example, extrinsic knowledge of results helps a cognitive learner understand the outcome, while varied practice helps an autonomous performer adapt to changing situations. 8.4 Transfer of learning

Transfer of learning is the effect of learning one skill on the learning of another. It can be positive (helpful), negative (harmful) or zero (no effect). Proactive transfer is when an earlier skill affects later learning; retroactive transfer is when later learning affects an earlier skill. Bilateral transfer is the transfer of learning from one limb or side of the body to the other. To optimise positive transfer , a coach can emphasise the common elements between skills, teach the underlying principles, and use varied practice. To limit negative transfer , a coach can highlight the differences between the skills, practise the two skills separately at first, and use gradual progression.

8.5 Motivation Intrinsic motivation comes from within the performer, from enjoyment, interest or a sense of achievement. It usually supports long-term participation and effort. Extrinsic motivation comes from outside, through tangible rewards (medals, money, equipment) or intangible rewards (praise, recognition, status). When you evaluate the types of motivation, consider the performer and the context. Extrinsic rewards can encourage a beginner to try a skill, but intrinsic motivation is usually more important for sustained practice. A reward that is controlling, such as a payment for winning, may reduce the performer’s enjoyment of the activity. Exam Tips

Exam tip When you evaluate a type of practice, give both an advantage and a disadvantage, and name the type of skill it suits. Exam tip For guidance, name the type and link it to the stage of learning: visual and verbal guidance dominate early learning, and manual guidance is usually reduced later. Exam tip For transfer, use the exact terms (positive, negative, zero, proactive, retroactive, bilateral) and give an example for each one you use. Exam tip For motivation, keep tangible and intangible rewards separate, and say which type a coach is using in your example. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it.

1 Explain the difference between massed and distributed practice. 2 marks Answer Model answer Massed practice has short rest periods between repetitions, while distributed practice has longer rest periods. Massed practice gives more repetitions in less time, but distributed practice usually gives better retention. 2 Evaluate the use of whole–part–whole practice for a learner in the associative stage. 4 marks Answer Model answer The whole skill is performed, giving the learner a sense of the whole action. The difficult part is then practised, which targets the element that is causing errors. The whole skill is performed again, so the part is placed back in context.

The method suits the associative stage, although it takes more time than whole practice alone. 3 Explain how a coach could optimise positive transfer between the forehand in tennis and the forehand in squash. 3 marks Answer Model answer Emphasise the common elements, such as the grip, the shoulder rotation and the timing of the swing. Teach the underlying principles of the stroke, which apply to both sports. Use varied practice so the learner can adapt the stroke to different situations. 4 Explain the difference between tangible and intangible rewards, and give one example of each. 2 marks Answer Model answer Tangible rewards are physical, such as medals or prize money.

Intangible rewards are non-physical, such as praise or recognition.
