Sociocultural Issues | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Theme 3 › Topic 9 Topic 9 Theme 3 · Sociocultural issues and technology AS Level 8386 Sociocultural Issues What sport and physical education are, the values and undesirable outcomes of sport, participation, and the pathways to excellence. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Sociocultural issues ask how sport and physical activity fit into society. You need to distinguish sport from physical education , explain the values and undesirable outcomes of sport, and explain why people do or do not take part in physical activity. The final part of the topic covers how countries and clubs try to produce elite performers. These are discussion topics. Examiners expect structured argument, use of examples and a clear judgement, especially when you evaluate. Specification content covered in this topic 9.1 The conceptual basis of sport and physical education 9.2 Sport 9.3 Physical education 9.4 Regular participation 9.5 Achieving excellence Key Terms

Sport A competitive, highly structured physical activity with complex rules, officials and predetermined boundaries. Physical education Planned, progressive learning of movement, delivered to all pupils as part of the school curriculum. Sociocultural influences Social, cultural and economic factors that shape who takes part in sport and how. Participation ethic The belief that taking part in sport is valuable in itself, whatever the result. Elite performer A performer at the top of the performance pyramid, of national, international or Olympic standard. Talent identification The process of identifying young performers with the potential to reach elite level. Presentations

9.1 Sport and Physical Education: Conceptual Basis 9.2 Sport: Characteristics, Values and Undesirable Outcomes 9.3 Physical Education in Schools 9.4 Regular Participation 9.5 Achieving Excellence Deep Dive 9.1 The conceptual basis of sport and physical education Sport and physical education share movement as their basis, but they differ in purpose. Sport is competitive, governed by complex rules and officials, and organised around tactics and strategies. Physical education is planned, progressive learning, delivered to all pupils, that aims to help them learn to move and become more physically competent, using a broad range of activities that are often teacher-led.

Discuss the interrelationship : physical education can introduce pupils to the skills and rules of sport, and sport can become a route into lifelong physical activity. Sport in its competitive form, however, is not the purpose of physical education, and the two are judged by different standards. 9.2 Sport The characteristics of sport are complex rules, a competitive nature, a highly structured form, predetermined boundaries, numbers, time constraints, equipment and roles, officials, and tactics and strategies.

Sport is valued for sportsmanship and fair play , a participation ethic , physical, mental and social health and well-being , self-realisation , and as a form of social control . Each value can be explained with an example, and each can be questioned: sport can also be used to channel or hide social problems. Sport can also have undesirable outcomes . For the individual , these include injury, pressure to win, and burnout. For the sport , they include corruption, violence and commercial distortion of its values. Explain each outcome and link it to a specific cause. 9.3 Physical education

Physical education is planned and progressive , so skills build over time. It is part of the school curriculum and is delivered to all pupils , regardless of ability. Its aim is learning to move and becoming more physically competent , across a broad range of activities . It is usually teacher-led . 9.4 Regular participation Participation is affected by several factors: Economic status : cost of equipment, membership and travel can exclude people with lower incomes. Sociocultural influences : cultural norms and attitudes shape which activities are seen as appropriate for different groups. Family and peers : parents and friends can encourage, model or discourage participation.

Facilities : the availability and quality of facilities determine what people can do locally. Age : participation often changes across the life course. Gender : opportunities and expectations can differ between men and women. Disability : access, equipment and adapted provision affect participation. Evaluate the benefits of regular participation for the individual (physical, mental and social health) and for society (for example reduced pressure on health services, stronger social networks and community cohesion). Weigh each benefit against the conditions that make it possible for different groups. 9.5 Achieving excellence

An elite performer is at the top of the performance pyramid, has reached excellence, is of national, international or Olympic standard, is often professional, and is achieved by few people. An elitist policy for excellence has benefits, such as medal success, role models and inspiration for others, but also limitations, such as high cost, a focus on a few performers at the expense of grassroots participation, and pressure on young athletes. Evaluate both before reaching a judgement.

The provision needed for excellence includes sufficient funding, high-quality facilities, high-quality coaches, high-level competition, and science support such as medicine, biomechanics, rehabilitation, nutrition and psychology. Pathways to excellence include specialist schools, clubs, academies, selection procedures and talent identification, college or university programmes, scholarships, (national) governing bodies, and regional and national squads. Explain how each pathway moves a performer from early participation towards elite level. Exam Tips

Exam tip When asked to discuss sport and physical education, state the similarities and the differences, then the interrelationship. A one-sided answer will not reach the top band. Exam tip For regular participation, name the factor, then explain how it affects a specific group in a specific way. Exam tip For elitist policy, give a benefit and a limitation, and reach a judgement that weighs them. Exam tip Use the pathway list in 9.5.4 to organise your answer on excellence: move from early participation to elite level in order. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it.

1 Describe two characteristics of physical education that distinguish it from sport. 2 marks Answer Model answer Physical education is planned, progressive learning delivered to all pupils, whereas sport is competitive. Physical education is teacher-led and aims to build physical competence, while sport is organised around predetermined rules and officials. 2 Explain how economic status can affect participation in physical activity. 3 marks Answer Model answer Costs of equipment, membership and travel can be a barrier for people on lower incomes. This reduces the range of activities that people can take part in. As a result, participation may be lower in the groups that can least afford it.

3 Evaluate the benefits and limitations of an elitist policy for excellence in sport. 6 marks Answer Model answer Benefit: successful elite athletes provide role models and can inspire participation. Benefit: investment can increase medal success and raise the profile of the sport. Limitation: the cost is high and may reduce money for grassroots participation. Limitation: people who are not selected may be excluded, which can reduce participation and inclusion. Limitation: a focus on a few performers may put pressure on young athletes. Judgement: the benefits depend on whether the policy also supports grassroots participation.

4 Explain the role of talent identification in the pathway to excellence. 3 marks Answer Model answer Talent identification selects young performers who have the potential to reach elite level. These performers are then placed on pathways such as academies, squads or scholarships. This allows the provision for excellence to be targeted at those most likely to succeed. Assessment requirements Assessed in the selection and application of skills and tactical awareness in competitive conditioned practices and formal competitive games. The range of skills may differ according to position.

Log of competitive participation Log every competitive match, including 11-a-side matches during lessons. Do not include training sessions in the log. The log must be completed for every candidate in the centre, and it supports the mark for each strand. Skills Outfield players Ball control: use of both feet, chest, thigh. Passing: short, long and lofted, including use of the non-dominant foot where appropriate. Shooting: short and long range, use of swerve and volley, including use of the non-dominant foot where appropriate. Dribbling: close control, to beat an opponent, to create space, use of both feet. Tackling: selection and timing of appropriate tackles, jockeying.

Marking: player with the ball and off the ball denying space, interceptions. Goalkeeper Ball control: use of both feet, chest, thigh. Handling: catching, parrying, punching. Passing: short, long and lofted, including the non-dominant foot. Kicking from the hand, throwing. Shot stopping: from different heights and distances. Diving and standing saves. Tactical awareness Selection of appropriate skills during competitive situations. Awareness of team tactics and strategies in attacking and defensive situations, including strengths and weaknesses of team formations. Positioning and organisation of the team at set pieces.

Awareness of the strengths and weaknesses of self and other performers, and use of strategies to enhance the chance of success. Awareness and application of the laws of the sport. Filming and evidence Evidence is likely to be made of multiple phases of involvement. Show how each phase started, how the candidate received the ball, how the candidate used it, and the result of that involvement.

Whatever the activity, the moderator must be able to identify the candidate. Use coloured bibs with contrasting numbers on the front and back, or the method the centre uses on its Centre Order of Merit form. Evidence may be edited to focus on a candidate and to remove periods of irrelevance, but it must not be edited to make the candidate look more consistent or more able than they normally are. The speed settings of filmed evidence must not be adjusted. Marking focus Each activity is marked using the generic assessment criteria, with the specific guidance above. The four strands are marked as follows:

Range of skills (5): how many of the skills above are performed in authentic competitive situations. Quality of skills (10): control, fluency and accuracy in the skills performed. Tactical awareness (10): selecting the most appropriate skills, tactics and strategies, and understanding the performance of others. Effective performance (10): maintaining the range and quality of skills under pressure, and the influence the candidate has on the outcome. This is supported by the log of competitive participation. Self-check Use this list before a filming session or before submitting evidence. Ball control: use of both feet, chest, thigh.

Passing: short, long and lofted, including use of the non-dominant foot where appropriate. Ball control: use of both feet, chest, thigh. Handling: catching, parrying, punching. Coursework | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Coursework Component 2 · 70 marks · 50% of AS Level Coursework Two physical activities, assessed in competitive conditions, with 35 marks for each. Internally assessed by your teacher and externally moderated by Cambridge. How the component works Candidates are assessed in two physical activities from the list in the syllabus, with 35 marks for each. Performance is assessed in competitive conditioned practices and in formal competitive games, competitions or situations. Centres must use the generic assessment criteria and the specific guidance for each activity.

Filming candidates and keeping the log of competitive participation throughout the course lets teachers select the best performances and keeps records if injury or illness occurs. The 16 physical activities Candidates must have knowledge of the full range of activities below. Choose any two. Each activity has its own page with its skills, tactical awareness, filming notes and marking focus. Association football Badminton Basketball Competitive swimming Cricket Cross-country running Field hockey Goalball Netball Olympic weightlifting Rugby union Squash Table tennis Tennis Track and field athletics Volleyball Assessment criteria

Each activity is marked out of 35 across four strands: range of skills (5) , quality of skills (10) , tactical awareness (10) and effective performance (10) . Each strand is assessed at a level, and the mark is chosen within that level’s range. Level Range of skills (5) Quality of skills (10) Tactical awareness (10) Effective performance (10) Exceptional 5 9–10 9–10 9–10 Very good 4 7–8 7–8 7–8 Good 3 5–6 5–6 5–6 Adequate 2 3–4 3–4 3–4 Limited 1 1–2 1–2 1–2 No evidence worthy of credit 0 0 0 0

The level descriptors in the syllabus describe what each level looks like, for example "demonstrates a full range of skills in authentic competitive performance situations" at the highest level. Consult the syllabus assessment criteria for the full wording. Using the levels If work convincingly meets the level, award the highest mark in that range. If it adequately meets the level, award a middle mark. If it just meets the level, award the lowest mark. Log of competitive participation

A log must be completed and submitted for every candidate entered by the centre, not only the sample. It records the level and frequency of competition in the two activities. Training sessions are not included. The mark is decided by the criteria and the activity guidance, not by how often a candidate competes. Competition can be within the centre, at an outside club, or at representative level. Examples include a lesson match, a club match, a club or squad trial, a schools final or a qualifying competition. Teachers may also submit supporting evidence, such as results, times or rankings. Filming

The moderator must be able to identify the candidate. Use coloured bibs with contrasting numbers, or the identifier the centre uses on its Centre Order of Merit form. Evidence may be edited to focus on the candidate and remove irrelevant periods, but must not be edited to make the candidate look more consistent or more able. Do not adjust the speed settings of filmed evidence. Continuous, unedited evidence is expected for badminton, table tennis and competitive swimming. For longer team sports and cross-country, include several phases of involvement showing how the candidate was involved and the result. Moderation and administration

Internal moderation. If more than one teacher marks coursework, arrange moderation or standardisation so that all candidates are assessed to a common standard. If only one teacher marks, no internal moderation is needed. External moderation. Cambridge externally moderates all internally assessed components. The centre submits the marks of all candidates, and the marked work of a sample. The samples database explains how the sample is chosen and how to submit. Samples database. The database at cambridgeinternational.org/samples gives the submission dates and methods, the forms to complete, and the instructions for Coursework 8386/02. Check it for each series. Authenticity and AI

Centres must make sure all assessed work is the candidate’s own. Candidates must cite and reference any material they use. Cambridge has a policy on generative AI in coursework: inappropriate use is treated as plagiarism, and the policy explains how to detect it and what action to take. Read it at cambridgeinternational.org/generative-ai-in-coursework. Safety and access

These activities are physically demanding. Centres must make sure candidates can cope with them, seek medical advice where there is doubt, and follow safe practice and the guidance of national governing bodies. Candidates with disabilities must not be prevented from taking part. Where an activity needs adaptation, contact Cambridge before teaching the course, so that the adaptation can be agreed. Retakes are allowed, and marks achieved in Component 2 can be carried forward to future series, subject to the rules in the Cambridge Handbook. Command Words | AS Level Sport & PE 8386 | Simply Sport Science Home › AS Level PE › Command Words AS Level 8386 · 20 command words Command Words Command words tell you what kind of answer the examiner wants. The meanings below are taken from the syllabus. The "how to answer" guidance is practical advice on building the answer. Assess Make an informed judgement. How to answer: Weigh the evidence and reach a judgement on the quality or value of the point being assessed. Give a clear judgement and the evidence for it. Calculate Work out from given facts, figures or information.

How to answer: Write the equation, substitute the values with units, show each step, and give the answer with its unit. Comment Give an informed opinion. How to answer: State a view, then support it with a reason from the science or the data. Keep the opinion tied to the statement given. Compare Identify and/or comment on similarities and/or differences. How to answer: Refer to both items in every point. Use "both" for similarities and "whereas" or "in contrast" for differences. Contrast Identify and comment on differences. How to answer: Concentrate only on differences, and refer to both items in each point. Define Give precise meaning.

How to answer: Give the exact meaning in one precise sentence. Do not add examples unless asked. Determine Establish an answer using the information available. How to answer: Use the information given to reach a specific answer. Show the reasoning that leads to it. Describe State the points of a topic, or give its characteristics and main features. How to answer: Give the main features in a logical order. Quantify where data is given. Do not explain why unless the question asks. Discuss Write about issue(s) or topic(s) in depth in a structured way. How to answer: Give several points on both sides, develop each with evidence, and link them to the question. A conclusion helps. Evaluate

Judge or calculate the quality, importance, amount or value of something. How to answer: Weigh the strengths against the limitations, and end with a judgement on which matters more and why. Explain Set out purposes or reasons, make the relationships between things clear, say why and/or how, and support with relevant evidence. How to answer: Build a chain of reasoning: state the fact, explain the link, and give the effect. Use evidence from the syllabus or the sport. Give Produce an answer from a given source or recall/memory. How to answer: Provide the answer directly from the information given or from memory. Keep it short and accurate. Identify Name, select or recognise.

How to answer: Name or select the correct answer. A short answer is enough. Justify Support a case with evidence or argument. How to answer: State the decision, then give two or three reasons supported by evidence. Outline Set out the main points. How to answer: List the main points briefly, in order. Include the key terms, but do not develop each one in detail. Predict Suggest what may happen based on available information. How to answer: State the likely outcome, and base it on the information given with a reason. Show (that) Provide structured evidence that leads to a given result.

How to answer: Set out the steps in order so that they lead to the result stated in the question. The final line should match the result given. Sketch Make a simple freehand drawing showing the key features, taking care over proportions. How to answer: Draw neatly and to scale in proportion, label the key features, and include units and axis labels for graphs. State Express in clear terms. How to answer: Give a short, clear answer. No explanation or working is needed. Suggest Apply knowledge and understanding to situations where there are a range of valid responses, in order to make proposals or put forward considerations.

How to answer: There may be more than one correct answer. Propose a sensible idea and link it to the knowledge in the syllabus. Note The use of a command word depends on the subject context. The same word can ask for different depths of answer in different questions, so always check the number of marks as well as the word. Students are eligible for grades a to e, and performance below grade e is reported as ungraded.

This hub is based on the 2024 to 2026 syllabus. Cambridge has also published syllabuses for 2027 to 2028 and 2029 to 2031. Check the syllabus for your exam year for any changes before you plan, and check the samples database for submission details in each series. What has changed Component 1 is now a 1 hour 45 minute combined question paper and answer booklet, and any question can sample any of the subject content. Component 2 candidates choose any two activities from the revised list, and no longer choose from activity profiles. The written action plan is no longer required, and a log of competitive participation is needed for every candidate. Performance is assessed in competitive conditioned practices and in formal competitive games, competitions or situations. Each activity is assessed against four strands, using the generic criteria and the guidance for that activity. A log is required for every candidate. It shows the level and frequency of competition in each of the two activities. Training sessions are not included. Filming and evidence The moderator must be able to identify the candidate. A.1.1 Inter-system Communication | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.1.1 A.1.1 Theme A · Communication SL & HL Inter-system Communication How the nervous and endocrine systems send messages around the body, and how they work together to prepare you for, and control you during, exercise. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Your body has two communication systems. The nervous system sends fast electrical signals along nerves. The endocrine system releases hormones into the blood, which act more slowly but last longer. In sport, the two systems work together: the nervous system gives instant control, while hormones keep the body's response going for as long as the exercise lasts. By the end of this topic you should be able to Outline the organisation of the nervous system. Describe how a nerve impulse travels and crosses to a muscle. Outline how the endocrine system communicates using hormones. Compare nervous and endocrine communication. Explain how both systems work together before and during exercise.

Key Terms Neuron A nerve cell that carries electrical impulses. Action potential The electrical impulse that travels along a neuron. Neurotransmitter A chemical released at a synapse to pass a signal on. Neuromuscular junction The synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fibre. Hormone A chemical messenger released by a gland into the blood. Target cell A cell with receptors for a specific hormone. Presentations A.1.1.1 The Nervous System A.1.1.2 The Endocrine System Deep Dive How the nervous system is organised

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. It processes information and makes decisions. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is every nerve outside the CNS. It carries information in from the senses (sensory neurons) and out to muscles and glands (motor neurons). The motor side splits into the somatic system, which controls voluntary skeletal muscle, and the autonomic system, which controls involuntary actions like heart rate. The autonomic system has two branches. The sympathetic branch prepares the body for action, and the parasympathetic branch calms it back down.

How the nervous system is organised. The sympathetic branch prepares the body for exercise; the parasympathetic branch returns it to rest. How a nerve impulse reaches a muscle A motor neuron carries an action potential , a wave of electrical charge, from the spinal cord along its axon. A fatty myelin sheath insulates the axon. The impulse jumps between the small gaps in the sheath, called the nodes of Ranvier , so it travels much faster than it would along an uninsulated axon.

When the impulse reaches the end of the neuron, it can't jump the tiny gap to the muscle. Instead, the neuron releases the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) . ACh crosses the gap at the neuromuscular junction , binds to receptors on the muscle fibre, and triggers a new action potential in the muscle that causes it to contract. The enzyme acetylcholinesterase then breaks ACh down, so the muscle fibre can relax until the next impulse arrives. A: a motor neuron carrying an impulse to a muscle fibre. B: how acetylcholine carries the signal across the neuromuscular junction. How the endocrine system communicates

Endocrine glands release hormones straight into the blood. The blood carries them everywhere, but they only affect target cells that have the right receptors. Key glands in sport include: Adrenal medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline raise heart rate and release glucose for energy. Pancreas: insulin lowers blood glucose, and glucagon raises it. Adrenal cortex: cortisol helps the body use fat and protein for fuel during long exercise. Pituitary gland: growth hormone supports tissue growth and repair. Nervous vs endocrine communication Nervous system Endocrine system Signal Electrical impulses plus neurotransmitters Hormones (chemicals) Route Along nerves In the bloodstream

Speed Very fast (milliseconds) Slower (seconds to minutes) Duration Short-lived Longer-lasting Target Specific muscle or gland Any cell with the right receptor Working together: a 400 m race Before the start: anticipation activates the sympathetic nervous system, so heart rate rises before you move (the anticipatory rise). Sympathetic nerves also stimulate the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline. During the race: sympathetic nerves raise heart rate and the force of each beat instantly. Adrenaline reinforces this and keeps it going, and it also helps release glucose from glycogen stores to fuel the working muscles.

After the race: the parasympathetic nervous system takes over and slows heart rate back towards resting levels, while hormone levels gradually fall. Exam Tips Name the specific hormone and gland "Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla" scores. "A hormone is released" doesn't. Make comparisons point by point For "compare" or "distinguish" questions, pair each point with its opposite: "Nervous signals are fast, whereas hormonal signals are slower." Always add a sporting example "Explain" questions reward application. Link your answer to a real event such as a sprint start or a penalty kick.

Read the command term "Outline" needs brief points. "Explain" needs a reason or mechanism for each point. Check the IB command terms . Common mistake Don't say the impulse "jumps to the muscle". It's carried across the neuromuscular junction by acetylcholine, a chemical. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Outline two differences between nervous and endocrine communication. 2 marks Answer Model answer — any two of Nervous signals travel along nerves, whereas hormones travel in the blood. Nervous communication is faster than endocrine communication. Nervous effects are short-lived, whereas hormonal effects last longer.

Nervous signals reach a specific target, whereas hormones can affect any cell with the right receptor. 2 Distinguish between the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. 2 marks Answer Model answer The sympathetic system prepares the body for action, for example by increasing heart rate. The parasympathetic system returns the body to rest, for example by decreasing heart rate. 3 Describe the role of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. 3 marks Answer Model answer The action potential reaches the end of the motor neuron and acetylcholine is released. Acetylcholine crosses the gap and binds to receptors on the muscle fibre.

This triggers an action potential in the muscle fibre, causing it to contract. 4 Outline how an action potential travels along a myelinated motor neuron. 3 marks Answer Model answer The impulse is a wave of electrical charge (depolarisation) along the axon. The myelin sheath insulates the axon. The impulse jumps between gaps in the myelin sheath, so it travels faster. 5 Explain how the nervous and endocrine systems work together to increase heart rate before and during a 400 m race. 4 marks Answer Model answer Before the race, anticipation activates the sympathetic nervous system, raising heart rate (the anticipatory rise).

Sympathetic nerves stimulate the adrenal medulla to release adrenaline. During the race, sympathetic nerves rapidly increase heart rate and the force of contraction. Adrenaline in the blood reinforces and sustains the raised heart rate for the rest of the race. A.1.2 Maintaining Homeostasis | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.1.2 A.1.2 Theme A · Communication SL & HL Maintaining Homeostasis How the body keeps its internal conditions stable, even when exercise pushes body temperature and blood glucose away from normal. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Homeostasis is the body keeping its internal environment stable, things like core temperature, blood glucose and water levels. Exercise constantly disturbs these conditions. Working muscles produce heat and use up glucose. The body detects these changes and corrects them, mainly through negative feedback , using the nervous and endocrine systems you met in A.1.1. By the end of this topic you should be able to Define homeostasis. Outline the parts of a negative feedback loop. Explain how core temperature is regulated during exercise. Describe the four ways the body loses heat. Explain how insulin and glucagon regulate blood glucose around exercise. Key Terms

Homeostasis Keeping the body's internal environment stable. Negative feedback A change triggers a response that reverses that change. Receptor Detects a change in a condition, e.g. temperature. Control centre Compares the change to normal and sends a response, e.g. the hypothalamus. Effector Carries out the response, e.g. sweat glands or blood vessels. Thermoregulation Keeping core body temperature stable, at about 37 °C. Presentation A.1.2 Maintaining Homeostasis Deep Dive Negative feedback: the body's correction system

Most homeostasis works through a negative feedback loop . When a condition moves away from its normal level, the body responds in a way that pushes it back. Every loop has the same parts: Stimulus: a change from normal, e.g. core temperature rises during a run. Receptors: detect the change, e.g. thermoreceptors in the skin and hypothalamus. Control centre: compares the change with the normal level and sends a response, e.g. the hypothalamus. Effectors: carry out the response, e.g. sweat glands and skin blood vessels. Response: the condition returns towards normal, and the loop switches off.

Negative feedback during exercise: a rise in core temperature is detected, processed and then reversed. Thermoregulation during exercise Muscles are inefficient. Around three quarters of the energy they use is released as heat , so core temperature rises quickly during exercise. The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat and triggers two main cooling responses: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels: more warm blood flows near the skin surface, where heat can escape. Sweating: sweat glands release sweat, and as it evaporates it carries heat away from the skin. The body loses heat in four ways: Mechanism How it works Sporting example

Evaporation Sweat turns to vapour, removing heat. This is the main method during exercise. A marathon runner sweating heavily Convection Moving air or water carries heat away from the skin. A cyclist cooled by the airflow Conduction Heat passes through direct contact with something cooler. A cold towel or ice vest at half-time Radiation Heat is given off as infrared energy to cooler surroundings. Heat radiating from the skin in the shade

Exercising in the heat is harder. When the air is hot, radiation and convection work less well, or even add heat to the body. In humid conditions, sweat can't evaporate easily, so it drips off without cooling you. More blood is sent to the skin, leaving less for working muscles, and heavy sweating causes dehydration (see A.2.1). Blood glucose regulation Blood glucose is controlled by two hormones from the pancreas , working in opposite directions: Insulin and glucagon act in opposite directions to keep blood glucose within its normal range. Insulin Glucagon Released when Blood glucose is too high, e.g. after a meal Blood glucose is too low, e.g. during long exercise

Main effect Cells take in glucose and the liver stores it as glycogen The liver breaks glycogen down and releases glucose into the blood Result Blood glucose falls Blood glucose rises During exercise, muscles take up glucose rapidly. Insulin release falls, while glucagon and adrenaline rise. Together they stimulate the liver to break down glycogen, which keeps blood glucose stable so the brain and muscles stay fuelled. If liver glycogen runs out in a long event, blood glucose can drop and performance suffers. This is one reason endurance athletes take on carbohydrate during races. Exam Tips

Use the loop language For feedback questions, name each part in order: stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response. Each step is usually worth a mark. Explain how, not just what "Sweating cools you" is incomplete. Say that evaporation of sweat removes heat from the skin. Link heat and hydration Questions on exercising in the heat often reward linking sweating to fluid loss, reduced blood volume and lower performance. Always add a sporting example Anchor your answer in a real situation, such as a marathon in hot, humid conditions. Common mistake Don't mix up glucagon and glycogen. Glucagon is the hormone, and glycogen is the stored carbohydrate it breaks down. Practice Questions

Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define homeostasis. 1 mark Answer Model answer The maintenance of a stable internal environment in the body, despite changes in external or internal conditions. 2 Identify four mechanisms of heat loss from the body. 2 marks Answer Model answer — all four for 2 marks Evaporation Convection Conduction Radiation 3 Outline the components of a negative feedback loop. 3 marks Answer Model answer Receptors detect a change from the normal level. A control centre compares the change with normal and sends a response. Effectors carry out the response, which returns the condition to normal.

4 Describe the role of glucagon during prolonged exercise. 3 marks Answer Model answer Blood glucose falls as working muscles take up glucose, so the pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to break down glycogen into glucose. Glucose is released into the blood, keeping blood glucose levels stable. 5 Explain how the body maintains core temperature during a marathon in hot conditions. 4 marks Answer Model answer Thermoreceptors detect the rise in core temperature and the hypothalamus triggers a response. Skin blood vessels vasodilate, so more blood flows near the surface and heat is lost. Sweat glands produce sweat, and its evaporation removes heat from the skin.

In hot conditions, radiation and convection are less effective, so the runner relies mainly on evaporation, which increases fluid loss. A.1.3 Transport | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.1.3 A.1.3 Theme A · Communication SL & HL Transport How the heart, blood vessels and lungs work together to deliver oxygen and nutrients, remove carbon dioxide and heat, and meet the rising demands of exercise. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Every cell in your body needs a delivery service. The cardiovascular system (heart, blood and blood vessels) pumps blood around the body. The respiratory system (airways and lungs) brings oxygen in and removes carbon dioxide. Together they transport oxygen, nutrients, hormones, waste products and heat. During exercise the demand rises, so heart rate, stroke volume, blood pressure, blood flow and breathing all change. The size of those changes depends on intensity, fitness, age, sex, body size and the type of activity. By the end of this topic you should be able to Describe the path of blood through the heart, lungs and body.

Define heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure, tidal volume, respiration rate and minute ventilation. Explain how each of these variables changes as exercise intensity rises. Explain how blood is redistributed during exercise, and how blood carries heat to the skin. Outline how gases are exchanged in the lungs and muscles and transported in the blood. Explain how age, sex, body size, fitness and type of activity affect these variables. Key Terms Cardiac output (Q) The volume of blood pumped by the heart each minute: Q = HR × SV. Stroke volume (SV) The volume of blood pumped out of the heart in one beat.

Blood pressure (BP) The force of blood against the walls of the arteries, written as systolic/diastolic. Blood redistribution Changing the share of cardiac output sent to each organ, by vasodilation and vasoconstriction. Tidal volume (TV) The volume of air breathed in or out in one breath. Minute ventilation (VE) The volume of air breathed per minute: VE = TV × respiration rate. Presentation A.1.3 Transport Deep Dive Why the body needs a transport system

Working muscles use oxygen and fuel quickly, and they produce carbon dioxide, waste products and heat. Diffusion alone is far too slow to move these over the distances involved, so the body uses the bloodstream as a delivery and collection service. The heart is the pump, the blood vessels are the pipes, and the lungs are where oxygen enters and carbon dioxide leaves. The heart and the two circuits

The heart is really two pumps side by side. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (the pulmonary circuit ). The left side pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body (the systemic circuit ). Valves between the chambers and at the exits make sure blood only flows one way. The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it must generate enough pressure to push blood around the whole body. The double circulation. Numbers show the order in which blood passes through the heart, lungs and body. This is a simplified flow diagram, not an anatomical drawing. Blood vessels Vessel Key features Role in transport

Arteries Thick, elastic, muscular walls; narrow lumen Carry blood away from the heart at high pressure Arterioles Smooth muscle in the walls Constrict or dilate to control how much blood reaches each tissue Capillaries Walls one cell thick; very large total surface area Exchange of gases, nutrients and waste with the tissues Veins Thinner walls; wide lumen; valves Return blood to the heart at low pressure; valves prevent backflow Heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output Heart rate (HR) is the number of beats per minute. Stroke volume (SV) is the volume of blood pumped out of the heart in one beat. Cardiac output (Q) is the volume pumped per minute: Q = HR × SV

At rest, a typical adult has a heart rate of about 70 beats per minute and a stroke volume of about 70 mL, giving a cardiac output of about 5 L per minute. As exercise intensity increases: Heart rate rises in a near-straight line with intensity. It starts to rise even before exercise begins (the anticipatory rise), driven by the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline (see A.1.1).

Stroke volume rises at first, then levels off at moderate to high intensity. It rises because more blood returns to the heart (the muscle pump and respiratory pump squeeze the veins, and veins constrict), so the ventricle fills more and contracts harder. Sympathetic stimulation also makes each contraction more forceful. It levels off because at very high heart rates there is less time to fill between beats. Cardiac output therefore rises sharply, first because both HR and SV increase, and later mainly because HR keeps increasing. Typical response of an untrained adult. Heart rate climbs steadily, stroke volume levels off, and cardiac output keeps rising because Q = HR × SV.

Variable Rest (untrained) Maximum (untrained) Maximum (elite endurance athlete) Heart rate (bpm) about 70 about 190 about 185 Stroke volume (mL) about 70 about 110 about 200 Cardiac output (L/min) about 5 about 21 about 37 Notice that the elite athlete's maximum heart rate is no higher than anyone else's. Their much larger maximum cardiac output comes from a much larger stroke volume, because endurance training enlarges the heart's chambers and increases blood volume. This is also why trained athletes have a lower resting heart rate: each beat moves more blood, so fewer beats are needed to give the same resting cardiac output. Blood pressure

Blood pressure is the force of blood against the artery walls. It is written as systolic pressure (when the ventricles contract) over diastolic pressure (when they relax). A typical resting value is about 120/80 mmHg. Dynamic exercise (running, cycling, swimming): systolic pressure rises with intensity because cardiac output rises. Diastolic pressure stays about the same, or falls slightly, because the arterioles in the working muscles dilate and lower resistance.

Resistance exercise (a heavy squat or deadlift): both systolic and diastolic pressure can rise sharply, especially if the lifter holds their breath (the Valsalva manoeuvre). This is why very heavy lifting is more demanding on the cardiovascular system than its energy cost suggests. Redistribution of blood flow Even at maximal effort the heart can only pump so much blood, so the body also changes where the blood goes. At rest, muscles receive only about 20% of cardiac output. In heavy exercise this rises to about 80%, while the digestive system and kidneys receive much less.

Vasoconstriction: sympathetic nerves narrow the arterioles supplying the digestive system and kidneys, so less blood reaches them. Vasodilation: in the working muscles, rising carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions (falling pH) and heat make the arterioles widen and open more capillaries, so far more blood flows through. Brain and heart: flow is maintained or increased, because these organs cannot go without oxygen. Heat transport: blood carries heat from the working muscles to the skin, where skin arterioles dilate so heat can be lost (see A.1.2).

Approximate blood flow to selected tissues at rest and in heavy exercise. Exact values vary between people; the pattern is what matters. Q = cardiac output. Pulmonary ventilation Tidal volume (TV) is the volume of air in one breath. Respiration rate (RR) is the number of breaths per minute. Minute ventilation (VE) is the volume of air moved per minute: VE = TV × RR

At rest, a typical adult breathes about 0.5 L per breath, 12 times per minute, so VE is about 6 L per minute. In maximal exercise, tidal volume can reach 2.5 L or more and respiration rate can reach 40 to 60 breaths per minute, so VE can exceed 100 L per minute. Tidal volume levels off at moderate to high intensity, so at the highest intensities most of the extra ventilation comes from breathing faster. Typical ventilation response of an untrained adult. Tidal volume levels off, respiration rate keeps rising, and minute ventilation increases roughly twenty-fold.

At rest, breathing in is driven by the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, and breathing out is passive. During exercise, extra muscles help: the sternocleidomastoid, scalenes and pectoralis minor assist inspiration, and the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles make expiration active and forceful. Breathing is controlled by the respiratory centre in the medulla. During exercise it responds to: Chemoreceptors that detect rising carbon dioxide and falling pH (the main driver of increased breathing). Proprioceptors in muscles and joints that signal that movement has started. Higher brain centres that cause an anticipatory increase before exercise begins.

Gas exchange and gas transport Gases move by diffusion , from an area of higher partial pressure to an area of lower partial pressure. In the lungs, oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. In the muscles the process reverses: oxygen leaves the blood and carbon dioxide enters it. The alveoli and capillaries have walls only one cell thick and a huge surface area, so exchange is fast. During exercise the gradients at the muscle become steeper because the muscle uses oxygen faster and produces more carbon dioxide, so more gas is exchanged. Location Partial pressure of O₂ (mmHg) Partial pressure of CO₂ (mmHg) Alveolar air about 104 about 40

Blood arriving at the lungs about 40 about 46 Blood leaving the lungs about 100 about 40 Working muscle below 40, and can fall to about 20 above 46 Almost all oxygen (about 98%) is carried bound to haemoglobin inside red blood cells, which is why having enough haemoglobin matters for endurance performance. A small amount dissolves in plasma. Most carbon dioxide (about 70%) is carried as bicarbonate in the plasma, with the rest bound to haemoglobin or dissolved in plasma. What changes the numbers? The values above are typical, not fixed. Each of the factors below shifts heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, blood pressure and ventilation. Factor Effect

Age Maximum heart rate falls with age, and maximum stroke volume and cardiac output decline. Resting blood pressure tends to rise. Sex Males usually have a larger heart and greater blood volume, so a larger stroke volume and higher maximum cardiac output. Females often have a higher heart rate at the same absolute workload. Body size Larger people usually have a larger stroke volume, cardiac output and minute ventilation in absolute terms. Smaller people may need a higher heart rate for the same output. Fitness Fitter people have a lower resting and sub-maximal heart rate, a larger stroke volume and a higher maximum cardiac output and minute ventilation.

Type of activity Resistance exercise causes larger blood pressure spikes than dynamic exercise. Swimming (horizontal) gives a larger stroke volume and lower heart rate than running (upright), because venous return is easier. Exercise using a small muscle mass (arms) produces a lower cardiac output than exercise using the legs. Intensity Heart rate, cardiac output, systolic blood pressure, blood redistribution and ventilation all increase as intensity increases. Putting it together: a 1500 m race

On the start line: anticipation raises heart rate and breathing before the gun fires. During the race: heart rate climbs towards its maximum, stroke volume rises then levels off, and cardiac output increases several-fold. Systolic pressure rises, blood is diverted from the gut and kidneys to the leg muscles, and minute ventilation increases roughly twenty-fold. Blood also carries heat from the legs to the skin. After the race: these variables fall back towards resting values over several minutes. Exam Tips

Use the precise term Write "cardiac output", not "the amount of blood pumped", and "minute ventilation", not "breathing more". Always include the equation (Q = HR × SV, VE = TV × RR) when it helps. Show your working and units For calculations, write the equation, substitute the numbers and give the units. Stroke volume is usually in mL, but cardiac output is in L per minute, so convert (1000 mL = 1 L). Quote the data when you describe a graph For "describe" or "interpret" questions on data, give the shape and figures from the graph: "Heart rate rose from 70 to 190 bpm, whereas stroke volume levelled off at about 110 mL."

Name the vessel change "Vasodilation of the arterioles supplying the working muscles" and "vasoconstriction of the arterioles to the gut and kidneys" score. "More blood goes to the muscles" doesn't explain anything. Check the IB command terms . Common mistake Don't say stroke volume keeps rising all the way to exhaustion. In most people it levels off at moderate to high intensity, so further increases in cardiac output come mainly from heart rate. Also remember that muscles get more blood from both a higher cardiac output and redistribution. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define cardiac output . 1 mark Answer Model answer

The volume of blood pumped by the heart (by each ventricle) per minute. Accept: heart rate × stroke volume. 2 Distinguish between arteries and veins. 2 marks Answer Model answer Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure, whereas veins return blood to the heart at low pressure. Arteries have thick, elastic, muscular walls, whereas veins have thinner walls and contain valves to prevent backflow. 3 Calculate the cardiac output, in L per minute, of an endurance cyclist with a heart rate of 180 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 190 mL. 2 marks Answer Model answer Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.

180 × 190 = 34 200 mL per minute = 34.2 L per minute (units required for the mark). 4 Describe how breathing changes between rest and maximal exercise in a distance runner. 3 marks Answer Model answer Tidal volume increases, for example from about 0.5 L to 2.5 L or more. Respiration rate increases, for example from about 12 to 40–50 breaths per minute. Because minute ventilation = tidal volume × respiration rate, minute ventilation increases greatly, for example from about 6 L per minute to over 100 L per minute. 5 Explain how blood flow is redistributed during exercise. 4 marks Answer Model answer

The sympathetic nervous system causes vasoconstriction of the arterioles to the digestive system and kidneys, reducing blood flow to them. In the working muscles, increased carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and heat cause vasodilation of the arterioles (and more open capillaries). As a result, the muscles receive a much larger share of cardiac output, about 80% in heavy exercise compared with about 20% at rest. This delivers more oxygen and nutrients to the muscles and removes more carbon dioxide, waste and heat, matching the muscles' increased demand. A.2.1 Water Balance & Electrolyte Balance | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.2.1 A.2.1 Theme A · Hydration & Nutrition SL & HL Water Balance & Electrolyte Balance How the body keeps its water and electrolytes in balance, what happens when exercise, heat or drinking habits upset that balance, and how it affects performance. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

About 60% of your body mass is water, and that water carries dissolved electrolytes : charged particles such as sodium, potassium and chloride. Together they keep blood volume up, allow nerves and muscles to work, and let you cool down by sweating. Water and electrolyte balance means that what enters the body closely matches what leaves it. Exercise, heat, humidity and altitude all push the body off balance, and drinking too little or too much can harm both health and performance. By the end of this topic you should be able to Outline how water and electrolytes enter and leave the body. Describe the roles of sodium, potassium and chloride in exercise.

Explain how the hypothalamus, pituitary gland and kidneys regulate water balance. Explain how the environment affects water and electrolyte balance in an athlete. Distinguish between dehydration, hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia, and explain their effects on performance and health. Outline how athletes can monitor hydration and rehydrate sensibly. Key Terms Electrolyte A charged particle (ion) dissolved in body fluids, such as Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻. Water balance The state in which water intake matches water loss. Dehydration A fall in total body water, caused by fluid loss exceeding fluid intake.

Hyponatraemia Abnormally low blood sodium, usually from too much water relative to sodium. (US spelling: hyponatremia.) Hypernatraemia Abnormally high blood sodium, usually from too little water relative to sodium. ADH Antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidneys reabsorb more water. Presentation A.2.1.1 Water and Electrolyte Balance Deep Dive Why water and electrolytes matter

Water is the medium for almost everything the body does. It makes up most of blood plasma, so it carries oxygen, nutrients and hormones. It is the raw material for sweat, so it allows cooling. It is also where chemical reactions happen inside cells. Electrolytes control how water is shared between the blood, the spaces around cells and the inside of cells, because water follows sodium by osmosis . They also carry the electrical signals that nerves and muscles rely on. Electrolyte Where it is mainly found Key roles in exercise Sodium (Na⁺) Blood plasma and the fluid around cells Sets blood volume and water distribution; needed for nerve impulses; lost in sweat

Potassium (K⁺) Inside cells Nerve impulses, muscle contraction and normal heart rhythm Chloride (Cl⁻) Blood plasma and the fluid around cells Works with sodium to keep fluid balance; lost with sodium in sweat Water and electrolyte intake and loss Intake comes from drinks, from the water in food (fruit, vegetables, soup) and from metabolic water , a small amount produced when the body breaks down fuel. Electrolytes come from food, and from sports drinks and oral rehydration products.

Loss happens through urine, sweat, breathing (water vapour in exhaled air) and faeces. At rest, urine is the biggest loss. In exercise, sweat becomes by far the largest, and sweat carries sodium and chloride with the water (and a little potassium). Sweat rates range from about 0.5 L per hour up to 2 L per hour or more in hard exercise in the heat, and sweat sodium varies hugely between individuals, roughly 0.5 to 2 g per litre. Breathing loss also rises because ventilation increases.

Typical daily water loss for an adult at rest compared with a day including two hours of hard exercise in the heat. Values are approximate and vary between people. Notice that the body cuts urine output to conserve water. How the environment changes the balance Heat: the body sweats more to lose heat, so water and electrolyte losses rise. Humidity: sweat evaporates poorly in humid air, so it drips off the skin. The athlete loses fluid and electrolytes without much cooling, and core temperature rises faster. Altitude: the air is drier and breathing is faster, so more water is lost through breathing, and urine output often increases.

Cold: thirst is often reduced and urine output can rise, so athletes can become dehydrated without noticing. Clothing and equipment: heavy kit (for example American football pads) traps heat and increases sweating. How the body regulates water balance

Water balance is controlled by negative feedback (see A.1.2). When body water falls, the blood becomes more concentrated. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect this and do two things. They trigger thirst , and they signal the posterior pituitary gland to release antidiuretic hormone (ADH) . ADH travels in the blood to the kidneys , where it makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water. More water is reabsorbed into the blood, so less urine is produced and it is darker and more concentrated.

Sodium is controlled partly by aldosterone , released by the adrenal cortex when blood volume or sodium falls. It makes the kidneys reabsorb more sodium, and water follows by osmosis, which helps maintain blood volume. Negative feedback control of water balance after sweat loss. ADH reduces further water loss through the kidneys, but only drinking can replace the water already lost. When the balance is lost Blood sodium concentration normally stays between about 135 and 145 mmol/L. Three problems matter in sport: Dehydration is a fall in total body water because fluid loss exceeds intake.

Hypernatraemia is blood sodium above the normal range. It usually means water has been lost faster than sodium, as in dehydration, because sweat contains proportionally more water than sodium. Hyponatraemia is blood sodium below the normal range. In sport it usually happens when an athlete drinks more fluid than they lose, so the sodium in the blood is diluted. Blood sodium concentration and what happens at each end of the scale. In hyponatraemia, water moves into cells by osmosis, which is why the brain is at particular risk. How dehydration affects performance

Performance often starts to fall once fluid loss reaches about 2% of body mass. A 70 kg athlete who finishes a hot training session weighing 68.6 kg has lost 1.4 kg, which is 2%. The main effects are: Lower blood volume: plasma volume falls, so less blood returns to the heart and stroke volume drops. Heart rate rises to compensate for the same effort (cardiovascular drift), and cardiac output is harder to maintain. Poorer temperature control: less blood is available to carry heat to the skin and less water is available to sweat, so core temperature rises faster.

Higher perceived effort: the same pace feels harder, and concentration, decision-making and skill (for example a footballer's passing) can decline. Muscle problems: heavy sweating with loss of sodium and other electrolytes is linked to fatigue and cramps. Severe dehydration with high body temperature can lead to heat illness, which is a medical emergency. Exercise-associated hyponatraemia

Hyponatraemia is most common in long events such as marathons, ultramarathons and Ironman triathlons, particularly in slower athletes who drink at every aid station. If they drink more than they sweat, and mainly plain water, the blood sodium is diluted. Water then moves into cells by osmosis and brain cells swell, causing headache, nausea, confusion, seizures and, in severe cases, collapse. Sports drinks contain some sodium but do not fully prevent hyponatraemia if far too much is drunk. The risk is reduced by drinking according to thirst or an individual plan that matches sweat loss, rather than drinking as much as possible. Monitoring hydration and rehydrating Method What it shows

Urine colour Pale straw suggests good hydration; dark yellow suggests dehydration. Quick and cheap, but some foods and supplements change the colour. Body mass change Weigh before and after exercise. Each 1 kg lost is about 1 L of fluid lost. Best used to learn your own sweat rate. Thirst A simple guide, but it lags behind actual fluid loss in hot conditions, and can be switched off by excitement or cold. Urine specific gravity Measures how concentrated the urine is. More accurate, but needs equipment. Before: start well hydrated, drinking steadily in the hours before rather than gulping just before the start.

During: replace some of the sweat loss, matched to the individual, aiming to limit body mass loss to under about 2% without overdrinking. Add sodium in long or very hot events. After: replace more than was lost (about 125–150% of the body mass lost) over the following hours, together with sodium from food or drinks, because urine continues to be produced. Exam Tips Name the ion and the direction of change "Plasma sodium falls below 135 mmol/L" scores. "Electrolytes are lost" doesn't. Always say which electrolyte, and whether it rises or falls.

Link the cause to the effect through osmosis For hyponatraemia, write that diluted blood makes water move into cells by osmosis, so cells (including brain cells) swell. That is the mechanism the mark scheme wants. Give a mechanism for environment questions "It's hot" isn't enough. Say why it matters: more sweating, poorer evaporation in humid air, or more breathing loss at altitude. Check the IB command terms . Use the sport and the numbers A marathon runner in heat, or a 2% body mass loss (1.4 kg for a 70 kg athlete), shows you can apply the idea.

Common mistake Don't say hyponatraemia is caused by "losing too much salt in sweat". The main cause is drinking too much fluid relative to sodium, which dilutes the blood. Sweat sodium loss can contribute, but dilution is the key point. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define dehydration . 1 mark Answer Model answer A reduction in total body water, which occurs when fluid loss is greater than fluid intake. 2 Outline two ways in which an athlete loses water during exercise. 2 marks Answer Model answer Sweat: water is lost as sweat evaporates to cool the body (along with sodium and chloride).

Breathing: water vapour is lost in exhaled air, and this increases as ventilation rises. Urine (reduced during exercise) is also accepted. Any two. 3 Outline the role of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) in maintaining water balance. 3 marks Answer Model answer The hypothalamus detects that the blood has become more concentrated (body water has fallen). The posterior pituitary gland releases ADH into the blood. ADH makes the kidneys reabsorb more water, so less, more concentrated urine is produced. 4 Explain how exercising in hot, humid conditions affects an athlete's water and electrolyte balance. 3 marks Answer Model answer

Heat increases the sweat rate, so more water, sodium and chloride are lost. High humidity reduces evaporation, so sweat drips off without cooling, and the athlete sweats even more to try to lose heat. If fluid intake does not match these losses, the athlete becomes dehydrated, and blood volume and plasma sodium balance are disrupted. 5 Explain how hyponatraemia can develop in a marathon runner and how it affects health and performance. 4 marks Answer Model answer The runner drinks more fluid than they lose in sweat, especially plain water with little sodium. This dilutes the blood, so plasma sodium falls below the normal range (about 135 mmol/L).

Water moves into cells by osmosis, so cells, including brain cells, swell. This causes headache, nausea, confusion and, in severe cases, seizures and collapse, so performance falls and health is at risk. A.2.2 Fuelling for Health & Performance | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.2.2 A.2.2 Theme A · Hydration & Nutrition SL & HL Fuelling for Health & Performance How carbohydrate, fat and protein fuel the body at rest and in exercise, how to time and plan fuelling, and what happens when energy intake is too low. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Food is the fuel and the building material for the body. The three macronutrients , carbohydrate, fat and protein, supply energy. Which one the body uses most depends on how hard and how long you exercise, and on how well fuelled you are. Athletes can improve performance by timing what they eat around training and competition, but eating too little for the energy they use causes low energy availability , which harms health and performance. At higher level you also study micronutrients and the gut microbiome . By the end of this topic you should be able to Outline the roles, energy values and food sources of carbohydrate, fat and protein.

Explain how exercise intensity, duration and other factors change which fuel is used. Describe fuelling strategies before, during and after exercise, including carbohydrate loading. Explain what low energy availability is, and how it affects health and performance. HL: Explain the roles of micronutrients in energy transfer and tissue synthesis. HL: Outline how the gut microbiome influences health and performance. Key Terms Macronutrient A nutrient needed in large amounts that provides energy: carbohydrate, fat or protein. Glycogen The stored form of carbohydrate, held in muscle and the liver. Carbohydrate loading Raising muscle and liver glycogen above normal before a long event.

Low energy availability (LEA) Too little energy left for normal body functions after the cost of exercise. Micronutrient (HL) A vitamin or mineral needed in small amounts; it does not provide energy itself. Gut microbiome (HL) The community of microbes living in the digestive tract. Presentations A.2.2.1 Macronutrients A.2.2.2 Micronutrients A.2.2.3 The Gut Microbiome Deep Dive The three macronutrients Macronutrient Energy per gram Main roles Typical sources Carbohydrate about 4 kcal (17 kJ) Main fuel for moderate to high intensity exercise; stored as glycogen in muscle and liver; the brain's preferred fuel Rice, pasta, bread, oats, fruit, potatoes

Fat (lipid) about 9 kcal (37 kJ) Main fuel at rest and low intensity; very large stores; absorbs vitamins A, D, E and K; protects organs Oils, nuts, oily fish, avocado, dairy Protein about 4 kcal (17 kJ) Growth and repair of tissue, enzymes and hormones; a small energy source, larger in long exercise or when carbohydrate is low Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, tofu Daily needs depend on training load. Endurance athletes may need roughly 3 to 12 g of carbohydrate per kg of body mass per day, from light to very heavy training, and about 1.2 to 2.0 g of protein per kg per day, with fat making up roughly 20 to 35% of energy intake. Which fuel is used? Intensity and duration

The body always uses a mixture of fuels. At rest and at low intensity, fat supplies the biggest share, because the demand for ATP is low and fat can be broken down slowly using oxygen. As intensity rises, ATP is needed faster. Carbohydrate can be broken down much more quickly, and it can supply energy both with and without oxygen, so its share rises. At high intensity it provides most of the energy. Protein supplies only a small share (about 5%) throughout. Approximate share of energy from each macronutrient. The exact mix varies with diet, fitness and the individual, but carbohydrate use always rises with intensity.

Body fat stores are huge, but glycogen stores are small : roughly 2000 kcal in muscle and liver combined, enough for about 90 to 120 minutes of hard endurance exercise. When glycogen runs low, power output, speed and concentration fall, which marathon runners call "hitting the wall". This is why carbohydrate availability matters so much for performance. Other factors that influence fuel use include: Duration: in long exercise, glycogen is gradually used up and the body relies more on fat (and a little more protein). Training status: trained endurance athletes use more fat at a given intensity, which spares glycogen.

Diet: a high-carbohydrate diet raises glycogen stores and carbohydrate use; low carbohydrate availability shifts the body towards fat and protein. Sex: on average, women use slightly more fat and less carbohydrate than men at the same relative intensity, but the differences between individuals are larger than the difference between sexes. Sex-related factors also affect energy availability and how the gut responds to eating during exercise. Environment: exercise in the heat tends to increase carbohydrate use. Fuelling strategies

The aim is to start exercise with enough carbohydrate available, to keep it topped up if the event is long, and to refuel afterwards, while avoiding stomach problems. Athletes should practise their strategy in training , never try new foods on competition day. Typical carbohydrate guidelines for an endurance athlete. Amounts are approximate and are individualised using body mass, event length and gut tolerance. Carbohydrate loading only helps events lasting longer than about 90 minutes, such as a marathon or a long cycling race. It raises glycogen stores so they last longer. It gives no benefit in a 100 m sprint.

Glycaemic index (GI): high GI foods raise blood glucose quickly and are useful during and straight after exercise. Low GI foods release glucose more slowly and are often chosen in the pre-exercise meal. Total intake, timing and tolerance matter as much as GI. After exercise: carbohydrate restores glycogen, and protein supplies amino acids for muscle repair and adaptation. Low energy availability and RED-S

Energy availability is the energy left for the body's normal functions after the energy cost of exercise has been subtracted from energy intake, expressed per kg of fat-free mass. Low energy availability (LEA) occurs when this is too low to support those functions. It can be unintentional (not realising how much energy training uses) or deliberate (dieting, or pressure to be lean in sports such as gymnastics, distance running or weight-class sports). It affects both female and male athletes. Prolonged LEA can lead to Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (RED-S) .

Worked example: an athlete with 50 kg of fat-free mass eats 2300 kcal per day and uses 800 kcal in training. Energy availability = (2300 − 800) ÷ 50 = 30 kcal per kg of fat-free mass per day , right at the threshold below which problems become likely. How energy availability is calculated, commonly used thresholds (these vary slightly between sources), and the body systems affected by prolonged low energy availability. Micronutrients HL Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts. They do not provide energy themselves. Instead, they have specific jobs in energy transfer (releasing and using the energy in food) and tissue synthesis (building and repairing tissue).

Micronutrient Role If intake is too low Iron Part of haemoglobin and myoglobin (oxygen transport) and of enzymes in aerobic energy production Anaemia, fatigue, lower aerobic capacity B vitamins Coenzymes in the release of energy from carbohydrate, fat and protein; B12 and folate help make red blood cells Fatigue, poor recovery, anaemia Vitamin C Needed to make collagen for tendons, ligaments and skin; antioxidant Slower tissue repair Calcium and vitamin D Bone formation; calcium is also needed for muscle contraction, and vitamin D helps absorb calcium Weaker bones, stress fractures Magnesium Helps enzymes that use ATP; muscle and nerve function Cramps, fatigue

Zinc Protein synthesis, tissue repair and immune function Slower recovery, more infections A varied diet usually provides enough. Supplements are most useful where a deficiency has been confirmed (for example iron or vitamin D) or diet is restricted (for example vitamin B12 for vegans). Taking more than needed gives no extra benefit, can be harmful (for example iron overload), and supplements can be contaminated with banned substances. The gut microbiome HL

Trillions of microbes live in the digestive tract, mostly in the large intestine. They ferment fibre to produce short-chain fatty acids , which feed the cells lining the gut and have anti-inflammatory effects. They also influence how nutrients are absorbed, immune function, inflammation and, through the gut–brain connection, mood. A healthy, diverse microbiome can therefore support fuel availability, recovery, immune health and general health. Very hard, prolonged exercise can cause stomach and bowel problems in some athletes, and a diet rich in varied plant foods and fibre supports a diverse microbiome. Research is still developing, and evidence that probiotic supplements improve performance is mixed.

Exam Tips Say how the fuel mix changes, not "which fuel" Fat is the main fuel at rest and low intensity; carbohydrate takes over as intensity rises. Never write that fat is used only at low intensity, because both are used all the time. Use the exact term Write "glycogen" for stored carbohydrate and "blood glucose" for carbohydrate in the blood. Say "energy availability", not just "not eating enough". For fuelling strategies, give timing, amount and reason "Eat about 1–4 g/kg of carbohydrate 1–4 hours before, to top up glycogen" scores. "Eat carbs before" doesn't. Check the IB command terms .

Match the strategy to the sport Carbohydrate loading suits a marathon or long road race, not a 100 m sprint or a 60-minute training run. Showing this is how you earn application marks. Common mistake (HL) Don't write that vitamins and minerals "give you energy". Micronutrients contain no usable energy. They help release energy from macronutrients and help build and repair tissue. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define macronutrient . 1 mark Answer Model answer A nutrient needed in large amounts that provides energy, i.e. carbohydrate, fat (lipid) or protein.

2 Outline two reasons why carbohydrate is the main fuel during high-intensity exercise. 2 marks Answer Model answer Carbohydrate can be broken down quickly, so ATP is resynthesised fast enough for high-intensity work. It can supply energy both with and without oxygen (anaerobically and aerobically). It is stored as glycogen in the muscles themselves, so it is immediately available. Any two. 3 Describe how the contributions of carbohydrate and fat to energy supply change as exercise intensity increases. 3 marks Answer Model answer At rest and at low intensity, fat provides the largest share of energy.

As intensity increases, the contribution of carbohydrate increases and the contribution of fat decreases. At high intensity, carbohydrate is the dominant fuel, while protein remains a small contributor throughout. 4 Explain the purpose of carbohydrate loading and identify one type of event for which it is suitable. 3 marks Answer Model answer Carbohydrate loading increases glycogen stores in the muscles and liver above normal levels. This delays glycogen depletion and fatigue, so the athlete can maintain intensity for longer. It is suitable for events lasting longer than about 90 minutes, such as a marathon.

5 Explain how low energy availability can affect the health and performance of an athlete. 4 marks Answer Model answer Low energy availability means energy intake is too low to cover the cost of exercise and still support normal body functions. It can reduce bone density and increase the risk of stress fractures. It can disrupt hormones (for example menstrual cycles in females or testosterone in males) and weaken immune function, leading to more illness. Performance falls because of reduced endurance and strength, and recovery is slower.
