A.2.3 Energy Systems | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.2.3 A.2.3 Theme A · Hydration & Nutrition SL & HL Energy Systems How the body makes ATP to power movement, how the three energy systems share the work from a sprint to a marathon, and what limits and follows aerobic exercise. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Every muscle contraction is powered by one molecule: ATP . Muscles store only a tiny amount, so ATP must be made again, continuously, by three energy systems . The phosphagen system is fastest but runs out in seconds. The glycolytic system supports hard efforts for up to a couple of minutes. The oxidative system uses oxygen and can keep going for hours. All three work at the same time, and the one that dominates depends on how intense and how long the activity is. At higher level you also study the lactate inflection point and excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) . By the end of this topic you should be able to Explain how ATP provides energy and how it is resynthesised.

Describe the phosphagen, glycolytic and oxidative systems, including fuel, oxygen use, rate, capacity and by-products. Explain the energy continuum and apply it to different sports. Explain the factors that affect maximal oxygen consumption (VO₂ max). HL: Explain the lactate inflection point and its significance. HL: Explain excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) and its role in recovery. Key Terms ATP Adenosine triphosphate: the molecule that releases energy for muscle contraction. Phosphagen system The ATP-PC system: resynthesises ATP using stored phosphocreatine, without oxygen.

Energy continuum All energy systems contribute at all times; their shares change with intensity and duration. VO₂ max The maximum rate at which the body can take in and use oxygen, in mL/kg/min. Lactate inflection point (HL) The intensity at which blood lactate starts to rise rapidly. EPOC (HL) Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption: oxygen used in recovery above resting levels. Presentations A.2.3.1 Energy Systems A.2.3.2 VO₂ Max A.2.3.3 The Lactate Inflection Point A.2.3.4 Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC) Deep Dive ATP: the energy currency

When the bond holding the end phosphate of ATP is broken, ATP becomes ADP (adenosine diphosphate) plus a phosphate, and energy is released for muscle contraction. Muscles hold only enough ATP for a couple of seconds of maximal effort, so ADP must be rapidly turned back into ATP. This needs energy, which comes from the breakdown of fuels (phosphocreatine, carbohydrate, fat and protein) by the three energy systems. ATP releases energy when it is broken down to ADP and phosphate. The three energy systems use the energy in different fuels to join them back together again. Comparing the three energy systems Phosphagen (ATP-PC) Glycolytic Oxidative (aerobic)

Fuel Stored ATP and phosphocreatine Glucose (blood) and glycogen (muscle) Carbohydrate and fat, plus a little protein Oxygen Not needed Not needed Needed Rate of ATP supply Fastest Fast Slowest ATP yield Very small (1 ATP per PC) Small (net 2–3 ATP per glucose unit) Very large (about 30–32 ATP per glucose; more from fat) Duration About 0–10 seconds About 10 seconds to 2 minutes Beyond about 2 minutes, for hours By-products Creatine (and phosphate) Lactate and hydrogen ions (H⁺) Carbon dioxide and water Recovery PC mostly restored within about 3 minutes Lactate cleared within about an hour; glycogen restored over 24 hours or more Glycogen restored over 24–48 hours

Sport examples 100 m sprint, shot put, vertical jump 400 m run, 100 m swim Marathon, 10 km run, long cycle The key trade-off is rate versus capacity . The systems that make ATP fastest can only make a little, and the system that can make a huge amount is slower. Notice also that lactate is not simply a waste product: it can be used as a fuel by the heart and by other muscle fibres. It is the accumulation of hydrogen ions, which lowers muscle pH, that is linked to fatigue in hard exercise. The energy continuum

The three systems do not switch on and off like lights. All three contribute at all times , but their share changes. The more intense the activity, the faster ATP is needed, so the phosphagen and glycolytic systems provide more. The longer the activity, the greater the share from the oxidative system. A sprinter's 10 seconds is mostly phosphagen, a 400 m is largely glycolytic, and a marathon is almost entirely oxidative. Approximate contribution of each energy system to maximal efforts of different durations. Values are estimates and vary between sources and individuals; the pattern is what matters.

Many sports are intermittent . A football player spends most of a match jogging and walking (oxidative), with repeated sprints that draw on the phosphagen and glycolytic systems. A strong oxidative system also helps players recover between sprints, because it restores phosphocreatine. Maximal oxygen consumption (VO₂ max)

VO₂ max is the maximum volume of oxygen the body can take in, transport and use per minute during exercise. It is usually given relative to body mass in mL per kg per minute , and it is the best single measure of aerobic fitness. Typical values are around 35–45 for untrained young adults, and 70–85 or more for elite endurance athletes (women typically about 10–15% lower than men). Factor How it affects VO₂ max Cardiac output Stroke volume and heart rate set how much oxygen-rich blood is delivered to the muscles (see A.1.3). This is the main limiter in most people. Oxygen-carrying capacity More haemoglobin and blood volume means more oxygen carried per minute.

Muscle oxygen use More capillaries and mitochondria, and more oxidative enzymes, mean the muscle can extract and use more oxygen. Muscle fibre type Slow-twitch fibres are better equipped for oxygen use than fast-twitch fibres. Training status Endurance training raises VO₂ max, usually by about 10–20% in previously untrained people. Genetics Heredity strongly influences both starting level and trainability. Age and sex VO₂ max falls with age after the mid-20s. Males tend to be higher, partly through larger hearts, greater blood volume and higher haemoglobin. Body composition More body fat lowers VO₂ max expressed per kg of body mass. Altitude Less oxygen in the air lowers VO₂ max.

Mode of exercise Using more muscle mass (running) gives a higher VO₂ max than using less (arm cranking). Lactate inflection point HL The body produces lactate all the time, even at rest, and also removes and uses it. At low intensities, production and removal are balanced, so blood lactate stays low and steady. The lactate inflection point (LIP) is the intensity at which blood lactate begins to rise rapidly , because production now exceeds removal. Beyond this point, hydrogen ions build up and the athlete tires quickly. Blood lactate against running speed. Training moves the lactate inflection point to the right, so the athlete can run faster before lactate accumulates.

The LIP matters for endurance athletes because it indicates the highest pace that can be sustained for a long time. Endurance training shifts the LIP to a higher speed or a higher percentage of VO₂ max, because trained muscles make less lactate and clear more of it. Coaches use the LIP to set training zones and race pacing, for example by training just below or at it to raise it further. Excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) HL

At the start of exercise, oxygen uptake takes a minute or two to rise to the level needed. During this time ATP is supplied partly by the anaerobic systems, creating an oxygen deficit . After exercise, oxygen uptake does not fall straight back to the resting level. It stays elevated, and the extra oxygen consumed above the resting level is the excess post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC) . Oxygen uptake before, during and after steady exercise. The shaded areas show the oxygen deficit at the start and the EPOC during recovery.

Fast component (the first few minutes): restoring ATP and phosphocreatine stores, replenishing oxygen stores in the blood and muscle (myoglobin), and a heart rate and breathing rate that are still raised. Slow component (can last for a long time after hard exercise): clearing lactate, a body temperature that is still raised, elevated hormones such as adrenaline, and tissue repair.

EPOC is larger after high-intensity and long exercise, because more of the body's stores have been used and more heat and lactate produced. It shows why the body needs time to recover between hard efforts: a footballer who sprints repeatedly builds up a large EPOC, which is why breathing stays heavy after the sprint is over. Exam Tips Say "dominant", not "only" All three systems contribute all the time. Write "the phosphagen system is the main contributor in the first 10 seconds", never "only the ATP-PC system is used".

Justify the system with intensity and duration Name the system, then give the reason: fuel, oxygen, rate of ATP supply and how long it lasts. Linking the sport to the continuum earns the application mark. Use correct units and terms VO₂ max is in mL/kg/min (relative) or L/min (absolute). Check the IB command terms to see whether you need to "outline" or "explain". Describe graphs in order (HL) For LIP and EPOC graphs, state the baseline, where the curve changes, and the direction and size of the change, then explain why using production and removal of lactate, or the fast and slow components.

Common mistake Don't say "lactic acid causes muscle soreness and fatigue". Lactate is a useful fuel and is not the cause of next-day soreness. The build-up of hydrogen ions, which lowers muscle pH, is linked to fatigue in hard exercise. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State the main fuel used by the phosphagen system. 1 mark Answer Model answer Phosphocreatine (PC) stored in the muscle (together with the small store of ATP). 2 Distinguish between the glycolytic and oxidative energy systems. 2 marks Answer Model answer

The glycolytic system breaks down glucose or glycogen without oxygen, producing a small amount of ATP and lactate with hydrogen ions. The oxidative system uses oxygen to break down carbohydrate and fat, producing a large amount of ATP with carbon dioxide and water as by-products. 3 Outline three factors that influence an athlete's VO₂ max. 3 marks Answer Model answer Any three of: genetics/heredity; training status (endurance training raises it); age (declines with age); sex (usually higher in males); body composition (more body fat lowers it per kg); altitude (less oxygen available).

Or physiological factors: stroke volume and cardiac output; haemoglobin and blood volume; capillary density and mitochondria in the muscle. 4 (HL) Explain what is meant by the lactate inflection point and why a higher value benefits an endurance athlete. 3 marks Answer Model answer The lactate inflection point is the exercise intensity at which blood lactate begins to rise rapidly, because lactate production exceeds removal. Below this intensity lactate production and removal are balanced, so the athlete can keep working at a steady state for a long time.

A higher inflection point means the athlete can sustain a faster pace or higher percentage of VO₂ max before lactate and hydrogen ions accumulate and cause fatigue. 5 Explain how the energy continuum applies to a 400 m sprint. 4 marks Answer Model answer All three energy systems contribute at all times, but the dominant system changes with the intensity and duration of the race. At the start, the phosphagen system supplies ATP most rapidly (using phosphocreatine) for the first few seconds, until PC runs low. As the race continues at high intensity, the glycolytic system becomes the main contributor, producing ATP quickly without oxygen but also lactate and hydrogen ions.

The oxidative system provides an increasing share as the race goes on, but it supplies ATP too slowly to be dominant in a 45–60 second effort. A.3.1 Qualities of Training | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.3.1 A.3.1 Theme A · Response SL & HL Qualities of Training The principles that make a training programme safe and effective, and how coaches design, measure and periodise training so the body adapts without breaking down. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Training works by applying a stress the body is not used to, then allowing time to recover and adapt. A good programme gets the balance right: enough stress to cause improvement, enough rest to recover, and a plan that matches the athlete and the sport. Coaches use a set of training principles (specificity, progressive overload, recovery, variety, reversibility and periodisation) and manipulate the frequency, intensity and duration of training. They also measure a baseline so that progress can be tracked, and they adjust the plan to suit factors such as fitness level, age and sex. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define and apply specificity, progressive overload, recovery, variety, reversibility and periodisation. Explain how frequency, intensity and duration can be changed to overload training safely. Explain why baseline values and progress measurement matter. Describe the structure of periodised training: macrocycles, mesocycles and microcycles. Explain how factors such as current fitness, age and sex affect programme design. Apply these ideas to design a programme for a named athlete or sport. Key Terms Specificity Training adaptations match the demands of the training: the sport, muscles, movements and energy systems used.

Progressive overload Gradually increasing the training stress so the body keeps adapting. Reversibility Fitness gains are lost when training stops or is reduced. Periodisation Planned variation of training across cycles to balance load, recovery and peak performance. Taper A planned reduction in training volume before a key event, keeping intensity high. Baseline value A starting measurement, used to set goals and judge progress. Presentation A.3.1.1 Training Design Deep Dive The training principles The principles work together. A programme that applies only one of them (for example, overload with no recovery) is likely to fail. Principle What it means Sporting example

Specificity Adaptations match what is trained: the energy system, muscle groups, movement pattern and goal. Not every exercise must copy the sport, as supporting exercises can build strength or stability. A marathon runner does long, steady runs; a sprinter does short, maximal sprints and power work. Progressive overload Training stress is increased gradually, by raising frequency, intensity or duration, so the body must keep adapting. Too fast risks injury; too slow causes a plateau. A runner adds a little distance or pace each week; a lifter adds a small amount of weight.

Recovery Adaptation happens during rest, not during the session. Sleep, nutrition and rest days allow repair and rebuilding. Too little leads to fatigue, poor performance and overtraining. Easy days and rest days between hard sessions; sleep and food after training. Variety Changing exercises or sessions in a planned way to keep the stimulus fresh, reduce overuse injury and maintain motivation, while still supporting the same goal. Random change is not variety. A cyclist adds hill sessions and strength work to long rides.

Reversibility "Use it or lose it": gains fall when training stops or is cut back, for example during injury or the off-season. A footballer's aerobic fitness drops after several weeks of no training. Periodisation Planned variation of training load across cycles, so that stress, recovery and peak performance are balanced. A swimmer builds a base in the preparation phase and peaks for the national championships. Overload, recovery and adaptation

When training stress is applied, performance drops temporarily because of fatigue. During recovery the body repairs and rebuilds, and adapts to be slightly better able to cope with the same stress. Timing is crucial. The graphs below use a simple model to show why training too often, at the right interval, and too rarely give very different results. An illustrative model, not real data. Triangles mark training sessions. Training again before recovery makes fatigue build up; well-timed sessions build performance; sessions too far apart let the gains fade (reversibility). Frequency, intensity and duration To overload safely, a coach changes the training variables, ideally one at a time:

Frequency: how often the athlete trains, for example sessions per week. Intensity: how hard the work is. It can be measured with heart rate (as a percentage of maximum heart rate), rating of perceived exertion (RPE), percentage of one-repetition maximum (1RM) for strength work, or running or cycling speed or power. Duration: how long each session lasts or, for strength training, how much work is done (volume = sets × repetitions × load).

Changing two at once, such as longer sessions at a higher intensity, creates a much bigger jump in load and raises the risk of injury and overtraining. A common rule of thumb is to increase weekly load by no more than about 10%, but this is only a guide and should be adjusted for the athlete. Many programmes also include easier recovery weeks. Baseline values and measuring progress A baseline value is a starting measurement, such as a fitness test result, resting heart rate or body mass. It allows a coach to choose a safe starting load, set realistic goals and later judge whether the programme is working. Good practice includes:

Using valid, reliable tests that match the goal (for example a 1RM test for strength or a timed run for aerobic fitness), carried out under the same conditions each time. Retesting often enough to guide decisions, but not so often that testing replaces training or causes fatigue. Using the results to change the plan: progress the load, vary the sessions, or ease off if the athlete is not coping. Designing a programme for an individual Programme design is a cycle: assess, plan, train, monitor and adjust. The training programme design cycle. The factors at the bottom shape every stage of the plan.

Current fitness level: beginners need a lower starting load and slower progression; trained athletes can tolerate higher intensity and more complex training. Age: affects recovery time, tolerance of load and injury risk. Young athletes are still growing and need careful loading, and older athletes usually need more recovery.

Sex and reproductive status: there are physiological differences between males and females (for example in body composition, hormones and energy needs), and some female athletes notice changes in energy or recovery across the menstrual cycle, or need adjusted training during pregnancy and after childbirth. Differences between individuals are often bigger than differences between the sexes, so plans should be individual and flexible. Training history, health and injuries: past injuries and medical conditions limit what is safe. Goals, sport and time available: the demands of the sport and the time the athlete has decide the content (specificity). Periodisation

Periodisation divides training into planned cycles so that load, recovery and peak performance are balanced across the year. Macrocycle: the long-term plan, such as a season or year, built around the main competition. Mesocycle: a block of several weeks within the macrocycle, with a particular focus (for example aerobic base, strength or speed). Microcycle: typically one week of sessions, mixing hard, moderate and easy days.

The macrocycle usually has three phases. In the preparation phase , training is first general (building a base with high volume at lower intensity) and then more specific to the sport. In the competition phase , intensity is high and volume is lower, with a taper before the key event to remove fatigue while keeping fitness. The transition phase gives active rest so the athlete can recover physically and mentally before the next cycle. A periodised plan, from the macrocycle down to a single week, with the typical shift from high volume and low intensity to low volume and high intensity. The curves are a simplified model. Exam Tips

Define, then apply to the sport named Give a short definition of the principle, then show it in action for the athlete in the question: "Specificity: a marathon runner mainly trains aerobically, with long runs." Name the variable you change For "explain how to apply overload", say which of frequency, intensity or duration changes, and by how much, for example "increase weekly distance by about 10%". Name the cycle and the phase For periodisation answers, say whether you mean the macrocycle, mesocycle or microcycle, and which phase (preparation, competition or transition). Check the IB command terms .

Link measurement to decisions Baseline values are used to set a safe starting load and to show progress. Say what the coach does with the result. Common mistake Progressive overload does not mean training harder every session. It means planned, gradual increases with recovery built in. Increasing too fast, or without rest, causes overtraining and injury. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define specificity . 1 mark Answer Model answer The principle that training adaptations are specific to the type of training done, so training should match the demands of the sport (for example its energy systems, muscles and movement patterns).

2 Outline two ways a coach could apply progressive overload for an endurance runner. 2 marks Answer Model answer Gradually increase the weekly distance (duration) of the runs. Gradually increase intensity, for example faster pace or interval sessions. Add an extra training session each week (frequency), or reduce recovery time between intervals. Any two, with the increase described as gradual. 3 Describe the structure of a periodised training plan using the terms macrocycle, mesocycle and microcycle. 3 marks Answer Model answer The macrocycle is the long-term plan, such as a whole season or year, built around the main competition.

A mesocycle is a block of several weeks within the macrocycle, with a particular training focus (for example aerobic base or strength). A microcycle is a short cycle, typically one week, made up of individual sessions with hard, moderate and easy days. 4 Explain why a coach must consider an athlete's current fitness level when designing a training programme. 3 marks Answer Model answer Baseline testing shows the athlete's starting level, so that a suitable starting load can be chosen. If the load is too high, the athlete risks injury, excessive fatigue or overtraining; if too low, there is no overload and so no adaptation.

The baseline allows progress to be measured later and the programme adjusted accordingly. 5 Explain how the principles of specificity and progressive overload could be applied in a 12-week programme for a recreational 5 km runner. 4 marks Answer Model answer Specificity: most sessions are running-based, using aerobic runs plus some interval sessions near race pace, so the training matches the energy systems and movements of a 5 km race. Progressive overload: weekly distance and/or intensity is increased gradually (for example by about 10% a week) rather than suddenly. Recovery weeks or rest days are included so the body can adapt and the risk of injury is reduced.

Progress is measured, for example with a baseline and repeat 5 km time trial, and the plan is adjusted using the results. A.3.2 Benefits to Health of Being Active | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.3.2 A.3.2 Theme A · Response SL & HL Benefits to Health of Being Active How regular physical activity protects health and well-being, what it does to the muscular and immune systems, and why inactivity carries real risks. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Being active is one of the most effective things a person can do for their health. Regular physical activity improves physical, mental and social well-being , strengthens the muscular system, supports the immune system and lowers the risk of non-communicable diseases such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis. Inactivity does the opposite. How active people are depends on many determinants : personal, social, environmental and economic. At higher level, you also study exercise prescription : how activity is planned for different people and conditions. By the end of this topic you should be able to Explain how physical activity supports physical, mental and social well-being.

Outline physical activity guidelines and the determinants of activity levels. Describe the effects of regular physical activity on the muscular and immune systems. Explain the health risks of inactivity and how activity protects against them. HL: Explain the principles and purposes of exercise prescription. HL: Apply exercise prescription to different target groups and conditions. Key Terms Physical activity Any movement by skeletal muscles that uses energy, including exercise, sport, play and active travel. Sedentary behaviour Low-energy sitting or lying while awake, such as long periods at a desk or screen.

Well-being A person's overall physical, mental and social health and quality of life. Non-communicable disease (NCD) A long-term disease that does not spread between people, such as heart disease or type 2 diabetes. Insulin sensitivity How effectively the body's cells respond to insulin and take up glucose. Exercise prescription (HL) An individual plan of activity (type, amount, intensity and progression) to meet a health or fitness goal. Presentations A.3.2.1 Active Lifestyle A.3.2.2 Prescribing Exercise Deep Dive Physical activity and well-being

Physical activity is any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that uses energy. Exercise is a planned, structured form of it. Sedentary behaviour (long periods of sitting) is a separate health risk, so a person who exercises for 30 minutes but sits for the rest of the day is still at some risk. Being active supports three areas of well-being: Physical: a fitter heart, lungs, muscles and bones, a healthier body composition and better sleep. Mental: lower stress, anxiety and depression, better mood and self-esteem, and improved concentration and thinking. Social: team sport, clubs and active travel build friendships, a sense of belonging and support. How much activity is enough?

The World Health Organization (WHO) gives these guidelines for health: Group Aerobic activity Strength and other activity Children and adolescents (5–17) An average of at least 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity, mostly aerobic Vigorous aerobic activity and muscle- and bone-strengthening activity on at least 3 days a week Adults (18–64) 150–300 minutes of moderate activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity, per week (or an equivalent mix) Muscle-strengthening activity at moderate or greater intensity on at least 2 days a week

Older adults (65+) The same as adults, as far as health allows Also multicomponent activity with balance and strength training on at least 3 days a week All groups should also limit sedentary time. Vigorous activity counts for roughly twice as much as moderate activity, so 10 minutes of running is about equal to 20 minutes of brisk walking. A useful check is the talk test: you can talk but not sing during moderate activity, and you can only say a few words during vigorous activity.

The shape of the relationship between weekly activity and the risk of early death, based on population studies. The values are approximate and the curve is illustrative. Some activity is better than none, and more is generally better up to a point. Determinants of activity levels Type Examples Personal Age, sex, health and disability, skills and confidence (self-efficacy), enjoyment, knowledge of the benefits, motivation Social Support and role models from family and friends, peer influence, culture and gender norms, school and workplace culture Environmental Access to safe parks, facilities and cycle or walking routes, climate and weather, air quality, how walkable the neighbourhood is

Economic and policy Cost of clubs and equipment, time available, work patterns, and government policy such as school PE and investment in facilities Effects on the muscular system Regular activity changes muscle in ways that depend on the type of training: Resistance training: increases muscle size (hypertrophy) and strength, partly through improved nervous system activation of muscle fibres. It also strengthens tendons and ligaments. Endurance training: increases capillaries and mitochondria in muscle, so more oxygen can be delivered and used, and improves the use of fat as a fuel. All types: improve insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake, balance and coordination.

Across life: keeping muscle mass and strength reduces the age-related loss of muscle (sarcopenia), reduces the risk of falls and helps people stay independent. Effects on the immune system The immune system defends the body against infection. Regular, moderate activity strengthens it: immune cells circulate more during and after exercise, so the body is better at detecting threats, and long-term activity reduces chronic low-grade inflammation (partly by reducing body fat). People who are regularly active tend to catch fewer upper respiratory infections such as colds.

The relationship is shown by the "J-curve" model. Very heavy training with too little rest, sleep or fuel can temporarily suppress immune function after exercise, so athletes in the middle of heavy blocks of training, or after marathons, may be more likely to pick up infections. The J-curve model of training load and infection risk. It is a simplified model: the lowest risk is at regular moderate activity, and very heavy load without recovery can raise risk above the sedentary level. Health risks of inactivity, and how activity protects

Physical inactivity is a leading risk factor for non-communicable diseases. Adults who do not meet the guidelines have around a 20–30% higher risk of death than those who do. Activity protects health through specific effects on body systems: Pathways from regular activity to the effects on body systems and the health outcomes. In exams, link activity to the physiological effect and then to the outcome. Condition Why inactivity raises the risk How activity protects Cardiovascular disease and hypertension Less demand on the heart, higher blood pressure, unhealthy blood fats, narrower arteries Stronger heart, lower resting blood pressure, improved blood fats and healthier blood vessels

Type 2 diabetes Muscles take up less glucose and insulin sensitivity falls, especially with excess body fat Contracting muscles take up glucose and become more insulin sensitive, and body fat falls Obesity Energy intake exceeds energy used Increases energy expenditure and helps maintain muscle mass, so supports healthy body composition Osteoporosis Bones that are not loaded lose density Weight-bearing and resistance exercise stimulate bone-building, raising peak bone mass and slowing loss Some cancers (for example colon and breast) Linked to excess body fat, hormone levels and inflammation Lowers body fat, inflammation and some hormone levels

Depression and anxiety Less stress relief, poorer sleep, less social contact Changes brain chemistry, improves sleep and self-esteem, and offers social contact Exercise prescription: principles and purposes HL Exercise prescription is an individual plan of activity designed to reach a goal. Its purposes include improving health and fitness, preventing and managing disease, supporting rehabilitation and improving performance. Good prescription: Starts with screening: health history, current activity, medication and risk factors, with medical clearance where needed. Is individual: it considers age, fitness, health, goals, preferences and what the person can keep doing.

Sets the FITT-VP variables: frequency, intensity, time (duration), type, volume and progression, and chooses a safe starting level. Progresses gradually and is monitored: intensity can be measured by heart rate, perceived exertion (RPE) or the talk test, and the plan is adjusted. Supports adherence: enjoyable, realistic activity with support is more likely to continue. Poor prescription can cause injury, overuse, dropout or little benefit. Exercise prescription for different groups and conditions HL Group or condition Key considerations

Children and adolescents Aim for about 60 minutes a day of varied, enjoyable activity and play, including bone- and muscle-strengthening on at least 3 days a week. Supervise strength training and technique. Older adults Combine aerobic, strength and balance training to reduce falls, preserve muscle and bone, and keep independence. Start gently and allow more recovery. Pregnancy Regular moderate activity is generally recommended with medical advice. Avoid contact or fall-risk activity and overheating, and adjust as pregnancy progresses.

Overweight and obesity Build up gradually, using lower-impact activities that protect the joints, and combine with diet changes. More time per week helps weight management. Type 2 diabetes Combine aerobic and resistance exercise on most days, and monitor blood glucose and its link with food and medication. Hypertension Regular moderate aerobic activity lowers blood pressure. Avoid heavy lifting with breath-holding, which sharply raises blood pressure. Established heart disease Start with medical clearance and supervision, at low to moderate intensity, and progress carefully. Exam Tips

Link activity → effect → outcome Don't just list benefits. Write the chain: "Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone-building, which raises bone density and lowers the risk of osteoporosis." Use the guideline numbers Quote them: adults need 150–300 minutes of moderate (or 75–150 minutes of vigorous) activity a week, with muscle-strengthening on at least 2 days. Numbers show precise knowledge. Classify determinants Sort factors into personal, social, environmental and economic, and give a specific example of each. Check the IB command terms .

For HL prescription questions, name the group's need Say why the plan differs: older adults need balance work to prevent falls, and people with hypertension should avoid breath-holding heavy lifts. Common mistake Don't write that "more exercise is always better for health". Gains get smaller at higher amounts, and very high loads with poor recovery can increase injury and infection risk. Moderate, regular activity is the key message. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State the minimum amount of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week recommended for adults by the World Health Organization. 1 mark Answer Model answer

150 minutes per week (the recommended range is 150–300 minutes of moderate activity, or 75–150 minutes of vigorous activity). 2 Outline two environmental determinants of physical activity levels. 2 marks Answer Model answer Access to safe parks, sports facilities and walking or cycling routes. Climate and weather, such as extreme heat or cold, which can reduce outdoor activity. Neighbourhood design and safety, for example how walkable it is, traffic, lighting or air pollution. Any two. 3 (HL) Outline three factors to consider when prescribing exercise for an older adult. 3 marks Answer Model answer

Health screening: medical history, medication and any conditions, with medical clearance where needed. Include balance and strength training as well as aerobic activity, to reduce the risk of falls and preserve muscle and bone. Start at a low intensity and progress gradually, allowing longer recovery between sessions. Any three. Enjoyment, social support and joint health are also accepted. 4 Explain how regular physical activity reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes. 3 marks Answer Model answer Muscle contraction increases glucose uptake into muscle cells, which lowers blood glucose. Regular activity increases insulin sensitivity, so cells respond better to insulin and less insulin is needed.

It reduces body fat, especially around the abdomen, which reduces insulin resistance. 5 Explain the relationship between training load and the risk of infection. 4 marks Answer Model answer The relationship is J-shaped: infection risk is lowest with regular moderate activity. Regular moderate activity improves immune function, for example by improving immune surveillance and reducing chronic inflammation, so the risk of infection is lower than for a sedentary person. Very heavy training loads with too little recovery, sleep or fuel can temporarily suppress immune function, so the risk of infection rises.

At very high loads the risk may exceed that of a sedentary person; adequate recovery and nutrition reduce this. A.3.3 Fatigue & Recovery (HL) | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme A › A.3.3 A.3.3 Theme A · Response HL only Fatigue & Recovery Why performance falls during exercise, how to tell when an athlete has recovered, and which nutrition, sleep and recovery techniques work best, and when. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

This whole topic is Higher Level only. Fatigue is a reduction in the ability to produce force or keep up performance. It can start in the brain and nervous system ( central fatigue ) or in the working muscles ( peripheral fatigue ), and it is influenced by fuel, hydration, electrolytes and energy availability. Recovery is the process of restoring the body and mind after exercise. Good recovery depends on matching the strategy (nutrition, sleep and techniques such as cooling or compression) to the cause of the fatigue, the time available and the individual athlete. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Distinguish between central and peripheral fatigue, and explain their neuromuscular and metabolic causes. Explain how hydration, electrolytes and energy availability influence fatigue. Describe recovery processes and timescales, and classify indicators of recovery. Outline hydration and nutritional strategies for recovery. Evaluate recovery techniques and the factors that influence recovery quality, including sleep. Key Terms Fatigue A reduction in the ability to produce force or maintain performance. Central fatigue Fatigue from the nervous system, with less neural drive to the muscles. Peripheral fatigue Fatigue within or near the working muscles, reducing force or speed.

Recovery Restoring the body and mind after exercise so performance can return. Active recovery Low-intensity exercise after hard exercise, such as a cool-down jog or easy cycling. DOMS Delayed onset muscle soreness: aching that peaks 24–72 hours after unfamiliar or hard exercise. Presentations A.3.3.1 Fatigue A.3.3.2 Recovery from Exercise Deep Dive Where does fatigue come from? For a muscle to contract, a signal has to travel from the brain, down the spinal cord and motor neuron, across the neuromuscular junction, through the muscle fibre membrane, and then the muscle needs energy to run the cross-bridges. Fatigue can arise at any point along this chain.

Where central and peripheral fatigue occur along the pathway from brain to muscle, and some possible causes. These are contributors; several often act together. Central fatigue Peripheral fatigue Site Brain and spinal cord (nervous system) Neuromuscular junction and muscle What goes wrong Reduced neural drive and voluntary activation, lower motivation, higher perceived effort The muscle produces less force or speed, even when the drive is high Examples Late in an ultramarathon in the heat; a long, monotonous session The last 30 m of a 100 m sprint (PC depletion, H⁺); the end of a marathon (glycogen) Metabolic causes, fuel, hydration and energy availability

Fuel: in very short, maximal efforts phosphocreatine runs down. In long events, falling muscle and liver glycogen means ATP cannot be made fast enough, and low blood glucose also affects the brain (central fatigue). Metabolic by-products: hydrogen ions (lowering pH), phosphate and ADP accumulate in intense exercise, impairing muscle contraction. Hydration and electrolytes: dehydration reduces blood volume and stroke volume, raises heart rate and core temperature, and makes the effort feel harder. Sodium and potassium imbalances impair nerve and muscle function (see A.2.1).

Energy availability: when energy intake is persistently too low for the training load, fatigue becomes chronic and recovery is poor (see A.2.2). Heat: a raised core temperature increases the sense of effort and reduces neural drive. Recovery processes and timescales Different systems recover at different speeds. Phosphocreatine is restored in a few minutes, so short rests between sprints help repeat performance. Glycogen and tissue repair take much longer, so they need days of planning during a tournament or heavy training block. Approximate recovery timescales on a logarithmic time axis. Real values depend on the exercise, the athlete and the recovery strategies used. Indicators of recovery

Strong answers classify the signs of recovery into three types: Type What it shows Examples Physiological Measurable body changes Heart rate and breathing back to resting; blood lactate returned to resting level; body temperature and hydration normal (urine colour, body mass); resting heart rate and heart rate variability; performance tests such as a jump height Symptomatic What the athlete feels in the body Muscle soreness and stiffness (DOMS), general tiredness, sleep quality, appetite Psychological Mood and readiness Motivation, mood, concentration and feeling ready to train, often tracked with simple daily wellness questionnaires

If an athlete's performance, mood and sleep keep getting worse and a raised resting heart rate or frequent illness appear despite rest, they may be overreaching or have overtraining syndrome , and the training load must be reduced. Hydration and nutritional strategies for recovery Strategy Purpose and typical guidance Fluids and sodium Replace sweat losses: drink about 125–150% of the body mass lost over the next hours, with sodium from food or drinks, because urine production continues.

Carbohydrate Restore glycogen. When there is less than about 8 hours before the next session, aim for roughly 1.0–1.2 g per kg of body mass per hour for the first 4 hours. If there is plenty of time, normal meals are enough. Protein Provides amino acids to repair and rebuild muscle. About 0.25–0.3 g per kg (roughly 20–25 g) in each meal, spread across the day. Combined with carbohydrate it can help refuelling when carbohydrate intake is low. Overall energy Eating enough total energy supports every recovery process (see A.2.2).

A strategy is only useful if it matches the demands of the event, the cause of fatigue, the time available and what the athlete can tolerate. A day-before-match recovery shake is helpful; the same plan after an easy session is probably unnecessary. Matching the main cause of fatigue to a suitable recovery strategy. This is a guide, not a rule: the right choice depends on the athlete and the schedule. Recovery techniques Active recovery and cool-down: light exercise keeps blood flowing and helps clear lactate faster than complete rest, and is a practical routine. It does not greatly speed up tissue repair.

Cold-water immersion: typically 10–15 minutes in water at about 10–15 °C. It can reduce soreness and perceived fatigue in the short term and lower core temperature after hot exercise. Repeated use straight after strength training may reduce muscle growth adaptations. Thermotherapy (heat or cold methods): heat such as a hot bath or sauna increases blood flow and promotes relaxation; contrast therapy alternates hot and cold. Evidence for performance benefits is limited. Compression garments: may modestly reduce soreness and perceived fatigue, with little clear effect on performance.

Massage and foam rolling: reduce soreness and improve how recovered an athlete feels, but evidence of faster physiological recovery is small. Sleep: the most important recovery tool. Growth hormone is released and tissue repair, learning and immune function all benefit. Most adults need about 7–9 hours, and athletes in heavy training often need more. Poor sleep impairs reaction time, decision-making, mood and recovery. Factors that influence recovery quality

Recovery is individual. Factors include the type, intensity and length of exercise (unfamiliar or eccentric work causes more muscle damage), age and training status , nutrition and hydration , sleep , psychological stress , the environment (heat and altitude) and the schedule , including travel across time zones. A good recovery plan is chosen using these factors and then reviewed, using the indicators above. Exam Tips Name the site of the fatigue Say "central: reduced neural drive from the brain" or "peripheral: phosphocreatine depleted in the muscle". Name the cause and the place.

Classify the indicators For recovery indicators, sort them into physiological, symptomatic and psychological, and give a measurable example of each. Evaluate with balance For "evaluate" or "discuss", give benefits and limits, then a conclusion that depends on the athlete, event and time available. Check the IB command terms . Match the strategy to the cause Glycogen depletion needs carbohydrate, dehydration needs fluid and sodium, and central fatigue needs sleep and reduced load. Show you can choose, not just list.

Common mistake Don't assume fatigue is only "the muscles running out of energy". Central fatigue matters too, especially in long, hot events. And don't claim that lactate causes next-day soreness: lactate is cleared within about an hour, and DOMS is linked to muscle damage and inflammation. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State one cause of peripheral fatigue during a 100 m sprint. 1 mark Answer Model answer Depletion of phosphocreatine in the muscle, or accumulation of hydrogen ions, phosphate and ADP in the muscle (any one). 2 Distinguish between central and peripheral fatigue. 2 marks Answer Model answer

Central fatigue occurs in the nervous system (brain and spinal cord), when there is reduced neural drive or voluntary activation to the muscles. Peripheral fatigue occurs at or within the muscle (including the neuromuscular junction), when the muscle produces less force even if the drive is high. 3 Outline three indicators of recovery, using the categories physiological, symptomatic and psychological. 3 marks Answer Model answer Physiological: for example heart rate returning to its resting level, or blood lactate returning to normal. Symptomatic: for example reduced muscle soreness or improved sleep quality. Psychological: for example improved mood, motivation or feeling ready to train.

4 Describe the hydration and nutritional strategies an athlete should use in the hours after a hard training session when they have a further session the next morning. 3 marks Answer Model answer Drink about 125–150% of the body mass lost as fluid, together with sodium, to restore hydration. Eat carbohydrate soon after exercise and in the following hours (about 1.0–1.2 g per kg per hour for the first 4 hours) to restore muscle glycogen. Include protein (about 20–25 g) in meals to supply amino acids for muscle repair. 5 Evaluate the use of cold-water immersion as a recovery technique. 4 marks Answer Model answer Benefit: it can reduce muscle soreness and perceived fatigue in the short term.

Benefit: it can lower core temperature quickly after hot exercise, which helps when there is a short time between events. Limitation: evidence that it speeds up physiological recovery or improves later performance is modest, and regular use after strength training may reduce muscle adaptations. Conclusion: it is most useful for short-term recovery between competitions or in hot conditions, and less suitable during a training block aimed at building strength; the decision depends on the athlete and the schedule. B.1.1 Anatomical Position, Planes & Movement | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.1.1 B.1.1 Theme B · Generating Movement in the Body SL & HL Anatomical Position, Planes & Movement The shared language of movement: how to describe where things are on the body, which way joints move, and in which plane and around which axis. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

To analyse movement, everyone needs the same reference system. The anatomical position is the standard starting point, and directional terms such as anterior and distal describe where one body part is relative to another. The skeleton gives the body its framework, and is split into an axial and an appendicular part. Movements at joints happen in planes (sagittal, frontal and transverse) and rotate around axes at right angles to those planes. At higher level, you also study anthropometry : measuring the size and proportions of the body and applying the results in sport and design. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Describe the anatomical position and use directional terms correctly. Outline the axial and appendicular skeleton and the functions of the skeleton. Identify the sagittal, frontal and transverse planes and the axis of rotation for each. Name the movements at the main joints and the plane in which each occurs. HL: Explain how anthropometric measurements are used in sport, health and design. Key Terms Anatomical position Standing upright, facing forward, arms by the sides, palms facing forward, feet together or slightly apart. Plane of movement An imaginary flat surface through the body in which a movement takes place.

Axis of rotation The imaginary line, at right angles to the plane, around which a body part rotates. Flexion A movement that decreases the angle at a joint. Abduction Movement of a limb away from the midline of the body. Anthropometry (HL) The measurement of the size, shape and proportions of the human body. Presentations B.1.1.1 The Human Skeleton B.1.1.2 Planes and Axes B.1.1.3 Anthropometry Deep Dive Anatomical position and directional terms

In the anatomical position the body stands upright and faces forward, with the arms by the sides, palms facing forward, and the feet together or slightly apart and pointing forward. All movement and location terms are described from this position, even when the performer is moving or upside down. This means the terms always mean the same thing to everyone. The figure is in anatomical position. The four pairs of directional terms describe where one structure is relative to another. Term Meaning Example Superior / inferior Towards the head / towards the feet The head is superior to the chest. Anterior / posterior Towards the front / towards the back The quadriceps are on the anterior thigh.

Medial / lateral Towards the midline / away from the midline The little toe is lateral to the big toe. Proximal / distal Nearer to / further from the trunk (or the point of attachment) The elbow is proximal to the wrist. Superficial / deep Nearer to / further from the surface of the body The skin is superficial to the muscles. The skeleton: axial and appendicular An adult skeleton has 206 bones. It is divided into two parts: Axial skeleton (80 bones) Appendicular skeleton (126 bones) Parts Skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum Pectoral (shoulder) girdle, arms and hands, pelvic girdle, legs and feet

Main roles Protects the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs; supports the head and trunk; central axis for posture Allows movement of the limbs, for locomotion and manipulation of objects Sport link Ribcage protects organs in contact sports; the spine supports the trunk in all lifting and throwing Leg bones act as levers in running and jumping; arm bones in throwing and hitting The skeleton as a whole has five main functions: support (framework for the body), protection of organs, movement (bones act as levers and muscles pull on them), storage of minerals such as calcium and phosphorus, and blood cell production in red bone marrow. Planes and axes

Movements at joints take place in planes , and the body part rotates around an axis . The axis is always at right angles to the plane of movement. The three planes through a figure in anatomical position, the three axes of rotation, and a summary of the movements in each plane. The axis is perpendicular to its plane. Sagittal plane: divides the body into left and right. Forward and backward movements such as flexion and extension happen here, around the frontal axis (also called the mediolateral axis).

Frontal plane (also called the coronal plane): divides the body into front and back. Sideways movements such as abduction and adduction happen here, around the sagittal axis (also called the anteroposterior axis). Transverse plane (also called the horizontal plane): divides the body into upper and lower parts. Rotation happens here, around the longitudinal axis (also called the vertical axis). Many sporting movements combine planes. A golf swing is mainly rotation in the transverse plane, with flexion and extension in the sagittal plane, and a tennis serve uses all three. Joint movements Movement Description Plane Example

Flexion Decreases the angle at a joint Sagittal Bending the elbow in a biceps curl Extension Increases the angle at a joint; hyperextension is extension beyond the normal range Sagittal Straightening the knee when kicking Abduction Moves a limb away from the midline Frontal Raising the arm sideways in a lateral raise Adduction Moves a limb towards the midline Frontal Bringing the leg back in after a star jump Medial (internal) and lateral (external) rotation Turning a limb towards or away from the midline around its long axis Transverse Rotating the arm in a tennis serve or throw

Horizontal flexion and extension With the arm at shoulder height, moving it forward across the body (flexion) or backward (extension) Transverse The forehand and backhand in tennis Circumduction A circular movement combining flexion, extension, abduction and adduction All planes A bowler's arm in cricket, or a swimmer's arm circle Plantarflexion and dorsiflexion Pointing the toes down / pulling the toes up towards the shin Sagittal Push-off in sprinting / landing from a jump Pronation and supination Forearm rotation so the palm faces down / up (when the elbow is bent) Transverse Top-spin and slice in tennis, or a screwdriver action

Inversion and eversion Turning the sole of the foot inwards / outwards Frontal Ankle sprains often involve too much inversion Elevation and depression Raising / lowering the shoulder girdle Frontal Shrugging the shoulders Schematic joint movements. Sagittal and frontal panels are side and front views (facing right); the transverse panels are top views, with the front of the body at the top. Grey dotted lines show the starting position. Anthropometry HL

Anthropometry is the measurement of the size, shape and proportions of the human body. Common measurements include height (stature), body mass, limb and segment lengths, arm span, circumferences, skinfold thickness and body composition, and indices such as body mass index (BMI) and waist-to-hip ratio. Application How it is used Talent identification and selection Some sports favour certain body dimensions, such as height and arm span in basketball and swimming, which helps coaches spot potential. It should be used with skill and fitness tests, because young athletes grow at different rates.

Equipment and workspace design (ergonomics) Bike frames, saddle height, bat and club length, and racing boat seats are fitted to body dimensions, improving efficiency and reducing injury risk. Biomechanical analysis Limb lengths and segment masses affect leverage, torque and movement efficiency, and are used in movement analysis. Health and growth monitoring BMI, waist circumference and body composition screen for health risks, and growth measurements track young athletes' development. Fair competition Body mass is used for weight categories in sports such as boxing and judo.

Anthropometric measures have limits. For example, BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so a muscular athlete can be labelled "overweight". Results should be combined with other information. Exam Tips Name the joint action first Identify the joint and its action (for example "knee extension"), then say the plane. Don't just say "the leg moves". Axis is perpendicular to the plane Say "sagittal plane, around the frontal axis". A quick check is that the axis always points in the one direction that is not in the plane.

Describe movements from anatomical position Say which way the body part moves relative to the anatomical position, even if the athlete is upside down mid-somersault. Check the IB command terms . Use precise terms in a sequence For a skill such as a jump, list the joints in order (hip, knee, ankle) and name the action at each, such as extension, extension and plantarflexion. Common mistake Don't confuse planes with axes. The movement in the sagittal plane (flexion and extension) happens around the frontal axis , not the sagittal axis. The sagittal axis is for abduction and adduction. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it.

1 Define anatomical position . 1 mark Answer Model answer The standard reference position for describing the body: standing upright, facing forward, with arms by the sides, palms facing forward and feet forward. 2 Identify the plane of movement and the axis of rotation for a biceps curl. 2 marks Answer Model answer Sagittal plane. Frontal (mediolateral) axis. 3 Distinguish between the axial and the appendicular skeleton. 2 marks Answer Model answer The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum, and mainly supports the trunk and protects organs such as the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs.

The appendicular skeleton is the limbs and the girdles that attach them (shoulder and pelvic girdles), and mainly allows movement. 4 Describe the joint actions at the hip, knee and ankle during the take-off phase of a vertical jump. 3 marks Answer Model answer Hip extension. Knee extension. Ankle plantarflexion. (All of these movements take place in the sagittal plane.) 5 (HL) Explain two ways anthropometric measurements can be used in sport. 4 marks Answer Model answer

Talent identification: measurements such as height or arm span can show whether a young athlete has dimensions that suit a sport (for example basketball or swimming), helping to select or guide them (1 mark for use, 1 for explanation). Equipment fitting and ergonomics: measurements of limb lengths are used to size equipment such as bike frames and saddle height or club length, which improves efficiency and reduces injury risk (1 mark for use, 1 for explanation). Other accepted uses: weight categories, monitoring growth in young athletes, or analysing leverage in technique. Back to ← Theme B Next topic B.1.2 Connective Tissues & Joints →

B.1.2 Structure & Function of Connective Tissues & Joints | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.1.2 B.1.2 Theme B · Generating Movement in the Body SL & HL Structure & Function of Connective Tissues & Joints The tissues that link muscle to bone and bone to bone, and the joints that trade off movement against stability. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Movement needs more than muscles and bones. Connective tissues link and support everything: tendons join muscle to bone, ligaments join bone to bone, cartilage cushions and smooths joint surfaces, and fascia wraps and connects muscles. Where bones meet, joints can be fibrous (fixed), cartilaginous (slightly movable) or synovial (freely movable). Each design is a trade-off: the more freedom a joint has, the more it relies on ligaments and muscles to keep it stable. By the end of this topic you should be able to Describe the structure and function of the main connective tissues: tendons, ligaments, cartilage, bone and fascia. Distinguish between fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints.

Describe the structure of a synovial joint and the function of each part. Name the classes of synovial joint, the movements each allows and an example of each. Explain the factors that affect joint stability and how connective tissues work together in movement. Key Terms Connective tissue Tissue that supports, connects and protects other tissues, made of cells in a fibre-rich matrix. Tendon A strong cord of connective tissue joining muscle to bone. Ligament A strong band of connective tissue joining bone to bone and stabilising a joint. Articular cartilage Smooth cartilage covering the ends of bones at a synovial joint. Synovial fluid The lubricating fluid in a synovial joint cavity.

Synovial joint A freely movable joint with a fluid-filled cavity between the bones. Presentation B.1.2 Connective Tissues and Joints Deep Dive Connective tissues: structure and function Connective tissues are made of cells scattered in an extracellular matrix . The matrix contains protein fibres: collagen gives strength when pulled (tensile strength), and elastin gives stretch and recoil. The arrangement of the fibres decides what each tissue is good at. Tissue Structure Function Sporting example

Tendon Dense regular connective tissue: tightly packed collagen fibres lined up in parallel, with few blood vessels Joins muscle to bone and transmits the force of muscle contraction to the bone; stores and releases some elastic energy The Achilles tendon in running and jumping Ligament Dense regular connective tissue: collagen fibres in parallel, with some elastin; a little more flexible than tendon; few blood vessels Joins bone to bone, stabilises joints and limits excessive or unwanted movement The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) in the knee when sidestepping

Cartilage Firm, flexible tissue with collagen in a gel-like matrix; no blood supply. Hyaline cartilage covers joint surfaces; fibrocartilage is tougher Reduces friction and absorbs shock; fibrocartilage forms discs and menisci that cushion joints Knee menisci absorbing landing forces Bone Collagen strengthened with calcium phosphate minerals, with a blood supply and marrow Support, protection, levers for movement, mineral storage, blood cell production The femur transmitting forces in running

Fascia Sheets of connective tissue wrapping muscles, groups of muscles and organs Holds muscles in place, reduces friction between them, and helps transmit force The thick fascia on the sole of the foot (plantar fascia) Tendons, ligaments and cartilage have a poor blood supply , so they heal slowly after injury. They also adapt slowly to training, which is one reason why training load should increase gradually. Tendon or ligament? Tendon Ligament Joins Muscle to bone Bone to bone Main role Transmits muscle force to move the bone Stabilises the joint and limits excess movement Injury Strain or tendinopathy (see B.3) Sprain (see B.3) Three types of joint

A joint (articulation) is where two bones, or bone and cartilage, meet. The three structural types are: The three structural types of joint. More freedom of movement means a more complex joint and a greater need for ligaments and muscles to keep it stable. Structure of a synovial joint Most of the joints used in sport are synovial. The bone ends are covered with smooth articular cartilage and enclosed in a capsule, with a fluid-filled space between them. A simplified synovial joint. Cartilage covers the bone ends, the capsule encloses the joint, and ligaments and tendons add stability and movement.

Articular cartilage covers the bone ends, giving a smooth, low-friction surface that absorbs some shock. Joint (synovial) cavity and synovial fluid: the fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction, supplies nutrients to the cartilage (which has no blood supply of its own), absorbs shock and removes waste. Synovial membrane: lines the capsule and makes the synovial fluid. Fibrous capsule: a tough sleeve of connective tissue that encloses the joint and holds the bones together. Ligaments: strengthen the capsule and stop movement beyond the normal range.

Other structures: menisci (fibrocartilage pads in the knee) deepen the joint and absorb shock, and bursae (small fluid-filled sacs) reduce friction between tendons, muscles and bone. Classes of synovial joint The shape of the bone ends decides how many ways a synovial joint can move. The six classes of synovial joint. The knee is usually described as a modified hinge, because it also allows a small amount of rotation when bent. Stability, mobility and training

There is a trade-off between mobility (range of movement) and stability (resistance to dislocation). The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint with a shallow socket, so it has a huge range but is easily dislocated and relies on ligaments and the surrounding muscles (the rotator cuff). The hip has a deep socket and strong ligaments, so it is more stable but has a smaller range. Joint stability depends on: the shape of the bone ends and how well they fit together; ligaments and the joint capsule ; the muscles and tendons crossing the joint, which can be strengthened by training; cartilage and fascia around the joint.

During an explosive movement such as a jump, these tissues work as a team: muscles contract and tendons transmit and store force, ligaments keep the joints in line, and cartilage and fascia absorb and spread the load on landing. Regular, gradually progressed training can increase the strength and stiffness of tendons and the strength of bone, and keeps cartilage healthy through moderate loading. A warm-up raises tissue temperature and makes it easier to stretch. Exam Tips Link structure to function Don't just define. Say why it suits the job: "Tendons have parallel collagen fibres, so they resist large pulling forces from the muscle."

Learn the synovial joint parts and a job for each Cartilage reduces friction, synovial fluid lubricates and feeds the cartilage, the capsule encloses the joint, and ligaments stabilise it. Check the IB command terms . Match joint class to movement Name the joint class, the movements it allows and an example, such as "hinge joint at the elbow: flexion and extension only". Use the stability and mobility trade-off For comparison questions (shoulder and hip, for instance), refer to the depth of the socket, ligaments and muscles.

Common mistake Don't mix up tendons and ligaments: tendons join muscle to bone , ligaments join bone to bone . And don't describe every joint as synovial: some are fibrous or cartilaginous. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State the function of a ligament. 1 mark Answer Model answer A ligament joins bone to bone, stabilising the joint and limiting excessive movement. 2 Outline two functions of synovial fluid. 2 marks Answer Model answer It lubricates the joint, reducing friction between the cartilage surfaces. It supplies nutrients to the articular cartilage and removes waste. It helps absorb shock. Any two.

3 Identify the class of synovial joint at the shoulder and at the elbow, and state the movement each allows. 3 marks Answer Model answer The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint. This allows movement in all planes: flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and rotation (and circumduction). The elbow is a hinge joint, allowing flexion and extension only. 4 Explain why the shoulder joint is more mobile but less stable than the hip joint. 3 marks Answer Model answer The shoulder socket is shallow and the head of the humerus is large relative to it, allowing a wide range of movement.

The hip socket is deep and the ball fits tightly, with strong ligaments, so the hip is more stable but has a smaller range. The shoulder therefore relies more on muscles, tendons and ligaments (the rotator cuff) for stability and is more prone to dislocation. 5 Discuss how connective tissues work together to support joint stability and efficiency during an explosive movement such as a jump. 4 marks Answer Model answer Tendons transmit the force of muscle contraction to the bones to produce movement, and can store and release elastic energy to improve jump efficiency. Ligaments hold the bones in position and limit excessive movement, especially on landing.

Articular cartilage and menisci reduce friction and absorb shock during take-off and landing. Fascia transmits force between muscles and supports them; together these tissues protect the joint and allow force to be produced and absorbed safely.
