B.1.3 Muscular Function | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.1.3 B.1.3 Theme B · Generating Movement in the Body SL & HL Muscular Function How the nervous system recruits muscle, how different fibre types and contraction types suit different tasks, and how muscles work in teams to move the body. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Skeletal muscles generate the force that moves the bones. Each muscle is controlled in motor units , and different muscle fibre types are suited to different jobs, from marathon running to sprinting. Muscles can produce force while shortening (concentric), lengthening (eccentric) or staying the same length (isometric). They also work in teams, with an agonist producing the movement, an antagonist controlling it, and other muscles assisting and stabilising. At higher level you also study the sliding filament theory , which explains how a muscle shortens at the molecular level. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Describe how a motor neuron activates a muscle, and define a motor unit. Compare type I, type IIa and type IIx muscle fibres and explain how they are recruited. Describe isometric, concentric, eccentric and isokinetic contractions with sporting examples. Identify agonist, antagonist, synergist and fixator roles, and explain reciprocal inhibition. HL: Explain the sliding filament theory, including the roles of calcium, ATP, actin, myosin, troponin and tropomyosin. Key Terms Motor unit A motor neuron and all of the muscle fibres it supplies. Concentric contraction The muscle shortens while producing force.

Eccentric contraction The muscle lengthens while producing force, usually to control a movement. Agonist The main muscle responsible for producing a movement (the prime mover). Reciprocal inhibition When the agonist contracts, the antagonist is signalled to relax so the movement is smooth. Sarcomere (HL) The basic contractile unit of a muscle fibre, from one Z-disc to the next. Presentations B.1.3.1 Muscular Contraction B.1.3.2 Sliding Filament Theory Deep Dive Motor units and recruitment

A muscle contracts when a nerve impulse travels along a motor neuron and crosses the neuromuscular junction, where acetylcholine triggers an action potential in the muscle fibres (see A.1.1). A motor unit is one motor neuron and every muscle fibre it supplies. When a motor neuron fires, all its fibres contract together (the all-or-none principle). Muscles that need fine control, such as those moving the fingers or eye, have small motor units with only a few fibres each. Muscles that need power, such as the quadriceps, have large motor units with hundreds or thousands of fibres.

The body controls force in two ways: by recruiting more motor units, and by firing each unit more often. Motor units are normally recruited from smallest to largest (the size principle ), so low-force tasks use small, slow units first, and large, fast units are only added when more force or speed is needed. Muscle fibre types Type I (slow oxidative) Type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic) Type IIx (fast glycolytic) Contraction speed Slow Fast Fastest Force produced Low Moderate to high Highest Resistance to fatigue High Moderate Low Mitochondria, capillaries and myoglobin Many (appears red) Many to moderate Fewer (appears paler)

Main energy system Oxidative Oxidative and glycolytic Phosphagen and glycolytic Sporting use Marathon running, posture 800 m, rowing, 100 m swim Sprinting, jumping, maximal lifts The proportion of each fibre type differs between people. It is strongly influenced by genetics, so elite endurance athletes tend to have more type I fibres in their leg muscles, and elite sprinters have more type II. Training can improve the fatigue resistance of type II fibres (for example, type IIx fibres take on type IIa features with endurance training), but it cannot change a person's fibre-type mix very much.

Recruitment by effort, following the size principle. Type I fibres are used at all effort levels; type IIa and IIx fibres are added as the demand for force rises. Percentages are approximate. Types of muscular contraction Type Muscle length Role in movement Example Concentric Shortens Produces movement and accelerates the body or a limb Lifting phase of a biceps curl; knee extension in a kick Eccentric Lengthens under tension Controls and slows movement, absorbs force and protects joints Lowering phase of a biceps curl; quadriceps on landing from a jump Isometric No change in length (joint does not move) Holds a position and stabilises joints Holding a plank or a gymnast's cross

Isokinetic Changes length at a constant speed against variable resistance Used mostly in testing and rehabilitation Muscle testing on an isokinetic dynamometer Concentric, eccentric and isometric contractions in a biceps curl. In all three the muscle is producing force: what differs is whether its length changes. Eccentric contractions can produce more force than concentric ones and use less energy, but they cause more muscle damage, which is the main cause of delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). In many sporting movements an eccentric contraction is followed straight away by a concentric one (for example in plyometric jumps), which gives extra power from the stored elastic energy.

How muscles work together Agonist (prime mover): the main muscle producing the movement. Antagonist: the muscle that opposes the agonist. It relaxes to allow the movement, and often works eccentrically to slow the limb down at the end. Synergist: a muscle that helps the agonist. Fixator (stabiliser): a muscle that holds a joint or bone steady so the agonist has a firm base to pull from. The nervous system coordinates this through reciprocal inhibition : when the agonist is signalled to contract, the antagonist is signalled to relax, so the movement is smooth and efficient. For control and safety, the antagonist is often active as well, braking the movement. Joint action Agonist Antagonist

Elbow flexion Biceps brachii Triceps brachii Knee extension Quadriceps Hamstrings Hip extension Gluteus maximus Hip flexors (iliopsoas) Ankle plantarflexion Gastrocnemius and soleus Tibialis anterior Shoulder abduction Deltoid Latissimus dorsi and pectoralis major Sliding filament theory HL A muscle fibre is packed with myofibrils , which are made of repeating units called sarcomeres . Each sarcomere contains thin filaments ( actin , with the proteins troponin and tropomyosin ) and thick filaments ( myosin ). In the sliding filament theory, the filaments slide past each other without changing length, which shortens the sarcomere and so the whole muscle.

A sarcomere relaxed and contracted. The thin filaments slide over the thick filaments, pulling the Z-discs closer together. The process, step by step: A nerve impulse reaches the muscle fibre and an action potential spreads along it, causing calcium ions (Ca²⁺) to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds to troponin , which makes tropomyosin move and expose the binding sites on actin . A myosin head, already holding ADP and phosphate, binds to actin and forms a cross-bridge . The head pivots (the power stroke ), pulling the actin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere, and ADP and phosphate are released.

A new ATP molecule binds to myosin, which makes the head detach from actin. The ATP is split, re-cocking the head so that it can bind again. The cycle repeats while calcium and ATP are available. When the nerve signal stops, calcium is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, tropomyosin blocks the binding sites again, and the muscle relaxes. The cross-bridge cycle. ATP is needed both for the power stroke cycle (to detach and re-cock the head) and to pump calcium back after contraction.

Without ATP, myosin heads cannot detach from actin, which is why muscles become stiff after death (rigor mortis). During exercise, running short of ATP, or an increase in the by-products of ATP use, contributes to fatigue (see A.3.3). Exam Tips Anchor each contraction type to length Always state what happens to muscle length: concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens under tension, isometric stays the same, with force produced in all three. Name the agonist and the antagonist Give both for a joint action, such as "knee extension: quadriceps (agonist), hamstrings (antagonist)", and mention reciprocal inhibition if asked about control.

Link fibre type to the sport Name the type, its feature (speed, force, fatigue resistance) and the activity it suits. Check the IB command terms . For sliding filament (HL), keep the sequence Calcium → troponin → tropomyosin moves → myosin binds actin → power stroke → ATP binds → detach. Name the job of each molecule. Common mistake Eccentric does not mean the muscle is relaxed or switched off. It lengthens while producing force. Likewise, the antagonist is not simply "off": it is often working eccentrically to control the movement. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define motor unit . 1 mark Answer Model answer

A motor neuron and all of the muscle fibres that it supplies (innervates). 2 Distinguish between concentric and eccentric muscle contractions. 2 marks Answer Model answer In a concentric contraction the muscle shortens while producing force, causing or accelerating movement. In an eccentric contraction the muscle lengthens while producing force, controlling or slowing the movement. 3 Outline three differences between type I and type IIx muscle fibres. 3 marks Answer Model answer Type I fibres contract slowly, whereas type IIx fibres contract fast. Type I fibres produce lower force, whereas type IIx fibres produce high force.

Type I fibres are highly resistant to fatigue, whereas type IIx fibres fatigue quickly. Type I fibres have more mitochondria, capillaries and myoglobin, and rely on the oxidative system; type IIx fibres rely on anaerobic energy systems. Any three. 4 Identify the agonist and antagonist during knee extension in a football kick, and explain the role of reciprocal inhibition. 3 marks Answer Model answer The agonist is the quadriceps and the antagonist is the hamstrings. Reciprocal inhibition is when the nervous system signals the antagonist to relax as the agonist contracts. This allows the agonist to move the joint smoothly and efficiently without working against the antagonist.

5 (HL) Explain the roles of calcium and ATP in the sliding filament theory. 4 marks Answer Model answer Calcium ions are released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and bind to troponin, which moves tropomyosin away and exposes the binding sites on actin. The myosin heads can then bind to actin, forming cross-bridges. The energy from splitting ATP is used to re-cock the myosin head (and powers the power stroke), which pulls the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere. A new ATP molecule must bind to myosin for the head to detach from actin, so that the cycle can repeat. B.1.4 Levers in Movement & Sport | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.1.4 B.1.4 Theme B · Generating Movement in the Body SL & HL Levers in Movement & Sport How bones, joints and muscles act as levers, why the body trades force for speed and range of movement, and how sports equipment extends the body’s own levers. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

A lever is a rigid bar that turns around a fixed point (the fulcrum ) when a force (the effort ) is applied to move a load . In the body, bones act as levers, joints as fulcrums and muscles provide the effort. The class of a lever depends on the order of the fulcrum, effort and load. The lengths of the effort arm and load arm decide whether the lever gives a mechanical advantage (less force needed) or a mechanical disadvantage (more force needed, but more speed and range of movement). Most levers in the body are third class, which is why human limbs are good at fast, wide movements. Sports equipment such as a bat or racket extends the body's own levers.

By the end of this topic you should be able to Identify the fulcrum, effort and load in a lever, inside and outside the body. Classify a lever as first, second or third class. Explain mechanical advantage and disadvantage using the effort arm and load arm. Calculate the effort force needed and the mechanical advantage using torque. Explain why most body levers are third class and how lever length affects speed. Key Terms Fulcrum The fixed point (pivot) about which a lever turns. In the body, a joint. Effort The force applied to move the load. In the body, usually muscle force. Load The resistance being moved, such as body weight or a weight held in the hand.

Torque (moment of force) The turning effect of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the fulcrum. Mechanical advantage Effort arm ÷ load arm. Above 1, less effort force is needed than the load. Lever arm The perpendicular distance from the fulcrum to the line of action of a force. Presentation B.1.4.1 Levers Deep Dive Levers in the body Every lever has three parts: a fulcrum (the pivot), an effort (the force that turns the lever) and a load (the resistance). In the body, a bone is the rigid bar, a joint is the fulcrum, a muscle (pulling through its tendon) provides the effort, and the load is the weight of the body part plus anything it carries or pushes against.

The distance from the fulcrum to the effort is the effort arm , and the distance from the fulcrum to the load is the load arm . Lever class is decided by the order of the three parts: The three classes of lever. The class tells you the order of fulcrum, effort and load. Whether there is a mechanical advantage depends on the lengths of the effort and load arms. Class Order Body example (fulcrum, effort, load) Typical effect First Effort – Fulcrum – Load Nodding the head back: the joint between the skull and spine, the neck extensor muscles, and the weight of the head Can change the direction of force; advantage or disadvantage depends on the arm lengths

Second Fulcrum – Load – Effort Rising onto the toes: the ball of the foot, the calf muscles pulling through the Achilles tendon, and body weight Always a mechanical advantage (the effort arm is longer), but slow and with a small range Third Fulcrum – Effort – Load Biceps curl: the elbow joint, the biceps pulling near the elbow, and the weight in the hand Mechanical disadvantage, but speed and a large range at the end of the limb Most levers in the body are third class , because muscles usually attach close to the joint they move. A first-class lever can have either an advantage or a disadvantage, depending on which arm is longer. Torque and mechanical advantage

Torque (the moment of force) is the turning effect of a force about a fulcrum: Torque = force × perpendicular distance from the fulcrum (N m) When a lever is balanced, the turning effect of the effort equals that of the load: Effort × effort arm = Load × load arm Mechanical advantage (MA) compares the arms: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm. If MA is more than 1, a small effort can move a bigger load (a mechanical advantage). If MA is less than 1, the muscle must produce more force than the load (a mechanical disadvantage). Two worked examples with illustrative values. In a biceps curl the biceps must produce seven times the load, whereas in a calf raise the effort is smaller than the load.

Why most body levers sacrifice force for speed and range A third-class lever has a mechanical disadvantage, so the muscle needs a lot of force. In return, a small shortening of the muscle swings the end of the limb through a large distance, so the hand or foot moves quickly and through a large range . This suits sport, where speed, reach and variety of movement matter, such as kicking, throwing, sprinting and swimming. Second-class levers give a force advantage but a small range and slow movement, so they are more suited to heavy, slow tasks such as pushing off the ground.

Because a muscle's line of pull changes as the joint angle changes, the effective effort arm also changes during a movement. The muscle gets better leverage at some angles than others, which is why an exercise may feel hardest at one point in the range. Levers outside the body: sports equipment

Bats, rackets, golf clubs and hockey sticks extend the body's own levers. A longer implement moves its tip faster for the same turning speed of the arms, which gives more speed at impact. However, the longer lever places the weight of the implement and the ball further from the fulcrum, so more torque is needed to swing it. Athletes and coaches choose the length and weight of equipment to balance the two. For the same turning speed, the end of a longer lever travels farther in the same time and so moves faster (v = ω × r). The cost is a greater torque requirement.

The same idea explains why a golfer hits a driver further than a short iron, and why a bowler or thrower using a straight arm can release the ball faster than with a bent arm. Exam Tips Label the three parts first Find the fulcrum, then the effort, then the load, then read off the order. Classify the lever only after that. Show calculation steps and units Write Effort × effort arm = Load × load arm, substitute, then give the answer in newtons (N). Keep distances in metres. Always state the trade-off For third-class levers, say "mechanical disadvantage (more force needed) but greater speed and range of movement". Check the IB command terms .

Use a sporting example Name the joint and muscle (biceps curl at the elbow) or the equipment (a hockey stick) so that your answer is applied, not just a definition. Common mistake Don't call third-class levers "inefficient" and stop there. They give up force but gain speed and range of movement. Also, class alone doesn't give mechanical advantage for a first-class lever: that depends on the lengths of the arms. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define torque . 1 mark Answer Model answer The turning effect of a force about a fulcrum (axis), equal to the force multiplied by its perpendicular distance from the fulcrum.

2 Outline why most levers in the human body are third class. 2 marks Answer Model answer Muscles attach close to the joint (fulcrum), so the effort arm is short and the effort is between the fulcrum and the load. This gives a mechanical disadvantage but allows the end of the limb to move quickly and through a large range of movement. 3 Identify the class of lever, and the fulcrum, effort and load, in a biceps curl. 3 marks Answer Model answer It is a third-class lever (the effort is between the fulcrum and the load). The fulcrum is the elbow joint. The effort is the force of the biceps, and the load is the weight of the forearm and the object in the hand.

4 A weight of 60 N acts at 0.30 m from the elbow. The biceps attaches 0.04 m from the elbow. Calculate the force the biceps must produce, and the mechanical advantage. 3 marks Answer Model answer Effort × effort arm = load × load arm, so E × 0.04 = 60 × 0.30. E = 18 ÷ 0.04 = 450 N. Mechanical advantage = 0.04 ÷ 0.30 = 0.13, which is a mechanical disadvantage (less than 1). 5 Explain how using a longer implement, such as a golf club, affects the speed of the club head at impact and the effort required to swing it. 4 marks Answer Model answer A longer implement is a longer lever, so for the same angular velocity the tip moves further in the same time.

Because tip speed = angular velocity × length, the club head moves faster, so there is more speed at impact. The weight of the club acts further from the fulcrum (the body), so the torque needed to swing it is greater. More muscular effort is needed, so there is a trade-off between speed and the force the performer can produce. B.2.1 Newton's Laws of Motion | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.2.1 B.2.1 Theme B · Forces, Motion & Movement SL & HL Newton's Laws of Motion How forces cause and change movement: the three laws, linear and angular motion, momentum and impulse, and at higher level collisions, friction, work, energy and power. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Every movement in sport follows Newton's three laws . They explain why an athlete needs a force to start moving, how force and mass decide acceleration, and how pushing on the ground moves the body. They apply to linear motion (in a straight line) and angular motion (rotation about an axis). Momentum and impulse link force, time and change of motion, which explains everything from landing safely to hitting a ball further. At higher level, you also study collisions , friction , and work, energy and power . By the end of this topic you should be able to State Newton's three laws and apply them to sport in both linear and angular contexts.

Distinguish between distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration, and interpret a velocity–time graph. Explain momentum and impulse, and use them to explain performance and injury risk. Explain angular motion, moment of inertia, angular momentum and the effect of an eccentric force. HL: Apply conservation of momentum to collisions. HL: Explain friction using the coefficient of friction, and calculate work, energy and power. Key Terms Momentum The quantity of motion of an object: mass × velocity (kg m/s). Impulse Force × time of application; it equals the change in momentum. Ground reaction force (GRF) The force the ground exerts back on a person who pushes on it.

Moment of inertia A body's resistance to a change in rotation; it depends on mass and how far it is from the axis. Angular momentum The quantity of rotation: moment of inertia × angular velocity. Eccentric force A force whose line of action does not pass through the centre of mass, causing rotation. Presentations B.2.1.1 Newton’s Laws of Motion B.2.1.2 Collisions and Momentum B.2.1.3 Friction B.2.1.4 Work Deep Dive Newton's three laws A force is a push or pull, measured in newtons (N). The net force is the total effect of all the forces on an object. The three laws explain how net force affects motion:

Newton's three laws with a sporting illustration of each. In the third law, the ground reaction force (GRF) is what drives a runner forward. First law (inertia): an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at constant velocity, unless a net external force acts on it. Inertia (resistance to a change in motion) increases with mass, so a heavy rugby forward is harder to stop or start than a light winger. Second law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to its mass: F = m × a (force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s²). A sprinter who pushes harder against the blocks accelerates more.

Third law: when one object exerts a force on another, the second exerts an equal and opposite force on the first. The two forces act on different objects. A runner pushes backwards and down on the track, and the ground reaction force pushes the runner forwards and up. A swimmer pushing back on the water is pushed forward. Linear motion and kinematics Quantity Meaning Type Unit Distance The total length of the path travelled Scalar m Displacement The straight-line change in position, with direction Vector m Speed Distance ÷ time Scalar m/s Velocity Displacement ÷ time Vector m/s Acceleration Change in velocity ÷ time Vector m/s²

A scalar has size only; a vector has size and direction. A runner who completes one 400 m lap in 50 s has covered a distance of 400 m, but their displacement is 0 m (they finish where they started), so their average speed is 8 m/s and their average velocity is 0 m/s. Velocity–time graph for a 100 m sprint (illustrative). The slope gives acceleration and the area under the curve gives displacement. Momentum and impulse Momentum is mass × velocity ( p = mv , in kg m/s). To change an object's momentum, a force must act for some time. The product is the impulse : Impulse = force × time = change in momentum

This explains many sporting techniques. A follow-through in golf, tennis or throwing lengthens the time the force is applied to the ball, which increases the impulse and so the speed of the ball. In the opposite case, when landing, the athlete must lose a fixed amount of momentum. Bending the knees makes the stopping time longer, so the peak force on the bones and joints is lower. Two landings with the same change in momentum (equal areas). The longer contact time of a bent-knee landing means a much lower peak force. Values are illustrative. Angular motion

Angular motion is rotation about an axis, such as a somersault (axis through the hips) or a golf swing. The key quantities are angular displacement (the angle turned, in degrees or radians), angular velocity (ω, the angle turned per second) and angular acceleration . Newton's laws have angular versions: a body keeps rotating at constant angular velocity unless an external torque acts, torque produces angular acceleration, and torques come in equal and opposite pairs.

Eccentric force: a force whose line of action passes through the centre of mass (a centric force) produces movement without rotation. An eccentric force , applied off-centre, creates torque and so rotation, as well as movement. A footballer who strikes the ball off-centre makes it spin. Moment of inertia (I): resistance to changes in rotation. It depends on the mass and on how far the mass is from the axis: the further away, the greater the moment of inertia. Angular momentum (L = I × ω): the quantity of rotation. In the air, when no external torque acts (ignoring air resistance), angular momentum is conserved .

Left: an off-centre force produces spin. Centre and right: the same angular momentum can be a slow spin with a large moment of inertia, or a fast spin with a small one. Because angular momentum is conserved in flight, a diver or gymnast can control rotation by changing shape. Tucking pulls mass towards the axis, reducing the moment of inertia, so angular velocity increases and the somersault speeds up. Extending the body before entry or landing increases the moment of inertia and slows the rotation. The angular momentum itself is created at take-off by an eccentric force pushing off the board or ground. Collisions and conservation of momentum HL

In a collision with no external force, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after ( conservation of momentum ): m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v₁′ + m₂v₂′. In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved (a bouncing superball); in an inelastic collision some is lost as heat and sound, and the objects may move together (a rugby tackle). Worked example: a 90 kg runner moving at 6 m/s tackles a stationary 100 kg player, and they move together. Momentum before = 90 × 6 = 540 kg m/s. Momentum after = 190 × v. So v = 540 ÷ 190 = 2.8 m/s . Friction HL

Friction is a contact force parallel to the surface that opposes motion or attempted motion between two surfaces. Its maximum size depends on the coefficient of friction (μ), which depends on the two surfaces, and on the normal reaction force (N) pressing them together: Friction = μ × N

For example, if μ = 0.8 and N = 700 N, the maximum friction is 0.8 × 700 = 560 N. Static friction (before sliding) is usually greater than kinetic friction (while sliding). Friction is essential for running, as without it the foot would slip and no forward push could be obtained. Athletes increase friction with studs, spikes and chalk, and reduce it where speed matters, as with skates on ice or waxed skis. A wet surface lowers μ and increases slipping and injury risk. Work, energy and power HL Quantity Equation Unit Example Work W = F × d (distance moved in the direction of the force) joule (J) Lifting 100 kg (about 1000 N) through 0.5 m is 500 J of work

Power P = W ÷ t (or F × v) watt (W) 500 J in 2 s is 250 W Kinetic energy KE = ½ m v² J A 70 kg sprinter at 10 m/s has 3500 J Gravitational potential energy GPE = m g h J A 70 kg high jumper raising their centre of mass 1 m gains about 690 J Power matters in sport because speed of movement matters as much as force: a weightlifter and a sprinter may both produce large forces, but the one who produces the same work in less time has more power. Exam Tips Name the law and apply it Say which law, state it briefly, then apply it to the sport: "Third law: the runner pushes back on the ground and the ground reaction force pushes the runner forward."

Use impulse for "time" questions For landing, follow-through or catching, say: impulse = force × time. A longer time reduces force for the same change in momentum. Link angular momentum to shape For somersaults, say that angular momentum is conserved, so a smaller moment of inertia (tuck) gives a larger angular velocity. Check the IB command terms . Show equations and units Write the equation, substitute, then give the answer with units (N, kg m/s, m/s², J, W). Don't mix up scalars and vectors. Common mistake Action and reaction forces act on different objects, so they don't cancel each other out. Also, don't write that a body "has" a force: say that a force acts on it. Practice Questions

Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State Newton's first law of motion. 1 mark Answer Model answer An object remains at rest, or continues to move at constant velocity, unless acted on by a net (unbalanced) external force. 2 State Newton's third law and give a sporting example. 2 marks Answer Model answer For every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. For example, a swimmer pushes back on the water and is pushed forward; or a runner pushes back and down on the track and the ground reaction force pushes the runner forward and up.

3 (HL) A 90 kg rugby player running at 6 m/s tackles a stationary 100 kg player and they move together. Calculate their velocity immediately after the tackle. 3 marks Answer Model answer Momentum is conserved: momentum before = momentum after. Momentum before = 90 × 6 = 540 kg m/s. 540 = (90 + 100) × v, so v = 2.8 m/s (units required). 4 Explain why bending the knees when landing from a jump reduces the risk of injury. 3 marks Answer Model answer The athlete must lose a fixed amount of momentum on landing, so the impulse is the same. Bending the knees increases the time over which the force acts.

Since impulse = force × time, a longer time means a lower average and peak force, so there is less stress on bones and joints. 5 Explain how a diver can increase the speed of rotation during a somersault and control the entry into the water. 4 marks Answer Model answer Angular momentum is created at take-off by an eccentric force from the board, and is conserved in the air because no external torque acts. Tucking moves mass closer to the axis, reducing the moment of inertia. Since angular momentum = moment of inertia × angular velocity, the angular velocity increases, so the diver rotates faster.

Extending the body before entry increases the moment of inertia and slows the rotation, allowing a controlled entry. B.2.2 Fluid Mechanics | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.2.2 B.2.2 Theme B · Forces, Motion & Movement SL & HL Fluid Mechanics How air and water push back on moving athletes and objects: projectile flight, drag, lift, spin and buoyancy, and how athletes use or avoid them. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Air and water are fluids , and anything moving through them is pushed on by them. For a projectile (a javelin, a ball, or a long jumper in flight) the path depends on release speed, angle and height and on the fluid forces acting on it. At higher level, you study how fluids act on athletes in more detail: drag slows movement, lift acts at right angles to the flow, spin causes the Magnus effect , and buoyancy pushes up on a body in water. Athletes, coaches and equipment designers use these effects to gain an advantage, and governing bodies regulate them. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Describe the factors that affect the flight path of a projectile and the forces that act on it. Explain how release angle, speed and height affect distance in sport. HL: Explain how environmental conditions change the forces acting on athletes and objects. HL: Explain surface, form and wave drag, and how athletes reduce drag. HL: Explain lift, Bernoulli's principle, angle of attack, the Magnus effect and buoyancy. HL: Discuss ethical and regulatory issues in using fluid mechanics to improve performance. Key Terms Projectile An object in flight that is acted on only by gravity and fluid forces such as air resistance. Drag A resistive force that opposes motion through a fluid.

Lift A force at right angles to the direction of fluid flow, caused by a pressure difference. Angle of attack The angle between an object and the direction of the fluid flow. Magnus effect A force that curves the path of a spinning object moving through a fluid. Buoyancy The upward force from a fluid, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. Presentations B.2.2.1 Projectile Motion B.2.2.2 Environmental Conditions B.2.2.3 Buoyancy, Lift and Drag Deep Dive Projectile motion

A projectile is an object moving through the air after release, such as a thrown javelin, a kicked ball or an athlete in the flight phase of a long jump. Once released, the only forces acting on it are its weight (gravity, always downwards) and fluid forces, mainly air resistance (and sometimes lift or a Magnus force). A projectile's initial velocity can be split into a horizontal part (v cos θ) and a vertical part (v sin θ). Without air resistance the horizontal velocity stays constant, while gravity changes the vertical velocity at 9.81 m/s² downwards, which gives the curved, parabola-shaped path. The factors that determine the flight path and distance are:

Release speed: the most important factor. Distance increases with the square of speed, so a small gain in speed gives a big gain in distance. Release angle: if release and landing are at the same height and there is no air resistance, 45° gives the greatest range, and angles that add up to 90° (such as 30° and 60°) give the same range. Release height: releasing from higher up gives a longer flight time and a longer distance. Air resistance, spin and lift: these change the path in real sport. Paths for five release angles at the same speed, with no air resistance and equal release and landing heights. 45° gives the greatest range, and complementary angles give equal ranges.

In real sport the best angle is usually less than 45° . In the shot put the shot is released well above the ground, and the best angle is about 35–40°. In the long jump the athlete takes off at about 20° because a steeper take-off would cost too much horizontal speed. The javelin is thrown at about 30–35°, partly because it generates lift. The path of a projectile released from 1.8 m, with and without air resistance (illustrative). Air resistance shortens the flight and makes the descent steeper. Environmental conditions HL

Air density: thinner air at altitude, or hot or humid air, gives less drag, so projectiles and runners meet less resistance. This helped long distances and sprints at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics. Wind: a tailwind reduces the air speed relative to an athlete and lowers drag; a headwind increases it. Wind affects projectiles and cyclists strongly. Water: the density of the water changes buoyancy. Salt water is denser than fresh water, so swimmers float higher in it. Water temperature also affects thickness (viscosity) and comfort. Drag HL

Drag is a force that opposes motion through a fluid. It increases with the speed (roughly with the square of speed), the frontal area of the body, the shape (streamlined shapes have less drag) and the density of the fluid. Water is much denser than air, so drag in water is far greater than in air. There are three types: The three types of drag. Athletes reduce drag with smoother surfaces, streamlined shapes and (in water) staying below the surface. Surface drag (skin friction): friction between the fluid and the surface of the body or equipment. Smooth suits, shaved skin and swim caps reduce it.

Form drag (pressure drag): caused by the shape and frontal area of the body, which leaves a low-pressure wake behind. A streamlined body position, such as a cyclist in an aerodynamic crouch, reduces it. Wave drag: energy used to make waves at the water surface. It matters for swimmers and rowers, and is reduced by swimming below the surface (as in the underwater phase after a swim start). Cyclists also reduce drag by drafting behind another rider. Drag is not always unwanted: swimmers use hand shape to create useful drag when pushing water backwards, and parachutes, and skydivers use it to slow down. Lift, Bernoulli's principle and the Magnus effect HL

Lift is a force at right angles to the direction of the fluid flow. According to Bernoulli's principle , where a fluid moves faster its pressure is lower, so if the flow is faster on one side of an object than the other, the higher pressure on the slower side pushes the object towards the faster side. The angle of attack (the angle between the object and the oncoming flow) controls how much lift and drag there are: a small angle can increase lift, but too large an angle causes the flow to separate and lift to fall. Discus and javelin throwers, ski jumpers and swimmers sculling their hands all use lift.

The Magnus effect is a sideways force on a spinning ball. The spin drags air round with it, so the air is slowed on one side and speeds up on the other, creating a pressure difference. With topspin the ball dips sooner (a topspin forehand in tennis); with backspin the ball floats further (a golf drive); and with sidespin the ball curves sideways (a bending free kick). Buoyancy is the upward force a fluid exerts on a body in it. It equals the weight of the fluid displaced, so it depends on the density of the fluid and the volume displaced . People with a higher body fat percentage or full lungs float higher, and a wetsuit adds buoyancy, helping a swimmer keep a flatter, less draggy position.
Lift, the Magnus effect and buoyancy. In the Magnus panel, the ball moves to the right, so the air moves to the left relative to the ball. Using fluid mechanics: ethics and regulation HL

Knowing fluid mechanics lets athletes and engineers improve performance through technique (body position, hand shape), equipment (smooth swimsuits, aerodynamic helmets and bikes) and environment (choosing a fast, high-altitude venue). This raises fairness questions. Equipment can be expensive, so wealthy athletes and nations may gain an advantage, and some technology can change results more than athletic skill. Governing bodies therefore set rules: for example, full-body polyurethane swimsuits, which gave large buoyancy and drag benefits, were banned in swimming after the 2008–2009 seasons, and cycling and javelin specifications are tightly controlled. Regulation tries to balance innovation with fair competition.

Exam Tips List the forces on a projectile Weight (gravity) and air resistance, plus lift or Magnus force if it spins. Say that weight always acts downwards. Link angle to the situation 45° is the best angle only for equal release and landing heights with no air resistance. In the shot put, long jump and javelin it is lower, so give the reason. Name the type of drag For "reduce drag" questions, say which type (surface, form or wave) and how: for example, "a tucked position reduces frontal area, so reduces form drag". Check the IB command terms .

Explain Magnus with pressure Describe which side the air is sped up (lower pressure) and which side it is slowed (higher pressure), and the direction of the resulting force on the ball. Common mistake Don't say heavier objects always fall faster or that 45° is always optimal. Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration, and optimal angles change with release height, lift and sport. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State the release angle that gives the greatest range for a projectile released and landing at the same height, ignoring air resistance. 1 mark Answer Model answer 45°.

2 Outline two forces that act on a projectile in flight. 2 marks Answer Model answer Weight (gravity), acting downwards. Air resistance (drag), acting against the direction of motion. (Lift or the Magnus force on a spinning projectile is also accepted.) 3 Describe three factors that influence the horizontal distance travelled by a projectile. 3 marks Answer Model answer Release speed: a higher speed gives a greater distance. Release angle: the angle should be close to the optimum for the situation (45° if heights are equal). Release height: a higher release gives a longer flight time and a longer distance. (Air resistance, spin and lift are also accepted.) Any three.

4 (HL) Explain how a cyclist can reduce form drag and surface drag. 3 marks Answer Model answer Adopting a low, tucked (aerodynamic) position reduces the frontal area, which reduces form drag. Wearing smooth, tight clothing and a helmet, or shaving the legs, reduces the friction between the air and the body, which reduces surface drag. Drafting behind another rider reduces the air resistance on the cyclist. Any three. 5 (HL) Explain how the Magnus effect causes a ball hit with topspin to dip. 4 marks Answer Model answer The ball spins forwards (topspin), so the top surface moves against the oncoming air flow.

The air above the ball is slowed, giving higher pressure on top; the air below is sped up, giving lower pressure underneath. The pressure difference creates a Magnus force acting downwards (from the high pressure to the low pressure). This force adds to gravity, so the ball dips sooner and a shorter, steeper path results. B.2.3 Movement Analysis & Its Applications | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.2.3 B.2.3 Theme B · Forces, Motion & Movement SL & HL Movement Analysis & Its Applications How coaches, scientists and therapists break a movement into phases, measure it and use the results to improve technique, reduce injury risk and guide rehabilitation. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Movement analysis means breaking a movement down so it can be described, measured and improved. Analysts divide a skill into phases (preparation, force production, the critical instant, and follow-through or recovery) and then judge each phase by qualitative methods (careful observation) and quantitative methods (numerical measurement with video, motion capture, force plates, wearable sensors or EMG). The results are used to improve technique, spot movement patterns that raise injury risk, and guide rehabilitation, for example through gait analysis. By the end of this topic you should be able to Describe the phases of movement for discrete and continuous skills.

Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative analysis. Outline the main tools used to analyse movement and what each measures. Interpret simple data such as a force plate graph. Explain how movement analysis is used to improve performance, reduce injury risk and guide rehabilitation. Key Terms Movement analysis Breaking down a movement so that it can be described, measured and improved. Critical instant The key moment of a skill, such as ball contact or release, that decides the outcome. Qualitative analysis Judging movement by observation, using descriptions rather than numbers. Quantitative analysis Measuring movement with numbers, such as angles, speed or force.

Force plate A platform that measures the ground reaction force over time. Gait analysis Analysis of the walking or running cycle, often to check recovery from injury. Presentation B.2.3.1 Phases of Movement Deep Dive Phases of movement Breaking a skill into phases makes it easier to see where a problem starts. For a discrete skill (one with a clear start and end, such as a kick, a throw or a jump) the phases are: Preparation: sets up the movement, with a stable stance, good balance and a backswing or wind-up that lets the muscles stretch.

Force production: the main movement, where muscles create force. The timing and sequence of joint actions, range of motion and the direction of force are key. Critical instant: the key moment that decides the outcome, such as ball contact in a kick or release in a javelin throw. Follow-through: the limb slows down safely after the critical instant, and its path shows the quality of the technique. For a continuous skill such as running, swimming or cycling, the movement repeats in a cycle, so the final phase is a recovery phase that returns the body to the start of the next cycle.

The phases of a football kick (a discrete skill). For each phase the analyst looks at different features, such as balance and posture in preparation and joint angles at the critical instant. Analysis can target joint position, timing, balance, coordination, range of motion, force application or body alignment. For example, in a tennis serve the preparation is the ball toss and the trophy position, the force production is the leg drive and arm swing, the critical instant is contact at full reach, and the follow-through is the racket slowing as it crosses the body. Qualitative and quantitative analysis Qualitative Quantitative

What it is Observation and description of movement quality, often by a coach, teacher or therapist Numerical measurement of movement, such as angles, speed, time and force Example "The elbow drops before release and the follow-through is short." Elbow angle 95° at release; ball speed 24 m/s; contact time 0.18 s Strengths Quick, cheap, needs no equipment, gives immediate feedback Objective, accurate and repeatable, so it can track progress Limitations Subjective and affected by the observer's experience and bias Costly, needs expertise and equipment, and may be hard to use in competition

The two approaches work best together: observation spots what to measure, and data confirms and quantifies it. Tools for analysing movement Some tools measure kinematics (the motion itself: positions, angles, velocity) and some measure kinetics (the forces causing it). Common methods of movement analysis, what each measures and a key limitation. Observation is qualitative; the others are quantitative. Using a force plate: a vertical jump

A force plate records the ground reaction force over time. In a countermovement jump, the graph shows the athlete first standing at body weight, then unweighting (force drops below body weight as they dip), then propulsion (force rises well above body weight to accelerate upwards), then flight (no contact, so zero force) and finally landing (a high force peak). Analysts can read off peak force, impulse and, from the flight time, jump height using h = g × t² ÷ 8 . Force–time graph of a countermovement jump for a 75 kg athlete (illustrative). A flight time of about 0.38 s gives a jump height of about 0.18 m. Applications of movement analysis

Improving technique and performance: comparing an athlete's movement with a model technique, or with their own previous data. For example, measuring release angle and speed in the shot put, or stroke rate in swimming. Reducing injury risk: finding movement patterns linked to injury, such as poor landing mechanics, the knee collapsing inwards (valgus) on landing, limited range of motion, a large difference between the two legs, or poor postural control. Rehabilitation and return to play: tracking recovery with objective measures such as jump force symmetry, range of motion and gait, and using them to decide when an athlete can safely return.

Monitoring load: wearable sensors track distance, speed and accelerations in training and matches, helping coaches manage fatigue and injury risk. Gait analysis The gait cycle runs from one heel strike to the next heel strike of the same foot. In walking, about 60% of the cycle is the stance phase (foot on the ground) and about 40% is the swing phase (foot in the air). Gait analysis, using observation, video, force plates or sensors, looks for asymmetry between the legs, reduced range of motion and poor weight transfer. It is widely used in rehabilitation. The gait cycle (walking). Analysing each phase helps to find problems and to track recovery after injury. Limitations and considerations

Technology is only useful if it is used well. Equipment can be expensive and needs training; lab results may not match what happens in competition; errors can come from poor marker placement, low camera frame rates or sensor drift; and large amounts of data are only helpful if they are interpreted correctly. Collecting personal movement and health data also raises privacy and consent issues, so athletes should know how their data is stored and used. Exam Tips Use the four phases in order For any skill, name the phases (preparation, force production, critical instant, follow-through or recovery) and say what happens in each, using the sport named.

Give both sides for qualitative and quantitative State what each is, an example, a strength and a limitation. Show that they complement each other. Check the IB command terms . Quote numbers when you interpret data For a force–time graph, refer to body weight, the peak force, the time of flight and what each shows about technique. Link the tool to the question Force plates measure force, video and motion capture measure movement, wearables measure load and EMG measures muscle activity. Match the tool to what needs measuring.

Common mistake Don't treat the follow-through as unimportant. It shows how the limb slows down safely and reveals the quality of the earlier phases. Also, the critical instant is a moment, not a whole phase. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State what is meant by the critical instant of a movement. 1 mark Answer Model answer The key moment in a skill, such as ball contact or release, which decides the outcome of the movement. 2 Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative movement analysis. 2 marks Answer Model answer Qualitative analysis is based on observation and descriptive judgement of movement, for example by a coach.

Quantitative analysis uses numerical measurement of movement, such as joint angles, speed, time or force. 3 Describe the phases of movement for a tennis serve. 3 marks Answer Model answer Preparation: the ball toss and trophy position, setting up balance and a stretched shoulder and trunk. Force production: the legs drive upwards and the trunk and arm swing the racket up to the ball (with timing and sequence of joints). Critical instant: contact with the ball at full reach. Follow-through: the racket slows down across the body. Any three phases described. 4 Explain how a force plate could be used to analyse a vertical jump. 3 marks Answer Model answer

The force plate records the ground reaction force over time, which shows the unweighting, propulsion and landing phases and the peak force. The flight time can be used to calculate jump height (h = g × t² ÷ 8). The impulse (or the difference between the legs) can be used to analyse technique, power or any imbalance, and to track progress. 5 Evaluate the use of wearable sensors and motion capture to reduce injury risk in a team sport. 4 marks Answer Model answer They provide objective, accurate data, for example on landing mechanics, asymmetry between the legs or accelerations, which can identify movements that increase injury risk.

Wearable sensors allow load and movement to be monitored in real training and matches, so coaches can adjust training. Limitations include cost, the need for expertise to interpret data, lab motion capture not matching match conditions, and privacy concerns. They are most useful when combined with coach and physiotherapist observation, as part of an overall injury-prevention programme. B.3.1 Causes of Injury | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.3.1 B.3.1 Theme B · Injury SL & HL Causes of Injury Why injuries happen: the risk factors that predispose an athlete, the mechanisms that cause acute and cumulative injuries, and how injury risk is assessed. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Injuries are rarely caused by one thing. They usually happen when several risk factors build up in one athlete, and then an event, the mechanism of injury, applies a load the tissue cannot tolerate. Risk factors are split into internal (within the athlete, such as previous injury, fitness or technique) and external (from the environment, such as training errors, equipment or the playing surface). Injuries are either acute , from one sudden event, or cumulative (overuse), from repeated stress over time. At higher level, you link overuse injury to technique and biomechanical maladaptation. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Distinguish between internal and external risk factors, with examples from sport. Explain how a risk factor predisposes an athlete to injury before the injuring event. Describe the mechanisms of acute and cumulative (overuse) injuries and give examples of each. Explain how risk can be assessed using screening and a risk matrix. HL: Explain how poor technique and biomechanical maladaptations can lead to chronic or overuse injuries. Key Terms Risk factor A variable that makes an individual more likely to be injured. Internal risk factor A factor within the individual, such as age, sex, fitness, previous injury or technique.

External risk factor A factor outside the individual, such as training errors, equipment, surfaces or weather. Acute injury An injury caused by one sudden event, such as a sprain, strain, fracture or dislocation. Cumulative (overuse) injury An injury that develops gradually from repeated stress, such as tendinopathy or a stress fracture. Biomechanical maladaptation (HL) A habitual movement or technique fault that places repeated, excessive stress on tissues. Presentations B.3.1.1 Internal and External Risk Factors B.3.1.2 Acute and Cumulative Trauma B.3.1.3 Chronic and Overuse Injuries Deep Dive Risk factors: a multifactorial picture

When analysing an injury, avoid blaming one cause. Instead, show how risk factors combine. Internal risk factors make a person more susceptible to injury, and external risk factors are variables in the environment. The model below shows how they lead to injury. A simple model of injury. Internal and external risk factors together predispose an athlete to injury. A mechanism of injury (the inciting event) then produces either an acute or a cumulative injury. Type Examples How it raises risk

Internal: sex Differences in anatomy, hormones, strength and flexibility, and neuromuscular control Can change the forces on joints and how well the body controls movement. Individual differences are often larger than the difference between sexes. Internal: previous injury A previous ankle sprain Can leave reduced proprioception (joint position sense), making the next landing less stable Internal: fitness and imbalance Low strength, poor flexibility, muscle imbalance between agonist and antagonist Joints and muscles are less able to absorb and control force

Internal: fatigue, sleep and nutrition Tiredness, poor sleep, low energy availability (see A.2.2) Reduces control, reaction time and tissue repair Internal: psychological High stress, risk-taking, distraction Affects concentration and decision-making in contact or fast play External: training Sudden increases in load, poor warm-up Tissues do not have time to adapt, so they are overloaded External: environment and equipment Wet or uneven surfaces, extreme heat, poor footwear, badly fitted protective equipment Reduces grip and stability, or increases the forces on the body

External: sport and opponents Level of contact, rules, supervision, another player's foot Creates the forces of collisions and tackles To identify risk factors from a scenario, separate the predisposing factors (those already present before the event) from the trauma that actually causes the injury. For example, a footballer with a previous ankle sprain who lands on another player's foot is predisposed by the old injury, and the landing on another player's foot is the mechanism. Mechanisms of injury: acute and cumulative

An acute injury comes from one identifiable event, usually with a clear onset. Typical acute injuries are sprains (ligament damage), strains (muscle or tendon damage), fractures, dislocations, contusions (bruises), lacerations (cuts) and concussion. A cumulative (overuse) injury develops slowly as a tissue is repeatedly loaded faster than it can repair. Typical cumulative injuries are tendinopathy, stress fractures and some shin pain. Tissue load against time for the two types of injury (schematic). Acute injury happens when one load exceeds tolerance. Cumulative injury happens when repeated loads wear tolerance down until a load that was previously tolerated causes damage.

The distinction matters for prevention. Acute injuries are reduced through safer techniques, equipment, rules and awareness of risk. Cumulative injuries are reduced by managing load: building training gradually, including recovery, and changing the stresses placed on the body. Many coaches avoid sudden large increases in training load, although the evidence for an exact weekly percentage is limited, so the rule should be applied to the individual. Assessing injury risk

Coaches and clinicians assess risk in two ways. Screening and fitness testing identify athletes with weaknesses, imbalances or poor movement patterns before injury occurs, for example through a range-of-motion test, a strength test or a landing assessment. A risk matrix ranks hazards by how likely they are and how severe the injury would be, so that the most important risks are dealt with first. A risk matrix. Risk is the product of likelihood and severity (each scored 1 to 3). Hazards in the high-risk cells are controlled first. Examples are illustrative. Technique and overuse injury HL

Many chronic injuries are linked to technique . A movement fault that is repeated thousands of times, such as an overstriding runner or a bowler with a poor front-foot landing, places large and repeated forces on the same tissues. Over time these tissues become overloaded and injured. This is a biomechanical maladaptation : the body adapts to the fault in a way that increases stress on a tissue.

Example chain: knee valgus (the knee collapsing inwards) on landing increases strain on the anterior cruciate ligament, so repeated landings with valgus can lead to ligament damage and, over time, knee pain. The predisposing factors might be weak hip muscles and fatigue, and the technique fault is the mechanism. For HL answers, explain how correcting biomechanical maladaptations reduces risk. Video analysis, force plates or coach observation can identify the fault, and drills, feedback and strength work can change the movement pattern. Changing technique reduces the repeated stress on the tissue, which allows it to recover. Psychological influences on injury risk

Stress and anxiety can increase muscle tension and reduce control, while high arousal can narrow attention and lead to mistakes. Athletes who have experienced injury may return to play with fear, which can change their movement pattern and increase the risk of re-injury. Coaches can reduce these risks through good communication, managed training loads and psychological support. Exam Tips Use the chain: risk factor → mechanism → tissue → outcome For example: previous ankle sprain → reduced proprioception → unstable landing → ligament sprain. This structure scores well on causation questions.

Separate predisposing factors from the trauma Say what made the athlete more likely to be injured, then say what event caused the injury. Check the IB command terms . Classify the factor and name the sport "Internal: muscle imbalance between the quadriceps and hamstrings, which increases strain on the knee in sprinting." Name the type and the example. For HL, tie technique to tissue Describe the fault, the repeated stress it causes, the tissue affected, and how correcting the technique reduces the risk.

Common mistake Don't blame injury on one factor, such as "too much training". Injuries are multifactorial. Also don't confuse the risk factor with the mechanism: fatigue is a risk factor; a collision is a mechanism. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 State one example of an internal risk factor for injury. 1 mark Answer Model answer Any one of: previous injury, low strength or flexibility, muscle imbalance, age, sex, fatigue or poor technique. 2 Distinguish between an acute injury and a cumulative (overuse) injury. 2 marks Answer Model answer An acute injury results from a single, sudden event (for example a sprain from a twisting landing).

A cumulative injury develops gradually from repeated stress that exceeds the tissue's ability to recover (for example tendinopathy). 3 Identify one external risk factor and explain how it could predispose an athlete to injury. 2 marks Answer Model answer For example, a wet or uneven playing surface, poor footwear or a sudden increase in training load. It reduces grip and stability, or overloads tissues before they can adapt, making injury more likely. 4 Explain how a previous ankle sprain can predispose a footballer to a further sprain. 3 marks Answer Model answer The previous injury can reduce proprioception (joint position sense) and control around the ankle.

This makes landing or changing direction less stable, so the ankle is more likely to roll. The sudden, uncontrolled landing (the mechanism) then causes a further ligament sprain. 5 (HL) Explain how poor technique can lead to a chronic (overuse) injury, and how a coach could reduce this risk. 4 marks Answer Model answer A repeated technique fault, such as knee valgus on landing, places repeated excessive stress on a tissue (for example the anterior cruciate ligament). Over time the tissue is overloaded faster than it can repair, causing damage and chronic injury.

The coach can identify the fault (for example through video analysis) and use drills, feedback and strength work to correct the movement pattern. Correcting the biomechanical maladaptation reduces repeated stress, so the tissue has time to recover. B.3.2 Interventions Related to Injury | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme B › B.3.2 B.3.2 Theme B · Injury SL & HL Interventions Related to Injury How injuries are prevented, treated and rehabilitated: managing force, reducing inflammation, staged recovery, safe return to sport and concussion management. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Injury interventions cover the whole injury cycle. Prevention reduces the risk of injury by managing the forces on the body, through training, technique, equipment and rules. Initial treatment manages pain, swelling and inflammation after an acute injury. Rehabilitation restores strength, range of movement and function, using therapeutic exercise and other modalities, and surgical repair is used for some severe injuries. A safe return to play depends on healing, function and psychological readiness, not just on whether pain has gone. Concussion needs its own staged return . By the end of this topic you should be able to

Explain how interventions reduce the magnitude, direction, rate and frequency of force. Distinguish between prehabilitation, rehabilitation, inflammation management and surgical repair. Explain the purpose of initial treatment, including the role of inflammation in healing. Describe the phases of rehabilitation and the criteria for a safe return to play. Describe a staged return-to-play protocol for concussion. Key Terms Prehabilitation Proactive training before injury to reduce its risk or severity. Rehabilitation Structured recovery after injury to restore strength, movement and function. Inflammation The early healing response that clears damaged tissue. It causes swelling, heat and pain.

Therapeutic modalities Treatments such as physiotherapy, manual therapy, taping and bracing used in recovery. Return to play A staged, criteria-based return to full training and competition. Graduated return (concussion) A step-by-step return in which each stage must be symptom-free before the next is started. Presentations B.3.2.1 Lowering Injury Risk B.3.2.2 Initial Injury Treatment B.3.2.3 Treatment of Concussion Deep Dive Lowering injury risk: managing force

Injury prevention is not simply avoiding impact. Injuries happen when the forces on tissues are too large, applied in the wrong direction, applied too quickly, or repeated too often. Interventions work by changing one or more of these four features: Force–time curves for a stiff and a soft landing with a similar impulse (illustrative). Spreading the force over a longer time lowers the peak. The table lists four ways that interventions manage force. Prevention therefore combines several approaches:

Warm-up and conditioning: raises tissue temperature and prepares muscles and joints. Strength and proprioceptive (balance and joint position) training improves the body's ability to absorb and control forces. Technique coaching: changes direction and rate of loading, for example landing with the knees bent and in line with the toes. Protective equipment: helmets, shin guards, mouthguards and padding reduce the magnitude of forces on the body. Equipment must fit and be maintained. Rule changes and supervision: limit dangerous tackles or contact, and make sure competition and training are controlled.

Load management: progressing training gradually and including rest and recovery reduces repeated stress and fatigue, which lowers the chance of both acute and cumulative injury (see B.3.1). Prehabilitation, rehabilitation, inflammation management and surgery Intervention When it happens Aim Example Prehabilitation Before injury Reduce the risk or severity of injury Hamstring strengthening for a sprinter with a previous strain Inflammation management Immediately after an acute injury Ease pain and swelling while keeping the healing response Compression, elevation and ice in the first days

Rehabilitation After the early injury phase Restore strength, range, balance and sport function Progressive strength and balance work after an ankle sprain Surgical repair When the injury needs it Repair structures that cannot heal well without surgery Reconstruction of a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament Surgery is usually followed by rehabilitation and physiotherapy, because the repaired tissue must be loaded gradually to become strong and functional again. Initial treatment and inflammation

After an acute soft-tissue injury such as a sprain or strain, inflammation starts straight away. Its job is to clear damaged tissue and start repair, so it should not be stopped completely. The early treatment goal is to control pain and swelling while protecting the injured area. RICE (rest, ice, compression and elevation) is a traditional approach. Current guidance tends to favour protecting the area, relative rest and early, pain-guided movement over complete immobilisation, so athletes should follow the advice of a medical professional rather than a fixed routine. Anti-inflammatory medication can reduce pain, but a medical professional should advise on its use, as some medication may affect healing.

The approximate stages of soft-tissue healing after an injury. The timescales vary with the tissue and the severity of the injury. Athletes must not return just because the pain has gone. Pain relief can mask tissue that is still healing, so return should consider the stage of healing, functional ability and the risk of re-injury. Therapeutic modalities and rehabilitation Rehabilitation uses a range of therapeutic modalities under the guidance of physiotherapists and sports medicine teams. These include: Therapeutic exercise: the core of rehabilitation, progressing from gentle movement to strength, balance and sport-specific tasks.

Manual therapy: hands-on techniques to improve joint movement and reduce stiffness or pain. Taping and bracing: support the joint and can limit unwanted movement while tissue heals or during return. Cryotherapy and other passive treatments: used for pain and swelling, but with limited evidence for long-term healing. Their role is mainly symptom control. Rehabilitation is usually organised in phases : Phase Main aims Typical activities 1: Protection and early recovery Control pain and swelling, protect the tissue, restore basic movement Gentle range-of-motion work, isometric contractions, support as needed

2: Strength and control Rebuild strength, endurance and balance (proprioception) Progressive resistance training, balance and stability exercises 3: Sport-specific return Restore sport skills and tolerate the demands of the activity Sport-specific drills, progressive loading, reactive and change-of-direction work Criteria for a safe return to play Return to play should be based on criteria , not a date alone. Common criteria include: Pain-free full range of movement at the injured joint. Strength that is close to the uninjured side . Many clinicians use a limb symmetry index of about 90% or more on tests such as a hop or a force measurement, but the test must suit the sport.

Functional performance in sport-specific tasks, such as sprinting, jumping, cutting and landing, without pain or compensation. Psychological readiness , including confidence in the injured area, and a plan for continued prevention work (see B.3.1 on psychological influences). Medical clearance from the appropriate professional. Returning too early increases the risk of re-injury, because the tissue is not yet strong enough for full loads and the athlete may change their movement to protect the injury, which can create new problems elsewhere. Concussion management

A concussion is a brain injury caused by a blow to the head or body that transmits force to the brain. Symptoms can include headache, dizziness, confusion and sensitivity to light or noise, and they may appear later. Recovery is not linear and varies between athletes. Any athlete with suspected concussion must be removed from play and assessed by a medical professional. Athletes then follow a graduated return , with each stage started only when there are no symptoms at the current stage, including after activity. Each stage increases the demand, and any return of symptoms means going back one stage.

A six-stage graduated return to play after concussion. Each stage must be symptom-free before moving on, and medical clearance is needed at each step. Psychological aspects of recovery Injury can cause frustration, anxiety, low mood and fear of re-injury. These can affect motivation and adherence to rehabilitation, and they can change movement during the return to sport. Good communication between the athlete, coach and medical team, goal-setting, and gradual exposure to sport all help the athlete recover both physically and mentally. Exam Tips

Link the intervention to the force Name the intervention, the feature of force it changes (magnitude, direction, rate or frequency), and the effect on the tissue. Check the IB command terms . Distinguish the four terms Prehabilitation is before injury; rehabilitation is after; inflammation management is the early response; surgery is a repair. Don't swap them. Describe return to play with criteria Give measurable criteria (range, strength symmetry, sport-specific function, psychological readiness, clearance), not just "when the pain stops".

Use the staged logic for concussion Each stage must be symptom-free before progressing, and symptoms mean stepping back. Explain why recovery is not linear. Common mistake Don't say inflammation is always harmful and must be stopped. It is part of healing. The aim is to manage its symptoms and protect the tissue while it does its job. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define prehabilitation . 1 mark Answer Model answer Proactive training or intervention before an injury occurs, to reduce its risk or severity. 2 State two ways that protective equipment reduces injury risk. 2 marks Answer Model answer

It reduces the magnitude of the forces transmitted to the body (for example padding absorbs impact). It protects vulnerable areas from direct contact (for example helmets and shin guards), and it can help distribute force. 3 Explain how a change in landing technique can reduce the risk of injury, using the terms magnitude, direction or rate of force. 3 marks Answer Model answer Landing with the knees bent and the body controlled increases the time over which force is absorbed, which reduces the rate of loading and the peak force. Keeping the knees in line with the toes changes the direction of force so that it is less likely to cause knee valgus and strain on the ligaments.

The lower peak force and better direction reduce the stress on the joint and the risk of injury. 4 Outline the purpose of inflammation in the healing of an acute soft-tissue injury. 2 marks Answer Model answer Inflammation clears damaged tissue and starts the repair process. The swelling, heat and pain signal the injury and protect the area while healing takes place. (Inflammation should be managed, not stopped completely.) 5 Discuss why an athlete should not return to play as soon as the pain has gone after an injury. 4 marks Answer Model answer Pain relief can mask tissue that is still healing, so the tissue may not be strong enough for full loads.

Return should be based on criteria, including pain-free range of movement, strength close to the uninjured side and sport-specific function. Returning too early increases the risk of re-injury, and athletes may compensate with altered movement that causes new problems. Psychological readiness and medical clearance should also be considered before a full return.
