C.1.1 Personality | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.1.1 C.1.1 Theme C · Individual Differences SL & HL Personality What personality is, how it is described and measured, how it interacts with the situation, and why no personality profile predicts sport performance on its own. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Personality is the set of characteristic patterns of thinking, feeling and behaviour that make one person different from another. Psychologists explain behaviour in three main ways. The trait approach sees personality as stable characteristics that drive behaviour across situations. The situational approach sees behaviour as shaped mainly by the environment, including what others do. The interactionist approach sees behaviour as the result of both. In sport, the most widely used trait framework is the Big Five . Athletes also learn behaviours by observing role models, and personality can change over time through experience and reflection. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Explain the trait-based approach and why traits are considered relatively stable. Identify and apply all five Big Five traits to sport and exercise examples. Explain social learning theory and apply it to a sporting example. Explain how personality can change through experience and reflection over time. Outline how personality is measured in sport, and the limitations of measurement. HL: Evaluate why no single personality profile predicts sport performance. Key Terms Personality Characteristic patterns of thinking, feeling and behaviour that differ between individuals. Trait A relatively stable characteristic that shows up in behaviour across many situations.

Big Five A trait model of five dimensions: openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. Interactionist approach The view that behaviour results from the interaction of personality and the situation. Social learning theory The view that behaviour is learned by observing and imitating models. Model A person whose behaviour is observed and copied, such as a coach, senior player or role model. Presentations C.1.1.1 Personality C.1.1.2 Social Learning Theory C.1.1.3 Personality Change Deep Dive Three approaches to behaviour

The trait approach describes personality as a set of relatively enduring characteristics. If an athlete is consistently competitive across training, matches and social situations, the trait view explains this as a stable tendency. Trait approaches describe broad, stable patterns of behaviour; they do not predict behaviour perfectly in every case.

The situational approach argues that the situation is the main influence on behaviour. A player who is aggressive on the pitch but calm in class is responding to the context, not showing a fixed trait. The interactionist approach combines the two: the same person may respond very differently depending on the situation, and different people respond differently to the same situation. Three explanations of sporting behaviour. The interactionist approach, shown at the bottom, is often considered the most balanced view. The Big Five in sport

The Big Five is the most widely used trait model. Each dimension is a continuum, so people sit at different points on each one. The table shows how each trait may be relevant to sport and exercise. The Big Five traits, with a description and illustrative sporting examples at high and low levels. These are tendencies, not guarantees of behaviour. Trait Possible effect on sporting behaviour Openness Willingness to learn new tactics or training methods; may be more adaptable to changing coaching Conscientiousness Consistency in training, preparation and following instructions; discipline in recovery

Extraversion Comfort in team settings, communication and leadership; may find long solitary training harder Agreeableness Cooperation, supporting teammates and resolving conflict within a team Neuroticism Tendency to experience anxiety and worry, which can affect performance under pressure (see C.4.1) Social learning theory

According to social learning theory (Bandura), people learn many behaviours by watching others and copying them, not only through their own experience. Learning from a model depends on four processes: attention (noticing the behaviour), retention (remembering it), reproduction (physically being able to copy it) and motivation (wanting to copy it, often because it is rewarded or admired). Social learning theory applied to sport. A model's behaviour is copied only if the learner attends to it, remembers it, can reproduce it and is motivated to do so.

In sport this explains how young athletes learn effort, discipline and sporting behaviour from coaches, senior players and professional role models. It also means that coaches and older teammates influence the behaviour of the whole group, so it matters what they model. Long-term changes in personality

Personality is relatively stable, but it is not fixed. Long-term sport participation can shape behaviours such as discipline, confidence, emotional control and cooperation. This happens through experience (repeatedly facing challenges and setbacks) and reflection (thinking about performance and deliberately changing how one responds). An athlete who learns to manage nerves before competition, for example, may become more emotionally controlled over several seasons. This change challenges the idea that traits are completely fixed. A balanced view is that core traits are relatively stable across time, while behaviour and how a person handles situations can develop.

Measuring personality in sport Personality is usually measured with self-report questionnaires , in which athletes rate statements about themselves. These are quick and easy to use, and they can be given to many people. However, they have limitations: Social desirability bias: athletes may answer in the way they think is expected or admirable. Situational specificity: a trait measured in general may not predict behaviour in a specific competitive situation. Response consistency: answers can change with mood, recent results or the setting in which the test is given, so reliability matters.

Ethics: personality data is personal. It should be collected with informed consent, used only for stated purposes, kept confidential and not used to exclude athletes from selection. Personality and performance HL A common idea is that elite athletes share a particular personality profile. Research has not supported this: no single personality profile predicts sport performance . Athletes in the same sport can have very different personalities, and the same personality can lead to different results in different situations. Performance depends on many factors, including skill, fitness, coaching, tactics, opportunity, health and the situation, and personality interacts with these.

Personality is still useful. It can help coaches understand how an athlete is likely to respond to feedback, pressure or a team role, and help them tailor support. The key evaluation is that personality should inform individual support, not be used as a fixed predictor of success or as the reason for choosing or rejecting an athlete. Exam Tips Name the approach first For "explain" questions, say whether you are using the trait, situational or interactionist approach, then apply it to the sport in the question.

Apply, don't list Name the Big Five trait and give a sporting effect, for example "high conscientiousness helps an athlete stick to a demanding training plan". Check the IB command terms . Use Bandura's four processes For social learning questions, name attention, retention, reproduction and motivation, and say which one is relevant to the example. Evaluate with limitations For measurement or performance questions, give social desirability, situational specificity or the lack of a predictive profile as a limitation. Common mistake Don't say a particular personality type guarantees success, or that elite athletes all share one profile. Also, traits are tendencies, not fixed behaviour.

Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define the term trait . 1 mark Answer Model answer A relatively stable characteristic of a person that influences their behaviour across many different situations. 2 Identify two of the Big Five personality dimensions and give a sporting example of each. 2 marks Answer Model answer Conscientiousness: a disciplined athlete who follows a training plan consistently. Extraversion: a sociable athlete who thrives in a team role and communicates well with teammates. (Any two dimensions with a valid example.) 3 Outline the interactionist approach to personality, using a sporting example. 3 marks Answer Model answer

Behaviour results from the interaction of personality (individual characteristics) and the situation (environment and demands). The same athlete may behave differently in different situations, and different athletes may respond differently to the same situation. Example: a nervous athlete may perform more calmly when a supportive coach is present than in a highly critical environment. 4 Explain how social learning theory can explain a young athlete adopting the behaviour of a respected senior player. 4 marks Answer Model answer Attention: the young athlete notices the senior player's behaviour, which is admired and similar to their own situation.

Retention: the athlete remembers the behaviour, for example through observation and mental rehearsal. Reproduction: the athlete has the physical ability to copy the behaviour through practice. Motivation: the athlete wants to copy it, because it is rewarded or valued by the team and coaches. 5 (HL) Evaluate the view that personality can be used to predict sporting success. 4 marks Answer Model answer No single personality profile has been shown to predict sport performance, and athletes in the same sport often have very different personalities. Performance depends on many factors, including skill, fitness, coaching, tactics and the situation, and personality interacts with these.

Self-report measures have limitations, such as social desirability bias and situational specificity, which make prediction less reliable. Personality is still useful for understanding how an athlete responds to pressure or feedback, but it should not be used as a fixed predictor or to exclude athletes. C.1.2 Mental Toughness | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.1.2 C.1.2 Theme C · Individual Differences SL & HL Mental Toughness What mental toughness is, how it helps athletes handle pressure and setbacks, and how beliefs, attributions and health connect to it. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Mental toughness is the psychological capacity to cope with the pressure, challenges and setbacks of sport, and to perform consistently as a result. It is usually described through five components: seeing pressure as a challenge , staying committed to goals, feeling in control , having confidence , and resilience to recover from setbacks. Mental toughness is not simply "trying harder". It shows in how an athlete appraises and responds to pressure. At higher level, you also study how beliefs and attributions can create self-fulfilling prophecies, and how mental toughness relates to health and well-being. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define mental toughness and identify its key components. Explain how mental toughness helps athletes handle pressure and challenges. Explain why mental toughness must be judged from thoughts, feelings and perceived control, not only from behaviour. HL: Explain the self-fulfilling prophecy and its effect on confidence and success. HL: Explain attribution and locus of control, and their effect on confidence. HL: Discuss the links between mental toughness and health and well-being. Key Terms Mental toughness The psychological capacity to cope with pressure, challenges and setbacks, and perform consistently.

Challenge appraisal Interpreting pressure as an opportunity to rise to, rather than only a threat. Perceived control The belief that one can influence one's own thoughts, emotions and actions. Resilience The ability to recover from setbacks and maintain effort and focus. Self-fulfilling prophecy (HL) A belief that leads to behaviour that makes the belief come true. Locus of control (HL) Whether a person sees outcomes as controlled by themselves (internal) or by outside forces (external). Presentations C.1.2.1 Mental Toughness C.1.2.2 The Self-fulfilling Prophecy C.1.2.3 Mental Toughness and Health C.1.2.4 Attribution Theory Deep Dive Defining mental toughness and its components

Mental toughness is generally described as a multidimensional characteristic, which means that several connected components make it up. The components below are usually discussed together, and none of them works alone. An athlete who is confident but has no commitment may give up after a setback; an athlete who is committed but feels no control may keep trying without changing their approach. The components of mental toughness. Resilience sits at the centre because it draws on the other four components when an athlete faces setbacks.

Mental toughness has a clear role in handling pressure and challenges . Pressure situations, such as a final, a penalty or a comeback, test whether an athlete can keep their focus, effort and decision-making. Athletes with greater mental toughness are more likely to maintain perceived control, effort and resilience when the situation becomes difficult. Appraising pressure: threat or challenge

How an athlete interprets a situation shapes their response. A threat appraisal sees the situation as something that might cause harm or failure, which tends to increase anxiety and narrow attention onto the risk. A challenge appraisal sees the same situation as an opportunity to show what they can do. The situation is the same; the appraisal and the athlete's perceived control differ. The same penalty shootout appraised as a threat or as a challenge (illustrative). The appraisal, and the perceived control that goes with it, shapes the response and the likely outcome. Evaluating mental toughness

Mental toughness is hard to observe directly, and it is measured mostly through questionnaires that ask athletes about their confidence, control, commitment and so on. A key evaluation point is that an athlete may look mentally tough from their behaviour, such as remaining calm in a tense moment, but this is not enough. True mental toughness requires evidence from thoughts, feelings and perceived control. A calm exterior may hide high anxiety, and an athlete who seems emotional may still be well in control.

Measurement also has limitations. Researchers do not agree on one definition, so different questionnaires measure slightly different things. Questionnaire answers can be affected by social desirability, mood and recent results. Some traits may also develop from repeated states, for example when repeated experience of calm under pressure becomes a stable tendency. Self-fulfilling prophecy HL

A self-fulfilling prophecy is a belief that leads a person to act in a way that makes the belief come true. An athlete who believes they can win may play with more confidence and take appropriate risks, and that performance can produce the win. The result then strengthens the belief. The same cycle works in reverse: an athlete who expects to lose may play tentatively and confirm their own expectation. This matters for mental toughness because the cycle of belief, behaviour and result can build confidence over time, or wear it down.

The self-fulfilling prophecy cycle, with a note on attribution. Internal and external attributions after success or failure affect how an athlete's confidence and perceived control develop. Attribution and locus of control HL

Attribution is the explanation a person gives for an outcome. Locus of control describes whether they see the cause as internal (within themselves, such as effort or strategy) or external (outside themselves, such as luck, the referee or the opponent). Athletes who make internal attributions for success and controllable attributions for failure, for example "I didn't prepare well enough, so I can change that", tend to keep their confidence and motivation. An external attribution can protect self-esteem briefly, but may reduce perceived control over future results.

Coaches can support mental toughness by helping athletes focus on controllable factors, such as preparation, effort and tactics, when they reflect on performance. Mental toughness, health and well-being HL

Mental toughness is linked to health and well-being outcomes. Athletes with stronger resilience and perceived control may cope better with the stress of competition, injury and the transition out of sport. Injury recovery is an example: mental toughness may support resilience and commitment to rehabilitation, but recovery also depends on injury severity, treatment and social support. The evidence is mainly correlational, so it cannot show that mental toughness causes better health on its own.

A penalty shootout illustrates the link between mental toughness and performance. A mentally tough performer keeps their confidence, uses positive self-talk and treats the penalty as a challenge rather than a threat. An athlete with lower mental toughness may focus on the consequences of a miss and become tense, which can affect technique. Both athletes face the same pressure; the difference lies in appraisal, control and confidence. Exam Tips Name the components, not just "trying hard" Include challenge appraisal, commitment, confidence, control and resilience in your definition. Check the IB command terms .

Apply to a pressure scenario For "explain how mental toughness helps" questions, use a named scenario (penalty, final, comeback) and link each component to the athlete's thoughts and actions. Judge toughness by evidence For evaluation, point out that behaviour alone does not show mental toughness. Refer to thoughts, feelings and perceived control, and to measurement limits. For HL, describe the cycle Belief → behaviour → result → confirmed belief. Then say whether it strengthens or weakens confidence, and link to attribution.

Common mistake Don't say that mentally tough athletes never feel anxious, or that mental toughness causes success. It is a set of components that supports performance under pressure, and its links to health are correlational. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define mental toughness . 1 mark Answer Model answer The psychological capacity to cope with the pressure, challenges and setbacks of sport and to perform consistently as a result. 2 Identify two components of mental toughness. 2 marks Answer Model answer Any two of: challenge, commitment, confidence, control, and resilience.

3 Explain what is meant by a challenge appraisal of pressure, and why it helps performance. 3 marks Answer Model answer A challenge appraisal interprets pressure as an opportunity to show ability, rather than only as a threat. This keeps attention on the task and effort, and supports the athlete's confidence and perceived control. As a result, the athlete is more likely to perform well under pressure, for example by committing to a penalty. 4 Explain why a coach should not judge an athlete's mental toughness from behaviour alone. 3 marks Answer Model answer An athlete may appear calm or tough in behaviour while experiencing high anxiety or low perceived control.

True mental toughness depends on thoughts, feelings and perceived control, which are harder to observe directly. Measurement is also limited by the lack of a single definition and by questionnaire problems, such as social desirability. 5 (HL) Explain how a self-fulfilling prophecy can affect an athlete's confidence over a season. 4 marks Answer Model answer A belief such as "I can win" leads the athlete to behave with confidence, for example by taking appropriate risks and committing fully. The behaviour can produce successful results, which confirm the belief. Repeated confirmation strengthens confidence and perceived control over the season.

In reverse, a negative belief can lead to tentative play and poor results, which lowers confidence. C.2.1 Motor Learning Processes | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.2.1 C.2.1 Theme C · Motor Learning SL & HL Motor Learning Processes How people acquire skills through practice and feedback: the information processing model, the three stages of learning, and how practice design supports transfer. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Motor learning is a relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill, brought about by practice and experience. It is different from performance, which can change temporarily because of fatigue, mood or conditions. The information processing model describes how a performer takes in information, decides what to do, produces a movement and uses feedback to improve the next attempt. Fitts and Posner describe three stages through which learners typically progress: cognitive, associative and autonomous. Coaches use these ideas to choose feedback, practice and cues that suit the learner's stage. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Distinguish between motor learning and performance. Describe the information processing model and apply it to a sporting skill. Describe the cognitive, associative and autonomous stages of learning, and their characteristics. Explain intrinsic and extrinsic (augmented) feedback, including knowledge of results and knowledge of performance. Explain how practice design (massed or distributed, constant or variable) affects learning and transfer. Apply these ideas to plan a coaching session for a learner at a given stage. Key Terms Motor learning A relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill, brought about by practice.

Information processing Taking in information, deciding what to do, producing movement and using feedback. Intrinsic feedback Information the performer gets from their own senses during or after a movement. Augmented (extrinsic) feedback Information from outside the performer, such as a coach's comment, video or the result. Transfer The influence of previous learning on the learning or performance of a new skill. Variable practice Practising the same skill under changing conditions, which supports transfer to new situations. Presentations C.2.1.1 Learning and Performance C.2.1.2 The Psychological Refractory Period C.2.1.3 Transfer of Learning Deep Dive Motor learning and performance

Learning is inferred from a relatively permanent change, which is why it is measured after practice, often in a retention test or a transfer test, rather than during practice. Performance is the temporary level shown on a particular day. A player may perform well in training because the conditions are easy, without having learned the skill. Coaches therefore design practice to produce learning, not just good performance during practice. The information processing model

The information processing model treats the performer as a system that moves through a sequence of stages. A performer takes in information from the environment, decides what to do, produces the movement, and receives feedback that updates the next attempt. Experienced performers process information more efficiently: they notice relevant cues quickly and need less decision time. The information processing model applied to a volleyball serve. Feedback from each attempt updates the next input, decision and movement. The three stages of learning (Fitts and Posner)

Fitts and Posner describe learning as three overlapping stages. Learners move through them at different speeds, and they may be at different stages for different skills. Cognitive stage: the learner works out what the skill involves. They think about each cue and body position, make many errors and feel clumsy. Coaching should use simple, clear cues, demonstrations, basic feedback and safe, low-pressure practice. Associative stage: the learner refines the skill. Errors fall, timing and consistency improve, and the learner starts to detect and correct their own mistakes. Coaching should give more specific feedback, vary the practice and encourage error detection.

Autonomous stage: the skill becomes largely automatic. It needs less attention, so the performer can focus on tactics, adapt to pressure and combine skills. Coaching should challenge the performer with changing and competitive conditions. The Fitts and Posner stages, with errors falling over time (a typical pattern, illustrative). The focus of coaching changes at each stage. Note that the autonomous stage is not always fully reached. A skill may appear automatic but break down under distraction or fatigue, so performance under pressure should be tested. Feedback

Feedback is information about a movement that helps the learner improve. It can be intrinsic , coming from the performer's own senses (proprioception, kinaesthesis, vision), or extrinsic , coming from outside. Extrinsic feedback is often called augmented feedback , and it includes: Knowledge of results (KR): information about the outcome of the movement, such as whether the shot went in or the time achieved. Knowledge of performance (KP): information about how the movement was made, such as the position of the elbow or the body shape at take-off, often from video or coach observation.

The learner's stage affects what feedback is useful. Beginners often need specific, frequent feedback on the form of the movement, because they cannot yet judge it. As the learner develops, too much augmented feedback can make them dependent on the coach, so feedback should be reduced and the learner encouraged to judge their own performance. This is known as the guidance or frequency effect: frequent feedback helps in the short term, but it may hinder long-term learning if it prevents the learner building their own error detection.

Intrinsic and extrinsic feedback, and the two main types of practice design. Massed and distributed practice differ in the rest between repetitions; constant and variable practice differ in whether conditions change. Practice and transfer How practice is organised affects how well a skill is learned: Massed practice (repetitions with short rest) can improve performance quickly in the short term, but may lead to fatigue and less retention. Distributed practice (repetitions spread out with longer rest, or across several sessions) usually gives better retention and long-term learning.

Constant practice (the same conditions every time) helps early learning, because the performer can build a clear movement pattern. Variable practice (changing conditions, such as different targets or opponents) helps learners build flexible patterns that transfer to new situations. Transfer is the influence of previous learning on a new skill. Positive transfer occurs when the earlier skill helps the new one, for example a tennis player learning badminton. Negative transfer occurs when the earlier skill interferes, for example a badminton player's shuttle-hitting action getting in the way of learning a tennis serve. Variable practice and clear links between skills help positive transfer.

Planning a coaching session To plan a session, identify the learner's stage first, then choose the features that suit it. A beginner in the cognitive stage may need a demonstration, one or two simple cues, short sets with rest, and plenty of positive, specific KR. An athlete in the associative stage may need more varied practice, feedback on the key details of the movement, and time to detect their own errors. An autonomous performer may practise under pressure, with tactical decisions added. Exam Tips Name the stage and its characteristics For stage questions, give the stage name and two features of it, then apply them to the sport. Check the IB command terms .

Match feedback to the stage Beginners need specific, frequent feedback on form. More advanced learners need less, so they can detect their own errors. Use the correct feedback term Say "knowledge of results" for the outcome and "knowledge of performance" for how the movement was made. Intrinsic feedback comes from the performer. Link practice to transfer Variable practice supports transfer to new situations. Distributed practice usually gives better retention than massed practice. Common mistake Don't confuse performance with learning. A good performance in practice does not prove that learning has occurred. Also, don't say that more feedback is always better. Practice Questions

Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define motor learning . 1 mark Answer Model answer A relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill, brought about by practice and experience. 2 State two characteristics of the associative stage of learning. 2 marks Answer Model answer Errors fall and the movement becomes more consistent. Timing improves and the learner starts to detect and correct their own errors. (Any two.) 3 Distinguish between knowledge of results and knowledge of performance . 2 marks Answer Model answer Knowledge of results is information about the outcome of the movement (for example whether the shot went in).

Knowledge of performance is information about how the movement was produced (for example the position of the elbow). 4 Explain why a coach might use distributed practice rather than massed practice when teaching a new skill. 3 marks Answer Model answer Distributed practice spreads repetitions out with longer rest, which reduces fatigue during practice. This usually leads to better retention and long-term learning than massed practice, which can improve short-term performance but may not last. Distributed practice therefore supports learning rather than just good performance in the session.

5 Discuss how a coach could adjust feedback and practice for a beginner in the cognitive stage compared with an athlete in the autonomous stage. 4 marks Answer Model answer Beginner (cognitive stage): simple cues and demonstrations, frequent specific feedback on form, short sessions with safe, low-pressure practice. Autonomous stage: less frequent feedback, so the athlete can detect their own errors, and practice that challenges them with pressure, tactics and variable conditions. Feedback is reduced as the learner develops, to avoid dependence on the coach and to build intrinsic error detection.

Coaches should check that the skill holds up under pressure and distraction, not just in calm conditions. C.2.2 Attentional Control | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.2.2 C.2.2 Theme C · Motor Learning SL & HL Attentional Control How athletes direct, maintain and shift their focus onto the cues that matter, and why pressure, arousal and distractions can disrupt it. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Attentional control is the ability to direct, maintain and shift focus onto the cues that matter most for a skill. Attention can be described along two dimensions: its width (broad or narrow) and its direction (external, on the environment or the outcome of a movement, or internal, on the body or thoughts). Effective skill execution depends on using the right focus at the right moment. Pressure, arousal, fatigue and distractions can narrow or scatter attention, and athletes can use strategies such as cue words and routines to keep their focus where it needs to be. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Distinguish between broad and narrow attentional focus, and between internal and external focus. Give a sporting example of each type of attentional focus. Explain how arousal and pressure can narrow attention and affect performance. Describe strategies that athletes use to control their attentional focus, such as self-talk and routines. Explain how external and internal distractors can impair performance. Explain why an external focus is often more effective than an internal focus for skilled motor performance. Key Terms Attentional control The ability to direct, maintain and shift focus onto the most relevant cues for successful skill execution.

Broad focus Attention spread across many cues at once, useful for scanning and decision-making. Narrow focus Attention restricted to one or two key cues, useful for precise execution. External focus Attention on the environment or the effect of the movement, such as the ball's flight. Internal focus Attention on the body, thoughts or feelings, such as the position of a joint. Self-talk Using spoken or silent cue words or phrases to direct attention, confidence and action. Presentation C.2.2.1 Execution of Skills Deep Dive Width and direction of attention

Attentional focus has two dimensions, and each combination suits a different demand. Broad focus takes in many cues, which helps with scanning, tactical awareness and decision-making in team sports. Narrow focus picks out one or two cues, which helps precise execution, such as a golf putt or a free throw. External focus is directed at the environment or at the outcome of the movement, while internal focus is directed at the body or at thoughts and feelings. The four combinations of attentional width and direction, with a sporting example for each. Athletes move between these as the demands of the situation change.

Each type has a use. In a fast team game, a player needs broad external focus to read teammates and opponents before choosing an action. A goalkeeper facing a penalty needs narrow external focus on the ball and the taker's movement. Broad internal focus helps with planning and analysing tactics or previous performance, while narrow internal focus can support breathing control, emotional regulation and mental rehearsal before a skill. External or internal focus in motor performance

Research on motor learning has found that an external focus on the intended outcome of a movement often leads to better performance and faster learning than an internal focus on body movements. For example, a basketball player focusing on the ball going through the hoop tends to perform better than one focusing on each joint of the shooting action. A plausible explanation is that an internal focus makes the performer consciously control movements that are better organised automatically, whereas an external focus allows movement to self-organise more naturally. The evidence is strongest for relatively simple, well-learned skills, so the effect should be applied with judgement.

Arousal, pressure and attentional narrowing Arousal (physiological and psychological activation) affects attention. At low arousal, attention may be wide but scattered, and relevant cues can be missed. At an optimal level of arousal, attention is focused on the relevant cues. At high arousal, such as the anxiety of a penalty in a final, attention tends to narrow , so the performer focuses on one thing, often the threat, and misses other relevant cues such as the goalkeeper's movement. This is linked to the arousal and anxiety topic (see C.4.1).

How arousal can affect attention in a penalty kick (illustrative). Attention is widest at low arousal, focused at optimal arousal, and narrowest at high arousal, when relevant cues are missed. Strategies to control attentional focus Athletes can learn to direct and control their attention with several strategies: Self-talk: a short cue word or phrase, spoken or silent, that directs attention and supports confidence and action. A cue such as "smooth" can keep a swimmer's attention on rhythm. Pre-performance routines: the same sequence of actions before each skill, which narrows attention to the task and manages arousal.

Mental rehearsal: imagining the skill before performing it, which focuses attention on the key cues and the feel of the movement (see C.5.2). Cue focus: choosing a relevant external cue, such as a target, rather than a list of technical points. Distractors and their effects

Distractors pull attention away from the relevant cues. External distractors include crowd noise, a heckling opponent, glare or a referee's whistle. Internal distractors include worry about the scoreline, thoughts about a previous mistake, fatigue and fear of failure. Distractors can impair performance by occupying attention that the skill needs, and by pushing the performer towards an internal focus at the wrong moment. Attentional control training helps athletes keep focus on relevant cues despite both kinds of distraction.

Internal and external cues for a basketball free throw, the strategies that help maintain focus, and examples of distractors. Strategies work by directing attention, not by ignoring the situation. Evaluating attentional control Attentional control can be measured with tests in which athletes respond to relevant and irrelevant cues, and with self-report questionnaires. Both have limits: laboratory tests may not reflect the pressure and noise of competition, and self-reports depend on how athletes perceive their own focus. Attentional strategies also differ between athletes and between skills, so coaches should test strategies in training before using them in competition. Exam Tips

Name both dimensions Describe attention by its width (broad or narrow) and its direction (internal or external). Give a sporting example of each. Check the IB command terms . Link arousal to narrowing For high-pressure questions, say that arousal can narrow attention onto a threat and cause relevant cues to be missed, then give the example. Match focus to the skill Use an external focus for simple, well-learned skills where the outcome is the cue. Use broad focus for scanning in team games.

Explain strategies with a cue For strategy questions, give the strategy, the cue or routine, and how it directs attention. For example: "a cue word such as 'smooth' keeps the swimmer's attention on rhythm." Common mistake Don't say that narrow focus is always better, or that broad focus is always worse. Each suits a different demand. Also, don't confuse internal focus with being "focused": an internal focus can be useful for some tasks, but may hurt skilled performance. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define attentional control . 1 mark Answer Model answer

The ability to direct, maintain and shift focus onto the most relevant cues for successful skill execution. 2 Identify the type of attentional focus used by a table tennis player watching the opponent's paddle, and justify your answer. 2 marks Answer Model answer Narrow external focus. The player focuses on one specific cue (the paddle movement) in the environment, which is narrow in width and external in direction. 3 Explain how high arousal can affect the attentional focus of a penalty taker. 3 marks Answer Model answer High arousal, such as the anxiety of a penalty in a final, causes attention to narrow onto one thing, often the threat or the outcome of the miss.

As a result, the penalty taker may miss relevant cues, such as the goalkeeper's movement or their own routine. This can lead to a rushed or poorly executed kick. 4 Outline two strategies an athlete could use to control their attentional focus. 2 marks Answer Model answer Self-talk: using a cue word or phrase (for example "smooth") to direct attention and action. Pre-performance routine: the same sequence of actions before each skill, which narrows attention to the task and helps manage arousal. (Mental rehearsal and cue focus are also accepted.) 5 Discuss why an external focus of attention may lead to better motor performance than an internal focus. 4 marks Answer Model answer

An external focus is directed at the outcome or effect of the movement (for example the ball's flight), which allows the movement to self-organise. An internal focus directs conscious control at body movements, which can interfere with automatic, well-learned movement patterns. Research suggests external focus often leads to better performance and faster learning, especially for simple, well-learned skills. However, the effect depends on the skill and the performer, so coaches should test it in context rather than apply it automatically. C.3.1 Achievement Motivation | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.3.1 C.3.1 Theme C · Motivation SL & HL Achievement Motivation Why athletes approach or avoid challenges: how personality and the situation combine, what drives task choice and persistence, and how coaches can change the balance. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Achievement motivation explains why people approach, persist in or avoid achievement situations, such as competitions, tests and difficult training. Atkinson's model proposes that this depends on two personality tendencies, the motive to achieve success and the motive to avoid failure , and on situational factors such as the probability of success and the incentive value of success. The balance between the approach and avoidance tendencies predicts how an athlete will feel and behave. Coaches can influence this balance by changing the situation, for example by setting tasks at a suitable level and focusing on personal progress. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Explain achievement motivation as the balance between approaching success and avoiding failure. Identify the personality and situational factors that combine in Atkinson's model. Explain the chain from personality and situation to resultant tendency, emotion and behaviour. Explain how achievement motivation affects task choice and persistence. Explain task orientation, and why task-oriented performers are more likely to persist after failure. Apply coaching strategies that increase approach motivation and reduce avoidance motivation. Key Terms Achievement motivation The psychological processes that drive a person to approach, persist in or avoid achievement situations.

Motive to achieve success (Ms) The personality tendency to seek success and the pride that comes with it. Motive to avoid failure (Maf) The personality tendency to avoid failure and the fear that comes with it. Probability of success (Ps) The likelihood of succeeding at a task. Probability of failure (Pf) = 1 − Ps. Resultant achievement motivation The balance of approach and avoidance tendencies for a particular task. Task orientation Judging success by self-referenced progress, effort, learning and mastery. Presentations C.3.1.1 Need Achievement Theory C.3.1.2 Goal Orientation Theory C.3.1.3 High Ego Orientation Deep Dive The personality and situation chain

Achievement motivation can be followed as a chain. The personality factors are the performer's tendency to seek achievement (Ms) and to avoid failure (Maf). The situational factors include the probability of success, the difficulty of the task, the importance of the outcome and the feedback given by others. Together they produce a resultant tendency : approach if the motive to achieve success is stronger, avoidance if the motive to avoid failure is stronger. This tendency then produces an emotion (pride and confidence, or fear and anxiety) and behaviour (choosing, persisting with or avoiding the task).

The chain from personality and situation to resultant tendency, emotion and behaviour, with a gymnastics example. The same situation can lead to very different responses in performers with different motives. Atkinson's model In Atkinson's model, the resultant tendency is often written as: Achievement motivation = Ms − Maf

The motive to achieve success is the product of the probability of success and the incentive value of success (Ms = Ps × Is). The motive to avoid failure depends on fear of failure, the probability of failure and the negative incentive value of failure. Because Ps + Pf = 1, a task that is easy (high Ps) carries little incentive for a performer who wants to succeed, and a task that is very hard (low Ps) carries little risk of a personal failure. This is why the two motives lead to different task choices. Task choice and persistence

The model predicts that performers with a strong motive to achieve success prefer tasks of moderate difficulty, where success is realistic but not certain, and that they persist longer in these tasks. Performers with a strong fear of failure prefer very easy or very hard tasks: very easy tasks protect against failure, and very hard tasks give a ready explanation for failing. This pattern is shown in the schematic curves below. The model is a simplified prediction; real preferences vary between individuals and situations.

Schematic task-choice preferences predicted by Atkinson's model. Approach-oriented performers prefer moderate difficulty; avoidance-oriented performers prefer very easy or very difficult tasks. In sport, this helps explain behaviour such as a player who avoids taking responsibility in a tense match, or an athlete who only enters races they are sure to win. Recognising the pattern lets a coach adjust the task instead of simply pushing the athlete harder. Task orientation

Performers also differ in how they define success. A task-oriented performer judges success by personal progress, skill development, effort and learning. An ego-oriented performer judges success by outperforming others. Task-oriented performers are more likely to persist after failure, because they interpret failure as information for improvement rather than as a judgement of their ability. This links to attribution and locus of control (see C.1.2). Coaching strategies Because achievement motivation depends on the situation as well as personality, coaches can shift the balance towards approach and away from avoidance by changing the environment:

Raise the probability of success: start with tasks the athlete can succeed at, and build the difficulty gradually. Make success meaningful: set personal targets and recognise progress, not only the final result. Reduce the cost of failure: treat errors as information, and avoid public blame or criticism. Build a task-focused climate: reward effort, learning and improvement, rather than only comparison with others. Four coaching strategies for changing the situation so that approach motivation increases and avoidance motivation falls. Examples are illustrative. Evaluating the model

Atkinson's model has been useful for explaining task choice, but it has limitations. It treats motives as fixed personality tendencies, although they can change with experience and coaching. The measures of motives and of the incentive value of success are hard to define and to test in real sport. The model also focuses on individual motivation, and does not fully capture team and social influences, or the role of goals and the coach. It is best used as one tool among several, to help understand and guide behaviour rather than to predict it exactly. Exam Tips

Use the chain for "explain" questions Personality (Ms and Maf) and situation (Ps and incentive) → resultant tendency → emotion → behaviour. Apply each step to the sporting example. Check the IB command terms . Show the balance Write Ms − Maf to show that achievement motivation depends on both motives. Say which is stronger for the athlete in the question. Link difficulty to task choice High Ms: moderate difficulty and persistence. High Maf: very easy or very hard tasks, and withdrawal from challenge. Give the reason for each. Apply the coaching strategies For coaching questions, name the strategy (for example graded difficulty) and explain how it changes Ps or the cost of failure.

Common mistake Don't say that high achievers always take the hardest challenges. Atkinson's model predicts moderate difficulty for high Ms. Also, don't describe motivation as a fixed trait that cannot change. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define achievement motivation . 1 mark Answer Model answer The psychological processes that drive a person to approach, persist in or avoid achievement situations in sport, exercise and health. 2 Identify two situational factors that affect achievement motivation. 2 marks Answer Model answer Probability of success (or difficulty of the task).

Importance or incentive value of the outcome, or feedback from others (any two). 3 Explain why an athlete with a high motive to achieve success might choose a task of moderate difficulty. 3 marks Answer Model answer A moderate task gives a realistic but uncertain chance of success, which makes success meaningful and rewarding. This maximises the incentive value of success for the athlete, so their motive to achieve success is most engaged. The athlete can also feel that success is due to their own ability and effort, which supports pride and persistence. 4 Explain how a coach could use the situation to increase approach motivation in an athlete who fears failure. 3 marks Answer Model answer

Start with tasks where success is likely (high probability of success), and build difficulty gradually. Focus feedback on personal progress and learning, and avoid public criticism, so that the cost of failure is reduced. These changes shift the balance of Ms and Maf towards approach over time. 5 (HL) Discuss the view that achievement motivation depends on both personality and the situation. 4 marks Answer Model answer Personality factors (Ms and Maf) determine the performer's tendency to approach or avoid achievement situations.

Situational factors, such as the probability of success, task difficulty and feedback from others, change how strongly those tendencies are expressed in a given task. For example, a high-Maf athlete may approach a task when the probability of success is high and the cost of failure is low, which shows the interaction. Limitations: the model treats motives as fixed and is hard to test in real sport, so it should be used as a guide rather than an exact prediction. C.3.2 Self-determination | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.3.2 C.3.2 Theme C · Motivation SL & HL Self-determination How autonomy, competence and relatedness drive motivation, how motivation ranges from amotivation to intrinsic, and how coaches can support self-determined athletes. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Self-determination theory (SDT) explains motivation by proposing that people naturally seek to satisfy three basic psychological needs : autonomy (feeling in control of one's actions), competence (feeling capable and effective) and relatedness (feeling connected to others). Motivation is not simply present or absent. It sits on a continuum , from amotivation , through four types of extrinsic motivation that differ in how internal they are, to intrinsic motivation , where the activity is done for its own enjoyment. Coaches who meet these needs tend to build more self-determined and persistent athletes. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define self-determination theory and describe the three basic psychological needs. Place examples of motivation on the continuum from amotivation to intrinsic motivation. Explain why intrinsic motivation supports enjoyment, self-regulation and persistence. Apply the needs to coaching strategies that support autonomy, competence and relatedness. HL: Describe the six mini-theories and explain the effect of rewards on intrinsic motivation. Key Terms Autonomy Feeling in control of one's own actions and choices, acting in line with one's values. Competence Feeling capable, effective and able to master challenges. Relatedness Feeling connected to, and cared for by, others.

Amotivation A lack of intention to act, with no sense that the action is worthwhile. Extrinsic motivation Acting to gain an outcome that is separate from the activity, such as a reward or avoiding punishment. Intrinsic motivation Acting for the enjoyment and interest of the activity itself. Presentations C.3.2.1 Self-determination Theory C.3.2.2 The Motivation Continuum C.3.2.3 Self-determination Meta-theories Deep Dive The three basic psychological needs SDT proposes that all people need to satisfy three basic psychological needs for optimal functioning and well-being. Satisfying them supports autonomous motivation; frustrating them tends to produce controlled motivation or amotivation.

The three basic psychological needs, what each means, and an example coaching approach for each. Meeting all three supports self-determined motivation. Autonomy is supported by choice and meaningful input: letting athletes select drills, set some of their own goals, or explain why a task matters. Controlling language, such as "you must", tends to undermine it. Competence is supported by achievable challenges and constructive feedback that highlights progress. A task that is far too difficult, or praise that is not connected to real improvement, does not support it. Relatedness is supported by a positive team climate, trust, cooperation and genuine care from coaches and teammates.

The needs work together. An athlete who is given choice but never succeeds may lose competence; one who succeeds in a cold, controlling environment may lose relatedness. Good coaching considers all three. The motivation continuum

SDT describes motivation as a continuum, which runs from less to more self-determined. Amotivation is the absence of intention. Extrinsic motivation covers four types, from least to most internalised: external (for a reward or to avoid punishment), introjected (to avoid guilt or protect self-worth), identified (because the activity is personally valued) and integrated (because it fits with the person's own values and identity). Intrinsic motivation is the most self-determined form, where the activity is enjoyed for its own sake. The motivation continuum, from amotivation to intrinsic motivation, with the four types of extrinsic motivation between them. Examples are illustrative.

Intrinsic and more internalised forms of motivation are associated with enjoyment, effort, persistence and self-regulation over time. A young player who is intrinsically motivated is more likely to keep practising when no one is watching, which supports long-term participation. Applying SDT to coaching

SDT can guide the design of training environments. A coach can move athletes towards more self-determined motivation by offering choice and explanation, providing achievable challenges with informative feedback, and building a supportive team culture. Coaches who rely mainly on external rewards and pressure may get short-term effort, but this is more likely to be controlled, and it can weaken when the pressure is removed. This does not mean that extrinsic rewards are always harmful. The effect depends on how the reward is perceived, which is part of the HL discussion below. The six mini-theories HL

SDT is often described as a meta-theory : a set of six related mini-theories that each explain part of motivation. Together they form a broader framework. The six mini-theories of self-determination theory, with a brief description and an application to sport. Each explains a different aspect of motivation.

Two of the mini-theories are especially useful for exam answers. Cognitive evaluation theory explains how rewards affect intrinsic motivation. A reward that feels informational , such as praise that recognises skill or improvement, can support the athlete's sense of competence and autonomy, and so support intrinsic motivation. A reward that feels controlling , such as a bonus that depends on winning, can make the athlete feel pressured and reduce their sense of autonomy, which can undermine intrinsic motivation. Goal contents theory distinguishes intrinsic goals (growth, relationships and community) from extrinsic goals (image, wealth and status). Intrinsic goals are linked to greater well-being.

Exam Tips Name all three needs when asked Autonomy, competence and relatedness. Then link each to a specific coaching behaviour in the sport in the question. Check the IB command terms . Place examples on the continuum For questions about types of motivation, say where the example sits (for example identified or introjected) and why. Don't just say "extrinsic" or "intrinsic". Evaluate rewards carefully For HL questions, say that informational rewards can support intrinsic motivation, while controlling rewards can undermine it. Give a sporting example of each.

Link needs to long-term outcomes Explain that meeting the needs supports self-determined motivation, which leads to enjoyment, persistence and long-term participation. Common mistake Don't say that extrinsic motivation is always bad. Some extrinsic motivation can be internalised and become self-determined. Also, don't describe the needs as only "fun" or "choice": competence and relatedness are equally important. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Identify two basic psychological needs in self-determination theory. 1 mark Answer Model answer Any two of: autonomy, competence and relatedness. 2 Define amotivation . 1 mark Answer Model answer

A lack of intention to act, with no sense that the activity is worthwhile or that the outcomes are controlled by the person. 3 Explain how a coach could support the need for autonomy in a training session. 3 marks Answer Model answer The coach can offer choices, such as the athlete selecting from a set of drills or choosing a goal area for the session. The coach can explain why the task is useful and use less controlling language, which lets the athlete feel their actions are their own. This supports autonomous motivation, so the athlete is more likely to persist and engage.

4 Place an athlete who trains only to avoid criticism from the coach on the motivation continuum, and explain your answer. 3 marks Answer Model answer This is external (or introjected) extrinsic motivation, because the athlete acts to avoid a negative consequence rather than for the activity itself. The athlete trains only to avoid criticism, so the behaviour depends on outside pressure rather than enjoyment or personal value. It sits towards the less self-determined end of the continuum, where the reason for acting is controlled by others. 5 (HL) Discuss how extrinsic rewards can affect an athlete's intrinsic motivation, using cognitive evaluation theory. 4 marks Answer Model answer

Informational rewards, such as praise for skill improvement, can support the athlete's sense of competence and autonomy, which supports intrinsic motivation. Controlling rewards, such as a bonus that depends on winning, can make the athlete feel pressured and reduce their sense of autonomy, which can undermine intrinsic motivation. The effect therefore depends on how the reward is perceived by the athlete, not only on the reward itself. Coaches should use rewards that recognise progress and effort, so that they support rather than replace intrinsic motivation. C.3.3 Motivational Climate | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.3.3 C.3.3 Theme C · Motivation SL & HL Motivational Climate How the psychological environment created by the coach shapes whether athletes focus on mastery and improvement or on comparison and winning. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

A motivational climate is the psychological environment that a coach (and the wider team) creates through session design, instructions, feedback, rewards and the way mistakes are handled. Climates are commonly described as mastery (task-involving) or ego (performance-involving). A mastery climate asks "How can we improve?" and values effort, learning and cooperation. An ego climate asks "Who is the best?" and values winning and outperforming others. The climate influences the goal orientation of each athlete, and through it their effort, teamwork, anxiety and enjoyment. The TARGET framework gives coaches six levers to build a mastery climate. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define motivational climate as the psychological environment created by the coach. Compare mastery and ego climates using effort, improvement, winning and comparison. Explain why mastery climates support enjoyment, teamwork and long-term participation. Explain why ego climates are linked to anxiety and dropout. Apply the TARGET framework to show how a coach can foster a mastery climate. Key Terms Motivational climate The psychological environment created by the coach through session design, instructions and feedback. Mastery (task-involving) climate An environment that emphasises personal or team development, effort and improvement.

Ego (performance-involving) climate An environment that emphasises winning and outperforming others. Goal orientation The way an individual defines success, as task (self-referenced) or ego (comparison with others). TARGET A framework of six levers (Task, Authority, Recognition, Grouping, Evaluation, Time) that shape the climate. Recognition The way praise and rewards are given, to individuals or to the team. Presentation C.3.3.1 Motivational Climate Deep Dive What is a motivational climate?

A motivational climate is not a personality trait. It is the environment that the coach creates, and it shapes how athletes judge success and failure. A coach creates it through what they choose to measure, how they give feedback, who receives praise, how mistakes are treated, and how decisions are made. Because athletes respond to the climate, the coach's choices affect the whole group, not only one athlete. Mastery and ego climates compared

In a mastery climate , success is defined by personal progress, skill development, effort and learning. Mistakes are seen as information for improvement, and recognition goes to effort and cooperation. In an ego climate , success is defined by outperforming others, mistakes are a reason for blame or embarrassment, and recognition goes to the top performer. The table below sets out these differences. Mastery (task) and ego (performance) climates compared across several aspects. Mastery climates are linked to enjoyment, persistence and teamwork; ego climates are linked to anxiety and dropout risk.

Mastery climates are linked to enjoyment , cooperation , sustained effort and better long-term development. Ego climates can produce short-term results for some athletes, but they are more likely to be linked to anxiety , fear of making mistakes, rivalry within the team and dropping out, especially for athletes who do not feel they are succeeding. A useful exam point is that a climate can be strong even when it is not stated. A coach who only rewards the top scorer, publicly compares players and puts winning above learning creates an ego climate, even if they never use the word "winning" in their instructions. The TARGET framework

TARGET sets out six areas in which coaches can structure instruction and practice to build a mastery climate: Task (the design and challenge of activities), Authority (how much athletes share in decisions), Recognition (how praise and rewards are given), Grouping (how athletes are organised), Evaluation (how progress and mistakes are judged) and Time (how much time is given to learn and how the pace is set). The TARGET framework, with a mastery approach and an ego approach for each of the six elements. A mastery climate is built by applying the TARGET elements consistently. How the climate shapes behaviour and outcomes

The climate influences the goal orientation that athletes adopt, and this shapes their behaviour. In a mastery climate, athletes tend to put in effort, cooperate, and keep trying after mistakes. In an ego climate, athletes may compare themselves with others, fear failure, and avoid risks that could help them learn. Over time these behaviours produce different outcomes: enjoyment, teamwork and long-term participation in the mastery pathway, and anxiety, reduced enjoyment and dropout risk in the ego pathway. The flow from motivational climate, to athlete goal orientation, to behaviour and outcomes. Individual differences also affect how an athlete responds to the same climate.

Applying the idea in team sport In team sports, a mastery climate can improve teamwork, because athletes are encouraged to cooperate and to value the team's development rather than only their own statistics. A coach who asks players to help each other learn a tactic, and recognises the support given to teammates, is building a mastery climate. Ego-focused selection and public ranking can damage team cohesion, because athletes may focus on their own position rather than the group. The climate can also be shaped by parents, peers and the wider environment, but the coach has the most direct influence through the choices made in each session. Exam Tips

Define the climate as the coach's environment Use the phrase "psychological environment created by the coach through session design, instructions and feedback". Check the IB command terms . Compare with the same terms each time Use effort, improvement, winning and comparison for both climates, so that your comparison is clear and balanced. Apply TARGET by name For questions on how a coach can create a mastery climate, name the TARGET element (for example Recognition) and give a specific coaching action for it. Link the climate to outcomes Explain the chain: climate → goal orientation → behaviour → outcomes, such as enjoyment, teamwork, anxiety or dropout.

Common mistake Don't say that an ego climate always produces poor results. It can work for some athletes in the short term, but it is linked to anxiety and dropout. Also, don't confuse the climate with the individual athlete's goal orientation: they are linked, but they are different. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define motivational climate . 1 mark Answer Model answer The psychological environment created by the coach through session design, instructions and feedback. 2 State two coaching behaviours that foster a mastery climate. 2 marks Answer Model answer Praising effort, improvement and learning rather than only the final result.

Treating mistakes as information for improvement, and giving athletes a role in decisions. (Any two, for example from TARGET.) 3 Compare a mastery climate with an ego climate in terms of how success is defined and how mistakes are treated. 3 marks Answer Model answer In a mastery climate, success is defined by personal progress, effort and learning; in an ego climate it is defined by outperforming others or winning. In a mastery climate mistakes are information for improvement; in an ego climate mistakes are a reason for blame or embarrassment. The mastery climate therefore supports persistence and learning, while the ego climate can increase fear of failure.

4 Explain how a coach could use the TARGET framework to make a basketball training session more mastery-focused. 3 marks Answer Model answer Task: set varied, challenging drills with clear skill goals, rather than one drill judged only on the result. Recognition: praise effort and improvement for all players, not only the top scorer. Evaluation: measure each athlete against their own previous performance, and treat errors as learning opportunities. 5 Discuss how a motivational climate can affect the enjoyment, teamwork and long-term participation of athletes. 4 marks Answer Model answer A mastery climate encourages effort, cooperation and learning, which supports enjoyment and teamwork.

Athletes in a mastery climate are more likely to persist after setbacks, which supports long-term participation. An ego climate can increase rivalry and fear of failure, which may reduce enjoyment and lead to anxiety or dropout, especially for athletes who feel they are not succeeding. The climate is shaped by the coach, so coaches are responsible for choosing approaches that support all athletes, not only the best performers. C.4.1 Arousal & Anxiety | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.4.1 C.4.1 Theme C · Stress & Coping SL & HL Arousal & Anxiety How arousal and anxiety relate to performance: the inverted-U hypothesis, individual zones, the two components of anxiety and why high anxiety can cause a sudden collapse. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Arousal is the level of physical and psychological activation, from deep sleep to intense excitement. Anxiety is a negative emotional state with worry and physical symptoms. The two are related but different: arousal can be positive, and anxiety is the unpleasant form of activation. The inverted-U hypothesis proposes that performance improves with arousal up to an optimal point and then declines. The individual zone of optimal functioning (IZOF) recognises that the optimal point differs between athletes and between tasks. At higher level, anxiety is split into cognitive and somatic components, and catastrophe theory explains why performance can collapse suddenly when both are high.

By the end of this topic you should be able to Define arousal as physical and psychological activation, and distinguish it from anxiety. Distinguish between cognitive and somatic anxiety, with examples. Distinguish between trait and state anxiety. Explain the inverted-U hypothesis, including the effect of task complexity, and the concept of IZOF. HL: Explain catastrophe theory, and compare it with the inverted-U hypothesis and IZOF. Key Terms Arousal The level of physical and psychological activation, which affects performance. Anxiety A negative emotional state involving worry and physical symptoms of arousal. Cognitive anxiety Mental worry, negative thoughts and self-doubt.

Somatic anxiety Physical symptoms of arousal, such as increased heart rate, muscle tension and sweating. Inverted-U hypothesis Performance rises with arousal to an optimal point, then falls when arousal is too high. IZOF Individual zone of optimal functioning: each athlete's own zone of arousal for peak performance. Presentations C.4.1.1 Arousal C.4.1.2 Anxiety Deep Dive Arousal: physical and psychological activation

Arousal has a physical side (heart rate, breathing, muscle tension, adrenaline release) and a psychological side (alertness, focus, readiness). It is controlled largely by the sympathetic nervous system and hormones such as adrenaline. Low arousal may leave an athlete flat and inattentive; high arousal may bring energy and readiness, but also tension. Arousal is not bad in itself. The question for performance is how much arousal there is compared with what the task needs. Anxiety: cognitive and somatic components

Anxiety is more than high arousal. It has two components that are often measured separately. Cognitive anxiety is the worry, negative thinking and fear of failure. Somatic anxiety is the physical experience of arousal that is interpreted as unpleasant, such as a racing heart, sweaty palms, butterflies or muscle tension. An athlete can have high physical arousal without anxiety, for example when excited, and anxiety can be present with little physical arousal. The components of anxiety: cognitive and somatic anxiety, and trait and state anxiety, with examples. Trait anxiety is a stable tendency; state anxiety is a temporary response to a situation. Trait and state anxiety

Trait anxiety is a stable personality tendency to perceive situations as threatening and to feel anxious across many situations. State anxiety is a temporary emotional state in a particular situation, which can rise and fall quickly, for example in the minutes before a final. A high-trait athlete is more likely to experience high state anxiety, but the two are not the same. Coaches and sport psychologists often measure state anxiety just before competition with questionnaires such as the Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2 (CSAI-2R), which assess cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety and self-confidence. The inverted-U hypothesis and IZOF

The inverted-U hypothesis proposes that performance increases as arousal increases, up to an optimal level, and then decreases as arousal becomes too high. Two points are important. First, the optimal level depends on the task : simple or gross motor tasks, such as a sprint start or a weightlift, tolerate and often need higher arousal, while complex or fine-motor tasks, such as a golf putt or a gymnastics balance, need lower arousal, because too much arousal disrupts precise control and attention. Second, the optimal point differs between athletes. The individual zone of optimal functioning (IZOF) proposes that each athlete has their own zone of arousal in which they perform best, and that this zone can be identified and used in training.

The inverted-U hypothesis for simple and complex tasks (schematic), with the individual zone of optimal functioning for one athlete shaded. The optimal arousal level is lower for complex tasks. The model links to attention (see C.2.2). Arousal beyond the optimal level tends to narrow attention, so an athlete may focus on the threat and miss relevant cues. Coaches can use IZOF to help athletes recognise their own signs of too much or too little arousal, and then use strategies to adjust it. Catastrophe theory HL

The inverted-U hypothesis predicts a gradual fall in performance after the optimal point. Catastrophe theory predicts something different when anxiety is involved. When cognitive anxiety is low , performance declines gradually as arousal rises past the optimal point, as the inverted-U predicts. When cognitive anxiety is high , performance may fall suddenly and severely once arousal passes a threshold, because the athlete's worry and physical arousal combine and the performance can collapse. This is why catastrophe theory explains the phrase "choking" under pressure.

Catastrophe theory compared with the inverted-U hypothesis (schematic). With low cognitive anxiety performance declines gradually; with high cognitive anxiety it drops suddenly once arousal passes the threshold. Comparing the theories HL Each theory explains a different part of the relationship: Theory Key idea Prediction for high arousal Limitation Drive theory Arousal increases the dominant response; skilled, well-learned responses improve while novel ones worsen Performance improves for well-learned skills, worsens for new ones Does not describe the optimal point clearly, and the drive-performance link is hard to test

Inverted-U hypothesis Performance is best at a moderate, optimal arousal level, and the optimal level depends on task complexity Gradual decline after the optimal point One optimal level is assumed for all athletes; the shape is hard to measure precisely IZOF Each athlete has a personal zone of optimal arousal Decline beyond the athlete's own zone Zones are hard to identify reliably, and can change over time Catastrophe theory Performance can collapse suddenly when cognitive and somatic anxiety are both high Sudden, severe drop once a threshold is passed Complex to test; the threshold is hard to define

A balanced evaluation shows that these theories are not in competition. Inverted-U and IZOF describe the basic relationship, and catastrophe theory explains when performance can fall sharply. The best approach for coaches is to combine them: identify each athlete's zone, and watch for cognitive anxiety, which can make the drop sudden. Exam Tips Name the optimal point Don't describe the inverted-U without naming the optimal arousal level and the decline after it. Say whether the task is simple or complex, because this changes the optimal level.

Separate arousal from anxiety Arousal is activation; anxiety is the unpleasant, worried form of it. Give one cognitive and one somatic example for anxiety. Check the IB command terms . Catastrophe theory needs both components Don't explain it as "high arousal only". It requires high cognitive anxiety combined with high somatic arousal, which causes a sudden drop. Evaluate the theories together For comparison questions, state what each theory predicts for high arousal and one limitation of each. Common mistake Don't say that all athletes have the same optimal arousal level, or that low arousal is always the best way to control anxiety. The optimal point differs between athletes and tasks.

Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define arousal in the context of sports performance. 1 mark Answer Model answer The level of physical and psychological activation (for example heart rate, alertness and readiness) that affects how well an athlete performs. 2 Identify two physiological signs of somatic anxiety. 2 marks Answer Model answer Increased heart rate or breathing rate. Muscle tension, sweating or butterflies in the stomach. (Any two.) 3 Outline how trait anxiety differs from state anxiety. 2 marks Answer Model answer Trait anxiety is a stable personality tendency to feel anxious across many situations.

State anxiety is a temporary emotional response to a particular situation, which can rise and fall quickly. 4 Explain how the inverted-U hypothesis describes the relationship between arousal and performance for a complex, fine-motor task. 3 marks Answer Model answer Performance improves as arousal increases up to an optimal point. Beyond this point, performance declines as arousal becomes too high. For a complex, fine-motor task the optimal arousal level is lower, because high arousal disrupts precise control and attention. 5 (HL) Explain how catastrophe theory explains a sudden fall in performance under pressure. 4 marks Answer Model answer

Catastrophe theory proposes that performance can fall suddenly and severely when arousal passes a threshold. This happens when cognitive anxiety (worry, fear of failure) is high alongside high somatic anxiety (physical arousal). With low cognitive anxiety, performance declines more gradually, as the inverted-U predicts. An athlete with high cognitive and somatic anxiety at a penalty may therefore suffer a sudden breakdown, which is sometimes described as choking.
