C.4.2 Coping | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.4.2 C.4.2 Theme C · Stress & Coping SL & HL Coping How athletes manage stressors and their emotional responses, which types of coping suit which stressors, and how coping works before, during and after competition. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Coping is the set of thoughts and behaviours an athlete uses to manage the demands of a stressful situation. Coping strategies are often grouped by what they target. Problem-focused coping alters or removes the stressor. Emotion-focused coping regulates the emotional response without changing the stressor, for example through relaxation, breathing or self-talk. Avoidance-focused coping moves attention or effort away from the stressor. Athletes use all three, often together. Which one works best depends on whether the stressor is controllable, and on the individual and the situation. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define coping and distinguish problem-focused, emotion-focused and avoidance-focused coping. Give examples of cognitive, somatic and social coping strategies. Explain how coping strategies can be used before, during and after competition. HL: Match problem-focused coping to controllable stressors and emotion-focused coping to uncontrollable stressors. HL: Explain why coping effectiveness varies between individuals and situations. Key Terms Coping The thoughts and behaviours used to manage the demands of a stressful situation. Stressor A demand or situation that an athlete perceives as stressful. Problem-focused coping Coping that alters or removes the stressor.

Emotion-focused coping Coping that regulates the emotional response without changing the stressor. Avoidance-focused coping Coping that moves attention or effort away from the stressor. Biofeedback A technique that uses sensors to show physiological responses, such as heart rate or muscle tension, so the athlete can learn to control them. Presentations C.4.2.1 Stressors C.4.2.2 Controllable and Uncontrollable Stressors C.4.2.3 Coping Strategies Deep Dive What coping is

A stressor is a demand the athlete perceives as stressful, such as a demanding opponent, an injury, a selection decision or a crowd. Stress arises when the athlete believes the demand exceeds their resources. Coping is the response: the effort to manage the demand or the emotions it creates. Effective coping reduces the negative effects of stress on performance, well-being and health. Three types of coping Coping strategies are often classified by what they target: Problem-focused, emotion-focused and avoidance-focused coping, with examples of each. The categories describe the aim of a strategy, not its quality.

Some strategies can belong to more than one category. Avoidance can be emotion-focused when it regulates anxiety, for example by telling oneself to stay calm, and seeking social support is emotion-focused when it provides reassurance and emotional regulation rather than practical help. Cognitive, somatic and social strategies Emotion-focused coping is often delivered through three kinds of strategy:

Cognitive strategies change how the athlete thinks. These include self-talk (cue words or phrases that direct attention and confidence), mental imagery (rehearsing a successful performance), and cognitive restructuring , which means identifying an unhelpful thought, such as "I always choke", and replacing it with a more balanced, useful one, such as "I've handled pressure before and I can focus on the next point".

Somatic strategies reduce physical arousal. These include progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) , in which the athlete tenses and then relaxes muscle groups in turn, slow diaphragmatic breathing (controlled breaths that lower heart rate and tension), and biofeedback , in which sensors show heart rate or muscle tension so the athlete can learn to control them. Social support comes from coaches, teammates, family and friends. It can provide reassurance, empathy and practical help. Emotional support is emotion-focused; practical advice on a tactic is problem-focused.

Routines are also important. A pre-performance routine combines cognitive and somatic elements, with a consistent sequence of breathing, cue words and imagery before each skill. It gives the athlete a familiar structure that reduces uncertainty and manages arousal. Coping across a competition Coping is not only needed during the event. Athletes can plan strategies for each stage: before (goal-setting, cue words and relaxation), during (refocusing, breathing and routines after mistakes) and after (reviewing performance, cooling down and seeking support). Planning across the whole competition helps athletes avoid being overwhelmed when a stressor appears.
Coping strategies across a competition. Each stage uses cognitive, somatic and social strategies, chosen to suit the stressor at that point. Matching coping to the stressor HL

Stressors differ in whether the athlete can change them. A controllable stressor is one the athlete can influence, such as a weak technique or a training plan. The best match is usually problem-focused coping , which changes the stressor: practising the skill, seeking coaching or adjusting tactics. An uncontrollable stressor is one the athlete cannot change, such as the weather, a referee's decision or an injury that is already happening. Here emotion-focused coping is usually more effective, because the aim is to manage the emotional response and focus on what can be controlled.
Matching coping types to controllable and uncontrollable stressors. Highlighted boxes show the best match; the fit depends on the individual and the situation. Effectiveness varies HL

No coping strategy works for everyone in every situation. Effectiveness depends on the individual , including their personality, experience, preferences and skills, and on the situation , including the sport, the stage of competition and the level of pressure. Relaxation may help a nervous archer before a shot, but be unhelpful for a boxer who needs energy in the ring. Some strategies can be maladaptive : avoidance that stops an athlete facing a problem, or excessive reliance on substances to cope, can increase stress in the long term. Coping should therefore be chosen, practised in training and reviewed, rather than used at random.

Coping can also be related to injury recovery. An injured athlete may use problem-focused coping, such as following a rehabilitation programme, alongside emotion-focused coping, such as managing frustration and fear of re-injury. Both are often needed. Exam Tips Name the type, then the aim "Problem-focused coping aims to alter the stressor". Name the coping type, say what it targets, then give a sporting example. Check the IB command terms . Say cognitive or somatic For emotion-focused strategies, say whether they work on thoughts (self-talk, imagery, cognitive restructuring) or on physical arousal (breathing, PMR, biofeedback).

Match the stressor first For HL questions, decide whether the stressor is controllable or uncontrollable before choosing the coping type. Then say why that match is appropriate. Evaluate with the individual and situation Say that effectiveness depends on the athlete and the context, and give one example where a strategy would help and one where it would not. Common mistake Don't say that relaxation is always the best coping strategy, or that problem-focused coping always works best. The match depends on whether the stressor can be changed. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define coping . 1 mark Answer Model answer

The thoughts and behaviours an athlete uses to manage the demands of a stressful situation. 2 Outline the difference between problem-focused and emotion-focused coping. 2 marks Answer Model answer Problem-focused coping alters or removes the stressor itself (for example by changing tactics or training). Emotion-focused coping regulates the emotional response to the stressor without changing it (for example by breathing control or self-talk). 3 Describe two somatic coping strategies used by athletes. 2 marks Answer Model answer Progressive muscle relaxation, in which muscle groups are tensed and relaxed in turn to reduce physical tension.

Slow diaphragmatic breathing, which lowers heart rate and muscle tension. (Biofeedback is also accepted.) 4 Explain how cognitive restructuring can help an athlete who believes they always fail under pressure. 3 marks Answer Model answer Cognitive restructuring identifies the unhelpful belief ("I always fail under pressure") and examines the evidence for it. The athlete replaces it with a more balanced, useful thought, such as recalling times they coped with pressure. This reduces cognitive anxiety, which can lower the emotional response and help the athlete focus on the task.

5 (HL) Explain why problem-focused coping is more appropriate for a controllable stressor, and give one example. 4 marks Answer Model answer A controllable stressor can be changed, so problem-focused coping, which alters or removes the stressor, addresses its cause. Changing the stressor usually reduces the stress more effectively than managing the emotional response alone. Example: a footballer with poor passing accuracy practises the skill with feedback from the coach, which removes the source of the stress. Emotion-focused coping still helps alongside this, but is less effective on its own when the stressor can be changed. Previous topic ← C.4.1 Arousal & Anxiety

C.5.1 Goal Setting | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.5.1 C.5.1 Theme C · Psychological Skills SL & HL Goal Setting How setting clear goals directs attention, sustains effort and builds confidence, and how outcome, performance and process goals work together. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Goal setting is a psychological skill that directs attention and effort to a specific task. Goals differ in their reference point : an outcome goal is judged against other performers, a performance goal against a personal, measurable standard, and a process goal against the technique or strategy being executed. Process and performance goals are usually more controllable than outcome goals, which depend on others. Effective goals are often SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound), arranged in a hierarchy from long-term to short-term, and reviewed and adjusted over time. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define goal setting as a psychological skill that directs attention to a task. Distinguish between outcome, performance and process goals by their reference point. Apply the SMART principles to write an effective goal. Explain how goal setting enhances motivation, attention and persistence. Explain the goal hierarchy and the value of combining short-term and long-term goals. HL: Explain goal adjustment, do-your-best goals and the goal-setting paradox. Key Terms Goal setting A psychological skill that directs attention and effort to a specific task. Outcome goal A goal focused on the result, usually judged against other performers.

Performance goal A goal focused on a personal, measurable standard. Process goal A goal focused on the technique or strategy being executed. SMART Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Goal hierarchy Long-term goals broken down into medium-term and short-term goals that lead towards them. Presentations C.5.1.1 Goal Setting C.5.1.2 The Goal-setting Paradox Deep Dive Goal setting as a psychological skill

Goal setting is a psychological skill because it can be learned, practised and refined, like a physical skill. A well-set goal does three things: it directs attention to the relevant parts of performance, it sustains effort when progress is slow, and it provides a standard against which the athlete can judge feedback and build confidence . Goal setting links closely to motivation, particularly to achievement motivation (see C.3.1), because a clear goal makes the chance of success more visible. Outcome, performance and process goals The three goal types differ in what they are measured against:

Outcome, performance and process goals, with the reference point, an example and how controllable each is. Athletes often combine all three. Outcome goals are judged against other performers, for example winning a race. They motivate, but depend on the opposition and on factors outside the athlete's control, so they can increase pressure and anxiety if they are the only focus. Performance goals are judged against the athlete's own previous standard, for example a personal best time. They are more controllable, because improvement depends largely on the athlete's own effort.

Process goals focus on the technique or strategy being carried out, for example a relaxed grip or even pacing. They are the most controllable, and they often lead to better performance and outcomes over time. A useful way to combine them is an outcome goal as the destination (qualifying for the final), a performance goal as the personal standard (running under 2:05), and a process goal as the action plan (maintaining even pacing and relaxed shoulders). The SMART principles

Effective goals are often written using the SMART principles. A goal should be specific about what is to be achieved; measurable so progress can be checked; achievable, challenging but realistic for the athlete; relevant to the sport and to the bigger goal; and time-bound, with a deadline or review date. The SMART principles, with a vague goal compared against a SMART version. The SMART version can be checked, reviewed and achieved or adjusted. The goal hierarchy

Long-term goals (for example making a national squad in three years) are most useful when they are broken down into medium-term goals (for example improving a scoring average this season) and short-term goals (for example a daily training target). Short-term goals give frequent feedback and a sense of progress, which maintains motivation, while the long-term goal gives direction. Goals should also be recorded, for example in a training diary, and reviewed regularly. The goal-setting cycle

Goal setting works best as a continuous cycle: set goals, plan the actions needed, monitor progress with logs, statistics or video, evaluate progress against the goal and the target date, and then adjust the goal or the plan. Adjustment is part of the process. Goals that are never checked are easily forgotten, and goals that are never adjusted may become unrealistic or stop being useful. The goal-setting cycle. Monitoring and evaluation feed directly into adjustment, which leads to new or revised goals. Goal adjustment, do-your-best goals and the paradox HL

Goal adjustment means changing a goal in the light of evidence: raising it if it has been reached easily, lowering it if it is unrealistic, or replacing it if circumstances have changed, for example after an injury. Adjustment should be based on objective evidence, not on a single bad result. Do-your-best goals set an aim to give full effort, without a specific numerical target. They avoid the pressure of a fixed standard, but they are less precise, so they give less clear direction and feedback than specific goals.

The goal-setting paradox refers to the observation that setting a goal can sometimes cause problems. A very difficult or highly visible goal may increase anxiety and cause the athlete to focus on the result and lose their process. An athlete may also set goals that make success depend on factors they cannot control, leading to frustration. Good goal setting therefore uses challenging but realistic targets, emphasises performance and process goals, and reviews the goal's effects on the athlete's emotions as well as their results. Exam Tips

Name the reference point Outcome goals are compared with others, performance goals with a personal standard, and process goals with technique or strategy. Say which applies. Check the IB command terms . Write goals in SMART form For a question about setting a goal, write one that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound, for the sport in the question. Link goals to motivation and attention Explain that goals direct attention to relevant performance cues and sustain effort, rather than just stating that goals "help". Include adjustment For evaluation questions, say that goals should be monitored, evaluated and adjusted, and why this matters.

Common mistake Don't say that outcome goals are always bad. They motivate, but they should not be the only focus, because they depend on others and can raise anxiety. Also, don't write a vague goal such as "do better" and call it SMART. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define goal setting in the context of sport. 1 mark Answer Model answer A psychological skill that directs attention and effort to a specific task, to improve motivation and performance. 2 Distinguish between outcome and process goals in sport. 2 marks Answer Model answer An outcome goal is judged against other performers and the result (for example winning the match).

A process goal focuses on the technique or strategy being executed (for example keeping a relaxed shoulder on serve). Process goals are more controllable. 3 Identify which element of SMART is missing from the goal "Improve my fitness this season", and rewrite the goal to include it. 3 marks Answer Model answer "Improve my fitness" is not measurable, and it has no time limit or specific target. A measurable target, such as a test result, lets progress be checked. Rewritten example: "Increase my 2 km rowing ergometer time from 8:10 to 7:50 by the end of the season in March." 4 Explain why a coach might combine outcome, performance and process goals for a sprinter. 3 marks Answer Model answer

The outcome goal (for example qualifying for the final) gives a clear destination and direction. The performance goal (a personal best time) gives a measurable standard that the sprinter controls more directly. The process goal (for example driving the arms and maintaining posture) gives daily actions that build towards the other goals. 5 (HL) Discuss why a goal that is too difficult or too visible may reduce performance, and how a coach could address this. 4 marks Answer Model answer A very difficult or highly visible goal can increase anxiety and cause the athlete to focus on the result rather than the process.

The athlete may feel that success depends on factors they cannot control, which can lower confidence and motivation. The coach can set challenging but realistic goals, emphasise performance and process goals, and adjust targets when evidence shows they are unrealistic. Reviewing the effect of the goal on the athlete's emotions, as well as their results, helps ensure that goals support rather than harm performance. C.5.2 Imagery | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Theme C › C.5.2 C.5.2 Theme C · Psychological Skills HL only Imagery How mental rehearsal, when made realistic, can improve skill execution, confidence and arousal control, and how to structure imagery for different purposes. 1 Overview 2 Presentation 3 Deep Dive 4 Exam Tips 5 Practice Questions Overview

Imagery is multisensory mental rehearsal of a skill or situation, carried out in the absence of actual physical performance. It uses sight, sound, touch and the feeling of movement, and can be seen through the athlete's own eyes ( internal ) or as if watching oneself from outside ( external ). Imagery can help improve skill execution, plan tactics, build confidence and control arousal. Paivio's framework classifies imagery by its function (cognitive or motivational) and its specificity (specific or general). The PETTLEP model describes how to make imagery as close as possible to real performance, which makes it more effective. By the end of this topic you should be able to

Define imagery as multisensory mental rehearsal in the absence of actual perception. Distinguish between internal and external imagery, and when each is most appropriate. Distinguish between cognitive and motivational imagery, and between specific and general imagery, using Paivio's framework. Explain the PETTLEP model and how it makes imagery more effective. Apply imagery to a sporting scenario, classifying its function and specificity. Key Terms Imagery Multisensory mental rehearsal in the absence of actual perception of the movement. Internal imagery Imagining the performance through one's own eyes, feeling the movement from inside.

External imagery Imagining oneself performing, as if watching from outside. Cognitive imagery Imagery used to rehearse skills and strategies. Motivational imagery Imagery used to achieve goals, regulate arousal or build confidence and control. PETTLEP A model of seven elements (physical, environment, task, timing, learning, emotion, perspective) for making imagery functionally equivalent to real performance. Presentation C.5.2.1 Imagery Deep Dive What imagery is

Imagery is multisensory : it involves more than a picture in the mind. A good image includes what the athlete sees, hears and feels, including the movement, the timing and the emotion. Imagery is sometimes called mental practice, visualisation or mental simulation. Its value comes from rehearsing a skill or situation without the physical effort, risk or cost of performing it, so it can be used when physical practice is not possible, for example during injury or before a competition. Internal and external perspective

The perspective chosen affects what is rehearsed. In internal imagery , the athlete sees the performance through their own eyes and experiences the movement from inside, which helps with the feel of the skill and its timing. In external imagery , the athlete watches themselves as if on video, which helps with technique, body position and how the performance looks. Many athletes use both, and choose the perspective that suits the aim of the session. Internal and external imagery, with an example and the aims each suits best. Paivio's imagery framework

Paivio's framework helps decide what imagery is for. It classifies imagery by function (cognitive or motivational) and specificity (specific or general): Cognitive specific (CS): rehearsing a specific skill, such as a golf swing sequence or a gymnastics element. Cognitive general (CG): rehearsing strategies, routines and game plans, such as a team's tactics for a set piece. Motivational specific (MS): imagining achieving a specific goal, such as a personal best time or a winning moment. Motivational general-arousal (MG-A): regulating stress, anxiety or activation, for example through calm breathing and relaxed imagery before competition.

Motivational general-mastery (MG-M): imagining confidence, coping and control under pressure, for example composed play when the score is close. Paivio's framework of imagery, showing the five categories with their function and an example for each. Choosing the right category helps the athlete match the imagery to the aim. Classifying imagery matters because it sets the content of the session. A coach who wants a player to improve a penalty technique would use cognitive specific imagery, whereas a player who is anxious before a penalty would benefit from motivational general-arousal imagery. Using the wrong type can waste time or fail to address the real need. The PETTLEP model

The PETTLEP model, proposed by Holmes and Collins (2001), gives seven elements for making imagery functionally equivalent to real performance. The more closely imagery reproduces the physical, environmental and emotional conditions of the actual performance, the more effective it is likely to be: The seven elements of PETTLEP: physical, environment, task, timing, learning, emotion and perspective. The elements are used together to make imagery close to real performance.

For example, a weightlifter using PETTLEP might tense the same muscles as in the lift, imagine the specific gym and the sound of the crowd, match the imagery to the time the lift takes, and update the image as their technique improves. The model supports an athlete returning from injury as well: imagery can rehearse the movement, and PETTLEP makes it closer to real performance as physical work is gradually restored. How imagery is used in practice

Effective imagery is planned and practised, not used at random. Athletes often start with a relaxed, quiet setting, rehearse a specific skill or routine, and then add detail and emotion. Regular practice makes imagery more vivid and controllable. Imagery is most useful when it is combined with physical practice, because it strengthens the planning and rehearsal of the skill, while physical practice develops the actual movement.

There are limits. Imagery cannot replace physical training, and its effects are usually larger for well-learned skills than for complex new ones. Vividness and controllability vary between athletes, and a poorly structured or unrealistic image may not help. Coaches should check that imagery supports, rather than replaces, the training programme. Exam Tips Define it as multisensory rehearsal Use the phrase "multisensory mental rehearsal in the absence of actual perception", then give one sporting example. Check the IB command terms .

Classify with both terms Name the function (cognitive or motivational) and the specificity (specific or general), for example "motivational general-arousal imagery". This is the core of Paivio questions. Choose the perspective with a reason Internal imagery suits feel and timing; external imagery suits technique and body position. Justify the choice for the athlete in the question. Apply PETTLEP to the scenario For "how to make imagery effective" questions, name the relevant PETTLEP elements and say how each would be applied to the sport.

Common mistake Don't describe imagery as "just visualising" or as a replacement for physical practice. It is multisensory and works best alongside physical training. Practice Questions Write your answer first, then open the model answer to check it. 1 Define imagery as a psychological skill. 1 mark Answer Model answer Multisensory mental rehearsal of a skill or situation in the absence of actual physical performance. 2 Distinguish between internal and external imagery. 2 marks Answer Model answer Internal imagery is seen through the athlete's own eyes and involves feeling the movement from inside.

External imagery is seen as if watching oneself from outside, for example on video, and focuses on technique and appearance. 3 A penalty taker imagines the exact technique of the kick before taking the penalty. Classify this imagery using Paivio's framework. 2 marks Answer Model answer Cognitive specific (CS) imagery: it rehearses a specific skill (the kicking technique). It is specific rather than general because the image is of one skill being performed, not a strategy or a general routine. 4 Explain how a motivational general-arousal imagery session could help a goalkeeper before a penalty shoot-out. 3 marks Answer Model answer

Motivational general-arousal imagery regulates stress and activation, so the goalkeeper can imagine calm breathing and a relaxed body. Imagining a composed state helps lower anxiety and bring arousal closer to the optimal level for the task. This supports focus and decision-making during the shoot-out, when stress is high. 5 (HL) Explain how the PETTLEP model could be used to make imagery more effective for a sprinter preparing for a final. 4 marks Answer Model answer Physical: the sprinter tenses and moves the muscles as in the start and drive phase. Environment and timing: they imagine the specific track and crowd, and match the duration of the imagery to the race.

Emotion and learning: they include the pressure of the final, and update the imagery as their technique improves. Perspective: they choose internal or external imagery depending on whether they are working on feel or on technique. IB Command Terms | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Command Terms 📖 IB Command Terms What Is the Question Asking You to Do? Every IB question contains a command term. It tells you what kind of answer to write and how much detail it needs. This guide explains each term, what the examiner is looking for, and how to build an answer that earns the marks. Terms covered Answer steps 1. How to use this guide Before you write a word, do three things with every question: Find the command term. It is usually the first word of the question (for example "Explain", "Outline", "Evaluate").

Check the depth it asks for. The same content can be asked at any level. "State" wants one fact; "Evaluate" wants a judgement. The mark allocation in brackets, such as [3], tells you how much to write. Plan the shape of the answer. Decide how many points you need and in what order, then write. This takes less time than rewriting. Command terms grouped by the depth of answer they require. Higher groups need a longer, more connected response. The rule that covers most questions Match the length and structure of your answer to the mark allocation. One mark usually means one precise point. Four marks usually means four developed points, or a chain of reasoning with a conclusion.

2. Rules that apply to every answer Use the sporting context. If the question names a sport, athlete or situation, refer to it in your answer. Generic answers lose marks. Use precise scientific terms. Write "ground reaction force", "type IIx fibre" or "knowledge of results", not "the push from the floor" or "the fast muscles". Include units and values. Give numbers with their units, and read values from graphs carefully (state the axis and the reading). Answer the question that is asked. If the question asks for the effect on performance, do not spend time on the mechanism unless "explain" is also asked.

Do not pad. Extra sentences that repeat a point, or add an unrelated fact, do not earn marks and can contradict what you have already written. Check the time. A two-mark question should take about two minutes. Move on and come back if you are stuck. 3. Quick reference Use the links to jump to the full guide for each term. Define State Identify Outline Describe Distinguish Explain Calculate Compare Compare and contrast Analyse Suggest Deduce Justify Evaluate Discuss To what extent Comment Draw, label and annotate Command term What it asks for Typical length Define A precise meaning One sentence State A name, value or brief fact A short phrase

Identify A choice or feature from options A word or phrase Outline Main points, brief 2–3 short points Describe Detailed account of what happens Several developed points Distinguish Clear differences 2–3 differences Explain Reasons or causes, as a chain A linked chain of 2–4 steps Calculate A number, with working and units Working plus answer Compare Similarities and differences 3–4 points about both items Analyse Parts, patterns and relationships, interpreted Linked observations with values Suggest A reasonable proposal, justified One justified idea Deduce A conclusion from given information A conclusion and short reason Justify A decision backed by evidence Conclusion plus 2–3 reasons

Evaluate Strengths and limitations weighed up Two sides plus judgement Discuss A balanced review with a conclusion Several arguments plus conclusion To what extent How far a claim is true, both sides Arguments both ways plus judgement 4. The terms, one by one Each entry gives the IB definition, what the examiner is looking for, a step-by-step method, the length to aim for, a worked example and a model answer. The model answers are examples of the standard expected, not the only correct wording. The length guides are typical allocations; check the number of marks on your paper. Define IB definition: Give the precise meaning of a word, phrase, concept or physical quantity.

What the examiner wants One accurate, precise sentence. Use the exact scientific wording, not a loose description. How to build the answer Write the term, then give its exact meaning in one sentence. Include units if the term is a quantity. Do not add examples unless asked; they earn no marks here and use time. Length guide 1 mark: one precise sentence. Example question: Define motor unit. [1] Model answer A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres that it supplies (innervates). Watch out A vague definition ("the unit that moves the muscle") will not earn the mark. Use the precise term. State IB definition: Give a specific name, value or other brief answer without explanation or calculation.

What the examiner wants The fact, name, value or unit, and nothing else. How to build the answer Give the answer first and stop. No reasons, no working, no extra sentences. If a value is requested, include its unit. Length guide 1 mark: a short phrase, name or value. Example question: State the name of the neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction. [1] Model answer Acetylcholine. Watch out Adding an explanation does not earn extra marks, and it can waste time. A contradictory extra statement can lose the mark. Identify IB definition: Provide an answer from a number of possibilities. Recognise and state briefly a distinguishing fact or feature. What the examiner wants

Pick out the correct answer or feature from what is given, briefly. How to build the answer Read every option or feature before you decide. State your choice clearly and briefly. In a data question, point to the specific value, line or label concerned. Length guide 1 mark per item: a brief answer, often a single word or phrase. Example question: Identify the type of muscle fibre with the greatest resistance to fatigue. [1] Model answer Type I (slow oxidative) fibres. Watch out Do not confuse identify with describe. "Identify" wants the name or feature; it does not want a paragraph. Outline IB definition: Give a brief account or summary. What the examiner wants

The main points only, in order, without detail or reasons. How to build the answer List the key points as short, linked statements. Keep each point to one clear idea. Use the correct terms; you do not need to explain them. Length guide 2 marks: two or three brief points. 3 marks: three points or a short summary sentence per step. Example question: Outline the role of calcium ions in muscle contraction. [2] Model answer Calcium is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the binding sites on actin. Watch out Outline is not the same as state. A single fact is usually too little; a full paragraph is usually too much. Describe

IB definition: Give a detailed account or picture of a situation, event, pattern or process. What the examiner wants The "what" and "how it looks": the features, sequence or pattern, with detail. Reasons are not needed, but a pattern in data must be quantified. How to build the answer Work through the process or pattern in order. Use precise terms and values where they are given. For graphs or data, state the trend, its size, and the range or period it covers. Length guide 2–4 marks: several developed points, often in sequence. Example question: Describe the change in heart rate during the first minute of exercise shown in the graph. [2] (illustrative graph)

Model answer Heart rate rises sharply from about 70 to about 120 beats per minute in the first 30 seconds, then rises more slowly and levels off at about 140 bpm by the end of the minute. Watch out Describe does not ask why. Keep reasons out unless the question also says "explain". Distinguish IB definition: Make clear the differences between two or more concepts or items. What the examiner wants Clear statements of how the items differ. Each difference should be stated, not just implied. How to build the answer Name both items at the start of each point. Write one difference per point, using a contrast word such as "whereas" or "unlike".

Make sure each difference is about the same feature (for example both about speed of contraction). Length guide 2 marks: two clear differences. 3 marks: three clear differences. Example question: Distinguish between type I and type IIx muscle fibres. [2] Model answer Type I fibres contract slowly, whereas type IIx fibres contract rapidly. Type I fibres have high resistance to fatigue, unlike type IIx fibres, which fatigue quickly. Watch out A list of features for each item separately is not a distinction. Compare the same feature side by side. Explain IB definition: Give a detailed account including reasons or causes. What the examiner wants

The "why" and "how": a chain of reasoning that links cause to effect, using the correct scientific principle. How to build the answer Start with the key fact or principle. Link each step to the next with "because", "so" or "this leads to". End with the effect on the performance or outcome asked about. Relate the chain to the sporting context in the question. Length guide 2 marks: a cause and an effect. 3–4 marks: a full causal chain, usually three or four linked steps. Example question: Explain why bending the knees on landing reduces the risk of injury. [3]

Model answer Bending the knees increases the time over which the athlete slows down. Because impulse equals force multiplied by time, the same change in momentum is achieved with a smaller average force. A lower peak force reduces the stress on bones, joints and ligaments, so the risk of injury falls. Watch out Listing reasons without connecting them is a common error. Show the link between each step. Calculate IB definition: Obtain a numerical answer showing the relevant stages in the working. What the examiner wants The correct number with its unit, and the working shown step by step. How to build the answer Write the equation you are using. Substitute the values with their units.

Show the intermediate steps, then state the answer with units and to a sensible number of significant figures. Length guide 2–3 marks: method marks for the equation and substitution, plus the final answer with units. Example question: Calculate the momentum of a 90 kg player running at 6 m/s. [2] Model answer Momentum = mass × velocity = 90 kg × 6 m/s = 540 kg m/s Watch out Method marks are often given for the right equation even if the final answer is wrong, so always show the working. Compare IB definition: Give an account of the similarities and differences between two or more items or situations, referring to both (all) of them throughout. What the examiner wants

Points about both items on each point, covering similarities and differences in the same structure. How to build the answer Choose a clear set of points to compare, such as speed, fatigue resistance and energy system. For each point, say what is true of item A and of item B in the same sentence. Use "both", "similarly" for similarities; "whereas" or "in contrast" for differences. Length guide 3–4 marks: three or four comparison points, each referring to both items. Example question: Compare the energy systems used during a 100 m sprint and a 10 km run. [3]

Model answer Both systems supply energy for exercise, and both use glucose. The sprint relies mainly on the phosphagen and anaerobic glycolysis systems, whereas the 10 km run relies mainly on the aerobic system. Sprinting produces energy faster but for a shorter time, while the aerobic system produces energy more slowly but for much longer. Watch out Writing about one item, then the other, without referring back, is weak. Refer to both items on every point. Compare and contrast IB definition: Give an account of the similarities and differences between two or more items or situations, referring to both (all) of them throughout. What the examiner wants

Both sides of the comparison, clearly marked. Make sure you cover both similarities and differences. How to build the answer Split your points into similarities first, then differences. Use the same structure as compare, but make sure every point has a similarity or a difference. Length guide As for compare, with at least one similarity and one difference in each part. Example question: Compare and contrast the roles of agonist and antagonist muscles. [3] Model answer Both are skeletal muscles that act across the same joint. However, the agonist shortens to produce the movement, whereas the antagonist lengthens and relaxes to allow it.

Watch out If the question says "compare and contrast", answering only with similarities or only with differences loses marks. Analyse IB definition: Break down in order to bring out the essential elements or structure. What the examiner wants The parts of the information, the relationships between them, and what they show. For data, the trends, comparisons and values that matter. How to build the answer Identify the key elements or variables in the information. Describe the pattern or relationship, with values. Interpret what the pattern shows, using the correct scientific terms. Avoid restating the data without comment. Length guide

3–5 marks: several linked observations, each with values and an interpretation. Example question: Analyse the data in the table on the effect of training on VO2 max. [4] (illustrative data) Model answer VO2 max increases in every training group, with the largest rise (from 45 to 52 ml/kg/min) in the high-intensity group. The control group changes by less than 1 ml/kg/min. This suggests that the training, rather than normal variation, caused the increase, and that higher intensity produced a larger adaptation. Watch out Analyse is different from describe. An analysis explains what the pattern shows and how the parts relate, not only what the numbers are. Suggest

IB definition: Propose a hypothesis or other possible answer. There may not be one correct answer. What the examiner wants A reasonable, justified proposal that uses the scientific context. Several answers may be accepted. How to build the answer Propose a possible explanation or action. Link it to the sport, the data or the theory. Say briefly why it is plausible. Length guide 1–2 marks: a sensible suggestion with a reason. Example question: Suggest one reason why the athlete's heart rate was higher than expected at the same workload. [1] Model answer The athlete may have been dehydrated, which reduces blood volume and raises heart rate for the same workload.

Watch out Do not treat suggest as "state the right answer". A plausible, well-justified idea scores; a guess with no link to the science does not. Deduce IB definition: Reach a conclusion from the information given. What the examiner wants A logical conclusion that follows directly from the data or statement given. How to build the answer Start from the information in the question or the data. Apply a relevant principle or rule. State the conclusion clearly. Length guide 1–2 marks: the conclusion with a short justification. Example question: Deduce the direction of the frictional force acting on a sprinter's foot during the push-off. [1]

Model answer Backwards, opposite to the direction of the foot's push on the track, because friction opposes the motion. Watch out Deduce means the answer should follow logically. A conclusion that does not come from the given information will not score. Justify IB definition: Give valid reasons or evidence to support an answer or conclusion. What the examiner wants A clear decision or conclusion, backed by reasons and evidence from the scientific context. How to build the answer State your answer or conclusion first. Give two or three reasons or pieces of evidence. Use values or science principles as evidence. Link the evidence back to the decision. Length guide

3–4 marks: a conclusion plus two or three supported reasons. Example question: Justify the use of a force plate, rather than video analysis, to measure the take-off of a long jump. [3] Model answer A force plate is the better choice because it measures the ground reaction force directly and allows the impulse and take-off velocity to be calculated. Video analysis can estimate the movement, but it cannot measure the force. Force plates also give precise timing of the take-off, which is needed to calculate velocity accurately. Watch out Do not just state the conclusion. Justify requires reasons that support it. Evaluate

IB definition: Make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations. What the examiner wants A judgement, reached by weighing strengths against limitations, usually ending with a conclusion. How to build the answer Give at least one strength and one limitation, each explained. Weigh them up: which matters more, and why? End with a clear judgement or conclusion. Length guide 4–6 marks: strengths and limitations, each developed, plus a judgement. Example question: Evaluate the use of wearable sensors to monitor training load. [4]

Model answer Strength: sensors give objective, continuous data on distance, speed and acceleration in real training, so load can be tracked over weeks. Limitation: accuracy varies between devices and the data may be hard to interpret without expertise. On balance, sensors are valuable for tracking trends, but they should support coaching judgement rather than replace it. Watch out Listing strengths and limitations without a judgement will not reach the top band. Always end with a conclusion. Discuss

IB definition: Offer a considered and balanced review that includes a range of arguments, factors or hypotheses. Opinions or conclusions should be presented clearly and supported by appropriate evidence. What the examiner wants Several viewpoints or factors, each supported by evidence, weighed against each other, with a conclusion. How to build the answer Present one argument or factor, then the evidence for it. Present a counter-argument or limitation, with its evidence. Weigh them up and reach a clear conclusion. Length guide 4–6 marks: a balanced review of at least two sides, with evidence and a conclusion.

Example question: Discuss whether intrinsic motivation is more important than extrinsic motivation for long-term participation in sport. [6] Model answer Intrinsic motivation supports enjoyment and self-determined effort, which predicts long-term participation (Self-determination Theory). However, extrinsic rewards such as selection or sponsorship keep some athletes involved, and they can be more important at early stages or for athletes with limited intrinsic interest. Overall, intrinsic motivation is more reliably linked to long-term participation, although the best approach combines both. Watch out Balanced does not mean giving every point equal weight. Make a clear judgement at the end.

To what extent IB definition: Consider the arguments for and against the claim, and reach a judgement. What the examiner wants A judgement about how far a claim is true, showing both sides of the argument. How to build the answer Give the strongest argument for the claim. Give the strongest argument against it. State how far you think the claim is true, and why. Length guide As for discuss: both sides, evidence, and a clear judgement. Example question: To what extent is training intensity the most important factor in improving VO2 max? [6]

Model answer Intensity is a major driver: high-intensity training produces larger increases in VO2 max than low-intensity training for the same time. However, duration, frequency and the athlete's starting fitness also affect the outcome, and the effect of intensity is limited for well-trained athletes. Intensity is therefore one of the most important factors, but not the only one. Watch out Do not answer with "yes" or "no" alone. Show the arguments and reach a graded judgement. Comment IB definition: Give a judgement based on a given statement or result. What the examiner wants A judgement about the statement or result, with a reason. How to build the answer

State whether you agree, disagree or see it as partly true. Give a reason based on the science or the data. Keep the judgement tied to the statement. Length guide 2–3 marks: a judgement and one or two supported reasons. Example question: Comment on the statement: "Stretching before exercise prevents all injuries." [2] Model answer This is not supported by the evidence. Stretching has not been shown to prevent all injuries, although a proper warm-up may reduce some types of injury. The statement overgeneralises. Watch out A judgement without a reason is not enough. Support the judgement with the science. Draw, label and annotate

IB definition: Draw: represent by means of a labelled, accurate diagram or graph. Label: add labels to a diagram. Annotate: add brief notes to a diagram. What the examiner wants An accurate, neat diagram, with labels and short notes where asked. How to build the answer Draw with a sharp pencil and use a ruler for straight lines. Make the diagram large enough to show detail. Add labels to each named part, and notes if asked to annotate. Give a title and any units for a graph. Length guide Marks are given for accuracy, labels and any required annotations. Example question: Draw and label a diagram of a sarcomere in the relaxed state. [3]

Model answer A labelled sketch showing Z-discs at each end, thin (actin) filaments, thick (myosin) filaments, the H zone and the A band, with the I band marked. Watch out A diagram with no labels, or with labels that do not match the diagram, will lose marks even if it is accurate. 5. Before you finish any answer Have I answered with the command term's depth (not more, not less)? Have I referred to the sport or situation in the question? Have I included units, values and correct scientific terms? If I was asked to evaluate, discuss or justify, did I reach a clear conclusion? Did I answer every part of the question, including every named item in "compare" or "distinguish"?

Internal Assessment Support | IB Sport Science | Simply Sport Science Home › IB Sport Science › Internal Assessment Support 🔬 Internal Assessment Scientific Investigation: Internal Assessment Support The IB SEHS internal assessment is an individual scientific investigation that you design, carry out and report on. This page takes you through every stage, from choosing a topic to checking your final report. 24% Of final grade ~10 hrs Practical time 3,200 Word limit (max) 1. What the internal assessment is

The internal assessment (IA), called the scientific investigation in the current course, is an open-ended task. You formulate your own research question, collect and analyse data to answer it, and write a report. It is marked against assessment criteria, with the strongest weight on conclusion and evaluation. Feature What to know Weighting 24% of the final SEHS grade, at both SL and HL Practical time About 10 hours, including developing the question, the method, data collection and processing Report length Maximum 3,200 words. Check your subject brief for what counts towards the limit (for example whether references and appendices are included)

Individual report Every student submits their own report, even if you worked in a group Group work Small groups may collaborate, and similar methods may be shared, provided the independent or dependent variable differs and each student's data is unique to them Marking emphasis Half of the marks are for conclusion and evaluation. Build your report around answering the question well and judging your own work Check your official source The IB subject brief for SEHS is the authority on mark allocations, criteria wording and word-count rules. This page is a practical guide that follows the published changes. Confirm the details with your teacher before you start.

The main stages of the investigation. Work through them in order, but expect to revisit earlier stages when results or evaluation show a problem. 2. Choosing a topic The best topics test one manageable factor, use equipment you can access in school, and produce enough repeated, reliable data to support a justified conclusion. Use this checklist before you commit: Safe: you can do it without unreasonable risk, and you have a risk assessment that your teacher has approved. Measurable: the dependent variable can be measured with a reliable, precise instrument. Controllable: you can keep the other factors constant. Feasible: you can get enough participants or trials within about 10 hours.

Ethical: participants give informed consent, and no one is pushed beyond a safe level of exertion or discomfort. Scientific: you can explain the expected result using SEHS theory from the syllabus. Examples Weaker topic Why it is weaker Stronger version Does music improve fitness? Too broad; "fitness" is not measurable Does playing fast-tempo music change the number of push-ups completed in 60 seconds? How does training change the heart? Requires long training periods and invasive measures Does a 2-minute warm-up change resting heart rate recovery after a set of step-ups?

Which shoe is best for running? Uncontrolled variables and no clear measure Does sole thickness change the contact time of a standing vertical jump? 3. Writing the research question A research question should be focused, testable, measurable and clearly linked to the variables. A common format is: Template How does [independent variable] affect [dependent variable] in [participants or context]? Make sure the question names the variables, states the units where relevant, and is possible to answer within your method. Avoid questions that can only be answered "yes" or "no", unless you then measure how much.

Good: How does a 1-minute versus a 3-minute rest interval affect the time taken for a 30 m sprint in Year 12 students? Too broad: What affects sprint performance? 4. Background and hypothesis Show that you understand the science behind your question. In the background section: Explain the relevant theory from the syllabus, using the correct terms. Summarise what other research has found, with references. Build a hypothesis that predicts the direction of the effect and gives a reason, based on the theory.

Example hypothesis: Longer rest between sprints will allow more phosphocreatine resynthesis, so sprint times will be faster after 3 minutes of rest than after 1 minute, because the phosphagen system is more fully restored. 5. Variables and method Identify your variables before you design the method. The independent variable is the one you change on purpose, the dependent variable is what you measure, and the controlled variables are kept the same. An example of variables for a sprint investigation. The rest interval is changed, the sprint time is measured, and the other factors are kept constant. Your method must be detailed enough for another student to repeat it. Include:

the participants (number, age, relevant characteristics) and how they were selected; the equipment, with its precision (for example timing gates to 0.01 s, not a stopwatch to 0.1 s); a step-by-step procedure, including warm-up, the number of trials, and the order of conditions; how each controlled variable was kept constant; the number of repeats, and how you dealt with fatigue and learning effects (for example randomising the order); safety measures and the risk assessment reference; how consent was obtained, and how personal data was stored and anonymised. 6. Recording data Good data is easy to read, complete and traceable. Follow these rules:

Design your table before you collect data. Use one column per variable, with the quantity and unit in the heading, for example "Sprint time (s)". Record raw data at the time, not afterwards. Write or type directly into the table. Keep the raw data unedited in an appendix. Use consistent decimal places that match the precision of your instrument. Record uncertainties for every measurement, for example ±0.01 s for a timing gate. Repeat trials. Three or more repeats per condition is usually a good minimum, so that you can calculate a mean and spread. Note anything unusual , such as a participant who stumbled or a timing error, in a comments column. Do not delete the result.

Keep a log of the date, time, conditions and equipment. A notebook or a shared digital log is fine; be consistent. Back up your data on a second device or cloud folder as you go. Example table layout Condition Trial Sprint time (s ± 0.01) Comments 1 min rest 1 4.82 – 1 min rest 2 4.91 – 3 min rest 1 4.67 Slight wind noted 7. Processing and analysing data Processing turns raw numbers into something you can interpret. Use the methods that suit your data and your question. Common calculations Calculation What it tells you How to do it Mean The typical value across repeats Sum of values ÷ number of values

Range and standard deviation The spread of the data (the sample standard deviation is used for a sample) Excel/Sheets: MAX − MIN for range; STDEV.S for standard deviation Percentage change How much a value changed, relative to the start (new − original) ÷ original × 100 Absolute and percentage uncertainty How precise a measurement or result is Absolute: the ± value. Percentage: absolute ÷ value × 100 Correlation The strength and direction of a relationship between two continuous variables Excel/Sheets: CORREL(x, y). Report r with its sign and interpret its size

t-test Whether two means differ by more than chance would suggest Excel/Sheets: T.TEST. Choose paired or unpaired to match your design Choosing a graph Scatter plot with a line of best fit for two continuous variables (for example rest time against sprint time). Bar chart with error bars for comparing means across categories (for example mean sprint time for each rest condition). Line graph for change over time (for example heart rate over a 10-minute recovery). Box plot to show the spread and median of each group.

Every graph needs a title, labelled axes with units, a sensible scale that uses most of the space, and a legend if there is more than one data set. Error bars should show the uncertainty or standard deviation, and the caption should say which. Tools that can help Tool Use it for Cost Microsoft Excel or Google Sheets Tables, means, standard deviation, t-tests, correlation, charts Free (Sheets) / school licence Desmos Plotting, curve fitting and regression lines Free GraphPad QuickCalcs Quick, checked t-tests and other statistics on the web Free Kinovea Frame-by-frame video analysis, timing and joint angles Free Tracker Video analysis of motion, with position and velocity data Free

Sensors (for example Vernier or smartphone sensor apps) Logging acceleration, force, heart rate or timing directly Varies; check school equipment first Check your working Recalculate one value by hand, and check that your spreadsheet formulas refer to the right cells. Small errors in formulas are a common cause of wrong conclusions. 8. Writing the conclusion The conclusion answers your research question directly, using your processed data. Make it: Direct: start with the answer, for example "The 3-minute rest condition produced faster sprint times than the 1-minute condition." Quantified: give the key values with their uncertainty, for example the mean difference and its spread.

Linked to the hypothesis: say whether the data supported your prediction, and why. Linked to theory: explain the mechanism using SEHS concepts, without overclaiming. Cautious about causation: a correlation or an effect in a small sample supports a conclusion; it does not prove it. 9. Writing the evaluation Evaluation is where you judge your own investigation. Half of the marks sit in conclusion and evaluation, so give it real effort. A strong evaluation: Identifies real limitations of the method, data or analysis, and explains how each one could affect the result.

Distinguishes random and systematic error. Random error varies unpredictably (for example reaction time when starting a stopwatch); systematic error pushes results consistently one way (for example a timing gate that is miscalibrated). Discusses sample size and representativeness (for example a small group of Year 12 students cannot represent all athletes). Judges the uncertainty of the result: is the difference between conditions larger than the uncertainty?

Suggests specific improvements , each linked to a limitation and explaining what it would change. "Use timing gates instead of a stopwatch, because hand timing adds human reaction error, often around 0.1–0.2 s, which is larger than some of the differences measured" is specific; "use better equipment" is not. Weak: The results may not be accurate because of human error. Strong: Hand timing introduces reaction-time error of around 0.1–0.2 s, which is comparable to the 0.15 s difference between conditions. Timing gates would reduce this error and would make the difference between conditions more reliable. 10. Referencing

Support your background, method and evaluation with sources. Use one consistent referencing style throughout (for example Harvard or APA), with: an in-text citation wherever you use another person's idea, data or image; a reference list at the end, with full details for each source. Good sources Use textbooks, peer-reviewed journal articles, official bodies (for example government health guidance or national sports organisations), and the IB syllabus. Be cautious with blogs and general websites: check the author, date and evidence. Wikipedia can help you find sources, but do not cite it as a primary source. Tools

Reference managers such as Zotero or Mendeley are free and can keep your references organised. Check whether your school allows a particular tool. Harvard template (book): Surname, Initial. (Year) Title of book . Edition. Place of publication: Publisher. Harvard template (journal): Surname, Initial. (Year) 'Title of article', Journal Name , volume(issue), pp. x–x. 11. Structure and word count A clear structure helps the examiner find the marks. A typical report includes these sections: Title, and research question Introduction and background (theory, prior research, hypothesis) Method (variables, participants, equipment, procedure, safety and ethics)

Data (raw data tables, with uncertainties) Data processing and analysis (calculations, graphs) Conclusion Evaluation (limitations and improvements) References and appendices Stay within the 3,200-word limit. A report that is too long usually has repetition, unnecessary background or raw data that belongs in an appendix. Check with your teacher what is counted. 12. Academic integrity The report, data and analysis must be your own work. Do not make up or alter data. Acknowledge any help, including the use of software, sources and any AI tools, in line with your school's policy and the IB's academic honesty rules.

If you collaborate, follow the group rules in the subject brief. Your data must be unique to you, and your report must be individual. 13. Before you submit Does my research question name the variables and the context? Can another student repeat my method from what I have written? Are my tables complete, with units and uncertainties? Are my graphs labelled, titled and appropriate for the data? Does my conclusion answer the research question directly, with values? Does my evaluation name specific limitations and specific improvements? Is every source cited in the text and listed in the references? Is the report within the word limit, and is the file named clearly? 14. Common mistakes

A research question that is too broad, or cannot be answered with the data collected. Method steps that are vague ("measure the athletes") and cannot be repeated. Raw data that is missing units or uncertainties. Graphs without axis labels, units or a title. A conclusion that claims more than the data shows, or restates results without answering the question. 1RM (One Repetition Maximum) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › 1RM (One Repetition Maximum) General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge 1RM (One Repetition Maximum) The gold-standard measure of maximal strength — the heaviest load you can lift once, and the basis for setting resistance training. 📖 What it means The one-repetition maximum (1RM) is the maximum weight a person can lift once, with correct technique , for a given exercise. It is the standard measure of maximal muscular strength .

It is used both to assess strength and to set training intensities : resistance training loads are commonly prescribed as a percentage of 1RM — for example, heavy loads (around 80–100% of 1RM) for maximal strength, and lighter loads (around 50–60%) for muscular endurance. A true 1RM test involves lifting genuinely maximal loads, which carries some injury risk and requires good technique , so 1RM is often estimated instead from the number of repetitions completed at a submaximal load using standard equations. 🏅 Sporting examples Setting loads A coach establishes a lifter's 1RM for the squat, then prescribes training at percentages of it — heavy loads for strength, lighter for endurance.

Monitoring Repeating a 1RM test across a training block shows whether an athlete's maximal strength is improving. Estimation Rather than a risky maximal lift, a coach may estimate 1RM from the reps a performer can complete at a submaximal weight. ✍️ Using the term in context Define 1RM and link it to strength testing and load prescription: "The one-repetition maximum is the greatest load that can be lifted once with correct technique, the standard measure of maximal strength; training loads are set as a percentage of 1RM, with heavy loads for strength and lighter loads for muscular endurance." Note the injury risk of true maximal testing and that 1RM can be estimated. 🔗 Related terms

30 Metre Sprint Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › 30 Metre Sprint Test General BTEC Sport 30 Metre Sprint Test Straight-line speed over 30 metres — a fast, field-based measure of acceleration and maximum sprint speed. 📖 What it means The 30 Metre Sprint Test is a field test measuring straight-line sprint speed over 30 metres, typically timed electronically with timing gates. The performer starts from a standing position and sprints maximally; the time is recorded. Abdominal Curl Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Abdominal Curl Test General BTEC Sport Abdominal Curl Test A simple, equipment-light field test of abdominal muscular endurance, popular in schools and BTEC assignments because a whole class can be tested at once. 📖 What it means The Abdominal Curl Test measures the muscular endurance of the abdominal muscles — how many controlled curl-up repetitions a performer can complete before fatigue or before they can no longer keep pace.

In its standardised form the test is progressive and paced to an audio signal : the performer completes one curl-up per bleep, and the required rate is fixed so that everyone is tested under identical conditions. The score is the number of correctly performed curl-ups completed in time. Because it isolates a single component of fitness in one muscle group, it is best used alongside other tests to build a full fitness profile, rather than as a stand-alone measure of overall fitness. 🏅 Sporting examples Rowing A rower needs strong abdominal endurance to maintain trunk stability through thousands of strokes, so this test helps monitor a key supporting quality across a training block. Gymnastics

Core endurance underpins held positions and controlled landings, making abdominal endurance testing a useful monitoring tool for a gymnast. School PE It appears constantly in PE and BTEC practicals because it needs only a mat and an audio track, and a whole group can be tested simultaneously. ✍️ Using the term in context Tie the test to the exact component it measures and comment on how useful it is: "The Abdominal Curl Test assesses abdominal muscular endurance. Abduction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Abduction General IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Abduction One of the fundamental joint movements every sport science student must be able to name, describe and spot in a sporting action. 📖 What it means Abduction is the movement of a limb away from the midline of the body. Raising your arm out to the side, or lifting a leg sideways, are both examples of abduction. It is produced by abductor muscles — for example, the deltoid abducts the arm at the shoulder, and the gluteus medius abducts the leg at the hip. Abduction always has an opposite movement, adduction , which returns the limb toward the midline.

Naming the movement correctly is only half the skill — in analysis questions you also need to identify the joint , the agonist muscle producing it, and the plane and axis in which it occurs (abduction happens in the frontal plane about a sagittal axis). 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming During the outsweep of a breaststroke arm pull, the arms move outward away from the midline — abduction at the shoulder. Gymnastics A star jump involves simultaneous abduction of both the arms and the legs, moving all four limbs away from the midline. Football A defender lifting their leg sideways to block a cross performs hip abduction, driven by the gluteus medius. ✍️ Using the term in context

In movement-analysis answers, always pair the movement with the joint, agonist and plane: "At the shoulder, the arm is abducted in the frontal plane about a sagittal axis; the agonist is the deltoid." Don't confuse abduction with adduction — a simple memory aid is that abduction 'takes the limb away', while adduction 'adds it back' toward the body. 🔗 Related terms Adduction Abductor Frontal Plane Agonist Planes of Movement Circumduction 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy © 2026 Simply Sport Science · simplysportscience.co.uk

Abductor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Abductor IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Abductor The muscle group responsible for moving a limb away from the body's midline — essential for lateral movement, balance and stability in almost every sport. 📖 What it means An abductor is any muscle whose action moves a limb away from the midline of the body (abduction). The most commonly cited examples are the deltoid at the shoulder and the gluteus medius and minimus at the hip.

The hip abductors are especially important in sport because they stabilise the pelvis during single-leg actions such as running and cutting — weak hip abductors are a common cause of poor movement mechanics and injury. Every abductor works against an adductor as its antagonist. Understanding these agonist–antagonist pairs is central to movement analysis and to designing balanced training programmes. 🏅 Sporting examples Football Strong hip abductors help a winger change direction sharply and keep the pelvis level when planting on one leg to cross the ball. Ice skating The powerful sideways push-off in skating is driven largely by the hip abductors moving the leg away from the midline. Netball

Landing on one foot after an interception relies on the hip abductors to stabilise the pelvis and prevent the knee collapsing inward. ✍️ Using the term in context Reference specific named abductors rather than saying 'the muscle': "The gluteus medius acts as an abductor at the hip, stabilising the pelvis during the single-support phase of running." In injury-prevention answers, link abductor strength to function: "Strengthening the hip abductors can reduce injury risk by preventing the knee from collapsing inward during landing and cutting movements." 🔗 Related terms Adductor Abduction Gluteus Maximus Agonist Antagonist Muscle Imbalance 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Ability — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ability AS Level / Cambridge General Ability A concept that trips up many students because it sounds like everyday language but has a precise meaning in skill acquisition — and is deliberately distinct from 'skill'. 📖 What it means In sport science, ability refers to an inherited, stable and enduring trait that underpins performance across a range of skills. Abilities are largely genetically determined and form the raw material on which skills are built.

The crucial distinction is that ability is innate, while skill is learned . A performer might have a high level of a general ability such as reaction time or coordination, but they still have to learn and practise the specific skills that draw on it. Abilities are often divided into gross motor abilities (underpinning strength, flexibility and movement, such as explosive strength or stamina) and psychomotor abilities (linking decision-making to movement, such as reaction time and limb coordination). 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A sprinter may possess a high level of the innate ability of speed, but they must still learn the skill of an efficient block start through years of practice. Tennis

Good innate hand-eye coordination is an ability that supports learning the skill of a serve, but does not guarantee it — the serve itself must be grooved. Basketball Two players with similar natural abilities can differ hugely in skill, because one has practised shooting technique far more than the other. ✍️ Using the term in context Keep the ability–skill distinction razor sharp in answers: "Ability is an inherited, stable trait, whereas skill is learned through practice. A performer's natural abilities determine their potential, but skills must be developed to realise it."

Avoid using 'ability' loosely to mean 'how good someone is' — in an exam it has the specific meaning of an innate underlying trait. 🔗 Related terms Skill Motor Learning Coordination Reaction Time Fitts and Posner's Stages of Learning Individual Differences 🎓 Where this appears AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy © 2026 Simply Sport Science · simplysportscience.co.uk

Absolute Strength — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Absolute Strength IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Absolute Strength How much force you can produce in total, with no adjustment for how heavy you are. 📖 What it means Absolute strength is the greatest force a muscle or muscle group can generate in a single maximal effort. It is measured in newtons or, more practically, as the heaviest load lifted for one repetition (1RM).

It does not take body mass into account. A heavy athlete will usually have higher absolute strength than a light athlete, which is why relative strength (strength divided by body mass) is used to compare athletes of different sizes. 🏅 Sporting examples Weightlifting An Olympic weightlifter's clean and jerk total is a direct measure of absolute strength, because the heaviest load lifted is what counts. Rugby forwards A prop forward needs high absolute strength for scrummaging, where total force matters more than body mass relative to opponents. Sprinting Absolute strength underpins the force a sprinter can apply to the blocks, although speed depends on how quickly that force is applied.

✍️ Using the term in context Define absolute strength and distinguish it from relative strength: "Absolute strength is the maximum force a muscle can produce, whereas relative strength takes body mass into account, so a lighter athlete may be stronger relative to their size." Acceleration Phase — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acceleration Phase IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Acceleration Phase The stage of a sprint when the athlete is building speed rather than holding top speed. 📖 What it means The acceleration phase is the period from the start until the athlete reaches maximum speed. The body leans forward, the step length is short, and the athlete pushes hard into the ground to generate horizontal force.

The phase relies heavily on power and the ability to apply force quickly at the start. Good technique, such as a low body angle and a strong drive from the front leg, improves how quickly the athlete reaches top speed. 🏅 Sporting examples 100 m sprint The first 30 to 40 metres of a 100 m sprint are the acceleration phase, and the best sprinters are often judged on how quickly they reach their peak speed. Rugby sevens A winger who accelerates quickly from a standing start gains an advantage over defenders, even if they do not reach the highest top speed. Netball A player who accelerates sharply out of a stand-still gets into space before the defender can react. ✍️ Using the term in context

Explain the acceleration phase of a 100 m sprint: "In the acceleration phase, the sprinter leans forward and applies large horizontal forces to the ground, so that speed increases rapidly until top speed is reached." Acceleration — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acceleration General IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Acceleration A cornerstone of biomechanics — the rate at which velocity changes — and the quantity that links force, mass and motion through Newton's second law. 📖 What it means Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity over time. Because velocity has direction, acceleration is a vector quantity — it describes speeding up, slowing down (deceleration), or changing direction. It is calculated as acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken , with units of metres per second squared (m/s²). A large acceleration means velocity is changing quickly.

Acceleration is central to Newton's second law , which states that the acceleration of a body is proportional to the force applied and inversely proportional to its mass (F = ma). This is why generating more force, or reducing mass, produces greater acceleration. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting In the first few metres out of the blocks, a sprinter produces very high acceleration, rapidly increasing velocity from a standstill before reaching top speed. Football A striker accelerating onto a through ball changes velocity quickly to beat a defender — the greater the force they apply against the ground, the greater their acceleration. Formula that matters

A shot putter applies maximum force to a fixed-mass shot to maximise its acceleration and therefore its release velocity. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish acceleration from speed and velocity precisely: "Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. In the drive phase of a sprint, the athlete generates large horizontal forces against the ground, producing high acceleration in line with Newton's second law." Remember that a body travelling at constant speed around a bend is still accelerating, because its direction — and therefore its velocity — is changing. 🔗 Related terms Velocity Speed Newton's Laws of Motion Force Momentum Law of Acceleration 🎓 Where this appears
