Acclimatisation to Altitude — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acclimatisation to Altitude IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Acclimatisation to Altitude How the body adjusts over time when it moves to a high-altitude environment. 📖 What it means At altitude, the air pressure is lower, so each breath delivers less oxygen. In the first days, breathing rate and heart rate rise to compensate. Over the following weeks, the body increases red blood cell production, which raises the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

Full acclimatisation takes several weeks and is not complete in a few days. Athletes who train at altitude before a competition often plan their timings around this process. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance athletes Distance runners travel to altitude training camps several weeks before a race so that their blood can carry more oxygen. Mountaineering Climbers ascend gradually to allow the body to acclimatise and reduce the risk of altitude sickness. Football A team arriving in a high-altitude city may schedule an extra day or two before a match to adjust, reducing fatigue. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the acclimatisation process for an athlete travelling to altitude:

"During the first few days, breathing and heart rate increase to compensate for lower oxygen, and over several weeks red blood cell production rises, so the blood carries more oxygen." Acclimatisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acclimatisation IB Sport Science General Acclimatisation The body's gradual adjustment to a challenging environment — a key planning consideration for any athlete competing in heat, humidity or at altitude. 📖 What it means Acclimatisation is the process of physiological adaptation that occurs when an athlete is exposed to a new environmental stress — typically heat, humidity or altitude — over a period of days to weeks.

In heat , acclimatisation improves the body's cooling ability: the athlete begins to sweat earlier and more efficiently, plasma volume increases, and heart rate at a given intensity falls. In altitude , the body increases red blood cell production to compensate for the reduced oxygen availability. Because these adaptations take time, athletes and coaches plan acclimatisation periods before major competitions in demanding environments, arriving early enough for the body to adjust and protect performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon running

A runner competing in a hot, humid city marathon will arrive one to two weeks early so their sweating response and plasma volume adapt, reducing the risk of heat illness. Football World Cup Teams travelling to tournaments in hot climates use acclimatisation camps so players can perform without excessive cardiovascular strain. Endurance cycling Cyclists preparing for a high-altitude stage race spend time at altitude beforehand to stimulate increased red blood cell production. ✍️ Using the term in context Link acclimatisation to specific physiological adaptations and to planning:

Acetylcholine — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acetylcholine IB Sport Science General Acetylcholine The chemical messenger that turns a nerve impulse into a muscle contraction — the crucial link between the nervous and muscular systems. 📖 What it means Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter : a chemical released by a motor neurone to pass a signal across the gap (synapse) to the next cell. At the muscle, this gap is called the neuromuscular junction .

When a nerve impulse reaches the end of a motor neurone, acetylcholine is released and diffuses across the neuromuscular junction to the muscle fibre. There it triggers an action potential in the muscle, which sets off the process of contraction. Without acetylcholine, the electrical signal in the nerve could not be transmitted to the muscle — it is the essential chemical bridge that allows the brain's commands to produce movement. 🏅 Sporting examples All explosive movement Every time a sprinter fires their muscles out of the blocks, acetylcholine is being released in huge quantities to recruit the motor units needed for a powerful contraction. Fine motor control

In a precise action such as a dart throw, acetylcholine transmission allows fine, coordinated firing of the small muscles controlling the hand. Fatigue link Reduced acetylcholine release is one proposed contributor to neuromuscular fatigue, where the muscle receives a weaker signal to contract. ✍️ Using the term in context Use acetylcholine to explain the nerve-to-muscle link precisely: "When the action potential reaches the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine is released and diffuses across the synapse, triggering an action potential in the muscle fibre and initiating contraction." Keep the sequence in order: nerve impulse → acetylcholine release → muscle action potential → contraction.

Achievement Motivation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Achievement Motivation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Achievement Motivation Why do some athletes relish a tough challenge while others shrink from it? Achievement motivation offers a framework for understanding competitive drive. 📖 What it means Achievement motivation describes an athlete's drive to succeed and their willingness to approach challenging, competitive situations . It is shaped by the balance between two tendencies: the motive to achieve success and the motive to avoid failure .

Athletes high in the motive to achieve success tend to seek out challenges , take risks, welcome feedback and persist after setbacks. Those dominated by the motive to avoid failure tend to choose easy or very hard tasks (where failure is unlikely or excusable) and avoid situations where they might be evaluated. This behaviour is not fixed — coaches can nurture approach behaviour by setting realistic, achievable goals , giving positive reinforcement, and attributing success to the athlete's own effort and ability. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis

A player high in achievement motivation actively wants to face a higher-ranked opponent, seeing it as a chance to test themselves, whereas a failure-avoidant player may feel relief at losing to a 'better' player. Athletics A high jumper who keeps raising the bar to challenge themselves, even risking failure, displays a strong motive to achieve success. Coaching application A coach builds approach behaviour in a nervous young athlete by setting attainable process goals and praising effort, gradually increasing the challenge. ✍️ Using the term in context Frame achievement motivation as the interaction of two motives:

"Achievement motivation reflects the balance between the motive to achieve success and the motive to avoid failure; performers high in the former approach challenges and persist after failure." Acid-Base Balance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acid-Base Balance IB Sport Science General Acid-Base Balance The body's tight control of its internal pH — a form of homeostasis that becomes critical during high-intensity exercise as acidity rises. 📖 What it means Acid-base balance is the maintenance of a stable blood pH , normally close to 7.4. It is a form of homeostasis , and the body has powerful mechanisms to keep pH within a narrow, safe range.

During high-intensity exercise, hydrogen ions accumulate as a by-product of anaerobic energy production, which tends to lower pH and make the blood more acidic. This rising acidity is a major contributor to fatigue , interfering with muscle contraction and enzyme activity. The body defends its pH using buffers (such as bicarbonate), by increasing breathing to remove carbon dioxide, and through the kidneys over longer periods. Training improves buffering capacity, helping athletes tolerate higher levels of acidity. 🏅 Sporting examples 400m running

A 400m runner finishes with very high blood acidity as hydrogen ions accumulate; their trained buffering capacity helps delay the fatigue this causes. Rowing The sustained maximal effort of a 2000m row generates large amounts of hydrogen ions, and buffering systems work hard to protect pH. Supplement link Some athletes use sodium bicarbonate as a legal buffer to help offset the drop in pH during high-intensity events. ✍️ Using the term in context Connect acid-base balance to fatigue and buffering: "During anaerobic exercise, hydrogen ions accumulate and lower blood pH; buffers such as bicarbonate resist this change, helping to delay fatigue and maintain muscle function."

Be precise: it is the accumulation of hydrogen ions, not lactate itself, that is most directly linked to the fall in pH. 🔗 Related terms Buffer Bicarbonate Buffering Blood Lactate Homeostasis Fatigue Anaerobic Glycolysis 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy © 2026 Simply Sport Science · simplysportscience.co.uk

Blood pH is normally kept tightly between about 7.35 and 7.45 ; a pH below 7.35 is acidosis. During hard exercise, hydrogen ions accumulate in muscle, lowering muscle pH ( muscle acidosis ). This slows enzymes, interferes with calcium release and contraction, and contributes to fatigue.

The body defends against it using buffers such as bicarbonate, by breathing out more carbon dioxide and through the kidneys. Actin — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Actin IB Sport Science General Actin One half of the molecular machinery of muscle contraction — the thin filament that slides over myosin to shorten the muscle. 📖 What it means Actin is the thin protein filament found within a muscle fibre's contractile units, the sarcomeres. It works together with the thick filament, myosin , to produce contraction. According to the sliding filament theory , muscle contraction occurs when the myosin heads attach to the actin filaments and pull them inward, sliding the actin over the myosin and shortening the sarcomere. Millions of these tiny movements together shorten the whole muscle.

Actin also carries the regulatory proteins that control when contraction can occur, so it is not just a passive rope but an active partner in the contraction process. 🏅 Sporting examples Every muscular action From a gentle golf putt to a maximal deadlift, actin filaments are being pulled across myosin to shorten muscle fibres and produce force. Strength training Resistance training increases the amount of contractile protein, including actin and myosin, contributing to muscle hypertrophy and greater force production. Sprinting The explosive contractions of a sprinter's fast-twitch fibres rely on rapid, repeated actin–myosin cross-bridge cycling. ✍️ Using the term in context

Reference actin as part of the sliding filament mechanism: "During contraction, the myosin heads bind to the actin filaments and pull them toward the centre of the sarcomere, shortening the muscle in line with the sliding filament theory." Action Potential — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Action Potential IB Sport Science General Action Potential The electrical nerve impulse that carries the command to move — the spark that travels down a neurone and ultimately fires a muscle. 📖 What it means An action potential is a rapid electrical signal that travels along a nerve cell (neurone). It is the way the nervous system transmits information at speed, including the commands that produce movement.

The action potential is an all-or-none event : once a stimulus reaches a certain threshold, a full impulse fires; below that threshold, nothing happens. It travels along the axon of the motor neurone toward the muscle. When the action potential reaches the neuromuscular junction, it triggers the release of acetylcholine , which generates a new action potential in the muscle fibre and sets off contraction. It is the essential electrical link in the chain from brain to movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Reaction starts When a sprinter reacts to the gun, action potentials race from the brain down motor neurones to fire the leg muscles as fast as possible. Skill precision

Fine skills such as a snooker cue action depend on precisely timed action potentials recruiting exactly the right motor units. Fatigue Neuromuscular fatigue can involve a reduced ability to generate or transmit action potentials effectively, weakening the contraction signal. ✍️ Using the term in context Place the action potential correctly in the sequence of movement: "A motor neurone carries an action potential to the neuromuscular junction, where acetylcholine is released; this generates an action potential in the muscle fibre, initiating contraction." Use the all-or-none principle when explaining motor unit recruitment. 🔗 Related terms

Activation Energy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Activation Energy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Activation Energy The energy barrier that must be overcome before a reaction, such as ATP breakdown, can begin. 📖 What it means In biochemistry, activation energy is the energy required to start a reaction. Enzymes reduce the activation energy needed, which allows reactions in the body to happen quickly at normal body temperature. In exercise physiology, enzymes such as those in glycolysis lower the activation energy of each reaction in the pathway, so energy can be released from glucose quickly enough to power muscle contraction. 🏅 Sporting examples

Muscle contraction The enzyme myosin ATPase lowers the activation energy for ATP breakdown, which releases the energy needed for the power stroke. Glycolysis Phosphofructokinase is a key enzyme that lowers the activation energy of a step in glycolysis, controlling how quickly glucose is broken down. Temperature and performance A rise in muscle temperature increases the rate of enzyme-catalysed reactions, partly because more molecules have the energy to overcome the activation barrier. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the role of enzymes in exercise metabolism:

Active Recovery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Active Recovery General IB Sport Science BTEC Sport Active Recovery Why elite athletes keep moving after a hard effort rather than collapsing — low-intensity activity that speeds up the body's return to normal. 📖 What it means Active recovery is low-intensity exercise performed after a hard effort — such as a gentle jog, cycle or swim — rather than complete rest. It is used both between intervals within a session and as a cool-down afterwards.

The main benefit is that keeping the muscles gently working maintains blood flow, which helps remove metabolic by-products such as hydrogen ions and lactate more quickly than passive rest, and keeps oxygen delivery high to support recovery. Active recovery also helps gradually lower heart rate and breathing , prevents blood pooling in the limbs, and can reduce muscle stiffness — which is why a structured cool-down is a standard part of a training session. 🏅 Sporting examples Interval training Between hard 400m repetitions, a runner jogs slowly rather than stopping, keeping blood flow high to clear by-products before the next effort. Swimming

Swimmers perform easy 'swim-down' laps after a race so that lactate is cleared more quickly than it would be by sitting still. Team sports Footballers do a light jog and mobility work after a match as active recovery to aid the return to resting physiology. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the mechanism, not just the practice: "Active recovery maintains elevated blood flow to the muscles, accelerating the removal of metabolic by-products such as hydrogen ions and supporting a faster return to homeostasis than passive rest." Contrast it with passive recovery and note that active recovery is generally more effective at clearing lactate. 🔗 Related terms

Active Stretching — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Active Stretching General BTEC Sport Active Stretching A flexibility method where the performer holds a stretch using their own muscle strength — no partner, no apparatus, just controlled effort. 📖 What it means Active stretching is a flexibility technique in which the performer uses the strength of their own opposing muscles to move a joint into a stretched position and hold it there, without any external assistance.

For example, lifting and holding a straight leg out in front uses the hip flexors and quadriceps (the opposing muscles) to stretch the hamstrings. Because the performer holds the position through muscular effort, active stretching also builds strength in the opposing muscle group . It contrasts with passive stretching , where an external force (a partner, a wall or gravity) moves the joint. Active stretches are typically held for shorter periods because the working muscles fatigue. 🏅 Sporting examples Gymnastics A gymnast holding a leg raised to the front or side is actively stretching — the lifting muscles hold the position while the opposite muscles are stretched. Dance

Dancers use active stretches to develop the controlled, held flexibility their routines demand without relying on a partner. Warm-up Active stretches can be incorporated into a warm-up because they combine mobility work with muscular activation. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish it clearly from passive stretching: "In active stretching the performer uses their own agonist muscles to hold the stretch, whereas in passive stretching an external force produces the movement." Active Transport — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Active Transport IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Active Transport Moving substances from low to high concentration, which needs energy. 📖 What it means Active transport moves molecules across a cell membrane from a region of lower concentration to a region of higher concentration. Nerve impulses The sodium–potassium pump restores the resting potential of a neurone, so it can fire again during rapid, repeated movements. Acute Exercise Response — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Acute Exercise Response IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Acute Exercise Response The body's immediate, short-term reaction to a single bout of exercise — distinct from the long-term adaptations that build up over weeks of training. 📖 What it means An acute exercise response is an immediate, temporary change that the body makes during a single session of exercise to cope with the increased demand. These responses appear quickly and disappear soon after exercise stops.

Typical acute responses include a rise in heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output , faster and deeper breathing, increased blood flow to the muscles, sweating, and a rise in body temperature. They exist to deliver more oxygen and remove more waste while the body works harder. The key exam distinction is between acute responses (short-term, during a single session) and chronic adaptations (long-term structural and functional changes that develop from repeated training over weeks and months). 🏅 Sporting examples Any first sprint As soon as a performer begins a sprint, heart rate, breathing rate and body temperature rise sharply — all acute responses to the sudden demand. Gym session

During a weights session, blood is redistributed to the working muscles and heart rate climbs; these changes return to normal shortly afterwards. Contrast with adaptation Over months of endurance training, resting heart rate falls — that is a chronic adaptation, not an acute response. ✍️ Using the term in context Keep the acute–chronic distinction explicit: "An acute response is an immediate, short-term change during a single exercise bout, such as increased heart rate, whereas a chronic adaptation is a long-term change resulting from repeated training." Adams' Closed Loop Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adams' Closed Loop Theory AS Level / Cambridge General Adams' Closed Loop Theory A classic motor-learning theory explaining how we refine skills by continuously comparing our movements against a stored 'correct' version. 📖 What it means Adams' closed loop theory proposes that skill learning depends on feedback . As a performer moves, they compare the sensory information from that movement against a stored memory of the correct action, and use any mismatch to make corrections.

The theory involves two memory 'traces'. The memory trace initiates the movement, while the perceptual trace is the stored reference of the correct movement, built up through practice, against which ongoing feedback is compared. Because it relies on feedback during the movement, the theory best explains slow, deliberate skills where there is time to detect and correct errors. Its main limitation is that it struggles to explain very fast, ballistic skills that are completed before feedback can be used. 🏅 Sporting examples Archery

An archer draws slowly and continuously compares the feel of their position against their stored perceptual trace, adjusting before release — a good fit for closed loop control. Golf putting A putter uses feedback throughout the slow stroke to refine the movement against their model of a correct putt. Limitation A boxer's fast jab is completed too quickly for feedback to guide it mid-movement, which is where the theory struggles. ✍️ Using the term in context Reference both memory traces and the role of feedback:

"Adams' closed loop theory suggests that the perceptual trace, built through practice, provides a reference against which feedback is compared, allowing errors to be detected and corrected during slow movements." Adaptation Energy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adaptation Energy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Adaptation Energy The extra energy the body needs to recover from training and grow stronger. 📖 What it means When training stresses the body, it uses energy to repair damaged tissue, synthesise new proteins and build new structures such as capillaries and mitochondria. This is the adaptation energy , and it comes on top of the energy needed for the training session itself. Adequate nutrition is needed to supply this energy. An athlete who does not eat enough may train hard but adapt poorly, because the body lacks the energy to build new tissue.

🏅 Sporting examples Resistance training After a heavy session, the body uses energy to repair muscle fibres and build new contractile proteins. Endurance training Building new mitochondria and capillaries uses energy, which is why aerobic adaptations take weeks to develop. This can involve dependence on exercise, misuse of substances such as stimulants or alcohol, or excessive use of performance-enhancing products.

Warning signs include continuing to train while injured, feeling anxious or irritable when unable to train, neglecting other responsibilities and needing more of the behaviour to get the same effect. Adductor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adductor IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Adductor The muscle group that draws the limbs back toward the body's midline — vital for controlling movement and a notorious site of injury in footballers. 📖 What it means An adductor is any muscle whose action moves a limb toward the midline of the body (adduction). The best-known examples are the adductor muscles of the inner thigh , which pull the leg inward. Adductors work as the antagonists to the abductors : as abductors move a limb away from the midline, adductors return it. Together they control side-to-side movement and stabilise the joint.

The hip adductors are heavily used in sports involving changes of direction, kicking and squeezing actions , and are one of the most commonly strained muscle groups in field sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Football A footballer performing a side-foot pass uses the hip adductors to bring the leg across the body — which is also why groin (adductor) strains are so common in the sport. Horse riding Riders use their adductors continuously to grip and stabilise against the horse. Swimming The inward squeeze of the legs in the breaststroke kick is driven by the hip adductors. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the muscle group and its action precisely:

Adenosine Diphosphate (ADP) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adenosine Diphosphate (ADP) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Adenosine Diphosphate (ADP) The 'spent' energy molecule that the body constantly recharges back into ATP — you cannot understand energy systems without it. 📖 What it means Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) is what remains when the energy-carrying molecule ATP loses one of its phosphate groups to release energy for muscle contraction. ADP has two phosphates; ATP has three.

The body cannot store much ATP, so it must constantly rebuild ATP from ADP by re-attaching a phosphate group. This resynthesis is the job of the three energy systems, which supply the energy and phosphate needed to turn ADP back into ATP. Understanding the ATP–ADP cycle is the foundation of energy-system questions: energy is released when ATP becomes ADP, and energy is required to convert ADP back into ATP. 🏅 Sporting examples Explosive efforts In a maximal lift, ATP is broken down to ADP almost instantly, and the ATP-PC system rapidly rebuilds ATP from ADP using phosphocreatine. Endurance

In a long run, the aerobic system continuously resynthesises ATP from ADP using carbohydrate and fat as fuels. Recovery After exercise, ADP is steadily converted back to ATP as phosphocreatine and glycogen stores are restored. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the cycle in both directions: "Energy is released when ATP is broken down to ADP and a phosphate; the energy systems then resynthesise ATP by re-attaching a phosphate to ADP." Be precise about phosphate numbers: ATP has three phosphates, ADP has two. 🔗 Related terms Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) Creatine Phosphate (PCr) ATP-PC System Energy Systems Glycolysis Phosphocreatine (PCr) 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Fibre types Fast-twitch fibres have higher myosin ATPase activity, which allows faster cross-bridge cycling and faster contraction. Sprinting The high ATPase activity of fast-twitch fibres supports the rapid contractions needed during a sprint. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why fast-twitch fibres contract faster than slow-twitch fibres:

Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) The universal energy currency of every muscle contraction — the single molecule that powers all human movement. 📖 What it means Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is the molecule that provides the immediate energy for muscle contraction . It is often called the body's 'energy currency' because it is the usable form of energy that muscles actually spend.

ATP releases energy when one of its three phosphate groups is broken off, forming ADP and a free phosphate. This released energy powers the cross-bridge cycling of actin and myosin that shortens the muscle. Because the body stores only enough ATP for a few seconds of maximal work, it must be continuously resynthesised by the three energy systems (ATP-PC, glycolytic and aerobic). Which system dominates depends on the intensity and duration of the exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Weightlifting A maximal lift uses stored ATP and the ATP-PC system to supply energy almost instantly for a few explosive seconds. 800m running

As the race continues past the first few seconds, the glycolytic and then aerobic systems resynthesise ATP to keep the muscles contracting. Marathon Over 26.2 miles the aerobic system produces the vast majority of ATP using fat and carbohydrate as fuels. ✍️ Using the term in context Establish ATP as the immediate energy source, then link to resynthesis: "ATP is the only immediately usable energy source for muscle contraction; because stores are very limited, the energy systems must continuously resynthesise ATP from ADP to sustain exercise." For any energy-system question, start from ATP and explain how each system rebuilds it. 🔗 Related terms

Adipose Tissue — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adipose Tissue IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Adipose Tissue The body's fat store — far more than padding, it's a major energy reserve and an active endocrine tissue. 📖 What it means Adipose tissue is a type of connective tissue that stores fat (triacylglycerol) as the body's main long-term energy reserve. It is found under the skin (subcutaneous) and around organs (visceral).

Its stored fat is an energy-dense fuel : gram for gram, fat provides more than twice the energy of carbohydrate. During low-to-moderate intensity and prolonged exercise, adipose tissue releases free fatty acids into the blood to be used aerobically by the muscles. Adipose tissue also provides insulation and protection , and acts as an endocrine tissue , releasing hormones involved in appetite and metabolism. The amount a person carries is a component of body composition. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance fuel During a long, steady run, adipose tissue releases fatty acids that the muscles oxidise aerobically, sparing limited glycogen stores. Body composition

The proportion of adipose tissue contributes to an athlete's body composition, which suits them to different sports. Fuel mobilisation Adrenaline stimulates the breakdown of stored fat in adipose tissue, mobilising fuel for exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe adipose tissue as an energy store and fuel source: "Adipose tissue stores fat as the body's main energy reserve; during prolonged, lower-intensity exercise it releases free fatty acids for aerobic metabolism, and it also provides insulation and acts as an endocrine tissue." Link it to fat metabolism and body composition. 🔗 Related terms Body Composition Fat Aerobic System Free Fatty Acids Body Fat Percentage Metabolism

Adrenal Gland — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adrenal Gland IB Sport Science General Adrenal Gland A small gland with a big role in exercise — the source of adrenaline and the body's stress hormones. 📖 What it means The adrenal glands are endocrine glands situated above the kidneys . They secrete several hormones central to the body's response to stress and exercise.

Each gland has two parts. The adrenal medulla (inner region) releases adrenaline and noradrenaline , which prepare the body for activity — increasing heart rate, mobilising fuel and redirecting blood to the muscles. The adrenal cortex (outer region) releases cortisol , involved in fat and protein metabolism during prolonged stress. The adrenal glands are a key part of the body's 'fight or flight' response , activated by the sympathetic nervous system, and their hormones drive many of the acute cardiovascular and metabolic responses to exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Anticipatory rise Before a race, the adrenal medulla releases adrenaline, causing the anticipatory rise in heart rate.

Fuel mobilisation Adrenaline from the adrenal glands mobilises glucose and fatty acids to fuel exercise. Prolonged exercise During long-duration effort, cortisol from the adrenal cortex supports fat and protein metabolism. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the gland's location and the hormones it releases: "The adrenal glands, situated above the kidneys, secrete adrenaline and noradrenaline from the medulla and cortisol from the cortex; these hormones drive the body's response to stress and exercise." Connect it to adrenaline's role in the cardiovascular response. 🔗 Related terms Adrenaline (Epinephrine) Hormone Endocrine System Cortisol Sympathetic Nervous System Anticipatory Rise

Adrenaline (Epinephrine) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Adrenaline (Epinephrine) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Adrenaline (Epinephrine) The body's readiness hormone — it primes the heart, lungs and muscles the moment exercise looms. 📖 What it means Adrenaline (also called epinephrine) is a hormone released by the adrenal medulla in response to stress or exercise. It is the chemical driver of the body's rapid preparation for activity.

Its effects include increasing heart rate and the force of cardiac contraction (raising cardiac output), causing vasodilation of vessels to the working muscles , and mobilising fuel by releasing glucose from the liver and fatty acids from adipose tissue. Adrenaline is responsible for the anticipatory rise in heart rate before exercise begins, and its wide-ranging effects make it central to the acute cardiovascular, respiratory and metabolic responses to exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Anticipatory rise Adrenaline released just before a sprint raises heart rate in advance, so the body is primed at the gun. Cardiac response

Adrenaline increases both heart rate and the force of contraction, boosting cardiac output during exercise. Fuel release Adrenaline mobilises glucose and fatty acids, ensuring fuel is available for the working muscles. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the source and list adrenaline's effects: "Adrenaline, released by the adrenal medulla, prepares the body for exercise by increasing heart rate and cardiac contraction force, causing vasodilation to the muscles, and mobilising glucose and fatty acids; it also drives the anticipatory rise." During prolonged or intense training, ACTH and cortisol levels rise. Cortisol helps mobilise energy, but long periods of high cortisol may suppress immune function and recovery, which is why training load needs to be managed. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance training Prolonged exercise increases ACTH and cortisol, which helps maintain blood glucose during long events. Aerobic Capacity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aerobic Capacity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Aerobic Capacity The ceiling on how much oxygen a body can use — the single best physiological predictor of endurance performance. 📖 What it means Aerobic capacity is the maximum ability of the body to take in, transport and use oxygen during sustained exercise. It reflects how well the heart, lungs, blood and muscles work together to supply the aerobic energy system.

It is most commonly quantified by VO₂ max — the maximum volume of oxygen a person can consume per minute. A higher aerobic capacity means a performer can work harder for longer before fatiguing. Aerobic capacity is improved through endurance training , which drives adaptations such as a larger stroke volume, greater capillary density and more mitochondria — all of which increase oxygen delivery and use. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running Elite marathon runners have among the highest aerobic capacities of any athletes, allowing them to sustain a fast pace aerobically. Cycling

A road cyclist's aerobic capacity determines how long they can hold a hard tempo on a climb before anaerobic fatigue sets in. Testing Aerobic capacity is estimated in the field with tests such as the Bleep Test or Cooper Test, and measured directly in a lab with a gas analyser. ✍️ Using the term in context Link aerobic capacity to its measure and its trainability: "Aerobic capacity, measured by VO₂ max, reflects the maximum rate of oxygen uptake and use; it improves with endurance training through adaptations such as increased stroke volume and capillary density." Don't confuse aerobic capacity (a maximum) with aerobic/lactate threshold (the intensity at which lactate rises). 🔗 Related terms

Aerobic Decoupling — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aerobic Decoupling AS Level / Cambridge BTEC General Aerobic Decoupling When the heart rate keeps rising but the power output no longer keeps pace, showing that the body is tiring. 📖 What it means Aerobic decoupling describes what happens during long exercise when heart rate continues to rise for the same power output, or when power output falls while heart rate stays high. It is a sign that the body is becoming less efficient at turning oxygen into work.

Causes include dehydration, rising body temperature and fatigue in the muscles. Coaches and athletes monitor decoupling in long events to judge when to adjust pace or fuelling. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A runner's heart rate creeps up at the same pace in the later stages, showing aerobic decoupling caused by dehydration and heat. Cycling A rider's power output falls while heart rate stays high during a long climb, a sign of decoupling. Aerobic Energy System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aerobic Energy System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Aerobic Energy System The body's long-distance engine — the oxygen-dependent system that produces the vast majority of energy for endurance exercise. 📖 What it means The aerobic energy system resynthesises ATP using oxygen . It is the dominant energy system for lower-intensity, longer-duration exercise , where oxygen supply can keep pace with demand.

It produces ATP through three stages: glycolysis , the Krebs cycle , and the electron transport chain , using carbohydrate and fat as fuels. Its by-products are carbon dioxide and water, which are easily removed. Its great strength is yield : it produces far more ATP per molecule of fuel than the anaerobic systems (around 36–38 ATP from one glucose molecule). Its limitation is speed — it cannot produce ATP fast enough for maximal efforts. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A marathon is fuelled almost entirely by the aerobic system, using a mix of carbohydrate and fat to sustain energy over hours. Triathlon

The long, steady demands of a triathlon rely on a highly developed aerobic system to supply continuous energy across all three disciplines. Recovery role Even during rest between sprints, the aerobic system works to restore the body and clear by-products from anaerobic efforts. ✍️ Using the term in context Emphasise the oxygen requirement, fuels, stages and high yield: "The aerobic system resynthesises ATP using oxygen via glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain, producing a high yield of around 36–38 ATP per glucose molecule, making it ideal for prolonged, submaximal exercise." Contrast its high yield but slow rate with the fast but low-yield anaerobic systems.

Aerobic Glycolysis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aerobic Glycolysis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Aerobic Glycolysis Glycolysis carried out when oxygen is available, so pyruvate goes on to the mitochondria. 📖 What it means Aerobic glycolysis is the first stage of carbohydrate breakdown, where glucose is split into two molecules of pyruvate, producing a small amount of ATP. In the presence of oxygen, the pyruvate enters the mitochondria and is converted into acetyl CoA for the Krebs cycle.

Because pyruvate is fully oxidised in aerobic conditions, aerobic glycolysis yields far more ATP per glucose molecule than the anaerobic pathway, which produces lactate instead. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance running A marathon runner relies on aerobic glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to produce ATP steadily over a long period. Recovery After intense exercise, the body uses aerobic glycolysis to clear lactate and restore energy stores. Aerobic Threshold — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aerobic Threshold IB Sport Science General Aerobic Threshold The gentle gear-change in exercise intensity where aerobic metabolism takes the lead. 📖 What it means The aerobic threshold is the exercise intensity at which the aerobic energy system becomes the primary source of ATP , and blood lactate first begins to rise slightly above resting levels. It sits at a relatively low-to-moderate intensity.

Below this threshold, energy demand is met almost entirely aerobically with minimal lactate. As intensity rises past the aerobic threshold, anaerobic contribution begins to increase, though lactate is still cleared effectively — that steeper accumulation comes later, at the anaerobic threshold . The aerobic threshold is useful for prescribing endurance training : sustained work around it develops aerobic efficiency and fat metabolism, forming the base of an endurance athlete's training. 🏅 Sporting examples Base training Endurance athletes do much of their training around the aerobic threshold to build aerobic efficiency and fat-burning capacity. Intensity marker

Below the aerobic threshold, effort feels comfortable and can be sustained for long periods. Two thresholds The aerobic threshold marks the first small rise in lactate; the anaerobic threshold marks the steeper accumulation at higher intensity. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the aerobic threshold and distinguish it from the anaerobic threshold: "The aerobic threshold is the intensity at which the aerobic system becomes the primary ATP source and lactate first rises slightly; it is lower than the anaerobic threshold, at which lactate accumulates rapidly, and is used to prescribe base endurance training." Aerodynamics — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aerodynamics IB Sport Science General Aerodynamics The science of moving through air — how drag and airflow shape performance in fast and flight-based sports. 📖 What it means Aerodynamics is the study of how air resistance and airflow affect moving objects , including athletes and sports equipment. It applies wherever speed through the air matters. The main aerodynamic force to overcome is drag , which increases with speed, frontal surface area and surface roughness. Athletes and designers reduce drag through streamlining — low body positions, smooth suits and shaped equipment.

Aerodynamics also involves generating and using lift , including the effects of spin (the Magnus effect) that curve a ball's flight. Understanding aerodynamics helps optimise technique, positioning and equipment in sports such as cycling, skiing and throwing. 🏅 Sporting examples Cycling A cyclist adopts an aerodynamic tuck and wears smooth clothing to reduce drag and go faster for the same effort. Throwing implements The aerodynamics of a discus or javelin — how it is angled to the airflow — affects how far it flies. Afterload — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Afterload IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Afterload The resistance the heart pumps against once blood starts to leave. 📖 What it means Afterload is the resistance against which the ventricles must pump to eject blood. In the left ventricle it is mainly the pressure in the aorta. Higher afterload means the heart has to work harder to achieve the same stroke volume. Afterload is affected by vascular resistance and blood pressure. Regular endurance training lowers resting blood pressure and reduces vascular resistance, which reduces the afterload the heart has to overcome. 🏅 Sporting examples Hypertension

A person with high blood pressure has a higher afterload, so their heart works harder for every beat. Endurance training Training reduces peripheral resistance, lowering afterload and making the heart more efficient. Heavy resistance training Heavy lifting can briefly raise blood pressure, increasing afterload during the effort. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how afterload affects stroke volume: "Higher afterload means the ventricle must generate more pressure to eject blood, so for the same contractility, the stroke volume is reduced." Aggression — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aggression IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Aggression Intent to harm outside the rules — a precisely defined concept in sport psychology, distinct from legitimate assertive play. 📖 What it means In sport psychology, aggression is behaviour intended to harm another person, outside the rules of the sport . The key features are the intention to harm and that it is against the rules .

It is carefully distinguished from assertion — forceful, competitive but rule-abiding play with no intent to harm. Aggression is also often split into hostile aggression (where harm itself is the goal, usually driven by anger) and instrumental aggression (where harm is used as a means to a sporting goal, such as intimidating an opponent). Several theories try to explain aggression, including instinct theory , the frustration–aggression hypothesis , and social learning theory (aggression is learned by observing others). Coaches manage it through strategies such as removing the aggressor, controlling arousal, and reinforcing assertive rather than aggressive behaviour. 🏅 Sporting examples

Hostile aggression A player deliberately striking an opponent in anger, intending to hurt them, is showing hostile aggression. Instrumental aggression A hard, illegal challenge aimed at intimidating an opponent to gain an advantage is instrumental aggression. Aggression vs assertion A fair but forceful, rule-abiding tackle with no intent to harm is assertion, not aggression. ✍️ Using the term in context Define aggression precisely and distinguish it from assertion:

"In sport, aggression is behaviour intended to harm another person outside the rules; it is distinguished from assertion, which is forceful but rule-abiding with no intent to harm, and is often divided into hostile and instrumental aggression." Agility — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Agility General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Agility The ability to change direction fast without losing control — a skill-related component of fitness that decides countless sporting contests. 📖 What it means Agility is the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while maintaining control and balance . It combines speed, balance, coordination and reaction, making it a skill-related component of fitness rather than a purely health-related one.

Agility matters most in sports with rapid, unpredictable changes of direction , where a performer must decelerate, reposition and accelerate again in a fraction of a second, often in response to an opponent. It is developed through drills that combine footwork, deceleration, and reactive movement , and it is assessed with tests such as the Illinois Agility Test that time a performer through a set course of turns. 🏅 Sporting examples Rugby A winger sidestepping a defender relies on agility to change direction sharply while keeping balance and control of the ball. Basketball A defender mirroring an attacker's movements uses agility to react and reposition constantly without being beaten.

Testing The Illinois Agility Test measures agility by timing a performer sprinting and weaving through a course of cones. ✍️ Using the term in context Define agility fully — it is more than just speed: "Agility is the ability to change direction quickly and accurately while maintaining balance and control; as a skill-related component of fitness, it is crucial in sports requiring rapid, reactive changes of direction." Agonist-Antagonist Paired Sets — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Agonist-Antagonist Paired Sets BTEC General Agonist-Antagonist Paired Sets Training opposing muscles one after the other, to save time and balance strength. 📖 What it means Agonist-antagonist paired sets pair an exercise for a muscle (the agonist) with one for the muscle that opposes it (the antagonist). The method is time-efficient and can increase total work. Agonist — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Agonist IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Agonist The 'prime mover' — the muscle doing the main work in any given movement, and the first thing to identify in movement analysis. 📖 What it means The agonist is the muscle primarily responsible for producing a movement at a joint. It is also called the prime mover because it generates the main force by contracting. Every agonist works in partnership with an antagonist — the muscle on the opposite side of the joint that relaxes and lengthens to allow the movement. This coordinated pairing is called reciprocal inhibition .

Which muscle is the agonist depends on the movement : in an upward biceps curl the biceps is the agonist, but as the weight is lowered under control the roles shift. Correctly identifying the agonist for a specific phase is a core movement-analysis skill. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps curl In the upward (lifting) phase of a biceps curl, the biceps brachii is the agonist, contracting to flex the elbow. Running During the drive phase, the quadriceps act as the agonist to extend the knee and propel the runner forward. Kicking As a footballer extends the knee to strike the ball, the quadriceps are the agonist and the hamstrings the antagonist. ✍️ Using the term in context

Always name the agonist for a specific movement and phase: "During elbow flexion in the upward phase of a curl, the biceps brachii is the agonist, while the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing to allow the movement." Air Resistance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Air Resistance IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Air Resistance The invisible brake on every fast-moving athlete — the frictional force of pushing through the air. 📖 What it means Air resistance is the frictional force that opposes a body's motion through the air . It acts in the opposite direction to movement, slowing the body or object down. It is a form of drag.

The size of air resistance increases with the velocity of the body, its frontal surface area, and its surface roughness (and with air density). Because it rises sharply with speed, it has the greatest effect in fast sports and on light, large objects. Air resistance affects projectiles, cyclists, sprinters and skiers . Athletes minimise it by streamlining — reducing frontal area and smoothing surfaces — while for some projectiles (like a discus) it also interacts with lift to shape the flight path. 🏅 Sporting examples Projectiles Air resistance shortens and distorts the flight of light, large-surface-area projectiles such as a shuttlecock far more than a dense shot. Cyclists

A cyclist crouches low to reduce frontal area and cut the air resistance opposing them at speed. Sprinting A headwind increases air resistance, slowing a sprinter, while a tailwind reduces it. ✍️ Using the term in context Define air resistance and the factors affecting it: "Air resistance is the frictional force opposing a body's motion through the air; it increases with velocity, frontal surface area and surface roughness, and is minimised by streamlining — most important in fast sports and for light, large objects." Treat it as a form of drag and link to streamlining. 🔗 Related terms Drag Aerodynamics Streamlining Projectile Air Resistance Fluid Mechanics 🎓 Where this appears

Alactic System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Alactic System IB Sport Science General Alactic System The 'lactate-free' energy pathway — another name for the ATP-PC system that fuels the most explosive efforts. 📖 What it means The alactic system is another name for the ATP-PC (phosphocreatine) energy system . 'Alactic' means without lactate — this pathway resynthesises ATP without producing lactic acid.

It uses stored phosphocreatine to rebuild ATP extremely rapidly and without oxygen, making it the fastest energy system. Because it produces no fatiguing by-products , fatigue in short maximal efforts comes from the depletion of phosphocreatine stores rather than acidity. It dominates very short, maximal efforts of up to around 8–10 seconds — sprints, jumps and single lifts — and its stores replenish quickly during recovery, allowing repeated short efforts. 🏅 Sporting examples Explosive efforts A shot put or a short sprint is fuelled by the alactic (ATP-PC) system, with no lactate produced. No acidity

Because the alactic system produces no lactate, fatigue in these efforts comes from depleted phosphocreatine, not acidity. Quick recovery Phosphocreatine stores replenish within a few minutes, letting an athlete repeat short maximal efforts. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the alactic system as the ATP-PC pathway: "The alactic system is another name for the ATP-PC system; 'alactic' means it resynthesises ATP without producing lactate, using phosphocreatine to fuel maximal efforts of up to around 8–10 seconds." Note that fatigue here comes from PC depletion, not acidity. 🔗 Related terms

Alcohol in Sport — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Alcohol in Sport BTEC General Alcohol in Sport How alcohol affects performers, teams and organisations, and what policies are used to manage it. 📖 What it means Alcohol affects sport in several ways. It impairs coordination, reaction time and decision-making, dehydrates the body and disrupts sleep and recovery. Even small amounts can reduce performance the following day. Many sports and organisations set alcohol policies for players, staff and spectators. These may include restrictions on drinking near training or competition, education on its effects and support for players who need help. 🏅 Sporting examples

Recovery Drinking after a match dehydrates the body and disturbs sleep, which slows recovery for the next session. Aldosterone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aldosterone IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Aldosterone The hormone that helps the body hold on to sodium and water during exercise. 📖 What it means Aldosterone is released from the adrenal cortex in response to falling blood pressure, low blood sodium or the renin–angiotensin system. It acts on the kidneys to increase the reabsorption of sodium, and water follows, which raises blood volume. During prolonged exercise with sweating, aldosterone helps conserve sodium and water. This supports blood volume and helps maintain blood pressure and cardiac output. 🏅 Sporting examples Long-distance events

Aldosterone helps retain sodium during a marathon, which reduces the risk of hyponatraemia. Heat exposure In hot conditions, aldosterone increases water retention, helping to maintain plasma volume. Dehydration Low blood volume triggers aldosterone release, which helps restore fluid balance. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the role of aldosterone during prolonged exercise in the heat: "Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the kidneys, so water is retained, which helps maintain plasma volume and blood pressure during sweating." All-or-None Law — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › All-or-None Law IB Sport Science General All-or-None Law A motor unit's on/off switch — when stimulated enough, it fires fully, or not at all. 📖 What it means The all-or-none law states that when a motor unit is stimulated above its threshold, all of its muscle fibres contract fully; if the stimulus is below threshold, none contract at all . There is no partial contraction of a motor unit. A motor unit is a motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it controls. When the neuron fires strongly enough to reach threshold, every fibre in that unit contracts maximally — it is all or nothing.

This means the body varies the strength of a whole-muscle contraction not by contracting units partially, but by recruiting more or fewer motor units (and by changing how frequently they fire). Greater force is produced by recruiting more motor units. 🏅 Sporting examples Grading force To lift a heavier weight, the body recruits more motor units — each contracting fully under the all-or-none law. Fine vs gross control Muscles needing fine control have small motor units, allowing precise grading of force through selective recruitment. Threshold A stimulus below a motor unit's threshold produces no contraction; above it, all its fibres contract fully. ✍️ Using the term in context

State the law and its implication for grading force: "The all-or-none law states that a motor unit contracts fully if stimulated above threshold, or not at all if below it; the body therefore grades whole-muscle force by recruiting more or fewer motor units, not by partial contractions." Altitude Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Altitude Training IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Altitude Training Training high to perform low — using reduced oxygen at altitude to boost the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity. 📖 What it means Altitude training is training at high altitude, where the air has a lower partial pressure of oxygen , in order to stimulate physiological adaptations that improve endurance performance. It is a legal physiological ergogenic aid.

The reduced oxygen availability at altitude prompts the body to increase its production of red blood cells and haemoglobin (via the hormone EPO), raising its oxygen-carrying capacity . On returning to sea level, the athlete may benefit from this enhanced ability to deliver oxygen to the muscles. Altitude training has drawbacks and complications : training intensity is reduced at altitude (which can cause some detraining), the benefits can be short-lived, and responses vary between individuals. Strategies such as 'live high, train low' aim to gain the adaptations while maintaining training quality. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance runners

Distance runners train at altitude to stimulate red blood cell production, aiming to improve oxygen delivery when they return to sea level. Live high, train low Athletes live at altitude to gain the blood adaptations but train lower down to maintain training intensity. Individual variation Because responses differ, some athletes benefit greatly from altitude training while others gain little. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the low-oxygen stimulus and the red-blood-cell adaptation:

"Altitude training exposes athletes to the lower oxygen pressure of high altitude, stimulating increased red blood cell and haemoglobin production to raise oxygen-carrying capacity; benefits can be offset by reduced training intensity, so strategies such as 'live high, train low' are used." Alveolar Membrane — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Alveolar Membrane IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Alveolar Membrane The very thin layer that separates the air in the lungs from the blood. 📖 What it means The alveolar membrane is the combined wall of the alveolus and the capillary it touches. It is extremely thin, which allows oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse quickly between the air and the blood. Factors that affect diffusion across the membrane include its thickness, its surface area and the partial pressure gradient. Thickening of the membrane, for example through fibrosis, reduces gas exchange and limits performance. 🏅 Sporting examples

Endurance Efficient gas exchange across the alveolar membrane supports high oxygen uptake during long events. Altitude At altitude, a lower partial pressure of oxygen reduces the diffusion gradient across the membrane. Alveoli — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Alveoli IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Alveoli The tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens — the lungs' vast surface for loading oxygen and offloading carbon dioxide. 📖 What it means The alveoli are the tiny air sacs at the end of the airways in the lungs , where gas exchange takes place . There are millions of them, surrounded by a dense network of capillaries. Their structure makes gas exchange highly efficient: they provide an enormous surface area , have extremely thin walls (one cell thick), and are surrounded by capillaries , creating a short diffusion distance and steep concentration gradients.

At the alveoli, oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood , and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air to be exhaled. During exercise, faster, deeper breathing and greater blood flow keep the gradients steep to speed this exchange. 🏅 Sporting examples Gas exchange During exercise, the large surface area of the alveoli allows huge volumes of oxygen to diffuse into the blood to meet demand. Structure and function The alveoli's thin walls and rich capillary supply create the short diffusion distance that makes gas exchange rapid. Endurance An endurance athlete's efficient alveolar gas exchange supports the high rates of oxygen uptake their sport demands.

Amino Acid Pool — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Amino Acid Pool IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Amino Acid Pool The store of amino acids the body can draw on to build and repair protein. 📖 What it means The amino acid pool is the collection of free amino acids in the blood and tissues. Amino acids come from diet, from the breakdown of body protein and from the synthesis of non-essential amino acids. The pool is used to build new proteins and to supply energy when needed.

Protein synthesis uses amino acids from the pool, so a well-fed athlete keeps the pool topped up. During prolonged exercise, some amino acids may be oxidised for energy, which is one reason protein needs rise with training. 🏅 Sporting examples Recovery After resistance training, amino acids from the pool are used to repair muscle proteins. Post-training meal Eating protein after exercise increases the amino acid pool available for muscle repair. Endurance Long events can increase amino acid oxidation, adding to protein needs. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why athletes need a protein-rich meal after training:

"Eating protein after training raises the amino acid pool in the blood, which supplies the building blocks needed to repair and build muscle protein." Amphiarthrosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Amphiarthrosis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Amphiarthrosis A joint that allows only a small amount of movement. 📖 What it means An amphiarthrosis is a cartilaginous or fibrous joint that allows slight movement. Examples include the pubic symphysis, where the two pubic bones meet, and the joints between the vertebrae, where discs allow limited movement. Amphiarthroses contrast with diarthroses, which are freely movable synovial joints, and with synarthroses, which do not move at all. Anaemia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anaemia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Anaemia Low haemoglobin and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. 📖 What it means Anaemia is a condition of low haemoglobin or red blood cell numbers , which reduces the blood's ability to carry oxygen. Anaerobic Capacity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anaerobic Capacity IB Sport Science General Anaerobic Capacity The body's total capacity for oxygen-free energy production — what powers repeated sprints and sustained high-intensity efforts. 📖 What it means Anaerobic capacity is the total amount of energy that can be produced by the anaerobic (oxygen-independent) energy systems — the ATP-PC and glycolytic systems combined. It determines how much high-intensity work a performer can do before the aerobic system must take over.

It underpins performance in short, maximal and repeated high-intensity efforts , such as sprinting, jumping and the explosive actions of team sports. A high anaerobic capacity allows a performer to sustain or repeat intense efforts and tolerate the resulting fatigue. It is developed through high-intensity and interval training , which improves the muscles' energy stores and their ability to buffer the acidity produced by anaerobic metabolism, delaying fatigue. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A high anaerobic capacity lets a sprinter or 400m runner sustain near-maximal effort and tolerate the fatigue it produces. Team sports

A footballer's anaerobic capacity supports repeated sprints and explosive efforts across a match. Training High-intensity interval training develops anaerobic capacity by improving energy stores and buffering ability. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it as the total anaerobic energy capacity and link to training: "Anaerobic capacity is the total energy the anaerobic systems can produce, underpinning short, maximal and repeated high-intensity efforts; it is developed through high-intensity and interval training, which improves energy stores and buffering of acidity." Anaerobic Glycolysis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anaerobic Glycolysis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Anaerobic Glycolysis Rapid energy without oxygen — the pathway that powers hard efforts once the ATP-PC system runs out, at the cost of rising acidity. 📖 What it means Anaerobic glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose to resynthesise ATP without oxygen . It is the energy pathway of the lactic acid (glycolytic) system, dominant in high-intensity efforts lasting from about ten seconds up to around three minutes .

It supplies ATP rapidly — faster than the aerobic system — but produces pyruvate that is converted to lactate , and the accompanying accumulation of hydrogen ions lowers muscle pH, contributing to fatigue. Its ATP yield is low compared with aerobic metabolism, and rising acidity limits how long it can be sustained. Trained athletes can better tolerate and buffer the acidity, delaying fatigue and allowing them to sustain high intensity for longer. 🏅 Sporting examples 400m running A 400m runner relies heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, generating the intense fatigue and acidity felt in the closing metres. Repeated sprints

In a game, anaerobic glycolysis supplies fast energy when efforts extend beyond the ATP-PC system's capacity. Training tolerance Trained middle-distance runners buffer acidity better, sustaining anaerobic effort longer before slowing. ✍️ Using the term in context State the process, duration, speed and by-product: "Anaerobic glycolysis breaks down glucose without oxygen to rapidly resynthesise ATP, dominating high-intensity efforts of around 10 seconds to 3 minutes; it produces lactate, and the accumulation of hydrogen ions lowers pH and causes fatigue." Be precise that it is hydrogen ion accumulation, not lactate itself, that most directly lowers pH. 🔗 Related terms

Anaerobic Threshold — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anaerobic Threshold IB Sport Science General Anaerobic Threshold The tipping point of hard exercise — where lactate starts piling up faster than the body can clear it. 📖 What it means The anaerobic threshold is the exercise intensity at which lactate begins to accumulate in the blood faster than it can be removed . Beyond it, blood lactate rises steeply and fatigue sets in more quickly.

It marks the intensity where the body relies increasingly on anaerobic glycolysis , producing lactate and hydrogen ions faster than they can be cleared and buffered. It is closely related to the lactate inflection point and OBLA. The anaerobic threshold is a strong predictor of endurance performance and a valuable training marker: training near or above it raises the threshold, allowing an athlete to sustain a higher intensity before fatiguing. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance predictor An athlete with a high anaerobic threshold can sustain a faster pace before lactate accumulates and forces them to slow. Threshold training

Training at or just below the anaerobic threshold raises it over time, improving sustainable pace. Related markers The anaerobic threshold is closely linked to the lactate inflection point and OBLA (around 4 mmol/L). ✍️ Using the term in context Define the anaerobic threshold and its significance: "The anaerobic threshold is the intensity at which blood lactate accumulates faster than it can be removed, causing a steep rise; it predicts endurance performance, and training near it raises the threshold so a higher intensity can be sustained." Angle of Release — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Angle of Release IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Angle of Release The launch angle that helps decide how far a projectile flies — one of the three factors governing projectile distance. 📖 What it means The angle of release is the angle at which a projectile is launched relative to the horizontal . Along with the speed of release and the height of release , it is one of the three factors that determine the horizontal distance a projectile travels.

For a projectile released and landing at the same height , the theoretically optimal angle for maximum distance is 45 degrees . However, when the release height is above the landing height (as in shot put, where the shot is released above the ground), the optimal angle is slightly less than 45 degrees . In practice, air resistance and aerodynamic lift further affect the ideal angle — for implements such as the discus and javelin, which generate lift, the optimal release angle differs from the simple projectile prediction. 🏅 Sporting examples Shot put Because the shot is released above the ground, its optimal release angle is slightly below 45 degrees rather than exactly 45. Long jump

A long jumper's take-off angle is a compromise, as the very high speeds involved make a true 45-degree angle impractical. Javelin The javelin's aerodynamic lift means its optimal release angle differs from the simple 45-degree projectile prediction. ✍️ Using the term in context State the three release factors and the 45-degree qualification: "The angle of release is one of three factors determining projectile distance, alongside speed and height of release; 45 degrees is optimal when release and landing heights are equal, but a greater release height lowers the optimal angle." Angular Momentum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Angular Momentum IB Sport Science General Angular Momentum The 'quantity of rotation' a body carries — the spinning equivalent of momentum, central to somersaults, spins and throws. 📖 What it means Angular momentum is the quantity of rotation a body possesses — the rotational equivalent of (linear) momentum. It depends on the body's moment of inertia (how its mass is distributed around the axis) and its angular velocity (how fast it is rotating).

A crucial principle is the conservation of angular momentum : once a body is airborne, its angular momentum stays constant (there is no external turning force to change it). So if the performer changes their moment of inertia, their angular velocity changes to compensate . This is why a rotating athlete spins faster when they tuck (bringing mass closer to the axis reduces moment of inertia, so angular velocity increases) and slower when they extend . It explains the control of rotation in diving, gymnastics and figure skating. 🏅 Sporting examples Diving

A diver generates angular momentum at take-off, then tucks to reduce their moment of inertia and spin faster, opening out to slow the rotation before entry. Figure skating A skater pulls their arms in to reduce moment of inertia and spin faster — conservation of angular momentum in action. Gymnastics A gymnast controls the speed of a somersault by tucking or extending to change their moment of inertia. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain conservation and the moment of inertia–angular velocity trade-off:

"Angular momentum is conserved once a body is airborne; because it equals moment of inertia multiplied by angular velocity, a diver who tucks reduces their moment of inertia, so their angular velocity increases and they spin faster." Angular Motion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Angular Motion IB Sport Science General Angular Motion Movement in a circle or rotation about an axis — one of the fundamental types of motion, alongside linear motion. 📖 What it means Angular motion is movement of a body in a circular path about an axis of rotation , where all parts turn through the same angle in the same time. It is rotation, as distinct from linear (straight-line) motion.

It occurs when a force is applied off-centre (not through the centre of mass), creating a turning effect called a torque or moment . Angular motion is described using angular quantities such as angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration . Angular motion is everywhere in sport — a somersault, a spinning skater, the rotation of a limb about a joint — and it frequently combines with linear motion , as when the angular motion of the legs produces the linear motion of a runner's body. 🏅 Sporting examples Somersault A gymnast performing a somersault rotates about an axis through their centre of mass — pure angular motion. Limb rotation

The rotation of the lower leg about the knee joint during a kick is angular motion. Combined A sprinter's legs rotate about their joints (angular motion) to drive the whole body forward in linear motion. ✍️ Using the term in context Define angular motion and its cause, and contrast with linear motion: "Angular motion is rotation about an axis, where all parts turn through the same angle in the same time; it results from a force applied off-centre, creating torque, and contrasts with linear motion, though the two often combine." Reference torque as the cause of angular motion. 🔗 Related terms Linear Motion Torque Angular Velocity Angular Momentum Centre of Mass Axes of Rotation

Angular Velocity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Angular Velocity IB Sport Science General Angular Velocity How fast a body rotates — the rotational counterpart of (linear) velocity, measured as angle turned per unit time. 📖 What it means Angular velocity is the rate at which a body rotates about an axis — the angle turned per unit of time. It is the rotational equivalent of linear velocity, measured in radians or degrees per second.

Angular velocity is a key component of angular momentum (moment of inertia × angular velocity). Because angular momentum is conserved in flight, a performer can increase their angular velocity by reducing their moment of inertia — for example, by tucking. High angular velocity of body segments is central to generating speed and force in throwing, striking and kicking — rapid rotation of the hips, trunk and limbs, summed in sequence, produces high end-point speed at the hand, foot or implement. 🏅 Sporting examples Diving/gymnastics A diver increases their angular velocity (spins faster) by tucking, reducing their moment of inertia while angular momentum is conserved. Throwing

The high angular velocity of the trunk and arm segments, summed in sequence, produces the fast release of a javelin or discus. Kicking Rapid angular velocity of the lower leg about the knee contributes to the speed of a football strike. ✍️ Using the term in context Define angular velocity and link it to angular momentum: "Angular velocity is the rate of rotation about an axis, the rotational equivalent of linear velocity; because angular momentum (moment of inertia × angular velocity) is conserved in flight, reducing moment of inertia increases angular velocity." Connect segment angular velocity to end-point speed in throwing and striking. 🔗 Related terms

Anisometrics — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anisometrics BTEC General Anisometrics Muscle contraction in which the muscle lengthens or shortens while it produces force. 📖 What it means Anisometric contractions are those in which the muscle changes length while producing force. They include concentric contractions, in which the muscle shortens, and eccentric contractions, in which it lengthens under load. Anisometric work is the basis of most sporting movements, as the muscle shortens to accelerate a limb and lengthens to control it. Eccentric work in particular is important for injury prevention and for controlling deceleration. 🏅 Sporting examples

Lowering a weight The biceps works eccentrically as the arm is lowered in a curl, controlling the movement. Running The quadriceps works eccentrically to absorb force as the foot lands. Ankylosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ankylosis BTEC General Ankylosis When a joint becomes stiff or fused, losing its range of movement. 📖 What it means Ankylosis is the stiffening or fusion of a joint, so that it loses its normal range of movement. It can be caused by injury, inflammation, disease such as arthritis or surgical fusion. In sport, ankylosis is a serious outcome of some injuries and conditions. Rehabilitation aims to restore movement before stiffness becomes permanent, and athletes with reduced joint mobility need tailored programmes to maintain function. 🏅 Sporting examples Arthritis

Anorexia Athletica — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anorexia Athletica BTEC General Anorexia Athletica Disordered eating driven by the pressure to perform or to look a certain way in sport. 📖 What it means Anorexia athletica describes restricted eating that is driven by sport. The athlete may believe that a lower body weight or a particular shape will improve performance or judging, and they restrict food even when they are already at a healthy weight.

The condition is serious. It can cause fatigue, injury, stress fractures, hormonal disruption and lasting harm to health. Coaches, parents and medical staff should watch for signs such as weight loss, avoidance of meals and a preoccupation with food and weight. 🏅 Sporting examples Gymnastics A gymnast who skips meals to keep a low weight may be showing signs of anorexia athletica. Endurance running A runner who restricts food despite high training loads may be at risk of stress fractures and fatigue. Judging sports Pressure to appear slim in judged sports can increase the risk of disordered eating. ✍️ Using the term in context

Anorexia Nervosa — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anorexia Nervosa BTEC General Anorexia Nervosa A serious mental health condition that involves severe food restriction and fear of weight gain. 📖 What it means Anorexia nervosa is a serious eating disorder in which a person restricts food intake to maintain a very low body weight, has an intense fear of gaining weight and experiences a distorted perception of their own body. It is a mental health condition with significant physical consequences.

Physical effects include a low heart rate, low blood pressure, electrolyte imbalance, hair loss and loss of bone density. Treatment involves medical and psychological support, and it is a condition that requires professional help rather than sports advice. 🏅 Sporting examples Athlete wellbeing A coach who suspects an athlete has anorexia nervosa should refer them to a doctor, not try to manage it through training. Team support A team may support a teammate by encouraging help-seeking and avoiding comments about food or weight. ✍️ Using the term in context
