Antagonist — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Antagonist IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Antagonist The muscle that relaxes and lengthens to allow movement to happen — the essential partner to every prime mover. 📖 What it means The antagonist is the muscle that opposes the agonist . As the agonist contracts to produce a movement, the antagonist relaxes and lengthens to allow that movement to occur smoothly. This coordinated relationship, where one muscle contracts while its opposite relaxes, is called reciprocal inhibition . Without it, opposing muscles would fight each other and movement would be jerky or impossible.

Like the agonist, the role of antagonist swaps depending on the movement . In elbow flexion the triceps is the antagonist; in elbow extension the biceps takes that role. Naming the correct antagonist for a specific action is a key analysis skill. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps curl During the upward phase of a curl, the triceps acts as the antagonist, relaxing to let the biceps flex the elbow. Sprinting As the quadriceps extend the knee to drive forward, the hamstrings act as the antagonist by relaxing and lengthening. Injury link If an antagonist fails to relax properly or is much weaker than its agonist, the resulting muscle imbalance can raise injury risk. ✍️ Using the term in context

Pair the antagonist with the agonist and the movement: "In elbow flexion, the biceps is the agonist and the triceps the antagonist, which relaxes and lengthens through reciprocal inhibition to allow the movement." Emphasise that the antagonist relaxes — it does not actively produce the movement. 🔗 Related terms Agonist Reciprocal Inhibition Muscle Imbalance Concentric Contraction Eccentric Contraction Fixator 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → BTEC Sport Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) The key ligament in the knee, often injured in sudden stops, turns and landings. 📖 What it means The anterior cruciate ligament runs diagonally inside the knee joint, connecting the femur to the tibia. It prevents the tibia from sliding forward relative to the femur and provides rotational stability to the knee.

ACL injuries are common in sports that involve sudden deceleration, cutting and landing, such as football, netball and basketball. Many occur without contact, when the knee collapses inwards during a landing or a change of direction. Recovery usually involves surgery and a long rehabilitation programme. 🏅 Sporting examples Netball A player who lands from a jump and changes direction quickly is at risk of an ACL injury. Football An ACL injury often happens when a player plants the foot and twists the knee. Prevention Neuromuscular training, which improves landing technique and knee control, reduces ACL injury risk. ✍️ Using the term in context

Anterior Pelvic Tilt — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anterior Pelvic Tilt BTEC General Anterior Pelvic Tilt A common postural pattern where the pelvis tips forward and the lower back arches. 📖 What it means Anterior pelvic tilt is a postural deviation in which the front of the pelvis rotates downwards and the back rotates upwards. This increases the lumbar curve, or lordosis, and often accompanies tight hip flexors and weak glutes and abdominal muscles.

It is common in people who sit for long periods. Over time, it can contribute to lower back pain and altered movement patterns. Exercise programmes often include hip flexor stretches and glute and core strengthening to address it. 🏅 Sporting examples Office workers A client who sits for many hours shows an anterior pelvic tilt with tight hip flexors. Anthropometry — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anthropometry IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Anthropometry The measurement of the body — the size, shape and composition data used to match athletes to sports and monitor change. 📖 What it means Anthropometry is the measurement of the size, shape, proportions and composition of the human body . Anticipation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anticipation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Anticipation Predicting events before they happen. 📖 What it means Anticipation is the ability to predict an event and prepare the response before it happens. It shortens reaction time and is a key part of expert performance. Spatial anticipation predicts what will happen (for example, where the ball will go), while temporal anticipation predicts when it will happen. Experts use cues from the opponent's posture and movement.

Anticipation improves with experience, practice and video-based training , and it is used to reduce the effect of the psychological refractory period. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis A returner reads the server's toss to predict the direction. Anticipatory Rise — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anticipatory Rise IB Sport Science General Anticipatory Rise The heart getting a head start — the pre-exercise jump in heart rate driven by nerves and hormones. 📖 What it means The anticipatory rise is the increase in heart rate that occurs before exercise actually begins . The heart starts to speed up in anticipation of the activity to come. It is caused by activation of the sympathetic nervous system and the release of adrenaline , often triggered by the psychological arousal of preparing to compete or train. It is a genuine, measurable rise above resting heart rate.

The anticipatory rise is a useful readiness response : it means the cardiovascular system is already elevated and primed at the moment exercise starts, so oxygen delivery can respond more quickly to the sudden demand. 🏅 Sporting examples On the blocks A sprinter's heart rate climbs on the starting blocks, before the gun — the anticipatory rise, driven by adrenaline. Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) The hormone that helps the body hold on to water. 📖 What it means Antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also called vasopressin) is released from the posterior pituitary when the body is dehydrated or the blood is concentrated. Antioxidants — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Antioxidants IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Antioxidants Compounds that protect cells from free radical damage. 📖 What it means Antioxidants are molecules that neutralise free radicals . They include vitamins C and E , beta-carotene, selenium and many plant compounds, and the body also makes its own antioxidant enzymes. Exercise increases free radical production. A diet rich in fruit and vegetables provides antioxidants naturally. High-dose antioxidant supplements are not recommended for most athletes: some research suggests they may blunt training adaptations . 🏅 Sporting examples Diet

An athlete eats berries, leafy greens and nuts as sources of antioxidants. Supplements High-dose vitamin C and E supplements may reduce some of the benefits of training. Recovery Tart cherry juice is a popular antioxidant-rich drink used by athletes. ✍️ Using the term in context Say what they do and the caution: "Antioxidants neutralise free radicals produced during exercise, but high-dose supplements may blunt training adaptations, so food sources are preferred." Common approaches include controlled breathing, progressive relaxation, imagery, positive self-talk and routines that help the performer feel prepared. Techniques work best when practised in training, not only before competition. A performer who has rehearsed a breathing routine many times is more likely to use it under pressure. 🏅 Sporting examples Penalty kicks

A footballer uses a set routine of breathing and a short cue word before each penalty to control nerves. Swimming A swimmer uses imagery of a smooth race to reduce pre-race anxiety. Team sport A coach introduces a team pre-match routine to help players feel calm and focused. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe an anxiety management routine for a performer before a competition: "Before competition, the performer uses controlled breathing and a positive self-talk cue to lower physical arousal and focus attention on the first task." Anxiety — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Anxiety IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Anxiety The negative emotional response that can wreck performance under pressure — and a concept students must be able to break into its cognitive and somatic parts. 📖 What it means Anxiety is a negative emotional state marked by worry, apprehension and heightened physiological arousal, often experienced before or during competition. It is closely linked to arousal, but is specifically the negative interpretation of that heightened state.

Anxiety has two components. Cognitive anxiety is the mental element — worry, negative thoughts and fear of failure. Somatic anxiety is the physical element — a racing heart, sweaty palms, tension and butterflies. Anxiety can also be viewed as a stable trait (a general tendency to feel anxious) or a temporary state (anxiety in a specific situation). Managing it uses techniques such as relaxation, imagery and self-talk. 🏅 Sporting examples Penalty taking A footballer facing a decisive penalty may experience cognitive anxiety (fear of missing) and somatic anxiety (a pounding heart), which can disrupt technique. Gymnastics

Before a beam routine, a gymnast's somatic anxiety might show as trembling, while cognitive anxiety appears as doubt about a difficult skill. Management An athlete uses progressive muscle relaxation to reduce somatic anxiety and positive self-talk to counter cognitive anxiety before competing. ✍️ Using the term in context Always split anxiety into its cognitive and somatic components: "Anxiety comprises cognitive anxiety, the mental worry and negative thoughts, and somatic anxiety, the physical symptoms such as increased heart rate; both can impair performance if not managed." Distinguish trait anxiety (a stable tendency) from state anxiety (situation-specific). 🔗 Related terms

Aorta — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aorta IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Aorta The body's main highway for oxygenated blood — the largest artery, carrying blood from the heart to the whole body. 📖 What it means The aorta is the largest artery in the body . It carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle out to the systemic circulation, branching into smaller arteries that supply the tissues.

Because it receives blood directly from the powerful left ventricle, the aorta withstands high pressure . Like all arteries, it has thick, elastic, muscular walls that stretch and recoil with each heartbeat, helping to maintain blood flow and smooth out the pressure. The aorta is the starting point of the systemic circuit — the route that delivers oxygen and nutrients to the body's tissues before blood returns, deoxygenated, to the heart. 🏅 Sporting examples Systemic circulation Oxygenated blood leaves the left ventricle through the aorta to begin its journey to the body's tissues. Withstanding pressure

The aorta's thick, elastic walls cope with the high pressure generated by the left ventricle's contraction. During exercise As cardiac output rises during exercise, a greater volume of blood is ejected into the aorta each minute. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the aorta's role and the blood it carries: "The aorta is the largest artery, carrying oxygenated blood from the left ventricle into the systemic circulation; its thick, elastic walls withstand the high pressure generated by the ventricle." Keep it clear that the aorta carries oxygenated blood (a common point of confusion). 🔗 Related terms Artery Left Ventricle Systemic Circulation Vena Cava Blood Pressure Cardiac Output

Aortic Valve — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aortic Valve IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Aortic Valve The valve that lets oxygenated blood out of the heart into the body. 📖 What it means The aortic valve is one of the four heart valves. It is a semilunar valve located at the exit of the left ventricle, where it opens to let oxygenated blood pass into the aorta and closes to stop it flowing back during diastole. Valve function matters for performance. A healthy aortic valve allows an efficient stroke volume, while a narrowed or leaky valve increases the workload on the left ventricle and can limit exercise tolerance. 🏅 Sporting examples

Stroke volume Each contraction of the left ventricle opens the aortic valve to eject the stroke volume into the aorta. Heart murmurs A clinician may detect a murmur through the aortic valve if blood flows abnormally, which can limit endurance and need investigation. Athlete screening Pre-participation screening may include listening to the heart for valve abnormalities. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the role of the aortic valve during exercise: "The aortic valve opens as the left ventricle contracts, allowing the stroke volume to enter the aorta, and closes during diastole to prevent backflow into the heart." Apathy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Apathy BTEC General Apathy A loss of drive or interest that can quietly undermine training and performance. 📖 What it means Apathy is a lack of interest, enthusiasm or motivation. In sport, a performer may stop caring about training, show little emotion about results or seem unwilling to make effort, even when they are physically able. Apathy can be a sign of burnout, overtraining, low mood or depression. Coaches should look at the cause rather than simply pushing the athlete harder, and a medical or psychological referral may be needed if low mood persists. 🏅 Sporting examples Burnout

A player who has trained hard for a long season may show apathy, with reduced effort and enjoyment. Mood A performer whose apathy continues for weeks may have a mood disorder that needs professional support. Team culture A squad with low expectations can develop apathy that spreads across the group. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe how a coach might respond to apathy in an athlete: "Rather than increasing the training load, the coach talks to the athlete about possible causes such as fatigue or stress, adjusts the programme and refers them if low mood persists." Aponeurosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aponeurosis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Aponeurosis The broad, flat tendon that spreads the pull of a muscle across a wide area. 📖 What it means An aponeurosis is a flattened sheet of dense connective tissue that acts like a broad tendon. It attaches a muscle to bone or to another muscle, and it spreads the force of contraction over a wider area than a rounded tendon would.

Examples include the aponeurosis of the abdominal muscles, which forms the linea alba, and the palmar aponeurosis in the hand. Aponeuroses store and transmit force efficiently, and they are important in muscles that work over broad areas. 🏅 Sporting examples Core The aponeurosis of the abdominal muscles transmits force across the trunk during twisting and flexion. Hand The palmar aponeurosis helps the grip by spreading force across the hand. Injury Strains of the aponeurosis can be painful and slow to heal, because the tissue has limited blood supply. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why an aponeurosis is useful in a broad muscle:

Different apoproteins define different lipoproteins, such as high-density (HDL) and low-density (LDL) lipoproteins. Their balance matters for cardiovascular health, which is relevant to endurance training and general health advice. 🏅 Sporting examples Cholesterol Apoprotein A-I is the main protein of HDL, which carries cholesterol away from the tissues. Appendicular Skeleton — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Appendicular Skeleton IB Sport Science General Appendicular Skeleton The part of the skeleton that lets you move — the limbs and the girdles that attach them to the body. 📖 What it means The appendicular skeleton is the part of the skeleton that includes the limbs and the girdles that attach them to the body — the arms and legs, the shoulder (pectoral) girdle and the pelvic girdle. It is distinguished from the axial skeleton (the central core: skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs). Together the two make up the complete skeleton.

The appendicular skeleton is central to movement : it provides the levers (the limb bones) that muscles pull on to produce the actions used in sport, and its joints allow the wide range of movement performers rely on. 🏅 Sporting examples Producing movement The bones of the arms and legs — part of the appendicular skeleton — act as levers for the muscles during throwing and running. Girdles The pelvic girdle, part of the appendicular skeleton, anchors the legs and transmits force during running and jumping. Contrast The appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles) is distinct from the axial skeleton (skull, spine, ribs). ✍️ Using the term in context

Aqua Running — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Aqua Running BTEC Sport General Aqua Running Running in water to keep fit without impact. 📖 What it means Aqua running (deep water running) is performed in the deep end of a pool, usually with a flotation belt , so that the feet do not touch the bottom. The athlete mimics the running action against the resistance of the water. Because the body is supported, there is almost no impact on the joints and bones . Heart rate for a given effort is lower in water, so it is normal to use perceived effort or adjusted heart rate zones to set the intensity.

It is widely used by runners to maintain aerobic fitness while injured and as a low-impact recovery session. Studies suggest well-trained runners can keep their fitness for several weeks using it. 🏅 Sporting examples Injured runner Aqua running replaces road sessions during a stress fracture recovery. Recovery A gentle session the day after a hard race. Interval work Hard and easy intervals in the pool. ✍️ Using the term in context Say why it is used: "Aqua running allows athletes to maintain cardiovascular fitness while avoiding the impact forces of land running." Mention that heart rate is typically lower in water, so use effort levels as well. 🔗 Related terms

Arousal Regulation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Arousal Regulation BTEC General Arousal Regulation Adjusting how activated you are so you perform at the right level for the task. 📖 What it means Arousal regulation is the use of techniques to move a performer's arousal towards the level that suits the task. Low arousal can be raised with activation methods such as music or self-talk, while high arousal can be lowered with breathing control or relaxation.

The optimal level differs by task. Fine, precise skills, such as archery or putting, usually need lower arousal, while strong, simple skills, such as a sprint, may benefit from higher arousal. Regulation works best when practised in training. 🏅 Sporting examples Archery An archer uses slow breathing to lower arousal before each shot. Sprinting A sprinter uses a bouncing routine and music to raise arousal before the start. Penalty taking A footballer uses a set routine to settle arousal and focus before a penalty. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe an arousal regulation strategy for a performer who is over-aroused:

Arousal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Arousal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Arousal The engine of readiness — the level of physiological and psychological activation that can make or break a performance, depending on how much of it there is. 📖 What it means Arousal is a state of physiological and psychological activation and alertness , ranging from deep sleep to intense excitement. In sport it describes how 'switched on' and energised a performer is.

Unlike anxiety, arousal is neutral — it is neither good nor bad in itself. Its effect on performance depends on how much there is and the type of task : too little and the performer is flat; too much and technique breaks down. Several theories describe this relationship, including drive theory (performance rises with arousal), the inverted-U hypothesis (an optimal mid-point), and catastrophe theory (a sudden drop-off when arousal is too high alongside cognitive anxiety). 🏅 Sporting examples Weightlifting A powerlifter deliberately raises arousal ('psyching up') before a maximal lift, because the simple, gross-motor task benefits from high activation. Golf putting

A golfer needs lower arousal for a delicate putt, as too much activation causes trembling and disrupts the fine motor control required. Optimal point A netball centre performs best at a moderate arousal level — alert and energised, but still able to make accurate decisions and passes. ✍️ Using the term in context Link arousal to task type and to a named theory: "According to the inverted-U hypothesis, performance improves as arousal increases up to an optimal point, beyond which it declines; the optimal level is higher for gross, simple skills than for fine, complex ones." Keep arousal (neutral activation) distinct from anxiety (a negative emotional state). 🔗 Related terms

Arteriole — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Arteriole IB Sport Science General Arteriole The body's traffic controllers — small vessels that fine-tune where blood flows during exercise. 📖 What it means An arteriole is a small blood vessel that branches from an artery and leads to the capillary beds. Arterioles are the key site for controlling how blood is distributed around the body. Their walls contain smooth muscle that can contract ( vasoconstriction ) or relax ( vasodilation ), narrowing or widening the vessel. This adjusts the resistance to flow and therefore how much blood passes into the capillaries beyond.

Arterioles are central to the vascular shunt mechanism during exercise: those supplying the working muscles vasodilate to increase flow, while those supplying inactive areas vasoconstrict to reduce it — redistributing blood to where it is needed. 🏅 Sporting examples Vascular shunt During exercise, arterioles feeding the muscles vasodilate while those feeding the gut vasoconstrict, redirecting blood to the muscles. Thermoregulation Arterioles in the skin vasodilate to increase blood flow and heat loss when the body overheats during exercise. Blood pressure By adjusting their diameter, arterioles influence resistance to flow and therefore blood pressure. ✍️ Using the term in context

Describe arterioles and their role in blood distribution: "Arterioles are small vessels branching from arteries whose smooth muscle walls vasodilate or vasoconstrict to control blood flow into the capillaries; they are central to the vascular shunt that redistributes blood during exercise." Arteriosclerosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Arteriosclerosis BTEC General Arteriosclerosis The stiffening of artery walls that makes it harder for blood to flow. 📖 What it means Arteriosclerosis is a general term for the thickening and hardening of artery walls. The arteries lose their elasticity, which raises blood pressure and makes the heart work harder to pump blood around the body. Arteriosclerosis is linked to ageing, high blood pressure, smoking, a poor diet and inactivity. Regular aerobic exercise helps keep arteries more elastic and supports healthy blood pressure. 🏅 Sporting examples Blood pressure

Stiffer arteries raise systolic blood pressure, increasing the afterload on the heart. Training benefits Regular endurance training helps maintain arterial elasticity, which supports healthy circulation. Risk factors A sedentary client with high blood pressure should be screened for arteriosclerosis before starting intense training. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why regular aerobic exercise helps arterial health: "Regular aerobic exercise helps keep artery walls elastic and lowers blood pressure, which reduces the strain of arteriosclerosis on the heart." Arteriovenous Oxygen Difference — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Arteriovenous Oxygen Difference IB Sport Science General Arteriovenous Oxygen Difference A measure of how greedily the muscles extract oxygen — the gap between what arteries deliver and veins return. 📖 What it means The arteriovenous oxygen difference (a-vO₂ diff) is the difference in oxygen content between the arterial blood arriving at the muscles and the venous blood leaving them . It reflects how much oxygen the tissues have extracted and used.

During exercise, the working muscles extract more oxygen from the blood, so the venous blood leaving them contains less — widening the arteriovenous oxygen difference . A larger difference means more efficient oxygen extraction and use. It is one of the factors that determines oxygen uptake (and therefore VO₂ max), alongside cardiac output. Endurance training increases the a-vO₂ difference through adaptations such as greater capillary and mitochondrial density, improving the muscles' ability to extract and use oxygen. 🏅 Sporting examples During exercise As exercise intensifies, the muscles extract more oxygen, widening the arteriovenous oxygen difference. Training adaptation

Endurance training increases the a-vO₂ difference by improving capillary and mitochondrial density in the muscles. VO2 max A greater a-vO₂ difference, alongside a higher cardiac output, contributes to a higher VO₂ max. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the a-vO₂ difference and its meaning: "The arteriovenous oxygen difference is the difference in oxygen content between arterial and venous blood, reflecting oxygen extraction by the tissues; it widens during exercise and is increased by endurance training, contributing to a higher VO₂ max." Artery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Artery IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Artery The high-pressure vessels that carry blood away from the heart — built strong and elastic to cope. 📖 What it means An artery is a blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart to the body's tissues. Most arteries carry oxygenated blood (the pulmonary artery, carrying deoxygenated blood to the lungs, is the exception). Arteries have thick, muscular and elastic walls to withstand and smooth out the high pressure of blood leaving the heart. Their elasticity lets them stretch as blood is ejected and recoil between beats, helping to maintain a steady flow.

Arteries branch into smaller arterioles and then capillaries , where exchange with the tissues occurs. As part of the vascular system, arteries and arterioles help control blood distribution and pressure. 🏅 Sporting examples Withstanding pressure An artery's thick, elastic walls cope with the surge of high-pressure blood each time the heart contracts. Articular Capsule — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Articular Capsule IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Articular Capsule The outer covering of a joint that keeps the bones in place and contains the synovial fluid. 📖 What it means The articular capsule is a sleeve of fibrous tissue that surrounds a synovial joint. Its outer layer is fibrous and strong, and its inner layer, the synovial membrane, produces synovial fluid that lubricates the joint. The capsule helps stabilise the joint, especially when combined with ligaments. A stretched or torn capsule can cause instability, which is common in shoulder injuries. 🏅 Sporting examples Shoulder

The articular capsule of the shoulder is loose, allowing wide movement, but it can be stretched in dislocations. Knee The capsule of the knee works with the ligaments to limit unwanted movement. Joint injury A joint effusion can cause the capsule to swell, which restricts movement and causes pain. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the role of the articular capsule in a synovial joint: "The articular capsule encloses the joint and holds the bones together, while the synovial membrane inside it produces fluid that lubricates the surfaces." Articular Cartilage — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Articular Cartilage IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Articular Cartilage The joint's shock absorber — smooth cartilage that lets bones glide and cushions every landing. 📖 What it means Articular cartilage is the smooth hyaline cartilage that covers the ends of bones where they meet at a synovial joint. It is one of the defining features of a freely movable joint. It performs two key functions: it reduces friction , allowing the bone ends to glide smoothly over one another, and it absorbs shock , cushioning the joint against the impact forces of running, jumping and landing.

Articular cartilage works alongside the other features of a synovial joint — synovial fluid, the joint capsule and ligaments — to allow smooth, protected movement. Damage to it (through injury or wear) can impair joint function. 🏅 Sporting examples Cushioning impact Articular cartilage in the knee absorbs the impact forces each time a runner's foot strikes the ground. Smooth movement The cartilage covering the bone ends lets the shoulder joint move smoothly through its wide range. Joint health Wear of articular cartilage over time can reduce its cushioning, affecting joint movement and comfort. ✍️ Using the term in context State where articular cartilage is found and its functions:

Assertion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Assertion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Assertion Forceful, competitive but fair play — the rule-abiding counterpart to aggression, with no intent to harm. 📖 What it means Assertion is forceful, competitive behaviour that stays within the rules of the sport and carries no intention to harm another person. It is legitimate, committed play — sometimes called 'assertive behaviour'.

It is the key contrast to aggression , which involves the intention to harm and breaks the rules. An assertive performer plays hard, competes strongly and may use legitimate physical force, but always within the laws of the game and without seeking to injure. The distinction matters because assertion is desirable and effective, whereas aggression is not . Coaches aim to channel a performer's competitive drive and arousal into assertive rather than aggressive behaviour, reinforcing hard but fair play. 🏅 Sporting examples Fair, forceful play A strong, legal shoulder-to-shoulder challenge for the ball is assertion — committed and physical, but within the rules and without intent to harm.

Competing hard A boxer boxing skilfully and forcefully within the rules is being assertive, not aggressive. Associative Stage of Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Associative Stage of Learning AS Level / Cambridge General Associative Stage of Learning The practice stage — the middle phase of learning where a skill is refined and errors gradually reduce. 📖 What it means The associative stage is the second of Fitts and Posner's three stages of learning . It is the practice phase, in which the learner has grasped the basics and now refines the skill through repeated practice .

Performance in this stage becomes more consistent and fluent , with fewer and smaller errors than in the cognitive stage. The performer relies less on conscious thought and begins to use their own intrinsic feedback to detect and correct errors, though they still benefit from external guidance. This is often the longest stage , and some performers remain in it and never reach the autonomous stage. Coaching focuses on refining technique and providing more detailed feedback (knowledge of performance) as the learner develops. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis A club-level player who serves fairly consistently but is still ironing out flaws in their technique is in the associative stage. Swimming

A learner who can complete a stroke reasonably well and is now refining timing and efficiency is in the associative stage. Coaching A coach gives associative-stage learners more detailed feedback on technique (knowledge of performance) to refine the skill. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the stage's characteristics and coaching: "In the associative stage, the second of Fitts and Posner's stages, the learner refines the skill through practice; performance becomes more consistent, errors reduce, and the performer begins using intrinsic feedback, aided by detailed knowledge of performance." Astrand Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Astrand Test General BTEC Sport Astrand Test A practical, submaximal way to estimate aerobic fitness — predicting VO₂ max from how the heart responds to cycling. 📖 What it means The Astrand Test is a submaximal cycle ergometer test that predicts VO₂ max from the heart rate response to a fixed workload. Because it is submaximal, the performer does not have to exercise to exhaustion.

The athlete cycles at a set resistance for a set time (typically six minutes), and their steady-state heart rate is recorded. Since heart rate and oxygen uptake rise together, a lower heart rate at the same workload indicates greater aerobic fitness , and VO₂ max is estimated from the result using standard tables or equations. As a submaximal test, it is safer and more practical than a maximal test, making it suitable for a wider range of people. However, it gives an estimate rather than a direct measure , and its accuracy depends on factors such as a stable heart rate and standardised conditions. 🏅 Sporting examples Estimating fitness

A performer cycles at a fixed resistance for six minutes; their steady-state heart rate is used to estimate VO₂ max. Submaximal advantage Because the Astrand Test is submaximal, it can be used with people for whom a maximal test would be unsuitable. Interpreting results A lower heart rate at the same workload indicates a higher predicted VO₂ max and better aerobic fitness. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and evaluate it: "The Astrand Test is a submaximal cycle ergometer test that predicts VO₂ max from the steady-state heart rate response to a fixed workload; it is safer and more practical than a maximal test but gives only an estimate."

Asymmetrical Movement — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Asymmetrical Movement BTEC General Asymmetrical Movement Movement in which the left and right sides of the body work differently. 📖 What it means An asymmetrical movement is one in which the two sides of the body perform different actions. Many sporting actions are asymmetrical, such as a tennis forehand, a one-arm throw or a single-leg kick. Asymmetry can create imbalances if one side is consistently stronger or more mobile. Coaches address this by including unilateral exercises and balanced training, which reduce the risk of injury caused by imbalance. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis

A forehand uses the dominant side strongly and the non-dominant side for balance, an asymmetrical pattern. Atherosclerosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Atherosclerosis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Atherosclerosis The build-up of fatty plaque inside arteries, which narrows them and restricts blood flow. 📖 What it means Atherosclerosis is a disease in which fatty deposits, or plaques, build up in the inner lining of arteries. The plaques narrow the artery, reduce blood flow and can rupture, forming a clot that blocks the vessel. Risk factors include high LDL cholesterol, high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and inactivity. Athlete Profiling — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Athlete Profiling General BTEC Sport Athlete Profiling Building a complete picture of a performer — the systematic assessment behind targeted training and talent decisions. 📖 What it means Athlete profiling is the systematic assessment of an athlete's physical, technical, tactical and psychological characteristics . A profile typically combines fitness testing (physical qualities), analysis of technical and tactical skills , and assessment of psychological attributes . The data is often compared against the demands of the sport or against normative benchmarks. Profiling is used to identify training needs, monitor progress, support talent identification and inform selection . By highlighting specific weaknesses, it allows training to be targeted and individualised rather than generic. 🏅 Sporting examples Targeting training An athlete's profile reveals that power is a relative weakness, so their programme prioritises explosive strength work. Athletic Identity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Athletic Identity BTEC General Athletic Identity How strongly an athlete's sense of who they are depends on being an athlete. 📖 What it means Athletic identity is the degree to which a person defines themselves as an athlete. A strong athletic identity can motivate training, but it can also make it hard to cope with injury, retirement or a loss of form. Athletes with a very strong identity may feel their worth depends entirely on performance. Supporting athletes to develop a balanced sense of self, with interests and relationships beyond sport, helps protect wellbeing. 🏅 Sporting examples Injury

An athlete whose identity is built on sport may struggle emotionally during a long injury. Retirement A former player who defined themselves only as a player may find the transition hard. ATP-PC System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › ATP-PC System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General ATP-PC System The body's instant-power system — the fastest energy pathway, fuelling the most explosive efforts for a few seconds. 📖 What it means The ATP-PC system (also called the alactic or phosphocreatine system) resynthesises ATP using phosphocreatine (PC), without oxygen and without producing lactate . It is the fastest energy system, providing energy almost instantly.

It dominates maximal, explosive efforts lasting up to about 8–10 seconds , because the muscle's stores of phosphocreatine are very limited. Phosphocreatine donates its phosphate to ADP to rapidly rebuild ATP. Its advantages are its speed and the absence of fatiguing by-products ; its limitation is its very short duration . Stores are replenished quickly during recovery (largely within a few minutes), allowing the system to be reused across a session. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A 100m sprint is fuelled predominantly by the ATP-PC system, providing near-instant energy for the maximal effort. Weightlifting

A single maximal lift draws on the ATP-PC system to resynthesise ATP explosively for the brief contraction. Repeated efforts Because phosphocreatine replenishes quickly, a footballer can repeat short sprints with adequate recovery between them. ✍️ Using the term in context State the fuel, duration, speed and by-products: "The ATP-PC system resynthesises ATP rapidly using phosphocreatine, without oxygen or lactate, dominating maximal efforts of up to around 8–10 seconds; it is the fastest system but very limited in duration, with stores replenished quickly during recovery." Position it as the dominant system at the explosive end of the energy continuum. 🔗 Related terms

Atrial Fibrillation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Atrial Fibrillation IB Sport Science General Atrial Fibrillation A common irregular heart rhythm — where the atria quiver chaotically instead of beating in time. 📖 What it means Atrial fibrillation is a type of irregular heart rhythm (arrhythmia) in which the atria beat chaotically and out of synchrony with the ventricles, rather than in a coordinated way. Instead of the organised impulse from the SA node driving a regular beat, disorganised electrical activity causes the atria to quiver . This makes the heartbeat irregular and often rapid, and reduces the efficiency with which the atria fill the ventricles.

In a sport and health context, atrial fibrillation is relevant to cardiovascular health and screening . It can reduce exercise capacity and, because it affects blood flow, carries health risks. Any suspected irregular rhythm warrants medical assessment. 🏅 Sporting examples Irregular rhythm In atrial fibrillation, the atria quiver out of time with the ventricles, producing an irregular, often rapid heartbeat. Reduced efficiency Because the atria do not contract effectively, they fill the ventricles less efficiently, which can reduce exercise capacity. Screening Cardiac screening of athletes can detect rhythm abnormalities such as atrial fibrillation, prompting medical follow-up.

✍️ Using the term in context Define atrial fibrillation as an irregular rhythm: "Atrial fibrillation is an irregular heart rhythm in which the atria beat chaotically and out of synchrony with the ventricles, producing an irregular, often rapid heartbeat and reducing the efficiency of ventricular filling." Atrioventricular Node (AVN) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Atrioventricular Node (AVN) IB Sport Science General Atrioventricular Node (AVN) The heart's relay and timekeeper — it delays the electrical impulse so the chambers pump in the right order. 📖 What it means The atrioventricular node (AVN) is part of the heart's electrical conduction system . It acts as a relay between the atria and the ventricles. When the impulse from the SA node reaches the AVN, the AVN briefly delays it . This delay is functionally important: it allows the atria to finish contracting and fully empty their blood into the ventricles before the ventricles contract .

From the AVN, the impulse passes down the bundle of His and through the Purkinje fibres , spreading through the ventricle walls and causing them to contract. The AVN's timing role is essential to the coordinated, efficient pumping of the heart. 🏅 Sporting examples Coordinated pumping The AVN's delay ensures the atria empty into the ventricles before the ventricles contract, making each beat efficient. Conduction pathway The impulse travels SA node → AVN → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres, coordinating the heartbeat. Myogenic control As part of the conduction system, the AVN helps the heart generate and coordinate its own beat (myogenic). ✍️ Using the term in context

State the AVN's role and why its delay matters: "The atrioventricular node relays the electrical impulse from the atria to the ventricles and briefly delays it, allowing the atria to finish emptying into the ventricles before the ventricles contract." Atrioventricular Valves — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Atrioventricular Valves IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Atrioventricular Valves The valves that stop blood flowing back from the ventricles into the atria. 📖 What it means The atrioventricular valves sit between the atria and the ventricles. The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart, and the bicuspid (mitral) valve is on the left. They open during diastole to let blood fill the ventricles and close during ventricular systole to prevent backflow.

The valves are held in place by chordae tendineae, which stop them from being pushed back into the atria. Healthy AV valves allow blood to flow efficiently through the heart during both rest and exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Filling The AV valves open during diastole to let blood move from the atria into the ventricles. Closure The AV valves close at the start of ventricular systole, producing the first heart sound. Valve disease A leaking mitral valve can reduce the efficiency of each beat, which limits aerobic capacity. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how the AV valves prevent backflow:

Atrium — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Atrium IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Atrium The upper chamber of the heart that collects blood before it moves into the ventricles. 📖 What it means The atria are the two upper chambers of the heart. The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the body through the vena cava, and the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs through the pulmonary veins. Each atrium contracts briefly to push blood into the ventricle below.

Atrial contraction adds a little extra blood to the ventricles at the end of diastole. The atria have thinner walls than the ventricles because they only need to push blood a short distance. 🏅 Sporting examples Venous return The right atrium receives blood from the body, which is essential for maintaining stroke volume during exercise. Atrophy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Atrophy IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Atrophy The wasting of muscle when it isn't used — the reverse of hypertrophy, and a consequence of the reversibility principle. 📖 What it means Atrophy is the wasting or reduction in size of muscle that occurs when it is not used, or is used much less than usual. It is the opposite of hypertrophy (muscle growth). It happens through disuse or detraining — for example during injury, illness, immobilisation (such as a limb in a cast) or a period without training. The muscle loses contractile protein, becoming smaller and weaker.

Atrophy is a direct consequence of the principle of reversibility ('use it or lose it'): the adaptations gained from training are lost when the stimulus is removed. It highlights the importance of maintaining training, and of rehabilitation to rebuild muscle after injury. 🏅 Sporting examples Injury layoff A limb immobilised in a cast after injury shows visible muscle atrophy, having lost size and strength through disuse. Detraining An athlete who stops training over a long off-season experiences some muscle atrophy, reversing earlier gains. Rehabilitation After injury, a structured rehabilitation programme rebuilds atrophied muscle through progressive resistance training.

✍️ Using the term in context Define atrophy and link it to reversibility: "Atrophy is the wasting of muscle through disuse or detraining, the opposite of hypertrophy; it is a consequence of the principle of reversibility, and highlights the need to maintain training and to rehabilitate muscle after injury." Attention Deficit — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Attention Deficit BTEC General Attention Deficit Difficulty keeping focus on the cues that matter, which can affect performance and learning. 📖 What it means In sport, an attention deficit describes a reduced ability to focus on relevant cues for a sustained period, especially under pressure. Attentional Focus — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Attentional Focus IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Attentional Focus Directing attention to the right things at the right time — a key mental skill that can make or break performance. 📖 What it means Attentional focus is the ability to direct and concentrate attention appropriately during performance — attending to the relevant cues while ignoring distractions. It is a crucial mental skill.

A widely used model describes attention along two dimensions: width (broad vs narrow) and direction (external vs internal). This gives four styles — for example, broad-external (reading a whole game situation), narrow-external (focusing on a single target), broad-internal (planning tactics), and narrow-internal (focusing on a feeling or cue). Skilled performers shift their attentional focus to match the demands of the moment, and use techniques such as cue words and pre-performance routines to maintain the right focus, particularly under pressure when attention can narrow or be captured by distractions. 🏅 Sporting examples Broad-external

A quarterback or playmaker uses a broad-external focus to read the whole field before deciding where to pass. Narrow-external A golfer putting narrows their focus to the ball and the line — a narrow-external focus on a single target. Shifting focus A skilled performer switches between broad and narrow focus as the situation changes, using cue words to stay on task. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the width and direction dimensions and shifting focus:

"Attentional focus is the ability to direct concentration appropriately; it varies in width (broad–narrow) and direction (external–internal), and skilled performers shift focus to match the situation, using cue words and routines to maintain it under pressure." Attentional Narrowing — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Attentional Narrowing IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Attentional Narrowing When high arousal shrinks your focus. 📖 What it means Attentional narrowing is the reduction in the range of cues a performer notices as arousal rises . Easterbrook's cue utilisation theory says that at low arousal, attention is broad and includes irrelevant cues; at optimal arousal it narrows to the relevant cues; at very high arousal it becomes too narrow and important cues are missed. This helps explain why over-aroused performers make poor decisions, such as a player who does not see an open teammate.

Coaches use arousal control techniques and practice under pressure to keep attention at the right width. 🏅 Sporting examples Football A nervous player fails to see an unmarked team-mate. Optimal arousal A golfer focuses on the key cues for the putt. Pressure practice Drills in noisy conditions build resilience. ✍️ Using the term in context Link arousal to attention: "At very high arousal, attention narrows too far and a performer may miss relevant cues, which impairs decision making." Attitudinal Body Image — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Attitudinal Body Image BTEC General Attitudinal Body Image How a person thinks and feels about their own body. 📖 What it means Attitudinal body image is the set of thoughts, feelings and attitudes a person holds about their own body. It includes body satisfaction, how much the person values their appearance and how much their self-worth depends on their shape or weight.

Attitudinal body image is linked to wellbeing and to disordered eating. In sport, pressure to achieve a particular shape can damage an athlete's attitudes towards their body. Coaches can support healthy attitudes by focusing on performance rather than appearance. 🏅 Sporting examples Judged sports A gymnast who feels their worth depends on their weight may develop a negative attitudinal body image. Team sport Positive feedback focused on skills rather than appearance supports a healthier body image. Wellbeing A coach who notices negative comments about the body should respond supportively and consider referral. ✍️ Using the term in context

Attribution Retraining — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Attribution Retraining BTEC General Attribution Retraining Teaching a performer to explain results in ways that keep motivation high. 📖 What it means Attribution retraining helps performers change how they explain their results. Performers who attribute failure to a stable, uncontrollable cause, such as lack of ability, tend to lose motivation. Retraining encourages them to attribute failure to changeable causes such as effort or strategy.

Attribution retraining works best when the performer practises new explanations after every session. Coaches can model the language and ask performers to identify what they can change next time. 🏅 Sporting examples Losing a match Instead of saying "I'm just not good enough", a player is encouraged to say "I need to improve my timing on the serve". Coaching feedback A coach asks a player to explain a mistake in terms of what they can control. Youth sport A young athlete who believes effort leads to improvement is more likely to keep practising. ✍️ Using the term in context Give an example of attribution retraining after a defeat:

"Rather than attributing the defeat to a lack of talent, the athlete identifies a controllable cause, such as their preparation, and sets a plan to change it." Attribution Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Attribution Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Attribution Theory How athletes explain their wins and losses — and why those explanations shape future motivation and confidence. 📖 What it means Attribution theory examines the reasons performers give for their successes and failures . The explanations they choose strongly influence their future motivation, confidence and persistence.

Attributions are commonly classified on two dimensions. The locus of causality asks whether the cause is internal (e.g. ability, effort) or external (e.g. luck, opponent difficulty). The stability dimension asks whether the cause is stable (unlikely to change, e.g. ability) or unstable (changeable, e.g. effort). The way athletes attribute outcomes matters because attributing failure to stable, internal, uncontrollable factors can lead to learned helplessness , while attributing it to unstable, controllable factors such as effort protects motivation. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis

A player who loses and blames a lack of effort (internal, unstable, controllable) is more likely to stay motivated than one who blames a lack of talent (internal, stable). Team sport A coach encourages players to attribute a defeat to correctable factors such as tactics or preparation, protecting confidence for the next game. Avoiding helplessness Reattributing repeated failure from 'I'm just not good enough' to 'I didn't train hard enough' helps break a cycle of learned helplessness. ✍️ Using the term in context Use the locus and stability dimensions explicitly:

"Attributing failure to internal, unstable and controllable factors such as effort protects motivation, whereas attributing it to stable, uncontrollable factors such as ability can lead to learned helplessness." Augmented Feedback — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Augmented Feedback IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Augmented Feedback Feedback from outside the performer, such as a coach or a camera. 📖 What it means Augmented feedback is information given to the performer from an external source. It includes knowledge of results (the outcome) and knowledge of performance (how the movement was made), given by coaches, video, timing systems or other devices.

Augmented feedback is most useful when it is specific, timely and reduced over time. Beginners often need frequent augmented feedback, while experienced performers learn to rely on intrinsic feedback from their own senses. 🏅 Sporting examples Video A swimmer watches video of their stroke, which gives them knowledge of performance. Timing A sprinter's split times give knowledge of results after each training run. Autogenic Inhibition — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Autogenic Inhibition IB Sport Science General Autogenic Inhibition A built-in safety brake for muscles — a reflex that makes a muscle relax when tension gets dangerously high. 📖 What it means Autogenic inhibition is a protective reflex that causes a muscle to relax when the tension within it becomes very high . It helps prevent the muscle or tendon from being damaged by excessive force. It is mediated by the Golgi tendon organs — sensory receptors in the tendons that detect tension. When they sense dangerously high tension, they trigger a reflex that inhibits the contracting muscle, causing it to relax .

Autogenic inhibition is the basis of certain flexibility techniques, particularly PNF stretching : contracting a muscle before stretching it triggers autogenic inhibition, allowing the muscle to then relax and stretch further. 🏅 Sporting examples PNF stretching In PNF stretching, contracting a muscle before relaxing it triggers autogenic inhibition, allowing a greater stretch. Injury protection Autogenic inhibition can cause a muscle under extreme tension to relax, helping protect it from tearing. Golgi tendon organs The Golgi tendon organs detect high tension and trigger the reflex relaxation of the muscle. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define autogenic inhibition and name the receptor involved: "Autogenic inhibition is a protective reflex, mediated by the Golgi tendon organs, that causes a muscle to relax when tension becomes very high; it underpins PNF stretching, where a pre-contraction allows a greater subsequent stretch." Autonomic Nervous System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Autonomic Nervous System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Autonomic Nervous System The part of the nervous system that runs the body's automatic processes. 📖 What it means The autonomic nervous system controls involuntary functions. It has two divisions: the sympathetic system, which prepares the body for action by raising heart rate and breathing, and the parasympathetic system, which slows the body down and supports digestion and recovery.

During exercise, sympathetic activity increases, and during recovery, parasympathetic activity returns. Monitoring this balance, for example through resting heart rate variability, can help coaches judge how well an athlete is recovering. 🏅 Sporting examples Warm-up As exercise begins, the sympathetic system raises heart rate and breathing. Recovery After exercise, parasympathetic activity slows the heart rate back towards rest. Monitoring A coach tracks resting heart rate, which reflects parasympathetic activity, to judge fatigue. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how the autonomic nervous system responds to exercise:

Autonomous Stage of Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Autonomous Stage of Learning AS Level / Cambridge General Autonomous Stage of Learning The expert stage — where a skill becomes automatic, freeing the mind to focus on tactics and the game. 📖 What it means The autonomous stage is the third and final stage of Fitts and Posner's stages of learning . Here the skill has become largely automatic , performed with little conscious thought.

Because execution requires little attention, the performer can focus on other things — tactics, opponents, and the wider game situation — rather than on the mechanics of the skill. Performance is consistent, fluent and efficient , and the performer can detect and correct their own errors using intrinsic feedback. Reaching this stage requires extensive practice , and not all performers get there. Coaching focuses on maintaining the skill, fine-tuning through precise feedback, and developing tactical and psychological aspects ; practice must continue or the skill can regress. 🏅 Sporting examples Professional performer

An elite footballer controls the ball automatically while scanning for passing options — autonomous-stage execution freeing attention for tactics. Automatic skill A skilled touch-typist or a professional server performs the skill without conscious thought about the mechanics. Coaching A coach helps an autonomous-stage athlete fine-tune technique and develop tactical and psychological skills, while maintaining practice. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe automaticity and freed attention:

"In the autonomous stage, the final stage of Fitts and Posner's model, the skill is largely automatic, freeing the performer to focus on tactics and the game situation; performance is consistent and fluent, and the performer uses their own intrinsic feedback." Note that reaching it needs extensive practice and that the skill can regress without maintenance. 🔗 Related terms Cognitive Stage of Learning Associative Stage of Learning Fitts and Posner's Stages of Learning Motor Learning Attentional Focus Knowledge of Performance (KP) 🎓 Where this appears AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Avascular Necrosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Avascular Necrosis BTEC General Avascular Necrosis Bone tissue dying because its blood supply has been cut off. 📖 What it means Avascular necrosis is the death of bone tissue caused by an interruption of its blood supply. It can follow a fracture or dislocation that damages the vessels, and it can also occur without a clear injury, for example with some medications or conditions. Early avascular necrosis may cause little pain at first. Over time, the affected bone can collapse, causing severe pain and joint damage. Athletes who have had a serious bone or joint injury should be monitored for signs of it.

🏅 Sporting examples Hip injury A hip fracture that disrupts the blood supply to the femoral head can lead to avascular necrosis. Monitoring An athlete with persistent joint pain after a serious injury should be assessed for avascular necrosis. Prevention Careful rehabilitation after a fracture helps protect the blood supply to the bone. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why persistent pain after a hip fracture should be investigated: "Persistent pain after a hip fracture may indicate avascular necrosis, where a loss of blood supply has caused bone to die, so the athlete should be referred for medical assessment." Avulsion Fracture — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Avulsion Fracture BTEC General Avulsion Fracture A bone fracture caused by a strong pull from a tendon or ligament. 📖 What it means An avulsion fracture occurs when a tendon or ligament pulls a fragment of bone away from its attachment site. It usually results from a sudden, forceful contraction or a strong pull, rather than a direct blow. Avulsion fractures are common in young athletes, whose growth plates and tendon attachments are still developing. They are often seen at the pelvis, such as the anterior superior iliac spine, and at the knee. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting

A hamstring pull in a sprint can cause an avulsion fracture at the ischial tuberosity in a young athlete. Kicking A forceful kick can pull a small fragment of bone from the pelvis at the attachment of a muscle. Youth sport A young footballer with pelvic pain after a sprint should be assessed for an avulsion injury. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how an avulsion fracture happens in a sprinting injury: "A sudden forceful contraction of the hamstring can pull a fragment of bone away at its attachment, causing an avulsion fracture that needs medical assessment." Axes of Rotation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Axes of Rotation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Axes of Rotation The lines that the body spins around. 📖 What it means An axis of rotation is an imaginary line around which a body turns . There are three main axes in the body. The longitudinal axis runs from head to toe, and rotation around it gives twists and spins , such as a pirouette. The transverse (frontal) axis runs from side to side, and rotation around it gives somersaults and flips . The sagittal (antero-posterior) axis runs from front to back, giving cartwheels .

Each axis is at right angles to a plane of movement : movement in a plane happens around the axis perpendicular to it. Gymnasts and divers use these to describe and analyse skills. 🏅 Sporting examples Pirouette A rotation about the longitudinal axis. Somersault A rotation about the transverse axis. Cartwheel A rotation about the sagittal axis. ✍️ Using the term in context Match axis and skill: "A somersault is a rotation about the transverse axis, whereas a twist occurs about the longitudinal axis." Axial Skeleton — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Axial Skeleton IB Sport Science General Axial Skeleton The central scaffold of the body — the skull, spine and ribcage that support and protect. 📖 What it means The axial skeleton is the central core of the skeleton , comprising the skull, vertebral column (spine), sternum and ribs . It forms the main axis of the body. Its primary roles are support and protection : it holds the body upright, supports the head and trunk, and protects vital organs — the skull protecting the brain, and the ribcage protecting the heart and lungs.

It is distinguished from the appendicular skeleton (the limbs and girdles). While the axial skeleton is more about support and protection, the appendicular skeleton is more about movement — though the two work together. 🏅 Sporting examples Protection The ribcage, part of the axial skeleton, protects the heart and lungs during contact sports. Support The vertebral column supports the trunk and transmits load during lifting and landing. Contrast The axial skeleton (skull, spine, ribs) is distinct from the appendicular skeleton (limbs and girdles). ✍️ Using the term in context Name the axial skeleton's components and roles:

Axon Terminal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Axon Terminal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Axon Terminal The point at the end of a nerve cell where the message is passed on chemically. 📖 What it means The axon terminal is the branched end of an axon. When an impulse reaches it, calcium ions enter, causing vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the membrane and release their contents into the synaptic cleft. The neurotransmitter crosses the gap and binds to receptors on the next cell, passing the signal on. In a neuromuscular junction, the axon terminal releases acetylcholine onto the muscle fibre, which triggers contraction. 🏅 Sporting examples

Muscle contraction At the neuromuscular junction, the axon terminal releases acetylcholine to start a contraction. Reaction time The speed of transmission at axon terminals contributes to reaction time. Fatigue A reduced supply of neurotransmitter at the axon terminal can contribute to fatigue during prolonged activity. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how the axon terminal starts a muscle contraction: "When an impulse reaches the axon terminal, calcium enters and vesicles release acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft, which binds to receptors on the muscle fibre and triggers contraction." Axon — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Axon IB Sport Science General Axon The signal cable of a nerve cell — it carries the electrical impulse that tells muscles to fire. 📖 What it means An axon is the long extension of a neuron (nerve cell) that conducts electrical impulses away from the cell body toward other neurons or, in the case of motor neurons, toward muscle fibres. In the context of movement, the axon of a motor neuron carries the impulse from the nervous system to the muscle, where it stimulates the muscle fibres to contract. Many axons are insulated by a myelin sheath that speeds conduction.

The axon is therefore a key link in the chain that turns a decision to move into an actual muscle contraction — part of the neuromuscular system that controls all sporting movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Triggering contraction A motor neuron's axon carries the impulse to the muscle fibres, stimulating them to contract. Fast conduction A myelin sheath around the axon speeds up impulse conduction, allowing rapid responses. Neuromuscular link The axon connects the nervous system to the muscle, part of the pathway that produces movement. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the axon and its role in movement:

Back Squat — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Back Squat General BTEC Sport Back Squat The king of lower-body lifts — a compound exercise that builds the leg and hip strength behind almost every athletic movement. 📖 What it means The back squat is a compound resistance exercise in which a barbell is held across the upper back while the performer bends at the hips and knees to lower into a squat, then drives back up to standing.

It is a multi-joint (compound) movement that works several major muscle groups together — chiefly the quadriceps, gluteals and hamstrings , with the core and back stabilising the load. This makes it highly effective for developing lower-body and hip strength. Because it trains the powerful hip and leg extension used in sprinting, jumping and changing direction , the back squat is a staple of strength programmes across many sports. Correct technique is essential to train safely and effectively. 🏅 Sporting examples Building leg power A sprinter uses back squats to develop the leg and hip strength that drives a powerful start. Compound efficiency

Because it works several muscle groups at once, the back squat is an efficient way to build lower-body strength. Load prescription Squat loads are set as a percentage of the performer's 1RM — heavy for maximal strength, lighter for endurance. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the back squat as a compound lower-body lift: "The back squat is a compound resistance exercise with a barbell across the upper back, working the quadriceps, gluteals and hamstrings together; it develops the lower-body and hip strength used in sprinting and jumping." Balance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Balance General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Balance The quiet foundation of every skill — keeping the body's line of gravity over its base, whether still or moving. 📖 What it means Balance is the ability to maintain equilibrium — keeping the body's line of gravity within its base of support. It is a skill-related component of fitness, essential across almost all sports. It comes in two forms: static balance (maintaining equilibrium while still, such as a gymnast holding a handstand) and dynamic balance (maintaining equilibrium while moving, such as a footballer changing direction).

Balance depends on information from the eyes, the inner ear (vestibular system) and proprioceptors , and on the biomechanical factors of stability — a lower centre of gravity and a larger base of support make balance easier to maintain. 🏅 Sporting examples Static balance A gymnast holding a handstand relies on static balance, keeping the line of gravity over a small base of support. Dynamic balance A netballer landing and pivoting uses dynamic balance to stay in control while moving. Testing Balance is commonly assessed with tests such as the standing stork test. ✍️ Using the term in context Define balance and distinguish static from dynamic:

"Balance is the ability to maintain equilibrium by keeping the line of gravity within the base of support; static balance is maintaining it while still, and dynamic balance is maintaining it while moving." Balke Treadmill Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Balke Treadmill Test IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Balke Treadmill Test A fitness test of aerobic fitness (VO2 max). 📖 What it means The Balke Treadmill Test is a graded treadmill test in which speed stays constant while the gradient rises at regular intervals until exhaustion, used to estimate VO2 max. Protocol: The athlete walks or jogs at a fixed speed while the incline increases every minute. The test ends at exhaustion and the total time is recorded.

Interpreting results: Time to exhaustion is entered into an equation to predict VO2 max. It is a maximal test, so it is not suitable for everyone, and the estimate is less accurate than direct gas analysis. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A runner's time to exhaustion is used to predict VO2 max. Training use Repeat tests across a season show the effect of aerobic training. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly.

✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures: "The Balke Treadmill Test assesses aerobic fitness (VO2 max); the result is compared with normative data or earlier scores to judge fitness or progress." Ball and Socket Joint — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ball and Socket Joint IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Ball and Socket Joint The most mobile joint in the body — the design that lets the shoulder and hip move in every direction. 📖 What it means A ball and socket joint is a type of synovial joint in which the rounded head of one bone (the 'ball') sits within the cup-shaped socket of another. The two main examples are the shoulder and the hip .

Its structure allows movement in all three planes — flexion and extension, abduction and adduction, and rotation — as well as circumduction. This makes it the most mobile type of joint in the body. There is a trade-off: the shoulder's great mobility comes at the cost of stability , making it more prone to dislocation, whereas the deeper socket of the hip sacrifices some range for greater stability. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming The front-crawl arm action uses the shoulder's ball and socket joint to circumduct the arm through a full range of motion. Football A footballer's hip (a ball and socket joint) allows the wide range of leg movements needed for kicking, sprinting and changing direction.

Gymnastics A gymnast's shoulder mobility, thanks to its ball and socket structure, enables the extreme ranges needed for many skills. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the joint type, an example, and the movements it allows: "The shoulder is a ball and socket joint, allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and rotation; its great mobility comes at the cost of reduced stability." Contrast it with a hinge joint, which permits movement in only one plane. 🔗 Related terms Synovial Joint Hinge Joint Joint Planes of Movement Circumduction Articular Cartilage 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → BTEC Sport

Ballistic Stretching — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ballistic Stretching General BTEC Sport Ballistic Stretching Stretching with bounce — an aggressive, controversial technique that uses momentum to push past normal range. 📖 What it means Ballistic stretching is a technique that uses bouncing or jerking movements to force a muscle beyond its normal range of motion . The momentum of the movement drives the stretch further than a held (static) stretch.

It contrasts with static stretching (holding a position) and dynamic stretching (controlled movements through the range). Because it uses uncontrolled momentum, ballistic stretching carries a higher risk of injury and can trigger the stretch reflex , which actually causes the muscle to contract against the stretch. For these reasons it is generally not recommended for most performers . Where it is used, it is typically by highly trained, well-warmed-up athletes in activities that demand extreme, fast ranges of movement (such as some martial arts or dance), and only with care. 🏅 Sporting examples Bouncing action

Bouncing repeatedly to touch the toes, using momentum to push further each time, is ballistic stretching. Injury risk The uncontrolled momentum of ballistic stretching can overstretch a muscle and cause injury. Limited use Only well-trained, thoroughly warmed-up athletes in extreme-range activities might use ballistic stretching, and with caution. ✍️ Using the term in context Define ballistic stretching and evaluate its risks: "Ballistic stretching uses bouncing or jerking movements to force a muscle beyond its normal range; the uncontrolled momentum carries a higher injury risk and can trigger the stretch reflex, so it is generally recommended only for well-trained athletes."

Ballistic Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ballistic Training BTEC General Ballistic Training Explosive training in which the body accelerates a load and releases it. 📖 What it means Ballistic training uses fast, explosive movements in which the athlete accelerates a load and releases it, so the load leaves the hand or foot. Examples include medicine ball throws, jump squats and kettlebell swings. Ballistic work develops rate of force development and power. Because the load is released, the athlete does not decelerate it, which makes ballistic exercises different from slow, controlled resistance training. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing

A medicine ball throw develops the explosive force needed for a shot put. Jumping Jump squats develop the power needed for jumping in netball or basketball. Sprinting Ballistic hip thrusts can develop the explosive hip drive used in acceleration. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why ballistic training develops power: "Ballistic training accelerates a load and releases it, so the athlete produces force rapidly without decelerating, which develops rate of force development and power." Bandura's Social Learning Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bandura's Social Learning Theory AS Level / Cambridge General Bandura's Social Learning Theory How we learn by watching others — an influential theory explaining how behaviour and skills are acquired through observation. 📖 What it means Bandura's social learning theory proposes that behaviour is learned from the environment through observing and imitating others (models), rather than being purely innate. It is central to explaining how performers acquire skills and behaviours by copying.

Bandura identified four processes required for observational learning : attention (noticing the model), retention (remembering what was observed), reproduction (being physically able to copy it), and motivation (having a reason to imitate). All four must be present for learning to occur. Imitation is more likely when the model is similar to the observer, of high status, or reinforced (rewarded) for the behaviour. The theory has wide applications in skill demonstration and in explaining how behaviours such as aggression or sportsmanship are learned. 🏅 Sporting examples Skill demonstration

A learner watches a coach's demonstration, remembers it, reproduces it and is motivated to copy it — Bandura's four processes in action. Role models A young player imitates the technique and conduct of an admired, high-status professional they see as similar to themselves. Learned behaviour Social learning theory explains how behaviours such as aggression can be learned by observing others being rewarded for them. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the four processes and the factors affecting imitation:

"Bandura's social learning theory states that behaviour is learned by observing and imitating models, requiring attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; imitation is more likely when the model is similar, high-status or reinforced."
