Baroreceptor Reflex — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Baroreceptor Reflex IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Baroreceptor Reflex The automatic control that keeps blood pressure steady during changes in activity. 📖 What it means The baroreceptor reflex monitors blood pressure through stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. If pressure rises, the reflex slows the heart and widens vessels. If pressure falls, it speeds the heart and narrows vessels, restoring pressure to the set point.

During exercise, the reflex is adjusted by the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems. It helps match cardiac output and vessel tone to the demands of the muscles while keeping blood pressure within a safe range. 🏅 Sporting examples Standing up On standing, the baroreceptor reflex speeds the heart to prevent a fall in blood pressure. Heavy lifting A sudden rise in pressure during a heavy lift triggers the reflex to slow the heart. Recovery After exercise, the reflex helps bring blood pressure back to resting levels. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how the baroreceptor reflex responds to a fall in blood pressure:

"When blood pressure falls, baroreceptors in the carotid sinus detect it, and the reflex increases heart rate and narrows the vessels to restore pressure." Baroreceptor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Baroreceptor IB Sport Science General Baroreceptor The body's blood-pressure sensors — receptors that detect pressure changes and trigger rapid cardiovascular adjustments. 📖 What it means A baroreceptor is a sensory receptor that detects changes in blood pressure . Baroreceptors are located in the walls of major blood vessels, particularly the aorta and carotid arteries. When they detect a change in blood pressure, they send signals to the cardiovascular control centre in the brain , which adjusts heart rate and blood vessel diameter to bring pressure back toward normal — a negative feedback response.

Baroreceptors help regulate the rapid cardiovascular responses at the start of exercise and on changing posture . Alongside chemoreceptors (which detect chemical changes), they are part of the system that keeps the cardiovascular system matched to the body's needs. 🏅 Sporting examples Regulating pressure When blood pressure rises, baroreceptors signal the control centre to slow the heart and widen vessels, lowering it again. Standing up Baroreceptors detect the pressure drop on standing quickly and trigger adjustments to prevent dizziness. Exercise onset Baroreceptors contribute to the rapid cardiovascular adjustments at the start of exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define baroreceptors and their role: "Baroreceptors are sensory receptors in the walls of major vessels that detect changes in blood pressure; they signal the cardiovascular control centre to adjust heart rate and vessel diameter, regulating blood pressure by negative feedback." Barriers to Participation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Barriers to Participation AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Barriers to Participation The factors that stop people taking part in sport — central to understanding participation, inclusion and sport development. 📖 What it means Barriers to participation are the factors that limit or prevent an individual from taking part in sport and physical activity . Identifying and reducing them is a central goal of sport development and inclusion policy.

Common barriers include cost (equipment, membership, travel), access (lack of facilities or transport), time (work and family commitments), and cultural or social factors (stereotypes, discrimination, lack of role models or confidence). Different groups face different barriers, so strategies to increase participation are often targeted — for example, subsidised sessions to address cost, or women-only sessions to address specific cultural barriers. 🏅 Sporting examples Cost A talented young athlete may be unable to progress in an expensive sport such as rowing or skiing because of the cost of equipment, coaching and travel. Access

People in rural areas may face barriers of distance and limited facilities, restricting the range of sports realistically available to them. Targeted schemes A national governing body runs subsidised 'come and try' sessions to lower cost and confidence barriers for underrepresented groups. ✍️ Using the term in context Categorise barriers and link them to targeted strategies: "Barriers to participation include cost, access, time and cultural factors; because different groups face different barriers, participation strategies are often targeted, such as subsidised sessions to reduce cost." Support each barrier with a specific example and a possible solution. 🔗 Related terms

Basal Ganglia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Basal Ganglia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Basal Ganglia The deep brain structures that help start, smooth and learn movement. 📖 What it means The basal ganglia are a group of nuclei deep within the brain. They help to select and smooth voluntary movements, and they play a key role in learning motor skills through repetition, which is why skills become more automatic with practice.

Damage to the basal ganglia can cause movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease, which affects the initiation and smoothness of movement. In sport, the basal ganglia contribute to the automation of skills that athletes develop through practice. 🏅 Sporting examples Skill automation A footballer who has practised a skill many times performs it with less conscious effort, a process involving the basal ganglia. Motor learning Repeated practice of a complex sequence strengthens the connections in the basal ganglia that control it. Movement control The basal ganglia help start and smooth a sprint start. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why skills become more automatic with practice:

Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) The energy cost of simply being alive — what the body burns at complete rest just to keep functioning. 📖 What it means Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the minimum energy the body requires at complete rest to maintain vital physiological functions — such as breathing, circulation, cell activity and temperature regulation.

It represents the largest portion of most people's daily energy expenditure . BMR is influenced by factors including body size, the amount of lean (muscle) mass, age and sex — more muscle mass raises BMR because muscle is metabolically active. BMR matters for energy balance and nutrition : total daily energy needs are BMR plus the energy used in physical activity and digestion. Understanding it helps athletes match their energy intake to their needs. 🏅 Sporting examples Resting energy Even lying completely still, the body uses energy at its basal metabolic rate to keep vital functions running. Muscle and BMR

An athlete with more lean muscle mass tends to have a higher BMR, as muscle is metabolically active. Energy balance Total daily energy needs are BMR plus the energy used in activity and digestion, guiding an athlete's intake. ✍️ Using the term in context Define BMR and note what affects it: "Basal metabolic rate is the minimum energy the body needs at complete rest to maintain vital functions; it is the largest part of daily energy expenditure and is raised by greater lean muscle mass." Base of Support — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Base of Support IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Base of Support A simple biomechanical idea with big consequences for balance — the area beneath a body that determines how stable it is. 📖 What it means The base of support is the area beneath a body that includes every point of contact with the supporting surface . For a person standing, it is the area bounded by their feet and the space between them.

The size and position of the base of support is one of the main factors affecting stability . A larger base of support generally makes a body more stable, because the centre of gravity can move further before it passes outside the base and balance is lost. Athletes deliberately adjust their base of support depending on whether they need stability (a wide base) or mobility to move quickly (a narrower base allowing faster acceleration). 🏅 Sporting examples Judo A judoka widens their stance to enlarge their base of support and lower their centre of gravity, making them harder to throw off balance. Sprint start

A sprinter uses a narrow base in the set position so their centre of gravity is high and forward, ready to drive out quickly — favouring mobility over stability. Gymnastics A gymnast holding a handstand keeps their hands slightly apart to widen the base of support and aid balance. ✍️ Using the term in context Link base of support to stability and to the demands of the skill: "A wider base of support increases stability by allowing the centre of gravity to move further before passing outside the base; a judoka widens their stance for this reason, while a sprinter uses a narrow base to favour rapid movement."

Behavioural Activation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Behavioural Activation BTEC General Behavioural Activation Using planned, rewarding activity to lift mood and re-engage with life and sport. 📖 What it means Behavioural activation is a therapy technique in which a person schedules and gradually increases activities that they find rewarding or meaningful. It is based on the idea that low mood and withdrawal are maintained by doing less, and that doing more meaningful activity can improve mood.

In sport, behavioural activation can help an injured or low-mood athlete re-engage with training, social contact and enjoyable activity. It is delivered by trained professionals, and it works best as part of a wider plan that includes support and, where needed, medical care. 🏅 Sporting examples Injury An athlete who has withdrawn from the team during rehabilitation is helped to schedule social and enjoyable activities alongside physiotherapy. Low mood A performer experiencing low mood plans small, rewarding activities each day and reviews how they feel. Team support A coach encourages a withdrawn player to rejoin team activities at a pace they can manage. ✍️ Using the term in context

Bench Press — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bench Press General BTEC Sport Bench Press The benchmark upper-body pushing lift — a compound exercise for chest, shoulder and arm strength. 📖 What it means The bench press is a resistance exercise performed lying on a bench, pressing a barbell or dumbbells upward from the chest until the arms are extended, then lowering under control. It is a compound (multi-joint) upper-body exercise that works the pectorals (chest), anterior deltoids (front of shoulder) and triceps together. This makes it a key movement for developing upper-body pushing strength.

The bench press is widely used to build upper-body strength and power for sports involving pushing, throwing or striking, and — like other lifts — its load is prescribed as a percentage of the performer's 1RM depending on the goal. 🏅 Sporting examples Upper-body strength A shot putter uses the bench press to build the pushing strength that helps drive the shot away. Compound movement The bench press works the chest, shoulders and triceps together, developing upper-body pushing power efficiently. Load prescription Bench press loads are set from the performer's 1RM — heavy for strength, lighter for muscular endurance. ✍️ Using the term in context

Benefits of Exercising — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Benefits of Exercising IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Benefits of Exercising What regular exercise does for body and mind. 📖 What it means Regular exercise brings physical benefits : a stronger heart and lungs, lower blood pressure, healthier blood fats, better control of body weight and blood sugar, stronger muscles and bones, and a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers and osteoporosis . It also brings psychological benefits such as lower stress, anxiety and depression, better sleep, improved mood and self-esteem, and sharper thinking.

Benson's Relaxation Response — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Benson's Relaxation Response BTEC Sport General Benson's Relaxation Response A simple meditation-style method for calming the body. 📖 What it means The relaxation response , described by cardiologist Herbert Benson , is the opposite of the stress response. It lowers heart rate, blood pressure and breathing rate. Benson's method has four elements : a quiet environment , a mental device such as a repeated word or phrase, a passive attitude (letting thoughts pass) and a comfortable position . It is practised for around 10 to 20 minutes.

Athletes use it to manage pre-competition anxiety and to recover and sleep better. It needs regular practice to work well. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-competition A gymnast uses a calming word and slow breathing the night before an event. Recovery A runner practises for 10 minutes after hard training. Stress A student uses it during exam preparation. ✍️ Using the term in context List the elements: "Benson's relaxation response uses a quiet place, a repeated word, a passive attitude and a comfortable position to reduce arousal." Bernoulli Principle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bernoulli Principle IB Sport Science General Bernoulli Principle The physics of fluid flow that explains lift — why a spinning or shaped object can curve, dip or rise through the air. 📖 What it means The Bernoulli principle states that faster-moving fluid (air or water) exerts lower pressure than slower-moving fluid. This pressure difference can create a force that pushes an object toward the low-pressure region.

In sport, it helps explain lift and swerve . When air travels faster over one side of a projectile than the other, the resulting pressure difference generates a force perpendicular to the direction of motion — lifting, dipping or curving the object. It is closely linked to the Magnus effect on spinning balls: the spin drags air around the ball, speeding airflow on one side and slowing it on the other, producing a Bernoulli pressure difference that curves the flight. 🏅 Sporting examples Football (free kick) A curling free kick relies on spin creating faster airflow on one side of the ball; the lower pressure there bends the ball's path around the wall. Discus

A discus is angled so air moves faster over the top, generating lift that keeps it airborne longer for a greater distance. Cricket Swing bowling exploits pressure differences created by the ball's seam and surface, causing it to deviate in flight. ✍️ Using the term in context State the principle and apply it to a lift or swerve example: "By the Bernoulli principle, faster-moving air exerts lower pressure; when a discus is angled so air moves faster over its upper surface, the pressure difference generates lift, increasing flight time and distance." Beta-Oxidation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Beta-Oxidation IB Sport Science General Beta-Oxidation How the body burns fat for fuel — the process that lets endurance athletes tap into their vast fat stores during prolonged exercise. 📖 What it means Beta-oxidation is the process by which fatty acids are broken down to be used as fuel in the aerobic energy system. It converts fat into a form (acetyl coenzyme A) that can enter the Krebs cycle and be used to resynthesise ATP.

Because it requires oxygen and takes place in the mitochondria , beta-oxidation only contributes meaningfully during low-to-moderate intensity, longer-duration exercise , when oxygen supply is plentiful and the pace allows fat to be mobilised. Fat is an enormous energy store — far larger than carbohydrate — so the ability to use it efficiently spares limited glycogen. Endurance training improves beta-oxidation, allowing trained athletes to use a greater proportion of fat at a given intensity. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon running In the steady middle miles of a marathon, beta-oxidation supplies a large share of the runner's energy, sparing precious glycogen for later. Long-distance cycling

An ultra-endurance cyclist relies heavily on fat metabolism through beta-oxidation to sustain hours of steady effort. Training effect Endurance training increases the number of mitochondria, boosting the capacity for beta-oxidation and improving fat use at a given pace. ✍️ Using the term in context Link beta-oxidation to intensity and glycogen sparing: "During prolonged, low-to-moderate intensity exercise, beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids for aerobic ATP resynthesis, sparing limited glycogen stores; endurance training enhances this capacity." Bicarbonate Buffer System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bicarbonate Buffer System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Bicarbonate Buffer System The blood's main defence against acidity, which helps keep pH within a narrow range. 📖 What it means The bicarbonate buffer system is the main buffer in blood. It uses bicarbonate ions to neutralise hydrogen ions, forming carbonic acid, which is broken down into water and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide is then removed by the lungs.

During high-intensity exercise, hydrogen ions accumulate, lowering blood pH. The bicarbonate buffer absorbs many of them, and increased breathing removes the carbon dioxide, which helps restore pH towards normal. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint intervals During repeated sprints, the bicarbonate buffer helps limit the fall in blood pH. Breathing Hyperventilation during exercise removes carbon dioxide, supporting the buffering effect. Sodium bicarbonate Some athletes take sodium bicarbonate to raise buffer capacity, though it can cause gut discomfort. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how the bicarbonate buffer responds to exercise:

Bicarbonate Buffering — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bicarbonate Buffering IB Sport Science General Bicarbonate Buffering The blood's acid-neutralising system — how the body mops up the hydrogen ions that cause fatigue. 📖 What it means Bicarbonate buffering is a chemical system in the blood that neutralises excess hydrogen ions produced during high-intensity exercise, helping to maintain a stable pH.

During intense exercise, anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate and hydrogen ions, and the accumulation of hydrogen ions lowers pH (increases acidity), contributing to fatigue. Bicarbonate ions bind with the excess hydrogen ions , neutralising them and limiting the fall in pH. This buffering capacity helps delay fatigue during high-intensity effort. It is also the rationale behind bicarbonate loading , a strategy some athletes use to increase buffering capacity and improve performance in events that heavily stress the anaerobic system. 🏅 Sporting examples Neutralising acidity As hydrogen ions accumulate during a hard 800m, bicarbonate binds with them, limiting the drop in muscle pH.

Delaying fatigue Greater buffering capacity allows an athlete to tolerate high-intensity effort for longer before fatiguing. Bicarbonate loading Some athletes ingest bicarbonate before anaerobic events to boost buffering capacity. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain bicarbonate buffering and its effect: "Bicarbonate buffering is a chemical system in the blood in which bicarbonate ions neutralise the excess hydrogen ions produced during high-intensity exercise, limiting the fall in pH and helping to delay fatigue." Biceps Brachii — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Biceps Brachii IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Biceps Brachii The muscle everyone knows by name — the elbow flexor at the front of the upper arm, and a textbook example for movement analysis. 📖 What it means The biceps brachii is the muscle at the front of the upper arm . Its main actions are to flex the elbow (bend the arm) and to supinate the forearm (turn the palm upward). It is the classic example used to teach agonist–antagonist pairing : when the biceps contracts to flex the elbow, its antagonist, the triceps, relaxes and lengthens. When the arm straightens, the roles reverse.

In movement analysis, the biceps is the agonist during the upward (lifting) phase of a curl , contracting concentrically; during the controlled lowering phase it contracts eccentrically to resist gravity. 🏅 Sporting examples Weight training In a biceps curl, the biceps brachii is the agonist, contracting to flex the elbow and lift the weight. Biceps Curl Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Biceps Curl Test BTEC Sport General Biceps Curl Test A fitness test of muscular endurance of the elbow flexors. 📖 What it means The Biceps Curl Test is a muscular endurance test in which the athlete performs as many controlled biceps curls as possible with a set weight in a given time. Protocol: The athlete sits or stands with a fixed dumbbell or barbell and curls to a set cadence, with the repetitions counted until form fails or time ends.

Interpreting results: A higher number of correct repetitions shows better local muscular endurance. Repetitions should only count when the full range is used. Bicuspid Valve — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bicuspid Valve IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Bicuspid Valve The two-flapped valve on the left side of the heart. 📖 What it means The bicuspid valve , also called the mitral valve, lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle. Its name comes from its two cusps, or flaps. It opens during diastole to let oxygenated blood from the lungs fill the left ventricle, and it closes during systole to prevent backflow. Because the left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, the bicuspid valve works under high pressure. Problems with it can reduce cardiac output and limit exercise performance.

🏅 Sporting examples Diastole The bicuspid valve opens as the left ventricle relaxes, allowing it to fill with blood. Systole The valve closes as the left ventricle contracts, forcing blood into the aorta. Valve disease A narrowed bicuspid valve can reduce blood flow into the left ventricle. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the role of the bicuspid valve in filling the left ventricle: "The bicuspid valve opens during diastole, letting oxygenated blood from the left atrium fill the left ventricle, and closes during systole to stop blood flowing back." Bilateral Deficit — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bilateral Deficit IB Sport Science General Bilateral Deficit Why two limbs together can produce less than the sum of their parts — a curious quirk of force production. 📖 What it means Bilateral deficit is the phenomenon where the force produced by both limbs working together is less than the sum of the forces each limb can produce alone . Two legs pushing together, for instance, may produce slightly less than double one leg's maximum.

It is thought to result from a reduction in the neural drive to the muscles when both limbs act simultaneously — the nervous system does not fully activate both sides at once as effectively as it activates one. The deficit is relevant to training and testing : it can be reduced with training that emphasises bilateral (two-limbed) maximal efforts, and it is a reason why single-limb and double-limb strength measures don't simply scale. 🏅 Sporting examples Less than double An athlete's two-legged jump produces less force than twice their single-leg effort — the bilateral deficit. Neural cause The deficit is attributed to reduced neural drive when both limbs are activated at the same time.

Training effect Regular heavy bilateral training can reduce the bilateral deficit over time. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the bilateral deficit and its likely cause: "The bilateral deficit is the phenomenon where the force produced by both limbs together is less than the sum of each limb alone, thought to result from reduced neural drive when both limbs are activated simultaneously." Bilateral Exercises — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bilateral Exercises IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Bilateral Exercises Exercises using both arms or both legs together. 📖 What it means Bilateral exercises use both sides of the body at the same time , for example the back squat, deadlift, bench press and pull-up. They let the athlete lift heavier loads than single-limb exercises, so they are efficient for building overall strength and power. They also place a greater demand on the trunk to keep the body stable.

One disadvantage is that a stronger side can compensate for a weaker one, hiding imbalances . Programmes therefore often combine bilateral and unilateral exercises. 🏅 Sporting examples Squat Both legs push against the barbell together. Bench press Both arms push the bar upwards. Bilateral Transfer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bilateral Transfer AS Level / Cambridge General Bilateral Transfer Learning on one side, gaining on the other — how a skill practised with one limb transfers to the opposite one. 📖 What it means Bilateral transfer is the transfer of a motor skill learned on one side of the body to the other side . Practising a skill with one limb can improve performance of the same skill with the opposite limb.

It is one type of transfer of learning . It occurs because the general pattern or 'schema' of the movement, once learned, can be applied to the other side of the body, even though that side has not directly practised it. Bilateral transfer has practical value in coaching: it can help develop a performer's weaker side and is one reason athletes are encouraged to practise skills with both limbs, aiding versatility in games. 🏅 Sporting examples Weaker side A footballer who has developed passing with their stronger foot finds their weaker foot improves partly through bilateral transfer. Learned pattern

The movement pattern learned on one side transfers to the other, even without direct practice there. Coaching use Coaches use bilateral transfer to help develop skills on a performer's weaker side. ✍️ Using the term in context Define bilateral transfer as a type of transfer of learning: "Bilateral transfer is the transfer of a motor skill learned on one side of the body to the other; the learned movement pattern (schema) can be applied to the opposite limb, which helps develop a performer's weaker side." Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) General BTEC Sport Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) Estimating body composition with a small electrical current — a fast, practical read on fat and lean mass. 📖 What it means Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) is a method of estimating body composition by measuring the resistance (impedance) to a small electrical current passed through the body .

It works because lean tissue, being high in water, conducts electricity well, while fat resists it . From the measured resistance, along with height, weight, age and sex, the device estimates body fat and lean mass. BIA is quick, non-invasive and practical , but its accuracy is affected by hydration status, recent food or drink, and recent exercise . For reliable results, it must be carried out under standardised conditions, and it gives an estimate rather than a precise measure. 🏅 Sporting examples Quick assessment A coach uses a BIA device to get a fast estimate of an athlete's body fat and lean mass. How it works

Because lean tissue conducts the current better than fat, the resistance measured reflects body composition. Standardising For consistent BIA results, the athlete must be measured in a standardised, well-hydrated state. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how BIA works and evaluate it: "Bioelectrical impedance analysis estimates body composition from the body's resistance to a small electrical current — lean tissue conducts well, fat resists; it is quick and practical but affected by hydration, so results must be standardised." Biomechanical Efficiency — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Biomechanical Efficiency IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Biomechanical Efficiency Achieving the movement goal with as little wasted energy as possible. 📖 What it means Biomechanical efficiency describes how well a movement uses energy to achieve its goal. A biomechanically efficient movement produces the required force or speed with minimal wasted motion, such as unnecessary arm swing or energy lost to excessive vertical movement.

Efficiency is improved through technique and strength. In running, for example, a shorter ground contact and a stable trunk reduce wasted energy, which helps the runner sustain a pace for longer. 🏅 Sporting examples Running A runner with good efficiency keeps vertical oscillation small, wasting less energy per stride. Cycling A cyclist with a stable upper body transfers more power to the pedals. Biphasic Sleep — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Biphasic Sleep BTEC General Biphasic Sleep Sleeping in two blocks during a day, rather than one continuous block. 📖 What it means Biphasic sleep is a sleep pattern in which the main sleep is split into two periods within 24 hours, often a longer sleep at night and a shorter rest during the day. Bleep Test (Multistage Fitness Test) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bleep Test (Multistage Fitness Test) General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Bleep Test (Multistage Fitness Test) The most widely used field test of aerobic fitness — cheap, simple, and able to test a whole squad at once. 📖 What it means The Multistage Fitness Test , universally known as the Bleep Test , is a maximal, progressive field test used to estimate aerobic capacity (VO₂ max). Performers run continuously between two lines 20 metres apart, turning in time with a recorded bleep.

The interval between bleeps gets progressively shorter, so the required running speed increases at each level. The performer continues until they can no longer keep up — failing to reach the line on two consecutive bleeps ends the test — and the level and shuttle reached is converted to an estimated VO₂ max. Its major strengths are that it is cheap, needs minimal equipment, and can test large groups at once . Its limitations are that it is maximal (unsuitable for some populations), affected by motivation and running technique , and only estimates VO₂ max rather than measuring it directly. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sports

The Bleep Test is a staple of pre-season testing because its stop-start, change-of-direction format mimics the demands of team sports and tests the whole squad at once. School PE It is one of the most common practical fitness tests in PE and BTEC assignments because it needs only a flat 20m space, cones and an audio track. Talent monitoring Coaches compare Bleep Test scores against normative tables and track them across a training block to monitor improvement. ✍️ Using the term in context Link the test to the component it measures and evaluate it:

"The Multistage Fitness Test estimates aerobic capacity (VO₂ max); it is a valid, highly practical field test for testing groups, but as a maximal, self-paced test its reliability depends on the performer's motivation and pacing." Blister — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blister BTEC General Blister A raised pocket of fluid under the skin, caused by friction or heat. 📖 What it means A blister is a small pocket of fluid that forms between layers of skin, usually after repeated friction, pressure or heat. The body fills the space with fluid as a protective response, and the top layer of skin lifts away from the tissue below. Blisters are common in running, rowing and racket sports. Prevention includes well-fitting footwear, moisture-wicking socks and protective dressings. Most blisters heal in a few days if they are kept clean and not burst. 🏅 Sporting examples Running

Block Periodisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Block Periodisation IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Block Periodisation Training in focused blocks — concentrating on a few fitness qualities at a time rather than everything at once. 📖 What it means Block periodisation is a training model that concentrates on a small number of fitness qualities in successive, focused blocks , rather than developing many qualities simultaneously across the whole programme.

Each block places a concentrated training load on one or two specific qualities (for example, a block emphasising strength, followed by a block emphasising power). The adaptations from one block are designed to carry over and support the next. It contrasts with traditional periodisation , which trains many qualities together throughout. Block periodisation is often used with advanced athletes , for whom concentrated loading can drive greater adaptation and allow more precise peaking for competition. 🏅 Sporting examples Focused blocks An athlete completes a strength-focused block, then a power-focused block that builds on the strength gained. Advanced athletes

Block periodisation suits advanced athletes who need concentrated stimulus to keep adapting. Peaking By sequencing blocks toward competition, an athlete can peak the right qualities at the right time. ✍️ Using the term in context Define block periodisation and contrast it with traditional periodisation: "Block periodisation concentrates on a small number of fitness qualities in successive focused blocks, with each block's adaptations supporting the next; it contrasts with traditional periodisation, which develops many qualities simultaneously." Block Start Settings — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Block Start Settings BTEC Sport General Block Start Settings How sprinters set their blocks for the best start. 📖 What it means In a sprint start , the athlete uses blocks with the front block about one to one-and-a-half foot lengths behind the line and the back block roughly two foot lengths from the line , with the exact distances adjusted to suit the athlete. The sprinter goes through 'on your marks', 'set' and the gun . In the set position the hips are raised slightly above the shoulders and the front leg knee angle is about 90 degrees and the rear about 120 degrees.

The aim is to apply as much horizontal force as possible, gaining the maximum acceleration while staying low in the first few strides. Individual settings vary with leg length and strength. 🏅 Sporting examples Medium start The most common spacing, a compromise between a bunched and an elongated start. Tuning A coach adjusts the spacing and checks the first steps on video. Set position The hips rise and the athlete leans forward over the hands. ✍️ Using the term in context Link settings to force: "Correct block settings allow the sprinter to push horizontally against the blocks, producing maximum acceleration out of the start." Blood Cholesterol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Cholesterol IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Blood Cholesterol A fatty substance in the blood with a good and a bad side — and one that regular exercise helps rebalance. 📖 What it means Blood cholesterol is a fatty substance carried in the blood . It is essential in small amounts, but the balance between its types is important for cardiovascular health.

Cholesterol is carried by lipoproteins: high-density lipoprotein (HDL, 'good' cholesterol) helps remove cholesterol from the arteries, while low-density lipoprotein (LDL, 'bad' cholesterol) can contribute to fatty deposits in the artery walls. A poor balance raises the risk of cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise can improve the cholesterol balance — typically raising HDL and helping to lower LDL — which is one of the ways physical activity reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease. This is a key health benefit of an active lifestyle. 🏅 Sporting examples Good vs bad HDL ('good') cholesterol helps clear cholesterol from the arteries, while LDL ('bad') can contribute to fatty deposits.

Exercise benefit Regular aerobic exercise tends to raise HDL and improve the overall cholesterol balance. Health risk A poor balance of blood cholesterol raises the risk of cardiovascular disease. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe blood cholesterol and the effect of exercise: "Blood cholesterol is a fatty substance in the blood; the balance between HDL ('good') and LDL ('bad') cholesterol affects cardiovascular health, and regular exercise improves this balance, typically raising HDL, reducing disease risk." Blood Doping — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Doping IB Sport Science General Blood Doping A banned method of boosting endurance by increasing oxygen-carrying capacity — a key example in any discussion of doping and ethics. 📖 What it means Blood doping is a prohibited method of artificially increasing the number of red blood cells in the body to boost oxygen-carrying capacity and therefore aerobic performance. It can be achieved by transfusing extra red blood cells (either the athlete's own, stored earlier, or a donor's) or by using substances such as EPO that stimulate red blood cell production. More red cells mean more oxygen delivered to the muscles.

Blood doping is banned because it provides an unfair advantage and carries serious health risks, including thickened blood that raises the danger of clots, stroke and heart failure. It is a central example in discussions of doping, ethics and deviance in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance cycling Blood doping has been most notoriously associated with professional cycling, where greater oxygen delivery offers a large advantage in mountainous stage races. Distance running In endurance running, increased oxygen-carrying capacity directly improves aerobic performance, making it a target for cheating. Ethics discussion

Blood doping is used as a case study in sport ethics because it combines unfair advantage with genuine danger to the athlete's health. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the mechanism and why it is banned: "Blood doping increases red blood cell count to raise oxygen-carrying capacity and aerobic performance; it is banned because it provides an unfair advantage and poses serious health risks such as blood clots." Blood Glucose — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Glucose IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Blood Glucose The level of sugar in the blood, which must be kept steady for energy supply. 📖 What it means Blood glucose is the concentration of glucose in the blood. The body keeps it within a narrow range, because the brain depends on glucose for energy and the muscles use it during exercise. Insulin lowers blood glucose after a meal, and glucagon, adrenaline and cortisol raise it when needed.

During prolonged exercise, the liver releases glucose to maintain blood glucose, especially when muscle glycogen stores are low. If blood glucose falls too low, fatigue, dizziness and poor concentration can result. 🏅 Sporting examples Long events A marathon runner needs carbohydrate during the race to maintain blood glucose in the later stages. Hypoglycaemia A fasting athlete may experience low blood glucose, causing dizziness and poor decisions. Recovery Eating carbohydrate after exercise helps restore blood glucose and replace glycogen. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why carbohydrate intake helps during a long event:

Blood Lactate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Lactate IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Blood Lactate The measurable by-product that tells coaches how hard the anaerobic systems are working — and a key marker for setting training zones. 📖 What it means Blood lactate is lactate that has diffused from the muscles into the bloodstream , where it can be measured with a small blood sample. It is produced during anaerobic glycolysis and rises as exercise intensity increases.

At low intensities, lactate is produced and cleared at similar rates, so blood lactate stays low. As intensity rises past a certain point, production outstrips clearance and blood lactate rises sharply — the lactate threshold or OBLA. Measuring blood lactate lets coaches identify these thresholds and set precise training intensities . Lactate itself is not simply a waste product — it can be shuttled to other tissues and used as a fuel. 🏅 Sporting examples Rowing Coaches take fingertip blood lactate samples during rowing step tests to pinpoint the intensity at which lactate rises sharply, then set training zones from it. Middle-distance running

An 800m runner finishes with very high blood lactate, reflecting heavy reliance on anaerobic glycolysis. Endurance monitoring Tracking blood lactate over a season shows whether an athlete's threshold is shifting to a higher intensity — a sign of improving fitness. ✍️ Using the term in context Connect blood lactate to threshold and training-zone setting: "Blood lactate rises sharply once production exceeds clearance, marking the lactate threshold; coaches measure it to set precise training intensities." Avoid calling lactate a simple 'waste product' — note it can be used as a fuel via the lactate shuttle. 🔗 Related terms

Blood Plasma — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Plasma IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Blood Plasma The liquid that carries the blood cells and dissolved substances around the body. 📖 What it means Blood plasma is the straw-coloured liquid that makes up around half of blood volume. It is mostly water, and it carries dissolved substances such as glucose, amino acids, hormones, electrolytes and waste products, along with blood proteins.

Plasma volume falls during exercise, especially in heat, as water is lost through sweat and some fluid moves out of the blood vessels. Maintaining plasma volume is important for cardiac output and temperature regulation. 🏅 Sporting examples Dehydration A fall in plasma volume during exercise reduces stroke volume and makes the heart work harder. Heat Sweating in the heat reduces plasma volume, increasing the strain on the cardiovascular system. Transport Plasma carries glucose and hormones from the digestive system and glands to the tissues. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why plasma volume matters during exercise in the heat:

Blood Pressure — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Pressure IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Blood Pressure The force that drives blood around the body — measured as two numbers, and a key indicator of both exercise response and long-term health. 📖 What it means Blood pressure is the force exerted by blood against the walls of the arteries . It is written as two numbers: systolic pressure (the higher value, when the heart contracts) over diastolic pressure (the lower value, when the heart relaxes), for example 120/80 mmHg.

During exercise, systolic pressure rises as cardiac output increases to push more blood to the muscles, while diastolic pressure usually stays relatively stable during aerobic work. Regular aerobic exercise is one of the most effective ways to lower resting blood pressure over time, reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease — an important link between physical activity and health. 🏅 Sporting examples Aerobic exercise During a steady run, systolic blood pressure rises to drive greater blood flow to the working muscles, while diastolic pressure remains fairly constant. Resistance training

During heavy lifting, blood pressure can spike sharply, which is why breathing technique matters and why it is monitored in some populations. Health benefit Someone who takes up regular aerobic exercise often sees their resting blood pressure fall, lowering their cardiovascular disease risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the two components and the exercise response: "Blood pressure is the force of blood against the artery walls, expressed as systolic over diastolic; during aerobic exercise systolic pressure rises to increase blood flow to the muscles." Blood Redistribution — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Redistribution IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Blood Redistribution How the body diverts its blood supply to where it's needed most during exercise — the vascular shunt that keeps working muscles fuelled. 📖 What it means Blood redistribution is the process of diverting blood flow toward the active muscles and away from less active organs during exercise. At rest, much of the blood supplies organs such as the gut; during exercise, the muscles' demand rises dramatically.

This is achieved by the vascular shunt mechanism : blood vessels supplying the working muscles vasodilate (widen) to increase flow, while vessels supplying inactive areas vasoconstrict (narrow) to reduce it. The redistribution ensures that oxygen and nutrients are delivered where they are most needed and waste products are removed efficiently, supporting sustained exercise. It is controlled by the nervous system and local chemical changes. 🏅 Sporting examples Running During a run, blood is shunted toward the leg muscles and away from the digestive system — which is why exercising too soon after a large meal can feel uncomfortable. Cycling

A cyclist's vascular shunt directs a huge proportion of cardiac output to the leg muscles during a hard climb. Thermoregulation link During prolonged exercise, some blood is also redistributed toward the skin to aid heat loss, which can compete with muscle demand. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the vascular shunt and the two opposing processes: "Blood is redistributed during exercise via the vascular shunt mechanism: vasodilation increases flow to the active muscles while vasoconstriction reduces flow to inactive organs." Blood Viscosity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Viscosity IB Sport Science General Blood Viscosity The thickness of blood — and how it affects the ease with which blood flows through the vessels. 📖 What it means Blood viscosity is the thickness and stickiness of the blood , which affects how easily it flows through the blood vessels. Thicker (more viscous) blood flows less easily. Viscosity is influenced by factors such as the proportion of red blood cells and the water (plasma) content . Dehydration, for example, reduces plasma volume and increases viscosity , making the blood harder to pump and reducing flow rate.

Blood viscosity is relevant to performance and health : during exercise, maintaining hydration keeps viscosity in check and supports efficient circulation, whereas increased viscosity places extra demand on the heart and can impair oxygen delivery. 🏅 Sporting examples Dehydration effect Dehydration reduces plasma volume, increasing blood viscosity and making the blood harder to pump. Flow rate More viscous blood flows less easily through the vessels, reducing the rate of oxygen delivery. Hydration Staying hydrated during exercise keeps blood viscosity in check, supporting efficient circulation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define blood viscosity and what affects it:

Blood Volume — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Blood Volume IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Blood Volume The total amount of blood in the body, which affects how much the heart can pump. 📖 What it means Blood volume is the total amount of blood in the circulatory system, typically around five litres in an adult. It comprises plasma and the cells suspended in it. Blood volume affects venous return, which determines how much blood fills the heart and so influences stroke volume.

Endurance training increases blood volume, mainly through an increase in plasma volume. A higher blood volume supports stroke volume and cardiac output, and it helps the body cope with heat stress. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance training Regular endurance training increases plasma volume, which raises the blood volume available to fill the heart. Dehydration Reduced blood volume from dehydration lowers stroke volume and increases heart rate. Altitude Some athletes at altitude see changes in blood volume as the body adapts to lower oxygen. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how endurance training increases stroke volume:

Body Composition — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Body Composition IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Body Composition What the body is actually made of — the balance of fat and lean tissue that underpins both health and sporting performance. 📖 What it means Body composition is the proportion of fat mass to fat-free (lean) mass in the body. Lean mass includes muscle, bone, organs and water; fat mass includes both essential fat and stored fat.

It is considered a health-related component of fitness , because an unhealthy body composition (too much stored fat) is linked to increased disease risk, while an appropriate composition supports both health and performance. Body composition is assessed using methods such as skinfold callipers , bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) , and more precise laboratory techniques. The ideal composition varies considerably between sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running Endurance runners typically have a low body-fat percentage and light frame, which improves their power-to-weight ratio for economical running. Rugby

A prop forward carries far more muscle mass than a marathon runner — a body composition suited to the strength and collisions of their position. Assessment A coach uses skinfold callipers or BIA to monitor an athlete's body composition across a season rather than relying on body weight alone. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it as the fat-to-lean ratio and note it is health-related: "Body composition is the ratio of fat mass to lean mass; as a health-related component of fitness, an appropriate composition supports both health and performance, and the ideal varies by sport." Body Density — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Body Density IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Body Density A measure that lets fat percentage be worked out. 📖 What it means Body density is body mass divided by body volume , usually in kg per litre. Fat is less dense than muscle and bone, so a person with more fat has a lower body density. Density is measured by hydrostatic (underwater) weighing or air displacement plethysmography (the Bod Pod), and then converted to a body fat percentage using an equation such as Siri's .

These methods are accurate but need specialist equipment, so skinfold measures and bioelectrical impedance are used more often in schools and clubs. 🏅 Sporting examples Sport science lab An athlete is weighed underwater to calculate body density. Body composition Density is used to estimate fat mass and fat-free mass. Comparison Muscular athletes have a higher density than people of the same weight with more fat. ✍️ Using the term in context State the equation: "Body density equals body mass divided by body volume; because fat is less dense than lean tissue, a lower density indicates a higher body fat percentage."

Body Fat Percentage — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Body Fat Percentage General BTEC Sport Body Fat Percentage The share of your body that's fat — a key component of body composition and a common fitness measure. 📖 What it means Body fat percentage is the proportion of total body mass made up of fat tissue . It is a component of body composition, complementing measures of lean (fat-free) mass. It is commonly estimated using methods such as skinfold callipers (measuring subcutaneous fat at specific sites), bioelectrical impedance analysis , or more precise laboratory techniques. Each varies in cost, practicality and accuracy.

Body fat percentage is relevant to both health and performance : an appropriate level supports health, while different sports are associated with different optimal ranges. It is more informative than body weight or BMI alone, because it distinguishes fat from muscle. 🏅 Sporting examples Body composition Two athletes of the same weight can have very different body fat percentages, and therefore different amounts of muscle. Measuring it A coach uses skinfold callipers to estimate an athlete's body fat percentage and track it over a season. Sport-specific Endurance athletes typically carry a lower body fat percentage than the general population, aiding power-to-weight ratio.

Body Mass Index (BMI) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Body Mass Index (BMI) General BTEC Sport Body Mass Index (BMI) A quick weight-to-height ratio — useful as a population health screen, but a blunt tool for athletes. 📖 What it means Body Mass Index (BMI) is a measure of body weight relative to height , calculated as mass in kilograms divided by height in metres squared ( kg/m² ). It is used as a general indicator of healthy weight. BMI places people into categories (such as underweight, healthy weight, overweight and obese). It is quick, cheap and easy to calculate, making it useful for screening large populations.

Its major limitation for athletes is that it does not distinguish muscle from fat . A very muscular athlete can be classified as 'overweight' despite low body fat, because muscle is dense and heavy. For this reason, body fat percentage is usually a more meaningful measure for athletes. 🏅 Sporting examples Population screening BMI is used to screen large populations quickly for weight-related health risk. Limitation for athletes A muscular rugby player may register as 'overweight' on BMI despite carrying little fat, because BMI ignores body composition. Better alternative For athletes, body fat percentage gives a more meaningful picture than BMI. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define BMI and evaluate its main limitation: "Body Mass Index is body weight relative to height (kg/m²), used as a general indicator of healthy weight; it is quick and cheap but does not distinguish muscle from fat, so it can misclassify muscular athletes as overweight." Bohr Effect — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bohr Effect IB Sport Science General Bohr Effect The elegant mechanism that makes haemoglobin release more oxygen exactly where hard-working muscles need it most. 📖 What it means The Bohr effect describes how haemoglobin releases oxygen more readily under the conditions found in exercising muscle. It is shown as a rightward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve . During exercise, working muscles produce more carbon dioxide , become more acidic (lower pH), and generate more heat . These conditions reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so it gives up its oxygen more easily to the tissues that need it.

The Bohr effect is a beautiful example of the body matching oxygen delivery to demand : the harder a muscle works, the more of these conditions it creates, and the more oxygen is released to it. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance running In a hard-working runner's leg muscles, raised CO₂, acidity and temperature trigger the Bohr effect, releasing more oxygen to sustain aerobic energy production. Any intense effort The more intensely a muscle contracts, the more it produces the conditions that make haemoglobin release oxygen to it. Curve interpretation On a graph, the Bohr effect shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, indicating easier oxygen release at a given pressure.

✍️ Using the term in context Name the three triggering conditions and the curve shift: "The Bohr effect shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right during exercise; increased carbon dioxide, acidity and temperature reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, releasing more to the working muscles." Bone Density — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bone Density IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Bone Density How much mineral is packed into bone — a measure of bone strength that exercise builds and disuse erodes. 📖 What it means Bone density is the amount of mineral matter per unit volume of bone . It is a key indicator of bone strength — denser bone is stronger and more resistant to fracture. Bone is a living tissue that adapts to the loads placed on it . Weight-bearing and resistance exercise increase bone density , because the mechanical stress stimulates bone to lay down more mineral. Conversely, disuse (through inactivity or immobilisation) reduces it.

Maintaining good bone density is important for long-term health as well as performance , helping to reduce the risk of fractures and conditions such as osteoporosis. It is one reason weight-bearing activity is recommended across the lifespan. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise builds bone Regular weight-bearing and resistance exercise increases bone density by stimulating the bone to lay down more mineral. Disuse Prolonged inactivity or immobilisation reduces bone density, weakening the bone. Health benefit Maintaining bone density helps reduce the risk of fractures and osteoporosis in later life. ✍️ Using the term in context Define bone density and how it responds to loading:

"Bone density is the amount of mineral matter per unit volume of bone, indicating its strength; weight-bearing and resistance exercise increase it by stimulating bone formation, while disuse reduces it." Bone Mineral Density (BMD) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bone Mineral Density (BMD) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Bone Mineral Density (BMD) How much mineral is packed into bone. 📖 What it means Bone mineral density (BMD) is the amount of mineral (mainly calcium and phosphate) in a given area or volume of bone. It is a main indicator of bone strength . It is measured with a DEXA scan and reported as a T-score or Z-score. Low BMD increases the risk of fracture and is the basis for diagnosing osteoporosis .

Weight-bearing and impact exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D, and enough energy intake all help build BMD, especially in adolescence. 🏅 Sporting examples Adolescent athletes Jumping and running activities help to build peak bone mass. Swimmers and cyclists Non-weight-bearing sports can have lower BMD than running or gymnastics. Female athlete Low energy availability and missed periods can reduce BMD. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe measure and factors: "BMD is measured by DEXA and is increased by weight-bearing exercise and adequate calcium, while low BMD raises the risk of stress fractures and osteoporosis."

Bone Remodelling — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bone Remodelling IB Sport Science General Bone Remodelling The lifelong rebuild of the skeleton — bone continuously broken down and rebuilt so it can adapt to demand. 📖 What it means Bone remodelling is the continuous process of bone formation and resorption (breakdown) that allows bones to adapt, repair and renew themselves throughout life. It involves a balance between cells that build new bone and cells that break bone down . This ongoing turnover lets the skeleton adapt to the mechanical loads placed on it — laying down more bone where it is repeatedly stressed, and repairing micro-damage.

Remodelling is the mechanism behind changes in bone density : regular weight-bearing and resistance exercise shifts the balance toward bone formation, strengthening the bone, whereas disuse shifts it toward resorption. It also enables the healing of bone after injury. 🏅 Sporting examples Adapting to load Bone remodelling lays down extra bone in areas repeatedly stressed by training, strengthening them over time. Repair Remodelling repairs the micro-damage bones accumulate through regular use. Density link Weight-bearing exercise shifts remodelling toward bone formation, increasing bone density. ✍️ Using the term in context Define bone remodelling and its function:

Borg Scale — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Borg Scale IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Borg Scale A simple way to put a number on how hard exercise feels — letting athletes and coaches monitor intensity without any equipment. 📖 What it means The Borg Scale is a tool for measuring rating of perceived exertion (RPE) — how hard a performer feels they are working. The original scale runs from 6 to 20 , a range chosen so that multiplying the rating by ten gives an approximate heart rate.

The performer simply reports the number that matches their sensations of effort, breathlessness and fatigue. It is subjective , but it correlates reasonably well with objective measures such as heart rate. Its great value is practicality : it needs no equipment, works anywhere, and lets athletes self-monitor and regulate intensity — particularly useful for those who cannot easily measure heart rate. 🏅 Sporting examples Interval training A runner uses the Borg Scale to check they are working near the top of the scale during hard intervals and lower during recovery. Rehabilitation

A coach uses RPE via the Borg Scale to keep a returning athlete's effort within a safe range without needing lab equipment. Everyday monitoring A recreational exerciser aiming for moderate intensity targets an RPE that feels 'somewhat hard' on the scale. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain what it measures and the heart-rate link: "The Borg Scale measures rating of perceived exertion on a 6–20 scale; multiplying the rating by ten gives an approximate heart rate, making it a practical way to monitor and regulate intensity without equipment." Brachial Artery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Brachial Artery IB Sport Science General Brachial Artery The main artery of the upper arm — and the standard site for measuring blood pressure. 📖 What it means The brachial artery is the major artery of the upper arm . It carries oxygenated blood down the arm, continuing from the arteries leaving the heart and supplying the tissues of the arm. It is best known as the site commonly used to measure blood pressure . When a blood pressure cuff is placed around the upper arm, it compresses the brachial artery, allowing systolic and diastolic pressures to be measured.

As part of the systemic circulation , the brachial artery is a practical, accessible point at which the pressure of the circulating blood can be assessed — a routine measure of cardiovascular health. 🏅 Sporting examples Blood pressure A blood pressure cuff around the upper arm compresses the brachial artery to measure systolic and diastolic pressure. Arm supply The brachial artery carries oxygenated blood down the arm to supply its tissues. Brachial Plexus — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Brachial Plexus IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Brachial Plexus The nerve network that supplies the arm. 📖 What it means The brachial plexus is a network of nerves formed from the spinal nerves C5 to T1 . It passes from the neck, through the armpit region, to supply the shoulder, arm, forearm and hand . It gives rise to the main nerves of the arm, such as the axillary, musculocutaneous, radial, median and ulnar nerves . Injury can occur when the head and shoulder are forced apart, as in tackles in rugby or American football (a 'burner' or 'stinger'), causing pain, numbness or weakness in the arm.

🏅 Sporting examples Rugby tackle A forceful tackle stretches the nerves, causing a stinger. Cycling A fall onto the shoulder can damage the plexus. Throwing Extreme throwing positions can irritate the nerves of the arm. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the source and target: "The brachial plexus arises from spinal nerves C5 to T1 and supplies motor and sensory nerves to the upper limb." Bradycardia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bradycardia IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Bradycardia A slow resting heart — often a sign not of a problem but of a highly trained cardiovascular system. 📖 What it means Bradycardia is a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute . While it can occasionally indicate a medical issue, in athletes it is very often a positive training adaptation .

In endurance-trained individuals, bradycardia results from cardiac hypertrophy — a larger, stronger heart with a greater stroke volume. Because more blood is pumped with each beat, fewer beats per minute are needed to maintain the same resting cardiac output, so heart rate falls. Athletic bradycardia is therefore a marker of an efficient, well-adapted cardiovascular system . Some highly trained endurance athletes have resting heart rates well below 50 beats per minute. 🏅 Sporting examples Training adaptation An endurance athlete's resting heart rate of 45 bpm reflects bradycardia caused by a larger, stronger heart. Stroke volume link

Because the trained heart pumps more blood per beat, fewer beats are needed at rest, lowering heart rate. Efficiency marker Athletic bradycardia indicates an efficient, well-adapted cardiovascular system. ✍️ Using the term in context Define bradycardia and explain its cause in athletes: "Bradycardia is a resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute; in endurance athletes it is a positive training adaptation, caused by cardiac hypertrophy and increased stroke volume — more blood per beat means fewer beats are needed at rest." Brainstem — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Brainstem IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Brainstem The part of the brain that keeps vital functions running. 📖 What it means The brainstem joins the brain to the spinal cord . It consists of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata . It controls automatic vital functions such as breathing, heart rate and blood pressure. The medulla contains the cardiac and respiratory control centres, which respond to signals from chemoreceptors and baroreceptors. All messages between the brain and body pass through it, and it also regulates sleep and alertness. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise

The respiratory centre in the medulla raises breathing rate when carbon dioxide rises. Heart rate The cardiac centre increases heart rate as exercise begins. Breathing Rate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Breathing Rate IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Breathing Rate How many breaths per minute — a simple respiratory measure that climbs steeply with exercise. 📖 What it means Breathing rate (breathing frequency) is the number of breaths taken per minute . At rest it is typically around 12–15 breaths per minute. It is one of the two components of minute ventilation (breathing rate × tidal volume). During exercise, breathing rate increases in proportion to intensity , working alongside a greater tidal volume to move much more air per minute.

The rise in breathing rate is one of the body's key acute respiratory responses to exercise, ensuring enough oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide removed. At higher intensities, increases in breathing rate contribute proportionally more to rising ventilation. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise response As a runner increases their pace, their breathing rate rises to help move more air per minute. Ventilation component Breathing rate and tidal volume together determine minute ventilation, both increasing during exercise. High intensity At high intensities, increases in breathing rate contribute proportionally more to the rise in ventilation. ✍️ Using the term in context

Breathing Rhythms — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Breathing Rhythms BTEC Sport General Breathing Rhythms Matching breathing to movement. 📖 What it means Breathing rhythm is the pattern in which breaths are taken in relation to movement. Runners may breathe in for two or three steps and out for two , and swimmers coordinate breathing with the stroke. A set rhythm helps the athlete stay relaxed, use the diaphragm and avoid breath-holding . At higher intensities the rate naturally speeds up, and the rhythm moves to a shorter pattern. Rhythmic breathing may also help reduce a stitch , particularly by alternating the foot on which the athlete breathes out.

🏅 Sporting examples Running A runner breathes in over three steps and out over two. Swimming A front-crawl swimmer breathes every three strokes to breathe on both sides. Brisk Walking — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Brisk Walking BTEC Sport General Brisk Walking A simple way to reach moderate-intensity exercise. 📖 What it means Brisk walking is walking fast enough to raise your heart rate and make you breathe harder, but still able to talk. Regular brisk walking lowers the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers, and helps weight management and mental health. 🏅 Sporting examples Health guideline

Bruce Protocol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bruce Protocol General BTEC Sport Bruce Protocol A standardised treadmill test that ramps up until you can't continue — a classic maximal measure of aerobic fitness. 📖 What it means The Bruce Protocol is a maximal treadmill test that increases speed and incline every three minutes in set stages until the performer reaches exhaustion. It is a widely used test of aerobic fitness. Because the workload rises in standardised stages, the time to exhaustion can be used to estimate VO₂ max from established equations. The progressive, standardised structure makes results comparable and repeatable.

As a maximal test , it requires the performer to work to exhaustion, giving a strong measure of aerobic capacity but demanding high effort and appropriate screening and supervision. It is often used in both sport and clinical settings. 🏅 Sporting examples Estimating VO2 max The longer an athlete lasts on the Bruce Protocol before exhaustion, the higher their estimated VO₂ max. Standardised stages Speed and incline increase every three minutes, so results are comparable between tests and people. Maximal effort Because it is a maximal test, the Bruce Protocol requires the performer to work to exhaustion under supervision. ✍️ Using the term in context

Buffer Capacity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Buffer Capacity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Buffer Capacity How much acid a system can absorb before its pH drops. 📖 What it means Buffer capacity is the amount of acid (hydrogen ions) a system can neutralise before its pH changes noticeably. The main buffers are bicarbonate , phosphate, proteins and haemoglobin. During high-intensity exercise, hydrogen ions accumulate. Athletes with a greater muscle buffer capacity can tolerate more acidity and keep going longer. Training at high intensity increases buffer capacity, and supplements such as sodium bicarbonate and beta-alanine can add to it.

🏅 Sporting examples 800m runner High buffer capacity helps delay the fall in pH in the closing stages. Interval training Repeated hard efforts raise muscle buffering. Supplements Sodium bicarbonate raises blood buffering capacity before competition. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it by effect: "A higher buffer capacity means more hydrogen ions can be neutralised before pH falls, delaying fatigue in high-intensity exercise." Buffer capacity is the amount of acid neutralised; a buffer is the substance itself. 🔗 Related terms Buffer Bicarbonate Buffering Hydrogen Ions Acid-Base Balance Lactate Threshold Fatigue 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub →

Buffer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Buffer IB Sport Science General Buffer A chemical pH stabiliser — substances that resist changes in acidity to keep the body's internal chemistry in check. 📖 What it means A buffer is a chemical that resists changes in pH . In the body, buffers help keep the blood and muscle pH within the narrow range needed for normal function, despite the acid produced during exercise. During high-intensity exercise, anaerobic glycolysis produces hydrogen ions that would otherwise sharply lower pH. Buffers such as bicarbonate neutralise these hydrogen ions, limiting the rise in acidity and thereby delaying fatigue .

An athlete's buffering capacity can be improved by training, particularly high-intensity training, which enhances the ability to tolerate and cope with the acidity produced during anaerobic effort. 🏅 Sporting examples Resisting pH change Buffers such as bicarbonate neutralise the hydrogen ions produced in hard exercise, keeping pH more stable. Delaying fatigue A greater buffering capacity lets an athlete sustain high-intensity effort for longer before acidity forces them to slow. Training effect High-intensity training improves the body's buffering capacity over time. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a buffer and its role in exercise:

"A buffer is a chemical that resists changes in pH; in the body, buffers such as bicarbonate neutralise the hydrogen ions produced during high-intensity exercise, limiting the fall in pH and delaying fatigue." Bulimia Nervosa — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bulimia Nervosa BTEC Sport General Bulimia Nervosa A serious eating disorder that follows a binge and compensate pattern. 📖 What it means Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder in which a person has repeated episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviour to avoid weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives, fasting or excessive exercise. It is often hidden, and body weight can be within the normal range, so it can be hard to spot. It is linked to a distorted body image and low self-esteem.

It can damage the teeth, the digestive system and the heart, and upset the balance of body salts. It is treatable, and early help from a doctor or specialist service makes a real difference. 🏅 Sporting examples Weight-sensitive sport Pressure to stay lean can make athletes more vulnerable. Warning signs Going to the bathroom straight after meals, secrecy about food and excessive exercise can be signs. Support A coach who is worried talks privately and encourages the athlete to see a doctor. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the pattern and the response: "Bulimia nervosa involves binge eating followed by compensatory behaviour, and it needs professional medical and psychological support."

Bundle of His — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bundle of His IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Bundle of His The wiring that carries the heartbeat signal down the heart. 📖 What it means The bundle of His is a group of specialised conducting fibres in the heart. It picks up the impulse from the atrioventricular node (AVN) and carries it down the septum between the ventricles. It divides into left and right bundle branches , which end in the Purkinje fibres in the ventricle walls. This allows the impulse to spread quickly so the ventricles contract together from the bottom upwards.

The sequence is: sinoatrial node, atrial walls, AVN (short delay), bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres, ventricular contraction. 🏅 Sporting examples Heartbeat The impulse reaches the ventricles via the bundle of His. ECG The spread of the impulse produces the QRS wave. Heart block Damage to the conducting system can slow or block the signal. ✍️ Using the term in context Put it in sequence: "After the delay at the atrioventricular node, the impulse passes along the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres, causing coordinated ventricular systole." Learn the whole conduction pathway in order. 🔗 Related terms

Burpee Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Burpee Test BTEC Sport General Burpee Test A fitness test of anaerobic and muscular endurance. 📖 What it means The Burpee Test is a whole-body endurance test in which the athlete performs as many burpees as possible in a set time. Protocol: The athlete moves from standing to a squat, kicks the legs back to a press-up position, returns and jumps up. The number of complete burpees in the set time is counted.

Interpreting results: More burpees indicate better whole-body muscular and anaerobic endurance. Counting rules (full chest-to-floor, full stand) must be kept the same each time. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Bursa — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bursa IB Sport Science General Bursa A tiny cushion at the joints — a fluid-filled sac that stops tendons and bones rubbing painfully together. 📖 What it means A bursa is a small, fluid-filled sac located near a joint . Its role is to reduce friction between structures that move against each other , such as tendons, bones, muscles and skin. By providing a cushioned, lubricated surface, bursae allow tendons to glide smoothly over bones during movement, protecting them from wear. They are found at many major joints, including the shoulder, knee and elbow.

Bursae can become inflamed through overuse or repeated pressure — a condition called bursitis — which causes pain and can limit movement. Healthy bursae are an important part of smooth, pain-free joint function in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Reducing friction A bursa in the shoulder lets the tendons glide smoothly over the bone during an overarm throw. Cushioning Bursae cushion the point where a tendon crosses a bone, protecting it from friction and wear. Overuse Repetitive movement or pressure can inflame a bursa (bursitis), causing pain around the joint. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a bursa and its function:

"A bursa is a small fluid-filled sac near a joint that reduces friction between tendons, bones and other structures, allowing them to glide smoothly during movement; overuse can inflame it, causing bursitis."
