Bursitis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Bursitis BTEC Sport General Bursitis Inflammation of the small fluid-filled cushions around joints. 📖 What it means Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa , a small fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between bones, tendons and muscles near joints. It is usually caused by repetitive movement or prolonged pressure , or by a direct blow. Common sites are the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee . Symptoms are pain, swelling and tenderness. Treatment includes rest, ice, compression and anti-inflammatory advice, followed by gradual return to activity. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimmer

Repeated overhead movement can inflame the shoulder bursa. Runner Hip bursitis can develop with a sudden increase in mileage. Kneeling Prolonged kneeling can lead to bursitis at the front of the knee. ✍️ Using the term in context State cause and treatment: "Bursitis is inflammation of a bursa, usually caused by repetitive overuse or pressure, and is treated with rest and gradual return to activity." Caffeine — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Caffeine IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Caffeine The everyday stimulant with genuine performance benefits — a legal ergogenic aid used across endurance and team sports. 📖 What it means Caffeine is a stimulant and a widely used legal ergogenic aid . It affects the central nervous system and can improve performance in a range of sporting contexts. Its main benefits appear to be reduced perception of effort and fatigue, improved alertness and concentration, and enhanced endurance performance . It may also promote greater use of fat as a fuel, helping to spare glycogen.

Caffeine is permitted in sport, but responses vary between individuals, and high doses can cause side effects such as anxiety, a raised heart rate, disrupted sleep and gastrointestinal upset, so dose and timing matter. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance events A cyclist may take caffeine before a long race to reduce perceived effort and delay fatigue over hours of riding. Team sports A footballer might use caffeine to improve alertness, reaction time and concentration during a match. Individual variation Because responses differ, an athlete trials caffeine in training first, since for some it causes jitters or stomach upset that harm performance. ✍️ Using the term in context

Summarise its main effects and note it is legal: "Caffeine is a legal stimulant that can reduce the perception of effort and fatigue, improve alertness, and enhance endurance performance; responses vary, and high doses can cause side effects such as anxiety and disrupted sleep." Calcium — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Calcium IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Calcium A mineral doing two vital jobs — building strong bone and triggering every muscle contraction. 📖 What it means Calcium is a mineral essential for bone strength, muscle contraction and nerve function . It is one of the key micronutrients for an active body. Most of the body's calcium is stored in the bones and teeth , where it provides structural strength and hardness. Adequate calcium, alongside weight-bearing exercise, supports bone density and helps reduce the risk of fractures and osteoporosis.

Calcium also plays a direct role in muscle contraction : it is released within the muscle fibre to expose the binding sites that allow the sliding filament mechanism to occur. Without calcium, muscles cannot contract, making it essential to movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Bone strength Adequate calcium, with weight-bearing exercise, supports bone density and reduces fracture risk. Muscle contraction Calcium released within the muscle fibre exposes the binding sites needed for the sliding filament mechanism. Dietary need Athletes ensure sufficient dietary calcium to support both bone health and muscle function. ✍️ Using the term in context State calcium's roles in bone and muscle:

Caloric Deficit — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Caloric Deficit BTEC Sport General Caloric Deficit Eating and drinking less energy than you use. 📖 What it means A caloric (energy) deficit occurs when energy intake is lower than energy expenditure . The body makes up the difference by using stored energy, mainly body fat and, if the deficit is large, also muscle. A moderate deficit is the basis of weight loss. A large or long deficit can cause fatigue, loss of lean mass, poor recovery and in athletes the risk of RED-S . Athletes who want to lose weight should do so out of season, gradually, and with professional guidance. 🏅 Sporting examples Weight management

A person loses weight by combining a small dietary reduction with more activity. Athlete A very large deficit during heavy training reduces performance and recovery. Making weight Combat athletes need careful planning to avoid harming health. ✍️ Using the term in context Use the term with balance: "A caloric deficit occurs when energy intake is less than expenditure, which causes weight loss, but a large deficit in athletes can impair performance and health." Calorie — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Calorie IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Calorie The unit commonly used for the energy in food. 📖 What it means A calorie is a unit of energy. Strictly, one calorie is the energy needed to heat 1 gram of water by 1°C, but in nutrition the 'calorie' on a label is a kilocalorie (kcal) , which is 1,000 calories . One kilocalorie equals about 4.18 kilojoules (kJ) . Energy values are about 4 kcal per gram for carbohydrate and protein, 9 kcal per gram for fat and 7 kcal per gram for alcohol. Energy balance is the relationship between the calories eaten and those used. 🏅 Sporting examples Food label

A snack bar lists 200 kcal per serving. Fuel Fat provides more than twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrate. Energy expenditure A run of 5 km uses roughly 300 to 400 kcal for an average adult. ✍️ Using the term in context Be exact about units: "Food energy is measured in kilocalories, and one kilocalorie is equal to about 4.18 kilojoules." Cancellous Bone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cancellous Bone IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Cancellous Bone The light, spongy bone found inside bones. 📖 What it means Cancellous bone (also called spongy or trabecular bone ) is the porous inner bone tissue made of a lattice of struts called trabeculae , with spaces filled with bone marrow . Capillarisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Capillarisation IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Capillarisation Growing more tiny blood vessels — a key endurance adaptation that boosts oxygen delivery to the muscles. 📖 What it means Capillarisation is the increase in capillary density within muscle tissue that occurs as an adaptation to endurance training. More capillaries surround each muscle fibre.

This adaptation improves the delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the muscles and the removal of waste products such as carbon dioxide. A greater capillary network provides more surface area and a shorter diffusion distance for exchange between blood and muscle. Capillarisation is one of the reasons endurance training improves aerobic performance and VO₂ max : by enhancing the muscles' ability to receive and use oxygen, it complements central adaptations such as increased stroke volume. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance adaptation Months of endurance training increase capillary density around the muscle fibres, improving oxygen delivery. Aerobic gains

Greater capillarisation contributes to a higher VO₂ max by helping the muscles receive and use more oxygen. Waste removal A denser capillary network also speeds the removal of carbon dioxide and other waste from the muscles. ✍️ Using the term in context Define capillarisation and its benefit: "Capillarisation is the increase in capillary density around muscle fibres from endurance training; it improves oxygen and nutrient delivery and waste removal, contributing to better aerobic performance and a higher VO₂ max." Capillary walls are one cell thick , which makes the exchange of gases, nutrients and waste fast. Blood flow through the network is controlled by precapillary sphincters , which open to send more blood to active tissue during exercise.

Endurance training increases capillarisation , the number of capillaries around each muscle fibre, so oxygen delivery and waste removal improve. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance training A runner develops more capillaries in the leg muscles. Capillary — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Capillary IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Capillary Where the real work happens — the microscopic vessels where oxygen, nutrients and waste cross between blood and tissue. 📖 What it means A capillary is the smallest type of blood vessel , forming networks that connect the smallest arteries (arterioles) to the smallest veins (venules). Capillaries are the site where exchange between the blood and the tissues takes place.

Their structure is ideal for this: walls only one cell thick and a vast network create a huge surface area and a very short diffusion distance . Here, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood into the tissues, and carbon dioxide and waste pass the other way. In the lungs, capillaries surround the alveoli for gas exchange; in the muscles, they deliver oxygen for energy production. Endurance training increases capillary density ( capillarisation ), improving this exchange. 🏅 Sporting examples Gas exchange Capillaries surrounding the alveoli allow oxygen to diffuse into the blood and carbon dioxide out. Muscle supply

Capillaries deliver oxygen to the working muscles and carry away carbon dioxide during exercise. Short diffusion distance Their one-cell-thick walls create the short diffusion distance that makes exchange rapid. ✍️ Using the term in context Define capillaries and describe why they suit exchange: "Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, where exchange between blood and tissues occurs; their one-cell-thick walls and vast network create a large surface area and short diffusion distance, allowing efficient exchange of gases, nutrients and waste." Carbohydrate Loading — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Carbohydrate Loading IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Carbohydrate Loading A strategic pre-event nutrition technique — maximising the body's glycogen stores to delay fatigue in endurance events. 📖 What it means Carbohydrate loading is a nutritional strategy used before endurance events to maximise muscle and liver glycogen stores . The aim is to delay the point at which glycogen runs low and fatigue sets in.

A common approach involves increasing carbohydrate intake while reducing training volume (tapering) in the days before competition, allowing the muscles to 'supercompensate' and store more glycogen than usual. Carbohydrate loading is most beneficial for events lasting longer than about 90 minutes , where glycogen depletion is a genuine limiting factor. For shorter events it offers little advantage, as glycogen stores are not the limiting factor. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon Marathon runners increase carbohydrate intake in the final days before a race to maximise glycogen stores and delay 'hitting the wall'. Long-distance triathlon

Ironman athletes carbohydrate load before racing because the extreme duration makes glycogen availability a key limiting factor. When not to use it A sprinter or a footballer playing a single short match gains little from full carbohydrate loading, as glycogen depletion is not their main limit. ✍️ Using the term in context Link the strategy to glycogen, event duration and tapering: "Carbohydrate loading raises carbohydrate intake while tapering training before an endurance event, maximising glycogen stores to delay fatigue; it benefits events lasting over about 90 minutes." Note it offers little benefit for short-duration events. 🔗 Related terms

Carbohydrate gives more ATP per unit of oxygen than fat, so it is the preferred fuel at higher exercise intensities.

The rate of carbohydrate oxidation rises as exercise intensity rises, and it can be estimated using the respiratory exchange ratio. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon Runners use carbohydrate oxidation as the main source of ATP at race pace. Carbohydrate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Carbohydrate IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Carbohydrate The body's premium fuel for hard exercise — the macronutrient that powers high-intensity efforts and is stored as glycogen. 📖 What it means Carbohydrate is a macronutrient and the body's main fuel for moderate-to-high intensity exercise . It is broken down to glucose, which is used to resynthesise ATP, and stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver.

Carbohydrate is the preferred fuel as intensity rises , because it can be broken down both aerobically and anaerobically and yields energy more quickly than fat. However, the body's glycogen stores are limited , lasting only around 90 minutes of hard exercise. Because glycogen is limited, carbohydrate intake and timing matter for performance — athletes fuel before, sometimes during, and after exercise to maintain and restore glycogen stores. 🏅 Sporting examples Football A footballer relies heavily on muscle glycogen for the repeated sprints of a match, which is why pre-match carbohydrate intake is emphasised. Marathon

Marathon runners take on carbohydrate during the race (gels, drinks) because their glycogen stores would otherwise run low — the cause of 'hitting the wall'. Recovery After a hard session, carbohydrate intake helps replenish depleted muscle glycogen ready for the next day's training. ✍️ Using the term in context Link carbohydrate to intensity, storage and its limited supply: "Carbohydrate is the body's main fuel for higher-intensity exercise, stored as glycogen in the muscle and liver; because glycogen stores are limited, carbohydrate intake and timing are important for sustained performance." Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) The waste gas of aerobic energy — produced by working muscles and carried to the lungs to be breathed out. 📖 What it means Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a metabolic waste product of aerobic respiration . As the muscles use oxygen to produce energy, they generate CO₂, which must be removed from the body.

CO₂ is transported in the blood to the lungs , where it diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is exhaled . During exercise, the greater rate of energy production increases CO₂ production, so ventilation increases to remove it. Rising CO₂ levels are an important signal for controlling breathing : chemoreceptors detect the increase and stimulate faster, deeper breathing to expel the extra CO₂ and maintain the body's pH balance. 🏅 Sporting examples Waste removal During exercise, the muscles produce more CO₂, which is carried to the lungs and breathed out. Breathing control Chemoreceptors detect rising CO₂ and stimulate faster, deeper breathing to remove it. Gas exchange

At the alveoli, CO₂ diffuses from the blood into the air to be exhaled, while oxygen diffuses in. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe CO₂ as a waste product and its removal: "Carbon dioxide is a waste product of aerobic respiration; it is transported in the blood to the lungs and exhaled, and rising CO₂ levels are detected by chemoreceptors, which increase breathing to remove it and maintain pH." Cardiac Cycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiac Cycle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Cardiac Cycle The sequence of filling and pumping in one heartbeat. 📖 What it means The cardiac cycle is everything that happens in one heartbeat . It has three stages: atrial systole (atria contract, filling the ventricles), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, ejecting blood into the aorta and pulmonary artery) and diastole (the whole heart relaxes and fills). At rest, a cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds at 75 beats per minute, with most of the time spent in diastole.

As heart rate increases in exercise, the cycle shortens, mainly by reducing the time in diastole. 🏅 Sporting examples Resting A heart beating at 70 bpm completes about 70 cycles per minute. Exercise At 180 bpm each cycle lasts about 0.33 seconds. Valves The opening and closing of heart valves cause the 'lub-dub' heart sounds. ✍️ Using the term in context Order the stages: "In the cardiac cycle, atrial systole fills the ventricles, ventricular systole ejects blood, then diastole allows the heart to refill." Remember that systole is contraction and diastole is relaxation. 🔗 Related terms Heart Rate Stroke Volume Cardiac Output Diastole Atrioventricular Valves 🎓 Where this appears

Cardiac Hypertrophy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiac Hypertrophy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General BTEC Sport Cardiac Hypertrophy The athlete's enlarged, more powerful heart — one of the most important long-term adaptations to endurance and resistance training. 📖 What it means Cardiac hypertrophy is the enlargement and thickening of the heart muscle (myocardium) as a long-term adaptation to training. It is a key reason trained athletes have such powerful cardiovascular systems.

Endurance training tends to enlarge the ventricular chamber , allowing the heart to fill with and eject more blood per beat — increasing stroke volume . This is a major cause of the trained athlete's high maximal cardiac output and low resting heart rate (bradycardia). It is a healthy, functional adaptation — sometimes called 'athlete's heart' — and is distinct from the harmful thickening of the heart that can occur in disease. It develops gradually over months of consistent training. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running Years of endurance training give a marathon runner an enlarged ventricle and a high stroke volume, contributing to a resting heart rate that can be below 40 bpm. Rowing

Rowers, who combine endurance and strength demands, develop pronounced cardiac hypertrophy supporting their very high cardiac outputs. Low resting HR Because a hypertrophied heart ejects more blood per beat, it needs to beat fewer times per minute at rest to circulate the same volume. ✍️ Using the term in context Link cardiac hypertrophy to stroke volume and resting heart rate: "Endurance training causes cardiac hypertrophy, enlarging the ventricle so that stroke volume increases; this raises maximal cardiac output and lowers resting heart rate (bradycardia)." Identify it clearly as a chronic adaptation, not an acute response. 🔗 Related terms

Cardiac Muscle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiac Muscle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Cardiac Muscle The specialised muscle that makes up the heart. 📖 What it means Cardiac muscle forms the wall of the heart (the myocardium ). It is involuntary , striated and is made of branching cells joined by intercalated discs , which let electrical signals spread quickly. It is myogenic : it can generate its own contractions, which the sinoatrial node coordinates. It has a rich blood supply and many mitochondria, so it is highly resistant to fatigue.

Endurance training causes cardiac hypertrophy , increasing the size of the left ventricle and its stroke volume. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance training An athlete's heart adapts with a larger left ventricle and a bigger stroke volume. Heart rate The sinoatrial node sets the heart rate, which the nervous system adjusts. Fatigue Unlike skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle keeps contracting for a lifetime. ✍️ Using the term in context Give three features: "Cardiac muscle is involuntary, striated and myogenic, with intercalated discs and many mitochondria, making it highly resistant to fatigue." Do not say it has no striations: cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle. 🔗 Related terms

Cardiac Output — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiac Output IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Cardiac Output The volume of blood the heart pumps each minute — one of the single most important numbers in exercise physiology. 📖 What it means Cardiac output (Q) is the total volume of blood the heart pumps out of the left ventricle in one minute. It is the product of heart rate (beats per minute) and stroke volume (blood ejected per beat): Q = HR × SV .

At rest, a typical cardiac output is around 5 litres per minute — close to the body's entire blood volume every minute. During maximal exercise, a trained endurance athlete can raise this to 30–40 litres per minute, as both heart rate and stroke volume increase. The key exam insight is that endurance training increases maximum cardiac output mainly by increasing maximum stroke volume : the heart becomes larger and stronger (cardiac hypertrophy) and fills more completely, delivering far more oxygen to the muscles at full effort. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running

A marathon runner's high maximal cardiac output delivers a large, continuous supply of oxygenated blood to the muscles; their large stroke volume also gives a low resting heart rate. Football A midfielder's cardiac output rises and falls repeatedly as they alternate between jogging and sprinting; a higher trained cardiac output aids recovery between efforts. Rowing Because rowing uses large muscle groups in the upper and lower body, elite rowers record some of the highest cardiac output values of any athletes. ✍️ Using the term in context Manipulate the equation and explain why it changes:

"As exercise intensity increases, cardiac output rises because both heart rate and stroke volume increase, delivering more oxygenated blood to the working muscles to meet the higher demand for aerobic energy production." Avoid confusing cardiac output with stroke volume or blood pressure — always tie back to Q = HR × SV. 🔗 Related terms Stroke Volume Heart Rate Cardiac Hypertrophy Cardiovascular Drift Venous Return Resting Heart Rate 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → BTEC Sport Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Cardiac Reserve — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiac Reserve IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Cardiac Reserve How much extra pumping the heart can do on demand. 📖 What it means Cardiac reserve is the difference between maximum cardiac output and resting cardiac output . It shows how much the heart can raise its output above rest. A typical untrained adult can raise cardiac output from about 5 litres per minute at rest to around 20 to 25 litres per minute , so the reserve is roughly four to five times resting output. Elite endurance athletes can exceed 35 litres per minute.

Endurance training raises cardiac reserve mainly by increasing stroke volume . 🏅 Sporting examples Untrained person Cardiac output rises from 5 to about 20 L/min. Elite cyclist A larger heart and stroke volume gives a much bigger cardiac reserve. Heart disease A reduced cardiac reserve limits exercise ability. ✍️ Using the term in context Write it as a difference: "Cardiac reserve is the difference between maximum and resting cardiac output, which increases with endurance training because stroke volume increases." Good cardiorespiratory endurance lowers the risk of heart disease and supports performance in endurance sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running A marathon runner relies on high cardiorespiratory endurance. Cardiovascular Disease — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiovascular Disease BTEC Sport General Cardiovascular Disease A group of heart and blood-vessel conditions — and one of the clearest health risks that exercise helps reduce. 📖 What it means Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a group of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels , including coronary heart disease, stroke and high blood pressure. It is a major cause of ill health worldwide. The risk of CVD is influenced by lifestyle factors such as physical inactivity, poor diet, smoking and being overweight, as well as factors like age and family history. Many of these risk factors are modifiable.

Regular physical activity reduces the risk of cardiovascular disease in several ways — by improving the cholesterol balance, helping to control blood pressure and body weight, and strengthening the heart. This makes reducing CVD risk one of the most important health benefits of an active lifestyle. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise benefit Regular aerobic exercise lowers CVD risk by improving cholesterol balance, blood pressure and body weight. Modifiable risk Many CVD risk factors — inactivity, poor diet, smoking — can be changed through lifestyle. Heart health Strengthening the heart through training is one way exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk. ✍️ Using the term in context

Cardiovascular Drift — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cardiovascular Drift IB Sport Science General Cardiovascular Drift Why heart rate creeps upward during steady exercise even when the pace stays the same — an important effect for pacing and monitoring. 📖 What it means Cardiovascular drift is the gradual rise in heart rate that occurs during prolonged, steady-state exercise , even when the intensity stays constant. It typically appears after around ten minutes of continuous work.

The main cause is fluid loss through sweating . As the body sweats to cool itself, plasma volume falls, which reduces the amount of blood returning to the heart. To maintain cardiac output, the heart compensates by beating faster , so heart rate drifts upward while stroke volume falls. Cardiovascular drift matters for pacing and monitoring — an athlete using heart rate to gauge effort must recognise that a rising heart rate during a long session may reflect drift and dehydration rather than a true increase in intensity. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A marathon runner holding a steady pace sees their heart rate slowly climb over the race as they lose fluid, illustrating cardiovascular drift.

Cycling On a long, hot ride, a cyclist's heart rate drifts upward at constant power output, signalling the need to drink to limit plasma volume loss. Pacing implication An athlete pacing by heart rate must account for drift, or they risk slowing unnecessarily as their heart rate rises without a real intensity increase. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the sweating–plasma–heart rate mechanism: "Cardiovascular drift is the gradual rise in heart rate during prolonged exercise; sweating reduces plasma volume, lowering venous return and stroke volume, so heart rate rises to maintain cardiac output." Link it to hydration and to the limitations of heart-rate-based pacing. 🔗 Related terms

Carotid Sinus — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Carotid Sinus IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Carotid Sinus A pressure sensor in the neck artery. 📖 What it means The carotid sinus is a small widening at the point where the common carotid artery divides in the neck. Its wall contains baroreceptors , which detect stretch caused by blood pressure. Signals go to the cardiac control centre in the medulla through the glossopharyngeal nerve . If blood pressure is too high, heart rate and vessel constriction are reduced; if too low, they increase.

This is the baroreceptor reflex , which keeps blood pressure steady, for example when standing up or starting to exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Standing up Baroreceptors detect a fall in pressure and raise heart rate. Exercise The set point is reset so that blood pressure can rise. Massage Pressing the neck over the carotid sinus can slow the heart rate, so avoid pressing there. ✍️ Using the term in context Link location to reflex: "Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus detect changes in blood pressure and send signals to the cardiac control centre to adjust heart rate." Cartilage — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cartilage IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Cartilage The body's flexible connective tissue — cushioning joints, shaping the nose and ears, and reducing friction. 📖 What it means Cartilage is a firm but flexible connective tissue . It is found at joint surfaces, in structures such as the nose and ears, and between the vertebrae, serving support and cushioning roles.

At synovial joints , a smooth type of cartilage (hyaline or articular cartilage) covers the ends of the bones, reducing friction and absorbing shock , allowing smooth, protected movement. Other types, such as the fibrocartilage of the intervertebral discs, absorb compressive loads. Because cartilage cushions and protects joints, keeping it healthy matters for pain-free movement in sport. It has a limited blood supply, so it can be slow to heal if damaged. 🏅 Sporting examples Joint cushioning Articular cartilage on the ends of bones at the knee cushions the joint against the impact of running and jumping. Reducing friction

The smooth cartilage covering bone ends lets a joint move fluently without friction. Catabolism — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Catabolism IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Catabolism Breaking big molecules down to release energy. 📖 What it means Catabolism is the part of metabolism in which large molecules are broken down into smaller ones , releasing energy. Examples are the breakdown of glucose, glycogen, fats and proteins. The energy released is used to resynthesise ATP and to produce heat. Catabolic processes are generally promoted by hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol .

It works alongside anabolism , which builds molecules up. Hard exercise is catabolic, while recovery, rest and nutrition allow anabolic repair and growth. 🏅 Sporting examples Training Glycogen is broken down during a hard run. Fasting The body breaks down fat and, if prolonged, protein for fuel. Overtraining Too much catabolic stress and too little recovery can reduce muscle mass. ✍️ Using the term in context Pair it with anabolism: "Catabolism breaks down molecules to release energy, whereas anabolism uses energy to build up tissues such as muscle." Catastrophe Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Catastrophe Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Catastrophe Theory A more sophisticated model of the arousal–performance link — explaining the sudden, dramatic collapses we sometimes see under pressure. 📖 What it means Catastrophe theory explains the relationship between arousal and performance , improving on the simpler inverted-U hypothesis. It proposes that performance depends on the interaction between physiological arousal and cognitive anxiety .

When cognitive anxiety is low , increasing arousal affects performance in the smooth, inverted-U way. But when cognitive anxiety is high , passing the optimal arousal point causes a sudden, dramatic 'catastrophic' drop in performance rather than a gradual decline. The theory also explains why recovery is difficult: once a performer has 'catastrophed', they cannot simply reduce arousal slightly to recover — arousal must drop substantially before performance can be rebuilt. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf A golfer with high cognitive anxiety who becomes over-aroused on the last hole may suddenly and completely lose their technique — a catastrophe rather than a gradual dip. Penalty shoot-out

A footballer's dramatic, sudden failure under extreme pressure illustrates the catastrophic collapse the theory predicts when arousal and cognitive anxiety are both high. Recovery difficulty After 'catastrophing', a performer struggles to recover mid-competition because arousal must fall a long way before performance returns. ✍️ Using the term in context Emphasise the interaction of arousal and cognitive anxiety: "Catastrophe theory proposes that when cognitive anxiety is high, exceeding the optimal arousal point causes a sudden, dramatic drop in performance rather than the gradual decline predicted by the inverted-U hypothesis."

Catecholamines — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Catecholamines IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Catecholamines The 'fight or flight' hormones, such as adrenaline. 📖 What it means Catecholamines are hormones and neurotransmitters including adrenaline (epinephrine), noradrenaline (norepinephrine) and dopamine . Their release rises with exercise intensity and with anticipation of competition, and they are central to the fight-or-flight response. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-race Adrenaline raises heart rate before the start (the anticipatory rise). Sprint High levels of adrenaline help mobilise glucose rapidly. Cavitation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cavitation BTEC Sport General Cavitation Bubbles forming in a liquid when pressure drops. 📖 What it means Cavitation is the formation of vapour or gas bubbles in a liquid when the pressure falls below the liquid's vapour pressure. The bubbles collapse when the pressure rises again. In sport and engineering it matters in water sports and boat propellers , where cavitation reduces efficiency and can damage surfaces. The popping sound when a joint is cracked is also often linked to gas bubbles forming in the synovial fluid. The exact mechanism is still debated, and it is not thought to cause arthritis.

🏅 Sporting examples Rowing and sailing Fast-moving blades and fins can cavitate and lose grip on the water. Propellers Cavitation pits the metal of boat propellers. Cellular Respiration — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cellular Respiration IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Cellular Respiration How cells turn food into usable energy. 📖 What it means Cellular respiration is the process by which cells release energy from nutrients and use it to make ATP . In aerobic respiration, glucose and oxygen produce carbon dioxide, water and ATP . It has three main stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix and the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Most ATP (around 30 to 32 per glucose) comes from the last stage.

Without enough oxygen, cells rely on anaerobic respiration (glycolysis, producing lactate), which gives much less ATP but works quickly. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon Aerobic respiration in muscle mitochondria supplies most energy. Sprint Anaerobic pathways add energy faster than oxygen can arrive. Training Endurance training increases mitochondria and respiratory enzymes. ✍️ Using the term in context Give the equation and locations: "Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen to form carbon dioxide, water and ATP, through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain." Centering — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Centering IB Sport Science General Centering A moment of calm control — a relaxation and focus technique athletes use to reset under pressure. 📖 What it means Centering is a relaxation and focus technique in which an athlete consciously directs their attention inward and controls their breathing to calm the body and refocus the mind, usually in a brief, deliberate moment. It typically combines controlled, deep breathing with a redirection of attention to a point of calm and to the relevant task cues, releasing tension (often on the out-breath). It can be performed quickly, making it useful in the flow of competition.

Centering is used to manage arousal and anxiety and regain focus — for example before a penalty, serve or free throw. As a psychological skill, it helps a performer reach and hold their optimal state under pressure. 🏅 Sporting examples Before a set play A rugby goal-kicker uses a centering routine — a deep breath and a refocusing of attention — before kicking. Resetting After a mistake, a tennis player centers to release tension and refocus for the next point. Quick technique Because centering takes only moments, it can be used within the flow of competition. ✍️ Using the term in context Define centering and its purpose:

Central Fatigue — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Central Fatigue IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Central Fatigue Tiredness that starts in the brain and nerves, not the muscle. 📖 What it means Central fatigue is a reduction in voluntary muscle activation caused by changes in the brain and spinal cord , so that less drive reaches the muscle even though the muscle itself could still work.

Possible causes include changes in neurotransmitters such as serotonin and dopamine, low blood glucose, heat and dehydration, and sleep loss. It contrasts with peripheral fatigue , which arises in the muscle through factors such as hydrogen ion build-up and fuel depletion. In long events, the brain may also reduce effort to protect the body, as proposed by the central governor theory. 🏅 Sporting examples Ultra-endurance Runners feel unable to continue though the muscles are not damaged. Heat Exercise in hot weather increases the perceived effort and reduces drive. Sleep loss Poor sleep reduces motivation and neural drive in training. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast the two types:

"Central fatigue reflects reduced neural drive from the central nervous system, whereas peripheral fatigue arises within the muscle itself." Central Governor Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Central Governor Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Central Governor Theory The idea that the brain slows you down to protect you. 📖 What it means The central governor theory was put forward by Tim Noakes . It proposes that the brain regulates exercise intensity by limiting muscle activation, in order to protect the body (especially the heart and brain) from damage.

Under this idea, fatigue is a feeling or conscious perception created by the brain, not just a result of the muscles running out of fuel. It explains why athletes can often produce a final sprint even when they seem exhausted. The theory is debated. Critics argue that peripheral factors in the muscle also set limits, and most researchers see fatigue as having both central and peripheral causes. 🏅 Sporting examples Final sprint A tired runner finds extra speed on seeing the finish line. Heat The brain may slow pace before core temperature becomes dangerous. Pacing Athletes set their pace in advance based on expected effort and distance. ✍️ Using the term in context Present it as a theory:

"According to the central governor theory, the brain limits muscle recruitment to protect the body, so fatigue is a protective mechanism, not only a muscle failure." Central Nervous System (CNS) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Central Nervous System (CNS) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Central Nervous System (CNS) The brain and spinal cord. 📖 What it means The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and the spinal cord . It receives sensory information, processes it and sends out instructions to the muscles and organs. The brain includes the cerebral cortex, cerebellum and brainstem . The spinal cord carries messages between brain and body and also controls simple reflexes without the brain.

It is linked to the body by the peripheral nervous system , whose sensory nerves bring information in and motor nerves carry instructions out. 🏅 Sporting examples Reaction A sprinter hears the gun, the CNS processes the signal and sends a command to the leg muscles. Reflex The spinal cord controls the stretch reflex without conscious thought. Training Neural adaptations improve how well the CNS recruits motor units. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the parts and roles: "The CNS comprises the brain and spinal cord; it processes sensory information and sends motor commands to the muscles." Centre of Buoyancy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Centre of Buoyancy BTEC Sport General Centre of Buoyancy The point where the upward force from water acts. 📖 What it means The centre of buoyancy is the point through which the upward buoyant force on a floating or submerged body acts. It is the centre of mass of the volume of fluid displaced . In a swimmer, the buoyant force acts at the centre of buoyancy, and the weight acts at the centre of gravity. If they are not in line, the body rotates : swimmers with heavy, dense legs tend to have the legs sink.

Swimmers can change their body position, such as by lifting the head less and kicking, to bring the two points closer together and reduce drag. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming The legs sink when the centre of gravity lies below the centre of buoyancy. Wetsuits Buoyant suits raise the hips and legs in the water. Floating A person floats horizontally when buoyancy and weight act in line. ✍️ Using the term in context Link it to the centre of gravity: "If the centre of buoyancy and the centre of gravity are not aligned, a torque rotates the swimmer so that the legs sink." Centre of Gravity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Centre of Gravity IB Sport Science General AS Level / Cambridge Centre of Gravity The single point where a body's weight acts — a concept at the heart of balance, stability and technique in every sport. 📖 What it means The centre of gravity is the single point at which a body's weight is considered to act , and around which its weight is evenly balanced. For a symmetrical object it lies at the geometric centre, but the human body's centre of gravity shifts as we change position.

Its position is crucial for stability : a body is stable as long as the line of gravity from its centre of gravity falls within the base of support . A lower centre of gravity generally increases stability. Because the body can change shape, the centre of gravity can even move outside the body — for example, when an athlete arches their back over a high-jump bar, allowing them to clear a height their centre of gravity passes beneath. 🏅 Sporting examples High jump A Fosbury-flop high jumper arches so their centre of gravity passes under the bar even as their body clears over it — a clever manipulation of centre of gravity. Judo

A judoka lowers their centre of gravity by bending their knees, increasing stability and making it harder for an opponent to unbalance them. Gymnastics A gymnast on a beam keeps their centre of gravity directly over the narrow base of support to maintain balance. ✍️ Using the term in context Connect centre of gravity to stability via the base of support: "A body remains stable while the line of gravity from its centre of gravity falls within the base of support; lowering the centre of gravity, as a judoka does by bending the knees, increases stability." Use the high-jump example to show the centre of gravity can move outside the body. 🔗 Related terms

Centre of Mass — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Centre of Mass IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Centre of Mass The balance point of a body's mass — closely related to centre of gravity and central to analysing motion and rotation. 📖 What it means The centre of mass is the single point at which a body's mass can be considered to be concentrated for the purposes of analysing its motion. On Earth, its position coincides with the centre of gravity.

Treating the whole body as a single point at its centre of mass simplifies motion analysis — for example, a projectile's centre of mass follows a smooth parabolic path even while the limbs move independently around it. Its position changes as the body changes shape , and it can lie outside the body. Rotation in the air (as in a somersault) occurs around the centre of mass, which is why understanding it is essential in gymnastics and diving. 🏅 Sporting examples Diving A diver's centre of mass follows a fixed parabolic path once they leave the board, while they rotate their body around that point to complete somersaults and twists. Long jump

In flight, a long jumper cannot change the path of their centre of mass, but they move their limbs around it to land in the most effective position. Gymnastics A somersault is rotation of the body around its centre of mass; tucking brings mass closer to the axis and speeds the rotation. ✍️ Using the term in context Use centre of mass to explain flight paths and rotation: "Once airborne, a jumper's centre of mass follows a fixed parabolic path; they cannot alter it, but they can rotate their body around the centre of mass and reposition their limbs." Centrifugal Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Centrifugal Force BTEC Sport General Centrifugal Force The outward 'pull' felt when moving in a circle. 📖 What it means Centrifugal force is the apparent outward force felt by a body moving in a circular path. It is not a real force: it is the result of the body's inertia , its tendency to keep moving in a straight line. The real force is the inward centripetal force . If it disappears, the body moves off along a tangent , not directly outwards. In sport, it is useful for explaining why a hammer thrower leans back, or why a cyclist leans into a bend. 🏅 Sporting examples Hammer throw

The thrower leans back to counter the pull from the hammer. Cycling Riders lean into the corner to balance the effect. Release When the hammer is released, it flies off along a tangent. ✍️ Using the term in context Be exact about the physics: "What feels like a centrifugal force is the inertia of the body resisting the inward centripetal force that causes circular motion." Centripetal Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Centripetal Force BTEC Sport General Centripetal Force The inward force that keeps something moving in a circle. 📖 What it means Centripetal force is the real, inward-acting force that makes a body follow a circular path. Cerebrospinal Fluid — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cerebrospinal Fluid IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Cerebrospinal Fluid The fluid that cushions the brain and spinal cord. 📖 What it means Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a clear fluid that fills the spaces around the brain and spinal cord and the cavities (ventricles) inside the brain. It cushions the brain against impact, helps support its weight by making it buoyant, and removes waste and supplies some nutrients. It is one reason the brain is protected from everyday knocks, but a hard blow can still move the brain inside the skull and cause concussion . 🏅 Sporting examples Heading a ball

The fluid cushions the brain from small impacts. Collision A heavy tackle can still cause the brain to hit the skull wall, causing concussion. Medical test A lumbar puncture samples the fluid for diagnosis. ✍️ Using the term in context State the main role: "Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord and reduces the effects of impact." Chaining — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chaining AS Level / Cambridge General Chaining Building a complex skill link by link — teaching parts, then joining them into the full sequence. 📖 What it means Chaining is a coaching method for teaching complex skills by linking together previously learned parts into the complete sequence. It is a form of part practice suited to serial skills. The performer first learns the individual sub-skills , then progressively links (chains) them together in the correct order until the whole skill can be performed fluently. The parts are joined one at a time, building up the full sequence.

Chaining is well suited to serial skills — those made up of several discrete parts in a set order, such as a gymnastics routine or a triple jump. It lets the performer master each element before combining them, which can build confidence and reduce errors. 🏅 Sporting examples Serial skills A triple jump can be taught by chaining — learning the hop, step and jump separately, then linking them. Building sequences A gymnastics routine is built by chaining individual skills together into the full sequence. Confidence Mastering each part before linking it can build confidence and reduce errors in complex skills. ✍️ Using the term in context Define chaining and the skills it suits:

"Chaining is a coaching method that teaches complex skills by learning the parts and progressively linking them into the whole sequence; it suits serial skills such as a triple jump or gymnastics routine." Chelladurai's Multidimensional Model of Leadership — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chelladurai's Multidimensional Model of Leadership IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Chelladurai's Multidimensional Model of Leadership Matching a leader's behaviour to the situation and the team. 📖 What it means Chelladurai's multidimensional model says leadership works best when three types of leader behaviour match : required behaviour (what the situation demands), actual behaviour (what the leader does) and preferred behaviour (what the group wants).

It is influenced by antecedents : characteristics of the situation, the leader and the members. When the behaviours are in line, performance and satisfaction are highest. Chemical Energy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chemical Energy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Chemical Energy Energy stored in food and fuel molecules. 📖 What it means Chemical energy is energy stored in the bonds between atoms in molecules. In the body, it is held in carbohydrates, fats, proteins, creatine phosphate and ATP . When bonds are broken during metabolism, the energy is released and used to produce ATP, which powers muscle contraction. Some is also released as heat . In the body, chemical energy is converted into kinetic energy (movement), heat and, in the case of elastic structures, elastic energy . 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinter

Stored ATP and creatine phosphate are broken down to fuel the first seconds of a sprint. Marathon Glycogen and fat are broken down to supply energy for hours. Throwing Chemical energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the javelin. ✍️ Using the term in context Trace the conversions: "Chemical energy in glucose is converted into ATP, which is used for muscle contraction, producing kinetic energy and heat." Remember that energy is transformed, not created or lost. 🔗 Related terms Kinetic Energy Elastic Energy Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) Conservation of Energy Glucose Energy Systems 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge

Chemoreceptor Reflex — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chemoreceptor Reflex IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Chemoreceptor Reflex The reflex that adjusts breathing when blood chemistry changes. 📖 What it means The chemoreceptor reflex begins with chemoreceptors that detect changes in carbon dioxide, hydrogen ion concentration (pH) and, to a lesser degree, oxygen in the blood. Central chemoreceptors are in the medulla and peripheral chemoreceptors in the aortic and carotid bodies.

When carbon dioxide rises during exercise, the receptors send signals to the respiratory centre in the medulla, which increases breathing rate and depth . The cardiac centre may also raise heart rate. This negative feedback loop returns blood CO2 and pH towards normal. 🏅 Sporting examples Running Rising CO2 in the blood increases breathing rate. Hyperventilation Over-breathing lowers CO2 and slows the drive to breathe. Altitude Low oxygen triggers peripheral chemoreceptors to increase ventilation. ✍️ Using the term in context Trace the loop: "Rising blood CO2 and falling pH stimulate chemoreceptors, which signal the medulla to increase breathing rate and depth."

Carbon dioxide is the strongest stimulus at sea level. 🔗 Related terms Chemoreceptor Brainstem Breathing Rate Negative Feedback Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Homeostasis 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → BTEC Sport Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy © 2026 Simply Sport Science · simplysportscience.co.uk

Chemoreceptor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chemoreceptor IB Sport Science General Chemoreceptor The body's chemical sensors — receptors that monitor the blood and drive changes in breathing and heart rate. 📖 What it means A chemoreceptor is a sensory receptor that detects changes in the chemical composition of the blood , particularly levels of carbon dioxide, oxygen and acidity (pH).

During exercise, chemoreceptors detect the rise in carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions (and fall in pH) as the muscles produce more waste. They signal the control centres in the brain, which increase breathing rate and depth, and heart rate , to remove CO₂ and deliver more oxygen. Chemoreceptors are therefore central to the regulation of breathing and the cardiovascular response to exercise . Alongside baroreceptors (which detect pressure), they help keep the body's internal environment matched to demand. 🏅 Sporting examples Controlling breathing As CO₂ rises during exercise, chemoreceptors detect it and stimulate faster, deeper breathing to remove it. Cardiovascular response

Chemoreceptors also help drive the increase in heart rate that delivers more oxygen during exercise. Detecting acidity Chemoreceptors sense the fall in pH from accumulating hydrogen ions and trigger corrective responses. ✍️ Using the term in context Define chemoreceptors and their role in exercise: "Chemoreceptors are sensory receptors that detect changes in blood chemistry — especially CO₂, oxygen and pH; during exercise they detect rising CO₂ and acidity and signal the brain to increase breathing and heart rate." Pair them with baroreceptors in exercise regulation. 🔗 Related terms Baroreceptor Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) Minute Ventilation Heart Rate Homeostasis pH 🎓 Where this appears

Chester Step Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chester Step Test General BTEC Sport Chester Step Test A simple stepping test that estimates aerobic fitness from how your heart responds to a rising workload. 📖 What it means The Chester Step Test is a submaximal, incremental step test used to predict VO₂ max . The performer steps up and down on a box in time with a set beat, and the stepping rate increases in stages.

At each stage, heart rate is recorded . Because heart rate and oxygen uptake rise together, the heart rate response across the increasing workloads is used to estimate VO₂ max — a lower heart rate at a given workload indicates greater aerobic fitness. As a submaximal test , it is safe, practical and requires minimal equipment, making it suitable for a wide range of people. Like other predictive tests, it gives an estimate rather than a direct measure , and depends on standardised procedures. 🏅 Sporting examples Estimating fitness A performer steps at increasing rates while their heart rate is recorded to estimate VO₂ max. Submaximal advantage

Being submaximal, the Chester Step Test can be used with people for whom a maximal test is unsuitable. Minimal equipment The test needs only a step and a metronome, making it practical in schools and clubs. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the Chester Step Test and evaluate it: "The Chester Step Test is a submaximal, incremental step test that predicts VO₂ max from the heart rate response to increasing workloads; it is safe, practical and needs little equipment, but gives an estimate rather than a direct measure." Group it with other submaximal predictors (Astrand, etc.). 🔗 Related terms

Chin-up Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chin-up Test BTEC Sport General Chin-up Test A fitness test of upper-body muscular strength and endurance. 📖 What it means The Chin-up Test is a test of upper-body strength endurance in which the athlete performs as many chin-ups or pull-ups as possible. Protocol: The athlete hangs from a bar with the arms fully extended and pulls up until the chin passes the bar, then lowers fully. Repetitions with full range are counted.

Interpreting results: A higher count shows better strength relative to body weight. Body mass strongly influences the score, so heavier athletes are at a disadvantage. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A climber completes 12 full chin-ups. Training use Assisted versions can be used with beginners. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures:

"The Chin-up Test assesses upper-body muscular strength and endurance; the result is compared with normative data or earlier scores to judge fitness or progress." Choice Reaction Time — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Choice Reaction Time IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Choice Reaction Time Reacting when you must choose between options. 📖 What it means Choice reaction time is the time between a stimulus and a response when there are several possible stimuli, each needing a different response , as in team sports. It is longer than simple reaction time (one stimulus, one response). Hick's law states that reaction time increases as the number of choices increases, in a logarithmic way. It can be reduced by practice, anticipation and better selective attention , which reduce the number of effective choices.

🏅 Sporting examples Football A midfielder chooses between pass, dribble and shoot. Boxing A boxer responds to different punches. Training Drills reduce the options the player needs to consider. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to Hick's law: "Choice reaction time rises as the number of response options increases, as described by Hick's law." Choline — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Choline IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Choline A nutrient needed by the nerves and brain. 📖 What it means Choline is an essential nutrient , grouped with the B vitamins in its effects. The body needs it to make acetylcholine , the neurotransmitter that triggers muscle contraction, and to build cell membranes . Good sources are eggs, liver, meat, fish, soya and some vegetables such as broccoli. Most people get enough from a varied diet. Choline supplements have been studied for endurance and mental performance, but the evidence of any benefit for healthy athletes is weak. 🏅 Sporting examples Diet

Eggs and meat give most adults enough choline. Nervous system Acetylcholine released at the neuromuscular junction needs choline to be made. Supplements Evidence for a performance boost in healthy athletes is limited. ✍️ Using the term in context State the role: "Choline is needed to make acetylcholine, which carries the signal from nerve to muscle at the neuromuscular junction." Chondrocyte — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chondrocyte IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Chondrocyte The cell that builds and maintains cartilage. 📖 What it means A chondrocyte is the main cell of cartilage . It makes and maintains the extracellular matrix , which contains collagen and other molecules that give cartilage its strength and elasticity. Chondrocytes sit in small spaces called lacunae . Cartilage has no direct blood supply, so chondrocytes get nutrients by diffusion and the tissue heals slowly. Joint loading, such as moderate exercise, stimulates chondrocytes, helping keep articular cartilage healthy. 🏅 Sporting examples

Joint health Regular moderate loading helps cartilage stay healthy. Injury Damaged cartilage heals slowly because chondrocytes have limited blood supply. Growth Chondrocytes in the growth plate help bones lengthen in children. ✍️ Using the term in context State the role: "Chondrocytes are the cells of cartilage that produce and maintain the matrix of collagen that gives cartilage its properties." Chronic Adaptation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chronic Adaptation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Chronic Adaptation The lasting changes training builds — the long-term adaptations that separate a trained body from an untrained one. 📖 What it means Chronic adaptations are the long-term physiological changes that result from consistent, repeated exercise over weeks and months. They are distinct from the immediate (acute) responses to a single bout of exercise.

They occur across the body's systems. Cardiovascular adaptations include cardiac hypertrophy, increased stroke volume and capillarisation ; respiratory and muscular adaptations include increased mitochondria and improved buffering . Together these improve performance and efficiency. Chronic adaptations are the goal of training and depend on the principles of training — particularly progressive overload and specificity. They are also subject to reversibility : if training stops, the adaptations are gradually lost. 🏅 Sporting examples Cardiovascular Months of endurance training produce chronic adaptations such as a larger heart and greater capillary density. Acute vs chronic

A single run raises heart rate (acute), but repeated training lowers resting heart rate over time (chronic). Reversibility Chronic adaptations are gradually lost if training stops, reflecting the principle of reversibility. ✍️ Using the term in context Define chronic adaptations and contrast with acute responses: "Chronic adaptations are the long-term physiological changes from consistent training, such as cardiac hypertrophy and capillarisation; they differ from acute responses to a single session and are lost if training stops (reversibility)." Give examples across body systems. 🔗 Related terms

Chronotropic State — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chronotropic State IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Chronotropic State A description of whether the heart rate is being sped up or slowed down. 📖 What it means Chronotropic describes anything that affects heart rate . A positive chronotropic effect speeds the heart up, and a negative chronotropic effect slows it down. Sympathetic stimulation and adrenaline are positive chronotropic factors. Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation is negative chronotropic. Chronotropic incompetence is the inability of the heart rate to rise properly with exercise, which may indicate heart disease.

🏅 Sporting examples Exercise start Sympathetic activity raises heart rate (positive chronotropic). Rest Vagal tone keeps heart rate low (negative chronotropic). Medication Beta blockers have a negative chronotropic effect and lower exercise heart rate. ✍️ Using the term in context Use the terms in pairs: "Adrenaline has a positive chronotropic effect on the heart, whereas vagal stimulation has a negative chronotropic effect." Chunking — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Chunking IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Chunking Grouping information to remember more. 📖 What it means Chunking means grouping small pieces of information into larger meaningful units . Circadian Rhythm — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Circadian Rhythm BTEC Sport General Circadian Rhythm The body's 24-hour internal clock. 📖 What it means A circadian rhythm is a cycle of about 24 hours in body processes such as sleep and wakefulness, body temperature, hormone release and alertness . It is controlled by an internal clock in the brain and is set by cues such as light . Body temperature, strength and reaction time tend to peak in the late afternoon or early evening , so many athletes perform best then. Travel across time zones ( jet lag ), shift work and poor sleep habits disrupt the rhythm and can reduce performance. 🏅 Sporting examples

Competition A swimmer used to training in the morning may perform better in the evening. Travel A team arrives early to adjust to a new time zone. Sleep Consistent bedtimes support recovery. ✍️ Using the term in context Link rhythm to performance: "Because body temperature and alertness peak in the late afternoon, many performance measures are higher at that time of day." Circuit Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Circuit Training General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Circuit Training A flexible, time-efficient training method built around stations — able to develop almost any fitness component depending on how it's set up. 📖 What it means Circuit training involves performing a series of exercises at different stations in sequence , with the performer moving from one to the next. A circuit can be repeated for several laps.

Its great strength is versatility : by choosing the exercises, work and rest periods, and loads, a circuit can be designed to develop strength, muscular endurance, aerobic fitness, or a mix — and to be highly sport-specific. It is also time-efficient and space-efficient , can train many people at once, and keeps sessions varied and engaging. Careful station ordering (e.g. alternating muscle groups) allows work to continue while some muscles recover. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sports A football pre-season circuit might mix agility ladders, press-ups, shuttle runs and core work to develop several components in one time-efficient session. Skill circuits

A basketball skill circuit alternates dribbling, shooting and passing stations, combining fitness and skill development. Strength endurance A circuit of resistance exercises with short rests and high repetitions targets muscular endurance. ✍️ Using the term in context Highlight the versatility and how design determines the outcome: "Circuit training uses a sequence of exercise stations; by adjusting the exercises, loads and work-to-rest ratios, it can be designed to develop strength, muscular endurance or aerobic fitness, and made sport-specific." Mention practical benefits: time-efficient, varied, and able to train groups. 🔗 Related terms

Circumduction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Circumduction IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Circumduction A circular sweep at a joint — the cone-shaped movement combining four others into one. 📖 What it means Circumduction is a circular movement at a joint that combines flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence, so the limb traces a cone shape. The end of the limb moves in a circle while the base stays relatively fixed. It occurs at joints with a wide range of movement, particularly ball and socket joints such as the shoulder and hip. Because it blends several movements, it produces the rounded, sweeping actions used in many sports.

Identifying circumduction is part of movement analysis : recognising it — and the joint that allows it — helps describe rounded actions such as an arm swing in a bowling or serving action. 🏅 Sporting examples Bowling The circular arm action in a cricket bowl involves circumduction at the shoulder. Arm circles Making large arm circles is circumduction — combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction. Ball and socket Circumduction occurs at ball and socket joints such as the shoulder and hip, which allow wide movement. ✍️ Using the term in context Define circumduction as a combined circular movement:

Closed Chain Kinematics — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Closed Chain Kinematics IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Closed Chain Kinematics Movement analysis where the end of the limb is fixed. 📖 What it means In a closed kinetic chain , the distal end of the limb is fixed (for example, the foot on the ground or the hands on a bar), so movement at one joint produces movement at the other joints. Closed chain kinematics describes the motion of the segments and joints in such movements. Examples are the squat, push-up and pull-up .

In an open chain movement, the end of the limb moves freely, as in a leg extension or a kick. Closed chain exercises are often used in rehabilitation because they load joints in a more functional and stable way. 🏅 Sporting examples Squat The feet are fixed on the floor and the hips, knees and ankles move together. Pull-up The hands are fixed on the bar while the body moves. Rehabilitation Closed chain exercises are used after knee injury to rebuild strength safely. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast with open chain: "In closed chain movements the distal segment is fixed, so joints move together, whereas in open chain movements the distal segment moves freely."

Closed Loop Control — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Closed Loop Control AS Level / Cambridge General IB Sport Science Closed Loop Control Movement guided by feedback — a control system that senses errors mid-action and corrects them. 📖 What it means Closed loop control is a motor control system that uses sensory feedback to detect and correct movement errors as the movement is happening . The 'loop' is closed because feedback returns to inform ongoing control.

During the movement, feedback from the senses and proprioceptors is compared against the intended action; any error is detected and the movement is adjusted. Because this feedback processing takes time, closed loop control suits slower, continuous movements where there is time to make corrections. It contrasts with open loop control , which runs a pre-programmed movement too fast to adjust mid-action. Closed loop control explains how performers make fine, ongoing adjustments — for example balancing or steadily tracking a target. 🏅 Sporting examples Balancing A gymnast on a beam uses closed loop control, constantly sensing and correcting their balance. Slow movements

Closed loop control suits slow, continuous actions where there is time to detect and fix errors. Contrast A fast, ballistic action such as a golf swing uses open loop control, being too quick to adjust mid-movement. ✍️ Using the term in context Define closed loop control and the movements it suits: "Closed loop control uses sensory feedback during a movement to detect and correct errors; because feedback takes time to process, it suits slower, continuous movements such as balancing, and contrasts with open loop control for fast actions." Contrast it with open loop control. 🔗 Related terms Open Loop Control Feedback Proprioception Motor Learning Motor Programme Kinaesthesis

Closed Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Closed Skill AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Closed Skill The counterpart to the open skill — a movement performed in a stable, predictable environment that the performer controls. 📖 What it means A closed skill is one performed in a stable, predictable and unchanging environment . The performer is not reacting to a shifting situation, so they can plan and repeat a well-grooved technique .

Closed skills are typically self-paced : the performer controls when and how the movement begins, rather than having the timing dictated by external factors. They rely less on decision-making and more on consistent, repeatable execution. Closed skills sit at one end of the open–closed continuum , opposite open skills. Because the environment is stable, they are best developed through repetitive, fixed practice that grooves the movement into a consistent motor programme. 🏅 Sporting examples Gymnastics A gymnast's vault is a closed skill — the apparatus and run-up are fixed, so the performer repeats a pre-planned, self-paced routine. Archery

Shooting an arrow is closed and self-paced: the target and conditions are stable, so the archer grooves a consistent technique. Free throw A basketball free throw is relatively closed — the distance and hoop never change, and the shooter controls the pace. ✍️ Using the term in context Justify the classification using environment and pacing: "A free throw is a closed skill because it is performed in a stable, predictable environment and is self-paced, allowing the performer to repeat a consistent, grooved technique." CNS Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › CNS Training IB Sport Science General CNS Training Training the nervous system, not just the muscle — maximal-effort work that sharpens the body's ability to produce force. 📖 What it means CNS (central nervous system) training refers to training methods — such as maximal-effort lifts and explosive efforts with full recovery — designed to improve the nervous system's ability to recruit and coordinate muscle, rather than primarily to build muscle size.

Strength and power depend not only on muscle size but on how effectively the nervous system activates the muscle — recruiting more motor units, firing them faster, and coordinating them. CNS-focused training targets these neural adaptations . Because it involves near-maximal efforts, CNS training requires full recovery between efforts and careful management to avoid excessive fatigue. It is used to develop maximal strength and power, and helps explain the strength gains that occur early in training before muscle size changes much. 🏅 Sporting examples Neural gains Heavy, maximal lifts with full recovery improve how well the nervous system recruits muscle, boosting strength.

Early strength gains CNS adaptations explain why strength can rise in the first weeks of training before muscle grows much. Full recovery Because efforts are near-maximal, CNS training requires long rests between efforts to stay effective. ✍️ Using the term in context Define CNS training and its target adaptation: "CNS training uses maximal-effort lifts and explosive efforts with full recovery to improve the nervous system's ability to recruit and coordinate muscle; it targets neural adaptations underpinning strength and power, rather than muscle size." Co-operativity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Co-operativity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Co-operativity How haemoglobin binds oxygen more readily once some oxygen is already attached. 📖 What it means Co-operativity describes how haemoglobin binds oxygen. Once one oxygen molecule binds, the shape of the haemoglobin changes so that it becomes easier for the next molecules to bind. This gives the characteristic S-shaped oxygen dissociation curve.

Cooperativity means haemoglobin is nearly saturated in the lungs, where oxygen is high, and releases oxygen readily in the muscles, where oxygen is low. This allows efficient oxygen loading and unloading during exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Lungs Haemoglobin loads oxygen efficiently in the lungs because of cooperativity. Muscle Cooperativity allows oxygen to be released in the muscles when pressure falls. Shift A rise in temperature or acidity shifts the curve, making more oxygen available to working muscles. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why the S-shaped dissociation curve helps exercise:

Coaching Styles — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coaching Styles General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Coaching Styles Different ways to lead learning — from telling to guiding to letting athletes discover for themselves. 📖 What it means Coaching styles are the distinct approaches a coach can take to instructing and developing performers. Common styles include command, reciprocal and guided discovery , which differ in how much control the coach retains and how actively the learner is involved.

In the command style , the coach makes the decisions and directs the learner — efficient and useful for beginners, large groups or safety-critical situations. In reciprocal style, learners work together giving each other feedback. In guided discovery , the coach sets problems for learners to solve, encouraging understanding and independence. The best style depends on the situation — the learners' stage, the task, the group size and safety. Effective coaches adapt their style, using more direction for beginners or dangerous skills and more discovery to develop understanding in experienced performers. 🏅 Sporting examples Command style

A coach uses the command style to give clear, safe instructions to a large beginner group. Guided discovery A coach poses tactical problems for experienced players to solve, developing their decision-making. Adapting An effective coach switches styles to suit the learners' stage, the task and safety needs. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the main coaching styles and note that choice depends on context: "Coaching styles include command (coach-directed), reciprocal (peer feedback) and guided discovery (problem-solving); the best choice depends on the learners' stage, the task, group size and safety, and effective coaches adapt their style." Coactivation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coactivation IB Sport Science General Coactivation Muscles bracing together — agonist and antagonist firing at once to lock and stabilise a joint. 📖 What it means Coactivation (co-contraction) is the simultaneous activation of agonist and antagonist muscles around a joint. Rather than one contracting while the other relaxes, both contract together. Its main purpose is to stabilise and stiffen a joint , providing control and protection. By tensing both sides of a joint at once, the body can hold a position firmly or resist unexpected forces.

Coactivation is important for stability, balance and injury protection — for example, bracing the muscles around the knee on landing, or stiffening the trunk during a heavy lift. It trades some efficiency of movement for greater joint control. 🏅 Sporting examples Joint stability On landing, the muscles around the knee coactivate to stiffen and stabilise the joint, protecting it. Bracing Coactivation of trunk muscles stiffens the core during a heavy lift, providing stability. Control Holding a steady position, such as a gymnast's balance, involves coactivation to lock the joints. ✍️ Using the term in context Define coactivation and its purpose:
