Coefficient of Friction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coefficient of Friction IB Sport Science General Coefficient of Friction A number that captures grip — how much two surfaces resist sliding, and therefore how much traction an athlete gets. 📖 What it means The coefficient of friction is a measure of the resistance between two surfaces in contact . A higher coefficient means more friction (more grip); a lower coefficient means less friction (more slide). It depends on the nature of the two surfaces in contact — their material and texture. In sport, it determines the traction between, for example, a shoe and the ground, or a ball and a surface.

The coefficient of friction has clear performance implications : high friction (grip) helps a sprinter drive off the track or a footballer change direction, while low friction (slide) benefits a curling stone or a skier. Athletes and equipment designers manipulate friction to suit the activity. 🏅 Sporting examples Traction A high coefficient of friction between studded boots and turf gives a footballer the grip to accelerate and turn. Low friction A curling stone glides because of the low coefficient of friction between the stone and the ice. Equipment design Grippy sole materials raise the coefficient of friction to improve traction for court sports. ✍️ Using the term in context

Coefficient of Restitution — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coefficient of Restitution IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Coefficient of Restitution A measure of how bouncy a ball or surface is. 📖 What it means The coefficient of restitution (COR) measures how much of an object's speed is retained after a collision . It is the speed after impact divided by the speed before impact (for a ball hitting a fixed surface). A value of 1 would be a perfectly elastic bounce, and 0 means the object does not bounce at all. A tennis ball has a high COR on a hard court and a lower COR on grass.

It depends on the material, temperature and pressure of the ball and the nature of the surface, and it is regulated in many sports to control the game. 🏅 Sporting examples Basketball A properly inflated ball bounces back to a set height. Tennis A new ball bounces higher than a worn one. Cricket The pitch affects how the ball bounces. ✍️ Using the term in context Define by ratio: "The coefficient of restitution is the ratio of the speed after a collision to the speed before it, and it indicates the bounciness of the object and surface." Cognitive Anxiety — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cognitive Anxiety IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Cognitive Anxiety The mental side of competitive nerves — the worry and negative thoughts that can undermine performance under pressure. 📖 What it means Cognitive anxiety is the mental or psychological component of anxiety . It involves worry, apprehension, negative thoughts, fear of failure and an inability to concentrate before or during performance. It is distinguished from somatic anxiety , which is the physical component (racing heart, sweating, tension). The two often occur together but respond to different management techniques.

According to catastrophe theory , high cognitive anxiety is particularly damaging when combined with high physiological arousal, potentially causing a sudden and dramatic drop in performance rather than a gradual decline. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf A golfer on the final putt experiencing racing negative thoughts and doubt about missing is showing cognitive anxiety, which can disrupt their focus. Exams of performance A gymnast worrying 'what if I fall?' before a routine is experiencing cognitive anxiety that can interfere with concentration. Management

Cognitive anxiety is best addressed with mental techniques such as positive self-talk, imagery and thought-stopping, rather than physical relaxation alone. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it as the mental component and pair it with somatic anxiety: "Cognitive anxiety is the mental component of anxiety, involving worry and negative thoughts, whereas somatic anxiety is the physical component; cognitive anxiety is best managed with strategies such as positive self-talk and imagery." Link it to catastrophe theory when high cognitive anxiety combines with high arousal. 🔗 Related terms Somatic Anxiety Anxiety Arousal Catastrophe Theory Self-Talk CSAI-2 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Cognitive Dissonance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cognitive Dissonance BTEC Sport General Cognitive Dissonance The uncomfortable feeling when beliefs and behaviour clash. 📖 What it means Cognitive dissonance , proposed by Leon Festinger , is the mental discomfort that arises when a person holds conflicting beliefs, attitudes or behaviours . People are motivated to reduce the discomfort by changing the belief, changing the behaviour or justifying the conflict. In sport and exercise, it can explain why people who believe exercise is important but do not exercise may start to downplay its value, and it is used to design interventions that change behaviour.

🏅 Sporting examples Exercise behaviour Someone who knows exercise is healthy but is inactive feels dissonance. Fair play A player who cheats but values honesty may justify it as 'everyone does it'. Cognitive Evaluation Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cognitive Evaluation Theory BTEC Sport General Cognitive Evaluation Theory The idea that rewards can undermine enjoyment. 📖 What it means Cognitive evaluation theory , part of self-determination theory (Deci and Ryan), explains how external rewards affect intrinsic motivation . If a reward is seen as controlling , it reduces the sense of autonomy and so lowers intrinsic motivation. If it gives information about competence (for example, praise for improvement), it can raise intrinsic motivation.

Coaches should therefore be careful with prizes and pressure for young players, and use feedback that supports competence. 🏅 Sporting examples Youth sport A child who loves playing is given money for each goal and loses interest when it stops. Cognitive Stage of Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cognitive Stage of Learning AS Level / Cambridge General Cognitive Stage of Learning The beginner's stage — the first phase of learning a new skill, defined by frequent errors and lots of thinking. 📖 What it means The cognitive stage is the first of Fitts and Posner's three stages of learning . It is the beginner phase, in which the performer is trying to understand and form a basic mental picture of what the skill involves.

Performance at this stage is characterised by frequent, large errors , slow and inconsistent execution, and a heavy reliance on conscious thought . The learner must think carefully about each part of the movement. Learners at this stage need clear demonstrations, simple instructions and lots of positive feedback , and benefit from breaking the skill into manageable parts. They rely heavily on external guidance to know whether they are doing it correctly. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis A beginner learning to serve is in the cognitive stage — they must think through the toss, grip and swing separately, and make many errors. Swimming

A novice swimmer concentrates hard on each element of a stroke, moving slowly and inconsistently as they build a basic understanding. Coaching approach A coach uses simple demonstrations and lots of encouragement with a cognitive-stage learner, breaking the skill into parts. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the stage's characteristics and the coaching it needs: "In the cognitive stage, the first of Fitts and Posner's stages, the beginner forms a mental picture of the skill, makes frequent large errors, and relies on conscious thought and clear demonstrations with positive feedback." Cohesion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cohesion BTEC General Cohesion The sense of unity that holds a team together and keeps it working towards shared goals. 📖 What it means Cohesion is the force that binds a group together. Cohesion develops through shared goals, clear roles, regular communication and positive experiences together. Cold Shock Response — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cold Shock Response BTEC General Cold Shock Response The sudden gasping and heart changes that happen when cold water hits the body. 📖 What it means The cold shock response is the body's immediate reaction to sudden immersion in cold water, typically in the first minute. It includes an involuntary gasp, hyperventilation, a rapid rise in heart rate and blood pressure, and a loss of breath control.

The response is a major cause of drowning in cold-water incidents, because a person who gasps and hyperventilates may inhale water. Preparation, controlled breathing and gradual entry reduce the risk for swimmers and sailors. 🏅 Sporting examples Open water A swimmer who jumps into cold open water may experience a strong cold shock response. Collateral Circulation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Collateral Circulation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Collateral Circulation Back-up blood vessels that take over when a main route is blocked. 📖 What it means Collateral circulation is a network of smaller blood vessels that provide an alternative route for blood when a main artery is blocked or narrowed. The collateral vessels can enlarge over time, and they help maintain blood supply to tissue that would otherwise be deprived of oxygen.

Regular endurance training can stimulate the growth of collateral vessels in the heart and other tissues. This is one reason well-trained athletes may cope better with some circulatory problems. 🏅 Sporting examples Heart Collateral vessels can develop around a narrowed coronary artery, supplying blood to the heart muscle. Commercialisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Commercialisation AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Commercialisation How modern sport became big business — the growing influence of money, media and marketing, with both benefits and drawbacks. 📖 What it means Commercialisation is the process by which sport has increasingly become driven by profit and business interests , through sponsorship, broadcasting rights, advertising and merchandising. It links sport tightly with the media and commerce — often called the 'golden triangle' of sport, sponsorship and media.

It brings clear benefits : greater funding for athletes and clubs, improved facilities, wider media coverage, and increased global exposure that can grow participation and revenue. It also brings drawbacks : sport may be shaped to suit sponsors and broadcasters rather than participants — rule changes, altered scheduling, over-commercialisation, and pressure that can encourage deviance such as doping to meet financial expectations. 🏅 Sporting examples Broadcasting Television deals have reshaped scheduling and even rules in many sports to make them more marketable and viewer-friendly. Sponsorship

Elite athletes and teams rely on sponsorship income, which funds their sport but can also create pressure and conflicts of interest. Balanced view Commercialisation has funded better facilities and wider coverage, but critics argue it can prioritise profit over the interests of grassroots participants. ✍️ Using the term in context Give a balanced account with benefits and drawbacks: "Commercialisation links sport with media and business through sponsorship and broadcasting; it increases funding and exposure, but can shape sport to suit commercial interests and create pressure that may encourage deviance." Commotio Cordis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Commotio Cordis BTEC General Commotio Cordis A sudden cardiac arrest caused by a direct blow to the chest at the wrong moment in the heartbeat. 📖 What it means Commotio cordis is a rare cause of sudden cardiac arrest in which a blow to the chest, most often from a ball or other object, disrupts the heart's rhythm. Acute compartment syndrome follows a serious injury and needs emergency treatment, often surgery to release the pressure. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome develops during exercise and eases with rest, and it is common in runners and cyclists in the lower leg. 🏅 Sporting examples Running A runner with pain that builds during training and eases with rest may have chronic exertional compartment syndrome. Complex Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Complex Skill AS Level / Cambridge General Complex Skill A demanding, many-part skill — one that requires attention, decisions and coordination all at once. 📖 What it means A complex skill is one that involves several interrelated parts, high information-processing demands, and significant attention and decision-making . Complex skills are harder to learn and perform than simple ones.

They sit at one end of the simple–complex continuum , along which skills are classified by their difficulty and the demands they place on the performer. A simple skill (like a sprint start) requires little decision-making; a complex skill (like a tennis rally shot) requires judging many cues and coordinating a precise response. Because complex skills demand more attention and processing, they are often best learned when the performer is at a lower level of arousal , using approaches such as breaking the skill down, and with plenty of practice to reduce the attention required as the skill becomes more automatic. 🏅 Sporting examples High demands

A tennis player selecting and executing a shot in a rally performs a complex skill with high processing demands. Contrast A complex skill (a gymnastics routine) contrasts with a simple skill (a forward roll) on the simple–complex continuum. Learning Complex skills are often broken down and practised extensively, and are best performed at lower arousal. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a complex skill on the simple–complex continuum: "A complex skill involves several interrelated parts, high information-processing demands and significant decision-making; it sits at one end of the simple–complex continuum and is harder to learn, often benefiting from being broken down."

Complex Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Complex Training IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Complex Training Pairing heavy and explosive — a method that uses a heavy lift to supercharge the power move that follows. 📖 What it means Complex training is a training method that pairs a heavy resistance exercise with a biomechanically similar explosive (plyometric) exercise , performed one after the other — for example, a heavy squat followed by jump squats.

It works through a phenomenon called post-activation potentiation : the heavy lift briefly primes the nervous system and muscles, so the explosive exercise that follows can be performed more powerfully than usual. Complex training is used to develop power , combining the strength stimulus of heavy lifting with the speed stimulus of plyometrics. Because it is demanding, it suits well-trained athletes and requires adequate recovery within and between sessions. 🏅 Sporting examples Heavy then explosive An athlete performs heavy squats, then immediately does jump squats, which feel more powerful (post-activation potentiation). Complex training combines strength and speed stimuli to develop explosive power. Components of Fitness — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Components of Fitness General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Components of Fitness The building blocks of physical fitness — the distinct qualities that together determine what a performer's body can do. 📖 What it means The components of fitness are the individual physical qualities that together make up a person's overall fitness . They are usually divided into two groups.

Health-related components are those linked to health and general function: cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition. Skill-related components are those linked to sporting performance: agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. Different sports demand different combinations and emphases of these components, so identifying the key components for a sport is the starting point for designing a relevant training programme and selecting appropriate fitness tests. 🏅 Sporting examples Gymnastics

Gymnastics demands a specific blend — high flexibility, balance, coordination and power — so training and testing focus on those components. Marathon For a marathon runner, cardiovascular endurance is by far the dominant component, so training and testing prioritise it. Concentration Gradient — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Concentration Gradient IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Concentration Gradient The difference in concentration that drives diffusion. 📖 What it means A concentration gradient is the difference in concentration of a substance between two regions. Diffusion moves particles from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration . The steeper the gradient, the faster the diffusion. In the body, gradients drive the movement of oxygen from alveoli to blood and from blood to muscle, and of carbon dioxide in the opposite direction.

Gradients are kept steep by blood flow and breathing , which constantly bring fresh oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. For gases, the concentration gradient is described as a partial pressure gradient. 🏅 Sporting examples Alveoli High oxygen in the alveoli, low in blood arriving from the body. Exercise Working muscle uses up oxygen, steepening the gradient. Training More capillaries shorten diffusion distances. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to gas exchange: "Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood down a concentration gradient maintained by ventilation and blood flow." Concentric Contraction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Concentric Contraction IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Concentric Contraction The muscle shortening under load — the 'lifting' phase that produces most positive work in sport. 📖 What it means A concentric contraction is a type of isotonic contraction in which the muscle shortens as it generates force . It is the contraction that produces movement against a resistance — the 'positive' or lifting phase.

For example, in the upward phase of a biceps curl, the biceps contracts concentrically, shortening to lift the weight. The muscle generates enough force to overcome the resistance, so it shortens. Concentric contractions are contrasted with eccentric contractions (the muscle lengthening under tension) and isometric contractions (no change in length). Identifying the type of contraction in each phase of a movement is a core part of movement analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Lifting phase In the upward phase of a biceps curl, the biceps contracts concentrically to lift the weight. Jumping The leg muscles contract concentrically to extend the joints and drive the body upward in a jump. Analysis

Analysing a press-up, the triceps work concentrically in the pushing-up phase. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a concentric contraction and give an example: "A concentric contraction is an isotonic contraction in which the muscle shortens as it generates force, as in the upward phase of a biceps curl; it produces movement against a resistance." Conconi Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Conconi Test General Conconi Test A running-based way to find your threshold — spotting where heart rate stops keeping pace with speed. 📖 What it means The Conconi Test is a field test that estimates the anaerobic threshold by identifying the point at which the relationship between heart rate and running speed changes.

The performer runs at progressively increasing speeds while heart rate is recorded. At lower speeds, heart rate rises in a fairly straight line with speed; at a certain intensity, the line deflects (flattens) as heart rate no longer keeps pace with speed. This deflection point is taken to estimate the anaerobic threshold. As a field test, the Conconi Test is practical and requires only a track and a heart rate monitor , making it accessible for endurance athletes. However, the deflection point can be difficult to identify clearly, so results are an estimate and depend on careful, standardised testing. 🏅 Sporting examples Finding the threshold

A runner's heart rate deflects from its straight-line rise at a certain speed, estimating their anaerobic threshold. Practical test The Conconi Test needs only a track and a heart rate monitor, making it accessible for endurance athletes. Training zones Knowing the estimated threshold from the test helps set training intensities. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the Conconi Test and what it estimates: "The Conconi Test estimates the anaerobic threshold by finding the running speed at which heart rate deflects from its straight-line rise; it is practical, needing only a track and heart rate monitor, but the deflection point can be hard to identify."

Concurrent Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Concurrent Training IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Concurrent Training Training that combines endurance and strength work in one programme. 📖 What it means Concurrent training combines endurance and strength training in the same programme. Athletes in many sports need both, but research suggests that endurance training can interfere with strength and power gains, especially when the two are heavy and performed close together.

Interference is smaller when sessions are separated, when the endurance work is low intensity and when the programme is planned around the athlete's goals. Good planning allows both adaptations to develop. 🏅 Sporting examples Rowing A rower combines heavy strength work with endurance intervals, planned on separate days to limit interference. Concussion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Concussion IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Concussion A serious brain injury that sport is taking increasingly seriously — essential knowledge for injury, welfare and safeguarding topics. 📖 What it means A concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head or a force transmitted to the head , producing a temporary disturbance of brain function. It does not require a loss of consciousness to be serious.

Symptoms can include headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea, blurred vision and memory problems , and may appear immediately or develop over the following hours. Because symptoms can be subtle, structured assessment protocols are used. Modern sport applies a cautious, welfare-first approach — summarised by the principle 'if in doubt, sit them out' — with graduated return-to-play protocols, because a second impact before recovery can cause severe, lasting harm. 🏅 Sporting examples Rugby Rugby has introduced Head Injury Assessments and strict return-to-play protocols to manage the high risk of concussion from tackles and collisions. Football

Concern over repeated heading and head clashes has led football to adopt concussion substitutes and cautious management guidelines. Welfare principle A coach removes a player showing any signs of concussion immediately, following 'if in doubt, sit them out', rather than risking a second impact. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it carefully and emphasise the cautious management approach: "Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow to the head; because a second impact before recovery can be severe, sport applies cautious protocols such as immediate removal and graduated return to play." Note that loss of consciousness is not required for a concussion to be serious.

Conduction (heat loss) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Conduction (heat loss) IB Sport Science General Conduction (heat loss) Losing heat by contact — body warmth passing directly into a cooler surface or object. 📖 What it means Conduction is the transfer of body heat to a cooler object or surface through direct contact . It is one of the ways the body loses heat to help regulate its temperature.

Heat flows from the warmer body to the cooler surface it touches. In sport, conduction is a relatively minor route of heat loss in most situations, but it becomes significant with direct contact with cold — for example, cold-water immersion , where heat is conducted rapidly into the surrounding water. Conduction is one of four heat-loss mechanisms, alongside convection, radiation and evaporation . During exercise, evaporation of sweat is usually the main route, but conduction contributes to overall thermoregulation and is exploited in some cooling and recovery strategies. 🏅 Sporting examples Cold-water immersion

In an ice bath, heat is lost rapidly by conduction from the body into the cold water. Direct contact Sitting on cold ground transfers body heat to the surface by conduction. Minor route In most exercise, conduction is a minor route of heat loss compared with sweating (evaporation). ✍️ Using the term in context Define conduction as a heat-loss mechanism: "Conduction is the transfer of body heat to a cooler object or surface through direct contact; it is usually a minor route of heat loss but becomes significant with cold-water immersion, and is one of four mechanisms alongside convection, radiation and evaporation." Connective Tissue — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Connective Tissue IB Sport Science General Connective Tissue The body's biological glue and scaffolding — tissue that supports, connects and separates everything else. 📖 What it means Connective tissue is tissue that supports, connects or separates different types of tissues and organs in the body. It is one of the main tissue types and takes many forms.

It includes structures highly relevant to movement: tendons (connecting muscle to bone), ligaments (connecting bone to bone), cartilage (cushioning joints), and even bone and adipose (fat) tissue . Each is specialised for its role of support, connection or storage. Because connective tissues such as tendons and ligaments transmit forces and stabilise joints, their health and strength matter for both performance and injury resistance . Like muscle, some connective tissue adapts to the loads placed on it through training. 🏅 Sporting examples Tendons and ligaments Tendons and ligaments are connective tissues that transmit force and stabilise joints during movement. Cushioning

Cartilage, a connective tissue, cushions the joints against impact. Adaptation Connective tissues such as tendons can strengthen in response to the loads of training. ✍️ Using the term in context Define connective tissue and give relevant examples: "Connective tissue supports, connects or separates other tissues and organs; examples relevant to movement include tendons, ligaments, cartilage and bone, which transmit force, stabilise joints and cushion impact." Conservation of Angular Momentum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Conservation of Angular Momentum IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Conservation of Angular Momentum The rule that spin stays constant unless an external turning force acts on the body. 📖 What it means The conservation of angular momentum states that the total angular momentum of a body stays constant when no external torque acts on it. If the body changes its shape or moment of inertia, its angular velocity must change to keep angular momentum the same.

In sport, divers and gymnasts use this principle. Pulling the limbs in reduces the moment of inertia, so rotation speeds up. Extending the body increases the moment of inertia, so rotation slows. 🏅 Sporting examples Diving A diver tucks in to increase rotation speed and extends to slow it before entry. Gymnastics A gymnast pulls into a tuck to complete more rotations in the air. Figure skating A skater pulls in their arms to spin faster. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why a diver tucks to increase rotation: "By tucking, the diver reduces their moment of inertia, and since angular momentum is conserved, their angular velocity increases, so they complete the somersault faster."

Conservation of Energy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Conservation of Energy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Conservation of Energy The rule that energy is never lost, only changed from one form to another. 📖 What it means The conservation of energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or converted from one form to another. In sport, chemical energy from food is converted into kinetic and potential energy, although some is always lost as heat.

The principle helps explain performance. A jump converts elastic energy stored in the muscles and tendons into gravitational potential energy as the body rises, and the energy is later converted back as the body falls. 🏅 Sporting examples Jump The energy from the muscles is converted into the potential energy of height as the athlete rises. Swing A pendulum-like arm swing converts kinetic into potential energy and back. Conservation of Momentum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Conservation of Momentum IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Conservation of Momentum The rule that the total motion of a system is unchanged unless an outside force acts on it. 📖 What it means The conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of a system remains constant if no external force acts on it. When two bodies collide, the momentum lost by one is gained by the other, so the total stays the same.

In sport, this principle explains collisions and pushes. A player who pushes against a team-mate in a rugby tackle changes their own momentum, and the opposing player's momentum changes in the opposite direction. 🏅 Sporting examples Collisions In a rugby tackle, the momentum of the two players combined is conserved. Recoil A kayaker pushing off the paddle gains momentum in one direction, with the water gaining it in the other. Continuous, Serial and Discrete Continuum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Continuous, Serial and Discrete Continuum AS Level / Cambridge General Continuous, Serial and Discrete Continuum One way to classify any skill — by how clearly it has a beginning and an end. 📖 What it means The continuous–serial–discrete continuum is a way of classifying skills by how clearly their start and end points are defined , and how they are structured.

A discrete skill has a clear beginning and end (a single, brief action such as a throw or a kick). A serial skill links several discrete skills together in a set order (such as a triple jump). A continuous skill has no clear start or finish and flows on repeatedly (such as running, cycling or swimming). Classifying a skill on this continuum helps guide how it is best practised — for example, serial skills often suit part practice or chaining, while continuous skills are typically practised as a whole. It is one of several ways of classifying skills, alongside the open–closed and simple–complex continua. 🏅 Sporting examples Discrete

A penalty kick is a discrete skill — one brief action with a clear start and end. Serial A triple jump is a serial skill, linking the discrete hop, step and jump in order. Continuous Running is a continuous skill, flowing on with no clear beginning or end. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the continuum and the three categories: "The continuous–serial–discrete continuum classifies skills by how clearly their start and end are defined: discrete skills have a clear beginning and end, serial skills link discrete skills in order, and continuous skills flow on with no clear start or finish." Continuous Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Continuous Training AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Continuous Training Steady, sustained work at a constant pace — the foundational method for building aerobic endurance. 📖 What it means Continuous training involves sustained exercise at a steady, moderate intensity without rest intervals , typically for 20 minutes or more. It is the classic method for developing aerobic endurance .

By keeping the heart rate in the aerobic training zone for a prolonged period, it drives adaptations such as increased stroke volume, capillary density and mitochondria , improving the body's ability to deliver and use oxygen. Its strengths are that it is simple, requires no special equipment, and is effective for base endurance . Its limitations are that it can be time-consuming and monotonous , and it does not develop anaerobic fitness or replicate the stop-start nature of many sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running A steady 45-minute run at a conversational pace is a classic continuous training session, building the aerobic base of a distance runner. A long, steady ride at a constant effort develops the aerobic endurance a road cyclist needs for extended events. Base building A footballer uses continuous training in pre-season to build the aerobic base that supports repeated sprints during matches. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the method and link it to aerobic adaptations: "Continuous training involves sustained, steady-intensity exercise without rest for at least 20 minutes, developing aerobic endurance through adaptations such as increased stroke volume and capillary density." Contractility — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Contractility IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Contractility How strongly the heart muscle can contract, beat by beat. 📖 What it means Contractility is the intrinsic ability of the heart muscle to contract with force. Increased contractility produces a stronger contraction and a larger stroke volume for the same filling pressure. It is increased by sympathetic activity and adrenaline.

Contractility is distinct from preload (the stretch of the ventricle before contraction) and afterload (the resistance to ejection). Together these factors determine stroke volume, and endurance training improves the heart's ability to contract strongly. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise Adrenaline increases contractility, which raises stroke volume during exercise. Training Endurance training improves contractility, helping the heart pump more blood per beat. Contrast Water Therapy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Contrast Water Therapy BTEC General Contrast Water Therapy Alternating hot and cold water immersion used to support recovery. 📖 What it means Contrast water therapy involves alternating immersion between hot and cold water, often in cycles of a few minutes each. It is used by athletes to ease soreness and support recovery, based on the idea that alternating vasodilation and vasoconstriction helps move fluid through the tissues.

Evidence on its effectiveness is mixed. Some studies report reduced soreness, while others find little benefit. It is best viewed as one option among several recovery methods, alongside sleep, nutrition and active recovery. 🏅 Sporting examples After a match A footballer uses contrast water therapy after a match, alternating hot and cold baths. Team recovery A squad uses contrast therapy as part of a recovery routine, combined with sleep and nutrition. Controlled Variable — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Controlled Variable IB Sport Science General Controlled Variable What you hold constant to keep a test fair — the factors kept the same so results are trustworthy. 📖 What it means A controlled variable is a factor kept constant during an investigation to ensure a fair test of the independent variable's effect on the dependent variable.

In an experiment, the researcher changes the independent variable and measures the dependent variable . Controlled variables are all the other factors that could affect the result and so must be kept the same across conditions — otherwise it would be impossible to know whether any change was due to the independent variable or to something else. Controlling variables is essential for valid, reliable results and is a key part of designing an investigation — for example, in the sport science internal assessment. Failing to control an important variable weakens the conclusions that can be drawn. 🏅 Sporting examples Fair test

Testing whether a warm-up affects sprint time, the researcher keeps the surface, footwear and time of day constant — these are controlled variables. Valid results Controlling other factors ensures any change in the dependent variable is due to the independent variable. Investigation design Identifying and controlling variables is a key part of designing a valid sport science investigation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a controlled variable and its purpose:

Contusion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Contusion IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Contusion A bruise from a blow — soft-tissue damage and bleeding beneath the skin, common in contact sport. 📖 What it means A contusion is a bruise caused by a direct blow that damages soft tissue and small blood vessels beneath the skin, without breaking the skin. It is a common acute injury in contact and collision sports. The blow ruptures small blood vessels, causing bleeding into the tissue that produces the characteristic discolouration, along with pain, swelling and tenderness . A deep contusion to a muscle can temporarily limit its function.

Immediate treatment follows the RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) to limit bleeding and swelling. Most contusions heal with time and appropriate management, though severe ones need medical assessment. 🏅 Sporting examples Contact sports A knock to the thigh in rugby can cause a contusion — a deep bruise with pain and swelling (a 'dead leg'). Direct blow A contusion results from a direct impact that ruptures small blood vessels under the skin. Convection (heat loss) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Convection (heat loss) IB Sport Science General Convection (heat loss) Losing heat to moving air or water — the cooling breeze effect that carries body warmth away. 📖 What it means Convection is the transfer of body heat to moving air or water passing over the skin . As cooler air or water moves across the body, it carries heat away, helping to regulate temperature.

The faster the air or water moves, the greater the heat loss — which is why a breeze, or the airflow created by cycling or running, feels cooling. Conversely, still, warm air reduces convective heat loss, making exercise in such conditions feel hotter. Convection is one of four heat-loss mechanisms, alongside conduction, radiation and evaporation . It contributes to thermoregulation during exercise, working with the redirection of blood to the skin to move heat from the core to the surface where it can be lost. 🏅 Sporting examples Cooling breeze A cyclist is cooled by convection as they move quickly through the air, carrying heat away from the skin. Airflow

The faster the air moves over the skin, the greater the convective heat loss. Still air Exercising in still, warm air reduces convective heat loss, making it feel hotter. ✍️ Using the term in context Define convection as a heat-loss mechanism: "Convection is the transfer of body heat to moving air or water passing over the skin; heat loss increases as the air or water moves faster, which is why a breeze or the airflow of cycling feels cooling." Coordination — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coordination General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Coordination Smooth, well-timed movement — using different body parts together efficiently to produce fluent action. 📖 What it means Coordination is the ability to use different parts of the body together smoothly and efficiently . Core Stability — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Core Stability General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Core Stability The foundation of efficient, injury-resistant movement — the trunk strength that lets the limbs work from a stable base. 📖 What it means Core stability is the ability of the muscles of the trunk to support the spine and pelvis , providing a stable base from which the limbs can move efficiently. A stable core allows force to be transferred effectively between the upper and lower body and helps maintain good posture and technique under load. Cori Cycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cori Cycle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Cori Cycle How the body recycles lactate back into fuel. 📖 What it means The Cori cycle is a metabolic pathway that moves the by-products of anaerobic glycolysis between muscle and liver. Working muscle produces lactate , which diffuses into the blood and travels to the liver . In the liver, lactate is converted back to glucose by gluconeogenesis. The glucose is released into the blood and can be taken up again by muscle to be used as fuel or stored as glycogen.

The cycle costs the liver energy (ATP) but allows muscle to keep producing energy anaerobically, and it helps clear lactate after hard exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Repeated sprints Lactate produced in the legs during a series of 200m efforts is partly cleared by the liver and returned as glucose. Recovery During a cool-down jog, lactate continues to be removed from the blood, partly through the Cori cycle. Endurance events In long events the liver's glucose output, supported by lactate recycling, helps maintain blood glucose. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the path and the purpose:

Coronal Plane — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coronal Plane IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Coronal Plane The vertical plane that runs side to side, where sideways movements take place. 📖 What it means The coronal plane , also called the frontal plane, is a vertical plane that divides the body into front and back halves. Coronary Artery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Coronary Artery IB Sport Science General Coronary Artery The heart's own blood supply — the vessels that feed the muscle that pumps for everything else. 📖 What it means The coronary arteries are the blood vessels that supply oxygenated blood to the heart muscle (myocardium) itself . Although the heart is full of blood, its muscular walls need their own dedicated supply. During exercise, the heart works much harder and so needs more oxygen ; blood flow through the coronary arteries increases to meet this demand. Healthy coronary arteries are essential for the heart to function under the stress of exercise.

The coronary arteries are central to heart health . If they become narrowed (for example by fatty deposits), the heart muscle's oxygen supply can be compromised — the basis of coronary heart disease. Regular exercise helps keep them healthy. 🏅 Sporting examples Feeding the heart The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself with oxygenated blood so it can keep pumping. During exercise Coronary blood flow increases during exercise to meet the hard-working heart's greater oxygen demand. Heart health Narrowing of the coronary arteries reduces the heart's oxygen supply — the basis of coronary heart disease. ✍️ Using the term in context State what the coronary arteries do:

Correlation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Correlation IB Sport Science General Correlation A key statistical idea for analysing data — how two variables change together, and the classic warning that it doesn't prove cause. 📖 What it means Correlation is a statistical relationship between two variables , describing how they change together. A positive correlation means both increase together; a negative correlation means one increases as the other decreases. The strength of a correlation is often expressed as a correlation coefficient between −1 and +1, where values near ±1 indicate a strong relationship and values near 0 indicate little or no relationship.

The essential caution is that correlation does not prove causation . Two variables may be related because one causes the other, because a third factor influences both, or by coincidence — so a correlation alone cannot establish cause and effect. 🏅 Sporting examples IB internal assessment A student investigating the relationship between training volume and VO₂ max would report the correlation between the two variables in their analysis. Fitness data A coach might find a positive correlation between players' sprint times and their leg power scores — but would be careful not to claim one directly causes the other. Avoiding the trap

Finding that two variables correlate does not prove one causes the other; a controlled experiment is needed to investigate causation. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the relationship and include the causation caveat: "The data showed a positive correlation between training volume and VO₂ max; however, correlation does not prove causation, as a third variable could influence both." Cortisol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cortisol IB Sport Science General Cortisol The body's main stress hormone — mobilising fuel during prolonged effort, but catabolic if it lingers. 📖 What it means Cortisol is a stress hormone released by the adrenal cortex . It is secreted in response to stress, including the stress of prolonged or intense exercise. Cortisol helps the body cope with prolonged demand by supporting the metabolism of fat and protein for energy and helping to maintain blood glucose. This is useful during long-duration exercise when carbohydrate stores are running low.

However, cortisol has catabolic effects — meaning it can break down tissue, including muscle protein — so chronically elevated cortisol (for example from overtraining or inadequate recovery) can impair adaptation and recovery. Balancing training stress with recovery keeps cortisol's effects beneficial. 🏅 Sporting examples Prolonged exercise During a long endurance event, cortisol supports fat and protein metabolism as carbohydrate stores deplete. Catabolic effect Chronically high cortisol, as in overtraining, can break down muscle protein and impair recovery. Recovery balance Adequate recovery helps keep cortisol from remaining elevated, protecting training adaptations.

✍️ Using the term in context Define cortisol and note its dual role: "Cortisol is a stress hormone from the adrenal cortex that supports fat and protein metabolism during prolonged exercise; however, it is catabolic, so chronically elevated cortisol from overtraining can impair recovery and adaptation." Cramp — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cramp General BTEC Sport Cramp A sudden, seizing muscle — the involuntary, painful contraction that can strike mid-effort. 📖 What it means Cramp is a sudden, involuntary and painful contraction of a muscle . The muscle tightens and will not relax, causing acute pain, and often occurs during or after exercise. Cramp is commonly associated with dehydration and the loss of electrolytes (such as sodium) through sweating, as well as with muscle fatigue . These factors are thought to disrupt the normal control of muscle contraction and relaxation.

Immediate relief usually comes from gently stretching and massaging the affected muscle . Prevention focuses on maintaining good hydration and electrolyte balance , adequate conditioning to reduce fatigue, and appropriate warm-up. 🏅 Sporting examples Late in a game A footballer's calf cramps late in a match, when fatigue and fluid and electrolyte loss are greatest. Relief Gently stretching and massaging the cramping muscle usually relieves it. Prevention Maintaining hydration and electrolyte balance helps prevent cramp during prolonged exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context Define cramp and its associated causes:

Creatine Kinase — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Creatine Kinase IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Creatine Kinase An enzyme that supports energy supply in muscle and is a marker of muscle damage. 📖 What it means Creatine kinase (CK) is an enzyme that catalyses the transfer of a phosphate between creatine phosphate and ADP, regenerating ATP. Creatine — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Creatine IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Creatine One of the most researched legal supplements in sport — aimed at boosting the body's rapid-energy system for explosive efforts. 📖 What it means Creatine is a naturally occurring compound , found in foods such as meat and made by the body, and one of the most widely used and researched legal ergogenic aids . Supplementing with creatine aims to increase the muscles' stores of phosphocreatine (PCr) , the fuel for the ATP-PC energy system. Greater PCr stores can support repeated short, high-intensity efforts and may aid gains in strength and muscle mass over time.

Creatine is most likely to benefit explosive, repeated-effort activities rather than endurance events. It is legal and generally considered safe, though possible side effects such as water retention should be considered. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting and jumps A sprinter or jumper may use creatine to support the repeated maximal efforts of training, drawing on the ATP-PC system. Team sports A rugby player might use creatine to support the repeated high-intensity sprints and collisions of training and matches. Critical Swim Speed — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Critical Swim Speed IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Critical Swim Speed A fitness test of swimming endurance and training pace. 📖 What it means The Critical Swim Speed is a measure of the fastest swimming speed an athlete can sustain aerobically, calculated from two timed swims of different distances. Interpreting results: The value is used to set training paces for endurance sets. It correlates with the lactate threshold, so it helps plan aerobic training in the pool. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A swimmer's 200m and 400m times are used to set a training pace. Training use Retest every few weeks to adjust the training paces. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Cryotherapy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cryotherapy IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Cryotherapy The therapeutic use of cold — ice and cold water used to reduce swelling, pain and speed recovery. 📖 What it means Cryotherapy is the therapeutic use of cold — such as ice packs, cold-water immersion (ice baths) or whole-body cold chambers — to reduce swelling, pain and inflammation and to aid recovery .

Applying cold causes vasoconstriction (narrowing of blood vessels), which reduces blood flow to the area. This helps limit swelling and inflammation and numbs pain , making it a common immediate treatment for acute injuries (the 'Ice' in RICE) and a popular recovery strategy after hard training. In injury management, cryotherapy is used soon after injury to control swelling; in recovery, cold-water immersion is used to reduce muscle soreness. Care is needed to avoid ice burns, and evidence for some recovery uses is mixed, so it is one tool among several. 🏅 Sporting examples Acute injury

An ice pack applied to a sprained ankle (the 'Ice' in RICE) uses cryotherapy to limit swelling and numb pain. Recovery An athlete takes an ice bath after a hard session to reduce muscle soreness. CSAI-2 — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › CSAI-2 IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General CSAI-2 A widely used questionnaire that measures the different faces of competitive anxiety — splitting it into mind, body and confidence. 📖 What it means The CSAI-2 (Competitive State Anxiety Inventory-2) is a questionnaire that measures an athlete's state anxiety before or during competition . It is a self-report tool completed close to the event.

It measures three separate subcomponents: cognitive anxiety (mental worry), somatic anxiety (physical symptoms), and self-confidence . Measuring them separately is useful because they behave differently and respond to different interventions. As a self-report measure it is quick and practical, but it relies on honest, accurate responses and only captures a snapshot in time. It is a common example of a psychological assessment tool in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-competition profiling A sport psychologist uses the CSAI-2 before events to see whether an athlete's problem is high cognitive anxiety, high somatic anxiety, or low confidence — then tailors the intervention.

Monitoring interventions By repeating the CSAI-2, a psychologist can check whether a relaxation programme has actually reduced an athlete's somatic anxiety. Research The CSAI-2 is frequently used in research investigating the relationship between anxiety subcomponents and performance. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the three subcomponents it measures: "The CSAI-2 is a self-report questionnaire measuring three subcomponents of competitive state anxiety: cognitive anxiety, somatic anxiety and self-confidence, allowing interventions to be targeted." Cue Utilisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cue Utilisation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Cue Utilisation Why attention narrows under pressure — Easterbrook's theory linking arousal to the cues we notice. 📖 What it means Cue utilisation is Easterbrook's theory that a performer's level of arousal affects the range of environmental cues they can attend to . As arousal changes, the number of cues the performer takes in changes with it.

At low arousal , attention is broad and the performer takes in too many cues , including irrelevant ones, which can impair performance. At an optimal level of arousal , attention narrows to focus on the relevant cues , improving performance. At very high arousal , attention narrows too far, so relevant cues are missed — a phenomenon called perceptual narrowing. Cue utilisation helps explain the arousal–performance relationship and the inverted-U: it provides a mechanism for why moderate arousal aids performance while too much harms it, by describing how arousal filters the information a performer processes. 🏅 Sporting examples Optimal arousal

At optimal arousal, a playmaker filters out distractions and focuses on the relevant cues, reading the game well. Over-arousal When over-aroused, a player's attention narrows too far and they miss relevant cues, such as a free teammate. Explaining the inverted-U Cue utilisation provides a mechanism for the inverted-U, linking arousal to the cues a performer can process. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain cue utilisation and its link to arousal:

"Cue utilisation is Easterbrook's theory that arousal affects the range of cues a performer attends to: low arousal lets in too many cues, optimal arousal narrows attention to the relevant ones, and very high arousal narrows it too far so relevant cues are missed." Cumulative Trauma Disorder — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cumulative Trauma Disorder BTEC General Cumulative Trauma Disorder An injury that builds up over time from repeated stress on the same tissue. 📖 What it means A cumulative trauma disorder develops gradually from repeated stress, strain or movement on a tissue over a long period. It is also called an overuse injury, and it typically affects tendons, nerves and joints that repeat the same action many times.

Prevention includes managing training load, varying movements, ensuring good technique and equipment, and allowing adequate recovery. Early symptoms are often ignored, so monitoring pain patterns is important. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming Repeated shoulder movements can lead to a cumulative trauma disorder of the rotator cuff. Protocol: The athlete runs at about 8 mph (12.9 km/h) up a 20% gradient. The time to exhaustion is recorded.

Interpreting results: A longer time shows greater anaerobic capacity, and the time can be used in an equation to estimate anaerobic performance. The test is very demanding and needs supervision. Curvilinear Motion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Curvilinear Motion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Curvilinear Motion Movement along a curved path, such as a thrown ball or a runner around a bend. 📖 What it means Curvilinear motion describes movement along a curved path, in which the direction of motion changes continuously. A projectile in flight follows a curved path because gravity acts on it, and a runner moving around a bend follows a curve because a centripetal force acts towards the centre.

Curvilinear motion can be analysed by splitting it into horizontal and vertical components. The horizontal velocity stays constant in the absence of air resistance, while the vertical velocity changes under gravity. 🏅 Sporting examples Projectile A thrown ball follows a curved path, with the vertical velocity changing under gravity. Running bend A runner on a bend follows a curvilinear path, with a centripetal force keeping them on track. Cytosol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Cytosol IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Cytosol The fluid inside the cell where many reactions, including glycolysis, take place. 📖 What it means The cytosol is the fluid that fills the cell, surrounding the organelles. It contains water, ions, enzymes and dissolved molecules, and many metabolic reactions take place there, including glycolysis and the synthesis of some molecules. Dead Space — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dead Space IB Sport Science General Dead Space The air that never reaches the lungs' business end — the volume sitting in the airways that can't exchange gases. 📖 What it means Dead space is the volume of air in the conducting airways that does not participate in gas exchange . This air fills the passages leading to the lungs — the trachea and bronchi — but never reaches the alveoli where exchange occurs.

Because a portion of each breath simply fills these conducting airways, only the air that reaches the alveoli is available for gas exchange. This is why breathing pattern matters: shallow, rapid breaths waste a greater proportion of each breath on dead space. Understanding dead space helps explain why deeper breathing is more efficient during exercise: increasing tidal volume means a larger share of each breath reaches the alveoli for gas exchange, rather than being 'wasted' filling the conducting airways. 🏅 Sporting examples Wasted volume Part of every breath fills the trachea and bronchi (dead space) and never reaches the alveoli to exchange gases. Deep vs shallow

Deep breaths deliver proportionally more air to the alveoli than shallow, rapid breaths, which waste more on dead space. Exercise efficiency Increasing tidal volume during exercise reduces the proportion of each breath lost to dead space. ✍️ Using the term in context Define dead space and its significance: "Dead space is the volume of air in the conducting airways (trachea and bronchi) that does not reach the alveoli and so does not take part in gas exchange; deeper breathing is more efficient because a larger share of each breath reaches the alveoli." Deadlift — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Deadlift General BTEC Sport Deadlift A raw test of whole-body strength — lifting a loaded barbell from the floor, working the whole posterior chain. 📖 What it means The deadlift is a compound resistance exercise in which a loaded barbell is lifted from the floor to a standing position, then lowered under control. It is one of the most effective whole-body strength exercises.

As a multi-joint (compound) movement , it works many major muscle groups together — particularly the gluteals, hamstrings, back and core (the 'posterior chain') — along with the grip. This makes it highly effective for building total-body and posterior-chain strength. Because it develops the powerful hip extension used in sprinting, jumping and lifting , the deadlift features in many strength programmes. Correct technique — particularly maintaining a neutral spine — is essential to lift safely. 🏅 Sporting examples Posterior chain The deadlift builds the gluteals, hamstrings and back — the posterior chain that drives sprinting and jumping. Compound strength

As a multi-joint lift, the deadlift develops whole-body strength efficiently. Technique Maintaining a neutral spine is essential to deadlift safely and effectively. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the deadlift as a compound posterior-chain lift: "The deadlift is a compound resistance exercise lifting a loaded barbell from the floor; it works the posterior chain — gluteals, hamstrings, back and core — building whole-body strength used in sprinting and jumping." Decision Making — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Decision Making AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science General Decision Making The mental process at the heart of open, game-based skills — choosing the right action, fast, in a changing situation. 📖 What it means Decision making is the cognitive process of selecting the most appropriate response from the available options in a given situation. In sport it is central to open skills, where the environment is constantly changing.

It is a key stage of the information processing model : after perceiving and interpreting information (input), the performer chooses a response (decision making) before executing it (output). The quality and speed of the decision strongly affect performance. Decision making is influenced by factors such as experience, the number of possible choices (see Hick's Law), anticipation, and arousal . Skilled performers make faster, better decisions partly because they read cues earlier and filter out irrelevant information. 🏅 Sporting examples Football

A midfielder receiving the ball must rapidly decide whether to pass, dribble or shoot, reading the positions of teammates and opponents — high-quality decision making. Rugby A fly-half decides in a fraction of a second whether to pass, kick or run, based on the defensive line in front of them. Expertise An experienced netball player makes faster decisions than a novice because they anticipate play and recognise patterns earlier. ✍️ Using the term in context Place decision making within the information processing model:

"Decision making is the stage of information processing in which the performer selects a response; in open skills, faster and more accurate decisions, aided by experience and anticipation, are crucial to performance." Dehydration — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dehydration IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Dehydration The performance-wrecking consequence of losing more fluid than you take in — a small percentage loss has a surprisingly large effect. 📖 What it means Dehydration is a deficit of body water that occurs when fluid losses (mainly through sweating) exceed fluid intake. It impairs both physiological function and performance.

Even relatively small losses have a marked effect: as little as a 2% loss of body mass through dehydration can measurably reduce performance . Dehydration reduces plasma volume, which lowers stroke volume and contributes to cardiovascular drift and impaired thermoregulation. Because sweat losses can be high during prolonged or hot-weather exercise, athletes follow a planned hydration strategy — drinking before, during and after exercise — and may replace electrolytes as well as fluid. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A marathon runner who fails to drink adequately becomes dehydrated, losing plasma volume and suffering a rising heart rate and falling pace. Hot conditions

In hot, humid competition, high sweat rates make dehydration a serious risk, so hydration planning becomes critical. Performance effect A 2% loss of body mass from dehydration is enough to measurably impair endurance and cognitive performance. ✍️ Using the term in context State the cause, the threshold and the effects: "Dehydration occurs when fluid loss exceeds intake; a loss of around 2% of body mass can impair performance by reducing plasma volume, lowering stroke volume and impairing thermoregulation." Link it to a planned hydration strategy and cardiovascular drift. 🔗 Related terms Hydration Strategy Electrolytes Cardiovascular Drift Thermoregulation Plasma Stroke Volume

Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC General Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS) The muscle ache that appears one to three days after a hard or unfamiliar session. 📖 What it means Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is muscle pain and stiffness that develops 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed or intense exercise. It is most strongly linked to eccentric work, where the muscle lengthens under load, and it is thought to involve micro-damage to muscle fibres and an inflammatory response.

DOMS usually peaks around two to three days and then resolves. Gradual progression, a warm-up and repeated exposure to the same type of exercise reduce its severity, which is known as the repeated bout effect. 🏅 Sporting examples Downhill running A runner who descends a steep hill for the first time feels strong soreness in the quadriceps two days later. Dependent Variable — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dependent Variable IB Sport Science General Dependent Variable The thing you measure in an experiment — a foundational idea for the IB internal assessment and any scientific investigation. 📖 What it means The dependent variable is the factor that is measured in an investigation , and which may change as a result of the independent variable. Detraining — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Detraining IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Detraining Losing what you built — the reversal of training adaptations when training stops or drops off. 📖 What it means Detraining is the partial or complete reversal of training adaptations that results from stopping or substantially reducing training . The fitness gained through training is gradually lost.

It is the practical expression of the principle of reversibility ('use it or lose it'). Adaptations such as increased stroke volume, capillarisation and muscle size begin to decline once the training stimulus is removed, and both aerobic and strength adaptations reverse , though at different rates. Detraining commonly occurs during injury, illness or an extended break . It highlights the importance of maintaining some training, and is a key reason for using cross-training or maintenance work during periods when normal training isn't possible. 🏅 Sporting examples After a break An athlete who stops training over a long off-season experiences detraining, losing aerobic fitness and muscle.

Injury During injury, detraining can be limited by cross-training or maintenance work on unaffected areas. Reversibility Detraining is the principle of reversibility in action — adaptations decline once the stimulus is removed. ✍️ Using the term in context Define detraining and link it to reversibility: "Detraining is the partial or complete reversal of training adaptations from stopping or reducing training; it is the principle of reversibility in action, and can be limited by maintenance work or cross-training during breaks." Deviance in Sport — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Deviance in Sport AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Deviance in Sport Behaviour that breaks sport's accepted norms — from cheating and violence to doping, and a central theme in sport and society. 📖 What it means Deviance in sport is behaviour that breaks the accepted rules, norms or values of sport . It ranges from breaches of the written rules to violations of the unwritten 'spirit' of a sport.

Deviance can be shown by players (violence, cheating, doping, match-fixing), by officials (bias, corruption) and by spectators (hooliganism, racism). It can be aimed at gaining an unfair advantage or driven by external pressures. The causes of deviance are often linked to the pressures of modern, commercialised sport — the rewards for winning can tempt athletes toward doping or cheating. Deviance is contrasted with positive values such as sportsmanship and fair play. 🏅 Sporting examples Doping Using banned substances to enhance performance is a clear form of deviance, breaking both the rules and the ethics of fair competition. Violence

Deliberately injuring an opponent goes beyond the accepted physical norms of a contact sport and constitutes deviant behaviour. Diastole — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diastole IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Diastole The relaxation phase of the heartbeat, when the chambers fill with blood. 📖 What it means Diastole is the phase of the cardiac cycle in which the heart muscle relaxes and the chambers fill with blood. Atrial diastole and ventricular diastole happen at different points, and the ventricles receive most of their filling during the relaxation that follows ventricular systole. Diastole is shortened at high heart rates, which reduces the time for filling. This is one reason stroke volume can plateau during maximal exercise, even as heart rate continues to rise.

🏅 Sporting examples Resting At rest, diastole takes up most of the cardiac cycle, allowing full ventricular filling. Exercise As heart rate rises, diastole shortens, so the ventricles have less time to fill. Filling Blood flows through the open AV valves during diastole. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain why stroke volume can plateau at high heart rates: "At high heart rates, diastole is shortened, so the ventricles have less time to fill, which limits stroke volume even as heart rate continues to rise." Diastolic Blood Pressure — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diastolic Blood Pressure IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General BTEC Sport Diastolic Blood Pressure The lower blood-pressure number — the pressure in the arteries while the heart relaxes between beats. 📖 What it means Diastolic blood pressure is the pressure in the arteries when the heart is relaxing between beats (during diastole). It is the lower of the two numbers in a blood pressure reading.

It represents the minimum arterial pressure , when the heart is refilling rather than contracting. It is reported alongside systolic pressure (the pressure during contraction) — for example, in a reading of 120/80, the 80 is the diastolic pressure. During aerobic exercise , diastolic pressure typically stays relatively stable or changes only slightly, even as systolic pressure rises — because the vessels supplying the working muscles dilate, offsetting the increased output. It is an important measure of cardiovascular health. 🏅 Sporting examples The lower number In a blood pressure reading of 120/80, the 80 is the diastolic pressure — the pressure between beats. Heart relaxing

Diastolic pressure is the arterial pressure while the heart relaxes and refills. During exercise In aerobic exercise, diastolic pressure often stays fairly stable while systolic pressure rises. ✍️ Using the term in context Define diastolic blood pressure and contrast with systolic: "Diastolic blood pressure is the arterial pressure when the heart relaxes between beats, the lower number in a reading; it contrasts with systolic pressure during contraction, and typically stays relatively stable during aerobic exercise." Diffusing capacity is measured clinically and is relevant to aerobic performance. Diffusion Gradient — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diffusion Gradient IB Sport Science General Diffusion Gradient The driving force behind gas exchange — the concentration difference that pushes gases across a membrane. 📖 What it means A diffusion gradient is the difference in concentration (or partial pressure) of a gas across a membrane , which drives the movement of that gas by diffusion from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated.

In gas exchange, a steep diffusion gradient speeds the movement of gases. At the alveoli, oxygen is at a higher partial pressure in the air than in the blood , so it diffuses into the blood; carbon dioxide, higher in the blood, diffuses out. The steeper the gradient, the faster the diffusion . During exercise, the body maintains steep diffusion gradients : fast, deep breathing keeps alveolar oxygen high and CO₂ low, while the working muscles use oxygen and produce CO₂ rapidly — keeping gas exchange fast to meet demand. 🏅 Sporting examples Driving exchange The higher partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli than in the blood creates the diffusion gradient that drives oxygen into the blood.

Steeper is faster The steeper the diffusion gradient, the faster the gas diffuses across the membrane. Exercise Fast breathing and rapid oxygen use during exercise keep the diffusion gradients steep, speeding gas exchange. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the diffusion gradient and its role: "A diffusion gradient is the difference in concentration or partial pressure of a gas across a membrane, driving its diffusion from high to low; steep gradients speed gas exchange, and the body maintains them during exercise to meet demand." Diffusion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diffusion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Diffusion The passive movement that drives gas exchange — how oxygen gets into the blood and carbon dioxide gets out, at the lungs and the muscles. 📖 What it means Diffusion is the movement of molecules from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration , down a concentration gradient, until they are evenly spread. It is a passive process, requiring no energy.

In sport physiology, diffusion is the mechanism of gas exchange . At the alveoli , oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out; at the muscles , oxygen diffuses from blood into tissue and carbon dioxide diffuses back. The steeper the concentration gradient , the faster diffusion occurs. During exercise, working muscles use oxygen rapidly and produce carbon dioxide, steepening the gradients and speeding up gas exchange to meet demand. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance exercise In a hard-working runner, muscles rapidly consume oxygen, creating a steep gradient that speeds oxygen diffusion from blood into the muscle tissue. At the lungs

During exercise, faster, deeper breathing keeps alveolar oxygen high, maintaining a steep gradient for oxygen to diffuse into the blood. Altitude At altitude, lower oxygen pressure reduces the diffusion gradient at the lungs, which is why oxygen uptake is harder until the body adapts. ✍️ Using the term in context Define diffusion and apply it to gas exchange gradients: "Diffusion is the passive movement of molecules down a concentration gradient; at the alveoli, oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide out, and exercise steepens these gradients to speed gas exchange." Discounting Principle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Discounting Principle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Discounting Principle The idea that multiple possible causes make each one seem less responsible for an outcome. 📖 What it means The discounting principle is an idea from attribution theory. It suggests that when several possible causes exist for a behaviour, the observer gives less weight to any one of them. In sport, a player who has several possible reasons for a poor result may attribute the cause differently from a player with a single clear reason.

Coaches can use the principle to help performers analyse results more accurately. Recognising multiple causes can prevent a single factor being blamed unfairly. 🏅 Sporting examples Result A team loses after poor tactics, injuries and bad weather, so each factor is seen as less responsible. Feedback A coach helps a player see several causes of a poor performance, not just one. It is a single, self-contained action that is over quickly and must be started again from the beginning to be repeated. Discrete skills sit on the discrete–serial–continuous continuum . Serial skills link several discrete actions into a sequence, and continuous skills have no obvious start or finish, flowing on repeatedly.

Dislocation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dislocation IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Dislocation A joint forced apart — a serious injury where the bones of a joint come out of position. 📖 What it means A dislocation is an injury in which the bones of a joint are forced out of their normal position . The joint surfaces are displaced so they are no longer properly aligned. Dislocations usually result from a strong force or impact , or an awkward fall, and commonly affect joints such as the shoulder and fingers . They cause intense pain, obvious deformity, swelling and loss of function , and often damage the surrounding ligaments and soft tissue.

A dislocation is a serious injury requiring prompt medical treatment — it should be relocated by a professional, not by the athlete, and is followed by immobilisation and rehabilitation. Repeated dislocations can leave a joint unstable and prone to further injury. 🏅 Sporting examples Shoulder A heavy fall onto an outstretched arm can dislocate the shoulder, forcing the joint out of position. Serious injury A dislocation causes intense pain and obvious deformity and needs prompt professional treatment.
