Displacement — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Displacement IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Displacement A precise biomechanical quantity that's easy to muddle with distance — how far a body is from where it started, and in what direction. 📖 What it means Displacement is the straight-line distance and direction from a body's starting position to its finishing position . Because it includes direction, it is a vector quantity .

It differs from distance , which is the total length of the path travelled and has no direction (a scalar). If a runner completes one lap of a 400m track, their distance is 400m but their displacement is zero, because they finish where they started. Displacement is used with time to calculate velocity (velocity = displacement ÷ time), just as distance is used to calculate speed. Keeping the two apart is essential for accurate biomechanical analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples 400m running A runner completing one lap covers 400m of distance but has zero displacement, because their start and finish positions are the same. Swimming

A swimmer doing lengths of a pool has a large distance but a small displacement if they finish near where they started. Long jump In the long jump, the horizontal displacement of the athlete's centre of mass largely determines the distance recorded. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast displacement with distance precisely: "Displacement is a vector describing the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish, whereas distance is a scalar describing the total path length; a runner completing a lap has zero displacement but 400m of distance." Distributed Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Distributed Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Distributed Practice Practice broken up with rest — usually the more effective way to learn and retain a skill, especially for beginners. 📖 What it means Distributed practice is a practice structure in which practice sessions or trials are spread out with rest intervals in between . The rest may be filled with recovery, feedback, or mental rehearsal.

It contrasts with massed practice , where the skill is practised repeatedly with little or no rest. Distributed practice is generally considered more effective for learning and retention , because the rests reduce fatigue and allow consolidation and feedback. Distributed practice is especially suitable for beginners, complex or dangerous skills, and physically demanding tasks , where fatigue and information overload would otherwise harm learning. 🏅 Sporting examples Learning to swim A beginner swimmer benefits from distributed practice — shorter efforts with rests — because the rests prevent fatigue and allow feedback between attempts. Complex gymnastics

A gymnast learning a demanding new skill uses distributed practice so fatigue does not cause dangerous errors. Diuresis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diuresis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Diuresis The process of making urine, which is how the kidneys remove excess water and waste. 📖 What it means Diuresis is the production of urine by the kidneys. Diuretic — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diuretic IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Diuretic A substance that makes the kidneys produce more urine, and which is banned in sport. 📖 What it means A diuretic is a substance that increases urine production, causing the body to lose water and electrolytes. Diuretics are prohibited in sport. They are classed by the World Anti-Doping Agency as masking agents, because they can dilute a urine sample and hide the presence of other substances. Diving Reflex — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Diving Reflex IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Diving Reflex The body's automatic response to the face being submerged, which slows the heart and conserves oxygen. 📖 What it means The diving reflex is a response triggered when the face is immersed in cold water. Dominant Response — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dominant Response AS Level / Cambridge General Dominant Response Your go-to reaction under pressure — the well-learned response that arousal makes more likely to emerge. 📖 What it means The dominant response is the most well-learned or habitual response to a stimulus — the action a performer is most likely to produce automatically in a given situation. It is central to drive theory (Hull's theory) , which states that increased arousal makes the dominant response more likely to occur. Whether this helps or harms performance depends on whether the dominant response is correct .

For a skilled performer (in the autonomous stage), the dominant response is usually the correct, well-grooved skill, so higher arousal aids performance. For a beginner , the dominant response may be an incorrect movement, so higher arousal makes errors more likely — which is why arousal affects skilled and novice performers differently. 🏅 Sporting examples Skilled performer Under high arousal, a skilled server's dominant response is the correct, well-practised technique, so performance improves. Doping — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Doping IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Doping The use of banned substances or methods to cheat — the most serious form of deviance in sport, and a core ethics topic. 📖 What it means Doping is the use of prohibited substances or methods to artificially enhance sporting performance . In sport science, double-blind designs are used to test supplements and recovery methods. Drag Co-efficient — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Drag Co-efficient IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Drag Co-efficient A number showing how streamlined a shape is, which sets how much drag it experiences. 📖 What it means The drag coefficient is a dimensionless number that describes how streamlined an object is. A lower drag coefficient means the object experiences less drag for the same speed and frontal area. It is one of the factors in the drag equation, together with air density, frontal area and velocity squared.

In sport, a lower drag coefficient is valuable in cycling, swimming and skiing. Athletes and equipment designers reduce it through posture, clothing and shape, because even small reductions can save energy over a long event. 🏅 Sporting examples Cycling A rider lowering the torso into an aero position reduces the drag coefficient of the body. Swimming Streamlined body position in the water reduces the drag coefficient and improves efficiency. Equipment Helmets and bike frames are designed to lower drag coefficient. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how an aero position helps a cyclist:

"An aero position lowers the drag coefficient of the rider, so less air resistance acts on them at a given speed, which saves energy over a long time trial." Drag — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Drag IB Sport Science General Drag The fluid's resistance to motion — the force pushing back on anything moving through air or water. 📖 What it means Drag is a resistive force acting on a body moving through a fluid (air or water) that opposes its motion . It acts in the opposite direction to movement, slowing the body down. The size of drag increases with the velocity of the body, its frontal surface area, and the roughness of its surface (and with the density of the fluid). Because it rises sharply with speed, drag is a major factor limiting performance in fast sports.

Athletes reduce drag through streamlining — adopting low, narrow body positions, wearing smooth suits, and using shaped equipment. Reducing drag is central to performance in swimming, cycling, skiing and sprinting. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming A swimmer keeps a long, streamlined body position to reduce the drag opposing them in the water. Cycling A cyclist crouches into an aerodynamic tuck to cut the drag of moving through the air at speed. Rises with speed Because drag increases sharply with velocity, it becomes an ever-greater force to overcome at higher speeds. ✍️ Using the term in context Define drag and the factors affecting it:

"Drag is a resistive force opposing a body's motion through a fluid; it increases with velocity, frontal surface area and surface roughness, and is reduced by streamlining — central to performance in swimming, cycling and sprinting." Drive Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Drive Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Drive Theory The simplest model of arousal and performance — more arousal means better performance, provided the skill is well learned. 📖 What it means Drive theory proposes a linear relationship between arousal and performance : as arousal increases, so does performance, in a straight-line fashion. The higher the drive (arousal), the greater the effort and output.

The crucial refinement is that arousal makes the performer's dominant response more likely. For a skilled performer, the dominant response is the correct one, so high arousal helps; for a beginner, the dominant response may be incorrect , so high arousal harms performance. Drive theory is often criticised as too simple — in reality, very high arousal usually impairs performance rather than continuing to improve it, which the inverted-U hypothesis and catastrophe theory address. 🏅 Sporting examples Skilled performer An expert weightlifter benefits from very high arousal, because their well-learned dominant response is the correct technique. Beginner

A novice under high arousal is more likely to produce their dominant (incorrect) response, so raising arousal harms their performance. Limitation Drive theory struggles to explain why elite performers can 'choke' when over-aroused, which the inverted-U and catastrophe theories address. ✍️ Using the term in context State the linear relationship and the dominant-response refinement: "Drive theory proposes that performance increases linearly with arousal, because arousal makes the dominant response more likely — beneficial for a skilled performer whose dominant response is correct, but harmful for a beginner." Note its main criticism: it does not explain the drop-off at very high arousal.

Coaches, teachers, officials and event organisers owe it to the participants. Static posture is judged while standing still, but dynamic posture matters in running, lifting and landing, where alignment must be held under changing forces. Dynamic Stretching — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dynamic Stretching General BTEC Sport Dynamic Stretching Stretching on the move — controlled movements through full range that prepare the body for action. 📖 What it means Dynamic stretching is stretching through controlled movements that take joints through their full range of motion , rather than holding a static position. The movements are smooth and deliberate, not bouncing.

Because it involves active, sport-like movement, dynamic stretching is particularly suited to the warm-up : it raises muscle temperature, mobilises the joints, and rehearses movement patterns, preparing the body for activity without the temporary reductions in power that prolonged static stretching can cause. It contrasts with static stretching (holding a position) and the risky ballistic stretching (bouncing). Examples include leg swings, walking lunges and arm circles, performed with control through a full, gradually increasing range. 🏅 Sporting examples Warm-up A sprinter does leg swings and walking lunges — dynamic stretches — to prepare the body before racing. Controlled movement

Dynamic stretching moves the joints through their full range with control, unlike bouncing ballistic stretches. Preparing to perform By mobilising joints and rehearsing movements, dynamic stretching readies the body for activity. ✍️ Using the term in context Define dynamic stretching and its best use: "Dynamic stretching uses controlled movements that take joints through their full range; it suits the warm-up because it raises muscle temperature, mobilises joints and rehearses movement patterns, unlike static stretching held in one position." Dynamometer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dynamometer IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Dynamometer A strength meter — the instrument that puts a number on how much force a muscle can produce. 📖 What it means A dynamometer is an instrument used to measure muscular strength or force output . It gives an objective reading of the force a muscle or muscle group can produce. The most common example is the handgrip dynamometer , which measures grip strength: the performer squeezes the device as hard as possible, and it displays the force produced. Other dynamometers measure the strength of other muscle groups.

Reliable results depend on standardised technique and procedure, and grip strength is sometimes used as a general indicator of overall strength. 🏅 Sporting examples Grip strength A handgrip dynamometer measures how hard a performer can squeeze, giving a reading of grip strength. Dyspnea — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Dyspnea IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Dyspnea The feeling of breathing hard or struggling to get enough air. 📖 What it means Dyspnoea (spelt dyspnea in US usage) is the subjective sensation of difficult or laboured breathing. It is a normal part of hard exercise, but when it is severe or occurs at low effort, it can indicate a lung, heart or other health problem. Dyspnoea is influenced by the balance between the work of breathing and the signals sent to the brain about carbon dioxide and oxygen. In sport, athletes who experience unexpected dyspnoea should be assessed by a clinician. 🏅 Sporting examples

Exercise A runner feels dyspnoea at the end of a hard sprint, which is normal. Warning sign Breathlessness at low effort may indicate a heart or lung problem that needs assessment. Eating Disorders — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Eating Disorders IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Eating Disorders Serious conditions in which eating behaviour harms health. 📖 What it means Eating disorders are mental health conditions involving unhealthy attitudes to food, weight and body shape. The main types are anorexia nervosa , bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder . They are more common among athletes in weight-sensitive or aesthetic sports , such as gymnastics, distance running, rowing (lightweight) and combat sports.

They can cause low energy availability, loss of bone density, hormone disruption and heart problems. Early recognition, supportive conversation and referral to professional help are important. 🏅 Sporting examples Gymnastics Pressure to stay light can contribute to disordered eating. Warning signs Secretive eating, obsession with weight and excessive exercise can be signs. Support A coach who is concerned talks privately and refers the athlete to a doctor or a specialist service. ✍️ Using the term in context Handle the topic with care:

Eccentric Contraction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Eccentric Contraction IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Eccentric Contraction The muscle lengthening under load — the braking phase that controls movement and builds strength. 📖 What it means An eccentric contraction is a muscle contraction in which the muscle lengthens while under tension . It acts as a brake , controlling or resisting a movement rather than producing it.

For example, in the downward phase of a biceps curl , the biceps contracts eccentrically — it is still generating tension, but lengthening to lower the weight under control against gravity. Eccentric contractions control the deceleration of movements and absorb force. Eccentric contractions are important in landing, decelerating and lowering , and are associated with delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) and with significant strength gains. They are contrasted with concentric (shortening) and isometric (no change in length) contractions. 🏅 Sporting examples Lowering phase In the downward phase of a biceps curl, the biceps contracts eccentrically to lower the weight under control. Landing

The quadriceps work eccentrically on landing, lengthening under tension to control the descent and absorb force. DOMS Eccentric contractions, such as running downhill, are strongly associated with delayed onset muscle soreness. ✍️ Using the term in context Define an eccentric contraction and give an example: "An eccentric contraction is one in which the muscle lengthens under tension, acting as a brake — as in the downward phase of a biceps curl; it controls and decelerates movement and is strongly associated with DOMS." Contrast it with concentric and isometric contractions. 🔗 Related terms

Ecological Validity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ecological Validity AS Level / Cambridge General Ecological Validity Does the test reflect the real thing? — how well a test or study mirrors actual sporting performance. 📖 What it means Ecological validity is the extent to which a test or research finding reflects performance in a real-world (or real sporting) setting . A test with high ecological validity closely resembles the actual demands of the sport.

It is a specific aspect of validity . A test may measure a quality reliably in the lab yet have low ecological validity if the conditions differ greatly from competition. For example, a treadmill test of a games player has lower ecological validity than a test that replicates the stop-start, multidirectional movements of their sport. Ecological validity matters because a test's results are only useful if they transfer to real performance . Choosing tests that resemble the sport's demands makes the results more meaningful for guiding training and selection. 🏅 Sporting examples Sport-specific

A stop-start, multidirectional fitness test has higher ecological validity for a games player than a straight-line treadmill test. Real-world reflection High ecological validity means the test closely reflects the demands of actual competition. Meaningful results A test with low ecological validity may give reliable numbers that don't transfer to real performance. ✍️ Using the term in context Define ecological validity as a form of validity: "Ecological validity is the extent to which a test or finding reflects real-world performance; a test high in ecological validity resembles the actual demands of the sport, making its results more meaningful for real performance."

Ectomorph — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ectomorph General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Ectomorph The lean, linear physique — one of the three somatotype extremes, characteristically slim and light. 📖 What it means Ectomorph is a body type (somatotype) characterised by a slim, narrow, linear frame with low levels of body fat and muscle . It is one of the three extremes of somatotype, alongside endomorph and mesomorph. Ectomorphs tend to be light and lean , which can favour a good power-to-weight ratio. Most people are a blend of the three body types rather than a pure ectomorph, and somatotype is scored on each component.

In sport, an ectomorphic build can suit activities where lightness and leanness are advantageous — such as endurance running or high jump. Effector — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Effector IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Effector The part that acts — the muscle or gland that carries out the body's response to a signal. 📖 What it means An effector is a muscle or gland that receives a motor signal and produces a response . It is the part of a control system that actually carries out the corrective action. Effectors are a key stage in control loops . In a reflex or homeostatic response, a receptor detects a change, a control centre processes the information, and the effector produces the response — a muscle contracting or a gland secreting a hormone.

In homeostasis , effectors carry out the corrections that keep variables near their set point — for example, sweat glands (an effector) secreting sweat to cool the body, or skin arterioles dilating. In motor control , the muscles are the effectors that execute the intended movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Thermoregulation When the body overheats, sweat glands act as effectors, secreting sweat to cool it down. Reflex response In a reflex, the muscle is the effector that contracts to produce the protective movement. Control loop The effector is the final stage of a control loop — receptor, control centre, then effector. ✍️ Using the term in context

Efficiency — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Efficiency IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC General Efficiency How much of the energy put in comes out as useful work. 📖 What it means Efficiency is the ratio of useful work or energy output to the total energy input. It is usually expressed as a percentage. In the human body, efficiency is typically around 20 to 25 per cent, because much of the energy from metabolism is lost as heat. Improving efficiency is a common aim in training and technique. Ejection Fraction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ejection Fraction IB Sport Science General Ejection Fraction How completely the heart empties — the share of the ventricle's blood pumped out with each beat. 📖 What it means Ejection fraction is the percentage of blood ejected from a ventricle with each contraction . It compares the volume pumped out (the stroke volume) with the total volume that filled the ventricle.

It is an indicator of how effectively the heart is pumping : a higher ejection fraction means the ventricle empties more completely with each beat. A healthy heart does not eject all its blood — some always remains — so ejection fraction is well below 100%. During exercise, ejection fraction can increase as the heart contracts more forcefully (helping to raise stroke volume), and endurance training tends to improve the heart's pumping effectiveness. It is also an important clinical measure of heart health. 🏅 Sporting examples Pumping effectiveness A higher ejection fraction means the ventricle empties more completely with each beat, indicating effective pumping. During exercise

Ejection fraction can increase during exercise as the heart contracts more forcefully, raising stroke volume. Not 100% Even a healthy heart does not eject all its blood, so ejection fraction is well below 100%. ✍️ Using the term in context Define ejection fraction and what it indicates: "Ejection fraction is the percentage of blood ejected from a ventricle with each contraction; it indicates how effectively the heart pumps, increasing during exercise as the heart contracts more forcefully, and never reaching 100%." Elastic Energy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Elastic Energy IB Sport Science General Elastic Energy Spring in the muscles — energy stored during the stretch of a movement and released to boost power. 📖 What it means Elastic energy is energy stored in stretched tendons and muscles during the eccentric (lengthening) phase of a movement, which can then be released to add to the force of the following concentric (shortening) phase .

This works like a spring : when a muscle-tendon unit is rapidly stretched, it stores elastic energy, and if it then shortens quickly, that stored energy is released to enhance the movement. This is the basis of the stretch-shortening cycle . Elastic energy is central to powerful, explosive movements such as jumping and sprinting — the quick counter-movement (a dip before a jump) stores elastic energy that boosts the jump. It is why plyometric training , which trains the stretch-shortening cycle, develops power effectively. 🏅 Sporting examples Jumping A quick dip before a jump stretches the leg muscles and tendons, storing elastic energy that boosts the upward drive. Stretch-shortening cycle

Elastic energy stored in the eccentric phase is released in the concentric phase to enhance force. Plyometrics Plyometric training develops the ability to store and use elastic energy, improving power. ✍️ Using the term in context Define elastic energy and how it is used: "Elastic energy is energy stored in stretched tendons and muscles during the eccentric phase, released to add force in the following concentric phase; this stretch-shortening cycle underpins powerful movements such as jumping and is trained by plyometrics." Elastic Limit — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Elastic Limit IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Elastic Limit The point beyond which a material or tissue stays permanently stretched or deformed. 📖 What it means The elastic limit is the point beyond which a material or tissue will not return to its original shape once the load is removed. Below the elastic limit, deformation is reversible. Beyond it, the material is permanently deformed, and if the load is greater still, it may fail.

In the body, tendons and ligaments behave elastically within a range. Excessive loading beyond their elastic limit can cause permanent stretch or damage, which is one reason injuries can happen suddenly under extreme force. 🏅 Sporting examples Tendon A tendon loaded beyond its elastic limit can be permanently stretched or tear. Ligament An ankle sprain happens when a ligament is stretched beyond its elastic limit. Elasticity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Elasticity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC General Elasticity The ability to spring back to shape after being stretched. 📖 What it means Elasticity is the ability of a material or tissue to return to its original shape after being stretched or compressed. Tendons, ligaments, arteries and some cartilage are elastic, which allows them to store and release energy and to cope with repeated loads. Elasticity declines with age and inactivity, and it can be improved through training. In blood vessels, elasticity keeps flow smooth between heartbeats, and loss of arterial elasticity raises blood pressure.

🏅 Sporting examples Tendon The elasticity of tendons allows them to store and release energy during running. Electrolytes — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Electrolytes IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Electrolytes The dissolved minerals that keep the body's fluids balanced and muscles firing — crucial to hydration and performance in hard exercise. 📖 What it means Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electrical charge when dissolved in the body's fluids , including sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride. They are essential for many physiological processes. In sport they matter because they help regulate fluid balance, nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction . During prolonged exercise, electrolytes — particularly sodium — are lost through sweat.

Significant electrolyte loss, especially when combined with fluid loss, can impair performance and contribute to problems such as muscle cramp and, in extreme cases, dangerous fluid imbalances . This is why many sports drinks contain added electrolytes. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance events A marathon runner loses sodium and other electrolytes through heavy sweating, which is why endurance sports drinks include electrolytes to aid rehydration. Electron Transport Chain — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Electron Transport Chain IB Sport Science General Electron Transport Chain The final, high-yield stage of aerobic energy production — where most of the body's ATP is actually made. 📖 What it means The electron transport chain is the third and final stage of aerobic ATP production , taking place in the mitochondria . It is where the largest amount of ATP is produced . It uses hydrogen carriers (produced during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle) and, crucially, oxygen . Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor, combining with hydrogen to form water — which is why the process only occurs aerobically.

Because it depends on oxygen and yields large amounts of ATP relatively slowly, the electron transport chain underpins the aerobic system's role in prolonged, endurance exercise . 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance events During a long-distance race, the electron transport chain produces the bulk of the runner's ATP, using oxygen to sustain energy over hours. Aerobic base A well-developed aerobic system, with many mitochondria, increases the capacity of the electron transport chain to resynthesise ATP. Water by-product The chain combines hydrogen with oxygen to form water, one of the aerobic system's harmless by-products alongside carbon dioxide. ✍️ Using the term in context

Endocrine System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Endocrine System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Endocrine System The body's hormonal network — glands that release chemical messengers to regulate function during exercise. 📖 What it means The endocrine system is the system of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream to regulate the body's functions. It controls slower, longer-lasting processes than the nervous system.

Its glands include the pituitary, adrenal glands, pancreas and thyroid , each releasing hormones that act on target cells with the appropriate receptors. Endomorph — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Endomorph General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Endomorph The rounder, softer physique — the somatotype extreme with a higher proportion of body fat. 📖 What it means Endomorph is a body type (somatotype) characterised by a rounder frame with higher levels of body fat and a tendency to store fat readily. It is one of the three extremes of somatotype, alongside ectomorph and mesomorph. Endomorphs tend to have a wider, softer, rounder physique . As with all somatotypes, most people are a blend rather than a pure endomorph, and physique is scored on each of the three components.

In sport, a predominantly endomorphic build may be less suited to activities requiring a high power-to-weight ratio , but greater mass can be an advantage where stability or momentum matters, such as certain positions in contact sports or events like the shot put (often combined with mesomorphy). Physique is only one factor among many in performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Greater mass A more endomorphic build's greater mass can aid stability or momentum in certain sports or positions. A blend Most athletes are a blend of somatotypes; a pure endomorph is uncommon. Endurance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Endurance General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Endurance The capacity to keep going — a foundational fitness quality that comes in both cardiovascular and muscular forms. 📖 What it means Endurance is the ability to sustain physical activity over a prolonged period while resisting fatigue. It is one of the fundamental qualities underpinning performance in most sports.

It has two main forms. Cardiovascular (aerobic) endurance is the ability of the heart, lungs and circulation to supply oxygen during sustained whole-body exercise. Muscular endurance is the ability of a specific muscle group to contract repeatedly or sustain a contraction without fatiguing. Endurance is developed through methods such as continuous, interval and Fartlek training , and is a key health-related component of fitness, closely linked to long-term cardiovascular health. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running Cardiovascular endurance is the dominant quality for a marathon runner, allowing them to sustain effort for hours. A rower needs both cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance to keep powering strokes throughout a race. Team sports A footballer relies on endurance to maintain work rate and keep repeating high-intensity efforts across ninety minutes. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish the two forms of endurance: "Endurance is the ability to sustain activity while resisting fatigue; cardiovascular endurance concerns oxygen supply during whole-body exercise, while muscular endurance concerns a muscle group contracting repeatedly." Energy Balance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Energy Balance IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Energy Balance Calories in versus calories out — the balance that determines whether body mass rises, falls or holds steady. 📖 What it means Energy balance is the relationship between energy consumed through food and energy expended through basal metabolism, physical activity and digestion. It determines changes in body mass.

There are three states: neutral balance (energy in equals energy out — body mass stays stable), positive balance (energy in exceeds energy out — body mass tends to increase), and negative balance (energy out exceeds energy in — body mass tends to decrease). Energy balance matters for managing body composition and fuelling performance . Athletes aim to match their intake to the demands of training, avoiding both under-fuelling (which impairs performance and recovery) and unwanted changes in body mass. 🏅 Sporting examples Stable mass When energy intake matches expenditure (neutral balance), body mass stays stable. Fuelling training

An athlete matches intake to training demands to avoid under-fuelling, which impairs performance and recovery. Managing mass A sustained positive or negative energy balance leads to a gain or loss in body mass respectively. ✍️ Using the term in context Define energy balance and its three states: "Energy balance is the relationship between energy consumed and energy expended; neutral balance keeps body mass stable, positive balance tends to increase it and negative balance to decrease it, and athletes match intake to training demands." Energy Continuum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Energy Continuum IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Energy Continuum Why no single energy system works alone — the sliding balance of the three systems as exercise intensity and duration change. 📖 What it means The energy continuum is the concept that all three energy systems contribute to ATP production at the same time , with the relative dominance of each shifting according to the intensity and duration of exercise .

At the start of maximal exercise, the ATP-PC system dominates; as effort continues, the glycolytic system takes over; and for prolonged, lower-intensity work the aerobic system becomes dominant. The switch is gradual, not a hard cut-off. Understanding the continuum lets a coach identify the predominant energy system for a given activity and design training that develops it — crucial for making training specific to the demands of the sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sports A footballer's match play moves constantly along the energy continuum — aerobic during jogging, ATP-PC and glycolytic during sprints and tackles. Middle distance

An 800m runner shifts along the continuum from mainly anaerobic early on to a greater aerobic contribution as the race progresses. Training design Identifying where an event sits on the continuum lets a coach target the dominant system, making training specific. ✍️ Using the term in context Emphasise simultaneous contribution and shifting dominance: "The energy continuum describes how all three energy systems contribute at once, with the dominant system shifting according to intensity and duration; identifying the predominant system allows training to be made specific." Energy Systems — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Energy Systems IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Energy Systems The three pathways that keep the muscles supplied with ATP — the framework behind every question about fuelling exercise. 📖 What it means The energy systems are the three metabolic pathways the body uses to resynthesise ATP for muscle contraction: the ATP-PC (alactic) system , the glycolytic (lactic acid) system , and the aerobic system .

They differ in speed, capacity and fuel . The ATP-PC system is fastest but lasts only seconds; the glycolytic system provides rapid energy for high-intensity efforts of up to a few minutes; the aerobic system is slower but produces the most ATP for prolonged exercise. All three systems are always working together , but their relative contribution shifts with the intensity and duration of the activity — this shifting balance is called the energy continuum. 🏅 Sporting examples 100m sprint A short sprint is fuelled predominantly by the ATP-PC system, providing near-instant energy for a maximal effort of a few seconds. 800m run

A middle-distance run draws heavily on the glycolytic system, with the aerobic system contributing more as the race continues. Marathon A marathon is almost entirely aerobic, the aerobic system resynthesising ATP from fat and carbohydrate over hours. ✍️ Using the term in context Name all three systems and note they work together: "The three energy systems — ATP-PC, glycolytic and aerobic — all contribute simultaneously, but their relative contribution shifts with the intensity and duration of the activity." Epiphyseal Plate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Epiphyseal Plate IB Sport Science General Epiphyseal Plate The growth plate — the region of cartilage near the ends of long bones where they lengthen during growth. 📖 What it means The epiphyseal plate (growth plate) is a region of cartilage near the ends of long bones where lengthwise bone growth occurs during childhood and adolescence. As a young person grows, new bone is laid down at the plate, lengthening the bone. Once growth is complete, the plate ossifies (turns to bone) and closes , and no further lengthwise growth is possible.

The epiphyseal plate is important in a sporting context because it is a relatively weak point in a growing bone . This is one reason care is taken with the type and load of training for young athletes, to reduce the risk of growth-plate injury. 🏅 Sporting examples Bone growth During adolescence, new bone is laid down at the epiphyseal plate, lengthening the long bones. Closure Once growth finishes, the epiphyseal plate ossifies and closes, ending lengthwise growth. Young athletes Because the growth plate is a weaker point in a growing bone, training loads for young athletes are managed carefully. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the epiphyseal plate and its significance:

EPOC (Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › EPOC (Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General EPOC (Excess Post-exercise Oxygen Consumption) Why you keep breathing hard after stopping — the extra oxygen the body uses to recover and repay its oxygen debt. 📖 What it means EPOC is the elevated oxygen consumption that continues after exercise has stopped , used to restore the body toward its pre-exercise resting state. It is the modern term for what was once called the 'oxygen debt'.

This extra oxygen is used to resynthesise ATP and phosphocreatine stores, remove and convert lactate, replenish oxygen bound to myoglobin, and support the raised metabolism from elevated heart rate, breathing and body temperature. EPOC has a fast component (rapid restoration of PCr and oxygen stores in the first few minutes) and a slow component (the longer-lasting elevated metabolism). HIIT

High-intensity interval training produces a large EPOC, meaning elevated oxygen use and calorie burn continue well after the session ends. Recovery use An athlete uses active recovery during EPOC to keep blood flow high and speed the restoration of the body toward rest. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain what the extra oxygen is used for: "EPOC is the elevated oxygen consumption after exercise, used to resynthesise ATP and phosphocreatine, remove lactate, replenish myoglobin stores and support raised metabolism; more intense exercise produces a larger EPOC." Ergogenic Aid — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ergogenic Aid IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Ergogenic Aid Anything used to gain a performance edge — a broad category spanning legal aids like caffeine and banned methods like doping. 📖 What it means An ergogenic aid is any substance, technique or device used to enhance sporting performance . The term covers a very wide range, from everyday legal aids to prohibited methods.

Ergogenic aids can be grouped by type — for example nutritional (caffeine, creatine, carbohydrate supplements), physiological (blood doping, altitude training), pharmacological (steroids, stimulants), and mechanical (specialised equipment or clothing). The key distinction is legal versus illegal (banned) . Legal aids such as caffeine and creatine are permitted; banned aids such as anabolic steroids and blood doping are prohibited because they provide an unfair advantage and/or endanger health. 🏅 Sporting examples Legal nutritional aid Caffeine is a legal ergogenic aid that can reduce perceived effort and improve endurance performance. Physiological aid

Altitude training is a legal physiological ergogenic aid, stimulating red blood cell production to improve oxygen delivery. Erythrocytes — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Erythrocytes IB Sport Science General Erythrocytes The oxygen carriers — red blood cells packed with haemoglobin that ferry oxygen to the muscles. 📖 What it means Erythrocytes are red blood cells . They contain haemoglobin and their main job is to transport oxygen around the body , from the lungs to the tissues. Oxygen binds to the haemoglobin inside erythrocytes for transport in the blood. The more erythrocytes (and haemoglobin) a person has, the greater their blood's oxygen-carrying capacity — a key factor in aerobic performance.

Evaluation Apprehension — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Evaluation Apprehension IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Evaluation Apprehension The nerves of being watched and judged — the anxiety that an audience's scrutiny can create. 📖 What it means Evaluation apprehension is anxiety caused by the perception of being judged by others . It is not simply the presence of an audience, but the sense that the audience is assessing the performance, that raises arousal and anxiety.

It is closely linked to social facilitation : the effect an audience has on performance is stronger when the performer believes they are being evaluated. This heightened arousal can help skilled performers but harm beginners or those performing complex skills. Understanding evaluation apprehension helps explain why performers may struggle in front of selectors, judges or critical crowds . Coaches manage it by gradually exposing learners to being watched, building skills to the autonomous stage, and using anxiety-management techniques. 🏅 Sporting examples Being judged A player performs worse in front of selectors because the sense of being evaluated raises their anxiety.

Evaporation (heat loss) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Evaporation (heat loss) IB Sport Science General Evaporation (heat loss) The body's main cooling system in exercise — heat carried away as sweat turns to vapour. 📖 What it means Evaporation is the loss of body heat as sweat turns from liquid to vapour on the skin surface . Converting sweat to vapour requires energy (heat), which is drawn from the body, cooling it.

It is the most important route of heat loss during exercise , when large amounts of heat are generated by the working muscles. The body sweats, and as that sweat evaporates, it removes heat from the skin, helping to keep core temperature within a safe range. Its effectiveness depends on the humidity of the air : in hot, humid conditions, sweat evaporates less readily, so evaporative cooling is less effective and the risk of overheating rises. This is why humid conditions feel especially challenging for performers. 🏅 Sporting examples Main cooling route During a hard run, most heat is lost by evaporation as sweat vaporises from the skin. Humidity

In humid conditions, sweat evaporates less readily, reducing evaporative cooling and raising the risk of overheating. Cooling mechanism Converting sweat to vapour draws heat from the body, lowering skin and core temperature. ✍️ Using the term in context Define evaporation as the main heat-loss route in exercise: "Evaporation is the loss of body heat as sweat turns to vapour on the skin, drawing heat from the body; it is the most important route of heat loss during exercise, but is less effective in humid conditions where sweat evaporates less readily." Eversion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Eversion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Eversion Turning the sole outward — the rotation of the foot away from the body's midline. 📖 What it means Eversion is the outward rotation of the sole of the foot away from the midline of the body — turning the sole to face outward. Excitation-Contraction Coupling — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Excitation-Contraction Coupling IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Excitation-Contraction Coupling How a nerve signal becomes a muscle contraction. 📖 What it means Excitation-contraction coupling is the sequence that turns an action potential into muscle contraction . The nerve signal crosses the neuromuscular junction and an action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules .

This causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium ions . Calcium binds to troponin , moving tropomyosin away from the binding sites on actin , so that myosin heads can form cross-bridges and pull the filaments past each other. When stimulation stops, calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the sites are covered again and the muscle relaxes. 🏅 Sporting examples Voluntary movement Each contraction starts with a signal from a motor neurone. Fatigue Impaired calcium release can reduce force. Relaxation Calcium is taken back up, so the muscle relaxes. ✍️ Using the term in context Give the order of events:

"An action potential triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum; calcium binds troponin, exposing actin sites for myosin cross-bridges." Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage Tiny muscle injuries after hard or unfamiliar exercise. 📖 What it means Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) is damage to the structure of muscle fibres, particularly after unaccustomed or eccentric exercise , such as downhill running or a new strength session. Exocytosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Exocytosis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Exocytosis How a cell releases substances by fusing a vesicle with its outer membrane. 📖 What it means Exocytosis is the process by which a cell releases substances from inside it. Neurotransmitters are released from nerve terminals this way, and so are many hormones. Exocytosis is an active process that uses energy. Expiration — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Expiration IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Expiration Breathing air out of the lungs. 📖 What it means Expiration is the movement of air out of the lungs. At rest, it is passive: the diaphragm and external intercostals relax and the elastic lungs recoil. During exercise and heavy breathing, expiration becomes active, with the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles pulling the ribs down and pushing the diaphragm up.

Efficient expiration matters in exercise, because more air must be moved out to clear carbon dioxide and make room for the next breath. Athletes who breathe out fully can improve ventilation during intense work. 🏅 Sporting examples Rest At rest, expiration is passive and needs no muscular effort. Exercise During intense exercise, the abdominal muscles help push air out. Extension — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Extension IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Extension The partner movement to flexion — the straightening of a joint that increases its angle, seen in every powerful pushing action. 📖 What it means Extension is a movement that increases the angle at a joint . External Feedback — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › External Feedback AS Level / Cambridge General External Feedback Information from outside — feedback about performance provided by a coach, teammate or video. 📖 What it means External feedback (also called extrinsic or augmented feedback) is information about performance provided by an outside source , such as a coach, a teammate, video analysis or a scoreboard.

It is distinguished from intrinsic feedback , which the performer senses themselves through their own body and senses. External feedback supplements what the performer feels, providing information they may not be able to detect alone — such as a coach pointing out a technical fault. External feedback is especially valuable for beginners , who cannot yet interpret their own intrinsic feedback well. As performers become more skilled, they rely more on intrinsic feedback, and coaches gradually reduce external feedback so learners can self-correct. 🏅 Sporting examples Coach's cue A coach telling a swimmer their arm entry is too wide is providing external feedback. Externally and Self-paced Skills — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Externally and Self-paced Skills IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Externally and Self-paced Skills Who controls the timing of a skill: the environment or the performer. 📖 What it means On the pacing continuum , an externally paced skill is one where the environment, an opponent or a teammate controls the timing, so the performer has to react. A self-paced skill is one where the performer decides when to start and how fast to move . Most skills sit somewhere in between. For example, a tennis return is externally paced while a golf putt or a gymnastic vault is self-paced .

Self-paced skills are usually closed skills, and externally paced skills are often open, but the classifications measure different things. 🏅 Sporting examples Football tackle Timing is set by the opponent, so this is externally paced. During exercise and dehydration, extracellular fluid volume changes. Extrinsic Feedback — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Extrinsic Feedback AS Level / Cambridge General Extrinsic Feedback Feedback from an outside source — the coach's word, the video, the scoreboard, guiding a learner's improvement. 📖 What it means Extrinsic feedback is feedback about performance that comes from an external source , such as a coach, teammate, video or scoreboard. It is essentially the same concept as external feedback.

It contrasts with intrinsic feedback , which the performer receives from their own senses and proprioceptors. Extrinsic feedback provides information from outside the performer, and can take the form of knowledge of results (about the outcome) or knowledge of performance (about the movement itself). Extrinsic feedback is particularly important for beginners , who cannot yet interpret their own intrinsic feedback effectively. Extrinsic Motivation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Extrinsic Motivation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Extrinsic Motivation Motivation that comes from outside — the rewards and pressures that drive behaviour, and their double-edged effect on long-term commitment. 📖 What it means Extrinsic motivation is motivation that comes from external sources rather than from within the performer. It includes tangible rewards (trophies, medals, prize money) and intangible rewards (praise, recognition, approval).

It contrasts with intrinsic motivation , which comes from the internal satisfaction and enjoyment of the activity itself. Both can be powerful, and they often operate together. Extrinsic motivation can be highly effective in the short term , but relying on it too heavily can undermine intrinsic motivation — if a performer comes to do an activity only for the reward, their enjoyment and long-term commitment may fall if the reward is removed. 🏅 Sporting examples Youth sport A young player motivated mainly by winning trophies (extrinsic) may lose interest if they stop winning, unlike a player who also enjoys the game itself. Professional sport

Prize money and contracts are powerful extrinsic motivators in elite sport, though the best performers usually retain strong intrinsic motivation too. Coaching balance A coach uses rewards carefully, so that extrinsic motivation supports rather than replaces a player's intrinsic love of the sport. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast it with intrinsic motivation and note the risk: "Extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards such as trophies or praise; it can be effective in the short term, but over-reliance can undermine intrinsic motivation and long-term commitment." Fartlek Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fartlek Training General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Fartlek Training 'Speed play' — a versatile continuous method that varies pace to develop both aerobic and anaerobic fitness in one session. 📖 What it means Fartlek training — Swedish for 'speed play' — is a form of continuous training in which the pace and intensity are varied throughout the session , without stopping for full rest.

By alternating between faster and slower efforts, often over varied terrain, Fartlek trains both the aerobic and anaerobic energy systems in a single session, making it more varied and sport-specific than steady continuous running. Its variety makes it engaging and flexible , and it closely mimics the changing pace of many team and racket sports , where players constantly shift between jogging, striding and sprinting. It can be structured or informal. 🏅 Sporting examples Football A footballer's Fartlek session might alternate jogging, striding and sprinting, closely replicating the stop-start pace of a match. Cross-country

Fascia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fascia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Fascia The web of connective tissue that surrounds and links the muscles. 📖 What it means Fascia is a continuous network of connective tissue that surrounds muscles, muscle groups, bones, nerves and organs. It helps transmit force between muscles, gives structure and support, and contains many sensory receptors, so it contributes to proprioception . Fascia can become tight or stuck after injury or inactivity. Foam rolling and massage are popular methods aimed at improving how it moves, though the research on exactly how they work is still developing.

🏅 Sporting examples Foam rolling A sprinter rolls the thigh to reduce stiffness before training. Plantar fascia Irritation of the plantar fascia under the foot causes heel pain in runners. Fast Feet Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fast Feet Test BTEC Sport General Fast Feet Test A fitness test of foot speed and coordination. 📖 What it means The Fast Feet Test is a test of foot speed in which the athlete makes as many rapid foot contacts as possible within a short time. Protocol: The athlete moves the feet as quickly as possible, usually touching or stepping over a line or on the spot, for a set time such as 10 seconds. The contacts are counted.

Interpreting results: A higher count indicates better foot speed. Technique and consistent scoring rules matter. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A footballer completes 40 contacts in 10 seconds. Training use Used as a progress check for agility drills. Fast-Twitch Fibres (Type II) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fast-Twitch Fibres (Type II) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Fast-Twitch Fibres (Type II) The muscle fibres built for power and speed — fast, forceful and quick to fatigue, they dominate explosive sport. 📖 What it means Fast-twitch fibres (Type II) are muscle fibres that contract rapidly and generate high force , but fatigue quickly . They are recruited for powerful, explosive and high-intensity efforts.

They rely mainly on the anaerobic energy systems , have fewer mitochondria and capillaries and less myoglobin than slow-twitch fibres, giving them a paler appearance. They are often subdivided into Type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic, more fatigue-resistant) and Type IIx (fast glycolytic, most powerful but fastest to fatigue). The proportion of fast- to slow-twitch fibres is largely genetically determined and influences the type of activity a person is naturally suited to — explosive athletes tend to have a higher proportion of fast-twitch fibres. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting

A 100m sprinter has a high proportion of fast-twitch fibres, enabling the rapid, powerful contractions needed for explosive speed. Weightlifting Fast-twitch fibres dominate a maximal lift, producing high force quickly, though they fatigue rapidly. Contrast A marathon runner, by contrast, relies on fatigue-resistant slow-twitch fibres for sustained aerobic effort. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe their characteristics and the efforts they suit: "Fast-twitch (Type II) fibres contract rapidly and produce high force but fatigue quickly, relying on the anaerobic systems; they dominate explosive activities such as sprinting and weightlifting."

Fat Burning Zone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fat Burning Zone BTEC Sport General Fat Burning Zone The lower-intensity range where fat provides a larger share of the energy. 📖 What it means The fat burning zone is a popular name for low-to-moderate intensity exercise (about 60–70% of maximum heart rate) where fat supplies a larger percentage of energy than at higher intensities. However, higher intensities burn more energy overall, so the total amount of fat used over a session can be as high or higher with harder exercise.

What matters most for fat loss is the overall energy balance across days and weeks, so the 'zone' should be treated as a guide rather than a rule. 🏅 Sporting examples Gym cardio A machine labels a heart rate range as the fat burning zone. Walking A steady walk uses a high proportion of fat but a small total amount of energy. Interval training A harder session burns more calories in the same time. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish percentage from total: "Lower intensities use a greater proportion of fat, but higher intensities burn more total calories and can lead to equal or greater fat use." Fat-free Body Mass — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fat-free Body Mass IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Fat-free Body Mass The mass of the body that is not fat. 📖 What it means Fat-free body mass (also called fat-free mass ) is total body mass minus fat mass . It includes muscle, bone, organs, connective tissue and body water. It is closely related to lean body mass , which sometimes includes a small amount of essential fat. It is estimated by methods such as skinfold measures, bioelectrical impedance, DEXA and underwater weighing.

Fat-free mass is a major determinant of resting metabolic rate , strength and power, so athletes often aim to increase it. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength training A rugby player increases fat-free mass through resistance training. Weight loss Crash dieting can reduce fat-free mass as well as fat. Assessment A DEXA scan separates fat, bone and lean tissue. ✍️ Using the term in context Give the equation: "Fat-free mass equals body mass minus fat mass, and includes muscle, bone, organs and water." Fat (Lipid) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fat (Lipid) IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Fat (Lipid) The body's largest energy store — a slow-burning fuel that powers low-intensity, long-duration exercise. 📖 What it means Fat (lipid) is a macronutrient and a major fuel for low-to-moderate intensity, long-duration exercise . It is stored as triglycerides in adipose tissue and within the muscles, and broken down via beta-oxidation for aerobic energy production.

Fat is an enormous energy store — far larger than the body's limited carbohydrate stores — but it releases energy slowly and requires more oxygen to metabolise, so it cannot fuel high-intensity efforts. As exercise intensity increases , the body shifts from using a higher proportion of fat toward using more carbohydrate. Endurance training improves the body's ability to use fat, helping to spare limited glycogen . 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance In the steady miles of a long run, fat provides a large share of the energy, sparing carbohydrate for later, higher-intensity efforts. Fuel shift

As a cyclist increases their pace up a climb, their body shifts from using more fat toward using more carbohydrate. Training effect Endurance training increases the capacity to use fat at a given intensity, improving glycogen sparing and endurance. ✍️ Using the term in context Link fat to low intensity, high yield and glycogen sparing: "Fat is a major fuel for low-to-moderate intensity exercise, providing a very large but slowly released energy store; as intensity rises the body shifts toward carbohydrate, and endurance training improves fat use to spare glycogen." Note fat requires more oxygen to metabolise than carbohydrate. 🔗 Related terms

Fatigue Index — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fatigue Index IB Sport Science General Fatigue Index A number that captures how quickly power drops — the measure of anaerobic power decline over repeated sprints. 📖 What it means The fatigue index is a measure of the percentage decline in power output over a repeated-sprint or power test , such as the Wingate Test. It quantifies how quickly performance deteriorates as fatigue sets in. It is calculated from the difference between peak power and minimum power over the test, expressed as a percentage of peak power. A high fatigue index means power drops rapidly; a low one means the performer maintains power well.

The fatigue index is relevant to sports with repeated, short, maximal efforts — such as team games and combat sports — where the ability to sustain power across efforts is important. Training to improve anaerobic capacity and buffering reduces the fatigue index. 🏅 Sporting examples Wingate Test The fatigue index is calculated from the Wingate Test as the percentage drop from peak to minimum power. Team sports A low fatigue index helps a footballer maintain sprint speed in the closing stages of a match. Training effect Improving anaerobic capacity and buffering reduces the fatigue index over repeated efforts. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the fatigue index and what it measures:

Fatigue — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fatigue IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Fatigue The body saying slow down — the temporary decline in performance capacity that follows sustained effort. 📖 What it means Fatigue is the temporary inability to maintain an expected power output or force . It is a complex, multifactorial phenomenon with both peripheral (within the muscle) and central (nervous system) components.

Peripheral causes include depletion of energy stores (particularly glycogen and phosphocreatine), accumulation of metabolic by-products such as hydrogen ions that impair muscle function, and dehydration . These disrupt the muscle's ability to generate force. Central fatigue refers to reduced drive from the central nervous system to the muscles. Whether peripheral or central, fatigue is protective — it prevents the body from damaging itself, and is followed by recovery and, with appropriate training, supercompensation . 🏅 Sporting examples Glycogen depletion As glycogen depletes in a marathon, the muscles can no longer sustain the required power output — fatigue. Metabolic by-products

Accumulation of hydrogen ions during a hard 400 m lowers muscle pH and impairs force production. Recovery After fatigue and adequate recovery, the body supercompensates — rebuilding to a higher level than before. ✍️ Using the term in context Define fatigue and name its main causes: "Fatigue is the temporary inability to maintain expected power output, caused by energy store depletion, accumulation of metabolic by-products such as hydrogen ions, and dehydration, as well as central nervous system factors; it is followed by recovery and supercompensation." Distinguish peripheral from central causes. 🔗 Related terms Lactate Blood Lactate Supercompensation Recovery Glycogen Depletion Dehydration

Fatmax — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fatmax IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Fatmax The intensity where the body burns the most fat per minute. 📖 What it means Fatmax is the exercise intensity at which absolute fat oxidation is highest . It is measured in a laboratory with an incremental test using gas analysis, from which fat oxidation rates are calculated. In most people it falls at a moderate intensity , roughly 45–65% of VO2 max, and it tends to be higher in well-trained endurance athletes. Above Fatmax, fat oxidation falls as carbohydrate takes over as the main fuel.

Fatmax varies a lot between individuals, so a single figure for everyone is only a rough guide. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance training A cyclist trains around Fatmax to improve the muscles' ability to use fat and spare glycogen. Fitness testing A lab test shows a runner's fat oxidation peaking at a steady jogging pace. Health Exercise around Fatmax is often used in weight-management programmes. ✍️ Using the term in context Link intensity to fuel use: "Fatmax is the intensity at which fat oxidation is at its peak; above it, the contribution from carbohydrate rises as exercise becomes more intense."

Feedback — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Feedback IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Feedback The information that lets a performer improve — the engine of skill learning, coming in several types with different uses. 📖 What it means Feedback is information a performer receives about their performance , used to detect and correct errors and to reinforce successful actions. It is essential to learning and refining skills.

Feedback is classified in several ways. Intrinsic feedback comes from the performer's own senses (how a movement felt); extrinsic (augmented) feedback comes from an outside source such as a coach or video. It can also be split into knowledge of results (the outcome) and knowledge of performance (the quality of the technique). The type and timing of feedback should match the learner : beginners rely heavily on extrinsic feedback and knowledge of results, while advanced performers can use their own intrinsic feedback and more detailed knowledge of performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Coaching a beginner

A coach gives a novice swimmer clear extrinsic feedback and simple knowledge of results, because the learner cannot yet interpret their own movements. Video analysis A gymnast uses video (extrinsic, knowledge of performance) to see exactly how their technique looked and where to improve. Expert intrinsic feedback An elite golfer often knows from the feel of the swing (intrinsic feedback) whether a shot was well struck before seeing the result. ✍️ Using the term in context Classify feedback and match it to the learner:

"Feedback can be intrinsic (from the performer's own senses) or extrinsic (from a coach or video), and can give knowledge of results or knowledge of performance; beginners rely on extrinsic feedback, while experts use their own intrinsic feedback." Fell Running — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fell Running BTEC Sport General Fell Running Running on steep mountain terrain. 📖 What it means Fell running is the sport of running over steep, rough hill and mountain terrain in the UK, often without marked paths, where runners may need to navigate using a map and compass and carry safety equipment. It places high demands on aerobic fitness, leg strength, balance and downhill control . Steep descents involve a lot of eccentric muscle work , which causes muscle soreness.

Safety is a major issue: weather can change quickly, so correct clothing, kit and navigation skills are vital. Races have rules about mandatory equipment. 🏅 Sporting examples Hill race A short, steep race up and down a fell. Training Hill repeats and strength work. Safety Compulsory waterproofs, map and whistle. ✍️ Using the term in context Mention demands: "Fell running combines endurance with strength and technique on steep ground, and the large amount of downhill running causes eccentric muscle damage." The triad is now understood more broadly within relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S). Fine Motor Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fine Motor Skill AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Fine Motor Skill Skills built on precision, not power — the small, accurate movements that decide sports like darts, archery and snooker. 📖 What it means A fine motor skill is one that involves small, precise movements using small muscle groups , requiring high levels of accuracy and control rather than large forces. Fine motor skills sit at one end of the gross–fine continuum of skill classification. At the other end, gross motor skills use large muscle groups to produce powerful, less precise movements.

Because they depend on precise control, fine motor skills are especially sensitive to factors such as arousal and anxiety — too much activation causes trembling and disrupts the delicate control they require. 🏅 Sporting examples Darts Throwing a dart is a fine motor skill, relying on precise, controlled movement of the hand and fingers rather than large muscular force. First-Class Lever — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › First-Class Lever IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General First-Class Lever The see-saw of the body — the lever arrangement where the pivot sits between the effort and the load. 📖 What it means A first-class lever is one in which the fulcrum (pivot) lies between the effort and the load — the arrangement of a see-saw. In the body, the joint acts as the fulcrum. The classic example in the body is the neck : the joint between the skull and the spine is the fulcrum, the weight of the head is the load, and the neck extensor muscles provide the effort, allowing the head to nod.

Depending on the exact position of the fulcrum, a first-class lever can favour either force or range and speed of movement . First-class levers are relatively uncommon in the human body compared with third-class levers. 🏅 Sporting examples Heading a ball Nodding the head to head a football uses a first-class lever at the joint between the skull and the top of the spine. Triceps extension Extension at the elbow via the triceps is sometimes classified as a first-class lever, with the joint between effort and load. General principle First-class levers can be arranged to favour force or to favour speed and range, depending on the fulcrum's position. ✍️ Using the term in context

State the arrangement and give the body example: "In a first-class lever the fulcrum lies between the effort and the load; in the body, nodding the head is an example, with the joint acting as the fulcrum between the neck muscles (effort) and the head (load)." Fitness Testing — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fitness Testing General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Fitness Testing The systematic measurement of fitness — how coaches establish a baseline, monitor progress and make training decisions on evidence. 📖 What it means Fitness testing is the systematic measurement of the components of fitness to assess a performer's current status and monitor change over time. It turns training decisions from guesswork into evidence.

Fitness testing is used to establish a baseline, identify strengths and weaknesses, set training goals, monitor progress, and compare an athlete against normative data or against their own past results. For a test to be worthwhile it must be valid (it measures what it claims to) and reliable (it gives consistent, repeatable results), and it should be specific to the demands of the sport and administered under standardised conditions. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-season A coach conducts a battery of fitness tests at the start of pre-season to establish a baseline and identify each player's weaknesses to target. Monitoring

Repeating the same tests across a season shows whether training is producing the intended improvements. Test selection For a sprinter, a coach selects speed and power tests (e.g. a 30m sprint and vertical jump) rather than an endurance test, ensuring specificity. ✍️ Using the term in context State the purposes and the quality criteria: "Fitness testing systematically measures the components of fitness to set baselines, monitor progress and guide training; tests must be valid, reliable and specific to the sport, and administered under standardised conditions." FITT Principle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › FITT Principle General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge FITT Principle A simple framework for turning training goals into a concrete programme — Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type. 📖 What it means The FITT principle is a framework for designing and progressing a training programme . FITT stands for Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what kind of training). By adjusting each of these four variables, a coach can apply progressive overload and shape training toward a specific goal — for example, increasing frequency or intensity over time to keep driving adaptation.

FITT works alongside the wider principles of training (such as specificity, progression and reversibility). The 'Type' element in particular ensures training is specific to the demands of the sport or fitness goal. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance goal To improve aerobic fitness, a coach might set Frequency at four sessions a week, moderate Intensity, Time of 40+ minutes, and Type as continuous running. Applying overload To progress, the athlete gradually increases one FITT variable at a time — for example, adding time or intensity — to keep overloading the body. Strength goal

For strength, the Type becomes resistance training, with Intensity set as a high percentage of 1RM and lower Time per set. ✍️ Using the term in context Spell out the four variables and link to overload: "The FITT principle — Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type — provides a framework for designing training; adjusting these variables applies progressive overload and shapes the programme toward a specific goal." Fitts and Posner's Stages of Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fitts and Posner's Stages of Learning AS Level / Cambridge General Fitts and Posner's Stages of Learning The classic three-stage map of how skills are learned — from clumsy beginner to automatic expert. 📖 What it means Fitts and Posner's stages of learning describe how a performer progresses through three stages as they acquire a motor skill : the cognitive, associative and autonomous stages.

In the cognitive stage , the beginner forms a basic mental picture of the skill and makes frequent large errors. In the associative stage , they refine the skill through practice, making fewer errors and relying less on conscious thought. In the autonomous stage , the skill becomes largely automatic, freeing attention for tactics and the environment. The model is useful because it tells a coach how to adapt their teaching at each stage — the type of practice, guidance and feedback that best suits a learner changes as they progress. 🏅 Sporting examples Cognitive stage A beginner tennis player thinking through every element of a serve, making many errors, is in the cognitive stage.

Associative stage A club-level player who serves fairly consistently but is still refining technique is in the associative stage. Autonomous stage A professional serving automatically while focusing on placement and tactics is in the autonomous stage. ✍️ Using the term in context Name all three stages and their characteristics: "Fitts and Posner identified three stages of learning: the cognitive stage (forming a mental picture, frequent errors), the associative stage (refining through practice), and the autonomous stage (automatic execution), each requiring different coaching." Link each stage to appropriate practice, guidance and feedback. 🔗 Related terms

Fixator — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fixator IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Fixator The stabiliser in the background — a muscle that holds the origin steady so the agonist can do its job. 📖 What it means A fixator is a muscle that stabilises the origin of the agonist , preventing unwanted movement there so that the agonist can act effectively at its insertion. Without fixators, contracting muscles would move the wrong bone.

For example, when the biceps curl lifts the forearm, the muscles around the shoulder act as fixators, holding the upper arm and shoulder steady so the biceps can flex the elbow. The fixator provides a stable base for the agonist's action. Fixators are part of the team of muscles — alongside agonist, antagonist, and synergist — that work together to produce controlled, efficient movement. Identifying fixators is part of the full analysis of a movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps curl The shoulder and rotator cuff muscles act as fixators during a biceps curl, keeping the upper arm stable. Providing a base By holding the origin steady, fixators give the agonist a firm base to pull from.

Movement analysis Full movement analysis identifies the agonist, antagonist, synergists and fixators. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a fixator and its role: "A fixator is a muscle that stabilises the origin of the agonist so it can act effectively; it holds the bone at the agonist's origin steady, providing a firm base for the movement."
