Fixed Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fixed Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Fixed Practice Repeating a skill in the same conditions over and over — the practice structure that grooves closed skills to automaticity. 📖 What it means Fixed practice involves repeatedly rehearsing a whole skill in the same, unchanging conditions . The performer practises the movement again and again to groove it into a consistent motor programme. It is sometimes called drill practice. It is best suited to closed, self-paced skills performed in stable, predictable environments, where the goal is to reproduce the same technique consistently every time.

It contrasts with variable practice , which changes the conditions between attempts to develop adaptability. Fixed practice builds consistency but does not develop the ability to adapt to changing situations, so it is less suitable for open skills. 🏅 Sporting examples Free throw A basketball player repeatedly practising the identical free-throw action uses fixed practice to groove a consistent closed skill. Javelin A javelin thrower drills the same throwing technique repeatedly, as the skill is closed and self-paced. Contrast A footballer developing dribbling would use variable practice instead, because dribbling is an open skill needing adaptability. ✍️ Using the term in context

Match fixed practice to closed skills and contrast with variable practice: "Fixed practice repeatedly rehearses a whole skill in unchanging conditions, suiting closed, self-paced skills such as a free throw; open skills are better developed through variable practice." Flexed Arm Hang Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Flexed Arm Hang Test General Flexed Arm Hang Test How long can you hold on? — a simple measure of upper-body muscular endurance. 📖 What it means The Flexed Arm Hang Test is a fitness test measuring upper-body muscular endurance by timing how long a performer can maintain their chin above a bar while hanging with elbows flexed. The performer holds the hanging position for as long as possible, and the time to failure is the score. Because it relies on the muscles holding the body up against gravity for a sustained time, it assesses the endurance of the biceps, forearms and shoulder muscles .

It is practical and requires minimal equipment — just a pull-up bar — and is suitable for a wide age range. Results are compared against normative data , though performance can be affected by body mass, so results are most useful for monitoring change over time. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance measure The longer a performer holds the flexed arm hang, the greater their upper-body muscular endurance. Minimal equipment The test needs only a bar and a timer, making it practical in schools and clubs. Normative comparison Results are compared against norms, but the test is most useful for tracking change over time. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures:

Flexibility — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Flexibility General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Flexibility The range of movement available at a joint — a health-related fitness component that underpins technique and helps prevent injury. 📖 What it means Flexibility is the range of motion available at a joint or series of joints . It is influenced by the structure of the joint, and by the length and elasticity of the surrounding muscles, tendons and ligaments.

It is a health-related component of fitness . Good flexibility allows a fuller, more efficient range of movement, can improve technique and performance, and may help reduce the risk of certain injuries. Flexibility is developed through stretching methods — static, dynamic, active, passive, ballistic and PNF — and is assessed with tests such as the sit and reach. The flexibility required varies greatly between sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Gymnastics Gymnastics demands exceptional flexibility, allowing the extreme joint ranges needed for splits, bridges and many skills. Hurdling A hurdler needs good hip flexibility to clear the barrier efficiently with minimal loss of speed. Assessment

The sit and reach test is commonly used to measure flexibility in the lower back and hamstrings. ✍️ Using the term in context Define flexibility and note the factors and methods: "Flexibility is the range of motion at a joint, influenced by joint structure and muscle length; as a health-related component of fitness, it is developed through stretching and assessed with tests such as the sit and reach." Name specific stretching methods and match the flexibility demand to the sport. 🔗 Related terms Static Stretching Dynamic Stretching Range of Motion (ROM) Sit and Reach Test Health-Related Fitness Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) 🎓 Where this appears BTEC Sport

Flexion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Flexion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Flexion One of the most common joint movements to identify in analysis — the bending of a joint that decreases its angle. 📖 What it means Flexion is a movement that decreases the angle at a joint . Bending the elbow to bring the hand toward the shoulder, or bending the knee, are both examples of flexion. It is produced by flexor muscles acting as the agonist — for example, the biceps flexes the elbow and the hamstrings flex the knee. Flexion has an opposite movement, extension , which increases the joint angle.

In movement analysis, correctly identifying flexion means also stating the joint, the agonist producing it, and the plane and axis — flexion and extension generally occur in the sagittal plane about a frontal axis. 🏅 Sporting examples Weight training The upward phase of a biceps curl is elbow flexion, driven by the biceps as the agonist, decreasing the angle at the elbow. Running During the recovery phase of the running stride, the knee flexes to bring the heel toward the buttock, driven by the hamstrings. Football A player draws their leg back to kick by flexing the knee, before extending it to strike the ball. ✍️ Using the term in context Pair flexion with joint, agonist and plane:

"At the elbow, flexion decreases the joint angle in the sagittal plane about a frontal axis; the agonist is the biceps brachii." Flow State — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Flow State IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Flow State Being 'in the zone' — the optimal psychological state of effortless, fully absorbed performance that athletes chase. 📖 What it means Flow state is an optimal psychological state of complete absorption in an activity , in which performance feels effortless and automatic. It is often described by athletes as being 'in the zone'. Flow is associated with features such as total concentration, a sense of control, loss of self-consciousness, an altered sense of time, and intrinsic enjoyment . Performance in flow is typically at or near the athlete's best.

Flow is more likely when there is a good match between the challenge of the task and the performer's skill level , when arousal is at an optimal level, and when the performer has clear goals and confidence. It cannot be forced, but conditions can be created to make it more likely. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running A runner in flow describes the miles passing effortlessly, fully absorbed in the rhythm of the run with no sense of strain. Team sport A player 'in the zone' reads the game instinctively, makes decisions automatically, and performs at their peak without conscious effort. Creating conditions

A coach helps make flow more likely by matching challenge to skill, setting clear goals and building the athlete's confidence. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe flow and the conditions that promote it: "Flow state is an optimal state of complete absorption in which performance feels effortless; it is more likely when the challenge matches the performer's skill level, arousal is optimal, and goals are clear." Flying 30 Metre Speed Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Flying 30 Metre Speed Test BTEC Sport General Flying 30 Metre Speed Test A fitness test of maximum running speed. 📖 What it means The Flying 30 Metre Speed Test is a sprint test in which the athlete builds up speed over a run-in and is timed over the next 30 metres, measuring maximum running speed. Protocol: After a run-in of 20 to 30 metres, the athlete sprints through timing gates placed 30 metres apart. The time over this section is recorded.

Interpreting results: Because acceleration is excluded, the test measures top speed separately from acceleration, which is useful for comparing sprinters. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A sprinter runs the flying 30m in 2.8 seconds. Training use Comparing flying and standing starts shows whether acceleration or top speed needs work. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Foam Roller Exercises (Self-myofascial Release) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Foam Roller Exercises (Self-myofascial Release) BTEC Sport General Foam Roller Exercises (Self-myofascial Release) Self-massage with a foam roller. 📖 What it means Foam rolling , a form of self-myofascial release , involves rolling a body part over a foam cylinder to apply pressure to the muscles and surrounding fascia. Common areas are the calves, quadriceps, iliotibial band, glutes and upper back.

Research suggests it can give short-term increases in range of motion without reducing muscle performance, and may reduce muscle soreness after hard exercise. The mechanisms are not fully understood. Roll slowly, pause on tender spots for 20 to 30 seconds, and avoid rolling directly over joints, bones or acute injuries . It does not replace a proper warm-up or stretching. 🏅 Sporting examples Warm-up Rolling the calves before running. Recovery Rolling the thighs after a match. Mobility Rolling the upper back to improve overhead mobility. ✍️ Using the term in context Be accurate on effect:

"Foam rolling produces short-term increases in range of motion and may reduce soreness, although how it works is still being researched." Food Composition — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Food Composition IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Food Composition What a food is made of. 📖 What it means Food composition describes the amounts of the different nutrients in a food: the macronutrients (carbohydrate, protein, fat), micronutrients (vitamins and minerals), fibre and water . It is shown on nutrition labels and in food composition tables, usually per 100 g and per serving, together with the energy value in kcal and kJ. Athletes use composition information to plan meals, for example choosing high-carbohydrate foods before endurance events and protein-rich foods for recovery.

🏅 Sporting examples Label reading A cereal bar lists carbohydrate, sugars, protein, fat and fibre per 100 g. Meal planning A runner picks pasta for its carbohydrate content. Force-Time Curve — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Force-Time Curve IB Sport Science General Force-Time Curve A graph of force over time — revealing how quickly force is developed and how much is produced. 📖 What it means A force-time curve is a graph showing how the force produced by a muscle or group changes over time during a contraction. The shape of the curve reveals important aspects of the contraction's quality.

Key features include peak force (the maximum force reached), the rate of force development (how quickly force rises — the steepness of the initial slope), and the impulse (the area under the curve — force × time). Together these describe both how much force is produced and how quickly. Force-time curves are used in performance analysis and research to assess the explosive qualities of muscle. Training to improve rate of force development is important in power sports where forces must be generated rapidly. 🏅 Sporting examples Rate of development A steep initial rise in the force-time curve indicates rapid force development — key in explosive actions. Impulse

The area under the force-time curve represents the impulse, the product of force and time. Performance analysis Force-time curves from force plates are used to assess jumping and sprinting mechanics. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe a force-time curve and its key features: "A force-time curve graphs force against time during a muscle contraction; its key features are peak force, rate of force development (how quickly force rises) and impulse (area under the curve); it is used to assess explosive performance." Link rate of force development to power sports. 🔗 Related terms Force Impulse Power Rate of Force Development Newton's Laws of Motion Plyometrics 🎓 Where this appears

Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Force IB Sport Science General AS Level / Cambridge Force The push or pull that changes motion — the single most important quantity in biomechanics, tying together Newton's laws. 📖 What it means Force is a push or pull that can change the state of motion of a body — starting it, stopping it, speeding it up, slowing it down or changing its direction. It is a vector quantity , having both magnitude and direction, and is measured in newtons (N).

Force is central to Newton's laws of motion . Newton's second law states that force equals mass multiplied by acceleration ( F = ma ), so a greater force produces a greater acceleration for a given mass. In sport, athletes generate and apply force to accelerate their own bodies or objects — pushing against the ground to sprint, or applying force to a ball or implement to project it. The size, direction and point of application of a force all affect the result. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A sprinter applies large horizontal forces against the ground; by Newton's third law the ground pushes back, accelerating the athlete forward. Shot put

A shot putter applies maximum force to the shot over the longest possible range to maximise its release velocity. Rugby In a scrum, the forward pack generates large forces against the opposition to drive them backward. ✍️ Using the term in context Define force as a vector and link it to Newton's second law: "Force is a push or pull that changes a body's motion; by Newton's second law, F = ma, so for a given mass a larger force produces a greater acceleration." Consider size, direction and point of application when analysing a sporting force. 🔗 Related terms Newton's Laws of Motion Acceleration Ground Reaction Force Impulse Momentum Net Force 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Fracture — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fracture General BTEC Sport Fracture A break in the bone — from a sudden impact or the cumulative damage of repeated stress. 📖 What it means A fracture is a break or crack in a bone . It can result from a sudden, excessive force (acute or traumatic fracture) or from repetitive, cumulative stress that the bone cannot withstand over time (stress fracture). Acute fractures occur from a single impact or force — for example, a collision in contact sport or a heavy landing. Stress fractures are overuse injuries where repeated sub-maximal loading gradually creates a crack, common in endurance runners.

Fractures require medical assessment and management, usually including immobilisation and rehabilitation . Maintaining bone density through weight-bearing exercise and avoiding overtraining helps reduce fracture risk. 🏅 Sporting examples Acute fracture A collision in rugby can cause an acute fracture — a bone broken by a single, excessive force. Stress fracture A runner who rapidly increases their training mileage may develop a stress fracture from cumulative loading. Prevention Good bone density and avoiding overtraining reduce the risk of fractures. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a fracture and distinguish acute from stress:

Frank Horwill's 4-Second Rule — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Frank Horwill's 4-Second Rule BTEC Sport General Frank Horwill's 4-Second Rule A pacing rule for keeping endurance sessions specific. 📖 What it means Frank Horwill , a British middle-distance coach, suggested a pacing guide for training. Some training should be run at a pace within about four seconds per 400m of the athlete's best pace for their event, so that the work is specific to racing. The idea is that pace too far below race pace does not train the energy systems and movement pattern needed for the event, while pace at the right level encourages the correct adaptations.

It is a rule of thumb used by coaches, not a scientific law. Training also needs easier work for recovery. 🏅 Sporting examples 800m runner Intervals are run within a few seconds per lap of target pace. Planning A coach sets session paces from a recent race time. Specificity The rule applies the principle of specificity to pace. ✍️ Using the term in context Treat it as a guide: "Horwill's 4-second rule suggests keeping some training pace within about four seconds per 400m of race pace to make training specific." Free Body Diagram — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Free Body Diagram IB Sport Science General Free Body Diagram A sketch of all the forces at play — a simple diagram that makes it easy to analyse what's pushing and pulling. 📖 What it means A free body diagram is a simplified diagram showing all the external forces acting on a single body or object , represented as arrows. Each arrow's direction shows where the force points, and its size can indicate the magnitude.

Common forces shown include weight (gravity), ground reaction force, drag, lift and friction . By isolating the body and showing all forces, the diagram makes it easy to identify the resultant force and predict how the body will move. Free body diagrams are a fundamental biomechanical analysis tool , used to understand what forces govern a sprint start, a jump landing or a projectile in flight. Drawing one is a practical application of Newton's laws. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint start A free body diagram of a sprinter on the blocks shows ground reaction force, gravity and the net force forward. Projectile

A diagram of a ball in flight shows gravity pulling down and air resistance opposing motion. Analysis tool Free body diagrams make it easier to see all the forces on a body and predict the resulting motion. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a free body diagram and its purpose: "A free body diagram shows all external forces acting on an isolated body as arrows, including weight, ground reaction force, drag and friction; it is a biomechanical tool for analysing the forces governing motion." Free Radicals — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Free Radicals IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Free Radicals Reactive molecules produced during metabolism that can damage cells. 📖 What it means Free radicals are highly reactive molecules with an unpaired electron . They are a natural by-product of using oxygen to produce energy, so production rises during exercise. In large amounts they can damage cell membranes, proteins and DNA (oxidative stress), but at moderate levels they act as signals that help the body adapt to training. The body's defence is antioxidants , which neutralise free radicals. 🏅 Sporting examples Hard training

Intense exercise raises free radical production and temporarily raises oxidative stress. Pollution and smoking External sources add to the free radical load. Overtraining Insufficient recovery may let oxidative stress build up. ✍️ Using the term in context Show both sides: "Exercise increases free radical production, which can cause oxidative damage if antioxidant defences are overwhelmed, but low levels help trigger adaptation." Frequency (training principle) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Frequency (training principle) General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Frequency (training principle) How often you train — the first variable in FITT and a key lever for managing load and recovery. 📖 What it means Frequency is the number of training sessions per week . It is the 'F' in the FITT principle and one of the key variables manipulated to apply progressive overload.

Training frequency must be balanced with recovery : sessions provide the training stimulus, but adaptation happens during rest. Too little frequency may be insufficient to drive adaptation; too much can prevent full recovery and risk overtraining. The optimal frequency depends on the type of training, the individual's fitness level, and the training goals . In periodisation, frequency is typically higher in the preparation phase and may be reduced during the competition phase or taper. 🏅 Sporting examples FITT Frequency is the 'F' in the FITT principle — one of four variables adjusted to apply progressive overload. Recovery balance

Increasing session frequency must be balanced with adequate recovery to allow adaptation. Periodisation Frequency may be higher in preparation phases and lower around key competitions. ✍️ Using the term in context Define frequency as a training variable: "Frequency is the number of training sessions per week, the 'F' in the FITT principle; it must balance the training stimulus with adequate recovery, and optimal frequency depends on training type, fitness level and goals." Friction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Friction IB Sport Science General Friction The resistance between surfaces — the force that gives athletes grip or makes objects slide. 📖 What it means Friction is a resistive force between two surfaces in contact that opposes relative motion between them . It acts parallel to the surfaces. There are two main types: static friction (preventing surfaces from beginning to slide against each other) and kinetic friction (slowing surfaces already moving against each other). The size of friction depends on the nature of the surfaces and the force pressing them together .

In sport, friction has dual relevance: too little can cause slipping (athletes seek high friction through studs, grip shoes and chalk), while in other contexts — a sliding tackle, a skiing turn — some friction is necessary but must be managed to control movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Grip A footballer's studded boots increase friction with the turf, preventing slipping on acceleration. Chalk and grip Climbers use chalk on their hands to increase friction between skin and rock. Sliding A swimmer minimises friction with the water through a streamlined position and smooth suit. ✍️ Using the term in context Define friction and its sporting implications:

"Friction is the resistive force between two surfaces in contact opposing relative motion; athletes use high friction for grip (studs, chalk) and reduce it where sliding or streamlining is needed." Frontal Plane — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Frontal Plane IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Frontal Plane One of the three planes of movement — the vertical divide between front and back, in which side-to-side movements occur. 📖 What it means The frontal plane is an imaginary vertical plane that divides the body into front and back halves . Movements that occur in this plane are side-to-side movements. The main movements in the frontal plane are abduction and adduction (moving limbs away from and toward the midline), along with side bending of the trunk. These movements occur about a sagittal axis (running front to back).

The frontal plane is one of the three planes of movement , alongside the sagittal (front–back) and transverse (top–bottom) planes. Identifying the correct plane is a key part of movement analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Star jump The out-and-in movement of the arms and legs in a star jump occurs in the frontal plane — abduction and adduction about a sagittal axis. Gymnastics A cartwheel is a classic frontal-plane movement, with the body moving sideways along the plane. Lateral raise A dumbbell lateral raise abducts the arms in the frontal plane. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the plane, the movements and the axis together:

Fuel Utilisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fuel Utilisation IB Sport Science General Fuel Utilisation The blend of fuels the body burns — and how intensity and duration shift the balance between carbohydrate and fat. 📖 What it means Fuel utilisation is the balance of carbohydrate and fat used to produce energy , which shifts with the intensity and duration of exercise. Both fuels are used, but their proportions change.

At higher intensities , carbohydrate dominates because it can be broken down rapidly, including anaerobically. At lower intensities and longer durations , fat contributes a greater proportion of energy — a phenomenon sometimes called the 'crossover point' as intensity rises. Understanding fuel utilisation guides nutrition strategies and training choices: endurance training adapts the body to use fat more efficiently (fat oxidation), sparing limited glycogen for higher-intensity bursts, and delayed glycogen depletion improves endurance performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Intensity effect

At marathon pace, a mix of fat and carbohydrate is used, whereas a sprint is almost entirely carbohydrate-fuelled. Training adaptation Endurance training increases fat oxidation, sparing glycogen during prolonged exercise. Nutrition Consuming carbohydrate during a long event helps maintain fuel availability as glycogen is used. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how fuel use shifts with intensity and duration: "Fuel utilisation is the balance of carbohydrate and fat used for energy; higher intensity increases reliance on carbohydrate, while lower intensity and longer duration shift the balance toward fat — endurance training improves fat oxidation, sparing glycogen."

Fulcrum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Fulcrum IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Fulcrum The pivot of a lever — in the body, always a joint. 📖 What it means The fulcrum is the pivot point of a lever system . In the human body, the fulcrum is always a joint — the fixed point around which the lever arm (a bone) rotates. Together with the effort (provided by the muscle) and the load (the resistance to be overcome), the fulcrum is one of the three components of a lever. The position of the fulcrum relative to the effort and load determines the class of lever .

Identifying the fulcrum correctly is the first step in analysing a lever system in the body — for example, the elbow joint is the fulcrum in elbow flexion and extension, while the ball of the foot is the fulcrum when rising onto the toes. 🏅 Sporting examples Elbow In a biceps curl, the elbow joint is the fulcrum — the pivot point around which the forearm rotates. Rising onto toes In plantar flexion, the ball of the foot acts as the fulcrum for the second-class lever. Lever class The position of the fulcrum relative to effort and load determines whether a first-, second- or third-class lever is used. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the fulcrum and its role in a lever:

Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) The air still in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath out. 📖 What it means Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the amount of air remaining in the lungs after a normal passive exhalation . It equals expiratory reserve volume + residual volume . FRC keeps the alveoli partly open and allows gas exchange to continue between breaths, so oxygen levels in the blood stay steady. 🏅 Sporting examples Quiet breathing Between breaths at rest, the lungs still hold the FRC. Spirometry

FRC is found by adding expiratory reserve volume to the residual volume. Posture FRC is lower when lying down than when standing, because of the effect of the abdomen on the diaphragm. ✍️ Using the term in context Show how it is built: "Functional residual capacity is the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume: the air left after a normal breath out." Gamesmanship — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gamesmanship AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Gamesmanship Bending the spirit of the rules without quite breaking them — the grey area between fair play and cheating. 📖 What it means Gamesmanship is the use of dubious but not strictly illegal tactics to gain an advantage . It involves bending the spirit of the rules and the conventions of fair play, without technically breaking the written rules. It contrasts with sportsmanship (fair, honourable conduct) and with outright cheating (breaking the rules). Gamesmanship sits in an ethical grey area — legal, but widely seen as against the spirit of the game.

Common examples include time-wasting, sledging (verbally unsettling an opponent), feigning injury, or deliberately breaking an opponent's concentration . Whether such tactics are acceptable is a live ethical debate in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Time-wasting A football team leading late in a match deliberately slows play at throw-ins and goal kicks — gamesmanship that bends the spirit of the game without breaking a rule. Sledging In cricket, verbally trying to unsettle a batter is a form of gamesmanship aimed at disrupting concentration. Ethical debate Feigning injury to gain a break or waste time raises questions about where competitive edge ends and unfair conduct begins.

✍️ Using the term in context Position gamesmanship between sportsmanship and cheating: "Gamesmanship involves dubious but not strictly illegal tactics such as time-wasting or sledging; it bends the spirit of the rules without breaking them, sitting ethically between sportsmanship and outright cheating." Gas Exchange — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gas Exchange IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Gas Exchange How oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it — the essential swap that happens at both the lungs and the muscles. 📖 What it means Gas exchange is the movement of oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out of it , achieved by the passive process of diffusion across thin membranes.

It happens in two key places. At the alveoli in the lungs, oxygen diffuses from the air into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out to be exhaled. At the muscles , oxygen diffuses from the blood into the tissue and carbon dioxide diffuses back into the blood. Gas exchange is efficient because of the large surface area and thin walls of the alveoli and capillaries, and the steep concentration gradients maintained by breathing and blood flow — gradients that steepen during exercise to speed the process. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance exercise During a run, rapid gas exchange at the alveoli keeps blood oxygen high, while at the muscles oxygen is offloaded quickly to meet the high demand.

Structure and function The huge surface area of the alveoli allows large volumes of gas to be exchanged quickly — vital during intense exercise. Altitude At altitude, lower oxygen pressure reduces the gradient for gas exchange at the lungs, making oxygen uptake harder until the body adapts. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe gas exchange at both sites via diffusion: "Gas exchange occurs by diffusion: at the alveoli, oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide out; at the muscles, oxygen moves into the tissue and carbon dioxide into the blood, aided by steep concentration gradients during exercise." Link efficient gas exchange to large surface area, thin membranes and steep gradients.

Gastrocnemius — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gastrocnemius IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Gastrocnemius The prominent calf muscle behind every jump and sprint step — a key plantar flexor at the ankle. 📖 What it means The gastrocnemius is the large, two-headed muscle that forms the bulk of the calf . Its main action is plantar flexion of the ankle (pointing the toes and pushing off the ground), and it also assists in flexing the knee . Because it crosses both the knee and ankle joints, it plays a major role in the powerful push-off during running and jumping , working with the deeper soleus muscle as part of the calf complex.

The gastrocnemius contains a high proportion of fast-twitch fibres in many people, suiting it to the explosive plantar flexion needed for sprinting and jumping. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting At each toe-off, the gastrocnemius plantar-flexes the ankle to push the sprinter forward off the ground. Jumping In a vertical jump, powerful plantar flexion by the gastrocnemius contributes to the final drive off the floor. Running economy The gastrocnemius and Achilles tendon store and return elastic energy with each stride, aiding efficient running. ✍️ Using the term in context Name its main action and its role in explosive movement:

General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) The body's blueprint for coping with stress — a three-stage response that training deliberately exploits. 📖 What it means General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) is Selye's model describing the body's three-stage response to a stressor , including the stressor of training. The three stages are alarm, resistance and exhaustion .

In the alarm stage , the body detects the stress and its initial performance may temporarily dip. In the resistance stage , it adapts and performance rises above the original level — the training effect. If stress continues without adequate recovery, the exhaustion stage is reached, where the body cannot cope and performance deteriorates — overtraining. GAS helps explain why training works: the alarm and resistance stages produce adaptation. It also explains why recovery is essential and why overtraining is harmful, providing a framework for periodisation . 🏅 Sporting examples Alarm The first session of a new training block causes an alarm response — temporary fatigue and soreness.

Resistance With repeated sessions and recovery, the body adapts and performance rises (the resistance stage). Exhaustion Too much training without recovery pushes the body into the exhaustion stage — overtraining. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the three stages and link to training: "General Adaptation Syndrome is Selye's three-stage model of the stress response — alarm (initial dip), resistance (adaptation and improvement) and exhaustion (overtraining from insufficient recovery); it explains how training works and why recovery is essential." Relate it to periodisation and overtraining. 🔗 Related terms

Glucagon — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glucagon IB Sport Science General Glucagon The blood sugar raiser — the pancreatic hormone that mobilises stored glucose when the body needs more. 📖 What it means Glucagon is a hormone secreted by the pancreas that raises blood glucose by stimulating the breakdown of glycogen to glucose (glycogenolysis) in the liver. It works in opposition to insulin : when blood glucose falls (as during prolonged exercise), glucagon is released to restore it. This antagonistic relationship between insulin and glucagon is a classic example of negative feedback control of blood glucose .

During prolonged exercise, glucagon is important for maintaining blood glucose supply to the brain and working muscles , helping to sustain performance as muscle glycogen depletes. 🏅 Sporting examples Blood glucose control As blood glucose falls during a long run, glucagon is released to break down liver glycogen and restore it. Antagonistic pair Glucagon and insulin work antagonistically to keep blood glucose stable — a classic negative feedback loop. Sustained exercise Glucagon helps maintain blood glucose during prolonged exercise, sustaining brain and muscle supply. ✍️ Using the term in context Define glucagon and contrast with insulin:

"Glucagon is a pancreatic hormone that raises blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown in the liver; it works antagonistically with insulin in a negative feedback loop, and is particularly important during prolonged exercise." Glucose — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glucose IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Glucose The simple sugar that muscles actually burn — the immediately usable form of carbohydrate that enters energy production. 📖 What it means Glucose is a simple sugar and the form of carbohydrate that the body uses directly for energy. It circulates in the blood and enters glycolysis to help resynthesise ATP. Glucose comes from the breakdown of dietary carbohydrate and from the breakdown of stored glycogen . Maintaining an adequate blood glucose level is important for sustaining exercise and for brain function.

During prolonged exercise, blood glucose can fall as stores deplete, contributing to fatigue — which is why athletes may take on carbohydrate (such as sports drinks or gels) during long events to maintain blood glucose. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance events A cyclist consumes carbohydrate during a long ride to maintain blood glucose and delay fatigue as glycogen stores fall. Gluteal Muscles — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gluteal Muscles IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Gluteal Muscles The buttock muscles that drive the hips. 📖 What it means The gluteal muscles are gluteus maximus, gluteus medius and gluteus minimus . Gluteus maximus is the largest and the main hip extensor , powerful in sprinting, jumping and climbing. Gluteus medius and minimus sit on the outer hip. They abduct the thigh and stabilise the pelvis on one leg, which is crucial in running and single-leg exercises.

Weak glutes are linked to knee and back problems and poor running mechanics. Common exercises include squats, hip thrusts, lunges, bridges and side-lying leg raises . 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting Gluteus maximus drives the hip into extension at push-off. Running Gluteus medius stops the pelvis dropping on the stance leg. Rehabilitation Bridges and side steps strengthen the glutes after injury. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the action: "Gluteus maximus extends the hip, while gluteus medius abducts the thigh and stabilises the pelvis during single-leg support." Gluteus Maximus — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gluteus Maximus IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Gluteus Maximus The body's largest and one of its most powerful muscles — the engine of hip extension behind sprinting and jumping. 📖 What it means The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle of the buttocks and one of the most powerful in the body. Glycaemic Index — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glycaemic Index IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Glycaemic Index A ranking of how fast foods raise blood sugar — a practical nutrition tool for fuelling and recovery around exercise. 📖 What it means The glycaemic index (GI) is a ranking of carbohydrate-containing foods by how quickly they raise blood glucose levels after eating. High-GI foods raise blood glucose rapidly; low-GI foods release glucose more slowly and steadily.

The GI is useful for timing nutrition around exercise . Low-GI foods before exercise can provide a slow, sustained release of energy, while high-GI foods during and immediately after exercise can quickly top up and replenish glycogen stores. It is one factor among many in sports nutrition — the overall amount and timing of carbohydrate, and the individual athlete's needs, also matter — but GI provides a practical guide for fuelling strategies. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-event An endurance athlete might choose a low-GI meal before competition for a slow, sustained release of energy. During and after

High-GI carbohydrate (such as a sports drink or gel) is useful during and immediately after exercise to rapidly supply and replenish glucose and glycogen. Recovery window Consuming high-GI carbohydrate soon after a hard session helps speed the replenishment of muscle glycogen. ✍️ Using the term in context Define GI and apply it to nutrition timing: "The glycaemic index ranks foods by how quickly they raise blood glucose; low-GI foods suit pre-exercise fuelling for sustained energy, while high-GI foods during and after exercise rapidly replenish glucose and glycogen." Glycogen Depletion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glycogen Depletion IB Sport Science General Glycogen Depletion Hitting the wall — when the body's carbohydrate stores run dry and endurance performance collapses. 📖 What it means Glycogen depletion is the exhaustion of the body's stored carbohydrate during prolonged exercise . Because glycogen stores are limited, they can be used up during sustained, moderate-to-high intensity effort. When glycogen is depleted — the moment endurance athletes call 'hitting the wall' — performance deteriorates sharply, because fat alone cannot sustain the same exercise intensity and cannot be broken down as quickly.

Strategies to delay or prevent glycogen depletion include carbohydrate loading before an event, consuming carbohydrate during exercise, and endurance training (which improves fat oxidation, sparing glycogen). Understanding glycogen depletion is fundamental to endurance sport nutrition. 🏅 Sporting examples Hitting the wall A marathon runner 'hitting the wall' around mile 20 is experiencing the sharp performance drop of glycogen depletion. Sparing glycogen Endurance training improves fat oxidation, sparing glycogen for higher-intensity moments. Nutrition strategy Consuming carbohydrate gels during a long race delays glycogen depletion and sustains performance. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define glycogen depletion and how to manage it: "Glycogen depletion is the exhaustion of stored carbohydrate during prolonged exercise, causing a sharp performance drop; it is managed by carbohydrate loading, consuming carbohydrate during exercise, and endurance training to improve fat oxidation." Glycogen — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glycogen IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Glycogen The stored form of carbohydrate — the body's readily available fuel tank for moderate and high-intensity exercise. 📖 What it means Glycogen is the storage form of carbohydrate in the body, held mainly in the muscles and the liver . When energy is needed, glycogen is broken down to glucose to fuel ATP resynthesis.

Glycogen is the main fuel for moderate-to-high intensity exercise , because carbohydrate can be broken down both aerobically and anaerobically and releases energy relatively quickly. However, glycogen stores are limited , lasting only around 90 minutes of hard exercise. When glycogen stores run low, fatigue sets in — the sensation endurance athletes call 'hitting the wall' . This is why carbohydrate intake, carbohydrate loading and refuelling after exercise are all important for performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A marathon runner's performance can collapse when muscle glycogen runs low — 'hitting the wall' — which is why they take on carbohydrate during the race. Team sports

A footballer relies on muscle glycogen for the repeated sprints of a match, making pre-match carbohydrate intake important. Recovery After training, carbohydrate intake replenishes depleted muscle glycogen ready for the next session. ✍️ Using the term in context Link glycogen to storage, intensity and its limited supply: "Glycogen is the stored form of carbohydrate in the muscles and liver and the main fuel for higher-intensity exercise; because stores are limited to around 90 minutes of hard exercise, depletion causes fatigue." Connect glycogen depletion to 'hitting the wall' and the need to refuel. 🔗 Related terms

Glycogenolysis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glycogenolysis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Glycogenolysis Breaking stored glycogen down into glucose. 📖 What it means Glycogenolysis is the breakdown of glycogen into glucose . It is triggered by adrenaline and glucagon at the start of exercise or when blood glucose falls. In the liver , the glucose is released into the blood to keep blood glucose steady. In muscle , the glucose (as glucose-6-phosphate) stays in the muscle cell and goes into glycolysis. It is the opposite of glycogenesis , the building of glycogen from glucose, which is stimulated by insulin. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint

Muscle glycogenolysis supplies fast fuel. Long run Liver glycogenolysis releases glucose to the blood. Recovery Glycogenesis restores glycogen stores. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast the two: "Glycogenolysis breaks glycogen down to glucose, and glycogenesis builds glycogen from glucose." Glycolysis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Glycolysis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Glycolysis The breakdown of glucose that fuels high-intensity exercise — the shared first stage of anaerobic and aerobic energy production. 📖 What it means Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose to produce ATP . It takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell and does not require oxygen to begin, making it central to high-intensity exercise.

Glycolysis produces a small, rapid yield of ATP and converts glucose into pyruvate . Without oxygen, pyruvate is converted to lactate (anaerobic glycolysis); with oxygen, pyruvate enters the Krebs cycle for much greater aerobic ATP production. Because it can operate anaerobically and produces ATP quickly, glycolysis is the key process of the glycolytic (lactic acid) energy system , dominant in high-intensity efforts lasting from about ten seconds to a few minutes. 🏅 Sporting examples 400m running A 400m runner relies heavily on anaerobic glycolysis to rapidly resynthesise ATP, producing lactate as the effort is sustained near-maximally. Repeated sprints

In a game of repeated sprints, glycolysis provides fast energy for each high-intensity burst. Aerobic link During steady endurance exercise, glycolysis still occurs, but pyruvate enters the Krebs cycle for aerobic ATP production rather than forming lactate. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the location, product and the two fates of pyruvate: "Glycolysis breaks glucose down to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, producing a rapid, small yield of ATP; without oxygen, pyruvate becomes lactate, whereas with oxygen it enters the Krebs cycle for further aerobic energy production." Position it as the shared first stage of anaerobic and aerobic metabolism. 🔗 Related terms

Goal Orientation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Goal Orientation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Goal Orientation What does success mean to you? — whether an athlete defines achievement by personal mastery or by beating others. 📖 What it means Goal orientation is an athlete's tendency to define success through personal mastery (task orientation) or through outperforming others (ego orientation) . A task-oriented athlete focuses on self-improvement and personal mastery — success means learning and developing skills. An ego-oriented athlete focuses on comparison with others — success means winning or performing better than peers.

Research suggests that a task orientation tends to be more adaptive , leading to greater persistence, intrinsic motivation and resilience when facing difficulty, whereas a strong ego orientation — especially when combined with low perceived ability — can lead to anxiety and avoidance. Many athletes hold both orientations to varying degrees. 🏅 Sporting examples Task orientation A task-oriented gymnast is satisfied when they improve a skill, regardless of where they finish in competition. Ego orientation An ego-oriented sprinter is motivated primarily by beating their rivals, not by personal improvement. Adaptive motivation

Task orientation is linked to greater persistence and resilience when progress is slow. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the two goal orientations and their implications: "Goal orientation describes how an athlete defines success: task orientation through personal mastery, ego orientation through outperforming others; task orientation tends to be more adaptive, linked to persistence and intrinsic motivation." Note that most athletes blend both orientations. 🔗 Related terms Achievement Motivation Motivation Self-Efficacy SMART Goals Attribution Theory Intrinsic Motivation 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub →

Goal Setting — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Goal Setting IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Goal Setting One of the most effective and widely used psychological tools — setting targets that direct effort, sustain motivation and build confidence. 📖 What it means Goal setting is the process of establishing specific targets to work toward . Used well, it is one of the most powerful techniques for improving motivation, focus, effort and confidence in sport.

Goals are often classified as outcome goals (the end result, e.g. winning), performance goals (a personal standard, e.g. a personal best time), and process goals (the specific actions or techniques to execute). Performance and process goals are largely within the athlete's control, making them especially valuable. Effective goals are commonly guided by the SMART principles — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound — ensuring they are clear, challenging but realistic, and able to be reviewed. 🏅 Sporting examples Athletics A runner sets a process goal (maintain a strong arm action), a performance goal (run under 12 seconds), and an outcome goal (win the race). Rehabilitation

An injured athlete uses short-term SMART goals to stay motivated and measure progress through a recovery programme. Control A coach emphasises performance and process goals because, unlike outcome goals, they remain within the athlete's control regardless of the opposition. ✍️ Using the term in context Classify goal types and reference SMART: "Goal setting directs effort and motivation; performance and process goals are especially valuable because they are within the athlete's control, and effective goals follow the SMART principles — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound." Golden Triangle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Golden Triangle BTEC Sport General Golden Triangle The link between sport, media and sponsors. 📖 What it means The golden triangle describes the interdependent relationship between sport, the media and sponsorship . Each corner gains from the others. Sport provides content and an audience for the media; the media give sport exposure and broadcasting income and attract sponsors; sponsors pay for access to the audience and fund sport and the media.

It has helped to make elite sport a global business, but critics argue it can change rules and schedules to suit broadcasters , make sport expensive to watch and favour wealthy clubs. 🏅 Sporting examples Premier League Television rights and sponsors bring huge income. Olympics Broadcasters and sponsors fund the Games. Scheduling Kick-off times are set to suit TV audiences. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain each corner: "In the golden triangle, sport provides an audience, the media provide exposure, and sponsors provide funding, so each benefits from the other two." Golgi Tendon Organ (GTO) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Golgi Tendon Organ (GTO) IB Sport Science General Golgi Tendon Organ (GTO) The body's built-in safety brake — a receptor that detects muscle tension and can trigger a protective relaxation. 📖 What it means The Golgi tendon organ (GTO) is a proprioceptor located in the tendons, near the junction with the muscle . It detects changes in muscle tension — how hard the muscle is pulling. When the GTO senses very high tension , it can trigger a reflex called autogenic inhibition , causing the muscle to relax. This is thought to be a protective mechanism , guarding against damage from excessive force.

The GTO's action is important in flexibility work: techniques such as PNF stretching deliberately use an isometric contraction to stimulate the GTO, producing autogenic inhibition and allowing a greater subsequent stretch. 🏅 Sporting examples PNF stretching In PNF stretching, an athlete contracts the muscle isometrically to activate the GTO; the resulting autogenic inhibition lets them stretch further afterwards. Heavy lifting The GTO's protective reflex can limit force output during a maximal lift, which training can partially adapt over time. Injury protection By triggering relaxation at very high tension, the GTO helps protect muscles and tendons from tearing under extreme load.

✍️ Using the term in context Name what it detects and the reflex it triggers: "The Golgi tendon organ is a proprioceptor in the tendon that detects muscle tension; at very high tension it triggers autogenic inhibition, causing the muscle to relax as a protective mechanism, which PNF stretching exploits." Contrast it with the muscle spindle, which detects stretch (length) rather than tension. 🔗 Related terms Muscle Spindle Autogenic Inhibition Proprioception Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) Stretch Reflex Flexibility 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Grassroots Sport — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Grassroots Sport AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Grassroots Sport The base of the pyramid — sport at community and amateur level where lifelong participation begins. 📖 What it means Grassroots sport refers to participation in sport at community and amateur level , forming the broad base of the participation pyramid. It includes school sport, club sport and recreational activity for the general population.

It is contrasted with elite or professional sport. Grassroots sport is primarily valued for its health, social and developmental benefits — building physical literacy, fostering social inclusion and forming the talent pool from which elite athletes emerge. Policy and investment in grassroots sport are central to sport development strategies, with the aim of increasing participation, widening access and reducing barriers so that more people remain active throughout their lives. 🏅 Sporting examples Participation base School sport clubs and local recreational teams are examples of grassroots sport. Grip Strength Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Grip Strength Test General BTEC Sport Grip Strength Test Squeeze as hard as you can — the quickest field test of upper-body muscular strength. 📖 What it means The Grip Strength Test is a test measuring the maximal force of the hand and forearm muscles using a handgrip dynamometer. The performer squeezes the device as hard as possible and the peak force is recorded. It is quick, safe and requires minimal equipment , and results can be compared against normative data . Grip strength is sometimes used as a general indicator of overall upper-body strength and is often measured in both hands for comparison.

Its main limitation is specificity — it only measures grip strength, and may not reflect the strength of other muscle groups. It is most useful for monitoring change over time or identifying differences between sides, rather than as a comprehensive measure of upper-body strength. 🏅 Sporting examples Quick test A handgrip dynamometer measures grip strength quickly and safely with minimal equipment. Both hands Testing both dominant and non-dominant hands allows comparison and identifies asymmetries. General indicator Grip strength is sometimes used as a proxy for overall upper-body strength. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and evaluate it:

Gross Motor Abilities — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gross Motor Abilities BTEC Sport General Gross Motor Abilities General abilities of large-muscle movement. 📖 What it means Gross motor abilities are the general capacities that support whole-body, large muscle movements , such as strength, speed, power, balance, agility, flexibility and endurance . They are inherited to a large extent but can be developed through practice. They underpin the performance of gross motor skills such as running, jumping and throwing. Abilities differ from skills: an ability is a general, stable trait, while a skill is learned and specific to a task. 🏅 Sporting examples Football

Speed and agility support dribbling and changes of direction. Gymnastics Balance and flexibility underpin routines. Gross Motor Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Gross Motor Skill AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Gross Motor Skill Skills built on power, not precision — the large-muscle movements that underpin running, jumping and throwing. 📖 What it means A gross motor skill is one that involves large muscle groups producing powerful movements , where the emphasis is on strength and power rather than fine precision . Gross motor skills sit at one end of the gross–fine continuum of skill classification. At the other end, fine motor skills use small muscle groups for small, precise, accurate movements.

Because they rely on large-muscle power rather than delicate control, gross motor skills are generally less disrupted by high arousal than fine motor skills — a useful point when discussing arousal and performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Running Sprinting is a gross motor skill — it uses large muscle groups to produce powerful movement, with precision playing a smaller role. Shot put Putting the shot is a gross motor skill, relying on the powerful contraction of large muscle groups. Rugby tackle A tackle uses large-muscle power to generate force, making it a gross motor skill. ✍️ Using the term in context Classify the skill and note the arousal implication:

Ground Reaction Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ground Reaction Force IB Sport Science General Ground Reaction Force Newton's third law in action — the force the ground pushes back with, and the source of all propulsion in running and jumping. 📖 What it means Ground reaction force (GRF) is the force exerted by the ground on a body in response to the force the body applies to the ground . It is a direct example of Newton's third law : for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

When an athlete pushes down and back into the ground, the ground pushes up and forward on them with an equal and opposite force — and it is this ground reaction force that propels them forward and upward. The size and direction of the ground reaction force determine the resulting motion. Athletes aim to apply force in the optimal direction (for example, more horizontally when accelerating) to maximise useful propulsion. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint start A sprinter drives back and down against the blocks; the ground reaction force pushes them forward and upward out of the start. Jumping

In a vertical jump, the athlete pushes hard into the floor, and the upward ground reaction force propels them into the air. Direction matters During acceleration a sprinter angles their force more horizontally, directing the ground reaction force to drive them forward rather than upward. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain GRF via Newton's third law and its role in propulsion: "By Newton's third law, when an athlete applies force to the ground, the ground exerts an equal and opposite ground reaction force; this force propels the athlete, and its direction determines the resulting motion." Group Cohesion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Group Cohesion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Group Cohesion The glue that holds a team together — the tendency to stick together and stay united in pursuit of shared goals. 📖 What it means Group cohesion is the tendency of a team to stick together and remain united in the pursuit of its goals . A cohesive team works together effectively and resists breaking apart under pressure.

Cohesion has two dimensions. Task cohesion is how well the team works together to achieve its performance goals . Social cohesion is how much team members like and get along with each other . The two do not always go together. Research suggests task cohesion is generally more strongly linked to performance than social cohesion, and that the relationship between cohesion and success works in both directions — cohesion can improve performance, and success can build cohesion. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sport A football team with high task cohesion coordinates effectively on the pitch, even if not all players are close friends off it. Social vs task

A group of good friends (high social cohesion) may still perform poorly if they lack the shared commitment to team goals (task cohesion). Building cohesion A coach uses shared goals, defined roles and team-building activities to strengthen cohesion, particularly task cohesion. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish task and social cohesion and their link to performance: "Group cohesion has two dimensions: task cohesion (working together toward goals) and social cohesion (interpersonal attraction); task cohesion tends to be more strongly associated with performance." GROW Model — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › GROW Model BTEC Sport General GROW Model A four-step framework for coaching conversations. 📖 What it means The GROW model (popularised by John Whitmore) structures a coaching conversation in four stages: G oal, R eality, O ptions and W ill (or Way forward). Goal : what does the athlete want to achieve? Reality : where are they now? Options : what could they do? Will : what will they actually do, and when? It supports athlete-centred coaching because the coach asks open questions and the athlete finds the answers, which builds ownership and motivation. 🏅 Sporting examples Mid-season review

A coach asks a player what they want to improve, how they currently perform and what options exist. Goal setting The athlete commits to a plan with dates. Growth Hormone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Growth Hormone IB Sport Science General Growth Hormone The body's growth and repair signal — a pituitary hormone that drives tissue building and fat metabolism. 📖 What it means Growth hormone is a hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland that stimulates tissue growth, protein synthesis and fat metabolism . It promotes the growth and repair of muscle and bone , and stimulates the use of fat as a fuel, sparing carbohydrate. Its secretion is increased by exercise, particularly high-intensity and resistance training , and also during sleep.

Because of its anabolic (tissue-building) effects, growth hormone is important for training adaptation and recovery . Synthetic forms have been misused as a doping substance to try to enhance muscle mass and recovery, though their effect on athletic performance is debated. 🏅 Sporting examples Tissue repair Growth hormone secreted after training promotes the repair and growth of muscle tissue. Fat metabolism Growth hormone stimulates fat oxidation, helping spare carbohydrate during prolonged exercise. Training stimulus High-intensity and resistance training increase growth hormone secretion. ✍️ Using the term in context Define growth hormone and its roles:

Guidance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Guidance AS Level / Cambridge General BTEC Sport Guidance The methods a coach uses to help a learner acquire a skill — visual, verbal, manual and mechanical, each with its own place. 📖 What it means Guidance refers to the methods a coach uses to help a performer learn or improve a skill . There are four main types, and the best choice depends on the learner and the skill.

Visual guidance (demonstrations, videos, diagrams) shows what the skill should look like. Verbal guidance (instructions, feedback) explains and directs. Manual guidance physically moves the performer through the movement. Mechanical guidance uses equipment (such as a harness or float) to support the action. The type of guidance should match the stage of learning : beginners benefit greatly from visual and, at times, manual or mechanical guidance, while more advanced performers rely more on precise verbal guidance and their own feedback. Over-reliance on manual or mechanical guidance can hinder independent performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Visual

A coach demonstrates a tennis serve so a beginner can form a clear mental picture of the correct action. Manual/mechanical A gymnastics coach physically supports a learner through a somersault (manual), or uses a harness (mechanical), to build confidence and safety. Verbal An experienced athlete receives precise verbal guidance to fine-tune a specific aspect of their technique. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the four types and match them to the learner:

"The four types of guidance are visual, verbal, manual and mechanical; visual and manual guidance suit beginners forming a mental picture, while advanced performers rely more on precise verbal guidance, and over-reliance on manual guidance can hinder independence." Haemoglobin — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Haemoglobin IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Haemoglobin The oxygen taxi of the blood — the protein in red blood cells that carries almost all the oxygen delivered to working muscles. 📖 What it means Haemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds and transports oxygen . The vast majority of the oxygen carried in the blood is bound to haemoglobin rather than dissolved in the plasma.

In the lungs, where oxygen is plentiful, haemoglobin binds oxygen to form oxyhaemoglobin. At the muscles, where oxygen is being used up, haemoglobin releases its oxygen — a release made easier during exercise by the Bohr effect. The amount of haemoglobin strongly affects oxygen-carrying capacity and therefore aerobic performance. This is why increasing red blood cell count — legally through altitude training or illegally through blood doping — can improve endurance. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance performance A distance runner's oxygen-carrying capacity depends heavily on haemoglobin; more haemoglobin means more oxygen delivered to the muscles. Altitude training

Altitude training stimulates red blood cell and haemoglobin production, legally boosting oxygen-carrying capacity. Bohr effect At the working muscles, raised carbon dioxide and acidity make haemoglobin release its oxygen more readily, matching supply to demand. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe haemoglobin's role in oxygen transport: "Haemoglobin is the protein in red blood cells that transports the majority of the blood's oxygen; it binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it at the muscles, and its concentration strongly affects oxygen-carrying capacity and aerobic performance." Link haemoglobin levels to altitude training and blood doping. 🔗 Related terms

Hammer Throw — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hammer Throw BTEC Sport General Hammer Throw Spinning with a heavy ball on a wire before release. 📖 What it means In the hammer throw , the athlete holds a metal ball attached to a wire and handle and makes preliminary swings, then three or four turns within the circle before releasing it. The ball weighs 7.26 kg for men and 4 kg for women . The hammer moves in a circle, so the athlete provides centripetal force through the wire. The faster the rotation, the greater the force that the athlete must resist, so they lean back. At release, the hammer travels along a tangent to its circular path.

Release speed, angle (about 40 to 44 degrees) and technique decide the distance. The event requires strength, rotational speed and balance . 🏅 Sporting examples Turns The thrower accelerates the hammer with each turn. Release The hammer leaves along a tangent to the circle. Safety Throws take place within a protective cage. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to circular motion: "The hammer thrower supplies a centripetal force through the wire, and at release the hammer flies off along a tangent to its path." Hamstrings — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hamstrings IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Hamstrings The powerful muscle group at the back of the thigh — vital for sprinting, and one of the most frequently injured muscles in sport. 📖 What it means The hamstrings are a group of three muscles at the back of the thigh . Their main actions are to flex the knee (bend the leg) and to extend the hip (drive the thigh backward). They are heavily involved in sprinting and jumping , working powerfully to extend the hip during the drive phase and to control the leg during the recovery phase. They act as the antagonist to the quadriceps at the knee.

The hamstrings are one of the most commonly strained muscle groups in sport, particularly during high-speed running, because of the large forces they absorb eccentrically as they decelerate the swinging lower leg. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A sprinter's hamstrings work powerfully to extend the hip and drive the body forward, and eccentrically to control the lower leg — which is where strains often occur. Football Hamstring strains are among the most common injuries in football, typically occurring during sprinting or stretching for the ball. Knee flexion In the recovery phase of running, the hamstrings flex the knee to bring the heel toward the buttock. ✍️ Using the term in context

Harvard Step Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Harvard Step Test General BTEC Sport Harvard Step Test A classic stepping test of cardiovascular fitness — measuring how quickly the heart recovers from effort. 📖 What it means The Harvard Step Test is a submaximal fitness test assessing cardiovascular fitness from heart rate recovery after stepping. The performer steps on and off a bench at a set rate for five minutes, then recovery heart rate is measured.

The recovery heart rate — measured in the minutes after stepping — is used to calculate a fitness index : a faster recovery (lower heart rate) indicates better cardiovascular fitness. This reflects the heart's ability to return to resting rate quickly. It is simple, practical and needs only a bench and a timer . As a submaximal test, it is safer than maximal tests for large groups, but recovery heart rate can be affected by factors including hydration and anxiety, so standardised conditions matter. 🏅 Sporting examples Recovery measure A faster heart rate recovery after the Harvard Step Test indicates better cardiovascular fitness. Practical

The test needs only a bench and a timer, making it practical for school and club settings. Fitness index The recovery heart rate is used to calculate a fitness index that reflects aerobic capacity. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the Harvard Step Test and what it assesses: "The Harvard Step Test is a submaximal cardiovascular fitness test that measures heart rate recovery after five minutes of stepping; faster recovery indicates better fitness, and it is practical but should be standardised to reduce variability." HDL and LDL Cholesterol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › HDL and LDL Cholesterol IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport HDL and LDL Cholesterol The 'good' and 'bad' cholesterol. 📖 What it means Cholesterol is carried in the blood by lipoproteins. LDL (low-density lipoprotein) carries cholesterol to the tissues and can build up in artery walls , leading to atherosclerosis. It is often called 'bad' cholesterol. HDL (high-density lipoprotein) carries cholesterol away from the tissues to the liver for removal, so higher levels are protective. It is often called 'good' cholesterol.

Regular aerobic exercise tends to raise HDL and lower LDL and triglycerides . Diet high in saturated fat can raise LDL. 🏅 Sporting examples Health check A blood test gives total cholesterol, HDL and LDL. Exercise Regular activity raises HDL. Diet Replacing saturated with unsaturated fat helps lower LDL. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast the two: "LDL deposits cholesterol in artery walls, increasing the risk of atherosclerosis, whereas HDL transports it back to the liver." Health-Related Fitness — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Health-Related Fitness General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Health-Related Fitness The fitness components tied to health and everyday function — the foundation on which sporting performance is built. 📖 What it means Health-related fitness refers to the components of fitness associated with good health and the ability to carry out everyday activities without undue fatigue. They benefit health regardless of sporting ability.

The health-related components are usually given as cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition . Together they underpin general physical wellbeing and reduce the risk of ill health. They contrast with the skill-related components (agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time, speed), which are more specific to sporting performance. Most sports draw on both groups, but health-related fitness forms the base. 🏅 Sporting examples General health Regular activity develops cardiovascular endurance and healthy body composition, lowering the risk of heart disease and improving daily function. Sporting base

A footballer's health-related fitness (endurance, strength) provides the base on which skill-related qualities such as agility and speed are built. Testing Health-related components are assessed with tests such as the multistage fitness test (endurance) and the sit and reach (flexibility). ✍️ Using the term in context List the health-related components and contrast with skill-related: "Health-related fitness comprises cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition; these underpin health and everyday function, in contrast to the skill-related components more specific to sporting performance."

Healthy Eating — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Healthy Eating BTEC Sport General Healthy Eating A balanced diet for health and performance. 📖 What it means Healthy eating means eating a balanced and varied diet that gives the body the energy and nutrients it needs. Heart Rate Reserve — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Heart Rate Reserve IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Heart Rate Reserve A more individualised way to set training intensity — the working range between resting and maximum heart rate. 📖 What it means Heart rate reserve (HRR) is the difference between a person's maximum heart rate and their resting heart rate . It represents the range over which heart rate can increase during exercise.

It is used to set training intensities more individually through the Karvonen method , which calculates a target heart rate as a percentage of the heart rate reserve added to the resting heart rate, rather than a simple percentage of maximum heart rate. Because it takes resting heart rate into account , HRR gives a more personalised target intensity — particularly useful for comparing individuals with different fitness levels, since a fitter person's lower resting heart rate changes their reserve. 🏅 Sporting examples Setting zones

A coach uses the Karvonen method with heart rate reserve to set a more individualised target heart rate for each athlete rather than a one-size-fits-all percentage. Fitness differences Two athletes with the same maximum heart rate but different resting heart rates will have different reserves, so HRR gives each a more appropriate target. Monitoring As an athlete's fitness improves and resting heart rate falls, their heart rate reserve increases, reflecting greater cardiovascular capacity. ✍️ Using the term in context Define HRR and link it to the Karvonen method:

Heart Rate Training Zones — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Heart Rate Training Zones IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Heart Rate Training Zones Training bands set by heart rate. 📖 What it means Heart rate training zones are ranges of heart rate calculated as a percentage of maximum heart rate (HRmax) or of heart rate reserve (the Karvonen method). A typical scheme is: 50–60% very light, 60–70% light aerobic, 70–80% moderate aerobic, 80–90% hard and 90–100% maximal. Estimated HRmax (such as 220 minus age) can be inaccurate for individuals, so zones are best set from a measured maximum or a field test. 🏅 Sporting examples Fitness class

Participants aim to stay in 60–80% of HRmax for fat and aerobic work. Interval training A runner works at 90%+ of HRmax in repetitions, then recovers to 60%.
