Heart Rate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Heart Rate IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Heart Rate The most accessible window into the cardiovascular response to exercise — how many times the heart beats each minute, and a foundation for monitoring training. 📖 What it means Heart rate (HR) is the number of times the heart beats per minute (bpm) . It is one of the simplest and most widely used measures of how hard the cardiovascular system is working.

Heart rate is one of the two components of cardiac output ( Q = HR × SV ). It rises before exercise (the anticipatory rise), climbs steeply as exercise begins, and levels off at a steady state during submaximal work before returning toward resting levels during recovery. Because it is easy to measure, heart rate is used to set and monitor training intensity — often as a percentage of maximum heart rate — and a low resting heart rate is a common sign of good aerobic fitness resulting from a larger stroke volume. 🏅 Sporting examples Training zones A runner uses a heart rate monitor to keep their effort within a target zone, for example 70–80% of maximum heart rate for aerobic development.

Fitness indicator An endurance athlete's low resting heart rate reflects a large stroke volume from cardiac hypertrophy — the heart needs fewer beats to circulate the same blood. Recovery How quickly heart rate falls after exercise (heart rate recovery) is used as an indicator of cardiovascular fitness. ✍️ Using the term in context Link heart rate to cardiac output and to training monitoring: "Heart rate is the number of beats per minute and one component of cardiac output (Q = HR × SV); it is widely used to set training intensity as a percentage of maximum heart rate, and a low resting heart rate indicates good aerobic fitness."

Adaptations include an increased plasma volume , earlier and greater sweating , more dilute sweat (less sodium lost), a lower heart rate and a lower core temperature at a given workload.

These improve exercise tolerance in hot environments and lower the risk of heat illness . Athletes can acclimatise by training in hot conditions or using heat chambers or hot baths. 🏅 Sporting examples Major event A team arrives early in a hot host country. Hick's Law — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hick's Law IB Sport Science General Hick's Law Why more choices mean slower reactions — a precise relationship at the heart of reaction time and decision making. 📖 What it means Hick's Law states that reaction time increases as the number of possible choices (stimulus–response alternatives) increases . The more options a performer must choose between, the longer it takes them to react.

The relationship is logarithmic rather than linear — reaction time rises predictably with the number of choices, but each additional choice adds progressively less time. Choice reaction time is longer than simple reaction time (one stimulus, one response). Hick's Law explains why performers try to increase the number of options they present to an opponent (to slow the opponent's reaction) while reducing their own uncertainty — for example through anticipation and reading cues. 🏅 Sporting examples Rugby An attacker with several passing and running options slows the defender's reaction, because the defender faces more choices — a direct application of Hick's Law. Tennis

A server who can place the ball in several different areas increases the returner's choices and therefore their reaction time. Reducing own uncertainty An experienced goalkeeper reads cues to anticipate a penalty, effectively reducing their own choices and speeding their reaction. ✍️ Using the term in context State the relationship and note it is logarithmic: "Hick's Law states that reaction time increases as the number of choices increases, in a logarithmic relationship; performers exploit this by presenting opponents with more options to slow their reactions while reducing their own uncertainty." High Jump — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › High Jump BTEC Sport General High Jump Jumping over a bar, using the Fosbury flop. 📖 What it means In the high jump , athletes run a curved approach and take off from one foot, then clear the bar head and back first and land on a mat. This is called the Fosbury flop , after Dick Fosbury, who used it at the 1968 Olympics. The curve helps the jumper lean away from the bar and rotate in the air. The body arches over the bar so the centre of mass can pass below the bar while the body goes over it, which is an efficient use of the energy in the jump.

Success needs speed, take-off power and good flexibility and body control . The jump is a good example of the use of rotation and angular momentum. 🏅 Sporting examples Approach A J-shaped curve builds speed and lean. Bar clearance The back arches over the bar. Landing Athletes land on a thick mat. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to centre of mass: "The Fosbury flop lets the high jumper clear the bar while the centre of mass passes under it, making best use of the jump." HIIT (High-Intensity Interval Training) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › HIIT (High-Intensity Interval Training) General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge HIIT (High-Intensity Interval Training) Short, hard efforts with brief recovery — a time-efficient method that improves both anaerobic and aerobic fitness. 📖 What it means High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a form of interval training that alternates short bursts of very high-intensity, near-maximal effort with periods of low-intensity recovery or rest .

Despite its short total duration, HIIT is highly effective: it improves both anaerobic and aerobic fitness , drives cardiovascular and metabolic adaptations, and produces a large EPOC (elevated post-exercise oxygen consumption and calorie burn). Its main strength is time efficiency — meaningful fitness gains in a short session — making it popular for busy individuals and for athletes needing sport-specific high-intensity conditioning. Because it is demanding, it must be programmed carefully to allow recovery. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sports A footballer uses HIIT to develop the ability to repeat high-intensity sprints, closely matching the demands of match play. Time-efficient fitness

A busy individual gains cardiovascular and metabolic benefits from a short HIIT session when they lack time for long continuous training. Programming Because HIIT is very demanding, a coach limits its frequency and ensures adequate recovery to avoid overtraining. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the work-rest structure and the benefits: "HIIT alternates short bursts of near-maximal effort with low-intensity recovery; it is highly time-efficient, improving both anaerobic and aerobic fitness and producing a large EPOC, but must be programmed to allow adequate recovery." Highlight time efficiency and sport-specific conditioning as key advantages. 🔗 Related terms

Hill Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hill Training IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Hill Training Using slopes to build power and endurance. 📖 What it means Hill training involves running repeats up an incline . Short, steep sprints of around 10 to 15 seconds develop power and running mechanics , while longer, moderate hills of one to three minutes build aerobic and muscular endurance . Running uphill increases the demand on the quadriceps, glutes and calves and encourages a high knee drive and forward lean, while the slower pace gives a lower impact than flat sprinting. Recovery is usually a jog or walk back down.

It is used in the pre-season to build strength before speed work. It should be introduced gradually to avoid overuse injuries to the Achilles tendon and calf. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinter Short, steep hill sprints to build acceleration power. Distance runner Hill repeats of two minutes for strength endurance. Rugby Hill sprints as conditioning with low impact. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to adaptation: "Hill repeats increase the resistance of running, which develops leg power and muscular endurance while reducing impact compared to flat sprints." Hinge Joint — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hinge Joint IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Hinge Joint The body's one-direction joint — the design at the elbow and knee that allows movement in a single plane. 📖 What it means A hinge joint is a type of synovial joint that allows movement in only one plane — essentially opening and closing like a door hinge. The main movements it permits are flexion and extension . The clearest examples in the body are the elbow and the knee (and the ankle). At the elbow, the joint allows the arm to bend and straighten; at the knee, it allows the leg to flex and extend.

Because it moves in only one plane, a hinge joint offers less range of movement but greater stability than a ball and socket joint. This trade-off between mobility and stability is a common theme in joint analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Weight training The elbow acts as a hinge joint during a biceps curl, allowing flexion and extension in a single plane. Running The knee, a hinge joint, flexes and extends repeatedly through the running stride. Stability vs mobility A hinge joint's single-plane movement gives it more stability but less range than the multi-directional ball and socket joint. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the joint type, its movements and examples:

Hip Flexion Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hip Flexion Test BTEC Sport General Hip Flexion Test A fitness test of hip flexibility. 📖 What it means The Hip Flexion Test is a flexibility test that measures the range of motion in the hip as the knee is brought towards the chest. Protocol: The athlete lies on their back and brings one knee towards the chest while the other leg stays flat. The angle or distance is measured with a goniometer or inclinometer.

Interpreting results: A larger range suggests greater hip flexibility, and differences between legs may point to tightness or imbalance. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A sprinter's left and right hip ranges are compared. Training use Used to design stretching and mobility work. Homeostasis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Homeostasis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Homeostasis The body's drive to keep its internal environment stable — the balancing act that exercise constantly challenges. 📖 What it means Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment within the body, despite changes in external conditions or activity. Key variables kept within narrow ranges include body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose and hydration.

It works through negative feedback : when a variable moves away from its normal set point, the body detects the change and activates responses to bring it back — for example, sweating to reverse a rise in body temperature. Exercise is a major challenge to homeostasis : it raises body temperature, alters blood pH, uses up glucose and loses fluid. Many of the body's acute responses to exercise (increased breathing, sweating, blood redistribution) are homeostatic mechanisms restoring balance. 🏅 Sporting examples Temperature During exercise, rising body temperature triggers sweating and blood redistribution to the skin — homeostatic responses that restore normal temperature (thermoregulation).

Blood pH As acidity rises during high-intensity exercise, buffering and increased breathing act to restore blood pH toward normal. Blood glucose Hormones regulate the release of glucose from glycogen to keep blood glucose within its normal range during exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context Define homeostasis and link it to negative feedback and exercise: "Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment through negative feedback; exercise challenges homeostasis by raising temperature and altering pH, and many acute responses such as sweating are homeostatic mechanisms restoring balance." Use temperature, pH or glucose as concrete examples of homeostatic control.

Hormone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hormone IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Hormone A chemical messenger in the blood — the body's way of sending instructions from glands to distant target cells. 📖 What it means A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the bloodstream to regulate the function of target cells or organs. Hormones are the signals of the endocrine system.

They travel in the blood to target cells that carry specific receptors for them. Only cells with the right receptors respond to a given hormone, giving hormonal control both reach and specificity. Hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting than neural ones. In exercise, key hormones include adrenaline (cardiovascular and fuel response), insulin and glucagon (blood glucose), cortisol (stress and catabolism) and growth hormone (repair and fat metabolism). Together they coordinate the body's adaptation to the demands of exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Adrenaline Adrenaline is a hormone that prepares the body for exercise by raising heart rate and mobilising fuel. Specificity

Only cells with the right receptors respond to a hormone, giving endocrine control its specificity. Slow but sustained Hormonal responses are slower than nerve impulses but longer-lasting, coordinating sustained adaptations. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a hormone and how it works: "A hormone is a chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood; it acts on target cells with specific receptors, producing responses that are slower but longer-lasting than neural control." Name key exercise-related hormones as examples. 🔗 Related terms Endocrine System Adrenaline (Epinephrine) Insulin Glucagon Cortisol Growth Hormone 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Hurdles — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hurdles BTEC Sport General Hurdles Sprinting over barriers. 📖 What it means Hurdling involves sprinting while clearing a series of evenly spaced barriers . Standard events are the 110m hurdles (men) and 100m hurdles (women), both with 10 hurdles , and the 400m hurdles for both, also with 10 hurdles. Technique focuses on a fast approach, a lead leg driven up and over, a trail leg brought through with the knee high and a quick return to sprinting . Athletes aim to lose as little speed as possible across each hurdle, using a fixed stride pattern between barriers.

Success relies on speed, rhythm, mobility in the hips and good coordination . 🏅 Sporting examples 110m hurdles Three strides between each hurdle. 400m hurdles Athletes keep a set number of strides, adjusting on tired legs. Drills Trail leg and lead leg drills improve technique. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the key demand: "Hurdling requires a consistent stride pattern and good hip mobility to clear each barrier with minimal loss of speed." Hydration Strategy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hydration Strategy IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Hydration Strategy Planning fluid intake around exercise — the deliberate approach to staying hydrated that protects performance and health. 📖 What it means A hydration strategy is a planned approach to fluid (and electrolyte) intake before, during and after exercise , designed to maintain hydration and offset the fluid lost through sweating.

The aim is to prevent dehydration — recall that even a 2% loss of body mass can impair performance — while also avoiding overdrinking. A good strategy considers the athlete's sweat rate, the duration and intensity of exercise, and the environmental conditions. Strategies typically involve drinking to start well-hydrated, taking fluid at regular intervals during prolonged exercise, and rehydrating afterwards , often with added electrolytes and sometimes carbohydrate for longer events. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A marathon runner plans to drink at regular intervals and includes electrolytes, matching intake to their known sweat rate and the weather. Hot conditions

In hot, humid competition, an athlete adapts their hydration strategy to account for a much higher sweat rate. Team sports A footballer takes on fluid at every opportunity during a match to limit the fall in plasma volume and delay cardiovascular drift. ✍️ Using the term in context Frame it as planned intake around exercise to prevent dehydration: "A hydration strategy plans fluid and electrolyte intake before, during and after exercise to prevent dehydration; it is tailored to the athlete's sweat rate, the exercise demands and the environmental conditions." Hydrogen Ions — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hydrogen Ions IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Hydrogen Ions The particles behind the acidity that builds up in hard exercise. 📖 What it means Hydrogen ions (H+) are released when ATP is broken down and during anaerobic glycolysis. As they build up, the pH of muscle falls and the muscle becomes more acidic. The extra acidity interferes with enzymes and with calcium release, so muscle contracts less forcefully and fatigue sets in. The body counters this with buffers such as bicarbonate. Training increases buffering capacity, which lets athletes tolerate more intense work. 🏅 Sporting examples 400m

Rapid accumulation of hydrogen ions in the final 100m causes the heavy, burning legs. Interval training Training near the lactate threshold improves buffering of hydrogen ions. Supplements Sodium bicarbonate is used to increase buffering capacity. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the true cause of the problem: "The accumulation of hydrogen ions lowers muscle pH, which inhibits enzyme activity and muscle contraction, causing fatigue." It is hydrogen ions, not lactate itself, that are most directly linked to the fall in pH. 🔗 Related terms Lactate Lactic Acid System Buffer Bicarbonate Buffering Acid-Base Balance Fatigue 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub →

Hypertension — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypertension IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Hypertension Persistently high blood pressure — a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease that exercise can help manage. 📖 What it means Hypertension is persistently elevated blood pressure , generally defined as a resting blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg . It is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke and kidney disease.

It is often called the 'silent killer' because it typically produces no obvious symptoms but causes progressive damage to the arteries and organs over time. Risk factors include inactivity, poor diet, obesity, smoking and age. Regular aerobic exercise is an effective way to reduce blood pressure and manage hypertension, by improving the elasticity of blood vessels and reducing resting heart rate. This is one of the most important health benefits of physical activity. 🏅 Sporting examples Risk factor Hypertension raises the risk of heart attack and stroke by placing sustained pressure on the arteries. Aerobic exercise

Regular aerobic exercise can lower resting blood pressure, helping to manage hypertension. Silent condition Hypertension typically produces no symptoms, so it often goes undetected without measurement. ✍️ Using the term in context Define hypertension and link it to exercise: "Hypertension is persistently elevated resting blood pressure above 140/90 mmHg, a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease; regular aerobic exercise can lower blood pressure, making physical activity one of the most effective management strategies." Hyperthermia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hyperthermia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Hyperthermia When the body overheats. 📖 What it means Hyperthermia is an elevated core temperature caused by heat production and gain exceeding heat loss, for example when exercising in hot or humid conditions. It ranges from heat cramps and heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, dizziness, headache) to heat stroke , where core temperature is above about 40°C and confusion or collapse may occur. Heat stroke is life-threatening.

Risk is reduced by acclimatisation, hydration, light clothing, avoiding the hottest part of the day and reducing intensity. Treatment is to cool the person quickly and seek emergency help. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A hot, humid race raises the risk. Pre-season training Players train in the heat before they acclimatise. Football Cooling breaks help manage temperature. ✍️ Using the term in context State symptoms and response: "Hyperthermia occurs when heat gain exceeds heat loss; heat stroke requires immediate cooling and emergency treatment." Hypertonic Drink — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypertonic Drink General BTEC Sport Hypertonic Drink A drink more concentrated than the body — high in carbohydrate but absorbed more slowly, suited to fuelling rather than rehydrating. 📖 What it means A hypertonic drink is a sports drink with a higher solute concentration than body fluids (above ~9g per 100ml). Its high carbohydrate content makes it effective for fuelling , but the high concentration slows gastric emptying and fluid absorption.

Because the gut must draw water from the body to dilute a hypertonic drink before it can be absorbed, it is less effective for rapid rehydration than isotonic or hypotonic drinks. This makes it less suitable during exercise when rapid fluid replacement is needed. Hypertonic drinks are best used before or after exercise as a carbohydrate source when hydration is not the primary concern — or in cooler conditions where sweat rates are lower and fuel rather than fluid is the priority. 🏅 Sporting examples Post-exercise fuelling A hypertonic drink after exercise replenishes carbohydrate stores, though rehydration may need plain water too. Slower absorption

The high concentration of a hypertonic drink slows absorption, so it should not be the main fluid source during exercise. Fuel focus In cool conditions with low sweat rates, a hypertonic drink can supply carbohydrate without major dehydration risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a hypertonic drink and its best use: "A hypertonic drink has a higher solute concentration than body fluids, providing good carbohydrate supply but slow absorption; it is less effective for rehydration than isotonic drinks and is best used before or after exercise." Hypertrophy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypertrophy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Hypertrophy The muscle growth that resistance training produces — the increase in muscle size that raises strength and power. 📖 What it means Hypertrophy is the increase in the size of muscle fibres , and therefore of the whole muscle, in response to training — particularly resistance training. It is a chronic adaptation, developing over weeks and months.

It occurs because the stress of resistance training stimulates an increase in contractile proteins (actin and myosin) within the muscle fibres. Larger fibres can generate greater force, so hypertrophy contributes to increased strength and power . The opposite process is atrophy , the wasting of muscle that occurs with disuse or detraining (an example of reversibility). Fast-twitch fibres generally show the greatest potential for hypertrophy. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength training A rugby forward follows a resistance programme to produce muscle hypertrophy, increasing size and strength for scrummaging and contact. Sprinting/power

Hypertrophy of fast-twitch fibres helps a sprinter or thrower generate greater force and power. Reversibility If training stops, the reverse process, atrophy, occurs and the muscle gradually loses the size it had gained. ✍️ Using the term in context Define hypertrophy as a chronic adaptation and link it to force: "Hypertrophy is the increase in muscle fibre size from resistance training, caused by an increase in contractile proteins; larger fibres generate greater force, improving strength and power. Hypoglycaemia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypoglycaemia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Hypoglycaemia Blood sugar that is too low. 📖 What it means Hypoglycaemia is a low blood glucose level , typically below about 4 mmol/L. Symptoms include hunger, shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion and poor coordination . In exercise, it can occur when glycogen stores are low or after a long period without food. It is more serious in people with diabetes who use insulin, who need to monitor their glucose and plan food and insulin around exercise.

The fix is to take fast-acting carbohydrate , such as glucose tablets or a sugary drink. Prevention includes eating before and during long exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance event A runner 'hits the wall' when carbohydrate is low. Diabetes A player checks blood glucose before play. Hyponatraemia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hyponatraemia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Hyponatraemia Low blood sodium. 📖 What it means Hyponatraemia means blood sodium is below the normal range (about 135 mmol per litre). In endurance athletes it is mostly caused by over-drinking , which dilutes the sodium in blood, sometimes with large sweat sodium losses. Fluid then moves into cells, causing swelling. Symptoms are headache, nausea, bloating, confusion and, in severe cases, seizures and coma . It is a medical emergency.

Prevention is to drink to thirst rather than as much as possible, and to include sodium in long events. It is also described as exercise-associated hyponatraemia. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon A slow runner drinks at every station and becomes ill. Ultra event Sodium tablets and drinks are used. Guidance Athletes should not drink beyond thirst. ✍️ Using the term in context Give the cause and the fix: "Hyponatraemia in endurance athletes is caused by excessive fluid intake diluting blood sodium; prevention is to drink to thirst and replace sodium." Hypothermia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypothermia BTEC Sport General Hypothermia When the body loses heat faster than it makes it. 📖 What it means Hypothermia is a condition in which core body temperature falls below about 35°C . It happens when heat loss exceeds heat production, in cold, wet and windy conditions or in cold water. Early signs are shivering, cold skin, tiredness and poor coordination ; later signs include confusion, slurred speech and loss of shivering. It is a medical emergency.

Outdoor and water sports participants reduce risk by wearing layered, waterproof clothing , staying dry, eating and drinking enough and monitoring group members. First aid is to shelter the person, remove wet clothing, insulate and call for help. 🏅 Sporting examples Hill walking Wet clothing and wind increase heat loss. Open-water swimming Cold water rapidly lowers core temperature. Expedition Leaders check for early signs in the group. ✍️ Using the term in context Give causes and prevention: "Hypothermia occurs when heat loss exceeds heat production, and can be prevented by layered clothing, staying dry and eating enough." Hypothesis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypothesis IB Sport Science General Hypothesis The testable prediction at the start of any investigation — essential for the IB internal assessment and all scientific method. 📖 What it means A hypothesis is a clear, testable prediction about the relationship between variables , made before an investigation. It states what the researcher expects to happen, and it can be supported or rejected by the data.

A good hypothesis is specific and testable , usually predicting how the independent variable will affect the dependent variable . Researchers often distinguish the experimental (alternative) hypothesis (predicting an effect) from the null hypothesis (predicting no effect). The hypothesis guides the whole investigation — shaping the method, the data collected and the analysis — and the conclusion states whether the evidence supports it or whether the null hypothesis should be retained. 🏅 Sporting examples IB internal assessment A student might hypothesise that increasing rest interval length will improve repeated-sprint performance — a testable prediction linking the two variables.

Null hypothesis The corresponding null hypothesis would state that rest interval length has no effect on repeated-sprint performance. Guiding the study The hypothesis determines which variables to manipulate and measure, and the conclusion reports whether the data support it. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a hypothesis as a testable prediction linking variables: "A hypothesis is a testable prediction about the relationship between the independent and dependent variables; the experimental hypothesis predicts an effect, while the null hypothesis predicts none, and the data determine which is supported." Hypotonic Drink — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypotonic Drink General BTEC Sport Hypotonic Drink A drink more dilute than the body — absorbed fastest of all, ideal when rapid rehydration is the priority. 📖 What it means A hypotonic drink is a sports drink with a lower solute concentration than body fluids (below ~4g per 100ml). Because it is more dilute, it is absorbed faster than isotonic or hypertonic drinks . The low concentration means it enters the body quickly, making it ideal when rapid rehydration is the priority — for example in high-sweat activities in hot conditions — though it provides less carbohydrate than the other drink types.

Hypotonic drinks suit short, high-intensity activities or situations where sweat rate is high and the main need is fluid rather than energy. They are also useful when plain water needs a small amount of electrolyte without significantly slowing absorption. 🏅 Sporting examples Rapid rehydration In a hot environment with high sweat rates, a hypotonic drink replaces fluid fastest. Less carbohydrate Hypotonic drinks provide less energy than isotonic or hypertonic options. Hypoxia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Hypoxia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Hypoxia Too little oxygen reaching the tissues. 📖 What it means Hypoxia is a state in which tissues do not get enough oxygen. It occurs at altitude , where the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, and in some health conditions. The body responds by raising breathing rate and heart rate and, over days to weeks, increasing erythropoietin (EPO) release, red blood cell numbers and haemoglobin. Athletes use altitude training or hypoxic tents to exploit these adaptations. Severe hypoxia causes dizziness, confusion and, at extreme heights, altitude sickness.

Illinois Agility Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Illinois Agility Test General BTEC Sport Illinois Agility Test A standard field test of agility — timing a performer through a set course of turns and weaves. 📖 What it means The Illinois Agility Test is a standardised field test that measures agility — the ability to change direction quickly while maintaining control. The performer sprints, turns and weaves through a set course of cones as fast as possible, and the total time is recorded.

The course has fixed dimensions and a fixed layout of cones, which makes the test reliable when administered under standardised conditions and allows results to be compared against normative data or an athlete's previous scores. Imagery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Imagery IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Imagery Creating or recreating experiences in the mind — a versatile mental technique that builds skills, confidence and calm. 📖 What it means Imagery is a psychological technique in which a performer creates or recreates an experience in their mind , using all the senses to make it vivid. It is closely related to mental rehearsal and visualisation.

Imagery can be internal (imagining the experience from one's own perspective, as if performing it) or external (seeing oneself from the outside, as if on video). It is used to rehearse skills and tactics, build confidence, control arousal and anxiety, and focus attention . It is thought to work by strengthening the neural pathways involved in the movement and by building positive associations and confidence. Immune System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Immune System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Immune System The body's defence against infection. 📖 What it means The immune system is the network of cells, tissues and organs that protects the body against pathogens . The innate system gives a fast, general response; the adaptive system produces a specific response with antibodies and memory cells.

Moderate regular exercise tends to improve immune function and reduce infections. After prolonged, intense exercise there can be a temporary dip, sometimes called the open window , when athletes are more susceptible to upper respiratory tract infections . Good sleep, adequate energy and carbohydrate, hygiene and managing stress help protect the immune system in athletes. 🏅 Sporting examples Marathon Runners are more prone to colds after the race. Training load Overtraining is linked with frequent infections. Travel Athletes take precautions on long journeys. ✍️ Using the term in context Link exercise to immunity:

Impulse — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Impulse IB Sport Science General Impulse The link between force and momentum — the biomechanical quantity that explains how athletes generate speed and absorb landings. 📖 What it means Impulse is the product of force and the time over which that force acts (impulse = force × time). It equals the change in momentum of a body, and is measured in newton-seconds (Ns).

The impulse–momentum relationship explains why applying a force for longer produces a greater change in momentum . To increase momentum (e.g. to accelerate), athletes apply force over as long a time and range as possible; to reduce it safely (e.g. on landing), they extend the time over which the force acts. On a force–time graph, impulse is the area under the curve . In sprinting, a net positive impulse increases forward momentum, while equal positive and negative impulses (as at foot strike) can leave momentum unchanged. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting

A sprinter maximises the forward impulse by applying force against the ground over the longest effective time and range, increasing forward momentum. Landing safely A gymnast bends the knees on landing to increase the time over which the landing force acts, reducing the peak force and injury risk — the same impulse spread over more time. Throwing A thrower applies force to an implement over the greatest possible range and time to maximise the change in its momentum and thus its release velocity. ✍️ Using the term in context State impulse = force × time and link it to momentum change:

"Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts, and equals the change in momentum; a sprinter increases forward momentum by applying force over a longer time, while a gymnast reduces peak landing force by extending the time of impact." Independent Variable — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Independent Variable IB Sport Science General Independent Variable The factor you deliberately change in an experiment — a foundational idea for the IB internal assessment and scientific method. 📖 What it means The independent variable is the factor the researcher deliberately changes or manipulates in an investigation to see what effect it has. It is the presumed 'cause' being tested. In a well-designed study, the researcher changes only the independent variable and measures the effect on the dependent variable , while holding all other controlled variables constant to ensure a fair test.

For example, in a study of how caffeine affects sprint time, the caffeine dose is the independent variable (the thing being changed) and the sprint time is the dependent variable (the thing being measured). 🏅 Sporting examples IB internal assessment A student investigating the effect of rest interval on repeated-sprint performance sets rest interval length as the independent variable. Training study In a study on how training intensity affects VO₂ max, training intensity is the independent variable that is deliberately varied. Fair test By changing only the independent variable and controlling the rest, the researcher can attribute any change in the dependent variable to it.

✍️ Using the term in context Define it against the dependent and controlled variables: "The independent variable is the factor deliberately manipulated in the investigation; in a study of how caffeine affects sprinting, the caffeine dose is the independent variable, while sprint time is the dependent variable measured in response." Individual Differences — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Individual Differences AS Level / Cambridge General Individual Differences No two athletes are the same — the principle that training and coaching must account for personal variation. 📖 What it means Individual differences is the principle that performers vary in their physical, psychological and social characteristics , and that training and coaching should account for these differences to be effective.

Factors that differ between individuals include fitness level, age, sex, training history, injury status, psychology and goals . A training programme or coaching approach designed without accounting for these differences may be ineffective or even harmful. Recognising individual differences underpins the principle of individualisation and is a reason why effective coaching involves assessing the performer's specific needs and tailoring the approach accordingly, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all method. 🏅 Sporting examples Fitness level A beginner and an advanced athlete need very different training loads to achieve the same adaptive effect. Age and sex

Training recommendations may differ between young and mature athletes, or between men and women. Tailored coaching Accounting for individual differences leads to coaching that targets each performer's specific needs. ✍️ Using the term in context Define individual differences as a training principle: "Individual differences is the principle that performers vary in physical, psychological and social characteristics; effective training and coaching must account for these differences rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach." Individualisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Individualisation General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Individualisation Training designed for you — the principle that programmes should be tailored to each person's specific needs. 📖 What it means Individualisation is a training principle stating that programmes should be tailored to the specific needs, fitness level, goals and characteristics of the individual , rather than using a generic approach.

It recognises that different people respond differently to the same training stimulus because of differences in fitness, age, genetics, psychology and training history. A programme that works well for one athlete may be ineffective or harmful for another. Individualisation is achieved through profiling, fitness testing and ongoing monitoring , adjusting the programme based on the performer's response. It is closely linked to the principle of individual differences and to effective, athlete-centred coaching. 🏅 Sporting examples Tailored loads An athlete recovering from injury needs a programme individualised to their current capacity rather than team training. Different responses

Two athletes following the same programme may adapt very differently due to genetics and training history. Inertia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Inertia IB Sport Science General Inertia The resistance to change — why a stationary object stays put and a moving one keeps going without a force. 📖 What it means Inertia is the resistance of a body to a change in its state of rest or motion . A body at rest tends to stay at rest; a body in motion tends to continue at the same speed and direction — unless acted on by an external force. Inertia is directly proportional to mass : a more massive body has greater inertia and is harder to start, stop or change direction. It is the property described by Newton's first law of motion .

Inertia is directly relevant to sport: it explains why heavier athletes are harder to move or stop , why initial acceleration requires large force, and why maintaining speed (once achieved) requires less effort than starting to move. 🏅 Sporting examples Starting A shot put at rest has inertia — the athlete must apply a large force to start it moving. Mass and inertia A heavier rugby player has greater inertia, making them harder to push off the ball. Newton's first law A moving ball continues in a straight line due to inertia until a force (such as gravity) changes it. ✍️ Using the term in context Define inertia and link it to Newton's first law:

"Inertia is a body's resistance to changes in its state of rest or motion, proportional to its mass and described by Newton's first law; greater mass means greater inertia, requiring more force to start, stop or change direction." Inflammation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Inflammation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Inflammation The body's first response to injury. 📖 What it means Inflammation is the immune response to tissue damage or infection . Its classic signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain and loss of function . Blood vessels widen and become leaky, so white blood cells and fluid reach the area to remove damaged tissue and begin repair. This is essential for healing after a sprain, strain or tissue damage.

Chronic inflammation , lasting weeks or months, can be harmful and is linked to overuse injuries and some diseases. Regular moderate exercise has an overall anti-inflammatory effect. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprained ankle Swelling and heat appear within hours. Training Hard sessions cause short-term inflammation as part of adaptation. Information Processing Model — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Information Processing Model AS Level / Cambridge General Information Processing Model A map of what happens between seeing and doing — how the brain turns sensory input into skilled movement. 📖 What it means The information processing model describes how a performer takes in information, makes a decision, and produces a response . It treats the performer like a system with input, processing and output stages.

A common version has several stages: input (detecting information from the environment through the senses), perception (interpreting and making sense of it), decision making (selecting a response from memory), output (executing the movement), and feedback (information about the result, which loops back to inform future actions). The model highlights the roles of selective attention (filtering relevant from irrelevant cues) and memory (comparing the situation with past experience), and explains why skilled performers process information faster and more effectively than beginners. 🏅 Sporting examples Cricket batting

A batter detects the ball (input), interprets its line and length (perception), selects a shot (decision making), plays it (output), and uses the result to inform the next ball (feedback). Selective attention A skilled netball player filters out crowd noise and irrelevant movement, attending only to the cues that matter — speeding their processing. Expertise Experienced performers move through the stages faster because they recognise patterns and anticipate, drawing efficiently on memory. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the stages and the feedback loop:

Insertion (muscle) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Insertion (muscle) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Insertion (muscle) Where the muscle attaches to the moving bone — the end that gets pulled toward the origin during contraction. 📖 What it means The insertion of a muscle is the end of the muscle attached to the bone that moves when the muscle contracts . It is the more distal (further from the body's centre) of the two attachment points.

When a muscle contracts, it pulls the insertion toward the origin (the fixed, more proximal end), shortening the muscle and producing movement at the joint between the two bones. Identifying origin and insertion is part of understanding how a muscle acts. For example, the biceps insertion is on the radius (lower arm) — when the biceps contracts, the radius is pulled toward the shoulder, flexing the elbow. The bone at the insertion moves; the bone at the origin stays relatively still. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps The biceps insertion on the radius is pulled toward the shoulder when the biceps contracts, flexing the elbow. The moving end

The insertion is the end of the muscle attached to the bone that moves during contraction. Movement analysis Identifying origin and insertion helps explain which bone moves and in what direction. ✍️ Using the term in context Define insertion and contrast with origin: "The insertion is the end of a muscle attached to the bone that moves during contraction — the more distal end; the muscle pulls the insertion toward the fixed origin, producing movement at the joint." Inspiratory Capacity (IC) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Inspiratory Capacity (IC) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Inspiratory Capacity (IC) The most air you can breathe in from a relaxed breath out. 📖 What it means Inspiratory capacity (IC) is the greatest volume of air that can be inhaled starting from the resting end-expiratory position . It is the sum of tidal volume + inspiratory reserve volume . Together with functional residual capacity it makes up the total lung capacity. 🏅 Sporting examples Spirometry A person breathes normally, then takes the deepest possible breath in; the total is the IC. Fitness

Respiratory muscle training aims to improve the ability to move more air in. Clinical IC is used to track changes in breathing in some lung conditions. ✍️ Using the term in context Show the sum: "Inspiratory capacity is tidal volume plus inspiratory reserve volume." It is typically around 3 litres in a young adult male at rest. During exercise, tidal volume rises partly by using this reserve, so IRV gets smaller while the person is working hard. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise A runner breathes deeper by drawing on the inspiratory reserve volume. Insulin — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Insulin IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Insulin The blood sugar lowerer — the pancreatic hormone that moves glucose into cells after a meal or during recovery. 📖 What it means Insulin is a hormone secreted by the pancreas that lowers blood glucose by promoting the uptake of glucose into cells and the storage of carbohydrate as glycogen. It works in opposition to glucagon : when blood glucose rises (after a meal), insulin is released to lower it. During exercise, insulin secretion tends to fall, allowing glucose to remain available in the blood for the working muscles.

After exercise, insulin plays an important role in recovery and refuelling — it promotes the uptake and storage of glucose in the muscles, helping to replenish glycogen stores. Understanding insulin is central to sports nutrition and blood glucose regulation. 🏅 Sporting examples After a meal Insulin is released after eating to lower blood glucose by promoting its uptake into cells. Falls during exercise Insulin secretion decreases during exercise, allowing blood glucose to remain available for the muscles. Recovery After exercise, insulin helps replenish muscle glycogen by promoting glucose uptake. ✍️ Using the term in context Define insulin and pair it with glucagon:

"Insulin is a pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose by promoting uptake into cells; it works antagonistically with glucagon in blood glucose regulation, secretion falls during exercise, and it supports glycogen replenishment in recovery." Intensity (training principle) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Intensity (training principle) General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Intensity (training principle) How hard you push — the effort level that determines which adaptations training produces. 📖 What it means Intensity is the level of effort in a training session and the 'I' in the FITT principle . It is one of the key variables manipulated to apply progressive overload.

It can be expressed in different ways depending on the training type: as a percentage of maximum heart rate or VO₂ max for cardiorespiratory work, or as a percentage of 1RM for resistance training. Higher intensity generally produces greater adaptations but requires more recovery. The appropriate intensity depends on the training goal : maximal strength requires high intensity (>85% 1RM), aerobic threshold training requires a moderate percentage of maximum, and speed work requires near-maximal efforts. Intensity must be progressively increased to continue driving adaptation. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength training A goal of maximal strength requires intensity at 85–100% of 1RM.

Heart rate zones Aerobic endurance training is prescribed at a percentage of maximum heart rate. Progressive overload Gradually increasing intensity ensures training continues to challenge the body and drive adaptation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define intensity and how it is prescribed: "Intensity is the level of effort in a training session, the 'I' in the FITT principle; it is expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate, VO₂ max or 1RM depending on the training type, and must increase progressively to continue driving adaptation." Interactionist Perspective — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Interactionist Perspective IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Interactionist Perspective Behaviour comes from the person and the situation together. 📖 What it means The interactionist perspective says that neither personality nor the environment alone determines behaviour; the two interact . Lewin's formula expresses this as B = f(P × E) : behaviour is a function of the person and their environment. It combines the trait approach (stable personality) and the social learning approach (situation). For example, an extrovert may be aggressive in one situation and quiet in another.

It is the most widely accepted view and is used to predict behaviour in sport, such as how an athlete will respond to pressure. 🏅 Sporting examples Competition A normally calm player becomes aggressive in a heated match. Coaching The coach adapts to the athlete and situation. Personality A trait is expressed differently in training and games. ✍️ Using the term in context Write the formula: "Lewin's formula B = f(P × E) shows that behaviour results from the interaction between the person and the environment." Internal and External Respiration — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Internal and External Respiration IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Internal and External Respiration The two sites where gases are exchanged. 📖 What it means External respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli of the lungs and the blood in the pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Internal respiration is the exchange between the blood and the tissue cells . Oxygen diffuses from the blood into the muscle and carbon dioxide diffuses into the blood.

Both rely on diffusion down concentration (partial pressure) gradients . Cellular respiration, which makes ATP, is a separate process inside the cell. 🏅 Sporting examples Lungs Oxygen enters the blood at the alveoli. Muscle Oxygen leaves the blood to fuel working cells. Exercise Steeper gradients speed up both exchanges. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish the sites: "External respiration occurs in the lungs, between alveoli and blood; internal respiration occurs in the tissues, between blood and cells." Interval Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Interval Training General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Interval Training Alternating work and rest to train hard efforts repeatedly — a flexible method that can target any energy system. 📖 What it means Interval training involves alternating periods of work with periods of rest or recovery . By manipulating the work and rest variables, it can be tailored to develop a specific energy system or fitness component.

The key variables are the intensity and duration of the work intervals, the duration and type of recovery, and the number of intervals and sets . Short, very intense intervals with full recovery develop the anaerobic systems; longer intervals with shorter recovery develop aerobic fitness. Interval training is highly versatile and time-efficient , allows a large volume of high-intensity work to be completed with recovery, and can be made sport-specific — which is why it is so widely used across endurance and team sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint intervals A sprinter performs short, maximal efforts with long recoveries to develop the ATP-PC and glycolytic systems. Aerobic intervals

A runner uses longer intervals with shorter recoveries to develop aerobic capacity while training at a higher intensity than continuous running. Team sports Interval training replicates the repeated high-intensity efforts of games, making it highly sport-specific for footballers and hockey players. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how manipulating the variables targets different systems: "Interval training alternates work and recovery; by adjusting the intensity and duration of work intervals and the recovery, it can be tailored to develop the anaerobic or aerobic systems, and made highly sport-specific."

Intrinsic Motivation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Intrinsic Motivation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Intrinsic Motivation Motivation that comes from within — doing an activity for the love of it, and the most durable driver of long-term commitment. 📖 What it means Intrinsic motivation is motivation that comes from within the performer — the internal drive to take part for the enjoyment, satisfaction and sense of achievement the activity itself provides, rather than for any external reward.

It contrasts with extrinsic motivation , which comes from external rewards such as trophies, money or praise. Intrinsic motivation is generally considered the more powerful and durable driver of long-term participation and commitment. A performer high in intrinsic motivation is more likely to persist, practise willingly and stay involved even without external rewards. Coaches try to foster it by making activities enjoyable, giving performers autonomy, and helping them experience competence and progress. 🏅 Sporting examples Lifelong participation An athlete who plays their sport purely for the enjoyment and challenge is intrinsically motivated and likely to stay involved for life. Practice

A young player who practises in their own time because they love the game shows strong intrinsic motivation. Fostering it A coach builds intrinsic motivation by making sessions enjoyable, offering choice, and helping players feel a growing sense of competence. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast it with extrinsic motivation and note its durability: "Intrinsic motivation comes from within — the enjoyment and satisfaction of the activity itself — and is generally a more powerful and durable driver of long-term commitment than extrinsic motivation from external rewards." Inverted-U Hypothesis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Inverted-U Hypothesis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Inverted-U Hypothesis The most widely taught model of arousal and performance — there's an optimal middle level, with too little or too much both harming performance. 📖 What it means The inverted-U hypothesis proposes that as arousal increases, performance improves up to an optimal point, after which further arousal causes performance to decline . Plotted on a graph, this produces an inverted U shape.

It improves on drive theory by recognising that too much arousal is harmful , not just helpful — at low arousal a performer is under-activated and flat, at moderate arousal they perform best, and at high arousal technique and focus break down. The optimal level of arousal varies with the task and the performer: it is higher for gross, simple skills (such as weightlifting) and lower for fine, complex skills (such as putting), and also depends on the performer's experience. 🏅 Sporting examples Gross skill A powerlifter performs best at high arousal, because their simple, gross-motor task tolerates — even benefits from — strong activation. Fine skill

A golfer putting needs lower arousal; too much activation causes trembling and disrupts the fine control required, illustrating the lower optimal point. Under-arousal A player who is flat and under-aroused early in a match performs below their best until their arousal rises toward the optimum. ✍️ Using the term in context State the optimal-point relationship and the task dependence: "The inverted-U hypothesis states that performance improves with arousal up to an optimal point, then declines; the optimal level is higher for gross, simple skills and lower for fine, complex skills." Compare it with drive theory (which it improves on) and catastrophe theory (which refines it further).

Iron — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Iron IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Iron An essential mineral for oxygen transport — without enough, haemoglobin can't be made and performance suffers. 📖 What it means Iron is a mineral essential for the formation of haemoglobin , the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Without adequate iron, haemoglobin production is impaired. Iron deficiency reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity , leading to anaemia (low haemoglobin). This impairs aerobic performance — less oxygen can be delivered to the muscles, so endurance and high-intensity effort suffer.

Athletes, particularly female athletes and endurance runners , are at higher risk of iron deficiency because of increased losses (through sweat, foot-strike haemolysis and menstruation) and increased demand. Dietary sources of iron include red meat, spinach and legumes. 🏅 Sporting examples Haemoglobin Iron is essential to make haemoglobin; without enough iron, less oxygen can be carried in the blood. Anaemia Iron deficiency anaemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity, impairing aerobic performance. At-risk athletes Endurance athletes and female athletes have higher iron requirements and are at greater risk of deficiency. ✍️ Using the term in context

Isokinetic Contraction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Isokinetic Contraction IB Sport Science General Isokinetic Contraction A constant-speed contraction against variable resistance — a specialised type used in testing and rehabilitation. 📖 What it means An isokinetic contraction is a muscle contraction performed at a constant speed against a variable resistance . The speed of movement is fixed, and the resistance automatically adjusts to match the force the muscle produces throughout the range of motion.

This differs from isotonic contractions (where the resistance is fixed but speed varies) and isometric contractions (no movement). Isokinetic contractions require specialised isokinetic dynamometers , which control the speed of movement and measure the force produced at each angle. Isokinetic testing and training are used mainly in rehabilitation and research — they allow precise assessment of muscle strength through the full range of motion and can identify weaknesses or imbalances at specific joint angles. 🏅 Sporting examples Constant speed An isokinetic leg extension machine controls the speed of movement while the resistance varies to match the force applied. Rehabilitation

Isokinetic dynamometers are used in rehab to assess and train strength through the full range at a controlled speed. Research use Isokinetic testing provides precise, reproducible strength measurements at each angle of movement. ✍️ Using the term in context Define an isokinetic contraction and its use: "An isokinetic contraction occurs at a constant speed against variable resistance, requiring a specialised dynamometer; it is used mainly in rehabilitation and research for precise strength assessment through the full range of motion." Contrast it with isotonic and isometric contractions. 🔗 Related terms

Isometric Contraction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Isometric Contraction IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Isometric Contraction Tension without movement — the muscle is working hard but the joint angle stays fixed. 📖 What it means An isometric contraction is a muscle contraction where tension is produced but there is no change in muscle length or joint angle . The muscle is generating force, but not shortening or lengthening.

It occurs when the force the muscle produces is matched by an equal opposing force — for example, pushing against an immovable wall, or holding a position still (such as a wall sit or a plank). The muscle works hard to maintain the position, but does not move. Isometric contractions are important in stability, posture and static holds , and are contrasted with isotonic contractions (which produce movement). They are also used in PNF stretching , where a pre-stretch contraction is isometric. 🏅 Sporting examples Wall sit In a wall sit, the quadriceps contract isometrically — generating tension to hold the position without shortening. Plank

Holding a plank position involves isometric contractions of the core muscles. PNF stretching The pre-stretch contraction in PNF stretching is isometric, triggering autogenic inhibition. ✍️ Using the term in context Define an isometric contraction and give an example: "An isometric contraction produces tension without a change in muscle length or joint angle — the muscle works without shortening; a plank or wall sit are examples, and it contrasts with isotonic contractions that produce movement." Isotonic Contraction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Isotonic Contraction IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Isotonic Contraction A contraction that produces movement — the umbrella term for both the lifting and the lowering phase. 📖 What it means An isotonic contraction is a muscle contraction that produces movement . It is the broad category that covers contractions where the muscle changes length — both concentric (shortening) and eccentric (lengthening).

It contrasts with isometric contractions (no change in length or movement). In everyday and sporting actions, most muscle contractions are isotonic — the muscle is actively contracting through a range of motion. Isotonic training (such as resistance exercises with free weights or machines) develops strength, hypertrophy and muscular endurance across the range of motion. Understanding that isotonic includes both concentric and eccentric phases is fundamental to movement analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps curl A full biceps curl involves isotonic contraction — the concentric lifting phase and the eccentric lowering phase. Isotonic contractions produce movement, distinguishing them from isometric contractions. Isotonic Drink — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Isotonic Drink General BTEC Sport Isotonic Drink The most sport-targeted drink — matching the body's own fluid concentration for fast absorption and fuel delivery. 📖 What it means An isotonic drink is a sports drink with a similar solute concentration to body fluids (around 4–8g carbohydrate per 100ml). This makes it absorbed at roughly the same rate as water while providing meaningful carbohydrate. The matching concentration means it enters the body efficiently, providing both fluid for rehydration and carbohydrate for energy . This balance makes isotonic drinks the most widely used option during exercise.

Isotonic drinks are suited to moderate-to-long duration, moderate-to-high intensity exercise where both fluid and fuel are needed. They are the middle ground between hypotonic drinks (fast absorption, less carbohydrate) and hypertonic drinks (more carbohydrate, slower absorption). 🏅 Sporting examples During exercise An isotonic drink during a football match provides fluid for hydration and carbohydrate for energy. Most popular Isotonic drinks are the most commonly used sports drinks because of their balance of fluid and fuel. Isotonic Muscle Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Isotonic Muscle Training IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Isotonic Muscle Training Training with a movement against a constant load. 📖 What it means In isotonic training , the muscle changes length while moving a constant load . It includes concentric (shortening) and eccentric (lengthening) phases. Examples are bicep curls, squats and bench presses with free weights or machines. It is the most common type of resistance training. The load is constant but the muscle's effort varies through the range, because leverage changes. 🏅 Sporting examples Bicep curl

The elbow flexes and extends with a constant dumbbell weight. Squat The thigh muscles shorten and lengthen against the barbell. Javelin Throw — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Javelin Throw BTEC Sport General Javelin Throw Throwing a spear-shaped implement after a run-up. 📖 What it means In the javelin throw , the athlete uses a run-up with a series of cross-steps before throwing a javelin that weighs 800 g for men and 600 g for women . The throw must be released over the shoulder and the javelin must land tip first. The distance is affected by release speed, angle and the aerodynamic behaviour of the javelin. Release angles are typically around 30 to 36 degrees. The whole-body sequence runs from the legs and hips through the trunk and shoulder to the arm and hand.

The event puts a large load on the elbow and shoulder , so strength training, mobility and careful load management are essential for injury prevention. 🏅 Sporting examples Run-up Speed builds the momentum for the throw. Block The front leg stops while the trunk and arm whip forward. Injury Throwers can develop elbow and shoulder problems. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the sequence: "In the javelin throw, force is generated from the run-up and transferred through the legs, trunk and arm in sequence to the release." Jerk — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Jerk IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Jerk How quickly acceleration changes. 📖 What it means Jerk is the rate of change of acceleration with respect to time. Velocity is the rate of change of position, acceleration the rate of change of velocity, and jerk the next step. It is measured in metres per second cubed (m/s³) . A high jerk means a sudden change in acceleration, as in a sharp stop or impact. In biomechanics, jerk is used to measure the smoothness of movement : skilled movement tends to be smoother with lower jerk than novice movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Skill learning

An expert's reach has a smoother, lower-jerk path than a beginner's. Impact A sudden stop in a collision involves very high jerk. Rehabilitation Smoother movement can show improving control. ✍️ Using the term in context Place it in the chain: "Jerk is the rate of change of acceleration, in m/s³; lower jerk indicates smoother movement." Joint Capsule — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Joint Capsule IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Joint Capsule The fibrous sleeve of a synovial joint — the structure that encloses and stabilises the joint. 📖 What it means The joint capsule is a fibrous sleeve that surrounds and encloses a synovial joint . Together with ligaments and other structures, it provides stability while allowing movement. It has two layers: an outer fibrous layer that gives structural strength and stability, and an inner synovial membrane that secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish the cartilage. The joint capsule effectively seals the joint cavity.

The joint capsule is one of the defining features of a synovial joint, alongside articular cartilage, synovial fluid and ligaments. It maintains the joint's integrity during movement and protects the structures within — damage to it can compromise joint stability. 🏅 Sporting examples Enclosing the joint The joint capsule encloses the knee joint, maintaining its integrity during loading. Synovial membrane The inner layer of the joint capsule secretes synovial fluid to lubricate the articular cartilage. Stability Together with ligaments, the joint capsule stabilises the joint while allowing the required range of movement. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define the joint capsule and its two layers: "The joint capsule is a fibrous sleeve surrounding a synovial joint; its outer layer provides structural stability and its inner synovial membrane secretes synovial fluid, sealing the joint cavity and working alongside ligaments to maintain integrity." Joint — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Joint IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Joint Where movement happens — the point at which bones meet, and the starting point of all movement analysis. 📖 What it means A joint (or articulation) is the point where two or more bones meet . Joints allow the skeleton to move and are the site at which all body movements occur.

Joints are classified by how much movement they allow: fixed (fibrous) joints permit no movement, slightly movable (cartilaginous) joints permit limited movement, and freely movable (synovial) joints — such as the knee, elbow, shoulder and hip — permit the wide range of movement used in sport. Synovial joints are the most important for movement analysis. Each type (hinge, ball and socket, etc.) allows specific movements in specific planes, so identifying the joint is the first step in analysing any sporting action. 🏅 Sporting examples Movement analysis Analysing a kick starts by identifying the joints involved — the hip and knee — before naming the movements, agonists and planes.

Synovial joints in sport The freely movable synovial joints of the knee, hip and shoulder produce almost all sporting movement. Joint type and movement A hinge joint such as the elbow allows flexion and extension, while a ball and socket joint such as the shoulder allows movement in all planes. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a joint and classify by movement allowed: "A joint is where two or more bones meet; synovial joints such as the knee and shoulder are freely movable and produce most sporting movement, so identifying the joint is the first step in movement analysis." Lead into naming the joint type, movements and plane for the specific action. 🔗 Related terms

Karvonen Method — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Karvonen Method IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Karvonen Method A way to calculate target heart rate for training. 📖 What it means The Karvonen method calculates a target heart rate using the heart rate reserve (maximum minus resting heart rate). The formula is: target HR = (HRmax − HRrest) × % intensity + HRrest . For example, a 20-year-old with an estimated HRmax of 200 and resting HR of 60 who wants to train at 70% has a target of (200 − 60) × 0.7 + 60 = 158 bpm .

It is more individual than a simple percentage of HRmax because it takes fitness (resting heart rate) into account. The result depends on an accurate HRmax. 🏅 Sporting examples Training zone A runner calculates 60% and 80% targets. Fitness class An instructor sets target ranges. Comparison Fitter people with low resting HR have a lower target. ✍️ Using the term in context Show the calculation: "Using the Karvonen formula, the target heart rate at 70% intensity is (200 − 60) × 0.7 + 60 = 158 beats per minute." Mention that HRmax estimates can be inaccurate. 🔗 Related terms

Kinaesthesia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Kinaesthesia IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Kinaesthesia The sense of your own movement — your body's internal awareness of position and motion without looking. 📖 What it means Kinaesthesia is the awareness of body position, movement and muscular effort derived from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons and joints. It is the 'feel' of movement — sensing where the body is and how it is moving without using vision.

It relies on receptors such as muscle spindles (detecting length and rate of change), Golgi tendon organs (detecting tension) and joint receptors . Together these give the nervous system moment-to-moment information about limb position and movement. Kinaesthesia is essential for skilled movement : it allows performers to detect errors in a movement by feel, to adjust mid-action without looking, and to build up the proprioceptive 'feel' of a well-executed skill. It is closely related to proprioception and is one basis for intrinsic feedback. 🏅 Sporting examples Feel of movement A gymnast who senses a balance error and corrects it mid-movement is using kinaesthesia. Skill development

As a skill develops, the performer builds a kinaesthetic 'feel' for the correct movement. Intrinsic feedback Kinaesthesia is the source of intrinsic feedback — the performer senses how the movement felt. ✍️ Using the term in context Define kinaesthesia and its role in skill: "Kinaesthesia is the awareness of body position, movement and effort from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons and joints; it provides intrinsic feedback, allowing performers to detect errors by feel and adjust mid-action without looking." Kinematic data come from video analysis, motion capture, timing gates and wearable sensors. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting Timing gates give split times and velocity along a 100m run. Gait Motion capture measures knee angle through a running stride. Swimming

Kinetic Chain — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Kinetic Chain IB Sport Science General Kinetic Chain The body as a chain of linked segments — how force flows from the ground up to produce explosive actions. 📖 What it means The kinetic chain is the linked system of body segments and joints working together to produce a movement . Force is generated and transferred through a sequence of body parts, each adding to the next.

In a throwing or striking action, force typically flows from the ground upward through the legs, hips, trunk and arm to the implement or ball . Each segment adds velocity to the next, and the total effect at the end of the chain is greater than any one segment alone could produce. The kinetic chain underpins the principle of summation of force and explains why full-body coordination — using the chain in the right sequence and timing — is so important for generating maximum power in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing In a javelin throw, force travels up the kinetic chain from the legs through the hips, trunk and arm to the implement. Sequence

Each segment of the chain adds velocity in the correct sequence, producing more speed than any part alone. Breakdown A weakness or poor technique in any link of the kinetic chain reduces power at the end point. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the kinetic chain and link it to summation of force: "The kinetic chain is the linked system of body segments and joints that transfer force sequentially from the ground upward; it underpins the summation of force, and effective technique requires each segment to contribute at the right moment." Use it to explain throwing, kicking or striking power. 🔗 Related terms

Kinetic Energy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Kinetic Energy IB Sport Science General Kinetic Energy The energy of motion — the faster and heavier a moving body, the more kinetic energy it carries. 📖 What it means Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses due to its motion . It depends on the body's mass and its velocity, given by the equation KE = ½mv² . Because velocity is squared in the equation, speed has a much greater effect on kinetic energy than mass — doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy. This is why high-speed collisions or impacts are so significant in sport, and why fast-moving objects carry so much energy.

Kinetic energy can be converted to other forms and vice versa: a ball thrown upward converts kinetic energy to potential energy as it rises, then back to kinetic as it falls. In sport, understanding kinetic energy helps analyse collisions, impacts and the transfer of energy between moving objects. 🏅 Sporting examples Speed squared A ball moving at twice the speed has four times the kinetic energy — the speed-squared relationship. Collision The high kinetic energy of a fast-moving tackle makes its impact greater. Energy transfer A thrown ball converts muscular energy into kinetic energy, which transfers to whatever it hits. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define kinetic energy and state the equation: "Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses due to its motion, given by KE = ½mv²; because velocity is squared, speed has a proportionally greater effect than mass, making fast-moving bodies disproportionately energetic."
