Knee Extension Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Knee Extension Test BTEC Sport General Knee Extension Test A fitness test of quadriceps strength. 📖 What it means The Knee Extension Test is a test of leg strength or endurance in which the athlete extends the knee against resistance, using a machine or dynamometer. Protocol: The athlete sits on a leg extension machine and lifts the heaviest weight possible through the range (1RM), or completes repetitions at a set weight. Isokinetic dynamometers can also be used.

Interpreting results: Results are compared between legs and with norms. A difference of more than around 10 to 15% between legs may indicate a risk of injury or incomplete rehabilitation. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A player's injured leg reaches 85% of the strength of the other leg. Training use Used to decide when a player is ready to return to sport. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Knowledge of Performance (KP) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Knowledge of Performance (KP) AS Level / Cambridge General Knowledge of Performance (KP) Feedback about the technique, not just the outcome — the how-well-you-did-it information that advanced performers thrive on. 📖 What it means Knowledge of performance (KP) is a form of extrinsic feedback about the quality of the movement or technique — how the action was performed — rather than simply its outcome.

It contrasts with knowledge of results (KR) , which reports the outcome. KP might tell a performer that their elbow was too low or their timing was slightly late — information about the technique that produced the result. Knowledge of performance becomes increasingly valuable as a performer advances . More skilled performers, who already achieve good outcomes, rely on detailed KP to refine technique, often delivered through coaching cues or video analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Video analysis A gymnast reviews footage with a coach to receive knowledge of performance about the exact shape and timing of their movements. Coaching cue

Telling a swimmer their catch was too shallow is knowledge of performance — information about technique rather than the outcome. Advanced performers An elite athlete relies on detailed KP to fine-tune technique, because they already produce good results. ✍️ Using the term in context Define KP as technique feedback and contrast with KR: "Knowledge of performance is extrinsic feedback about the quality of the technique, such as a coaching cue about body position; unlike knowledge of results, it concerns how the movement was performed, and is especially valuable for advanced performers." Knowledge of Results (KR) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Knowledge of Results (KR) AS Level / Cambridge General Knowledge of Results (KR) Feedback about the outcome — did the shot go in? — the most basic and beginner-friendly form of performance information. 📖 What it means Knowledge of results (KR) is a form of extrinsic feedback about the outcome of a movement — the end result of the action. It tells the performer what happened , such as whether a shot scored or how far a throw travelled.

It contrasts with knowledge of performance (KP) , which is feedback about the quality of the technique that produced the result. KR concerns the result; KP concerns how it was achieved. Knowledge of results is especially valuable for beginners , who cannot yet judge their own performance. It gives them clear, simple information about whether they succeeded, which they can use to adjust their next attempt. 🏅 Sporting examples Basketball Seeing whether a free throw goes in is knowledge of results — the outcome of the shot, regardless of how the technique looked. Archery Knowing which ring the arrow hit is knowledge of results, telling the archer the outcome of their shot. Beginners

A novice relies on knowledge of results because they cannot yet evaluate the quality of their own technique. ✍️ Using the term in context Define KR as outcome feedback and contrast with KP: "Knowledge of results is extrinsic feedback about the outcome of a movement, such as whether a shot scored; it differs from knowledge of performance, which concerns the quality of the technique, and is especially useful for beginners." Kolb's Learning Cycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Kolb's Learning Cycle General BTEC Sport Kolb's Learning Cycle Learning by doing and reflecting — a four-stage model of experiential learning relevant to coaching and sport. 📖 What it means Kolb's Learning Cycle is a model of experiential learning describing four stages : concrete experience (doing or having an experience), reflective observation (reflecting on it), abstract conceptualisation (drawing conclusions or forming concepts) and active experimentation (trying out the new understanding).

The model suggests that learning is most effective when a learner cycles through all four stages — experiencing, reflecting, theorising and experimenting — rather than only reading or being told. This underpins experiential and discovery-based learning approaches . In sport and coaching contexts, Kolb's cycle supports reflection on performance, analysis of what went wrong, and deliberate adjustment — it helps explain why guided discovery and problem-solving coaching can be more effective than purely directive instruction for developing understanding. 🏅 Sporting examples Performance review

After a game, a player reflects on what happened (reflective observation), analyses why (abstract conceptualisation), then tries a new approach (active experimentation) — Kolb's cycle in action. Coaching use A coach using guided discovery prompts reflection and conceptualisation, supporting the full cycle. All four stages Learning is deepest when all four stages are completed, not just the doing. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the four stages and explain the cycle's value:

Krebs Cycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Krebs Cycle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Krebs Cycle The central hub of aerobic energy production — the second stage of the aerobic system, feeding the electron transport chain. 📖 What it means The Krebs cycle (also called the citric acid cycle) is the second stage of aerobic ATP production , taking place in the mitochondria . It follows glycolysis and precedes the electron transport chain.

In the Krebs cycle, the products of glycolysis (and of fat breakdown) are further broken down. The cycle produces a small amount of ATP directly , releases carbon dioxide as a by-product, and — most importantly — generates hydrogen carriers that are passed to the electron transport chain, where the bulk of ATP is produced. Because it requires oxygen and occurs in the mitochondria, the Krebs cycle only operates aerobically , underpinning energy production for prolonged, endurance exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance events During a long-distance run, the Krebs cycle continuously processes fuel in the mitochondria, feeding the electron transport chain to sustain aerobic energy production.

Aerobic base A well-developed aerobic system with many mitochondria increases the capacity of the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. Fuel entry Both carbohydrate (via pyruvate) and fat (via beta-oxidation) feed into the Krebs cycle, showing how it integrates different fuels. ✍️ Using the term in context Place the Krebs cycle as the second aerobic stage and state its products: "The Krebs cycle is the second stage of aerobic energy production in the mitochondria; it produces a little ATP and carbon dioxide, but mainly generates hydrogen carriers for the electron transport chain, where most ATP is made." Stress its oxygen dependence and its role feeding the electron transport chain.

Food sources include meat, fish, eggs, dairy and some plant foods, and a diet high in protein provides plenty. 🏅 Sporting examples Heavy training Blood glutamine falls after prolonged exercise. Protocol: Three cones are placed in an L shape, 5 yards (about 4.6 m) apart. The athlete sprints, touches lines, weaves around the cones and returns. The time is recorded.

Interpreting results: A shorter time shows better agility and ability to decelerate and re-accelerate. It is commonly used in American football testing. Lactate Inflection Point — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lactate Inflection Point IB Sport Science General Lactate Inflection Point The training-prescription threshold — the intensity where lactate starts accumulating faster than the body can clear it. 📖 What it means The lactate inflection point (LIP) is the exercise intensity at which blood lactate begins to accumulate exponentially , because production exceeds the rate of removal and buffering.

At low intensities, the aerobic system handles most energy production and lactate stays low. As intensity rises, anaerobic glycolysis contributes more and lactate rises — initially slowly, then rapidly at the LIP. This point represents the practical limit of sustained, predominantly aerobic effort. The LIP is used to prescribe training zones, monitor fitness and predict endurance performance . Training at and around the LIP raises the threshold, allowing higher intensities to be sustained before lactate accumulates — a central goal of endurance conditioning. 🏅 Sporting examples Training zone

An athlete trains just below their LIP to develop aerobic capacity without heavy lactate accumulation. Performance predictor A higher LIP (occurring at a greater fraction of VO₂ max) predicts better endurance performance. Testing The LIP is identified from blood lactate samples at increasing workloads during a step test. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the LIP and its training application: "The lactate inflection point is the intensity at which blood lactate begins to accumulate rapidly; it predicts endurance performance, guides training zone prescription, and is raised by training at or near the threshold." Relate it to OBLA and the anaerobic threshold. 🔗 Related terms

Lactate Shuttle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lactate Shuttle IB Sport Science General Lactate Shuttle Lactate as fuel, not just waste — how the body redistributes and uses lactate between tissues. 📖 What it means The lactate shuttle is the process by which lactate produced in one tissue (such as fast-twitch fibres or white muscle) is transported in the blood and used as a fuel by other tissues (such as slow-twitch fibres, the heart or the liver).

This challenges the older view of lactate as simply a waste product. Lactate is actually a valuable fuel source that is actively moved between tissues — taken up by oxidative (aerobic) tissues and used in the aerobic energy pathway. Understanding the lactate shuttle explains why low-intensity exercise aids recovery from high-intensity effort: gentle aerobic activity helps clear lactate from the blood by providing the aerobic tissues with the conditions to take it up and use it. It also underpins how trained athletes tolerate and clear lactate more effectively . 🏅 Sporting examples Fuel, not waste

Lactate produced by fast-twitch fibres during a sprint is taken up by slow-twitch fibres and the heart as fuel. Active recovery Low-intensity exercise post-sprint keeps aerobic tissues working, clearing lactate via the shuttle. Training effect Endurance training improves the lactate shuttle, allowing better lactate clearance. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the lactate shuttle and its implications: "The lactate shuttle is the process by which lactate produced in one tissue is transported and used as fuel by others; this means lactate is not just a waste product but a valuable fuel, and low-intensity active recovery aids clearance by promoting uptake."

Lactate Threshold — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lactate Threshold IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Lactate Threshold The tipping point where lactate starts to pile up — one of the best predictors of endurance performance and a key training target. 📖 What it means The lactate threshold is the exercise intensity at which blood lactate begins to accumulate rapidly , because its rate of production starts to exceed the rate at which the body can clear it.

It is often expressed as a percentage of VO₂ max . A performer who can work at a high percentage of their VO₂ max before reaching their lactate threshold can sustain a faster pace aerobically — making the threshold one of the best predictors of endurance performance, sometimes even better than VO₂ max alone. The lactate threshold can be improved through training , particularly training performed at or near threshold intensity, which pushes the threshold to a higher percentage of VO₂ max and allows a faster sustainable pace. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running

Two runners with the same VO₂ max will differ in performance if one has a higher lactate threshold, allowing them to sustain a faster pace before lactate accumulates. Threshold training A cyclist performs sustained efforts at threshold intensity to push their lactate threshold higher over time. Testing Coaches identify the threshold from a step test with blood lactate sampling, then set training zones around it. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it and explain why it predicts endurance performance:

"The lactate threshold is the intensity at which blood lactate rises rapidly as production exceeds clearance; a higher threshold, expressed as a percentage of VO₂ max, allows a faster sustainable pace, making it a strong predictor of endurance performance." Lactate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lactate IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Lactate Long misunderstood as a mere waste product — in fact a useful fuel, and a key marker of exercise intensity. 📖 What it means Lactate is a product of anaerobic glycolysis , formed when glucose is broken down for energy without sufficient oxygen. It is produced whenever the rate of energy demand is high.

Contrary to the old view of lactate as simply a fatiguing 'waste product', it is now understood that lactate can be transported to other tissues and used as a fuel (the lactate shuttle), and can be converted back to glucose in the liver. It is the accompanying accumulation of hydrogen ions , not lactate itself, that is most closely linked to the drop in pH and fatigue. The point at which lactate begins to accumulate rapidly in the blood — the lactate threshold — is an important marker of endurance fitness and is used to set training intensities. 🏅 Sporting examples High-intensity exercise

During a hard 800m, lactate is produced rapidly as the anaerobic systems supply energy, and it can be shuttled to other muscle fibres to be used as fuel. Endurance testing Coaches measure blood lactate to find the intensity at which it rises sharply — the lactate threshold — and set training zones from it. Recovery During active recovery, lactate is cleared and used as a fuel by the heart and other tissues. ✍️ Using the term in context Correct the 'waste product' myth and note the hydrogen ion point:

"Lactate is produced during anaerobic glycolysis and can be used as a fuel via the lactate shuttle; it is the accumulation of hydrogen ions, rather than lactate itself, that is most closely associated with the fall in pH and fatigue." Link lactate accumulation to the lactate threshold as a fitness marker. 🔗 Related terms Blood Lactate Lactate Threshold Anaerobic Glycolysis Lactic Acid System Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation (OBLA) Lactate Shuttle 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Lactic Acid System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lactic Acid System IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Lactic Acid System The engine of sustained high-intensity effort — the anaerobic system that powers efforts too long for the ATP-PC system. 📖 What it means The lactic acid system (anaerobic glycolytic system) resynthesises ATP by breaking down glucose without oxygen , through anaerobic glycolysis. It is the dominant system for high-intensity efforts lasting from about ten seconds up to around three minutes .

Because it works anaerobically, it supplies ATP rapidly — faster than the aerobic system — but its by-product is the accumulation of hydrogen ions (associated with lactate), which lowers muscle pH and contributes to fatigue. Its ATP yield is low compared with the aerobic system, and it cannot be sustained for long before rising acidity forces a reduction in intensity. Trained athletes can better tolerate and buffer the acidity, delaying fatigue. 🏅 Sporting examples 400m running A 400m sprint relies heavily on the lactic acid system, producing the intense fatigue and acidity felt in the closing stages. Repeated efforts

The repeated hard sprints in a game draw on the lactic acid system when efforts extend beyond the ATP-PC system's capacity. Training tolerance Trained middle-distance runners tolerate higher levels of acidity, allowing them to sustain the effort longer before slowing. ✍️ Using the term in context State the fuel, duration, speed and by-product: "The lactic acid system resynthesises ATP anaerobically by breaking down glucose, dominating high-intensity efforts of around 10 seconds to 3 minutes; it supplies ATP rapidly but accumulates hydrogen ions, lowering pH and causing fatigue." Be precise: it is hydrogen ion accumulation, not lactate itself, that most directly causes the fall in pH.

Lactose Intolerance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lactose Intolerance BTEC Sport General Lactose Intolerance Trouble digesting the sugar in milk. 📖 What it means Lactose intolerance happens when the body makes too little lactase , the enzyme that breaks down lactose (milk sugar). Undigested lactose causes bloating, wind, cramps and diarrhoea . It is common worldwide, especially in adults. It is not the same as a milk allergy, which involves the immune system. Athletes who are intolerant can use lactose-free products or other sources of calcium and protein , such as fortified plant milks, tofu and fish with bones. 🏅 Sporting examples Recovery drink

An athlete swaps milk for a lactose-free or soy alternative. Calcium Fortified plant drinks help to maintain calcium intake. Lateral Change of Direction Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lateral Change of Direction Test BTEC Sport General Lateral Change of Direction Test A fitness test of lateral agility and speed. 📖 What it means The Lateral Change of Direction Test is an agility test in which the athlete shuffles sideways between two lines as many times as possible in a set time. Interpreting results: More crossings show better lateral quickness. It suits sports such as basketball, tennis and squash. Latissimus Dorsi — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Latissimus Dorsi IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Latissimus Dorsi The large muscle of the back that powers every pulling action — from a swimmer's stroke to a climber's pull-up. 📖 What it means The latissimus dorsi (or 'lats') is a large, flat muscle covering the lower and middle back . Its main actions at the shoulder are adduction, extension and medial rotation of the arm — essentially, powerful pulling movements that bring the arm down and back.

It is heavily recruited in pulling and rowing actions , and in any movement that draws the arm downward or backward against resistance. It acts as an antagonist to muscles that raise the arm. Because of its size and power, the latissimus dorsi is a major contributor to performance in swimming, climbing, rowing and gymnastics , and is a common focus in movement analysis of pulling actions. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming The latissimus dorsi provides much of the propulsive power in the pull phase of front crawl, drawing the arm down and back through the water. Climbing A climber's lats work powerfully to pull the body upward toward the next hold. Weight training

A lat pull-down or pull-up strongly recruits the latissimus dorsi to adduct and extend the arm at the shoulder. ✍️ Using the term in context Name its main actions and its role in pulling movements: "The latissimus dorsi adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder; it provides powerful pulling force in actions such as the front-crawl pull and a pull-up." Law of Acceleration — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Law of Acceleration IB Sport Science General Law of Acceleration Newton's second law — more force means more acceleration, but mass fights back. 📖 What it means The law of acceleration is Newton's second law of motion : the acceleration of a body is proportional to the net force applied to it and inversely proportional to its mass . Stated as the equation: F = ma (force = mass × acceleration).

A larger net force produces greater acceleration; a greater mass reduces acceleration for the same force. This means a lighter athlete accelerates more easily for the same muscular force, and that greater muscular force is needed to accelerate a heavier body or a heavier object. It is central to analysing starting, sprinting and throwing : how fast a sprinter accelerates off the blocks, or how far a shot is thrown, both depend on the force applied relative to the mass being moved. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A greater force from the legs produces greater acceleration of the sprinter's body off the blocks. Throwing

The acceleration of a shot is determined by the force applied and the mass of the implement. Lighter athlete For the same muscular force, a lighter athlete accelerates more readily than a heavier one. ✍️ Using the term in context State the law and the equation: "The law of acceleration is Newton's second law: acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass (F = ma); greater force produces greater acceleration, but greater mass reduces it." Apply it with the equation and a sporting example. 🔗 Related terms Newton's Laws of Motion Force Acceleration Momentum Mass Law of Inertia 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub →

Law of Inertia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Law of Inertia IB Sport Science General Law of Inertia Newton's first law — a body stays put or keeps going until something changes it. 📖 What it means The law of inertia is Newton's first law of motion : a body remains at rest, or continues moving at constant velocity in a straight line, unless acted upon by an external unbalanced force . A stationary ball stays still until kicked; a rolling ball would continue in a straight line forever without friction and air resistance to slow it. The property that makes a body resist change is its inertia , which is proportional to its mass.

In sport, the law of inertia explains why it takes effort to start, stop or change direction of a body or object, and why a more massive body requires more force to change its motion than a lighter one. 🏅 Sporting examples Starting A stationary ball requires a force to start it moving — it stays at rest due to inertia (first law). Changing direction A player must apply force to change direction because their body tends to continue in its current path. Mass and inertia A heavier athlete is harder to change direction because their greater mass gives greater inertia. ✍️ Using the term in context State the law of inertia:

"The law of inertia is Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or moves at constant velocity in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force; greater mass means greater inertia and more force is needed to change motion." Law of Reaction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Law of Reaction IB Sport Science General Law of Reaction Newton's third law — every push gets pushed back, and that reaction is what moves athletes. 📖 What it means The law of reaction is Newton's third law of motion : for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction . When one body exerts a force on another, the second body exerts an equal and opposite force on the first.

The ground reaction force is the most sporting example: when a runner pushes down and back on the ground, the ground pushes up and forward on the runner with equal force — propelling them forward. The same applies to swimming (pushing water backward propels the swimmer forward) and rowing. The law also applies to collisions : in any impact, both objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other, which is why tackling a larger, more massive opponent can be more damaging for the tackler. 🏅 Sporting examples Running A runner pushes back on the ground; the ground reaction force pushes them forward — Newton's third law. Swimming

A swimmer pulls water backward; the reaction force propels them forward. Collision In a collision, both bodies exert equal forces on each other, regardless of their sizes. ✍️ Using the term in context State the law of reaction with a sporting example: "The law of reaction is Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction; when a runner pushes back on the ground, the equal ground reaction force propels them forward." Leadership — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Leadership General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Leadership The ability to direct and inspire others — a key quality in captains, coaches and team environments. 📖 What it means Leadership is the process of influencing others toward goal achievement in a sport or team environment. Effective leadership shapes the team's motivation, cohesion and performance.

Leadership styles range from autocratic (leader makes decisions, directive) to democratic (decisions made collectively with the group) to laissez-faire (leader takes a hands-off approach). The most effective style depends on the situation — the task, the team's experience and the leader's characteristics. Chelladurai's multidimensional model of leadership suggests that effective leadership results from a fit between the leader's actual behaviour, required behaviour (what the situation demands) and preferred behaviour (what athletes want). Leader-member exchange and transformational leadership are also relevant frameworks. 🏅 Sporting examples Autocratic style

A coach uses an autocratic style with a beginner group, making clear decisions and directing activities safely. Democratic style A captain uses a democratic style with experienced players, involving them in tactical decisions. Situational fit The most effective leadership style changes with the situation — task complexity, group experience and time pressure all matter. ✍️ Using the term in context Define leadership styles and note that effectiveness is situational:

Lean Body Mass — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lean Body Mass General BTEC Sport Lean Body Mass The body without its fat — the muscle, bone, organs and water that make up the active portion of body mass. 📖 What it means Lean body mass is the mass of the body excluding fat tissue , comprising muscle, bone, organs, water and other non-fat tissues. It is sometimes called fat-free mass. Lean body mass is the metabolically active component: muscle, in particular, increases basal metabolic rate and is central to strength, power and performance. A higher lean body mass relative to fat mass is generally associated with better athletic performance.

It is measured or estimated as part of body composition assessment , using methods such as skinfolds, BIA or DEXA. Resistance training increases lean body mass; disuse and ageing tend to reduce it. 🏅 Sporting examples Metabolic rate Greater lean body mass raises basal metabolic rate, because muscle tissue burns more energy at rest. Performance A higher lean-to-fat ratio generally supports power and endurance performance. Measurement BIA and skinfold tests estimate body fat percentage and, from it, lean body mass. ✍️ Using the term in context Define lean body mass and link to performance:

Learned Helplessness — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Learned Helplessness IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Learned Helplessness The belief that failure is inevitable and out of one's control — a damaging psychological state that can end participation. 📖 What it means Learned helplessness is a belief that failure is inevitable and beyond one's control , developed after repeated failures. The performer comes to feel that no amount of effort will lead to success, so they stop trying.

It is closely linked to attribution theory : learned helplessness tends to develop when a performer attributes their failures to internal, stable and uncontrollable factors — such as believing 'I'm just not good at sport' — rather than to controllable factors such as effort. It can be general (across all sport) or specific (to one activity). Coaches counter it through attribution retraining — helping performers re-attribute failure to controllable factors — and by setting achievable goals to rebuild confidence and a sense of control. 🏅 Sporting examples Giving up

A young player who repeatedly loses and concludes 'I'll never be any good' has developed learned helplessness and stops making an effort. Specific helplessness A performer confident in most sports may feel helpless in one specific activity, such as swimming, after repeated poor experiences. Reversing it A coach uses attribution retraining and achievable goals to help a helpless performer see that success is within their control. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it and link to attribution and its remedy:

Learning Styles — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Learning Styles General BTEC Sport Learning Styles How people prefer to take in information — a framework for matching guidance to the learner. 📖 What it means Learning styles are theoretical categories describing how individuals prefer to receive and process information . The most commonly cited model in sport and PE is the VAK model: visual (learning by seeing), auditory (learning by hearing) and kinaesthetic (learning by doing).

The idea is that matching instruction to a learner's preferred style can improve learning — so visual learners benefit most from demonstrations, auditory from verbal explanation, and kinaesthetic from physical practice. It is important to note that the scientific evidence for fixed learning styles is mixed , and many learners benefit from multiple modes rather than one. In coaching practice, using a variety of guidance methods — demonstrations, verbal cues, and physical practice — is generally the most effective approach regardless of preferred style. 🏅 Sporting examples Visual Showing a video analysis of a skill benefits visual learners who prefer to see the action first. Kinaesthetic

Letting a beginner physically try the skill immediately (kinaesthetic guidance) can work well alongside other methods. Mixed modes Most effective coaching combines demonstrations, verbal cues and physical practice, catering to all preferences. ✍️ Using the term in context Define learning styles and note the evidence caveat: "Learning styles are theoretical categories (commonly visual, auditory and kinaesthetic) describing how individuals prefer to receive information; matching instruction to style may help, though evidence is mixed and using multiple modes is generally most effective." Leg Press — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Leg Press IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Leg Press A machine-based leg strength exercise. 📖 What it means The leg press is a machine exercise in which the athlete sits or lies back and pushes a loaded platform away by extending the hips and knees. It works mainly the quadriceps and gluteus maximus , with help from the hamstrings and calves. It is a closed chain exercise. The back is supported, so heavier loads can be used with less demand on the trunk, which makes it useful for beginners and in rehabilitation.

Technique points are to keep the lower back flat against the pad , push through the whole foot and avoid locking the knees. Because it does not train balance and core, it is often used alongside free-weight squats. 🏅 Sporting examples Rehabilitation Used to rebuild leg strength after a knee injury. Hypertrophy High-repetition sets to build the quadriceps. Levers — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Levers IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Levers The body's machines for movement — the bone-joint-muscle arrangements that let us generate force and speed. 📖 What it means A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a pivot to produce movement. In the body, bones act as the levers, joints as the pivots (fulcrums), and muscles provide the effort to move a load (usually the weight of a body part or an external resistance).

Every lever has three components: the fulcrum (pivot), the effort (muscle force) and the load (resistance). Levers are classified into first, second and third class according to the arrangement of these three components. Levers allow the body to gain either mechanical advantage (moving a large load with less effort) or speed and range of movement . Most levers in the body are third-class, which favour speed and range over force. 🏅 Sporting examples Third-class lever A biceps curl uses a third-class lever — the effort (biceps) lies between the fulcrum (elbow) and the load (forearm and weight) — favouring speed and range. Second-class lever

Rising onto the toes uses a second-class lever at the ball of the foot, giving mechanical advantage to lift the body's weight. Speed vs force The body's mostly third-class levers sacrifice force for the speed and range of movement useful in throwing and kicking. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the three components and the classification principle: "A lever consists of a fulcrum, effort and load; in the body, bones are levers, joints are fulcrums and muscles provide effort. Levers are classed as first, second or third class by the arrangement of these components, and most in the body are third-class, favouring speed and range." Link lever class to whether it favours force or speed/range.

Lift Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lift Force IB Sport Science General Lift Force The perpendicular push from a fluid — the force that can keep a projectile aloft or curve a ball's path. 📖 What it means Lift force is an aerodynamic or hydrodynamic force acting perpendicular to the direction of motion through a fluid. It is not simply 'upward' — it acts at right angles to the direction of travel. Lift is generated when fluid flows faster over one surface of an object than another, creating a pressure difference (the Bernoulli principle ). This can result from the shape of the object or the angle at which it meets the fluid .

In sport, lift can be beneficial or directional : a discus angled to the airflow generates lift that extends its flight; a topspin tennis ball gets lift directed downward, making it dip; a spinning football curves sideways. Understanding lift is part of projectile and ball-flight analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Discus A discus angled to the airflow generates lift that extends its range. Topspin Topspin on a tennis ball produces downward lift (via the Magnus effect), making it dip sharply. Perpendicular Lift acts perpendicular to direction of travel — not always upward. ✍️ Using the term in context Define lift force and note its direction:

"Lift force is an aerodynamic force acting perpendicular to the direction of motion, generated by pressure differences when fluid flows faster over one side; it can extend projectile flight or curve a ball's path, acting in any direction perpendicular to travel." Ligament — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ligament IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Ligament Bone-to-bone connective tissue — the tough straps that hold joints together and prevent dislocation. 📖 What it means A ligament is a band of dense connective tissue connecting bone to bone across a joint . Its primary role is to stabilise the joint and limit excessive or unwanted movement . Ligaments are strong and relatively inelastic — they hold bones in position while allowing the normal range of movement. When a joint is forced beyond its normal range , ligaments can be overstretched or torn, producing a sprain .

Because ligaments have a limited blood supply , healing can be slow. Key ligaments in sport include the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and medial collateral ligament (MCL) of the knee, which are commonly injured in cutting and contact sports. 🏅 Sporting examples Joint stability The ligaments of the knee hold the joint bones together and prevent the tibia sliding excessively on the femur. Sprain Twisting the ankle beyond its range overstretches its ligaments — a lateral ankle sprain. ACL The ACL is a major stabilising ligament of the knee, commonly torn in pivoting sports. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a ligament and note its injury:

Line of Gravity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Line of Gravity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Line of Gravity The invisible plumb line from the centre of mass — where it falls relative to the base of support determines stability. 📖 What it means The line of gravity is an imaginary vertical line running downward from the body's centre of mass , indicating where gravity's effect is directed. Stability depends on where this line falls.

When the line of gravity falls within the base of support , the body is in balance and stable. When it falls outside the base of support , the body will topple unless a correcting movement is made. The closer the line of gravity is to the centre of the base, the more stable the body. Athletes deliberately position their body so the line of gravity falls where they need it: centred for stability, at the edge for readiness to move . For example, a sprinter leans forward so the line of gravity is at the front of their base, primed to accelerate. 🏅 Sporting examples Stability A goalkeeper in a wide, low stance keeps the line of gravity centred over a large base, staying very stable. Toppling

When a gymnast loses balance, the line of gravity has fallen outside their base of support. Sprinter A sprinter's forward lean moves the line of gravity to the front of the base, ready to accelerate. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the line of gravity and its link to stability: "The line of gravity is an imaginary vertical line from the centre of mass downward; when it falls within the base of support the body is stable, and the closer to the centre of the base, the greater the stability." Combine with centre of gravity and base of support in stability analysis. 🔗 Related terms Centre of Gravity Base of Support Stability Balance Centre of Mass Angular Motion 🎓 Where this appears

Linear Motion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Linear Motion IB Sport Science General Linear Motion Movement in a straight (or curved) line — one of the fundamental types of motion in biomechanics. 📖 What it means Linear motion is movement in which all parts of a body move the same distance, in the same direction, in the same time . It occurs when a force is applied through the body's centre of mass. Linear motion can follow a straight line (rectilinear motion) or a curved line (curvilinear motion) . It is described using linear quantities such as distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.

It contrasts with angular motion (rotation about an axis). Many sporting movements combine the two — for example, angular motion of the limbs producing linear motion of the whole body. 🏅 Sporting examples Skating A speed skater gliding across the ice in a straight line shows linear (rectilinear) motion, all parts of the body moving together. Projectile flight A shot in flight follows a curved path — curvilinear linear motion of its centre of mass. Combined motion A sprinter's legs rotate (angular motion) to drive the whole body forward in linear motion. ✍️ Using the term in context Define linear motion and distinguish it from angular motion:

Long Jump — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Long Jump BTEC Sport General Long Jump Jumping for distance after a sprint run-up. 📖 What it means The long jump has four phases: the approach run , the take-off , the flight and the landing . Speed at take-off is the most important factor in the distance achieved. The best take-off angle is around 20 to 22 degrees , much lower than the theoretical 45 degrees, because the jumper takes off with a high horizontal speed and cannot generate much vertical velocity. In the air, jumpers use the hang or hitch-kick technique to stay balanced and prepare to land.

The distance is measured from the take-off board to the closest mark in the sand. It is a good example of projectile motion and the conversion of horizontal speed into distance. 🏅 Sporting examples Take-off The jumper plants the foot flat and drives the free knee upward. Flight A hitch-kick keeps the body from rotating forward. Landing The feet are extended forward to gain extra distance. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to physics: "In the long jump, the speed and angle of take-off determine the flight path, and a low take-off angle is used because of the high approach speed." Long Term Athlete Development (LTAD) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Long Term Athlete Development (LTAD) General BTEC Sport Long Term Athlete Development (LTAD) A roadmap from playground to podium — a framework structuring how athletes should be trained across their lifespan. 📖 What it means Long Term Athlete Development (LTAD) is a multi-stage framework for structuring training, competition and recovery across an athlete's lifespan , from childhood to senior performance and retirement.

It typically describes stages such as Active Start, FUNdamentals, Learn to Train, Train to Train, Train to Compete, Train to Win and Active for Life . Each stage has age-appropriate training priorities — early stages emphasise developing fundamental movement skills; later stages progress to specialised, high-performance training. LTAD promotes the idea that early specialisation can be harmful , advocating for a broad physical foundation and enjoyable participation in the early years. It is widely used in national sport development policies and talent pathways. 🏅 Sporting examples Early stages

LTAD's FUNdamentals stage for young children emphasises basic movement skills and enjoyment rather than sport-specific training. Avoiding early specialisation LTAD warns against early specialisation, which can cause burnout and overuse injury. Talent pathway National governing bodies use LTAD to structure junior and senior development pathways. ✍️ Using the term in context Define LTAD and its key principle: "LTAD is a multi-stage framework structuring athlete development from childhood to retirement, emphasising age-appropriate training priorities; it advocates against early specialisation, promoting broad physical foundations early and progressive sport-specific training later."

Lung Volume and Capacity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Lung Volume and Capacity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Lung Volume and Capacity The set of measurements that describe how much air the lungs can hold and move. 📖 What it means Lung volumes are the four separate amounts of air: tidal volume , inspiratory reserve volume , expiratory reserve volume and residual volume . They do not overlap. Lung capacities are combinations of two or more volumes: vital capacity , inspiratory capacity , functional residual capacity and total lung capacity .

A spirometer measures most of these, but residual volume cannot be breathed out, so it needs a different technique to measure. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise During exercise tidal volume rises by using up some of the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes. Testing A spirometer test records vital capacity and forced expiratory measures. Swimming Swimmers often have larger lung volumes, partly through training and partly through body size. ✍️ Using the term in context Separate volumes from capacities: "Vital capacity is the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume and expiratory reserve volume; residual volume stays in the lungs." Macrocycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Macrocycle IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Macrocycle The big picture of a training year — the longest planning phase that houses all the smaller cycles. 📖 What it means A macrocycle is the longest phase of a periodised training plan , typically spanning a full year or an Olympic quadrennial. It contains all the mesocycles and microcycles that make up the programme.

It is structured around key target competitions — everything within the macrocycle is designed to ensure the athlete peaks at the right moments. The typical macrocycle contains preparation, competition and transition phases , each with different training emphases. The macrocycle gives the whole plan its shape and direction, and is the unit within which periodisation is applied — manipulating volume, intensity and type of training over time to produce planned peaks and avoid overtraining. 🏅 Sporting examples Annual plan An athlete's full-year plan — from pre-season preparation to post-season recovery — is their macrocycle. Target competition

The macrocycle is built backward from the target event, ensuring the athlete peaks at the right time. Phases Within the macrocycle, preparation builds fitness, the competition phase maintains and peaks it, and transition allows recovery. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a macrocycle and place it in the periodisation hierarchy: "A macrocycle is the longest phase of a periodised plan, typically a year, containing all the mesocycles and microcycles; it is structured around target competitions and divided into preparation, competition and transition phases." Macronutrient — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Macronutrient IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Macronutrient The big three of nutrition — carbohydrates, fats and proteins that provide the body's energy and raw materials. 📖 What it means Macronutrients are the major categories of nutrients required in large amounts : carbohydrates, fats and proteins . They provide energy (carbohydrates and fats) and the raw materials for growth and repair (proteins).

Each macronutrient has a distinct role. Carbohydrates are the body's preferred fuel for moderate-to-high intensity exercise, stored as glycogen. Fats provide a large energy reserve used at lower intensities. Proteins are essential for muscle repair and growth, and act as a minor fuel source. Understanding macronutrients is fundamental to sports nutrition : the right balance, timing and amount of each supports performance, recovery and long-term adaptation. 🏅 Sporting examples Carbohydrate A runner's pre-race meal is carbohydrate-rich to maximise glycogen stores for the effort ahead. Fat During long, steady effort, fat provides the majority of energy, sparing limited glycogen. Protein

A post-training protein intake supports the repair and growth of muscle tissue. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the three macronutrients and state their main roles: "Macronutrients are carbohydrates, fats and proteins — the major nutrients needed in large amounts; carbohydrate is the primary fuel for moderate-to-high intensity exercise, fat for sustained lower-intensity effort, and protein for growth and repair." Magnus Effect — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Magnus Effect IB Sport Science General Magnus Effect Why a spinning ball swerves, dips or lifts — the aerodynamic force behind curling free kicks and topspin forehands. 📖 What it means The Magnus effect is the force generated on a spinning object moving through the air , which causes it to deviate from a straight path — to swerve, dip or lift depending on the direction of spin.

It arises because the spin drags a thin layer of air around the ball , making the air travel faster on one side and slower on the other . By the Bernoulli principle, this creates a pressure difference , and the ball is pushed from the high-pressure side toward the low-pressure side. The direction of the swerve depends on the axis of spin: topspin makes a ball dip more quickly, backspin makes it stay in the air longer, and sidespin makes it curve sideways. 🏅 Sporting examples Football A curling free kick uses sidespin; the Magnus effect creates a pressure difference that bends the ball's flight around the wall. Tennis

A topspin forehand dips sharply because the Magnus effect from the topspin pushes the ball downward, letting it clear the net yet land in. Cricket / golf Backspin on a well-struck golf ball generates lift via the Magnus effect, keeping it airborne longer for greater carry. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the spin–pressure mechanism and the effect of spin direction: "The Magnus effect is the force on a spinning ball that causes it to swerve; the spin makes air travel faster on one side, creating a pressure difference (Bernoulli principle) that pushes the ball — topspin causes it to dip, backspin to stay airborne, sidespin to curve." Link it explicitly to the Bernoulli principle.

Margaria-Kalamen Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Margaria-Kalamen Test General BTEC Sport Margaria-Kalamen Test Run up the stairs as fast as you can — a stair-sprint test of explosive anaerobic leg power. 📖 What it means The Margaria-Kalamen Test is a test of anaerobic leg power measuring the time taken to run up a set of stairs as fast as possible. Power is calculated from the performer's mass, the height gained and the time taken.

Because it involves a maximal, explosive stair sprint, it tests the ability of the legs to produce power rapidly — the ATP-PC system primarily — over a very short duration. It provides a calculated power output rather than simply a time. It is a practical, direct measure of explosive leg power requiring only stairs and a timer. However, it involves a maximal sprint effort and needs a suitable staircase, limiting where it can be administered. 🏅 Sporting examples Explosive power The Margaria-Kalamen Test measures how powerfully an athlete can drive up stairs — an explosive anaerobic effort. Power calculation Mass, height and time are combined to give a calculated power output in watts.

ATP-PC system The very short, maximal effort primarily taxes the ATP-PC energy system. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures: "The Margaria-Kalamen Test measures anaerobic leg power by timing a maximal stair sprint and calculating power from mass, height and time; it tests the explosive power of the legs but requires a maximal effort and a suitable staircase." Massage Techniques — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Massage Techniques BTEC Sport General Massage Techniques The strokes used in sports massage. 📖 What it means Sports massage uses several standard strokes. Effleurage is long, gliding strokes used to warm the tissue and move blood and lymph. Petrissage is kneading and squeezing of the muscle. Friction uses small, deep movements to loosen tight areas or adhesions. Tapotement is rhythmic tapping, such as hacking and cupping, and is stimulating. Vibration is shaking or trembling of the tissue.

Massage is used before events to stimulate, after events to aid recovery, and in treatment of injury. It must be avoided on acute injury, infection and certain medical conditions. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-event Light effleurage and tapotement to warm and stimulate. Massed Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Massed Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Massed Practice Practice packed together with little rest — efficient for grooving simple, well-learned skills, but demanding. 📖 What it means Massed practice is a practice structure in which a skill is rehearsed repeatedly with little or no rest between attempts . The practice is concentrated into a solid block. It contrasts with distributed practice , which spaces attempts out with rest intervals. Massed practice is time-efficient and good for grooving and automating simple, well-learned skills , and for helping performers practise under fatigue.

However, because there is little rest, massed practice can cause fatigue and reduced motivation , and is less suitable for beginners, complex skills or dangerous skills , where fatigue would harm learning or safety. The choice depends on the learner and the skill. 🏅 Sporting examples Grooving a simple skill An experienced player repeatedly practising a simple, well-learned closed skill uses massed practice to reinforce automaticity. Practising under fatigue A coach uses massed practice to help an athlete perform a skill even when tired, replicating late-game demands. When to avoid it

For a beginner learning a complex or dangerous skill, distributed practice is safer, as massed practice would cause fatigue and errors. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast massed with distributed practice and state when it suits: "Massed practice rehearses a skill repeatedly with little rest; it is time-efficient and suits grooving simple, well-learned skills and practising under fatigue, but is less suitable for beginners or complex skills, where distributed practice is preferable." It contrasts with a performance (ego) climate , where success means beating others and ability is compared. Mastery climates are associated with greater enjoyment, persistence, intrinsic motivation and lower anxiety .

Coaches create it by giving feedback on effort and progress , letting athletes help in decisions, valuing mistakes as part of learning and avoiding public comparison. 🏅 Sporting examples Youth sport A coach praises improvement, not only the winner. Students set personal goals. Protocol: Examples include the multistage fitness (bleep) test run to exhaustion, a treadmill VO2 max test and a 1RM lift. Motivation and a thorough warm-up are important.

Interpreting results: Maximal tests give direct, accurate results, but they are demanding, carry more risk for untrained people and depend on the athlete's willingness to give full effort. Maximum Heart Rate (HRmax) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Maximum Heart Rate (HRmax) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Maximum Heart Rate (HRmax) The ceiling on how fast the heart can beat — the reference point for setting exercise intensity from heart rate. 📖 What it means Maximum heart rate (HRmax) is the highest number of beats per minute an individual's heart can reach during maximal exercise. It is largely determined by age and is relatively unaffected by training.

It is commonly estimated using the formula 220 minus age , though this is only an approximation with considerable individual variation; a maximal exercise test gives a more accurate figure. HRmax tends to decline gradually with age . HRmax is important because it provides the reference point for setting training intensities — target heart rate zones are often expressed as a percentage of HRmax (for example, 60–80% for aerobic development). 🏅 Sporting examples Setting zones A coach estimates a 20-year-old's HRmax as about 200 bpm (220 − 20) and sets an aerobic training zone of roughly 140–160 bpm (70–80%). Age effect

As an athlete ages, their maximum heart rate gradually falls, so their target training zones shift downward over the years. Accuracy Because 220 − age is only an estimate, a coach may use a maximal test for a more accurate individual HRmax. ✍️ Using the term in context Define HRmax, give the estimate and its use: "Maximum heart rate is the highest heart rate an individual can reach, estimated by 220 minus age; it provides the reference point for setting training intensities as a percentage of HRmax, though the formula is only an approximation." Mean — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mean IB Sport Science General Mean The arithmetic average — the sum of all values divided by how many there are. 📖 What it means The mean is the arithmetic average of a set of values , found by adding all the values together and dividing by the number of values . It is the most commonly used measure of central tendency. It gives a single representative value for a data set, summarising the typical score. However, the mean is sensitive to extreme values (outliers) — a single very high or very low score can pull the mean far from the typical value.

In sport science investigations, the mean is reported alongside measures of spread (such as standard deviation or range) to give a fuller picture of the data. Together, central tendency and spread characterise a distribution. 🏅 Sporting examples Calculating it Five sprint times of 10.1, 10.3, 10.0, 10.2, 10.4 give a mean of 10.2 seconds. Representative value The mean sprint time summarises the group's typical performance in one number. Outlier effect One very slow sprint time pulls the mean up, making it seem less typical of the group. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the mean and note its limitation:

"The mean is the arithmetic average of a data set, found by dividing the sum of values by the number of values; it is the most common central tendency measure but is sensitive to outliers, so should be reported alongside standard deviation." Mechanical Advantage — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mechanical Advantage IB Sport Science General Mechanical Advantage Getting more out than you put in — the lever's ability to multiply force or speed depending on arrangement. 📖 What it means Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load arm to the effort arm in a lever system , indicating whether the lever favours force or speed.

A mechanical advantage greater than 1 means the lever multiplies force — a small effort can move a large load (as in a second-class lever). A mechanical advantage less than 1 means force is not multiplied but speed and range of movement are favoured instead (as in most body third-class levers). Most levers in the body have a mechanical advantage less than 1 , sacrificing force for the speed and range that sporting movements need. This is why muscles must generate large forces to produce relatively small external loads — the lever arrangement favours speed over force. 🏅 Sporting examples Second-class lever

Rising onto the toes uses a second-class lever with a mechanical advantage >1, allowing the calf to lift body weight. Mechanoreceptor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mechanoreceptor IB Sport Science General Mechanoreceptor Receptors that feel force and movement — the sensory cells behind pressure, stretch and position sense. 📖 What it means A mechanoreceptor is a sensory receptor that responds to mechanical stimuli such as pressure, stretch, deformation and vibration. They translate physical forces into nerve signals.

In sport and movement, mechanoreceptors include the muscle spindles (detecting muscle length and rate of change), Golgi tendon organs (detecting tension), and joint receptors . Together they are the foundation of proprioception and kinaesthesia — the body's sense of its own position and movement. They also include skin mechanoreceptors that detect pressure and texture, contributing to the 'feel' of grip and contact. Mechanoreceptors provide the constant stream of information the nervous system uses to control and adjust movement during sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Muscle spindle Muscle spindles are mechanoreceptors that detect stretch, contributing to proprioceptive sense. Grip feel

Skin mechanoreceptors provide the sensation of grip on a racket or bat. Proprioception Mechanoreceptors in muscles and joints give the body its sense of position and movement. ✍️ Using the term in context Define mechanoreceptors and give sporting examples: "Mechanoreceptors are sensory receptors responding to mechanical stimuli such as pressure and stretch; they include muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs, underpinning proprioception and kinaesthesia." Medicine Ball Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Medicine Ball Training BTEC Sport General Medicine Ball Training Power and core training with weighted balls. 📖 What it means Medicine ball training uses balls of about 1 to 5 kg in throws, slams, catches and rotational movements. It develops explosive power, trunk strength and coordination . Throws can be ballistic , for example overhead throws and chest passes against a wall, or rotational , such as side throws, which train the trunk to transfer force. They can be done as plyometric exercises, with the catch and re-throw using the stretch-shortening cycle.

The ball weight should be light enough to allow fast, safe movement. It is used in sports that need rotational power, such as tennis, golf, cricket and throwing events. 🏅 Sporting examples Tennis Rotational throws to develop the strength for groundstrokes. Rugby Chest passes against a wall for upper-body power. Core Slams and twists for trunk strength. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to power: "Medicine ball throws develop explosive power and trunk rotation because they allow fast movement with a light external load." Meniscus — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Meniscus IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Meniscus The shock-absorbing cartilage pads in the knee. 📖 What it means Each knee has two menisci : a medial and a lateral , made of tough fibrocartilage . They sit between the femur and tibia. They absorb shock, spread load across the joint, deepen the socket and help stability. Because they have little blood supply, tears heal slowly. Meniscus tears often occur with a twist while the foot is planted, as in football, rugby and skiing, causing pain, swelling and sometimes locking. Treatment ranges from rehabilitation to surgery. 🏅 Sporting examples Football

A twisting tackle tears the medial meniscus. Rehabilitation Strengthening the thigh muscles protects the joint. Ageing Menisci wear with age, increasing osteoarthritis risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the function: "The menisci cushion the knee by absorbing shock and distributing load between the femur and tibia." Menstrual Cycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Menstrual Cycle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Menstrual Cycle The monthly hormone cycle and why it matters for female athletes. 📖 What it means The menstrual cycle is a repeating cycle of about 28 days (range roughly 21–35) controlled by oestrogen and progesterone , with the follicular phase before ovulation and the luteal phase after it. The cycle begins with menstruation. Hormone levels can affect energy, mood, sleep, temperature, injury risk and perceived effort , though the effects on performance are small on average and vary a lot between individuals.

Missed or absent periods ( amenorrhoea ) in an athlete can signal low energy availability and need medical attention, as in the female athlete triad and RED-S. 🏅 Sporting examples Tracking An athlete records symptoms across the cycle to plan harder and easier training. Warning sign Missed periods in a distance runner prompt a medical check for low energy availability. Injury Some research links the phase of the cycle to ligament laxity and injury risk, but the evidence is not yet clear. ✍️ Using the term in context Be balanced about the evidence:

"Hormonal changes across the menstrual cycle may influence how an athlete feels, but effects on performance vary between individuals, so training is best adapted to the athlete." Mental Rehearsal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mental Rehearsal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Mental Rehearsal Practising in the mind's eye — a psychological technique in which athletes rehearse a skill mentally to improve performance and confidence. 📖 What it means Mental rehearsal is a psychological technique in which a performer mentally practises a skill or performance without physically moving — vividly imagining themselves executing the action successfully.

It is a form of imagery , and is thought to work by strengthening the neural pathways involved in the movement, reinforcing correct technique, and building confidence and focus . It can be used to rehearse technique, tactics, or coping with pressure. Mental rehearsal is most effective when the imagery is vivid and controllable , using all the senses, and when it is combined with physical practice rather than used as a replacement for it. It is widely used in pre-performance routines. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-performance A high jumper mentally rehearses their entire run-up and jump before each attempt, reinforcing the correct technique and focusing their attention. Building confidence

A penalty taker vividly imagines scoring, building confidence and reducing anxiety before stepping up. Combined with practice A gymnast uses mental rehearsal alongside physical training to reinforce a complex routine between sessions. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it as mental practice and explain how it helps: "Mental rehearsal involves mentally practising a skill without moving; as a form of imagery, it strengthens neural pathways, reinforces technique and builds confidence, and is most effective when vivid and combined with physical practice." Mental Toughness — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mental Toughness General BTEC Sport Mental Toughness Thriving under pressure — the psychological resilience that lets athletes perform when it matters most. 📖 What it means Mental toughness is a psychological attribute enabling athletes to cope consistently with demands and perform at or near their best , under pressure and adversity. It is often described as one of the most important psychological qualities for high-level performance.

It encompasses resilience, self-belief, motivation, focus and the ability to bounce back from setbacks . Mentally tough athletes maintain composure under pressure, persist through difficulty, and are less affected by distractions or failure. Mental toughness can be developed through psychological skills training (such as goal setting, imagery, self-talk and routines), although it also has trait-like characteristics. Coaches foster it by creating challenging but supportive training environments. 🏅 Sporting examples Composure A mentally tough athlete maintains focus and composure in the deciding moments of a match. Bouncing back

After a mistake, a mentally tough performer resets quickly rather than dwelling on the error. Development Goal setting, imagery and self-talk training all contribute to developing mental toughness. ✍️ Using the term in context Define mental toughness and its components: "Mental toughness is the ability to cope consistently with demands and perform at or near best under pressure; it involves resilience, self-belief, focus and the ability to bounce back, and can be developed through psychological skills training." Mesocycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mesocycle IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Mesocycle A training block within the plan — typically lasting weeks to months, targeting a specific fitness quality. 📖 What it means A mesocycle is a mid-length training phase within a periodised plan , typically lasting between three and twelve weeks . It sits within the macrocycle and is made up of individual microcycles (usually weeks).

Each mesocycle has a specific training objective — for example, building aerobic base, developing strength, or sharpening speed and power. The training content and volume/intensity are structured to achieve that objective over the block's duration. The sequencing of mesocycles within the macrocycle is carefully planned so that each block builds on the previous one, progressively targeting the qualities needed for competition — the basis of block periodisation . 🏅 Sporting examples Strength block A four-week mesocycle focused on maximal strength comes before a power mesocycle, providing the base for it. Sequencing

Metabolism — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Metabolism IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Metabolism All the chemical processes that keep the body running — from energy production to tissue building. 📖 What it means Metabolism encompasses all the chemical processes in the body used to maintain life , including energy production and the building and breaking down of substances. It has two sides: catabolism (breaking down complex molecules to release energy — as in the breakdown of glycogen or fat for ATP production) and anabolism (building complex molecules from simpler ones — as in muscle protein synthesis after training).

Metabolic rate is how fast these processes occur; it is influenced by factors such as muscle mass, physical activity, age and hormones . Understanding metabolism underpins nutrition, training and recovery in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Catabolism Breaking down glycogen to produce ATP during exercise is a catabolic process. Anabolism Rebuilding muscle protein after training is an anabolic process. Metabolic rate A greater muscle mass raises metabolic rate, increasing energy demand even at rest. ✍️ Using the term in context Define metabolism and distinguish catabolism from anabolism:

METS — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › METS IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport METS A simple unit that compares the cost of an activity with resting energy use. 📖 What it means A MET (metabolic equivalent of task) is a multiple of your resting metabolic rate . 1 MET is the energy cost of sitting quietly and is about 3.5 ml of oxygen per kilogram of body weight per minute . Activities are rated by how many METs they require: for example light activity is under 3 METs , moderate is 3 to 6 and vigorous is above 6 . METs allow different activities to be compared and are used to estimate energy expenditure and to set exercise guidelines.

Microcycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Microcycle IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Microcycle The training week — the shortest repeating unit of a periodised plan. 📖 What it means A microcycle is the shortest phase of a periodised training plan , typically a single week . It is the basic repeating unit that makes up a mesocycle. Within a microcycle, the coach plans the individual sessions, their sequence, and the balance between work and recovery . Sessions are ordered to avoid unnecessary fatigue accumulation — for example, not placing two hard sessions back-to-back.

Microcycles allow the coach to vary daily and weekly load to manage fatigue while maintaining the training stimulus. Adjusting microcycle structure is one of the main tools for optimising training within a mesocycle. 🏅 Sporting examples Weekly plan A microcycle typically shows a full week's training schedule — which sessions fall on which days. Recovery management Placing easy or rest days after hard sessions within the microcycle helps manage fatigue. Building block Microcycles build into mesocycles, which build into the macrocycle. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a microcycle and its role:

"A microcycle is the shortest unit of a periodised plan, typically a week, planning individual sessions and the balance of work and recovery; microcycles build into mesocycles and macrocycles." Micronutrient — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Micronutrient IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Micronutrient The small but mighty dietary essentials — vitamins and minerals that regulate the body without providing energy. 📖 What it means Micronutrients are nutrients required by the body in small amounts , including vitamins and minerals . They do not provide energy (unlike macronutrients) but are essential for regulating metabolism, supporting immunity and maintaining health.

Key micronutrients relevant to sport include iron (haemoglobin formation), calcium (bone and muscle), vitamin D (calcium absorption and bone health) and B vitamins (energy metabolism). Deficiency in any of these can impair performance. A varied, balanced diet is the most reliable way to meet micronutrient needs. Athletes with higher training loads may have elevated requirements for some micronutrients and should ensure their diet supports them. 🏅 Sporting examples Iron Iron is a micronutrient essential for haemoglobin; deficiency impairs oxygen transport and endurance. Calcium Calcium supports bone density and muscle contraction — critical for athletic health. Balanced diet

A varied diet of whole foods is the best way to meet micronutrient needs. ✍️ Using the term in context Define micronutrients and give sport-relevant examples: "Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts; they regulate metabolism and health without providing energy, and key ones for athletes include iron, calcium and vitamin D, with deficiency impairing performance." Minute Ventilation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Minute Ventilation IB Sport Science General Minute Ventilation The total volume of air breathed each minute — the headline measure of how hard the respiratory system is working. 📖 What it means Minute ventilation (also called pulmonary ventilation, VE) is the total volume of air breathed in or out of the lungs per minute . It is the product of tidal volume (the air moved per breath) and breathing frequency (breaths per minute): VE = tidal volume × frequency.

At rest, minute ventilation is around 6–8 litres per minute. During maximal exercise it can rise dramatically — to well over 100 litres per minute in trained athletes — as both tidal volume and breathing frequency increase to meet the demand for oxygen and the need to remove carbon dioxide. The increase in minute ventilation during exercise is one of the body's key acute responses , ensuring gas exchange keeps pace with the working muscles' demands. 🏅 Sporting examples Intense exercise As a rower approaches maximal effort, minute ventilation rises steeply as both deeper and faster breathing move far more air per minute. Rest to exercise

Moving from rest into hard exercise, minute ventilation can increase more than tenfold to supply oxygen and clear carbon dioxide. Components Early in exercise, minute ventilation rises mainly through increased tidal volume; at higher intensities, breathing frequency increases more. ✍️ Using the term in context State the formula and the exercise response: "Minute ventilation is the volume of air breathed per minute, equal to tidal volume multiplied by breathing frequency; it rises sharply during exercise as both increase, ensuring gas exchange meets the demand for oxygen and removal of carbon dioxide." Note how the components contribute at different intensities. 🔗 Related terms

Mitochondria — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Mitochondria IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Mitochondria The cell's power stations — where oxygen-based energy production happens and endurance is made. 📖 What it means Mitochondria are organelles within cells where aerobic ATP production takes place . Often called the 'powerhouses of the cell', they are the site of the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation . They use oxygen to break down carbohydrate and fat, producing large amounts of ATP. The more mitochondria a muscle fibre has (and the larger they are), the greater its aerobic capacity and endurance .

Endurance training causes a significant increase in the number and size of mitochondria (mitochondrial biogenesis) in the trained muscles — one of the most important peripheral adaptations. This directly increases the muscles' ability to produce ATP aerobically. 🏅 Sporting examples Aerobic ATP Mitochondria use oxygen to produce large amounts of ATP from carbohydrate and fat. Training adaptation Endurance training increases the number and size of mitochondria, raising aerobic capacity. Slow-twitch fibres Slow-twitch fibres have many mitochondria, which is why they are resistant to fatigue. ✍️ Using the term in context Define mitochondria and the training adaptation:

Moment of Inertia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Moment of Inertia IB Sport Science General Moment of Inertia Resistance to rotation — how mass distribution around an axis determines how hard something is to spin or stop. 📖 What it means Moment of inertia is a body's resistance to changes in its rotational motion . Like inertia in linear motion, it opposes changes in angular velocity — but it depends not just on mass but on how the mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation .

The further the mass is from the axis, the greater the moment of inertia. A tucked diver has a smaller moment of inertia than an extended one because their mass is closer to the axis, so they spin faster for the same angular momentum. Because angular momentum = moment of inertia × angular velocity , and angular momentum is conserved, changing the moment of inertia changes the angular velocity. This explains the classic spin speed changes in diving, gymnastics and figure skating. 🏅 Sporting examples Tuck position A diver in a tight tuck reduces their moment of inertia, so their angular velocity increases (they spin faster). Extended position

Extending the arms and legs increases the moment of inertia, slowing rotation. Conservation Angular momentum is conserved, so reducing moment of inertia speeds up the spin. ✍️ Using the term in context Define moment of inertia and link to angular momentum: "Moment of inertia is a body's resistance to changes in rotational motion, determined by mass and its distribution around the axis; because angular momentum (= moment of inertia × angular velocity) is conserved, reducing moment of inertia increases angular velocity." Use the diver's tuck as the main example. 🔗 Related terms Angular Momentum Angular Velocity Angular Motion Torque Centre of Mass Conservation of Angular Momentum
