Momentum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Momentum IB Sport Science General Momentum The 'quantity of motion' a body carries — the product of mass and velocity, central to collisions, throws and running. 📖 What it means Momentum is the quantity of motion a body possesses , calculated as mass multiplied by velocity (momentum = mass × velocity). It is a vector quantity , having both magnitude and direction, measured in kilogram-metres per second.

A body has more momentum if it has more mass, more velocity, or both. Momentum is changed by impulse (force × time), so applying a force over time changes a body's momentum — the basis of accelerating, decelerating and striking objects. The conservation of momentum means that in a collision, the total momentum is conserved; this explains what happens when players collide or when a bat strikes a ball, with momentum transferred between the bodies involved. 🏅 Sporting examples Rugby collision A heavier player running at the same speed as a lighter one carries greater momentum, making them harder to stop in a tackle. Striking a ball

In a tennis serve, momentum is transferred from the fast-moving racket to the ball, sending it forward at high velocity. Sprinting A sprinter builds forward momentum by applying impulse against the ground; the greater the impulse, the greater the change in momentum. ✍️ Using the term in context State momentum = mass × velocity and link to impulse: "Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, a vector quantity; it is changed by impulse (force × time), which is how athletes accelerate their bodies or transfer momentum to strike an object." Reference conservation of momentum when analysing collisions. 🔗 Related terms Impulse Force Velocity Newton's Laws of Motion Acceleration Angular Momentum

Motivation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Motivation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Motivation The drive behind everything an athlete does — the internal and external forces that direct and energise behaviour. 📖 What it means Motivation is the drive to initiate and sustain behaviour toward a goal — the forces that determine the direction of effort (what we choose to do) and its intensity (how hard we try). It is fundamental to participation and performance.

Motivation is commonly divided into intrinsic motivation (the internal drive from enjoyment and satisfaction of the activity itself) and extrinsic motivation (from external rewards such as trophies, money or praise). Both influence behaviour, often together. Because motivation drives effort and persistence, coaches try to develop and maintain it — particularly durable intrinsic motivation — through enjoyable activities, achievable goals, positive reinforcement and helping performers experience competence and progress. 🏅 Sporting examples Persistence A highly motivated athlete trains willingly, persists through setbacks, and keeps working toward long-term goals. Intrinsic vs extrinsic

One player is driven mainly by love of the game (intrinsic), another by the prospect of a trophy (extrinsic); the strongest performers usually have both. Coaching A coach sustains motivation by making sessions enjoyable, setting achievable goals and reinforcing progress. ✍️ Using the term in context Define motivation and split it into intrinsic and extrinsic: "Motivation is the drive that directs and energises behaviour toward a goal; it can be intrinsic, from the enjoyment of the activity itself, or extrinsic, from external rewards, and coaches aim to develop durable intrinsic motivation." Motor Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Motor Learning IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Motor Learning The relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill — what practice is actually trying to achieve. 📖 What it means Motor learning is the relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill , resulting from practice or experience. The key word is permanent — learning is distinguished from a temporary change in performance.

This matters because performance and learning are not the same . A performer might do well on one day due to favourable conditions (good performance) without having genuinely learned; true learning shows as a lasting improvement that persists over time and transfers to new situations. Motor learning is described by models such as Fitts and Posner's stages of learning , and is influenced by the type of practice, guidance and feedback used. Retention and transfer tests are used to check whether genuine learning, rather than temporary performance change, has occurred. 🏅 Sporting examples Learning vs performance

A player who performs brilliantly once but cannot repeat it has not necessarily learned the skill; genuine motor learning shows as consistent, lasting improvement. Stages A learner progresses through the cognitive, associative and autonomous stages as motor learning takes place. Checking learning A coach uses a retention test days later to confirm that practice produced lasting learning, not just a temporary lift. ✍️ Using the term in context Stress the permanence and the learning–performance distinction:

"Motor learning is a relatively permanent change in the ability to perform a skill, resulting from practice; it is distinct from performance, which can change temporarily, so retention and transfer are used to confirm genuine learning." Motor Neurone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Motor Neurone IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Motor Neurone The nerve cell that commands muscles — carrying the signal from the brain to the muscle fibres. 📖 What it means A motor neurone is a nerve cell that carries impulses from the central nervous system to muscle fibres , causing them to contract. It is the final link in the pathway from thought to movement.

Each motor neurone serves a number of muscle fibres together forming a motor unit . When the neurone fires, all the fibres in its unit contract (the all-or-none law). The neurone reaches the muscle at the neuromuscular junction , where the neurotransmitter acetylcholine triggers the contraction. The size of motor neurones and the fibres they serve varies: small motor neurones supply slow-twitch fibres (lower threshold, recruited first); large motor neurones supply fast-twitch fibres (higher threshold, recruited for powerful efforts). 🏅 Sporting examples Command to contract A motor neurone carries the signal from the brain to the quadriceps, causing the leg to extend in a kick. Motor unit

Each motor neurone and the muscle fibres it controls form a motor unit. Recruitment order Smaller motor neurones to slow-twitch fibres are recruited first; larger ones to fast-twitch fibres follow at higher intensity. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a motor neurone and its role: "A motor neurone is a nerve cell carrying impulses from the CNS to muscle fibres, causing contraction; with its fibres it forms a motor unit, and small motor neurones to slow-twitch fibres are recruited first, large ones to fast-twitch fibres at higher intensity." Motor Programme — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Motor Programme IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Motor Programme A stored plan for a movement. 📖 What it means A motor programme is a memorised set of instructions for a movement, held in long-term memory . Once triggered, it controls the movement, with the muscles in the correct sequence and timing, with little conscious attention. This is called open-loop control . Schmidt's schema theory proposes generalised motor programmes , which hold the general rules for a class of actions (for example, a throw) and can be adjusted with parameters such as speed and force.

Fast, ballistic skills such as a golf swing or a tennis serve rely heavily on motor programmes because there is not enough time for feedback during the movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf swing The sequence is run as a single programme. Sprint start The movement is too fast for feedback. Practice Repetition strengthens the stored programme. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to open-loop control: "A motor programme is a stored set of commands that runs without feedback during the movement, as in open-loop control." Motor Unit — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Motor Unit IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Motor Unit The functional unit of muscle contraction — a single motor neurone and all the fibres it controls, working together in an all-or-none fashion. 📖 What it means A motor unit is a single motor neurone together with all the muscle fibres it stimulates . It is the basic functional unit through which the nervous system controls muscle contraction.

Motor units work on the all-or-none principle : when a motor neurone fires, all the muscle fibres in its unit contract fully, or none do . The strength of a whole muscle's contraction is varied not by contracting fibres partially, but by controlling how many motor units are recruited and how frequently they fire. The size of motor units varies with the muscle's role: muscles needing fine control (such as those of the eye or hand) have small motor units (few fibres per neurone), while powerful muscles (such as those of the leg) have large motor units. 🏅 Sporting examples Graded force

To lift a light object then a heavy one, the body recruits progressively more motor units, increasing the force produced. Fine control The small motor units of the hand allow the precise control needed for a delicate skill such as a dart throw. Explosive power A maximal effort such as a jump recruits many large motor units of the leg muscles simultaneously for maximum force. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the motor unit and explain the all-or-none principle:

"A motor unit is a motor neurone and all the muscle fibres it stimulates; it obeys the all-or-none principle, so whole-muscle force is graded by recruiting more motor units and increasing their firing frequency, not by partial fibre contraction." Multi-Store Memory Model — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Multi-Store Memory Model IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Multi-Store Memory Model The three-stage model of how memory works. 📖 What it means The multi-store model (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968) describes memory as three separate stores : the sensory register , short-term memory (STM) and long-term memory (LTM) . The sensory register holds information from the senses for a very short time. If attention is paid, it moves to the STM , which holds a limited amount for a short time unless it is rehearsed . Rehearsal and practice move it to the LTM , which has a large capacity and long duration.

The model is simple and helps to explain how coaches should present information, but it is criticised as too simple, and other models (such as the working memory model) give more detail. 🏅 Sporting examples Coaching A learner's attention is captured by a demonstration. Practice Repetition moves a skill into long-term memory. Multidimensional Anxiety Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Multidimensional Anxiety Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Multidimensional Anxiety Theory The theory that treats anxiety as having separate mental and physical parts. 📖 What it means Multidimensional anxiety theory (Martens, 1990) splits anxiety into cognitive anxiety (worry) and somatic anxiety (physiological arousal), plus self-confidence . It predicts that cognitive anxiety has a negative, linear relationship with performance: more worry means worse performance. Somatic anxiety shows an inverted-U relationship, and self-confidence has a positive link with performance.

It differs from the single-dimension inverted-U hypothesis. Research support is mixed, and it does not fully explain why anxiety affects individuals differently. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf putt High cognitive anxiety about missing leads to a poorer putt, even when physical arousal is moderate. Multistage Abdominal Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Multistage Abdominal Test General BTEC Sport Multistage Abdominal Test A progressive core endurance test — timed curl-ups to a rising beat until failure. 📖 What it means The Multistage Abdominal Test (also called the Progressive Abdominal Curl Test) is a progressive test of abdominal muscular endurance in which the performer completes curl-ups in time with an audio signal that gradually increases in speed.

The performer completes as many curl-ups as possible, maintaining correct technique, until they can no longer keep up with the beat. The stage reached before failure gives the score, which can be compared against normative data. It is a simple, practical field test requiring minimal equipment, useful for assessing and monitoring core endurance. It specifically tests the abdominal muscles' endurance, rather than their maximal strength, and is sensitive to changes in core conditioning over a training programme. 🏅 Sporting examples Progressive speed The beat increases stage by stage; the performer matches it until they cannot maintain technique. The test measures how long the abdominals can sustain repeated efforts — endurance, not maximal strength. Monitoring Repeating the test across a training block shows whether abdominal endurance is improving. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures: "The Multistage Abdominal Test is a progressive curl-up test of abdominal muscular endurance in which the performer matches a rising beat until failure; the stage reached is the score, and it is practical and sensitive to changes in core conditioning." Muscle Fibre Recruitment — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Muscle Fibre Recruitment IB Sport Science General Muscle Fibre Recruitment How the body calls up exactly the right muscle power for the job — recruiting motor units in an orderly sequence as demand rises. 📖 What it means Muscle fibre recruitment is the process by which the body activates motor units to produce the required force . As the demand for force increases, more motor units are recruited , and the fibres within them contract on the all-or-none principle.

Recruitment follows an orderly sequence (the 'size principle'): smaller, slow-twitch motor units are recruited first for low-intensity work, with larger, fast-twitch motor units recruited progressively as the force requirement rises toward maximal. This orderly recruitment lets the body match energy use and fatigue to the task — using efficient, fatigue-resistant slow-twitch fibres for light work and only calling on powerful, quickly-fatiguing fast-twitch fibres when high force is genuinely needed. 🏅 Sporting examples Light to heavy

Lifting a light weight recruits mainly slow-twitch fibres; as the weight increases toward maximal, more fast-twitch motor units are recruited to produce the extra force. Endurance Steady jogging relies on continuous recruitment of fatigue-resistant slow-twitch motor units, sparing fast-twitch fibres. Sprinting A maximal sprint recruits large numbers of fast-twitch motor units to generate explosive force quickly. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain graded recruitment and the size principle:

"Muscle fibre recruitment matches force to demand by activating more motor units as required; following the size principle, slow-twitch motor units are recruited first, with fast-twitch units added as the force requirement rises." Muscle Fibre — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Muscle Fibre IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Muscle Fibre The individual contractile cells that make up a muscle — and whose type largely determines what a performer is built for. 📖 What it means A muscle fibre is an individual muscle cell . Skeletal muscles are made up of many muscle fibres bundled together, and it is the coordinated contraction of these fibres that produces force and movement.

Muscle fibres are broadly classified into types with different properties: slow-twitch (Type I) fibres, which are fatigue-resistant and suited to endurance, and fast-twitch (Type II) fibres, which contract quickly and powerfully but fatigue rapidly, suited to explosive efforts. The proportion of fibre types a person has is largely genetically determined and strongly influences the activities they are naturally suited to — though training can improve the qualities of the fibres they possess. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance vs power A marathon runner typically has a high proportion of slow-twitch fibres, while a sprinter has more fast-twitch fibres. Recruitment

During exercise, motor units recruit muscle fibres according to demand — slow-twitch first for low intensity, adding fast-twitch for higher force. Training Training cannot easily change fibre-type proportions much, but it can improve the endurance or power qualities of the fibres a person has. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the fibre and note the two main types: "A muscle fibre is an individual muscle cell; fibres are classified as slow-twitch (Type I), fatigue-resistant and suited to endurance, or fast-twitch (Type II), fast and powerful but quick to fatigue, with the proportion largely genetically determined." Link fibre-type proportion to the activities a performer is suited to.

Muscle Imbalance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Muscle Imbalance General BTEC Sport Muscle Imbalance When one side is stronger or tighter than the other — a common cause of injury and inefficiency in athletes. 📖 What it means Muscle imbalance is a difference in strength or flexibility between opposing muscle groups or between the same muscle group on opposite sides of the body. It is common in athletes who train repetitively in one pattern.

Imbalances can arise from sport-specific overuse (one side or one movement pattern dominating), injury , or poor training design . They alter joint mechanics and movement patterns, increasing the risk of overuse injury and reducing performance efficiency. Identifying and correcting muscle imbalances through balanced training, stretching and targeted strengthening is an important part of injury prevention and long-term athletic development. 🏅 Sporting examples Quad-hamstring A footballer who over-develops the quadriceps relative to the hamstrings has a muscle imbalance that raises hamstring strain risk. Side-to-side

A tennis player may develop greater strength in the dominant arm, creating a bilateral imbalance. Correction Targeted unilateral training and stretching can correct imbalances and reduce injury risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Define muscle imbalance and its consequences: "Muscle imbalance is a difference in strength or flexibility between opposing muscle groups or sides of the body; it alters movement mechanics, increases overuse injury risk, and is corrected through balanced training, stretching and targeted strengthening." Give a common sporting example. 🔗 Related terms Strength Flexibility Overtraining Strain Proprioception Resistance Training 🎓 Where this appears BTEC Sport

It is closely related to what clinicians call a trigger point . They often develop in the neck, shoulders and upper back, and after repeated or heavy use of a muscle. Self-care includes stretching, heat, massage and foam rolling. Persistent or severe pain should be checked by a physiotherapist or doctor. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimmer A knot in the shoulder after hard training sessions. Office worker

Neck and shoulder knots from long periods at a desk. Weightlifter A tight spot in the lower back after heavy deadlifts. ✍️ Using the term in context Use the technical term where needed: "Commonly called muscle knots, these tender, contracted areas are known as myofascial trigger points." Muscle Spindle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Muscle Spindle IB Sport Science General Muscle Spindle The body's stretch detector — a receptor that senses muscle length and triggers the reflex that protects against overstretching. 📖 What it means The muscle spindle is a proprioceptor located within the muscle belly that detects changes in muscle length and the rate of that change — essentially, how far and how fast a muscle is being stretched.

When a muscle is stretched rapidly, the muscle spindles trigger the stretch reflex (myotatic reflex), causing the muscle to contract to resist the stretch. This is a protective mechanism that guards against overstretching and injury. The muscle spindle is important in flexibility work: ballistic and fast stretching can trigger the stretch reflex , causing the muscle to contract against the stretch, whereas slow, controlled stretching avoids provoking it, allowing a greater range of movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Stretch reflex If a muscle is stretched suddenly, the muscle spindles trigger a reflex contraction to protect it — the basis of the knee-jerk reflex. Ballistic stretching risk

Bouncing (ballistic) stretches can activate the stretch reflex, causing the muscle to contract against the stretch and increasing injury risk. Contrast with GTO The muscle spindle detects stretch (length), while the Golgi tendon organ detects tension — a common comparison in exam questions. ✍️ Using the term in context Name what it detects and the reflex it triggers: "The muscle spindle is a proprioceptor that detects changes in muscle length; rapid stretch triggers the stretch reflex, a protective contraction, which is why slow controlled stretching is safer than ballistic stretching for developing flexibility." Contrast it with the Golgi tendon organ (which detects tension).

Muscular Endurance — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Muscular Endurance General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Muscular Endurance The staying power of a muscle — the ability to keep contracting repeatedly or hold a contraction without tiring. 📖 What it means Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to sustain repeated contractions, or to hold a contraction, over a period of time without fatiguing . It is a health-related component of fitness. It differs from muscular strength (the maximum force a muscle can exert in a single effort) — muscular endurance concerns repeated or sustained submaximal effort rather than one maximal contraction.

It is developed through training with lighter loads and high repetitions , or activities involving repeated contractions, and is assessed with tests such as timed press-up or sit-up tests. It is important in almost every sport for maintaining performance and technique over time. 🏅 Sporting examples Rowing A rower needs high muscular endurance to keep powering strokes throughout a race without the muscles fatiguing. Team sports A footballer relies on muscular endurance in the legs to keep sprinting and changing direction late in a match. Testing Muscular endurance is commonly assessed with a timed press-up test or the abdominal curl test. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define it and distinguish from muscular strength: "Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle to sustain repeated or prolonged contractions without fatiguing, unlike muscular strength, which is the maximum force in a single effort; it is developed with lighter loads and high repetitions." Muscular Strength — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Muscular Strength General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Muscular Strength The raw force a muscle can produce — the maximum a muscle group can exert in a single, all-out effort. 📖 What it means Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert in a single contraction . It is a health-related component of fitness and underpins power and many sporting actions.

It differs from muscular endurance (repeated submaximal contractions) — strength is about maximal force on one occasion . It is often measured by the one-repetition maximum (1RM) , the heaviest load that can be lifted once with correct technique, or with dynamometers. Muscular strength is developed through resistance training with heavy loads and low repetitions , which drives adaptations including hypertrophy and improved motor unit recruitment. It is essential in strength and power sports and important for injury prevention. 🏅 Sporting examples Weightlifting A weightlifter's performance depends directly on muscular strength — the maximum force they can exert to lift a heavy barbell once.

Rugby A prop forward needs high muscular strength for scrummaging and holding their ground in contact. Measurement Muscular strength is commonly assessed with a 1RM test or a grip dynamometer. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it, distinguish from endurance, and note how it's trained and measured: "Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle group can exert in a single contraction, unlike muscular endurance; it is developed with heavy loads and low repetitions and commonly measured by the one-repetition maximum (1RM)." Link strength to hypertrophy and improved motor unit recruitment. 🔗 Related terms

Myocardium — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Myocardium IB Sport Science General Myocardium The heart muscle itself — the specialised cardiac tissue that contracts relentlessly to pump blood. 📖 What it means The myocardium is the muscular wall of the heart responsible for contracting to pump blood. It is made of specialised cardiac muscle — distinct from skeletal and smooth muscle — that can contract powerfully and repeatedly without fatiguing. The myocardium of the left ventricle is the thickest , because it must generate the highest pressure to pump blood around the entire body. The right ventricle's wall is thinner, as it only pumps blood to the lungs.

Endurance training thickens the myocardium (cardiac hypertrophy), particularly the left ventricle, increasing its strength and stroke volume. This is one of the key chronic cardiovascular adaptations to training. 🏅 Sporting examples Cardiac muscle The myocardium contracts with every heartbeat without voluntary control — cardiac muscle never fully fatigues. Left ventricle wall The left ventricle's thick myocardium generates the force needed to push blood around the body. Training adaptation Endurance training causes the myocardium to thicken (cardiac hypertrophy), increasing stroke volume. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the myocardium and its training adaptation:

Myofibril — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Myofibril IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Myofibril The contractile threads inside a muscle fibre. 📖 What it means A myofibril is a long cylindrical bundle of protein filaments inside a muscle fibre. Each fibre contains hundreds to thousands of myofibrils running along its length. A myofibril is made of a chain of sarcomeres , the basic contractile units, each containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments, which give skeletal muscle its striped appearance. Hypertrophy from resistance training mainly involves adding more myofibrils and contractile proteins within each fibre. 🏅 Sporting examples

Strength training Fibres grow by adding myofibrils. Microscopy Stripes are visible because of the pattern of sarcomeres. Contraction Sarcomeres in each myofibril shorten together. ✍️ Using the term in context Place it in the hierarchy: "A muscle fibre contains many myofibrils, each made of sarcomeres containing actin and myosin filaments." Myoglobin — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Myoglobin IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Myoglobin Muscle's own oxygen store — a protein that holds oxygen inside the cell, ready for aerobic work. 📖 What it means Myoglobin is an oxygen-binding protein in muscle cells that stores oxygen and releases it to the mitochondria as needed for aerobic ATP production. It is the muscle's own oxygen reserve. Like haemoglobin in the blood, myoglobin binds oxygen and gives red muscle its characteristic colour. It has a very high affinity for oxygen — it holds onto it even when blood oxygen falls, releasing it only to the mitochondria when needed.

Muscles with high aerobic demand — particularly slow-twitch fibres — are rich in myoglobin, reflecting their reliance on aerobic energy production. Endurance training can increase myoglobin content, improving oxygen availability within the muscle. 🏅 Sporting examples Muscle oxygen store During exercise, myoglobin releases its stored oxygen to the mitochondria for aerobic energy production. Red muscle colour The high myoglobin content of slow-twitch fibres gives them their red colour. Training effect Endurance training can increase myoglobin content in muscle, improving aerobic capacity. ✍️ Using the term in context Define myoglobin and contrast with haemoglobin:

Myosin — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Myosin IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Myosin The thick protein that pulls the filaments in muscle contraction. 📖 What it means Myosin is the protein that forms the thick filaments of a sarcomere. Each myosin molecule has a tail and a head that can bind to actin to form a cross-bridge . The head contains ATPase , an enzyme that splits ATP. The energy released lets the head pivot (the power stroke), pulling the thin actin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere. ATP is also needed to release the head so it can reattach.

Repeated cycles of attach, pull, release and reattach shorten the sarcomere and so the muscle. Without ATP, myosin stays attached, as in rigor mortis . 🏅 Sporting examples Contraction Myosin heads pull actin in a ratchet action. Fibre types Fast fibres have a faster form of myosin ATPase. Training Resistance training increases the amount of contractile protein. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the cycle: "Myosin heads bind to actin, pivot to pull the filament using energy from ATP, and then detach to repeat the cycle." Mention the role of ATP in both pulling and release. 🔗 Related terms Actin Sliding Filament Theory Sarcomere Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) Muscle Fibre Myofibril

Negative Feedback — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Negative Feedback IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Negative Feedback The body's self-correcting loop — detecting a change and triggering a response that reverses it. 📖 What it means Negative feedback is a homeostatic mechanism where the body responds to a change from the set point by triggering a response that opposes and reverses the change , returning the variable toward normal.

The three components are a receptor (detects the change), a control centre (processes the signal), and an effector (produces the corrective response). Once the variable returns to normal, the stimulus is removed and the response switches off. It underpins the regulation of many physiological variables during exercise — body temperature, blood glucose and blood pressure are all maintained by negative feedback. It is 'negative' because the response negates the original change. 🏅 Sporting examples Thermoregulation When core temperature rises, negative feedback triggers sweating and vasodilation, reducing it back toward normal. Blood glucose

When blood glucose falls, glucagon is released and raises it — negative feedback restoring the set point. Self-limiting The response switches off as the variable returns to normal, preventing overcorrection. ✍️ Using the term in context Define negative feedback and name its components: "Negative feedback is a homeostatic mechanism where a receptor detects a change, a control centre triggers a corrective response by the effector, reversing the change back toward the set point; it is self-limiting because the response switches off as normal conditions return." Apply it to thermoregulation and blood glucose as examples. 🔗 Related terms

Negative Transfer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Negative Transfer AS Level / Cambridge General Negative Transfer When learning one skill gets in the way of another — the unhelpful side of transfer that coaches work to minimise. 📖 What it means Negative transfer is when the learning or performance of one skill hinders the learning or performance of another . It is the opposite of positive transfer. It tends to occur when two skills are similar in some respects but require different responses , so a habit learned in one interferes with the other. It is often temporary and can usually be overcome with practice and clear coaching.

Coaches aim to minimise negative transfer by making learners aware of the differences between skills, and by structuring practice carefully — for instance, avoiding teaching two conflicting skills at the same time. 🏅 Sporting examples Racket sports A tennis player learning squash may experience negative transfer, as the tennis habit of a firm wrist interferes with the wristy squash action. Similar but different A skill that looks similar but needs a different timing or response can produce negative transfer until the new pattern is learned. Minimising it A coach highlights the key differences between the two skills and avoids teaching them together to reduce interference.

✍️ Using the term in context Define it against positive transfer and note when it occurs: "Negative transfer is when the learning of one skill hinders another, often occurring when skills are similar but require different responses; coaches minimise it by highlighting the differences and structuring practice carefully." Net Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Net Force IB Sport Science General Net Force The single resultant of all forces — what's left when you add every push and pull acting on a body. 📖 What it means The net force is the overall force resulting from the combination of all forces acting on a body . It is the vector sum of all individual forces.

When forces act in the same direction they add together ; when they act in opposite directions they partially or fully cancel . A net force of zero means the body is in equilibrium (not accelerating); a non-zero net force produces acceleration in the direction of the net force, as described by Newton's second law (F = ma). In sport, analysing the net force on an athlete reveals the cause of acceleration or deceleration — for example, the net force on a sprinter from the ground reaction force, gravity and drag determines how fast they accelerate. 🏅 Sporting examples Equilibrium An athlete holding a static position has a net force of zero — all forces balance. Acceleration

A non-zero net force produces acceleration: a sprinter with a large forward net force accelerates. Combining forces The net force on a swimmer is found by adding thrust forward and drag backward as vectors. ✍️ Using the term in context Define net force and link it to Newton's second law: "Net force is the vector sum of all forces acting on a body; a net force of zero produces equilibrium, while a non-zero net force produces acceleration in that direction (Newton's second law, F = ma)." Neuromuscular Junction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Neuromuscular Junction IB Sport Science General Neuromuscular Junction The bridge between nerve and muscle — where the electrical signal becomes a chemical one to trigger contraction. 📖 What it means The neuromuscular junction is the synapse where a motor neurone meets a muscle fibre and transmits the signal to contract . It is the interface between the nervous system and the muscular system.

When a nerve impulse arrives, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine is released and crosses the tiny gap (synapse) to receptor sites on the muscle fibre. This triggers an electrical change in the muscle fibre that leads to calcium release and muscle contraction (the sliding filament mechanism). The neuromuscular junction is fundamental to all voluntary movement: every muscle contraction — from a whisper-light touch to a maximal lift — passes through this junction. Understanding it completes the pathway from nervous system signal to physical action. 🏅 Sporting examples Trigger point

At the neuromuscular junction, a motor neurone releases acetylcholine, which triggers contraction of the muscle fibre. Acetylcholine The neurotransmitter acetylcholine crosses the synapse and binds to the muscle fibre membrane. Full pathway The neuromuscular junction is the final link: brain → motor neurone → neuromuscular junction → muscle contraction. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the neuromuscular junction and its role: "The neuromuscular junction is the synapse between a motor neurone and a muscle fibre; the neurotransmitter acetylcholine is released and triggers calcium release and contraction, completing the pathway from nervous system to muscle."

Newton's Laws of Motion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Newton's Laws of Motion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Newton's Laws of Motion The three laws that govern all movement — the bedrock of biomechanics, explaining how and why bodies move as they do. 📖 What it means Newton's laws of motion are three fundamental principles describing the relationship between forces and motion. They underpin the whole of biomechanics.

Newton's first law (inertia) states that a body remains at rest or moving at constant velocity unless acted on by an external force. Newton's second law (acceleration) states that the acceleration of a body is proportional to the force applied and inversely proportional to its mass (F = ma). Newton's third law (action–reaction) states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Together the laws explain why athletes must apply force to start, stop or change motion, why greater force produces greater acceleration, and why pushing against the ground propels the body — making them essential for analysing almost any sporting movement. 🏅 Sporting examples First law (inertia)

A stationary rugby ball stays still until a player applies a force to it; a rolling ball keeps moving until friction or another force stops it. Second law (F = ma) A sprinter who applies greater force against the ground accelerates more quickly, in line with F = ma. Third law (action–reaction) When a swimmer pushes water backward, the water pushes them forward with an equal and opposite force. ✍️ Using the term in context Name and apply all three laws: "By Newton's third law, when a sprinter drives force into the blocks, the ground exerts an equal and opposite force that propels them forward; by the second law, the greater that force relative to their mass, the greater their acceleration."

Nitrate (Beetroot Juice) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Nitrate (Beetroot Juice) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Nitrate (Beetroot Juice) Beetroot juice and its effect on exercise efficiency. 📖 What it means Dietary nitrate is found in beetroot, spinach, rocket and lettuce . The body converts it to nitric oxide , which widens blood vessels and can lower the oxygen cost of exercise. Research suggests a small benefit for endurance performance of a few minutes' duration, especially in recreational athletes, with less clear effects in elite athletes.

It is usually taken as concentrated beetroot juice 2 to 3 hours before exercise . Side effects include red urine and stools and occasional stomach upset. 🏅 Sporting examples Time trial A cyclist drinks beetroot juice before a 10-mile time trial. Normative Data — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Normative Data General BTEC Sport Normative Data The reference chart for fitness testing — population averages that let you rate and compare results. 📖 What it means Normative data are reference values from a large sample population used to compare and rate an individual's test results . They allow a performer's score to be placed in context — categorised as excellent, above average, average, below average or poor.

Normative data are collected from large, representative samples and are usually broken down by age and sex , since these strongly influence fitness test results. Using age- and sex-appropriate norms gives a fair comparison. The value of normative data is in interpretation : a score without reference data is just a number, but compared against norms it becomes meaningful. They also allow tracking of whether a performer is improving relative to their peers. 🏅 Sporting examples Rating a result A 20-metre sprint time is compared against normative tables to rate a player as 'excellent', 'average' or 'poor'. Age and sex

Normative data are separated by age group and sex to ensure a fair, relevant comparison. Nutrition — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Nutrition IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Nutrition The science of eating for performance and health — the fuel, raw materials and regulators in every meal. 📖 What it means Nutrition is the process of consuming and utilising food and drink to support health, performance and recovery . It encompasses the intake and use of macronutrients, micronutrients, water and other dietary components.

For athletes, nutrition serves multiple roles: fuelling exercise (primarily carbohydrates and fats), supporting recovery and adaptation (protein and micronutrients), maintaining hydration (water and electrolytes) and sustaining long-term health . Sports nutrition tailors dietary choices to the demands of training and competition — timing, quantity and composition of food and drink all influence performance and adaptation. It works alongside training as the foundation of athletic development. 🏅 Sporting examples Fuelling A runner's carbohydrate-rich diet ensures glycogen stores are full before training and competition. Obesity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Obesity IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Obesity Excessive body fat accumulation — a health condition that increases disease risk and that physical activity helps prevent. 📖 What it means Obesity is a condition of excessive body fat , conventionally defined as a BMI above 30 . It is associated with significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, some cancers and other conditions.

It typically results from a sustained positive energy balance — energy intake consistently exceeding expenditure — often combined with low physical activity levels. Genetic, environmental and behavioural factors all contribute. Regular physical activity is one of the most effective tools for preventing and managing obesity, alongside dietary change. It increases energy expenditure and can improve metabolic health even before large changes in body weight occur. 🏅 Sporting examples Health risk Obesity significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and musculoskeletal problems. Energy balance

Sustained excess energy intake over expenditure gradually leads to greater fat accumulation. Activity benefit Regular physical activity helps prevent obesity by increasing energy expenditure and improving metabolic health. ✍️ Using the term in context Define obesity and its health link, with activity's role: "Obesity is a condition of excessive body fat (BMI > 30) associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes; regular physical activity is one of the most effective strategies for prevention and management." Observational Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Observational Learning IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Observational Learning Learning by watching others. 📖 What it means Observational learning is learning by watching a model and imitating their behaviour. Albert Bandura described four conditions, often remembered as ARMM : attention to the demonstration, retention of it in memory, motor reproduction (being able to perform it) and motivation to do so. A model is more effective if they are skilled, similar to the learner, of high status, and consistent . Demonstrations should be accurate and highlight key points.

It is the basis of visual guidance : coaches demonstrate skills and use video and peer models. 🏅 Sporting examples Coaching A coach demonstrates a golf swing while the learner watches. Olympic Lift — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Olympic Lift General BTEC Sport Olympic Lift The clean, jerk and snatch — technically demanding, full-body explosive lifts at the heart of power training. 📖 What it means Olympic lifts are a category of explosive, technical resistance exercises — primarily the clean and jerk and the snatch — that develop whole-body power, coordination and rate of force development. Olympic lifts are widely used in strength and conditioning for power sports (such as sprinting, throwing and team sports). Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation (OBLA) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation (OBLA) IB Sport Science General Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation (OBLA) A precise marker on the lactate curve — the intensity at which blood lactate reaches a defined concentration, used to guide training. 📖 What it means OBLA (onset of blood lactate accumulation) is the exercise intensity at which blood lactate concentration reaches a specific level , conventionally taken as 4 millimoles per litre (4 mmol/L) . It provides a standardised marker for comparing performers and setting training.

It is closely related to the lactate threshold : both mark the point at which lactate begins to accumulate as production outstrips clearance. OBLA fixes a specific concentration (4 mmol/L) as the reference, giving a repeatable, objective marker. A performer who reaches OBLA at a higher percentage of their VO₂ max can sustain a faster aerobic pace, making OBLA a useful indicator of endurance fitness and a target for threshold training. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance testing In a step test, a coach records the intensity at which blood lactate reaches 4 mmol/L — OBLA — and uses it to set training zones. Comparing athletes

Two runners can be compared by the pace at which each reaches OBLA; the one who reaches it at a higher pace has better endurance fitness. Training target Threshold training aims to push OBLA to a higher intensity, allowing a faster sustainable pace before lactate accumulates. ✍️ Using the term in context Define OBLA at 4 mmol/L and relate it to the lactate threshold: "OBLA is the intensity at which blood lactate reaches 4 mmol/L, a standardised marker closely related to the lactate threshold; reaching OBLA at a higher percentage of VO₂ max indicates better endurance fitness." Open and Closed Continuum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Open and Closed Continuum AS Level / Cambridge General Open and Closed Continuum From fixed to unpredictable — classifying skills by how much the environment influences them. 📖 What it means The open–closed continuum is a way of classifying skills by how much the environment affects their performance . At one extreme are closed skills , performed in a stable, predictable environment; at the other are open skills , performed in a changing, unpredictable environment.

A closed skill (such as a free throw or a gymnastic vault) is performed the same way each time in a controlled setting. An open skill (such as a tackle or a rally shot) must be constantly adapted to the changing situation — opponents, teammates, surface and ball flight all vary. The classification guides how a skill should be practised : closed skills suit fixed, repetitive practice; open skills suit variable practice that builds adaptability. Most real skills sit somewhere along the continuum rather than at the extremes. 🏅 Sporting examples Closed skill A gymnast's vault is a closed skill — the environment is stable and the movement is the same each time. Open skill

A footballer's tackle is an open skill — constantly adapted to the opponent's movement. Practice choice Open skills benefit from variable practice; closed skills from fixed, repetitive practice. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the continuum and explain how it guides practice: "The open–closed continuum classifies skills by environmental predictability: closed skills are performed in stable, predictable settings and suit fixed practice, while open skills must adapt to changing conditions and suit variable practice." Open Loop Control — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Open Loop Control AS Level / Cambridge General Open Loop Control Movement that runs on a pre-set programme — the control theory that explains fast, ballistic skills executed too quickly for feedback. 📖 What it means Open loop control is a model of motor control in which a movement is executed from a pre-programmed set of instructions (a motor programme) without relying on feedback during the action . The whole movement is sent as one command.

Because it does not wait for feedback, open loop control is fast , making it well suited to rapid, ballistic skills that are completed too quickly to be adjusted mid-movement — such as a golf drive or a kick. Its limitation is that errors cannot be corrected once the movement has started . It contrasts with closed loop control , which uses feedback during slower movements to detect and correct errors as they occur. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf drive A full golf swing is largely open loop — executed as a pre-programmed action too fast to adjust once it has begun. Kicking A powerful kick is run as a motor programme; the movement is completed before feedback could be used to change it. Contrast

A slow, controlled putt uses closed loop control, with feedback guiding the movement, unlike the ballistic drive. ✍️ Using the term in context Define open loop control and contrast it with closed loop: "Open loop control executes a movement from a pre-programmed motor programme without using feedback during the action, suiting fast, ballistic skills; unlike closed loop control, errors cannot be corrected once the movement has begun." Match open loop to fast/ballistic skills and closed loop to slow, feedback-guided ones. 🔗 Related terms Adams' Closed Loop Theory Closed Loop Control Motor Learning Schema Theory Reaction Time Feedback 🎓 Where this appears AS Level / Cambridge

Open Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Open Skill AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Open Skill A skill performed in an unpredictable, changing environment where the performer must adapt continually. 📖 What it means An open skill is one performed in an unpredictable, constantly changing environment . The performer cannot simply repeat a pre-planned movement — they must read the situation and adapt their action to what is happening around them, often responding to opponents, teammates or the ball.

Open skills are externally paced : the timing of the action is controlled by factors outside the performer's control. Because the environment is always shifting, open skills involve high levels of perception and decision-making , relying on selecting the right response at the right moment. Open skills sit at one end of the open–closed continuum . At the opposite end, closed skills are performed in a stable, predictable environment. Most real sporting skills fall somewhere along this continuum rather than at the extremes, and open skills are best developed through variable practice. 🏅 Sporting examples Rugby

A tackle in open play is a classic open skill — the tackler continually adjusts their body position, timing and angle as the ball carrier changes speed and direction. Football Dribbling past a defender is open because the defender's movements are unpredictable, unlike a stationary set-piece. Netball Intercepting a pass requires reading the passer, tracking the ball and timing a movement to a situation that is different every time. ✍️ Using the term in context Justify the classification using environment and pacing:

Using the stimulus-response-reinforcement (S-R) bond, a correct response that is reinforced (praised or rewarded) becomes more likely to be repeated. Optimum Arousal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Optimum Arousal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Optimum Arousal The performance sweet spot — the exact level of activation where an athlete performs at their peak. 📖 What it means Optimum arousal is the level of physiological and psychological activation at which an individual performs best for a given task. It is the peak of the inverted-U curve. The optimal level is not the same for everyone or every task . It is higher for simple, gross, strength-based skills and lower for complex, fine, precision skills . Individual differences also mean some performers thrive at higher arousal than others.

Finding and reaching optimum arousal is a key aim of pre-performance psychology : performers use arousal-management techniques (such as centering, self-talk or imagery) to reach and maintain their individual optimum, whether that means calming down or psyching up. 🏅 Sporting examples Task-specific A shot putter's optimum arousal is higher than an archer's — gross power versus fine precision. Individual Two teammates may need different pre-match routines to reach their own optimal arousal level. Management A performer who over-arouses uses centering and breathing to reduce arousal toward their optimum. ✍️ Using the term in context

Origin (muscle) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Origin (muscle) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Origin (muscle) Where the muscle is anchored — the fixed proximal end that stays put while the insertion moves. 📖 What it means The origin of a muscle is its proximal attachment — the end attached to the bone that remains relatively fixed when the muscle contracts. It is the muscle's anchor point. When a muscle contracts, it shortens, pulling the insertion toward the origin. The bone at the insertion moves; the bone at the origin stays relatively still (stabilised by fixator muscles).

Correctly identifying origin and insertion helps explain which bone moves, in which direction . For example, the biceps brachii has its origin on the shoulder (scapula) and its insertion on the radius; when it contracts, it pulls the radius (and forearm) toward the shoulder, flexing the elbow. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps The biceps origin is on the scapula — it stays fixed as the muscle contracts and flexes the elbow. Fixed point The origin is the anchor; the insertion is what moves when the muscle shortens. Movement analysis Identifying origin and insertion is the starting point for explaining a muscle's action. ✍️ Using the term in context Define origin and contrast with insertion:

"The origin is the proximal attachment of a muscle — the end fixed to the bone that stays relatively still during contraction; the muscle shortens, pulling the insertion toward the origin and producing movement at the joint." Orthostatic Heart Rate Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Orthostatic Heart Rate Test IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Orthostatic Heart Rate Test A fitness test of recovery and autonomic fatigue. 📖 What it means The Orthostatic Heart Rate Test is a recovery monitoring test in which heart rate is measured lying down and again after standing up, to check for fatigue or overtraining. Protocol: The athlete rests lying for several minutes and records heart rate, then stands and records it again after a set time (for example 15 seconds to 2 minutes).

Interpreting results: A rise in heart rate that is much larger than the athlete's usual response can indicate incomplete recovery. Trends over several days are more useful than a single reading. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A rower's standing heart rate is much higher than normal after a hard week. Training use Used to guide rest days. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Describe the test and what it measures: "The Orthostatic Heart Rate Test assesses recovery and autonomic fatigue; the result is compared with normative data or earlier scores to judge fitness or progress." Osmosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Osmosis IB Sport Science General Osmosis Water following concentration — the movement of water across membranes that underpins fluid balance. 📖 What it means Osmosis is the movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to a region of higher solute concentration . Water moves to dilute the more concentrated solution. It is the mechanism underlying fluid balance in cells and across body compartments . When fluid concentrations are unequal — as happens with dehydration or after drinking different types of sports drinks — osmosis drives water movement to restore balance.

In sports nutrition, osmosis explains why the concentration of a sports drink (isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic) affects how quickly it is absorbed and how it influences fluid balance. It also explains why excessive fluid or salt intake can disrupt cellular function. 🏅 Sporting examples Sports drinks A hypertonic drink draws water into the gut before absorption, slowing rehydration — osmosis in action. Dehydration As plasma becomes more concentrated during dehydration, water moves out of cells by osmosis. Fluid balance Osmosis helps equalise fluid concentrations across the body's compartments. ✍️ Using the term in context Define osmosis and link it to hydration:

"Osmosis is the movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration; it underlies fluid balance and explains how sports drink concentration affects absorption rate and hydration." Ossification — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ossification IB Sport Science General Ossification Cartilage turning to bone — the developmental process that builds and closes the skeleton. 📖 What it means Ossification is the process by which cartilage is replaced by bone during growth and development. It is the means by which the skeleton forms and matures. In growing children and adolescents, ossification occurs at the epiphyseal plates (growth plates) of long bones, lengthening them. It also occurs during bone repair, when fractures are healed.

Ossification is relevant to sport in two ways: because growing bone is less dense and more vulnerable than mature bone, young athletes are at greater risk of growth-plate injuries, and training loads should be managed accordingly. Additionally, once the growth plates ossify and close, lengthwise growth ends. 🏅 Sporting examples Bone growth During adolescence, ossification at the epiphyseal plates lengthens the long bones. Closure When growth is complete, the epiphyseal plates ossify and close, ending lengthwise growth. Young athletes Because growing bone is still ossifying, growth-plate injuries are a risk in young athletes. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define ossification and its sporting relevance: "Ossification is the replacement of cartilage by bone during growth, occurring at the epiphyseal plates; because bone is still ossifying in young athletes, growth plates are at risk of injury and training loads should be carefully managed." Osteoblasts and Osteoclasts — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Osteoblasts and Osteoclasts IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Osteoblasts and Osteoclasts The cells that build and break down bone. 📖 What it means Osteoblasts are the cells that form new bone by laying down collagen and minerals. Osteoclasts are large cells that break down and remove old bone , releasing calcium. Together they control bone remodelling . Mechanical loading from exercise stimulates osteoblasts to lay down more bone, increasing density and strength.

If osteoclast activity outweighs osteoblast activity, as in osteoporosis or low energy availability, bone density falls and fracture risk rises. 🏅 Sporting examples Impact sports Running and jumping stimulate osteoblasts. Fracture repair Osteoclasts and osteoblasts remodel the healing site. Ageing Bone loss exceeds bone formation. ✍️ Using the term in context Contrast the two: "Osteoblasts build bone and osteoclasts remove it; weight-bearing exercise shifts the balance towards bone formation." Osteoporosis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Osteoporosis IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Osteoporosis Bones becoming thin and brittle — a condition of low density that makes fractures far more likely. 📖 What it means Osteoporosis is a condition of low bone density and strength that significantly increases the risk of fractures, particularly of the spine, hip and wrist. Bones become porous and fragile. It typically develops with age, after menopause in women, and due to inactivity . Reduced oestrogen levels accelerate bone loss after menopause, making osteoporosis more common in older women.

Weight-bearing and resistance exercise throughout life is one of the most effective strategies for reducing osteoporosis risk, by stimulating bone formation and maintaining density. It is one of the key long-term health benefits of an active lifestyle. 🏅 Sporting examples Fracture risk Osteoporosis makes bones brittle, so a minor fall can cause a hip fracture that would not harm healthy bone. Menopause Reduced oestrogen after menopause accelerates bone loss, increasing osteoporosis risk in older women. Prevention Weight-bearing exercise such as running and resistance training builds bone density, reducing osteoporosis risk. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define osteoporosis and the role of exercise: "Osteoporosis is a condition of low bone density that greatly increases fracture risk; weight-bearing and resistance exercise throughout life helps prevent it by stimulating bone formation — a key long-term health benefit of activity." Outcome Goal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Outcome Goal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Outcome Goal A goal focused on the end result — winning or beating others — motivating but largely outside the athlete's control. 📖 What it means An outcome goal is a goal focused on the end result of a competition, usually in comparison with others — such as winning a match, finishing first, or beating a specific opponent.

Outcome goals can be motivating , but they have a key drawback: they depend heavily on factors outside the performer's control , especially the opposition. An athlete can perform brilliantly and still not achieve an outcome goal if the opponent is better. For this reason, outcome goals are usually best used alongside performance and process goals , which focus on the athlete's own standards and actions and remain within their control — protecting motivation and confidence regardless of the result. 🏅 Sporting examples Winning 'Win the league' is an outcome goal — motivating, but dependent on how every other team performs, not just the athlete. Beating an opponent

Aiming to beat a specific rival is an outcome goal that can raise anxiety because the result is not fully controllable. Balanced use A coach pairs an outcome goal with process and performance goals so the athlete stays focused on what they can control. ✍️ Using the term in context Define outcome goals and note the control limitation: "An outcome goal focuses on the end result, such as winning; it can motivate but depends on factors outside the performer's control, so it is best combined with performance and process goals that remain within the athlete's control." Contrast it with performance and process goals. 🔗 Related terms

Overload — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Overload General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Overload The core principle that makes training work — the body only adapts when asked to do more than it is used to. 📖 What it means Overload is the principle that, to improve fitness, the body must be made to work harder than it is normally accustomed to . Training at or below the usual level maintains fitness but does not improve it; exceeding it forces adaptation.

Overload is applied by manipulating the FITT variables — increasing Frequency, Intensity or Time , or adjusting Type . The extra stress disrupts the body's balance, and during recovery it adapts to cope better next time (supercompensation). Overload must be applied progressively : it works hand in hand with the principle of progression, gradually increasing the load as the body adapts. Too much overload too quickly risks injury and overtraining; too little produces no improvement. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength training A lifter overloads their muscles by lifting heavier than they are used to; the muscles then adapt during recovery, becoming stronger. Endurance

A runner overloads their aerobic system by gradually increasing distance or pace beyond their current comfortable level. Applying FITT Overload is applied by increasing frequency, intensity or time — for example, adding an extra session or lifting more weight. ✍️ Using the term in context Define overload and link it to FITT and progression: "Overload is the principle that the body must work harder than it is accustomed to in order to improve; it is applied by increasing the FITT variables and must be progressive, working alongside the principle of progression." Note that too much overload too soon risks injury and overtraining. 🔗 Related terms

Overreaching — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Overreaching IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Overreaching Pushing training load hard for a short period. 📖 What it means Overreaching is a short-term increase in training load that causes a temporary fall in performance. With adequate recovery , performance then rises above its previous level; this is functional overreaching , linked to supercompensation. If recovery is not enough, it becomes non-functional overreaching (fatigue lasts weeks) and, if it continues, overtraining syndrome , which can last months and affect health and mood.

Coaches use overreaching in training camps and follow it with a taper or recovery week . Monitoring sleep, mood and heart rate helps to avoid going too far. 🏅 Sporting examples Training camp Two weeks of heavy training followed by a rest week. Warning signs Persistent tiredness and poor mood. Monitoring A coach tracks recovery scores daily. ✍️ Using the term in context Place it on the continuum: "Functional overreaching is a planned load increase followed by recovery and improvement, whereas overtraining syndrome follows when recovery is inadequate." Name signs to monitor. 🔗 Related terms Overtraining Supercompensation Recovery Total Quality Recovery (TQR) Periodisation Tapering

Overtraining — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Overtraining IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Overtraining Too much training and too little recovery — the state where performance falls instead of rising, and health suffers. 📖 What it means Overtraining is a state of chronic fatigue and declining performance caused by training too hard or too often without adequate recovery . It occurs when the training load consistently exceeds the body's ability to recover and adapt.

Symptoms can include persistent fatigue, a decline in performance, elevated resting heart rate, disturbed sleep, frequent illness or injury, and loss of motivation . Overtraining reflects a breakdown of the balance between stress and recovery that normally drives adaptation. It highlights the importance of recovery, rest and periodisation in a training programme. The principle is that adaptation happens during recovery (supercompensation), so without enough recovery, progress reverses rather than continues. 🏅 Sporting examples Declining performance An athlete who keeps increasing training without rest may find their performance falling rather than improving — a hallmark of overtraining.

Warning signs A rising resting heart rate, poor sleep and frequent minor illnesses can be early warning signs of overtraining. Prevention Building recovery days and periodisation into a programme prevents overtraining by allowing adaptation to occur. ✍️ Using the term in context Define overtraining and link it to recovery and adaptation: "Overtraining is chronic fatigue and declining performance caused by insufficient recovery relative to training load; because adaptation occurs during recovery, adequate rest and periodisation are essential to prevent it." List recognisable symptoms (fatigue, raised resting HR, poor sleep, illness). 🔗 Related terms

Overuse Injury — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Overuse Injury IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Overuse Injury Damage from too much too soon — injuries that build up gradually from repetitive stress without enough recovery. 📖 What it means An overuse injury results from repetitive stress on a tissue over time without adequate recovery . Unlike acute injuries from a single event, overuse injuries develop gradually as cumulative micro-damage exceeds the body's ability to repair.

Common examples include stress fractures (bone), tendinopathy (tendon), shin splints and bursitis. They are particularly common when training load is increased too rapidly , without appropriate recovery or variety. Prevention focuses on gradual progression, adequate recovery, balanced training, good technique and appropriate equipment . The principles of progressive overload and specificity must be applied carefully — too much, too soon is the central cause. 🏅 Sporting examples Stress fracture A runner who rapidly increases mileage may develop a stress fracture — an overuse injury from cumulative loading. Tendinopathy

Repetitive jumping without adequate recovery can lead to patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee). Prevention Gradual load progression, cross-training and adequate rest help prevent overuse injuries. ✍️ Using the term in context Define overuse injury and its prevention: "An overuse injury results from repetitive stress accumulating faster than the body can repair it, developing gradually; prevention involves gradual progression, adequate recovery, balanced training and good technique." Contrast with acute injuries from a single event. 🔗 Related terms Stress Fracture Tendinopathy Principle of Progression Recovery Cross-Training Overtraining 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Oxygen Debt — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Oxygen Debt IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Oxygen Debt The body's post-exercise oxygen 'repayment' — the older term for the extra oxygen consumed to recover after hard effort. 📖 What it means Oxygen debt is the volume of oxygen consumed after exercise, above resting levels, to restore the body to its pre-exercise state . It is the traditional term for what is now more commonly called EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption).

During high-intensity exercise, the anaerobic systems supply energy without oxygen, creating a 'debt' that must be 'repaid' afterwards. The extra oxygen is used to resynthesise ATP and phosphocreatine, remove lactate, replenish myoglobin oxygen stores, and support the raised heart rate, breathing and temperature . The concept has two parts: the fast (alactic) component , restoring PCr and oxygen stores quickly, and the slow (lactacid) component , associated with clearing lactate and the longer-lasting raised metabolism. More intense exercise produces a larger oxygen debt. 🏅 Sporting examples After sprints

Following hard sprints, a runner keeps breathing heavily as they repay the oxygen debt, restoring PCr and clearing the by-products of anaerobic work. Recovery use Active recovery during the repayment of oxygen debt keeps blood flow high, speeding the return toward rest. Intensity effect A maximal effort creates a larger oxygen debt than a moderate one, meaning a longer period of elevated oxygen consumption afterwards. ✍️ Using the term in context Define oxygen debt, equate it with EPOC, and state its uses:

"Oxygen debt, now usually called EPOC, is the excess oxygen consumed after exercise to restore the body; it is used to resynthesise ATP and phosphocreatine, remove lactate and replenish oxygen stores, with a fast and a slow component." Oxygen Deficit — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Oxygen Deficit IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Oxygen Deficit The oxygen shortfall at the start of exercise. 📖 What it means At the start of exercise, oxygen uptake does not rise instantly to the level needed. The oxygen deficit is the difference between the oxygen required and the oxygen consumed during this period, before a steady state is reached. During the deficit, ATP is supplied mainly by anaerobic sources: the ATP-PC system and anaerobic glycolysis. This leads to depletion of phosphocreatine and some lactate production.

A smaller deficit is seen in trained athletes, because their aerobic system responds faster. The deficit is repaid after exercise as EPOC . 🏅 Sporting examples Start of a run Oxygen uptake lags behind the demand for the first minutes. Warm-up A warm-up reduces the deficit by raising oxygen uptake early. Trained athlete A faster rise in VO2 means a smaller deficit. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to EPOC: "The oxygen deficit at the start of exercise is repaid during recovery as excess post-exercise oxygen consumption." Oxyhaemoglobin Dissociation Curve — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Oxyhaemoglobin Dissociation Curve IB Sport Science General Oxyhaemoglobin Dissociation Curve The graph that captures how haemoglobin loads and unloads oxygen — and how exercise shifts the balance toward the muscles. 📖 What it means The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve is a graph showing the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen and the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen . Its characteristic S-shape reflects how readily haemoglobin binds and releases oxygen at different oxygen pressures.

Where oxygen pressure is high (as in the lungs), haemoglobin is almost fully saturated , loading up with oxygen. Where oxygen pressure is low (as in working muscle), haemoglobin releases its oxygen to the tissues. During exercise the curve shifts to the right (the Bohr effect): increased carbon dioxide, acidity and temperature at the muscles reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so more oxygen is released exactly where it is needed most. 🏅 Sporting examples At the lungs The high oxygen pressure in the lungs sits on the flat, upper part of the curve, where haemoglobin is nearly fully saturated as it loads oxygen. At the muscles

In hard-working muscle, low oxygen pressure and the rightward Bohr shift mean haemoglobin releases much more of its oxygen to the tissue. Exercise shift As exercise raises CO₂, acidity and temperature, the curve shifts right, increasing oxygen release to match demand. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the curve and the exercise (Bohr) shift: "The oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve shows haemoglobin's oxygen saturation against oxygen pressure; during exercise it shifts right (the Bohr effect), as raised carbon dioxide, acidity and temperature reduce haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, releasing more to the muscles." Link the shape to loading in the lungs and unloading at the muscles.

Parasympathetic Nervous System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Parasympathetic Nervous System IB Sport Science General Parasympathetic Nervous System The rest-and-digest system — the division of the autonomic nervous system that calms the body and promotes recovery. 📖 What it means The parasympathetic nervous system is the division of the autonomic nervous system that promotes rest, recovery and digestion . It is often called the 'rest-and-digest' system, in contrast to the sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' system.

It lowers heart rate, promotes digestion, reduces blood pressure and generally restores the body to a calm state after stress or exercise. Parasympathetic activity dominates at rest and during recovery. After exercise, the return of parasympathetic dominance drives the fall in heart rate. A trained athlete's heart often shows stronger parasympathetic tone at rest, contributing to bradycardia . Managing the balance between sympathetic (exercise) and parasympathetic (recovery) activity is central to training periodisation. 🏅 Sporting examples After exercise The parasympathetic nervous system drives heart rate back to resting levels after exercise ends. Bradycardia

Strong resting parasympathetic tone in endurance athletes contributes to their low resting heart rate. Rest-and-digest Digestion is active when parasympathetic activity dominates — why eating just before intense exercise can cause discomfort. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the parasympathetic nervous system and contrast with sympathetic: "The parasympathetic nervous system promotes rest, recovery and digestion, contrasting with the sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' system; it lowers heart rate and blood pressure after exercise, and strong resting parasympathetic tone contributes to athletic bradycardia." Part Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Part Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Part Practice Breaking a skill into chunks to learn them separately — a practice method suited to complex or dangerous skills. 📖 What it means Part practice is a method in which a skill is broken down into its component parts, which are practised separately before being combined into the whole skill. It is especially useful for complex skills with distinct parts, or dangerous skills , where practising the whole action at once would overload the learner or pose a risk. It lets the performer master each element before linking them.

Part practice contrasts with whole practice (practising the entire skill at once) and combinations such as whole–part–whole . It suits skills that are 'low in organisation' — whose parts are relatively independent — and is often more useful for beginners. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming A swimmer learns the leg kick, arm action and breathing of a stroke separately before combining them — part practice for a complex skill. Dance routine A complex routine is broken into sections, each practised separately before being linked together. Contrast A simple, highly-organised skill such as a golf swing is better practised as a whole, since its parts are hard to separate. ✍️ Using the term in context
