Passive Stretching — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Passive Stretching General BTEC Sport Passive Stretching Letting something else do the stretch — using an external force to extend range beyond what muscles alone can reach. 📖 What it means Passive stretching is stretching in which an external force — a partner, apparatus or body weight — moves a joint beyond its active range of motion while the performer remains relaxed.

Because the performer's own muscles are not driving the stretch, passive stretching can achieve a greater range of movement than active stretching alone. However, it carries a slightly higher risk of injury if the external force is applied too aggressively. It contrasts with active stretching (the performer's own muscles move the limb) and is a component of techniques such as PNF stretching . Passive stretching is commonly used in cool-down and flexibility development sessions. 🏅 Sporting examples Partner stretch A physiotherapist moving a player's hamstring into a stretch while the player relaxes is passive stretching. Greater range

Passive stretching can reach a greater range than the performer's own muscles can achieve. Cool-down Passive stretches are commonly included in cool-down routines to improve flexibility. ✍️ Using the term in context Define passive stretching and contrast with active: "Passive stretching uses an external force — a partner or apparatus — to move a joint beyond its active range while the performer relaxes; it achieves a greater range than active stretching but carries slightly higher injury risk if applied too forcefully." Peak Flow Experience — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Peak Flow Experience IB Sport Science General Peak Flow Experience Being 'in the zone' — the rare state of effortless, absorbed, optimal performance. 📖 What it means A peak flow experience is a state of exceptional, seemingly effortless performance accompanied by deep focus, a sense of control and complete absorption in the task. It is often called being 'in the zone' or 'in flow'.

Csikszentmihalyi described flow as occurring when perceived challenge and perceived skill are both high and well-matched : the task is demanding enough to require full engagement, but the performer has the skills to meet the demand. It is associated with a loss of self-consciousness and a distorted sense of time. Flow tends to arise spontaneously but can be encouraged by setting challenging-but-achievable goals, maintaining optimal arousal, using pre-performance routines and narrowing attentional focus . It is a sought-after state for peak athletic performance. 🏅 Sporting examples In the zone

A tennis player who seems unbeatable, moving effortlessly and anticipating everything, is in a flow state. Challenge-skill balance Flow arises when challenge and skill are both high and well-matched — neither too easy nor too hard. Encouraging flow Routines, goal setting and attentional focus techniques can create conditions that encourage flow. ✍️ Using the term in context Define peak flow and name its conditions: "Peak flow is a state of effortless, deeply focused, exceptional performance (being 'in the zone'), occurring when perceived challenge and skill are both high and well-matched; it can be encouraged through goal setting, optimal arousal and pre-performance routines."

Peaking — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Peaking IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Peaking Timing form to arrive at its best for the big event. 📖 What it means Peaking is the process of timing training so that peak performance occurs at the most important competition . It is the aim of the final stage of a periodised plan. It usually includes a taper (reducing volume while keeping intensity), race-specific sharpening , good nutrition and sleep and a plan for travel and the competition day. Athletes cannot peak all year, so they plan one to three peaks per season.

If the timing is wrong, the athlete may peak too early or arrive tired. Monitoring and flexibility are key. 🏅 Sporting examples Championships A swimmer tapers over two weeks. Season plan Training builds towards a major event. Double peak A runner plans peaks for the national and international events. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to the plan: "Peaking uses a taper and race-specific preparation at the end of a periodised plan so that form is highest at the main competition." Pectoralis Major — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Pectoralis Major IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Pectoralis Major The large chest muscle behind every pushing and throwing action — a prime mover at the shoulder. 📖 What it means The pectoralis major is a large muscle covering the front of the chest . Its main actions at the shoulder are horizontal adduction (bringing the arm across the body), flexion and medial rotation of the arm. It is heavily recruited in pushing and throwing actions — any movement that drives the arm forward or across the body against resistance. It acts as an agonist in these actions and works with other shoulder muscles.

Because of its size and power, the pectoralis major is central to performance in sports involving pushing, throwing and striking , and is a common focus in movement analysis of the upper body. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing The pectoralis major contributes power to an overarm throw or a shot put by driving the arm forward across the body. Boxing A boxer's straight punch uses the pectoralis major to drive the arm forward powerfully. Weight training A bench press or press-up strongly recruits the pectoralis major to push the arms forward against resistance. ✍️ Using the term in context Name its actions and role in pushing/throwing:

Perception — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Perception IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Perception Making sense of the senses — the process of interpreting sensory information to guide action. 📖 What it means Perception is the process of interpreting sensory information to make decisions about appropriate responses . It is the second stage of information processing (after input), transforming raw sensory data into a meaningful understanding of the environment.

Skilled performers perceive situations more efficiently than novices: they are better at selectively attending to relevant cues, recognising patterns and predicting what will happen next (anticipation). This allows quicker, more accurate decision-making. Perception is influenced by arousal and attention : at optimal arousal, relevant cues are attended to; at very high arousal, attentional narrowing (cue utilisation) can cause relevant cues to be missed. Improving perceptual skills is an important part of developing expertise. 🏅 Sporting examples Pattern recognition An experienced footballer perceives patterns in play quickly, reading the game faster than a novice. Anticipation

A skilled cricketer's perception of the bowler's action helps them anticipate the delivery early. Arousal effect Over-arousal narrows attention so that relevant perceptual cues are missed. ✍️ Using the term in context Define perception in the information processing model: "Perception is the process of interpreting sensory information to understand a situation and guide decisions; skilled performers perceive more efficiently through pattern recognition and anticipation, and arousal affects which cues are attended to." Place it in the input → perception → decision → output model. 🔗 Related terms

Performance Goal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Performance Goal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Performance Goal A goal measured against your own standards, not others' — within the athlete's control, and a powerful motivator. 📖 What it means A performance goal is a goal focused on improving on one's own previous performance or reaching a personal standard , rather than on the outcome against others. An example is beating a personal best time.

Its key advantage over an outcome goal is that it is largely within the athlete's own control — it does not depend on how opponents perform. This makes it a more reliable source of motivation and confidence, especially when facing stronger opposition. Performance goals work well alongside process goals (focused on technique and actions) and outcome goals . Together, they let an athlete pursue results while keeping their focus on the controllable standards and actions that produce them. 🏅 Sporting examples Personal best Aiming to run a personal-best time is a performance goal — measured against the athlete's own standard, regardless of who wins. Facing stronger opponents

Against a superior opponent, a performance goal keeps an athlete motivated and confident even if winning is unlikely. Combined goals A swimmer sets a performance goal (a target time) alongside process goals (technique cues) to focus on what they control. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it and stress that it is within the athlete's control: "A performance goal focuses on improving on one's own previous performance, such as a personal best; because it does not depend on opponents, it is within the athlete's control and a reliable source of motivation and confidence." Contrast it with outcome goals and pair it with process goals. 🔗 Related terms

Performance Profiling — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Performance Profiling General BTEC Sport Performance Profiling Rating yourself against the ideal — an athlete-led tool for identifying strengths and setting development goals. 📖 What it means Performance profiling is a self-assessment technique in which an athlete rates their own qualities against an ideal profile , identifying discrepancies between current and desired levels. It was developed by Butler and Hardy.

The athlete (often with a coach) first identifies the key qualities needed for success in their sport or position, then rates their own level on each. The gap between 'ideal' and 'actual' scores highlights the areas needing most attention. It promotes athlete ownership , self-awareness and motivation, because the athlete is actively involved in identifying their own development needs rather than having them imposed. The profile can guide goal setting and programme design. 🏅 Sporting examples Self-assessment A footballer rates their speed, agility, positioning and composure — the gap between ideal and actual guides training. Athlete involvement

Because athletes define the qualities themselves, performance profiling increases ownership and motivation. Goal setting The discrepancy scores from a profile directly inform SMART goals for the training period. ✍️ Using the term in context Define performance profiling and its benefits: "Performance profiling is a self-assessment technique where an athlete rates their qualities against an ideal profile; the gap between ideal and actual highlights development needs and promotes athlete ownership and motivation." Periodisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Periodisation IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Periodisation Structuring a training year into phases — the long-term planning that peaks an athlete for the right moment. 📖 What it means Periodisation is the organisation of training into structured phases or cycles across a season or year , each with a specific focus, in order to optimise performance and peak at the right time while managing fatigue.

Training is typically divided into cycles: the macrocycle (the long-term plan, often a whole season or year), mesocycles (blocks of several weeks with a particular focus, such as building strength), and microcycles (short units, often a week, of individual sessions). A common structure moves from a general preparation phase (building a base) through a competition phase (sharpening and peaking, often via tapering) to a transition phase (recovery). Periodisation helps apply progressive overload, avoid overtraining, and ensure the athlete peaks for key events. 🏅 Sporting examples Peaking

A sprinter periodises their year so that their fitness peaks precisely for the major championships, via a competition phase and taper. Base building During the preparation phase (a mesocycle), an athlete builds a general fitness base before moving to more specific, higher-intensity work. Avoiding overtraining By structuring hard and easy phases, periodisation manages fatigue and reduces the risk of overtraining. ✍️ Using the term in context Define periodisation and name the cycles and phases:

"Periodisation organises training into phases across a season — macrocycles, mesocycles and microcycles — moving from a preparation phase to a competition phase and a transition phase, to peak performance at the right time and manage fatigue." Periosteum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Periosteum IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Periosteum The tough skin that covers a bone. 📖 What it means The periosteum is a tough double-layered membrane that covers the outer surface of bone, except at the joint surfaces where articular cartilage is found. It has a rich blood and nerve supply (which is why bone injuries hurt), contains osteoblasts for bone growth in width and repair, and provides the attachment point for tendons and ligaments . Damage to it, as in a bruised shin bone, is painful. The periosteum plays an important role in fracture healing. 🏅 Sporting examples Fracture healing

Cells in the periosteum form new bone. Kick to the shin A direct blow to the bone surface is very painful. Personality — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Personality IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Personality The stable patterns that make each athlete distinct — and a long-debated question of how much it shapes sporting behaviour. 📖 What it means Personality is the relatively stable and enduring set of characteristics that makes an individual unique and influences how they think, feel and behave. In sport, psychologists ask how personality relates to participation and performance.

Several approaches attempt to explain it. Trait theories argue personality is made up of stable, inherited traits that are consistent across situations. Social learning theory argues behaviour is largely learned from the environment and others. The interactionist approach combines the two, proposing that behaviour results from the interaction of personality traits and the situation (often summarised as B = f(P, E)). The interactionist view is the most widely accepted today, because it explains why an athlete might behave differently in different situations despite having stable underlying traits — useful for predicting and managing behaviour. 🏅 Sporting examples Trait vs situation

A normally calm player (trait) may behave aggressively in a heated derby (situation) — an interactionist explanation of their behaviour. Predicting behaviour A coach uses the interactionist approach to anticipate how a player's traits might combine with a high-pressure situation. Learned behaviour Social learning theory would explain a young athlete copying the conduct of an admired role model. ✍️ Using the term in context Outline the main approaches, favouring the interactionist view:

"Personality is the stable set of characteristics that makes an individual unique; trait theories, social learning theory and the interactionist approach explain it differently, with the interactionist view — that behaviour results from the interaction of traits and situation — most widely accepted." Use B = f(P, E) to summarise the interactionist position. 🔗 Related terms Bandura's Social Learning Theory Trait Anxiety Aggression Achievement Motivation Self-Confidence Motivation 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy

Phosphocreatine (PCr) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Phosphocreatine (PCr) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Phosphocreatine (PCr) The muscle's instant-energy reserve — the compound that regenerates ATP within seconds for the most explosive efforts. 📖 What it means Phosphocreatine (PCr) , also called creatine phosphate, is a high-energy compound stored in the muscles that rapidly resynthesises ATP by donating its phosphate group to ADP. It is the fuel of the ATP-PC energy system.

The reaction is very fast and requires no oxygen , providing energy almost instantly for maximal efforts — but PCr stores are very limited , supplying only around 8–10 seconds of all-out work before they are depleted. After exercise, PCr stores are rapidly replenished using aerobic energy , largely within a few minutes. This quick recovery is why the system can be reused repeatedly across a session with adequate rest, and why it forms the fast component of EPOC. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A 100m sprinter relies on phosphocreatine to resynthesise ATP for the explosive, maximal effort of the race. Weightlifting

A single maximal lift draws on PCr to regenerate ATP almost instantly for the brief, powerful contraction. Repeated efforts Because PCr replenishes quickly, a footballer can repeat short sprints across a match provided there is enough recovery between them. ✍️ Using the term in context Link PCr to the ATP-PC system, its duration and recovery: "Phosphocreatine rapidly resynthesises ATP by donating a phosphate to ADP in the ATP-PC system, fuelling maximal efforts of around 8–10 seconds; stores replenish quickly during recovery, allowing repeated efforts." Note it forms the fast (alactic) component of EPOC. 🔗 Related terms

Phosphocreatine Recovery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Phosphocreatine Recovery IB Sport Science General Phosphocreatine Recovery Refilling the fast tank — how quickly the ATP-PC system recharges between explosive efforts. 📖 What it means Phosphocreatine (PC) recovery is the rapid resynthesis of phosphocreatine stores during recovery , largely using aerobic energy production. PC stores are depleted during maximal, explosive efforts and must be replenished before the ATP-PC system can support another maximal effort.

PC recovery is rapid : around 50% is restored within 30 seconds and near-full recovery occurs within 3–5 minutes of rest. This rapid timescale allows repeated maximal efforts when appropriate rest is provided. Understanding PC recovery is important for structuring interval training and repeated-sprint sessions : the rest period between maximal efforts should be long enough to allow near-complete PC replenishment if the goal is to train the ATP-PC system at full intensity. 🏅 Sporting examples Speed of recovery About 50% of phosphocreatine is replenished within 30 seconds of rest. Interval training A coach provides 3–5 minutes' rest between maximal sprint efforts to allow PC stores to recover.

Aerobic role The aerobic system provides the energy to resynthesise PC during recovery — connecting the systems. ✍️ Using the term in context State the timescale of PC recovery and its training implication: "Phosphocreatine recovery is rapid — around 50% within 30 seconds and near-complete within 3–5 minutes; this timescale guides the rest periods between maximal efforts in interval training, allowing near-full recovery for subsequent sprints." Physical Activity Guidelines — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Physical Activity Guidelines BTEC Sport General Physical Activity Guidelines The recommended minimum — the evidence-based guidance on how much activity is needed for health benefits. 📖 What it means Physical activity guidelines are recommended minimum amounts of moderate or vigorous physical activity for maintaining and improving health. They are issued by health bodies and governments based on scientific evidence.

For adults, guidelines typically recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week , plus muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. Children typically need more activity than adults. They are a benchmark for health promotion — informing policy, coaching, exercise prescription and public health campaigns . They also contextualise barriers to participation and the health consequences of inactivity. 🏅 Sporting examples Adult minimum 150 minutes of moderate activity per week is the typical adult guideline for health benefit. Children

Children's guidelines typically specify 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity every day. Policy Physical activity guidelines inform national sport and health promotion policies. ✍️ Using the term in context State the guidelines and their purpose: "Physical activity guidelines recommend minimum amounts of activity for health — typically 150 minutes of moderate or 75 of vigorous aerobic activity per week for adults, plus strengthening activities; they underpin health promotion and exercise prescription." Piriformis Muscle Syndrome — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Piriformis Muscle Syndrome BTEC Sport General Piriformis Muscle Syndrome Buttock muscle tightness that irritates the sciatic nerve. 📖 What it means The piriformis is a small muscle deep in the buttock that rotates the hip outward . The sciatic nerve runs close to it, and in some people through it. In piriformis syndrome , a tight or irritated muscle puts pressure on the nerve, causing buttock pain and sometimes pain, tingling or numbness down the back of the leg (sciatica-like symptoms).

It is associated with running, cycling and long sitting. Treatment includes rest, stretching, strengthening the hip muscles, massage and sometimes medical treatment. Persistent or severe symptoms need a clinician's assessment. 🏅 Sporting examples Runner Pain in the buttock after increasing mileage quickly. Pivot Joint — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Pivot Joint IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Pivot Joint A rotating joint — allowing spin around a single axis, like the head turning or the forearm rotating. 📖 What it means A pivot joint is a synovial joint that allows rotational movement around a single axis . One bone rotates within a ring formed by another. The most common sporting examples are the proximal radioulnar joint (allowing pronation and supination of the forearm) and the atlantoaxial joint in the neck (allowing the head to rotate — turning left and right).

As a type of synovial joint, a pivot joint has the same features as other synovial joints (joint capsule, synovial fluid, articular cartilage) but allows only uniaxial rotation . It is one of the six types of synovial joint. 🏅 Sporting examples Forearm rotation Pronating the forearm — rotating the palm to face downward — uses the pivot joint at the proximal radioulnar joint. Head rotation Turning the head to look over the shoulder uses the atlantoaxial pivot joint. Uniaxial Pivot joints allow only rotation around one axis — unlike ball and socket joints, which allow movement in all directions. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a pivot joint and give the sporting example:

Planes of Movement — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Planes of Movement IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Planes of Movement The three imaginary planes that divide the body — the framework for describing exactly how and where a movement occurs. 📖 What it means The planes of movement are three imaginary flat surfaces that divide the body , used to describe the direction in which movements occur. There are three: sagittal, frontal and transverse.

The sagittal plane divides the body into left and right, and contains front-to-back movements such as flexion and extension. The frontal plane divides front from back, and contains side-to-side movements such as abduction and adduction. The transverse plane divides top from bottom, and contains rotational movements. Each plane has an associated axis of rotation that runs perpendicular to it. Identifying the correct plane (and axis) is a core part of movement analysis, allowing precise description of a sporting action. 🏅 Sporting examples Sagittal plane A biceps curl or a running stride occurs mainly in the sagittal plane — flexion and extension viewed from the side. Frontal plane

A star jump moves in the frontal plane, with abduction and adduction of the limbs. Transverse plane A discus thrower's or a gymnast's twist occurs in the transverse plane — rotation about the long axis of the body. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the three planes and their movements: "There are three planes of movement: the sagittal plane (flexion and extension), the frontal plane (abduction and adduction), and the transverse plane (rotation); identifying the correct plane and axis is central to movement analysis." Pair each plane with its associated axis when a detailed answer is required. 🔗 Related terms Sagittal Plane Frontal Plane Transverse Plane Flexion Abduction Axes of Rotation

Plasma — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Plasma IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Plasma The liquid part of blood — the watery carrier for cells, nutrients, hormones and waste. 📖 What it means Plasma is the liquid component of blood in which blood cells, nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products are suspended and transported. It makes up roughly 55% of blood volume. Plasma is largely water, containing dissolved proteins, electrolytes, nutrients (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids), hormones, gases (including CO₂) and waste products . It plays a central role in transport, fluid balance and immune function.

During exercise, plasma volume can decrease as fluid is lost through sweating and shifts into the muscles. This increases blood viscosity and places extra strain on the cardiovascular system. Endurance training tends to increase plasma volume , improving oxygen delivery and reducing cardiovascular strain. 🏅 Sporting examples Transport medium Plasma carries glucose to the muscles and removes carbon dioxide as blood circulates. Exercise response Sweating during exercise reduces plasma volume, increasing blood viscosity. Training adaptation Endurance training increases plasma volume, improving the blood's ability to carry oxygen. ✍️ Using the term in context Define plasma and link to exercise:

Plyometric Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Plyometric Training General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Plyometric Training Training that harnesses the muscle's elastic 'stretch–shorten' action to build explosive power. 📖 What it means Plyometric training is a method that develops muscular power using exercises based on the stretch–shortening cycle — a rapid eccentric (lengthening) contraction immediately followed by a powerful concentric (shortening) contraction.

The rapid pre-stretch stores elastic energy in the muscle and tendon and triggers the stretch reflex , both of which add to the force of the following concentric contraction — producing a more powerful, explosive movement than the concentric action alone. Typical plyometric exercises include bounding, depth jumps and hopping . Because it is high-impact and demanding, plyometric training must be built up gradually and used with adequate recovery to avoid injury, and suits athletes who already have a strength base. 🏅 Sporting examples Jumping sports A basketball or volleyball player uses depth jumps to develop the explosive power needed for higher jumps. Sprinting

Bounding drills develop the powerful, elastic push-off that contributes to sprint acceleration. Progression A coach introduces plyometrics gradually and ensures recovery between sessions, because the high impact carries injury risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the stretch–shortening cycle mechanism: "Plyometric training develops power using the stretch–shortening cycle, in which a rapid eccentric contraction stores elastic energy and triggers the stretch reflex, adding to the force of the following concentric contraction for a more explosive movement." Note the high-impact nature and the need for gradual progression and recovery. 🔗 Related terms

Pole Vault — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Pole Vault BTEC Sport General Pole Vault Vaulting over a bar with a flexible pole. 📖 What it means In the pole vault , the athlete sprints down a runway, plants the pole in a box and is swung up and over a high bar . The pole bends under load and then recoils, returning stored elastic energy . The vault converts kinetic energy from the run-up into elastic strain energy in the pole, and then into gravitational potential energy as the vaulter rises. Phases are the approach, plant, take-off, swing-up, turn, bar clearance and landing on a mat.

It demands speed, upper-body strength, gymnastic body control and coordination , and is a high-risk event that needs expert coaching and proper safety equipment. 🏅 Sporting examples Run-up The athlete builds a controlled sprint. Pole bend The pole stores elastic energy as it flexes. Bar clearance The vaulter turns and extends over the bar. ✍️ Using the term in context Trace the energy: "A pole vaulter converts kinetic energy from the run-up into elastic energy in the pole and then into gravitational potential energy at the top." POMS (Profile of Mood States) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › POMS (Profile of Mood States) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General POMS (Profile of Mood States) A mood snapshot before competition — a questionnaire measuring an athlete's emotional state across key dimensions. 📖 What it means The Profile of Mood States (POMS) is a psychological questionnaire measuring an athlete's current mood across several dimensions , typically including tension, depression, anger, vigour, fatigue and confusion.

In sport psychology research, POMS has been used to describe the 'iceberg profile' of successful athletes: higher than average vigour and lower than average scores on all the negative dimensions, producing a distinctive shape on a profile chart. As a self-report tool, POMS is quick and practical but depends on honest, accurate responses and can be affected by a performer's desire to appear in a certain state. It gives a snapshot of current mood rather than a stable trait. 🏅 Sporting examples Iceberg profile Elite athletes tend to show the POMS 'iceberg profile' — high vigour and low tension, depression, anger, fatigue and confusion. Pose Running Technique — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Pose Running Technique BTEC Sport General Pose Running Technique A running style based on falling forward and pulling the foot up. 📖 What it means The Pose method was developed by Dr Nicholas Romanov . It is based on three elements: the pose (the body in an S-shape on the support foot), the fall (leaning forward so gravity pulls the runner ahead) and the pull (lifting the support foot up from the ground under the hip). It encourages midfoot landing under the body's centre of mass , a high cadence and little ankle push-off. Supporters say it can reduce overstriding and impact loading.

Research has not shown that it makes runners more economical or injury free, and changing technique can cause calf and Achilles problems if made quickly. Any change should be gradual. 🏅 Sporting examples Overstriding A runner reduces braking by landing under the hips. Transition Switching from heel strike takes months. Drills Pull-up drills teach the foot-lift action. ✍️ Using the term in context Be balanced: "The Pose method promotes midfoot landing under the body with a high cadence, but evidence that it improves efficiency or reduces injury is limited." Positive Transfer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Positive Transfer AS Level / Cambridge General Positive Transfer When learning one skill helps another — the useful side of transfer that good coaches deliberately exploit. 📖 What it means Positive transfer is when the learning or performance of one skill aids the learning or performance of another . It happens because skills share common elements that carry over usefully. It is most likely when two skills have similar components, movement patterns or perceptual demands — for example, the overarm throw and the tennis serve share a similar action, so learning one can help the other.

Coaches actively exploit positive transfer by pointing out similarities between skills, teaching fundamental movement skills that underpin many sports, and ensuring practice conditions resemble the target situation so the learning carries over. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing to serving A performer who can throw overarm well often learns a tennis serve more easily, because the two actions share a similar pattern — positive transfer. Fundamental skills Learning to catch and throw benefits many sports, so teaching these fundamentals produces broad positive transfer. Practice design A coach makes practice resemble the game so that skills learned in training transfer positively to competition.

Power — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Power General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Power Strength delivered fast — the explosive combination of force and speed that decides jumps, sprints and throws. 📖 What it means Power is the ability to exert force quickly — it combines strength and speed . In physics terms, power is the rate of doing work (work ÷ time), and in sport it is often described as the product of force and velocity.

Power is a skill-related component of fitness essential to explosive actions such as jumping, sprinting, throwing and striking . An athlete may be very strong, but without the ability to apply that force rapidly, they lack power. It is developed through methods such as plyometric training, Olympic-style lifts and resistance training performed explosively , and is commonly assessed with tests such as the vertical jump test. 🏅 Sporting examples Jumping A high jumper needs power — applying large force very quickly — to convert their run-up into height at take-off. Power is often assessed with the vertical jump test, which measures explosive leg power. ✍️ Using the term in context Define power as force × speed and give the fitness context: "Power is the ability to exert force quickly, combining strength and speed; as a skill-related component of fitness it underpins explosive actions such as jumping and throwing, and is developed through plyometrics and explosive resistance training." Press-up Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Press-up Test BTEC Sport General Press-up Test A fitness test of upper-body muscular endurance. 📖 What it means The Press-up Test is a muscular endurance test in which the athlete performs as many press-ups as possible with correct form. PRICE — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › PRICE General BTEC Sport PRICE An updated first-aid protocol for soft-tissue injuries — Protection first, then Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. 📖 What it means PRICE is an extended acute injury protocol standing for Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation . It builds on the classic RICE protocol by adding an initial Protection step.

Protection means stopping the activity and protecting the injured area from further harm — removing the athlete from risk before the rest of the protocol is applied. The remaining steps limit swelling, pain and tissue damage: Rest prevents further stress, Ice reduces inflammation and numbs pain, Compression limits swelling, and Elevation reduces blood pooling. PRICE should be applied in the first 24–72 hours after a soft-tissue injury such as a sprain or strain. It is a practical first-aid approach used in sports settings and updated in some guidance to POLICE (Protection, Optimal Loading, Ice, Compression, Elevation). 🏅 Sporting examples Ankle sprain

After an ankle sprain, PRICE is applied: the player stops (Protection), rests, applies ice, uses a bandage (Compression) and raises the ankle (Elevation). Protection first The P in PRICE ensures the athlete is removed from further risk before other treatment begins. Short-term management PRICE is for immediate management; medical assessment follows if the injury is significant. ✍️ Using the term in context Expand the acronym and explain each step: "PRICE is an acute injury protocol — Protection (stop and protect), Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation; applied in the first 24–72 hours after a soft-tissue injury, it limits swelling, pain and further damage."

Principle of Progression — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Principle of Progression General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Principle of Progression The rule that training must get gradually harder — the key to continued improvement without injury or burnout. 📖 What it means The principle of progression (progressive overload) states that training must be gradually and progressively increased over time for adaptation and improvement to continue. As the body adapts to a given load, the load must rise to keep challenging it.

The word gradually is crucial: increases must be appropriately sized and timed . Progressing too quickly risks injury, overtraining and burnout; progressing too slowly (or not at all) leads to a plateau where no further adaptation occurs. Progression is applied by adjusting the FITT variables — increasing frequency, intensity, time or adjusting type — and works alongside other training principles such as overload, specificity and reversibility. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength training A lifter gradually increases the weight lifted as they get stronger, applying progressive overload to keep driving adaptation. Endurance

A runner slowly builds their weekly mileage over weeks, progressing gradually to avoid injury while improving fitness. Avoiding a plateau Without progression, an athlete's body fully adapts to the current load and improvement stalls at a plateau. ✍️ Using the term in context State the principle and stress gradual, appropriate increases: "The principle of progression states that training load must be increased gradually over time for adaptation to continue; progressing too fast risks injury and overtraining, while too little leads to a plateau." Process Goal — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Process Goal IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Process Goal A goal about the actions and technique themselves — the most controllable, focus-directing type of goal. 📖 What it means A process goal is a goal focused on the specific actions, techniques or behaviours a performer must execute to perform well — for example, keeping a high elbow in a swimming stroke.

Process goals are the most fully within the athlete's control , because they concern exactly what the performer does. They are excellent for directing attention to the key technical points during performance and for building skills, especially in learners. They work best combined with performance and outcome goals : the process goals guide the actions, the performance goals set the personal standard, and the outcome goal provides the ultimate target — with the process goals being what the athlete concentrates on in the moment. 🏅 Sporting examples Technique focus 'Keep the head still through the putt' is a process goal directing a golfer's attention to a specific controllable action.

Progressive Muscle Relaxation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Progressive Muscle Relaxation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Progressive Muscle Relaxation Tense to relax — a systematic technique that works through the body's muscles to release physical tension. 📖 What it means Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR) is a relaxation technique involving the sequential tensing and releasing of muscle groups throughout the body, to reduce physical tension and somatic anxiety.

The performer systematically tenses each muscle group for a few seconds, then releases the tension , working progressively from one part of the body to another. The contrast between tension and relaxation enhances the awareness of relaxation and deepens it. PMR is used to manage somatic anxiety and physical tension before or during competition. Projectile — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Projectile IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Projectile Any body launched into the air — and the physics of how far and how well it flies, from a javelin to a jumper. 📖 What it means A projectile is any body launched into the air and subject to the forces of gravity and air resistance . It may be an object (a javelin, a ball) or the athlete's own body (a long jumper).

Once airborne, a projectile's centre of mass follows a parabolic (curved) flight path that cannot be changed. The distance and height achieved depend on three factors at the moment of release or take-off: the speed of release, the angle of release, and the height of release . For most projectiles aiming for maximum distance, an angle of release around 45 degrees is theoretically optimal , though the ideal angle changes when release and landing heights differ, and air resistance and lift (as on a discus) further complicate real flight. 🏅 Sporting examples Javelin

A javelin is a projectile; the thrower manipulates release speed, angle and height, and the implement's aerodynamics, to maximise distance. Long jump A long jumper's body is a projectile whose centre of mass follows a fixed parabola once they leave the board — they cannot change its flight path in the air. Shot put Because the shot is released above the ground, its optimal release angle is slightly below 45 degrees. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the three release factors and the parabolic path:

Proprioception — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Proprioception IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Proprioception Your body's internal GPS — the sense of position and movement that lets you move without looking. 📖 What it means Proprioception is the body's ability to sense its own position, movement and forces acting within it , without using vision. It is sometimes called the 'sixth sense'. It relies on information from proprioceptors — sensory receptors in the muscles, tendons and joints (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint receptors) — that continuously feed the nervous system with data about body position and movement.

Proprioception is essential for balance, coordination and skilled movement , and it underpins the intrinsic feedback that allows skilled performers to detect and correct errors by feel. It can be improved through training , particularly balance and stability exercises. 🏅 Sporting examples Balance Standing on one leg requires proprioception — continuous sensory feedback about position and adjustments. Skilled movement A skilled gymnast uses proprioception to sense body position mid-air without seeing themselves. Training Balance boards and unstable surfaces train proprioception by challenging the sensory-motor system. ✍️ Using the term in context Define proprioception and its sources:

Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) The most effective static flexibility technique — using muscle contraction to unlock greater stretch. 📖 What it means Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) is an advanced flexibility technique combining passive stretching with isometric contraction of the muscle being stretched, to achieve a greater range of movement than static stretching alone.

A common method involves: (1) the muscle is stretched to its limit (passive), (2) the performer contracts it isometrically against resistance for several seconds, (3) the contraction is released, and (4) the muscle is stretched further into the new range. The prior contraction exploits autogenic inhibition (via the Golgi tendon organs), causing the muscle to relax and allow a greater stretch. PNF is highly effective for increasing flexibility and is used in rehabilitation and advanced sport. It requires a partner or apparatus and should be applied carefully to avoid injury. 🏅 Sporting examples Hamstring PNF

A partner stretches a player's hamstring, the player pushes against the resistance for 6 seconds, then the partner stretches further. Autogenic inhibition The prior contraction triggers autogenic inhibition, causing the muscle to relax and allow a greater stretch. Advanced technique PNF is more effective than static stretching but requires a partner and care to avoid overstretching. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe PNF and the mechanism behind it: "PNF is an advanced flexibility technique that passively stretches a muscle, has the performer contract it isometrically, then stretches it further; the contraction triggers autogenic inhibition, relaxing the muscle for a greater range."

Proprioceptor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Proprioceptor IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Proprioceptor The sensory receptors behind proprioception — the detectors in muscles, tendons and joints reporting position and movement. 📖 What it means A proprioceptor is a sensory receptor in muscles, tendons and joints that provides information about body position, movement and internal forces . The main proprioceptors relevant to sport are muscle spindles (detecting muscle length and rate of change, triggering the stretch reflex), Golgi tendon organs (detecting tension, mediating autogenic inhibition) and joint receptors (detecting joint angle and movement). Protein Synthesis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Protein Synthesis IB Sport Science General Protein Synthesis Building new proteins after training — the cellular process that turns exercise stress into muscle adaptation. 📖 What it means Protein synthesis is the cellular process of building new proteins , using amino acids, central to muscle repair and adaptation after training. It is the mechanism behind muscle hypertrophy and recovery .

After resistance exercise or heavy training, muscle fibres are damaged. Protein synthesis repairs this damage and, with repeated training, builds stronger, larger fibres . It requires a sufficient supply of dietary protein and amino acids , along with anabolic hormones such as growth hormone and testosterone. The rate of protein synthesis is elevated after exercise for several hours. Timing protein intake — particularly consuming protein soon after training — can maximise this response and support the adaptations that training aims to produce. 🏅 Sporting examples Post-training repair Protein synthesis rebuilds the muscle fibres damaged by resistance training, making them stronger.

Hypertrophy Over time, repeated bouts of protein synthesis in response to training lead to muscle hypertrophy. Timing Consuming protein soon after training elevates amino acid availability when protein synthesis rates are high. ✍️ Using the term in context Define protein synthesis and link to adaptation: "Protein synthesis is the cellular process of building new proteins from amino acids; after exercise it repairs and rebuilds muscle fibres, driving adaptation and hypertrophy, and is optimised by adequate protein intake and timing." Protein — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Protein IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Protein The body's building and repair material — the macronutrient central to muscle growth and recovery. 📖 What it means Protein is a macronutrient made up of amino acids , essential for the growth, repair and maintenance of body tissues — especially muscle. It also has roles in making enzymes and hormones and in the immune system.

In sport, protein is particularly important for repairing the muscle damage caused by training and for building new muscle tissue (hypertrophy) , making adequate intake important for strength and power athletes and for recovery in all athletes. Protein is not a major fuel for exercise under normal conditions, contributing only a small proportion of energy; its main sporting role is in recovery and adaptation rather than as an energy source. Intake is best spread through the day, including after training. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength training A strength athlete ensures adequate protein intake to support the repair and growth of muscle tissue stimulated by resistance training. Psychological Refractory Period — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Psychological Refractory Period IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Psychological Refractory Period The delay when a second signal arrives too soon. 📖 What it means The psychological refractory period (PRP) is the delay in responding to a second stimulus that follows closely after a first. The brain is still dealing with the first one. It happens when the second stimulus arrives within about half a second of the first. The response to it is then slower, and this is why performers can be 'fooled' by a dummy or feint.

Performers reduce the PRP by anticipating , practising, focusing attention on key cues and making fewer choices. Attackers use it, for example by faking a shot. 🏅 Sporting examples Dummy pass The defender responds to the dummy and is slow to react to the real pass. Tennis A disguised drop shot after a series of deep shots. Fencing A feint creates the delay. ✍️ Using the term in context Define and apply: "The psychological refractory period is the delay in responding to a second stimulus presented before the first has been processed, as when a defender is deceived by a dummy." Pulmonary Ventilation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Pulmonary Ventilation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Pulmonary Ventilation The mechanics of breathing — moving air in and out of the lungs, and the total volume shifted each minute. 📖 What it means Pulmonary ventilation is the process of moving air into and out of the lungs — breathing. The term is also used for the total volume of air breathed per minute (minute ventilation, VE). As a volume, it equals tidal volume × breathing frequency — the air moved per breath multiplied by the number of breaths per minute. At rest it is around 6–8 litres per minute, rising sharply during exercise.

During exercise, pulmonary ventilation increases dramatically as both tidal volume and breathing frequency rise, ensuring enough oxygen is taken in and enough carbon dioxide removed to support the working muscles. This increase is a key acute response to exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Intense exercise As a rower nears maximal effort, pulmonary ventilation rises steeply through deeper and faster breathing to meet the oxygen demand. Pyruvate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Pyruvate IB Sport Science General Pyruvate The crossroads of energy metabolism — the molecule that decides whether energy goes aerobic or anaerobic. 📖 What it means Pyruvate is the end product of glycolysis — the breakdown of glucose. What happens to pyruvate next determines whether energy production proceeds aerobically or anaerobically.

When oxygen is available and demand is not excessive, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA and enters the Krebs cycle in the mitochondria for aerobic ATP production. When oxygen is insufficient or demand is high, pyruvate is converted to lactate instead — allowing glycolysis to continue at speed. Pyruvate is thus the gateway between anaerobic glycolysis and aerobic metabolism . The point at which the balance tips from aerobic to lactate production is related to the lactate threshold . 🏅 Sporting examples Aerobic route At moderate intensity, pyruvate enters the Krebs cycle for full aerobic ATP production. Anaerobic route

During intense exercise, pyruvate is converted to lactate, allowing rapid glycolysis to continue. Crossroads Pyruvate is the decision point — whether metabolism goes aerobic or produces lactate depends on oxygen availability and demand. ✍️ Using the term in context Define pyruvate and its two metabolic fates: "Pyruvate is the end product of glycolysis; with adequate oxygen it enters the Krebs cycle as acetyl-CoA for aerobic ATP production, but when oxygen is limited or demand is high it is converted to lactate, allowing glycolysis to continue." Frame it as the aerobic/anaerobic decision point. 🔗 Related terms

Q Angle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Q Angle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Q Angle A measure of how the thigh and shin line up at the knee. 📖 What it means The Q angle (quadriceps angle) is the angle formed between a line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the centre of the kneecap and a line from the kneecap to the tibial tuberosity . It is generally larger in females because of a wider pelvis. A larger Q angle is associated with greater side-ward forces on the kneecap and is linked with patellofemoral pain and kneecap problems , though the link is debated. It is measured with a goniometer, with the person standing relaxed.

🏅 Sporting examples Female athletes A wider pelvis gives a larger Q angle on average. Knee pain Clinicians check the Q angle when kneecap pain is reported. Biomechanics A large Q angle can place extra stress on the knee in cutting movements. ✍️ Using the term in context State the definition: "The Q angle is the angle between the line of pull of the quadriceps and the patellar tendon, and is typically greater in females." Quadriceps — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Quadriceps IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Quadriceps The powerful muscle group at the front of the thigh — the prime mover of knee extension behind kicking, sprinting and jumping. 📖 What it means The quadriceps are a group of four muscles at the front of the thigh . Their main action is extension of the knee (straightening the leg), and one of them also assists in flexing the hip.

They are the prime movers in powerful lower-body actions such as kicking, sprinting, jumping and squatting, generating much of the force that straightens the knee. They act as the antagonist to the hamstrings at the knee. The quadriceps work concentrically to extend the knee (e.g. driving upward in a jump) and eccentrically to control knee flexion (e.g. absorbing a landing or decelerating), making them central to both producing and controlling movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Kicking In a football kick, the quadriceps act as the agonist, contracting powerfully to extend the knee and strike the ball. Jumping

The quadriceps drive knee extension in a jump, and control the landing eccentrically as the knee bends. Sprinting The quadriceps extend the knee powerfully in the drive phase of a sprint to propel the athlete forward. ✍️ Using the term in context Name their action and role in a specific movement: "The quadriceps extend the knee and act as the agonist in kicking; they contract concentrically to straighten the knee and eccentrically to control landings, working as the antagonist to the hamstrings." Qualitative Analysis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Qualitative Analysis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Qualitative Analysis Analysis by observation and description — the non-numerical eye of the coach watching performance. 📖 What it means Qualitative analysis is descriptive, non-numerical analysis of movement or performance based on observation . It focuses on the quality, technique and characteristics of a performance rather than producing data in numbers.

It is the basis of coaching observation : a coach watching and describing technique, identifying deviations from the ideal model, and giving feedback. It can be supported by video analysis , slow-motion replay and notation, which allow deeper observation. Qualitative analysis is valuable because many important aspects of performance cannot be easily quantified — fluency, coordination, decision-making and technique all require a trained observational eye. Its limitation is subjectivity; findings can vary between observers. 🏅 Sporting examples Coaching feedback A coach watching a swimmer's stroke and describing what's wrong — poor catch, dropping elbow — is qualitative analysis. Video review

Using slow-motion video to identify the exact point of a technical error is qualitative analysis. Subjectivity Two coaches may observe the same performance differently, highlighting qualitative analysis's main limitation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define qualitative analysis and contrast with quantitative: "Qualitative analysis is non-numerical, descriptive analysis of movement based on observation; it assesses technique and quality, is valuable for aspects that cannot easily be quantified, but is subjective and may vary between observers." Quantitative Analysis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Quantitative Analysis IB Sport Science General Quantitative Analysis Analysis by numbers — measurable, objective data that puts precise figures on performance. 📖 What it means Quantitative analysis is numerical, measurable analysis of performance using data such as speed, time, distance, force or frequency . It provides objective, comparable figures.

It includes data from timing gates, force plates, GPS trackers, heart rate monitors and notational analysis . Because the data are objective, results can be compared, tracked over time and statistically analysed — making conclusions more reliable and less subject to personal interpretation. Quantitative analysis is contrasted with qualitative analysis. While it provides objective precision, it can miss aspects of performance that numbers cannot capture — such as technique, decision-making and fluency. Best practice combines both approaches. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint timing A 40m sprint time of 4.82 seconds is a quantitative analysis — an objective, numerical measure of speed. Force data

Force plate data from a jump test gives a quantitative measure of power output. Combined Effective performance analysis combines quantitative data with qualitative observation of technique. ✍️ Using the term in context Define quantitative analysis and contrast with qualitative: "Quantitative analysis uses measurable, numerical data — such as speed, time, force and distance — to objectively assess performance; it provides comparable, statistically analysable data but may miss qualitative aspects like technique." Protocol: The participant steps up and down a step of about 41 cm for three minutes at a set rate (slightly faster for men than women). Heart rate is counted soon after finishing.

Interpreting results: A lower recovery heart rate indicates better fitness, and the result can be used in a formula to estimate VO2 max. It is a simple test for groups. It takes less than a minute, so it can be used before a free throw, penalty, serve or start as part of a pre-performance routine. Radiation (heat loss) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Radiation (heat loss) IB Sport Science General Radiation (heat loss) Heat escaping as infrared waves — how the body sheds warmth without contact or airflow. 📖 What it means Radiation is the transfer of body heat to the surroundings as infrared energy, without contact . The body emits heat waves in all directions; the cooler the surroundings, the greater the radiation.

It is one of four heat-loss mechanisms (alongside conduction, convection and evaporation). At rest and in cool conditions, radiation is a significant route of heat loss. During intense exercise, evaporation becomes the dominant route , though radiation continues. In hot conditions, the body can also gain heat by radiation from the sun or hot surfaces. This makes thermoregulation more challenging in radiant-heat environments such as outdoor sport in direct sunlight. 🏅 Sporting examples Cool environment In a cool room at rest, much of the body's heat is lost by radiation to the cooler surroundings. Radiant gain

Competing in direct sunlight, the athlete both loses heat by radiation and gains it from the sun. One of four Radiation works alongside conduction, convection and evaporation in the body's heat-loss system. ✍️ Using the term in context Define radiation as a heat-loss mechanism: "Radiation is the transfer of body heat as infrared energy to cooler surroundings, without contact; it is one of four heat-loss mechanisms and can work in reverse in hot, sunny conditions when the body may gain heat." List it alongside the other three heat-loss mechanisms. 🔗 Related terms Conduction (heat loss) Convection (heat loss) Evaporation (heat loss) Thermoregulation Homeostasis Dehydration 🎓 Where this appears

RAMP Protocol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › RAMP Protocol General BTEC Sport RAMP Protocol A structured warm-up that does more than raise the heart rate — progressively preparing the whole athlete for action. 📖 What it means The RAMP Protocol is a structured warm-up framework consisting of four phases: Raise (increase heart rate, body temperature and blood flow), Activate (switch on key muscle groups), Mobilise (move joints through their required ranges) and Potentiate (gradually increase the intensity of sport-specific movements).

It is a more comprehensive approach than a simple pulse-raiser and stretch, because it systematically targets all aspects of physical preparation — cardiovascular, neuromuscular and movement-specific — and culminates in explosive, sport-specific activity that primes the nervous system. The RAMP Protocol is widely used in sport and strength-and-conditioning settings because it is evidence-based, adaptable and more effective than traditional warm-ups at preparing the body and reducing injury risk. 🏅 Sporting examples Raise Light jogging raises heart rate and body temperature in the first RAMP phase. Activate and Mobilise

Glute bridges, ankle circles and dynamic lunges activate and mobilise the key muscles and joints. Potentiate Building to short accelerations and sport-specific movements primes the nervous system at the end of the RAMP warm-up. ✍️ Using the term in context Expand the acronym and explain its advantage: "The RAMP Protocol is a structured warm-up: Raise (temperature and heart rate), Activate (key muscles), Mobilise (joints) and Potentiate (sport-specific intensity); it is more comprehensive than a traditional warm-up, systematically preparing the cardiovascular, neuromuscular and movement systems." Random Error — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Random Error IB Sport Science General Random Error Unpredictable measurement wobble — natural variation that affects precision but doesn't bias results in one direction. 📖 What it means A random error is an unpredictable variation in measurement that affects precision . Unlike systematic errors, random errors vary in size and direction from measurement to measurement, causing results to scatter around the true value.

Sources include natural biological variation, imprecise timing, inconsistent technique or environmental fluctuations. They do not bias results consistently in one direction — they are equally likely to cause over- or under-measurement. Random errors reduce reliability but can be reduced by repeated measurement and averaging . They are contrasted with systematic errors (which consistently shift all results in one direction). 🏅 Sporting examples Timing variation A hand-timed sprint test produces slightly different results each attempt due to reaction-time variation in the timer — a random error. Averaging

Taking three measurements and averaging them reduces the impact of random error on the result. Contrast A miscalibrated stopwatch shifts all times by the same amount (systematic), while timing reaction variability is random. ✍️ Using the term in context Define random error and distinguish from systematic: "A random error is unpredictable variation in measurement that causes results to scatter around the true value; unlike systematic errors, they do not bias in one direction and can be reduced by repeated measurements and averaging." Contrast clearly with systematic error. 🔗 Related terms Systematic Error Reliability of Data Validity Controlled Variable Mean Standard Deviation

Range of Motion (ROM) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Range of Motion (ROM) General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Range of Motion (ROM) How far a joint can move — the full arc of movement available, and a key marker of flexibility. 📖 What it means Range of motion (ROM) is the full extent of movement possible at a joint , measured in degrees. It is the standard measure of flexibility at a specific joint. ROM depends on joint structure, surrounding muscles, tendons, ligaments and connective tissue . It can be measured actively (the performer moves through the range using their own muscles) or passively (an external force moves them).

Adequate ROM supports performance and injury prevention : insufficient ROM restricts movement patterns and can increase injury risk, while appropriate flexibility training can improve ROM. It is assessed using goniometry or functional flexibility tests. 🏅 Sporting examples Flexibility measure A physiotherapist measures a footballer's hip ROM with a goniometer after an injury to assess recovery. Active vs passive Active ROM is how far the performer moves themselves; passive ROM, with external help, is usually greater. Performance A swimmer's shoulder ROM directly affects the efficiency of their pull phase. ✍️ Using the term in context Define ROM and link it to flexibility:

RAST (Running-based Anaerobic Sprint Test) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › RAST (Running-based Anaerobic Sprint Test) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport RAST (Running-based Anaerobic Sprint Test) A fitness test of anaerobic power and fatigue. 📖 What it means The RAST (Running-based Anaerobic Sprint Test) is a running test of anaerobic power and fatigue in which the athlete completes six 35 metre sprints with 10 seconds recovery between each. Rate of Force Development — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rate of Force Development IB Sport Science General Rate of Force Development How fast you can produce force — the explosive quality that separates athletes in sprint starts, tackles and jumps. 📖 What it means Rate of force development (RFD) is the speed at which a muscle or group can generate force from the onset of contraction . It describes how quickly peak force is reached, not just how much force is produced.

In many sporting actions the time available to apply force is extremely short — ground contact in sprinting lasts milliseconds. A high RFD means large forces are produced in the brief time available , which is often more important than absolute maximal strength. RFD is developed through explosive and ballistic resistance training, Olympic lifts and plyometrics , and is measured by the slope of the early portion of the force-time curve. It is a key quality underpinning power in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint start An explosive start requires rapid RFD — the ability to push hard against the blocks in a very short contact time. Plyometrics

Plyometric training improves RFD by training the muscle to generate force rapidly through the stretch-shortening cycle. Force-time curve RFD is shown by the slope of the early portion of the force-time curve. ✍️ Using the term in context Define RFD and distinguish from maximal strength: "Rate of force development is how quickly force can be generated from the start of a contraction; in explosive actions where ground contact is brief, RFD is often more important than maximal strength, and is developed through Olympic lifts and plyometrics." Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) Putting a number on how hard exercise feels — a simple, equipment-free way to gauge and control intensity. 📖 What it means Rating of perceived exertion (RPE) is a subjective measure of how hard a person feels they are working during exercise, based on sensations such as effort, breathlessness and fatigue.

It is most commonly measured using the Borg Scale , traditionally running from 6 to 20 (where multiplying the rating by ten gives an approximate heart rate), or a simpler modified 0–10 scale. The performer simply reports the number matching how they feel. RPE is valued for its practicality — it needs no equipment, works anywhere, and lets athletes self-regulate intensity. Although subjective, it correlates reasonably well with objective measures such as heart rate, making it a useful everyday monitoring tool. 🏅 Sporting examples Self-regulation A runner uses RPE to keep hard intervals near the top of the scale and recovery efforts low, without needing a heart rate monitor. Rehabilitation

A coach uses RPE to keep a returning athlete's effort within a safe range using only their subjective feedback. Monitoring load Multiplying RPE by session duration gives a simple measure of training load that can be tracked over time. ✍️ Using the term in context Define RPE and link it to the Borg Scale: "Rating of perceived exertion is a subjective measure of how hard exercise feels, usually measured on the Borg Scale; it is practical, requires no equipment, and correlates reasonably with objective measures such as heart rate." Rational Recreation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rational Recreation BTEC Sport General Rational Recreation The Victorian shift to organised, rule-based sport. 📖 What it means Rational recreation describes the organised, regulated sport that emerged in 19th-century Britain, replacing older popular recreations that were often violent, local and unregulated. It was led by the middle class and public schools , with codified rules, clubs, governing bodies, set times and venues . Factories and churches provided facilities and teams to encourage moral, healthy and disciplined behaviour.

It grew with the Industrial Revolution , urbanisation , better transport, and the Saturday half-day. It created the basis of modern sport, including football and rugby. 🏅 Sporting examples Football Codified rules in 1863 by the Football Association. Factories Works teams provided healthy recreation. Reaction Time — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reaction Time General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Reaction Time The split-second between stimulus and response — a skill-related component of fitness that decides sprints, saves and returns. 📖 What it means Reaction time is the time taken to initiate a response to a stimulus — the interval between a stimulus appearing (such as the starter's gun) and the start of the movement in response. It is a skill-related component of fitness.

It is distinguished from movement time (the time to complete the movement) and response time (reaction time + movement time). Reaction time can be simple (one stimulus, one response) or choice (several possible stimuli and responses), and choice reaction time is longer — as described by Hick's Law. Reaction time is influenced by factors including the number of choices, anticipation, arousal, experience and the intensity of the stimulus . Skilled performers effectively speed their reactions by reading cues early and anticipating. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprint start

A sprinter's reaction time is the interval between the gun and their first movement out of the blocks — a simple reaction time situation. Goalkeeping A goalkeeper facing a penalty has a choice reaction, and anticipates cues to react faster, effectively reducing their reaction time. Batting A cricket batter reads the bowler's cues early to anticipate the ball, giving themselves more time to respond. ✍️ Using the term in context Define reaction time and distinguish it from movement and response time:

Reciprocal Inhibition — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reciprocal Inhibition IB Sport Science General Reciprocal Inhibition When the agonist contracts, the antagonist must relax — the neural mechanism behind smooth, coordinated movement. 📖 What it means Reciprocal inhibition is the neuromuscular process by which contraction of an agonist muscle causes reflex inhibition (relaxation) of the antagonist , allowing smooth movement.

When the nervous system sends a signal to the agonist to contract, it simultaneously sends an inhibitory signal to the antagonist, suppressing its activity. This prevents the two muscles from fighting against each other and allows efficient, fluid movement. Reciprocal inhibition is also exploited in active stretching techniques : contracting the agonist causes the antagonist to relax, allowing it to be stretched further. It contrasts with the simultaneous activation of both in coactivation . 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps curl As the biceps (agonist) contracts to flex the elbow, reciprocal inhibition relaxes the triceps (antagonist). Smooth movement

Reciprocal inhibition prevents agonist and antagonist fighting each other, producing smooth, efficient movement. Active stretching Contracting the quadriceps causes reciprocal inhibition of the hamstrings, allowing them to be stretched. ✍️ Using the term in context Define reciprocal inhibition and its effect: "Reciprocal inhibition is the neural process by which contraction of an agonist causes reflex inhibition of its antagonist, allowing smooth movement; it is contrasted with coactivation, and is exploited in active stretching." Recovery Oxygen Consumption — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Recovery Oxygen Consumption IB Sport Science General Recovery Oxygen Consumption The oxygen debt after exercise — the extra oxygen the body takes in after stopping to restore itself. 📖 What it means Recovery oxygen consumption (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption, EPOC ) is the elevated oxygen uptake after exercise used to restore the body toward its resting state . The body continues to consume more oxygen than at rest for a period after exercise ends.

This extra oxygen is used for processes such as replenishing phosphocreatine stores, removing lactate, restoring oxygen levels in myoglobin and blood, and returning elevated heart rate and temperature toward baseline . EPOC is greater after high-intensity exercise — particularly anaerobic efforts — than after moderate aerobic activity. It is one mechanism by which high-intensity training contributes to greater total energy expenditure even after the session ends. 🏅 Sporting examples Post-sprint Breathing heavily for several minutes after a maximal sprint is EPOC in action. Phosphocreatine Part of EPOC goes toward replenishing the phosphocreatine depleted during the sprint. Higher EPOC

High-intensity exercise produces greater EPOC than steady-state aerobic work. ✍️ Using the term in context Define EPOC and name its components: "EPOC (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) is the elevated oxygen uptake after exercise used to replenish phosphocreatine, remove lactate and restore blood oxygen and body temperature; it is greater after high-intensity exercise." Recovery Position — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Recovery Position BTEC Sport General Recovery Position A first-aid essential — the position that keeps an unconscious casualty safe until help arrives. 📖 What it means The recovery position is a first-aid body position used to keep an unconscious but breathing casualty's airway open and clear , while waiting for emergency help.

It involves turning the casualty onto their side, with the head tilted back and the chin lifted to keep the airway open, the upper leg bent forward to prevent rolling onto the front, and the upper arm extended to support the position. It prevents the tongue or vomit from blocking the airway. It is a key skill in sports first aid — coaches and staff may encounter injured or unconscious athletes and need to act quickly. The recovery position should be applied if a casualty is unconscious but breathing, and emergency services should be called immediately. 🏅 Sporting examples Unconscious casualty

An unconscious player who is breathing is placed in the recovery position to keep their airway clear while waiting for help. Preventing blockage The side-lying position prevents the tongue or vomit from blocking the airway. Sports first aid Coaches learn the recovery position as a key sports first-aid skill for managing pitch-side emergencies. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the recovery position and when it is used: "The recovery position places an unconscious but breathing casualty on their side with the airway open and clear, preventing the tongue or vomit from obstructing breathing; it is used in sports first aid while awaiting emergency services."

Recovery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Recovery General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Recovery The other half of training — the process during which the body adapts, repairs and comes back stronger. 📖 What it means Recovery is the process by which the body restores itself after exercise and adapts to the training stress . It is when the beneficial adaptations to training actually occur — not during the session itself, but during the recovery afterwards.

Recovery involves restoring energy stores (ATP, phosphocreatine and glycogen), removing metabolic by-products, repairing tissue, and rehydrating . The concept of supercompensation describes how, with the right balance of stress and recovery, the body rebuilds to a level slightly higher than before. Because adaptation depends on recovery, insufficient recovery leads to overtraining and declining performance , while adequate recovery — through rest, sleep, nutrition, hydration and methods such as active recovery — allows continued improvement. 🏅 Sporting examples Supercompensation

After a hard session and adequate recovery, an athlete's fitness rebuilds to a slightly higher level than before — the basis of improvement. Nutrition and sleep Refuelling with carbohydrate and getting good sleep are key parts of recovery that allow adaptation to occur. Too little recovery An athlete who trains hard without enough recovery slides toward overtraining and worsening performance. ✍️ Using the term in context Frame recovery as when adaptation happens:

"Recovery is the process by which the body restores energy stores, repairs tissue and adapts to training stress; adaptation occurs during recovery through supercompensation, so inadequate recovery leads to overtraining rather than improvement."
