Rectus Abdominis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rectus Abdominis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Rectus Abdominis The 'abs' — the paired vertical abdominal muscle that flexes the trunk and stabilises the core. 📖 What it means The rectus abdominis is a paired muscle running vertically along the front of the abdomen . It is the muscle most visible as the 'six pack' when body fat is low. Its primary action is trunk flexion — bringing the chest toward the hips (as in a crunch). It also assists with posterior pelvic tilt and contributes to core stability and intra-abdominal pressure, protecting the spine during effort.

Together with the other abdominal muscles (obliques and transverse abdominis), the rectus abdominis forms the abdominal wall , which is essential for core stability, force transfer and posture in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Trunk flexion A sit-up or crunch is driven by the rectus abdominis, which flexes the trunk. Core stability The rectus abdominis contributes to core stability during lifting, throwing and sprinting. Abdominal wall As part of the abdominal wall, it supports the spine and transfers force between the lower and upper body. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the rectus abdominis and its action:

"The rectus abdominis is the paired vertical abdominal muscle that produces trunk flexion (as in a crunch) and contributes to core stability and force transfer; it forms part of the abdominal wall alongside the obliques and transverse abdominis." RED-S — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › RED-S IB Sport Science General RED-S When the energy tank runs too low — a syndrome affecting athletes who don't eat enough for their training load. 📖 What it means RED-S (Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport) is a syndrome caused by insufficient energy intake relative to energy expenditure , impairing multiple physiological functions. It is the current, broader term replacing the older 'Female Athlete Triad'.

When energy availability is chronically low, the body prioritises survival over performance, leading to impaired bone health, hormonal function, immunity, cardiovascular health, psychological wellbeing and muscle function . In female athletes, menstrual disruption is a key indicator. RED-S affects athletes of any sex and is common in sports emphasising leanness or weight categories. Early recognition and adequate fuelling are essential, as chronic RED-S can cause long-term health and performance consequences including stress fractures and hormonal disruption. 🏅 Sporting examples Under-fuelling An endurance athlete who significantly restricts intake to reduce weight may develop RED-S.

Bone health Low energy availability impairs bone formation, increasing stress fracture risk. Recognition Menstrual disruption in female athletes is a warning sign of RED-S requiring medical review. ✍️ Using the term in context Define RED-S and its consequences: "RED-S is a syndrome of insufficient energy intake relative to expenditure, impairing bone health, hormonal function, immunity, cardiovascular health and performance; it affects all athletes but is particularly recognised in sports emphasising leanness." Note it replaces the female athlete triad and affects all sexes. 🔗 Related terms Energy Balance Bone Density Stress Fracture Nutrition Overtraining Lifestyle Choice

Reflex — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reflex IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Reflex An automatic reaction to a stimulus — the body bypassing the brain to respond fast. 📖 What it means A reflex is an automatic, involuntary motor response to a sensory stimulus, mediated via the spinal cord rather than the brain. Because the signal does not need to travel to the brain and back, reflexes are extremely fast.

A reflex arc consists of: a receptor (detects the stimulus) → a sensory neurone → the spinal cord (processes and relays) → a motor neurone → the effector (muscle contracts). The classic example is the stretch reflex , triggered by rapid muscle elongation. Reflexes are important in sport for protective responses (catching oneself in a fall, protecting a joint) and for movements that need to be faster than conscious control allows. Understanding reflexes explains why certain stretching and training techniques work the way they do. 🏅 Sporting examples Stretch reflex A rapid stretch of a muscle triggers the stretch reflex — an involuntary contraction — before conscious control can intervene.

Protection A reflex snatch of a falling object is completed via the spinal cord before the brain fully registers the event. Speed Reflexes are faster than voluntary movements because they bypass the brain. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a reflex and describe the reflex arc: "A reflex is an automatic, involuntary response mediated by the spinal cord, faster than voluntary movement; the reflex arc runs receptor → sensory neurone → spinal cord → motor neurone → effector, as in the stretch reflex." Give the stretch reflex as the prime sporting example. 🔗 Related terms Stretch Reflex Autogenic Inhibition Motor Neurone Proprioceptor Muscle Spindle All-or-None Law 🎓 Where this appears

Reinforcement — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reinforcement IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Reinforcement What makes a behaviour more likely to be repeated. 📖 What it means Reinforcement strengthens the link between a stimulus and a response, so that the behaviour becomes more likely to be repeated. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant after the behaviour, such as praise or a reward. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant, for example, a coach stops criticising when the performer does the skill correctly.

Punishment is different: it aims to make behaviour less likely, either by adding an unpleasant consequence or removing something pleasant. Positive reinforcement is generally considered the most effective for learning. 🏅 Sporting examples Praise A coach says 'well done' after a good pass (positive). Relief Criticism stops once a technique is corrected (negative). Punishment A player misses a session after a rule break. ✍️ Using the term in context Do not mix up the terms: "Positive reinforcement rewards correct responses to make them more likely, whereas negative reinforcement removes an unpleasant stimulus when the correct response is made." Reliability of Data — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reliability of Data IB Sport Science General Reliability of Data Consistency you can trust — data is reliable if you get the same result repeating the same test. 📖 What it means Reliability is the consistency and repeatability of measurements . A test or measurement is reliable if it produces the same (or very similar) results when repeated under the same conditions.

It is assessed through methods such as test-retest reliability (repeating the test at a later time) and inter-rater reliability (consistency between different observers). Statistical measures such as intraclass correlation coefficients can quantify reliability. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for a good test — a measure can be reliable without being valid . A bathroom scale with a consistent 2 kg offset is reliable but not accurate. Good data needs both reliability and validity. 🏅 Sporting examples Test-retest A grip strength test repeated twice gives values of 42 kg and 43 kg — the consistency indicates high reliability. Standardisation

Standardising conditions (same time of day, same equipment) improves reliability. Reliability vs validity A test can be reliable without being valid — consistency does not mean accuracy. ✍️ Using the term in context Define reliability and distinguish from validity: "Reliability is the consistency and repeatability of measurements; a reliable test produces similar results when repeated under the same conditions, and is improved by standardisation, but a test can be reliable without being valid." Always pair reliability with validity. 🔗 Related terms Validity Random Error Systematic Error Normative Data Standardisation Fitness Testing 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Reliability — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reliability General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Reliability Whether a test gives consistent, repeatable results — one of the two essential qualities of any worthwhile fitness test. 📖 What it means Reliability is the extent to which a test produces consistent, repeatable results . A reliable test, if repeated under the same conditions, will give the same or very similar results each time.

Reliability depends on standardising the test conditions — the same equipment, procedure, instructions, tester and environment — so that any change in the result reflects a real change in the performer, not a change in how the test was run. It is distinct from validity (whether a test measures what it claims to). A test can be reliable but not valid, and a good fitness test must be both — consistent and measuring the right thing. Reliability is essential for meaningfully monitoring progress over time. 🏅 Sporting examples Standardised conditions

To keep a bleep test reliable, a coach uses the same audio track, surface, instructions and procedure every time, so changes in score reflect real fitness changes. Monitoring A reliable test lets a coach compare an athlete's results across a season with confidence that differences are genuine. Reliable but not valid A test could give very consistent results (reliable) yet still not measure the intended component of fitness (not valid). ✍️ Using the term in context Define reliability and distinguish it from validity:

"Reliability is the extent to which a test gives consistent, repeatable results under standardised conditions; it is distinct from validity, and a good fitness test must be both reliable and valid." Residual Volume — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Residual Volume IB Sport Science General Residual Volume The air you can never breathe out — the volume that stays in the lungs even after a maximal exhalation. 📖 What it means The residual volume is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal exhalation . It cannot be voluntarily expired, and so it is not part of the vital capacity . The residual volume prevents the lungs from completely collapsing, maintains the structural integrity of the alveoli and keeps them ready for the next breath. It is typically around 1.0–1.5 litres in adults.

It is relevant when calculating total lung capacity (vital capacity + residual volume). Understanding it matters for interpreting lung volume measures: vital capacity is the usable portion; total lung capacity includes the air that always remains. 🏅 Sporting examples Cannot expire Even after blowing out as hard as possible, residual volume remains — it cannot be voluntarily removed. Total lung capacity Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume. Preventing collapse Residual volume keeps the alveoli slightly inflated, preventing their walls from sticking together. ✍️ Using the term in context Define residual volume and its role:

"Residual volume is the air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation, typically around 1.0–1.5 litres; it prevents alveolar collapse and is not included in vital capacity but is part of total lung capacity." Resistance Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Resistance Training General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Resistance Training Training against a load to build strength, power and muscle — a versatile method adaptable to almost any goal. 📖 What it means Resistance training is training in which muscles work against an external resistance — such as free weights, machines, resistance bands or body weight — to develop strength, power, muscular endurance or muscle size.

The adaptation depends on how the variables are set. Heavy loads and low repetitions develop maximal strength and power; lighter loads and high repetitions develop muscular endurance. Over time, resistance training drives adaptations including hypertrophy and improved motor unit recruitment . It is highly versatile and can be made sport-specific by selecting exercises that mimic the movements and muscle actions of the sport. It is important not only for performance but also for injury prevention and general health. 🏅 Sporting examples Strength/power sports A rugby forward uses heavy resistance training to build the strength and power needed for contact and scrummaging. Muscular endurance

An endurance athlete uses lighter loads and higher repetitions to build muscular endurance in key muscle groups. Injury prevention Targeted resistance training strengthens muscles and connective tissue, helping to prevent injuries such as hamstring strains. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain how load and repetitions determine the adaptation: "Resistance training works muscles against an external load; heavy loads with low repetitions develop strength and power, while lighter loads with high repetitions develop muscular endurance, with adaptations including hypertrophy and improved motor unit recruitment." Note it can be made sport-specific and aids injury prevention. 🔗 Related terms

Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Respiratory Exchange Ratio (RER) A gas-analysis ratio that shows whether fat or carbohydrate is fuelling exercise. 📖 What it means The respiratory exchange ratio (RER) is VCO2 ÷ VO2 , measured from expired air at the mouth. It is closely related to the respiratory quotient (RQ), which is measured at cell level. A value of about 0.7 indicates mainly fat use; about 1.0 indicates mainly carbohydrate . Values between show a mix of the two.

During very hard exercise RER can rise above 1.0 because hyperventilation blows off extra CO2 from buffering lactate, so it is not a pure fuel measure at that point. A rise above 1.0 is often used as a sign of maximal effort in VO2 max tests. 🏅 Sporting examples Rest At rest RER is about 0.8, showing a mix of fat and carbohydrate. Steady jog A low RER during an easy run shows a high contribution from fat. VO2 max test An RER above 1.1 is commonly taken as evidence the athlete has reached maximal effort. ✍️ Using the term in context Give the formula and interpret it:

"RER is the ratio of carbon dioxide produced to oxygen consumed; a value near 0.7 shows fat is the main fuel, while a value near 1.0 shows carbohydrate." RER and RQ are not identical: RER is measured at the mouth, RQ at the cells. 🔗 Related terms Respiratory Quotient (RQ) Fuel Utilisation Fatmax VO2 Max Carbohydrate Beta Oxidation 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → AS Level / Cambridge Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library Home · A–Z Library · Teacher Hub · YouTube · About · Privacy © 2026 Simply Sport Science · simplysportscience.co.uk

Respiratory Pump — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Respiratory Pump IB Sport Science General Respiratory Pump Breathing as a circulatory aid — how the pressure changes of ventilation help push blood back to the heart. 📖 What it means The respiratory pump is the mechanism by which pressure changes during breathing assist the return of venous blood to the heart . It is one of the mechanisms that aids venous return.

During inhalation , the thoracic cavity expands and pressure inside it falls. This lowered pressure is transmitted to the large veins and the right heart, creating a suction effect that draws blood toward the heart . During exhalation, pressure rises and the veins are gently compressed. Together with the skeletal muscle pump , venoconstriction and venous valves, the respiratory pump helps maintain venous return — particularly during exercise when breathing becomes faster and deeper, amplifying the pumping effect. 🏅 Sporting examples Inhalation suction When a runner inhales deeply, the fall in thoracic pressure draws venous blood toward the heart. Deep breathing

Faster, deeper breathing during exercise amplifies the respiratory pump's contribution to venous return. Combined pumps The respiratory and skeletal muscle pumps work together to maintain venous return during exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the respiratory pump and link it to venous return: "The respiratory pump aids venous return through the pressure changes of breathing; inhalation reduces thoracic pressure and draws blood toward the heart, and its effect is amplified during exercise by faster, deeper breathing." Pair it with the skeletal muscle pump. 🔗 Related terms Venous Return Skeletal Muscle Pump Stroke Volume Starling's Law Venoconstriction Cardiac Output

Respiratory Quotient (RQ) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Respiratory Quotient (RQ) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Respiratory Quotient (RQ) The cellular version of the exchange ratio, linked to the fuel being burned. 📖 What it means The respiratory quotient (RQ) is the volume of CO2 produced divided by the volume of O2 used in metabolism at cell level. The value depends on the fuel: carbohydrate about 1.0 , fat about 0.7 and protein about 0.8. A reading between 0.7 and 1.0 shows a mixture. In practice the ratio is measured from the breath, and this measure is called the respiratory exchange ratio (RER). The two are equal only in a steady state.

🏅 Sporting examples Rest A resting RQ of about 0.8 shows fat and carbohydrate both contributing. High intensity An RQ approaching 1.0 shows carbohydrate is now the main fuel. Fasted exercise A lower RQ shows greater use of fat when glycogen stores are low. ✍️ Using the term in context State the values: "An RQ of 0.7 shows fat is being oxidised; an RQ of 1.0 shows carbohydrate is being oxidised." Resting Heart Rate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Resting Heart Rate IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Resting Heart Rate The heart rate at complete rest — a simple, powerful indicator of aerobic fitness and, tracked over time, of recovery. 📖 What it means Resting heart rate is the number of times the heart beats per minute when the body is completely at rest , ideally measured on waking. A typical adult value is around 60–80 bpm.

It is a useful indicator of aerobic fitness : endurance-trained individuals tend to have a low resting heart rate (bradycardia) , sometimes below 40 bpm, because cardiac hypertrophy has increased their stroke volume — the heart pumps more blood per beat, so it needs to beat fewer times to circulate the same volume. Tracked over time, resting heart rate is also used to monitor recovery and detect overtraining or illness : an unexpectedly elevated morning resting heart rate can be an early warning sign that the body has not fully recovered. 🏅 Sporting examples Fitness indicator

An endurance athlete's low resting heart rate reflects a large stroke volume from cardiac hypertrophy — a hallmark of good aerobic fitness. Monitoring training A coach tracks athletes' morning resting heart rate; a sustained rise can flag overtraining or oncoming illness. Improvement As a beginner's aerobic fitness improves over months, their resting heart rate gradually falls. ✍️ Using the term in context Link a low resting heart rate to stroke volume and fitness: "Resting heart rate is the heart rate at complete rest; a low value (bradycardia) indicates good aerobic fitness, resulting from cardiac hypertrophy and a larger stroke volume, and a rise can signal overtraining or illness."

Resting Metabolic Rate — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Resting Metabolic Rate IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Resting Metabolic Rate Energy at rest — similar to BMR but measured in slightly less strict conditions. 📖 What it means Resting metabolic rate (RMR) is the energy the body uses at rest to sustain basic functions , measured under standardised but less strict conditions than the basal metabolic rate (BMR). It typically gives a slightly higher value than BMR.

Like BMR, it accounts for the majority of total daily energy expenditure and is influenced by lean body mass, age, sex and hormones . Greater muscle mass raises RMR because muscle is metabolically active even at rest. RMR is useful for guiding energy intake : total daily energy needs are RMR plus the energy cost of physical activity and digestion. Understanding it helps athletes and coaches plan nutrition to meet training demands without over- or under-fuelling. 🏅 Sporting examples Most of daily expenditure RMR accounts for 60–75% of most people's total daily energy use. Muscle raises it An athlete with greater lean mass has a higher RMR, burning more energy even at rest. Nutrition planning

Knowing their RMR helps an athlete estimate total daily energy needs. ✍️ Using the term in context Define RMR and distinguish from BMR: "Resting metabolic rate is the energy used at rest to maintain basic functions, slightly higher than BMR due to less strict conditions; it makes up most daily energy expenditure and is raised by greater lean body mass." Reversibility — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Reversibility General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Reversibility Use it or lose it — the principle that fitness gains are lost when training stops. 📖 What it means The principle of reversibility states that the fitness adaptations gained through training are gradually lost when training stops or is significantly reduced . In short, 'use it or lose it'.

When training ceases ( detraining ), the body reverses its adaptations: aerobic gains such as increased stroke volume and mitochondrial density decline, and strength gains reduce as muscle atrophies. Aerobic fitness tends to be lost relatively quickly , while strength is generally retained a little longer. Reversibility explains why consistency matters and why injury layoffs and off-seasons cause a loss of fitness. It is one of the core principles of training, alongside progression, overload and specificity. 🏅 Sporting examples Injury layoff An injured athlete who cannot train loses aerobic fitness within weeks, illustrating reversibility — which is why cross-training is used where possible.

Off-season A player returning from an off-season break finds their fitness has declined and must be rebuilt. Detraining rates After stopping training, aerobic adaptations are lost faster than strength adaptations. ✍️ Using the term in context State the principle and note the differing loss rates: "The principle of reversibility states that fitness adaptations are lost when training stops (detraining); aerobic fitness is generally lost more quickly than strength, which is why consistency is important." Link reversibility to injury layoffs and off-seasons. 🔗 Related terms Principle of Progression Overload Specificity Atrophy Periodisation Detraining 🎓 Where this appears BTEC Sport

RICE — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › RICE General BTEC Sport RICE The first-aid protocol for acute soft-tissue injuries — Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. 📖 What it means RICE is a widely taught immediate treatment protocol for acute soft-tissue injuries such as sprains and strains. The letters stand for Rest, Ice, Compression and Elevation . Rest protects the injury from further damage; Ice reduces pain and limits swelling by constricting blood vessels; Compression (e.g. a bandage) helps control swelling; and Elevation raises the injured part to reduce blood flow to it and limit swelling.

RICE is used in the immediate period after an acute injury to control pain and swelling and support early recovery. It is a starting point for managing minor soft-tissue injuries, with more serious injuries requiring professional medical assessment. 🏅 Sporting examples Ankle sprain A player who rolls their ankle applies RICE — resting, icing, compressing with a bandage and elevating the leg — to control pain and swelling. Muscle strain RICE is used immediately after a muscle strain to limit swelling and protect the injured tissue. Limits For a suspected serious injury, RICE is only a first step before seeking professional medical assessment. ✍️ Using the term in context

Expand the acronym and explain each element's purpose: "RICE — Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation — is the immediate treatment for acute soft-tissue injuries such as sprains; it controls pain and swelling, with rest protecting the injury and ice, compression and elevation limiting swelling." Ringelmann Effect — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ringelmann Effect IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Ringelmann Effect The bigger the group, the less each person pulls — the social phenomenon behind individual effort in teams. 📖 What it means The Ringelmann Effect is the tendency for individual effort to decrease as group size increases . Ringelmann found that the total pulling force in a rope-pulling task did not increase proportionally as more people were added — individuals pulled less hard in a larger group.

It is closely related to social loafing : people work less hard when in a group, partly because individual contribution becomes less identifiable and accountability decreases. The larger the group, the more pronounced the effect. In sport, coaches counter the Ringelmann effect by identifying individual contributions, setting individual goals within the team, and making each person's effort visible and valued . It highlights why team size alone does not guarantee proportional improvement in performance. 🏅 Sporting examples Rope pulling In Ringelmann's original study, individual force in a tug-of-war decreased as group size grew. Team sport

A large squad may see more players contributing less than they would individually — the Ringelmann effect. Counter-strategy Tracking individual statistics and setting personal targets helps counter the effect. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the Ringelmann effect and link to social loafing: "The Ringelmann effect is the tendency for individual effort to decrease as group size increases; related to social loafing, it occurs because individual contributions become less identifiable, and is countered by making individual effort visible and valued." Pair it with social loafing. 🔗 Related terms Social Loafing Group Cohesion Motivation Task Cohesion Leadership Achievement Motivation

Rockport Walk Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rockport Walk Test General Rockport Walk Test An accessible fitness test for all — estimating aerobic capacity from a 1-mile walk time and heart rate. 📖 What it means The Rockport Walk Test is a submaximal fitness test that estimates VO₂ max from the time taken to walk one mile (1.6 km) as fast as possible, combined with the heart rate measured immediately after.

It is particularly useful for less fit populations, older adults or those returning from injury , for whom maximal tests are unsuitable. Walking briskly produces an elevated heart rate, and along with the time and the performer's age, sex and body mass, VO₂ max is estimated from an equation. Like other submaximal tests, it gives an estimate rather than a direct measure . It is simple, safe and needs only a measured course and a timer, making it accessible in many settings. 🏅 Sporting examples Less fit populations The Rockport Walk Test suits older or less fit individuals who cannot safely complete a maximal test. Estimating VO2 max

Heart rate at the end of the walk, combined with time and personal details, gives a VO₂ max estimate. Minimal equipment The test needs only a measured 1-mile course and a heart rate monitor. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and its target population: "The Rockport Walk Test estimates VO₂ max from 1-mile walk time and post-walk heart rate; safe and practical for less fit or older populations where maximal tests are unsuitable, it gives an estimate rather than a direct measure." Rotation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rotation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Rotation Turning on an axis — the movement of a bone around its own long axis. 📖 What it means Rotation is the turning movement of a bone around its own longitudinal axis . It differs from circumduction (which traces a cone) by spinning the bone in place rather than sweeping it through a range. Rotation occurs at joints that allow it, particularly pivot joints and ball and socket joints . Examples include medial (inward) and lateral (outward) rotation of the shoulder, and the rotation of the head at the atlantoaxial joint.

It is one of the movements analysed in movement analysis and planes of movement : rotation occurs in the transverse plane about a longitudinal (vertical) axis . 🏅 Sporting examples Shoulder Medial and lateral rotation of the shoulder occur in many throwing and swimming actions. Head turn Turning the head to look over the shoulder is rotation at the atlantoaxial pivot joint. Transverse plane Rotation occurs in the transverse plane about a longitudinal axis. ✍️ Using the term in context Define rotation and name the plane and axis:

Rotator Cuff — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rotator Cuff IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Rotator Cuff The group of small muscles that stabilise the shoulder — unglamorous but essential, and a frequent site of injury in throwing sports. 📖 What it means The rotator cuff is a group of four small muscles surrounding the shoulder joint . Their main role is to stabilise the shoulder — holding the head of the upper arm bone securely in its socket — and to assist in rotation of the arm.

Because the shoulder is a highly mobile ball and socket joint, it sacrifices stability for range of movement, and the rotator cuff provides much of the dynamic stability that keeps the joint secure during movement. The rotator cuff is heavily used and commonly injured in overhead and throwing sports , where the repeated high-speed rotation places great demand on these muscles. Strengthening them is important for both performance and injury prevention. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing sports A javelin thrower or baseball pitcher relies on the rotator cuff to stabilise the shoulder through repeated high-speed throwing — and these athletes commonly suffer rotator cuff injuries. Swimming

A swimmer's rotator cuff stabilises the shoulder through thousands of overhead strokes, making it prone to overuse injury. Injury prevention Athletes in overhead sports include rotator cuff strengthening to stabilise the shoulder and reduce injury risk. ✍️ Using the term in context State its stabilising role and injury vulnerability: "The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles that stabilise the shoulder, holding the arm securely in its socket; it is heavily used and commonly injured in overhead and throwing sports, so strengthening it aids performance and injury prevention." Rowing Step Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Rowing Step Test IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Rowing Step Test A fitness test of aerobic fitness for rowers. 📖 What it means The Rowing Step Test is a submaximal test on a rowing ergometer in which the athlete rows through several stages of increasing workload while heart rate is recorded. Protocol: Each stage lasts a few minutes at a set power or pace, with heart rate recorded at the end. The test stops before maximal effort.

Interpreting results: Heart rate at set workloads, or the power at a fixed heart rate, is compared across tests to track aerobic fitness. A lower heart rate at the same power means improved fitness. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A rower is tested every six weeks to track fitness. Training use Results help set training zones for steady-state rowing. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Ruler Drop Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ruler Drop Test General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Ruler Drop Test How fast can you catch a falling ruler? — a simple test of reaction time. 📖 What it means The Ruler Drop Test is a simple test of reaction time measuring how quickly a person can catch a dropped ruler. The performer holds their fingers around the lower end of a ruler; the tester releases it without warning and the performer catches it as quickly as possible. The distance the ruler falls before being caught gives the reaction time.

It is quick, cheap and requires no equipment beyond a ruler , making it practical for school and club use. Results can be compared against normative data or used to monitor individual change over time. Its main limitation is specificity : it measures a simple, single-limb response to a visual stimulus, which may not reflect the reaction time demands of complex, multidirectional sport. It is best used as an indicator, not a comprehensive measure. 🏅 Sporting examples Simple to administer A ruler and a partner are all that's needed to test reaction time in a class or training session. Distance = time The further the ruler falls before being caught, the slower the reaction time. Limitation

Catching a falling ruler is a simple visual-motor task that may not reflect reactive demands in sport. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the Ruler Drop Test and evaluate it: "The Ruler Drop Test measures reaction time by recording how far a dropped ruler falls before being caught; it is quick, cheap and needs only a ruler, but has low ecological validity for sport-specific reaction demands." Running Economy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Running Economy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Running Economy How cheaply a runner can run at a set speed. 📖 What it means Running economy is the oxygen cost of running at a particular steady speed, usually in ml of oxygen per kg per kilometre. A lower oxygen cost means better economy . It helps explain why runners with a similar VO2 max can perform very differently. Factors include biomechanics, muscle-tendon stiffness, body composition, footwear and training. Economy improves with high mileage, strength and plyometric training and hill work. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running

Two runners with the same VO2 max race at 5 km; the one with better economy finishes ahead. Strength training A runner improves economy through heavy resistance work and plyometrics. Sagittal Plane — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sagittal Plane IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Sagittal Plane One of the three planes of movement — the vertical divide between left and right, in which flexion and extension occur. 📖 What it means The sagittal plane is an imaginary vertical plane that divides the body into left and right halves . Movements that occur in this plane are front-to-back movements. The main movements in the sagittal plane are flexion and extension — such as bending and straightening the elbow or knee. These movements occur about a frontal (mediolateral) axis , which runs from side to side.

The sagittal plane is one of the three planes of movement , alongside the frontal and transverse planes. Many common sporting actions — running, cycling, a biceps curl — occur predominantly in the sagittal plane. 🏅 Sporting examples Running The forward-and-back movements of the legs during a running stride occur in the sagittal plane — flexion and extension about a frontal axis. Biceps curl A biceps curl occurs in the sagittal plane, flexing and extending the elbow. Somersault A forward somersault is a sagittal-plane rotation, the body rotating front-to-back about a frontal axis. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the plane, its movements and axis together:

Sarcomere — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sarcomere IB Sport Science General Sarcomere The basic contractile unit of muscle — the microscopic segment that shortens to produce force. 📖 What it means A sarcomere is the basic functional (contractile) unit of a muscle fibre . Muscle fibres are made up of many sarcomeres arranged end to end, and it is their shortening that produces muscle contraction. Each sarcomere contains overlapping thin filaments (actin) and thick filaments (myosin) . During contraction, described by the sliding filament theory, the actin filaments are pulled over the myosin, and the sarcomere shortens .

Because a whole muscle contains millions of sarcomeres in series and in parallel, the tiny shortening of each sarcomere sums to shorten the entire muscle , producing the force and movement used in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Contraction When a bicep contracts in a curl, millions of sarcomeres shorten simultaneously to shorten the whole muscle. Building blocks The repeating sarcomere structure gives skeletal muscle its striped (striated) appearance under a microscope. Force production The number and arrangement of sarcomeres influences how much force and over what range a muscle can produce. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define the sarcomere as the contractile unit and link to sliding filaments: "A sarcomere is the basic contractile unit of a muscle fibre, containing overlapping actin and myosin filaments; during contraction the actin slides over the myosin, shortening the sarcomere, and the summed shortening of millions of sarcomeres shortens the whole muscle." Sarcoplasmic Reticulum — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sarcoplasmic Reticulum IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Sarcoplasmic Reticulum The calcium store inside a muscle fibre. 📖 What it means The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is a network of membrane-bound tubes wrapped around each myofibril in a muscle fibre. It is the muscle's store of calcium ions . When an action potential travels down the T-tubules , the SR releases calcium into the sarcoplasm, which triggers contraction. Afterwards, calcium pumps actively return calcium to the SR, which needs ATP.

Fast-twitch fibres have a more extensive SR and release and take up calcium faster, which helps explain their quicker contraction and relaxation. 🏅 Sporting examples Contraction Calcium release from the SR starts the cycle. Relaxation Calcium pumps return it to the SR. Fibre types Fast fibres have a better developed SR. ✍️ Using the term in context State its function: "The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium and releases it when stimulated, allowing actin and myosin to interact and the muscle to contract." Scalar Quantity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Scalar Quantity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Scalar Quantity A quantity with size but no direction — one half of a fundamental biomechanics distinction. 📖 What it means A scalar quantity is a quantity that has magnitude (size) only, and no direction . It is fully described by a number and a unit. Common scalar quantities in sport biomechanics include distance, speed, mass and energy . For example, saying a runner covered '400 metres' or ran at '5 metres per second' describes magnitude without any direction.

Scalars contrast with vector quantities , which have both magnitude and direction (such as displacement, velocity, acceleration and force). Correctly distinguishing scalars from vectors is essential for accurate biomechanical analysis and calculation. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance The 400m a runner covers is a scalar — it states how far, with no direction (unlike displacement, which does). Speed Running at 5 m/s is a scalar quantity; velocity, which adds direction, is its vector counterpart. Mass A shot's mass is a scalar — a magnitude only — whereas the force applied to it is a vector. ✍️ Using the term in context Define scalars and contrast with vectors, with examples:

SCAT (Sports Competition Anxiety Test) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › SCAT (Sports Competition Anxiety Test) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General SCAT (Sports Competition Anxiety Test) A questionnaire that measures how anxious an athlete tends to get in competition — a measure of competitive trait anxiety. 📖 What it means The SCAT (Sport Competition Anxiety Test) is a self-report questionnaire that measures a performer's competitive trait anxiety — their general tendency to become anxious in competitive situations.

Because it measures trait anxiety, it assesses a relatively stable predisposition , in contrast to the CSAI-2, which measures situation-specific state anxiety before a particular event. A high SCAT score suggests a performer is generally prone to competition anxiety. As a self-report tool, the SCAT is quick and practical , but it relies on honest, accurate responses and gives only a general trait measure rather than capturing anxiety in a specific moment. It is a common example of a psychological assessment in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Identifying prone athletes A coach uses the SCAT to identify athletes with high competitive trait anxiety, who may need extra anxiety-management support.

Trait vs state The SCAT gives a general picture of an athlete's anxiety tendency, while the CSAI-2 would capture their anxiety just before a specific match. Guiding support A high SCAT score prompts a coach to introduce relaxation and confidence-building strategies before competition. ✍️ Using the term in context Define SCAT as a measure of competitive trait anxiety and contrast with CSAI-2: "The SCAT is a self-report questionnaire measuring competitive trait anxiety — a stable tendency to become anxious in competition — in contrast to the CSAI-2, which measures situation-specific state anxiety." Schema Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Schema Theory AS Level / Cambridge General Schema Theory An influential theory of how we adapt skills to new situations — using stored 'rules' rather than fixed motor programmes. 📖 What it means Schema theory proposes that we do not store a separate motor programme for every possible movement, but instead store general rules, or 'schemas', that can be adapted to produce movements in new situations . This explains how performers cope with novel variations of a skill.

A schema is built from four sources of information : the initial conditions (the situation), the response specifications (what to do), the sensory consequences (how it felt), and the response outcome (the result). From these, two schemas develop: the recall schema (to produce the movement) and the recognition schema (to evaluate it). The practical implication is powerful: because schemas are built by experiencing varied situations , schema theory strongly supports the use of variable practice — practising a skill in many different conditions — to build adaptable, transferable skills. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing

A player who has thrown from many distances and angles has a well-developed schema, letting them adapt to a throw they have never made before. Variable practice Schema theory explains why practising passing from many positions and distances builds a more adaptable skill than repeating one fixed pass. Open skills Schema theory helps explain how performers of open skills constantly adapt their movements to new game situations. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain schemas as adaptable rules and link to variable practice:

"Schema theory proposes that performers store general rules (schemas) that can be adapted to new situations, built from information such as initial conditions and response outcomes; because varied experience builds richer schemas, the theory supports variable practice." Second-Class Lever — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Second-Class Lever IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Second-Class Lever The lever that gives mechanical advantage — the wheelbarrow arrangement, letting a large load be moved with less effort. 📖 What it means A second-class lever is one in which the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort — the arrangement of a wheelbarrow. This arrangement always gives a mechanical advantage . Because the effort arm is longer than the load arm, a second-class lever allows a large load to be moved with a relatively small effort — it favours force over speed and range of movement.

The classic example in the body is plantar flexion at the ankle when rising onto the toes : the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, the body's weight is the load, and the calf muscles provide the effort. Second-class levers are relatively uncommon in the body. 🏅 Sporting examples Rising onto the toes Standing on tiptoe uses a second-class lever at the ball of the foot, giving the calf muscles a mechanical advantage to lift the body's weight. Mechanical advantage The second-class lever lets a relatively small muscular effort move the large load of body weight. Force over speed This lever favours force, sacrificing the speed and range that third-class levers provide. ✍️ Using the term in context

State the arrangement and the mechanical advantage: "In a second-class lever the load lies between the fulcrum and the effort, giving a mechanical advantage; rising onto the toes is the body's example, with the ball of the foot as the fulcrum, allowing a small effort to move a large load." Sedentary Lifestyle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sedentary Lifestyle BTEC Sport General AS Level / Cambridge Sedentary Lifestyle A life without enough movement — the single most modifiable risk factor for a range of major health conditions. 📖 What it means A sedentary lifestyle involves little physical activity and extended periods of sitting or low-energy behaviour . It is strongly associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, some cancers and poor mental health.

Physical inactivity is one of the leading causes of preventable ill health worldwide. Even meeting exercise guidelines does not fully offset the harm of prolonged sitting : breaking up sedentary time regularly is recommended in addition to structured activity. In sport and PE contexts, tackling sedentary behaviour is a key rationale for participation programmes and physical activity guidelines. Understanding its health consequences underpins health education across all course specifications. 🏅 Sporting examples Health risks A sedentary lifestyle is associated with cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and poor mental health. Breaking sitting time

Even small breaks from prolonged sitting have measurable health benefits. PE rationale One core aim of PE is to counteract sedentary behaviour by building lifelong physical activity habits. ✍️ Using the term in context Define sedentary lifestyle and link to health risk: "A sedentary lifestyle involves little physical activity and extended inactivity, strongly associated with cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes and obesity; regular activity and breaking up prolonged sitting both reduce the risk." Self-Confidence — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Self-Confidence IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Self-Confidence The belief that you can succeed — a broad psychological quality strongly linked to performance under pressure. 📖 What it means Self-confidence is a performer's general belief that they can achieve success . It tends to be broader and more stable than task-specific self-efficacy, though the two are closely related.

Self-confidence strongly influences performance: confident athletes tend to set challenging goals, persist through difficulty, maintain focus under pressure and interpret nerves positively . Low confidence can create anxiety and a fear of failure, harming performance. It is built through many of the same routes as self-efficacy — experiencing success, positive reinforcement, good preparation, imagery and positive self-talk — and is a key subcomponent measured by anxiety questionnaires such as the CSAI-2. 🏅 Sporting examples Under pressure A confident penalty taker stays composed and focused, while low confidence can trigger anxiety and disrupt technique. Building it

A coach builds confidence through good preparation, achievable early successes, positive feedback and imagery of successful performance. Interpreting nerves A self-confident athlete interprets pre-competition nerves as a sign of readiness rather than a threat. ✍️ Using the term in context Define self-confidence and link it to performance and its development: "Self-confidence is the general belief that one can succeed; it improves performance by increasing persistence, focus and positive interpretation of nerves, and is built through success, preparation, positive reinforcement, imagery and self-talk." Relate it to self-efficacy (task-specific) and note it is measured by the CSAI-2.

Self-Determination Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Self-Determination Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Self-Determination Theory Why people stay motivated — a theory built on the three needs of autonomy, competence and relatedness. 📖 What it means Self-Determination Theory (SDT) is a theory of motivation proposing that people are most motivated when three basic psychological needs are met: autonomy, competence and relatedness .

Autonomy is the need to feel in control of one's actions; competence is the need to feel effective and capable; relatedness is the need to feel connected to others. When these are satisfied, intrinsic motivation is high — people engage because they find the activity inherently rewarding. When external controls undermine autonomy or feedback undermines competence, motivation can become external (extrinsic) or fade altogether. Coaches promote SDT-aligned motivation by giving athletes choices, building skills progressively, and creating a supportive team environment. 🏅 Sporting examples Autonomy

Allowing athletes to have input into training design supports their autonomy and intrinsic motivation. Competence Progressive skill challenges that are achievable — but not too easy — build competence and motivation. Relatedness A team culture of support and belonging satisfies the relatedness need, sustaining motivation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the three SDT needs and link to intrinsic motivation: "Self-Determination Theory proposes that intrinsic motivation thrives when autonomy (feeling in control), competence (feeling capable) and relatedness (feeling connected) are met; coaches promote these by giving choices, building skills and fostering belonging."

Self-Efficacy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Self-Efficacy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Self-Efficacy Confidence in your ability to succeed at a specific task — a powerful, situation-specific predictor of performance. 📖 What it means Self-efficacy is a performer's belief in their ability to succeed at a specific task or in a specific situation . Unlike general self-confidence, it is situation-specific — a performer may have high self-efficacy for one skill and low for another.

According to Bandura , self-efficacy is built from four main sources: past performance accomplishments (previous success, the most powerful source), vicarious experience (seeing others like oneself succeed), verbal persuasion (encouragement from others), and emotional/physiological states (interpreting arousal positively). High self-efficacy tends to increase effort, persistence and performance , so coaches deliberately build it — for example by ensuring early success, using appropriate role models, giving genuine encouragement, and helping performers read their nerves as readiness rather than fear. 🏅 Sporting examples Past success

A gymnast who has previously landed a skill has high self-efficacy for it, boosting their confidence and performance next time. Vicarious experience Seeing a similar teammate succeed at a vault raises a performer's belief that they too can do it. Building it A coach ensures a nervous beginner experiences early success and offers genuine encouragement to build task-specific self-efficacy. ✍️ Using the term in context Define self-efficacy as task-specific and name Bandura's four sources:

"Self-efficacy is the belief in one's ability to succeed at a specific task; Bandura identified four sources — past performance accomplishments, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion and emotional states — with previous success the most powerful." Self-Fulfilling Prophecy — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Self-Fulfilling Prophecy IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Self-Fulfilling Prophecy When expectations create the result they predict. 📖 What it means A self-fulfilling prophecy occurs when an expectation leads to behaviour that makes it come true . It is also called the Pygmalion effect when it is a positive expectation. A coach who believes a player is talented may give them more attention, practice and feedback , so the player improves. A coach who expects little may give less, and the player falls behind, confirming the belief.

Coaches should review their expectations , give each athlete fair attention and set high but realistic standards for all. 🏅 Sporting examples Selection The 'star' player gets more coaching time. Low expectations A pupil told they are not sporty stops trying. Pygmalion Positive expectation raises performance. ✍️ Using the term in context Show the cycle: "A coach's high expectations led to more feedback and opportunity, which improved the player's performance and confirmed the expectation." Self-Talk — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Self-Talk IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Self-Talk The inner voice as a performance tool — deliberately using positive statements to boost confidence and focus. 📖 What it means Self-talk is the internal (or spoken) dialogue a performer has with themselves , used deliberately as a psychological technique to improve performance. It can be positive (helpful) or negative (harmful).

Positive self-talk is used to build confidence, maintain focus, control arousal and counter negative thoughts . It includes motivational statements ('I can do this') and instructional cues ('watch the ball') that direct attention to the task. A key application is thought-stopping combined with reframing — recognising a negative thought, halting it, and replacing it with a positive or instructional one. Self-talk is particularly useful for managing cognitive anxiety . 🏅 Sporting examples Confidence Before a serve, a tennis player uses positive self-talk — 'I've practised this, I'm ready' — to build confidence and calm nerves. Instructional cue

A high jumper repeats an instructional cue ('fast and tall') to focus attention on the key technical point. Countering negativity A performer catches a negative thought ('I'll miss'), stops it, and reframes it positively ('smooth and controlled'). ✍️ Using the term in context Define self-talk and its uses, distinguishing positive from negative: "Self-talk is a performer's internal dialogue used as a technique; positive self-talk, whether motivational or instructional, builds confidence, maintains focus and counters negative thoughts, making it effective for managing cognitive anxiety." Serial Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Serial Skill AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Serial Skill A skill made of several discrete actions linked in sequence — one of the three ways of classifying skills by continuity. 📖 What it means A serial skill is one made up of several discrete skills linked together in a specific sequence to form a longer, integrated movement. The order of the sub-skills matters. Serial skills sit in the middle of the discrete–serial–continuous continuum . A discrete skill has a clear start and end; a serial skill chains several discrete skills together; a continuous skill flows on with no clear start or finish.

Because they are made of parts in sequence, serial skills are often well suited to being learned through part practice or whole–part–whole practice , mastering the individual elements before linking them smoothly. 🏅 Sporting examples Triple jump The triple jump is a serial skill — the hop, step and jump are discrete actions performed in a set sequence to form the whole. Gymnastics routine A floor routine chains together many discrete skills in a specific order, making it a serial skill. Lay-up A basketball lay-up links dribbling, picking up the ball, stepping and shooting into a sequence. ✍️ Using the term in context Classify the skill on the continuity continuum:

"The triple jump is a serial skill because it links several discrete skills — the hop, step and jump — in a set sequence; this sits between discrete and continuous skills on the continuum." Shaping — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Shaping AS Level / Cambridge General Shaping Rewarding small steps toward a big skill — a coaching technique that builds complex behaviour through gradual approximations. 📖 What it means Shaping is a coaching technique that reinforces successive approximations of a target skill , progressively moving toward the full, correct performance. Rather than waiting for the perfect action, small steps in the right direction are rewarded.

It is rooted in behaviourist principles — reinforcing approximations encourages the performer to get progressively closer to the target. Each step is rewarded only once the previous has been achieved, raising the bar progressively. Shaping is useful when the target skill is too complex for the learner to produce all at once . It is closely linked to part practice and can be combined with other guidance and feedback approaches to build complex skills systematically. 🏅 Sporting examples Complex skill Teaching a young gymnast a back handspring: each step (arms back, jump, back bend) is reinforced before combining. Gradual progression

Shaping rewards close approximations of the target, raising the bar as each is achieved. Behaviourist roots Shaping builds on operant conditioning — reinforcing successive approximations toward the target. ✍️ Using the term in context Define shaping and link it to part practice: "Shaping is a technique that reinforces successive approximations of a target skill, progressively raising the standard; it is useful for complex skills too difficult to produce all at once, and is related to part practice." Shin Splints — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Shin Splints General BTEC Sport Shin Splints Pain along the shin — a common overuse injury in runners and jumping athletes from excessive impact loading. 📖 What it means Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) is pain along the shin bone (tibia) caused by overuse , commonly affecting runners, jumpers and military personnel. It results from repetitive impact stress on the periosteum (bone lining) and surrounding tissues.

Common causes include rapid increases in training load, hard surfaces, inadequate footwear and excessive pronation . Pain is typically felt along the inner edge of the tibia and worsens with activity. Management involves relative rest, ice and gradual return to activity . Prevention focuses on progressive training load increases, appropriate footwear, surface variation and addressing any biomechanical issues such as overpronation. 🏅 Sporting examples Runner's pain A runner who rapidly increases their mileage may develop shin splints — pain along the inner tibia. Causes Hard surfaces, excessive pronation and sudden load increases are common contributing factors. Prevention

Gradual progression, appropriate footwear and addressing biomechanical issues help prevent shin splints. ✍️ Using the term in context Define shin splints and its causes: "Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) is pain along the tibia from repetitive impact overuse, common in runners; causes include rapid load increases, hard surfaces and overpronation, and it is managed with rest and a gradual return." Short and Long-term Memory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Short and Long-term Memory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Short and Long-term Memory Where information is held briefly and where it is stored for good. 📖 What it means Short-term memory (STM) holds a limited amount of information (about 7 ± 2 items ) for roughly 20–30 seconds unless it is rehearsed. Long-term memory (LTM) has a very large capacity and stores information, such as learned skills and motor programmes, for a long time. Information passes from STM to LTM through rehearsal and practice . A stored motor programme can then be recalled and used.

Coaches help learners by giving few cues at a time, chunking information, and repeating practice so skills are stored in LTM. 🏅 Sporting examples Learning a skill A beginner can remember only one or two coaching points at a time. Shot Put — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Shot Put BTEC Sport General Shot Put Pushing a heavy ball as far as possible. 📖 What it means In the shot put , the athlete pushes (does not throw) a metal ball from the shoulder: 7.26 kg for men and 4 kg for women, from a circle 2.135 m across. Simple Sets (Training System) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Simple Sets (Training System) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Simple Sets (Training System) The standard way to organise a lifting session. 📖 What it means In the simple set system (also called straight sets), the athlete performs a set number of repetitions of one exercise , rests, and repeats for the planned number of sets before moving to the next exercise. The load, repetitions, sets and rest are chosen to match the training goal: heavy loads with low repetitions and long rests for strength, moderate loads with 8 to 12 repetitions for hypertrophy and lighter loads with higher repetitions for endurance. Simple Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Simple Skill AS Level / Cambridge General Simple Skill A skill with low demands — requiring little decision-making or information processing to perform. 📖 What it means A simple skill is one with low information-processing demands, requiring little decision-making or attention . It sits at one end of the simple–complex continuum. Simple skills are typically gross, predictable and easily automated . They can be executed with high arousal without impairing performance, because little cognitive processing is needed. Examples include a squat, a straight sprint or a basic throw.

Because they are easily learned and automated, simple skills are well suited to fixed, repetitive practice and can be performed at higher arousal levels. They contrast with complex skills, which require fine control and decision-making and suit lower arousal. 🏅 Sporting examples Gross action A maximal squat is a simple skill — it requires little decision-making and is performed the same way each time. Higher arousal A simple skill such as a sprint start benefits from high arousal, as the dominant response is correct. Contrast A simple skill (forward roll) sits at the opposite end of the continuum from a complex skill (gymnastics routine). ✍️ Using the term in context

Single Channel Hypothesis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Single Channel Hypothesis IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Single Channel Hypothesis The idea that the brain handles one decision at a time. 📖 What it means The single channel hypothesis (Welford) says that the decision-making part of the brain, the translatory mechanism , can deal with only one stimulus at a time . If a second stimulus arrives before the first has been dealt with, it must wait , causing a delay called the psychological refractory period (PRP) . The second response is therefore slower.

This explains why a dummy or feint works: an opponent who responds to the dummy is delayed in responding to the real move. The hypothesis is simple, but not everyone agrees that processing is always one at a time. 🏅 Sporting examples Basketball A pump fake delays the defender's response. Boxing A feint then a real punch gives a delayed response. Rugby A dummy pass fools the defender. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to feints: "Because only one stimulus can be processed at a time, a second stimulus after a dummy has to wait, causing the psychological refractory period." Sinoatrial Node (SAN) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sinoatrial Node (SAN) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Sinoatrial Node (SAN) The heart's natural pacemaker — where every heartbeat begins. 📖 What it means The sinoatrial node (SAN) is the heart's natural pacemaker, located in the right atrium . It generates the electrical impulse that initiates each heartbeat, making the heart myogenic — capable of beating without nervous system input.

The impulse from the SAN spreads across both atria, causing them to contract. It then reaches the atrioventricular node (AVN) , which relays it to the ventricles. Heart rate is controlled by the autonomic nervous system modulating the SAN's firing rate. During exercise, the sympathetic nervous system and adrenaline increase the SAN's firing rate , raising heart rate. At rest and during recovery, the parasympathetic nervous system slows it . Endurance training can lower the SAN's intrinsic rate (contributing to bradycardia). 🏅 Sporting examples Pacemaker The SAN generates the initial electrical impulse that triggers each heartbeat — it is the heart's pacemaker. Exercise

Sympathetic stimulation and adrenaline increase the SAN's firing rate, raising heart rate during exercise. Myogenic The SAN means the heart is myogenic — it generates its own rhythm without requiring the brain. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the SAN and its role in heart rate control: "The sinoatrial node is the heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium, generating the impulse that initiates each heartbeat; heart rate is modulated by the autonomic nervous system acting on the SAN — sympathetic stimulation raises it, parasympathetic lowers it." Note it makes the heart myogenic. 🔗 Related terms

Sit and Reach Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sit and Reach Test General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Sit and Reach Test The classic field test of flexibility — a simple measure of how far you can reach, targeting the lower back and hamstrings. 📖 What it means The Sit and Reach Test is a field test that measures flexibility , specifically of the lower back and hamstrings . The performer sits with legs straight and reaches forward as far as possible along a measuring box, and the distance reached is recorded.

It is simple, cheap and quick , needing only a sit-and-reach box, and produces a score that can be compared against normative data or the performer's own previous results to monitor flexibility over time. Its main limitation is that it only assesses flexibility in one specific region (lower back and hamstrings) and does not indicate flexibility elsewhere in the body. Results are also affected by limb-length differences, so it is best used to monitor change rather than for absolute comparison. 🏅 Sporting examples Monitoring flexibility A coach uses the Sit and Reach Test to track a performer's lower-back and hamstring flexibility across a training block. School PE

It is a common practical test in PE and BTEC because it needs only a sit-and-reach box and is quick to administer. Comparison Results are compared against normative tables to rate flexibility for age and sex. ✍️ Using the term in context State what it measures and evaluate its scope: "The Sit and Reach Test measures flexibility of the lower back and hamstrings; it is simple, cheap and reliable when standardised, but only assesses flexibility in one region and is affected by limb-length differences." Sit-ups — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sit-ups BTEC Sport General Sit-ups A classic abdominal exercise and its limits. 📖 What it means A sit-up involves lying on the back with the knees bent and lifting the trunk up to a sitting position . It works the rectus abdominis and the hip flexors (psoas and iliacus). A full sit-up involves heavy use of the hip flexors, which can pull on the lower back , so many coaches prefer curl-ups or crunches , planks and other core exercises for training the abdominals with less spinal stress. Sit-ups are still used in some fitness tests, so they need to be performed with a consistent, controlled technique. 🏅 Sporting examples

Fitness test A set number of sit-ups in one minute. Alternative A curl-up with only the shoulder blades lifted. Skeletal Muscle Pump — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Skeletal Muscle Pump IB Sport Science General Skeletal Muscle Pump Muscles squeezing blood back to the heart — the contracting leg muscles that boost venous return. 📖 What it means The skeletal muscle pump is the mechanism by which contracting skeletal muscles squeeze the veins running through them , propelling blood toward the heart and aiding venous return.

Veins have one-way valves that prevent blood from flowing backward. When muscles contract, they compress the surrounding veins; when they relax, the veins refill with blood from the periphery. This rhythmic squeeze-and-release action drives blood upward toward the heart. During exercise, particularly in the legs during running or cycling, the skeletal muscle pump makes a major contribution to venous return , helping raise stroke volume via Starling's law. It is one reason an abrupt stop after vigorous exercise can cause dizziness — the pump stops suddenly. 🏅 Sporting examples Leg muscles

The pumping action of the calf and thigh muscles during running squeezes veins and drives blood toward the heart. Venous valves One-way valves in the veins ensure blood squeezed by muscles flows toward the heart, not back. Cool down An active cool-down keeps the skeletal muscle pump working, preventing blood pooling when intensity drops. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the skeletal muscle pump and link to venous return: "The skeletal muscle pump is the mechanism by which contracting muscles squeeze veins and, aided by one-way valves, propel blood toward the heart; it makes a major contribution to venous return during exercise and is why an active cool-down prevents blood pooling."

Skeletal Muscle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Skeletal Muscle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Skeletal Muscle The muscle that moves the body — the voluntary, striated tissue attached to bone that produces all sporting movement. 📖 What it means Skeletal muscle is the voluntary muscle attached to the skeleton that produces movement by contracting and pulling on bones. It is one of the three muscle types, alongside cardiac and smooth muscle, and is the type used in all sport.

It is described as striated (striped in appearance) and voluntary (under conscious control). It is made up of bundles of muscle fibres , which contain the contractile units (sarcomeres) that shorten to produce force via the sliding filament mechanism. Skeletal muscles work by pulling, not pushing , and usually in antagonistic pairs — as one muscle (the agonist) contracts, its partner (the antagonist) relaxes. This coordinated action, across many muscles, produces controlled movement. 🏅 Sporting examples All movement Every sporting action, from a sprint to a throw, is produced by skeletal muscles contracting to pull on bones. Antagonistic pairs

At the elbow, the biceps and triceps are skeletal muscles working as an antagonistic pair to flex and extend the joint. Fibre types Skeletal muscle contains slow- and fast-twitch fibres in proportions that suit a performer to endurance or explosive activities. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe skeletal muscle as voluntary, striated and attached to bone: "Skeletal muscle is voluntary, striated muscle attached to the skeleton that produces movement by pulling on bones; it works in antagonistic pairs and contracts via the sliding filament mechanism." Note it pulls rather than pushes, hence the need for antagonistic pairs. 🔗 Related terms

Skill-Related Fitness — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Skill-Related Fitness General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Skill-Related Fitness The fitness components tied to sporting performance — the qualities that separate athletes beyond basic health. 📖 What it means Skill-related fitness refers to the components of fitness particularly associated with performing sporting skills successfully , beyond the basic requirements of health. The skill-related components are usually given as agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed . These qualities enable the quick, precise, powerful and well-timed movements that skilled performance demands.

They contrast with the health-related components (cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, body composition). Most sports draw on both, but skill-related fitness is what often distinguishes higher-level performers, and different sports emphasise different components. 🏅 Sporting examples Games players A footballer relies heavily on skill-related components — agility, speed, coordination and reaction time — to beat opponents and control the ball. Gymnastics Balance, coordination and power are the key skill-related components for a gymnast. Testing

Skill-related components are assessed with tests such as the Illinois Agility Test (agility) and the vertical jump test (power). ✍️ Using the term in context List the skill-related components and contrast with health-related: "Skill-related fitness comprises agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed; these enable skilled sporting performance, in contrast to the health-related components, and different sports emphasise different ones." Skill — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Skill AS Level / Cambridge General Skill A learned ability to produce a result with certainty and efficiency — and, crucially, distinct from innate 'ability'. 📖 What it means In sport science, skill is a learned ability to bring about a predetermined result with maximum certainty, often with minimum outlay of time and energy . The key point is that skill is learned , not innate.

This distinguishes skill from ability , which is an inherited, stable trait. A performer's abilities provide the raw material, but skills must be developed through practice to realise that potential. Skilled performance is typically consistent, efficient, fluent, accurate and goal-directed. Skills can be classified in several ways — by environment (open/closed), by muscular involvement (gross/fine), and by continuity (discrete/serial/continuous) — and these classifications guide how a skill is best practised and coached. 🏅 Sporting examples Learned, not innate A tennis serve is a skill: even a performer with high natural coordination (ability) must practise for years to serve skilfully.

Efficiency A skilled swimmer moves through the water fluently and efficiently, achieving the result with minimal wasted effort. Consistency Skilled performance is consistent — a skilled free-throw shooter scores reliably, not just occasionally. ✍️ Using the term in context Define skill as learned and distinguish it from ability: "Skill is a learned ability to produce a result with maximum certainty and efficiency; unlike ability, which is innate, skill must be developed through practice, and skilled performance is consistent, fluent and goal-directed." Reference how skills are classified to guide practice. 🔗 Related terms

Skinfold Testing (Yuhasz Technique) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Skinfold Testing (Yuhasz Technique) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Skinfold Testing (Yuhasz Technique) A fitness test of body fat. 📖 What it means The Skinfold Testing (Yuhasz Technique) is a body composition method that measures the thickness of skinfolds at several sites on the body, using callipers, to estimate body fat. Protocol: The Yuhasz method uses skinfolds at sites such as the triceps, subscapular, supraspinale, abdomen, front thigh and calf, measured with calipers by a trained tester.

Interpreting results: The sum of skinfolds is used in an equation to estimate body fat percentage, or tracked as a total over time. Accuracy depends on the skill of the tester and consistent sites. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A rower's sum of six skinfolds is tracked every month. Training use Tracking the sum of skinfolds avoids the error of equations. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

Sleep Hygiene — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sleep Hygiene BTEC Sport General Sleep Hygiene Habits that help you sleep well. 📖 What it means Sleep hygiene covers the habits and environment that support good sleep . Sleep is vital for recovery, hormone release, learning and immune function . Teenagers generally need about 8 to 10 hours and adults 7 to 9. Good practice includes a regular bedtime and wake time , a dark, quiet, cool room , avoiding caffeine and large meals late in the day, limiting screens before bed and winding down with a relaxing routine.

Athletes who sleep too little have slower reactions, poorer mood, higher injury risk and slower recovery . Naps can help, but long late naps can disrupt night sleep. 🏅 Sporting examples Evening matches Athletes plan a wind-down routine after late games. Travel Light and a regular schedule help adjust to new time zones. Screen time Devices are switched off before bed. ✍️ Using the term in context Link sleep to performance: "Good sleep hygiene supports recovery, mood and reaction time, so athletes follow consistent routines and limit caffeine and screens before bed."
