Sliding Filament Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sliding Filament Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Sliding Filament Theory How a muscle actually shortens — the molecular mechanism in which filaments slide over one another to produce contraction. 📖 What it means The sliding filament theory explains how a muscle contracts at the microscopic level. It states that muscle shortening occurs when the thin filaments (actin) slide over the thick filaments (myosin) within the contractile units, the sarcomeres.

During contraction, the myosin heads form cross-bridges with the actin filaments and pull them inward , toward the centre of the sarcomere. This shortens each sarcomere, and the combined shortening of millions of sarcomeres shortens the whole muscle. The filaments themselves do not shorten — they slide past each other. The process requires calcium (to expose the binding sites on actin) and ATP (to power the cross-bridge cycling). It is the fundamental mechanism behind every muscular contraction in sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Every contraction From a gentle putt to a maximal lift, the sliding filament mechanism is shortening the muscles by pulling actin over myosin. Cross-bridge cycling

In a sprinter's explosive contractions, myosin heads rapidly and repeatedly attach to actin and pull, cycling many times per second. ATP requirement Because cross-bridge cycling needs ATP, the energy systems must continuously resynthesise ATP to sustain contraction. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe filaments sliding via cross-bridges: "According to the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction occurs when the myosin heads form cross-bridges with the actin filaments and pull them toward the centre of the sarcomere, shortening it; the filaments slide rather than shorten, and the process requires calcium and ATP." Keep actin (thin) and myosin (thick) correctly paired. 🔗 Related terms

Slow-Twitch Fibres (Type I) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Slow-Twitch Fibres (Type I) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Slow-Twitch Fibres (Type I) The muscle fibres built for endurance — fatigue-resistant and oxygen-hungry, they power sustained aerobic effort. 📖 What it means Slow-twitch fibres (Type I) are muscle fibres that contract relatively slowly and produce less force, but are highly resistant to fatigue . They are suited to prolonged, lower-intensity, aerobic activity.

They rely mainly on the aerobic energy system and are well equipped for it: they have many mitochondria and capillaries and a high myoglobin content (which gives them a red appearance), allowing efficient oxygen delivery and use. The proportion of slow- to fast-twitch fibres is largely genetically determined and influences the activities a person is suited to — endurance athletes tend to have a high proportion of slow-twitch fibres. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running A marathon runner typically has a high proportion of slow-twitch fibres, enabling sustained aerobic effort with strong resistance to fatigue. Posture

Slow-twitch fibres are also important in postural muscles, which must contract continuously without tiring. Contrast A sprinter, by contrast, relies on fast-twitch fibres for explosive, powerful but quickly-fatiguing efforts. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe their characteristics and the efforts they suit: "Slow-twitch (Type I) fibres contract slowly and produce less force but resist fatigue, relying on the aerobic system with many mitochondria and capillaries; they dominate endurance activities such as distance running." SMART Goals — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › SMART Goals General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge SMART Goals A checklist for setting goals that actually work — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. 📖 What it means SMART goals are goals set according to five principles that make them effective: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound . The framework turns vague intentions into clear, workable targets.

Specific goals state exactly what is to be achieved; Measurable goals can be quantified so progress is trackable; Achievable goals are challenging but realistic; Relevant goals relate to the performer's wider aims; and Time-bound goals have a deadline. Applying the SMART principles improves motivation, focus and the ability to review progress , because a well-formed goal is clear, trackable and appropriately challenging. SMART is often applied to performance and process goals in particular. 🏅 Sporting examples Vague vs SMART 'Get fitter' is vague; 'reduce my 5km time by 30 seconds within eight weeks' is SMART — specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. Rehabilitation

An injured athlete uses SMART goals to structure their recovery with clear, measurable milestones and deadlines. Reviewing progress Because a SMART goal is measurable and time-bound, the athlete can objectively review whether they are on track. ✍️ Using the term in context Expand the acronym and explain the benefit: "SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound; applying these principles improves motivation and focus and makes progress trackable, turning vague intentions into clear, workable targets." Smooth Muscle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Smooth Muscle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Smooth Muscle The involuntary muscle in blood vessels and the digestive system. 📖 What it means Smooth muscle is found in the walls of blood vessels, the digestive tract, airways and the bladder . It is involuntary and has no striations . It contracts slowly and can maintain contraction for long periods with little energy use. It is controlled by the autonomic nervous system and hormones. In exercise, smooth muscle in the arterioles controls vasoconstriction and vasodilation , shunting blood to the working muscles. 🏅 Sporting examples Blood flow

Social Facilitation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Social Facilitation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Social Facilitation How an audience changes performance — for better or worse, depending on the skill and the performer. 📖 What it means Social facilitation is the effect that the presence of others — an audience or co-performers — has on performance . The effect can be positive (facilitation) or negative (inhibition).

The presence of others tends to increase arousal , and by drive theory this makes the performer's dominant response more likely . For skilled performers and simple/gross skills , the dominant response is correct, so an audience helps; for beginners and complex/fine skills , the dominant response may be incorrect, so an audience harms performance (social inhibition). Related concepts include evaluation apprehension (the effect is stronger when performers feel they are being judged). Coaches manage these effects by gradually exposing learners to audiences and building their skills to the autonomous stage before performing under scrutiny. 🏅 Sporting examples Skilled performer

An experienced athlete often raises their game in front of a big crowd, as the increased arousal enhances their well-learned dominant response. Beginner A novice may perform worse when watched, because the raised arousal makes their incorrect dominant response more likely (social inhibition). Managing it A coach gradually introduces small audiences during practice so learners habituate before performing in front of large crowds. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the arousal–dominant response mechanism and who it helps or harms:

"Social facilitation is the effect of others' presence on performance; it raises arousal, making the dominant response more likely — helping skilled performers of simple skills but harming beginners or those performing complex skills (social inhibition)." Social Loafing — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Social Loafing IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Social Loafing Why some players hide in a team — the tendency to try less hard when individual effort goes unnoticed. 📖 What it means Social loafing is the tendency for individuals to reduce their effort when performing as part of a group , compared with when they perform alone. It can undermine team performance and cohesion.

It tends to occur when a performer believes their individual contribution is not being identified or valued — they feel their effort will go unnoticed, or that others will 'carry' them. It is linked to a loss of motivation and to reduced accountability within a group. Coaches counter social loafing by highlighting and monitoring individual contributions (for example, through statistics or defined roles), giving specific feedback, setting individual as well as team goals, and fostering a culture where every player's effort is recognised. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sport A player who coasts during a game, letting more motivated teammates do the work, is displaying social loafing.

Highlighting contribution A coach uses performance statistics to make each player's individual contribution visible, reducing loafing. Defined roles Giving each player a clear, accountable role helps ensure their effort is noticed and valued, countering social loafing. ✍️ Using the term in context Define social loafing and give strategies to reduce it: "Social loafing is the tendency to reduce individual effort in a group, often when a performer's contribution is not identified or valued; it is countered by monitoring and highlighting individual contributions, giving specific feedback and setting individual goals." Link it to motivation and accountability within a group. 🔗 Related terms

Socialisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Socialisation BTEC Sport General Socialisation How we learn the values around us. 📖 What it means Socialisation is the process of learning the norms, values and behaviours of a society. Primary socialisation occurs in early childhood within the family , while secondary socialisation comes later through school, peers, the media, religion and clubs . It shapes attitudes to sport and exercise, such as whether participation is seen as normal for girls and boys , and which sports are seen as suitable. It also influences gender, class and ethnic stereotypes .

Active parents and positive role models raise the likelihood that children participate. Social change can come from new role models and policies. 🏅 Sporting examples Family A child who plays with active parents tends to be active. School PE lessons shape attitudes to exercise. Media Role models influence interest in sport. ✍️ Using the term in context Distinguish primary and secondary: "Primary socialisation within the family introduces sporting values, which are reinforced by secondary agents such as school, peers and the media." Somatic Anxiety — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Somatic Anxiety IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Somatic Anxiety The physical side of competitive nerves — the racing heart and tense muscles that signal the body's response to pressure. 📖 What it means Somatic anxiety is the physical component of anxiety — the bodily symptoms a performer experiences under pressure, such as an increased heart rate, sweating, muscle tension, butterflies and nausea . It is distinguished from cognitive anxiety , the mental component (worry and negative thoughts). The two often occur together but respond to different management techniques.

Somatic anxiety is closely linked to physiological arousal , and is best managed with physical relaxation techniques such as progressive muscle relaxation, controlled breathing and biofeedback, rather than the cognitive techniques used for mental worry. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-competition A sprinter on the blocks feeling a pounding heart, tense muscles and butterflies is experiencing somatic anxiety. Management An athlete uses progressive muscle relaxation and controlled breathing to reduce the physical symptoms of somatic anxiety before competing. Paired with cognitive

A performer may feel both somatic anxiety (racing heart) and cognitive anxiety (fear of failure), each needing a different management approach. ✍️ Using the term in context Define it as the physical component and pair with cognitive anxiety: "Somatic anxiety is the physical component of anxiety, such as increased heart rate and muscle tension, whereas cognitive anxiety is the mental worry; somatic anxiety is best managed with physical relaxation techniques." Match the management technique (relaxation, breathing) to the type of anxiety. 🔗 Related terms Cognitive Anxiety Anxiety Arousal State Anxiety Progressive Muscle Relaxation CSAI-2 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science

Somatotype — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Somatotype General BTEC Sport IB Sport Science Somatotype A way of classifying body build — the balance of three physique types that suits different sports. 📖 What it means Somatotype is a system for classifying and describing a person's body type or physique . It rates a physique on three components, each scored to give an overall somatotype. The three components are endomorphy (a rounder, higher-fat physique), mesomorphy (a muscular, wider-shouldered, athletic physique), and ectomorphy (a lean, slender, linear physique). Most people are a blend, scored on each component.

Somatotype is relevant in sport because certain physiques suit certain activities — for example, a strong mesomorphic build suits power sports, while a lean ectomorphic build can suit endurance running or high jump. It is one factor among many, alongside training, skill and psychology. 🏅 Sporting examples Power sports A sprinter or weightlifter typically shows a strongly mesomorphic somatotype, with a muscular, powerful build. Endurance A distance runner often has a more ectomorphic build — lean and light, aiding their power-to-weight ratio. Blends Most athletes are a blend of the three components, scored to give their overall somatotype. ✍️ Using the term in context

Name the three components and link physique to sport: "Somatotype classifies physique on three components — endomorphy, mesomorphy and ectomorphy — with most people a blend; certain physiques suit certain sports, such as a mesomorphic build for power events, though it is only one factor in performance." Spatial Summation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Spatial Summation IB Sport Science General Spatial Summation More motor units firing at once — one of two ways the body increases the force a muscle produces. 📖 What it means Spatial summation is the increase in muscle force produced by recruiting a greater number of motor units simultaneously . More motor units firing at the same time produces more total force. It is one of two mechanisms of force gradation (alongside temporal summation / wave summation, where the same motor unit is fired more rapidly). The nervous system uses both to control the graded force output of a muscle.

Because of the all-or-none law , each motor unit either fires fully or not at all. The only way to increase force is therefore to recruit more units (spatial summation) or fire existing ones faster (temporal/wave summation). Most force gradation in practice involves both. 🏅 Sporting examples Heavier lift To lift a heavier weight, the nervous system recruits more motor units simultaneously — spatial summation. Gradual force increase As demand increases, more motor units are recruited progressively (the size principle). Combined In most sporting actions, both spatial and temporal summation contribute to producing the required force. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define spatial summation and contrast with temporal: "Spatial summation is the increase in muscle force from recruiting more motor units simultaneously; alongside temporal summation (firing motor units more rapidly), it is one of two mechanisms the nervous system uses to grade muscle force." Specificity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Specificity General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Specificity The principle that training must match the demands of the sport — train the way you want to perform. 📖 What it means The principle of specificity states that training adaptations are specific to the type of training performed . To improve at a particular sport, training must match its specific demands — the muscle groups, movement patterns, energy systems and components of fitness it uses.

This means training should replicate the relevant energy systems (e.g. anaerobic work for a sprinter), the muscle groups and actions used, and the skills and movement patterns of the sport. Generic training produces generic gains; specific training produces sport-specific improvement. Specificity must be balanced with variety and a broad base, but it is a core principle of programme design — captured in the 'Type' element of the FITT principle — ensuring training transfers effectively to competition. 🏅 Sporting examples Energy systems

A sprinter trains the anaerobic systems with short, maximal efforts, while a marathon runner trains the aerobic system with sustained work — specificity in action. Movement patterns A swimmer does much of their conditioning in the water so that training matches the specific muscles and actions of swimming. FITT link The 'Type' of training in the FITT principle is chosen to be specific to the sport's demands. ✍️ Using the term in context State the principle and what training should replicate:

"The principle of specificity states that adaptations are specific to the training performed; training should replicate the energy systems, muscle groups, actions and skills of the sport so that gains transfer to competition." Speed-Agility-Quickness (SAQ) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Speed-Agility-Quickness (SAQ) General BTEC Sport Speed-Agility-Quickness (SAQ) Training rapid multi-directional movement — a method that develops the fast-feet skills needed in games. 📖 What it means Speed-Agility-Quickness (SAQ) training is a training approach that develops rapid multi-directional movement through drills focusing on acceleration, deceleration, change of direction and reaction.

It uses equipment such as ladders, cones and hurdles to create drills that challenge foot speed, coordination and explosive direction changes. The aim is to improve the neuromuscular qualities underpinning agile, reactive movement. SAQ training is widely used in team and racket sports where rapid changes of direction and fast footwork are decisive. It complements strength and conditioning work by developing the movement-specific speed and agility that general fitness training alone does not fully address. 🏅 Sporting examples Ladder drills Agility ladder drills develop foot speed and coordination, key SAQ qualities. Cone drills

T-cone and Illinois agility drills challenge change of direction and acceleration under SAQ training. Sport transfer SAQ training improves the rapid footwork and direction changes needed in football and basketball. ✍️ Using the term in context Define SAQ training and its purpose: "SAQ training develops speed, agility and quickness through multi-directional drills using ladders, cones and hurdles; it improves the neuromuscular qualities underpinning rapid direction changes and reactive movement in team and racket sports." Speed — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Speed General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Speed How quickly a performer can move — a skill-related component of fitness decisive in sprints, breaks and reactions. 📖 What it means Speed is the ability to move all or part of the body as quickly as possible . It is a skill-related component of fitness, essential in any sport where covering ground or moving a limb rapidly confers an advantage. Speed depends on factors including muscle fibre type (a high proportion of fast-twitch fibres favours speed), strength and power, technique, and the anaerobic energy systems that fuel rapid, maximal efforts.

It is developed through sprint training, resistance and plyometric work, and technique drills , and is commonly assessed with timed sprints over a set distance (such as a 30m sprint test). In biomechanics, speed is distinct from velocity, which also includes direction. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting A 100m sprinter's performance depends directly on speed — moving the whole body over the ground as fast as possible. Team sports A footballer uses speed to break away from a defender or chase down an attacker. Testing Speed is commonly assessed with a timed 30m sprint test. ✍️ Using the term in context Define speed and note what it depends on and how it's tested:

"Speed is the ability to move the body or a limb as quickly as possible; as a skill-related component of fitness it depends on fast-twitch fibres, power, technique and the anaerobic systems, and is measured with timed sprints." Spirometer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Spirometer IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Spirometer The instrument used to measure lung volumes. 📖 What it means A spirometer records the volume and flow of air a person breathes in and out. Modern digital models use a mouthpiece and flow sensor; older ones used a floating chamber and a trace on a rotating drum. It can measure tidal volume, vital capacity, inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes and forced measures such as FEV1. It cannot measure residual volume , because that air stays in the lungs. 🏅 Sporting examples Fitness testing A student breathes into a spirometer to find vital capacity.

Asthma checks FEV1 and FVC are measured with a spirometer. Training Changes in respiratory measures after a training block can be tracked with spirometry. ✍️ Using the term in context Say what it can and cannot measure: "A spirometer measures lung volumes such as tidal volume and vital capacity, but not residual volume." Sponsorship — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sponsorship AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Sponsorship Money in exchange for exposure — the commercial relationship that funds sport and shapes how athletes perform and appear. 📖 What it means Sponsorship is a commercial arrangement in which a business provides funding or resources to an athlete, team or event in exchange for promotional exposure . It is a major funding mechanism for sport at all levels.

It benefits both parties: sponsors gain brand visibility and association with sport's values ; athletes, teams and events gain income, equipment, support services and platform . However, it creates commercial pressures that can influence decision-making and behaviour. Sponsorship is part of the wider commercialisation of sport and has been both a positive enabler (funding athletes and grassroots sport) and a source of ethical tension — particularly where unhealthy products are sponsored, or where performance or independence is compromised. 🏅 Sporting examples Athlete sponsorship A kit deal provides an athlete with equipment and income in exchange for wearing the brand's logo. Event funding

Sponsors fund major events, enabling prize money and media coverage. Ethical tension Sponsorship by gambling or alcohol brands raises ethical questions about sport's values. ✍️ Using the term in context Define sponsorship and note its dual nature: "Sponsorship is a commercial arrangement providing funding or resources in exchange for promotional exposure; it enables sport through funding but can create ethical tensions, particularly where sponsors conflict with sport's values." Sports Massage — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sports Massage General BTEC Sport Sports Massage Hands-on recovery — manual soft-tissue work used to aid recovery, reduce tension and prepare for performance. 📖 What it means Sports massage is manual soft-tissue manipulation used to aid recovery, reduce muscle tension and soreness, and prepare athletes for performance . It can be applied before competition (to warm and stimulate), after competition (to aid recovery, reduce soreness and remove metabolic waste) or during a training phase as a regular recovery tool. Techniques include effleurage (stroking), petrissage (kneading) and deep tissue work.

Evidence suggests sports massage can reduce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), improve flexibility and enhance psychological recovery . It does not replace adequate rest and nutrition but is a valued complementary recovery strategy. 🏅 Sporting examples Post-exercise Sports massage after a match can help reduce DOMS and aid recovery. Pre-competition A stimulating pre-competition massage warms the muscles and enhances readiness. Complement Sports massage complements rest and nutrition as part of a comprehensive recovery strategy. ✍️ Using the term in context Define sports massage and its uses:

Sports Vision — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sports Vision IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Sports Vision The eye skills athletes depend on. 📖 What it means Sports vision covers the visual abilities that matter in sport. Vision can be tested and, to some extent, trained.

Visual training programmes are popular, but the evidence that they transfer to better performance in competition is mixed. 🏅 Sporting examples Cricket Batters track the ball using early cues from the bowler. Sportsmanship — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sportsmanship AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Sportsmanship Fair, honourable conduct in sport — respecting opponents, officials and the spirit of the game. 📖 What it means Sportsmanship is fair, honest and generous conduct in sport — competing hard while respecting opponents, officials, the rules and the spirit of the game. It reflects the positive values that sport aims to embody. It includes behaviours such as respecting opponents and officials, accepting decisions gracefully, competing within both the letter and the spirit of the rules, and showing generosity in victory and dignity in defeat .

Sportsmanship contrasts with gamesmanship (bending the spirit of the rules for advantage) and deviance (breaking the rules). It is a central positive value in discussions of ethics and fair play, though it can be under pressure in highly commercialised, win-at-all-costs environments. 🏅 Sporting examples Fair play Kicking the ball out so an injured opponent can be treated, or applauding an opponent's good play, are acts of sportsmanship. Sportsmanship can be tested in high-stakes, commercialised sport, where the pressure to win may tempt performers toward gamesmanship. ✍️ Using the term in context Define sportsmanship and contrast it with gamesmanship and deviance: "Sportsmanship is fair, honest and respectful conduct that honours the spirit of the game; it contrasts with gamesmanship, which bends the spirit of the rules, and with deviance, which breaks them." Sprain — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sprain General BTEC Sport Sprain A stretched or torn ligament — one of the most common acute joint injuries in sport, treated initially with RICE. 📖 What it means A sprain is an injury to a ligament — the tough tissue connecting bone to bone at a joint — caused by overstretching or tearing it, usually when a joint is forced beyond its normal range of movement. Sprains commonly occur at the ankle, knee and wrist , often from a twist, awkward landing or impact. Symptoms include pain, swelling, bruising and reduced function at the joint, and they are graded by severity from mild overstretch to complete rupture.

Immediate treatment follows the RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) to control pain and swelling. A key distinction for exams: a sprain affects a ligament , whereas a strain affects a muscle or tendon . 🏅 Sporting examples Ankle sprain A player who rolls their ankle on landing may sprain the ligaments on the outside of the joint — a very common sporting injury. Knee A twist of the knee can sprain its ligaments; a severe sprain may involve a ligament such as the ACL. Treatment A sprained wrist is treated immediately with RICE to limit pain and swelling. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a sprain and distinguish it from a strain:

"A sprain is the overstretching or tearing of a ligament, commonly at the ankle or knee, causing pain and swelling; it is distinguished from a strain, which affects a muscle or tendon, and is treated initially with RICE." Sprint Interval Training — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sprint Interval Training IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Sprint Interval Training Very short, all-out sprint sessions. 📖 What it means Sprint interval training (SIT) uses maximal 'all-out' efforts , typically 20 to 30 seconds (for example on a cycle ergometer), with long recoveries of a few minutes. Stability — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stability IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Stability How resistant a body is to being knocked off balance — a biomechanical quality athletes manipulate constantly. 📖 What it means Stability is the ability of a body to resist being moved or knocked off balance . It depends on several biomechanical factors that athletes adjust according to whether they need to hold firm or move quickly.

Stability is increased by a lower centre of gravity , a larger base of support , keeping the line of gravity within the base of support , and a greater mass . The closer the line of gravity is to the centre of the base, the more stable the body. There is a trade-off with mobility : a very stable position (low, wide) is hard to move quickly from, so athletes choose the amount of stability to match the task — firm and stable to resist a force, or less stable and ready to move fast. 🏅 Sporting examples Judo A judoka lowers and widens their stance to increase stability, making it harder for an opponent to unbalance them. Sprint start

A sprinter adopts a less stable, forward-leaning position so their line of gravity is near the edge of the base, ready to move quickly. Gymnastics A gymnast holding a balance keeps their line of gravity centred over a small base of support to stay stable. ✍️ Using the term in context List the factors affecting stability and the mobility trade-off: "Stability is the ability to resist being moved; it increases with a lower centre of gravity, a larger base of support, keeping the line of gravity within the base, and greater mass — but greater stability reduces mobility, so athletes match it to the task." Combine centre of gravity, base of support and line of gravity in a full answer.

Standard Deviation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Standard Deviation IB Sport Science General Standard Deviation A measure of how spread out data are — an essential statistic for the IB internal assessment and interpreting results. 📖 What it means Standard deviation is a measure of the spread or dispersion of a set of data around the mean (average) . It shows how much the individual values typically differ from the average.

A small standard deviation means the data are clustered closely around the mean (consistent, less variable), while a large standard deviation means the data are more spread out (more variable). It gives far more insight than the mean alone. In sport science investigations, standard deviation is used to describe the consistency of results and to compare variability between groups or conditions — for example, showing whether one training method produced more consistent improvements than another. 🏅 Sporting examples Consistency Two groups may have the same mean sprint time, but the group with the smaller standard deviation performed more consistently. IB internal assessment

A student reports the standard deviation alongside the mean to show how spread out their measured data were. Comparing conditions A larger standard deviation in one condition indicates its results were more variable than the other's. ✍️ Using the term in context Define standard deviation as spread around the mean: "Standard deviation measures the spread of data around the mean; a small value indicates consistent, tightly clustered results, while a large value indicates greater variability, giving more insight than the mean alone." Use it to compare the consistency of results between conditions. 🔗 Related terms Mean Correlation Hypothesis Independent Variable Dependent Variable Range

Starling's Law — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Starling's Law IB Sport Science General Starling's Law The rule that links blood returning to the heart with the force of the next beat — the mechanism behind rising stroke volume. 📖 What it means Starling's law (the Frank–Starling mechanism) states that the more the heart's ventricle is stretched by incoming blood, the more forcefully it contracts , and so the greater the stroke volume. The key link is venous return — the volume of blood returning to the heart. Greater venous return stretches the ventricle wall more, and this increased stretch produces a stronger contraction, ejecting more blood per beat.

This mechanism explains why stroke volume rises during exercise : exercise increases venous return (through the muscle and respiratory pumps and venoconstriction), stretching the ventricle and increasing the force of contraction to match the greater demand. 🏅 Sporting examples Onset of exercise As exercise begins and venous return rises, Starling's law causes the ventricle to contract more forcefully, increasing stroke volume. Muscle pump The muscle pump squeezes veins during exercise, boosting venous return and, via Starling's law, stroke volume. Matching demand

Starling's law helps the heart automatically match its output to the amount of blood returning, supporting the increased demand of exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context State the stretch–contraction relationship and the venous return link: "Starling's law states that greater stretch of the ventricle, caused by increased venous return, produces a more forceful contraction and a larger stroke volume; this is why stroke volume rises during exercise." Use it to explain increases in stroke volume rather than stating it in isolation. 🔗 Related terms Stroke Volume Venous Return Cardiac Output Muscle Pump Cardiac Hypertrophy Heart Rate 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub →

State Anxiety — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › State Anxiety IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General State Anxiety Anxiety in the moment — the temporary, situation-specific nerves a performer feels in a particular event. 📖 What it means State anxiety is a temporary, situation-specific emotional state of anxiety experienced at a particular moment. It fluctuates depending on the situation — rising before a big competition and falling afterwards.

It contrasts with trait anxiety , which is a stable, enduring personality characteristic — a general predisposition to become anxious. A performer high in trait anxiety is more likely to experience high state anxiety in a given situation. Like anxiety generally, state anxiety has both a cognitive component (in-the-moment worry) and a somatic component (physical symptoms). It is commonly measured by questionnaires such as the CSAI-2, completed close to the event. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-competition A gymnast feeling intense nerves in the minutes before a major final is experiencing high state anxiety, which subsides once they finish. Trait link

A performer high in trait anxiety tends to experience greater state anxiety before an important match than a calmer teammate. Measurement State anxiety is measured with the CSAI-2 shortly before competing, capturing that moment's cognitive and somatic anxiety. ✍️ Using the term in context Define state anxiety and contrast it with trait anxiety: "State anxiety is a temporary, situation-specific state of anxiety that fluctuates with circumstances, unlike trait anxiety, which is a stable predisposition; performers high in trait anxiety tend to experience higher state anxiety." Note it has cognitive and somatic components and is measured by the CSAI-2. 🔗 Related terms

Static Flexibility Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Static Flexibility Test BTEC Sport General Static Flexibility Test A fitness test of joint flexibility. 📖 What it means The Static Flexibility Test is a test of the range of motion at a joint when the athlete holds a stretched position, with no movement during the measurement. Protocol: The athlete moves slowly into the end position of a joint, for example in a sit and reach, and holds it while the distance or angle is measured with a ruler or goniometer.

Interpreting results: Comparing sides and joints identifies tight areas. Static flexibility does not always predict how well someone moves in sport, which is dynamic. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A gymnast's hamstring flexibility is measured with the sit and reach. Training use Results guide stretching and mobility programmes. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures:

Static Stretching — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Static Stretching General BTEC Sport Static Stretching Hold the stretch — the classic flexibility technique of taking a muscle to its end range and holding it there. 📖 What it means Static stretching is stretching by slowly extending a muscle to the point of mild tension and holding for a period , typically 15–60 seconds. It is the most common and best-recognised stretching technique.

It is most effective for developing flexibility when performed regularly , particularly in the cool-down or in dedicated flexibility sessions. It can temporarily reduce muscle force production immediately after stretching, so prolonged static stretching immediately before power-dependent sport is generally not recommended before competition. Static stretching is contrasted with dynamic stretching (active movement) and ballistic stretching (bouncing). It is categorised as active (the performer's own muscles hold the position) or passive (an external force holds it). 🏅 Sporting examples Cool-down Holding a hamstring stretch for 30 seconds in a cool-down develops flexibility over time.

Before vs after Prolonged static stretching before explosive sport can temporarily reduce power — dynamic stretching is preferred pre-activity. Flexibility development Regular static stretching increases ROM over weeks and months. ✍️ Using the term in context Define static stretching and note its timing: "Static stretching extends a muscle to the point of mild tension and holds it, typically 15–60 seconds; it is effective for developing flexibility in cool-down or dedicated sessions, but prolonged static stretching before explosive sport may temporarily reduce power." Contrast with dynamic stretching for warm-up. 🔗 Related terms

Steiner's Model of Group Effectiveness — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Steiner's Model of Group Effectiveness IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Steiner's Model of Group Effectiveness Why teams often perform below their potential. 📖 What it means Steiner's model says actual productivity = potential productivity − faulty processes . Potential productivity is the best a team could achieve with the resources (skills, fitness) of its members. Faulty processes are the losses that prevent this. They include coordination losses (poor teamwork or timing) and motivation losses (such as social loafing ).

Coaches can improve productivity by building cohesion, clear roles and communication and giving individual accountability. The Ringelmann effect is a related idea. 🏅 Sporting examples Relay A poor baton change is a coordination loss. Team sport A player who coasts causes a motivation loss. Fix Clear roles and tracked contributions reduce loafing. ✍️ Using the term in context Write the equation: "According to Steiner, actual productivity equals potential productivity minus faulty processes such as coordination and motivation losses." Name an example of each type of loss. 🔗 Related terms Ringelmann Effect Social Loafing Group Cohesion Task Cohesion Group Dynamics Leadership

Stitch — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stitch IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Stitch The sharp pain in the side that can stop you mid-run. 📖 What it means A stitch , or exercise-related transient abdominal pain (ETAP) , is a sharp, cramping or stabbing pain, usually in the side of the abdomen , that occurs during exercise, most often running, swimming and horse riding. The exact cause is not fully understood . Theories include irritation of the lining of the abdominal cavity and strain on the ligaments connected to the diaphragm. Eating a large meal or drinking concentrated sugary drinks shortly before exercise makes it more likely.

Relief methods include slowing down, changing breathing pattern, pushing on the painful area and bending forwards . It usually passes quickly. 🏅 Sporting examples Running A stitch appears after eating a big meal an hour before. Prevention Allow time after eating and warm up gradually. Relief Slow down and breathe deeply until it eases. ✍️ Using the term in context Be honest about the cause: "A stitch is a transient pain in the side of the abdomen during exercise; its exact cause is not fully understood but is linked to eating and drinking before exercise." Avoid stating a single proven cause. 🔗 Related terms Breathing Rhythms Cramp Warm-Up Hydration Strategy Dehydration 🎓 Where this appears

Strain — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Strain General BTEC Sport Strain A stretched or torn muscle or tendon — the 'pulled muscle' familiar to every athlete, distinct from a ligament sprain. 📖 What it means A strain is an injury to a muscle or tendon — commonly called a 'pulled muscle' — caused by overstretching or tearing the tissue, often during a sudden, forceful or awkward movement.

Strains frequently affect muscles that cross two joints or absorb large forces, such as the hamstrings, calf and groin (adductors) , and often occur during sprinting, jumping or rapid changes of direction. Symptoms include pain, tenderness, swelling and reduced strength or movement . Immediate treatment follows the RICE protocol . The key exam distinction is that a strain affects a muscle or tendon , whereas a sprain affects a ligament . Gradual progression of training and thorough warm-ups help reduce the risk of strains. 🏅 Sporting examples Hamstring strain A sprinter straining a hamstring during a fast run is a classic muscle strain, caused by the large eccentric forces involved.

Groin strain A footballer changing direction sharply may strain the adductor (groin) muscles. Prevention A thorough warm-up and gradual progression of training load help reduce the risk of muscle strains. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a strain and distinguish it from a sprain: "A strain is the overstretching or tearing of a muscle or tendon, such as a hamstring strain during sprinting; it is distinguished from a sprain, which affects a ligament, and is treated initially with RICE." Streamlining — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Streamlining IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Streamlining Shaping the body to cheat the fluid — reducing drag by presenting the smallest, smoothest profile possible. 📖 What it means Streamlining is the process of shaping a body or adopting a posture to reduce air or water resistance (drag) . It minimises frontal surface area and surface friction, reducing the force opposing motion.

In sport, streamlining is achieved through body position, clothing and equipment design : a cyclist adopts an aero tuck, a swimmer keeps a horizontal body position, a skier crouches. Even small reductions in drag have a significant effect at high speeds because drag increases with velocity squared. Streamlining is a central concept in fluid mechanics and aerodynamics, and is a key principle in sports where moving through a fluid is the performance task — swimming, cycling, skiing and sprinting. 🏅 Sporting examples Cycling An aero tuck reduces the cyclist's frontal area and drag, allowing faster speeds for the same power. Swimming

A streamlined body position cuts drag in the water, contributing significantly to swimming performance. Equipment Aerodynamic helmets, skin suits and shaped handlebars all streamline the cyclist against the air. ✍️ Using the term in context Define streamlining and link it to drag: "Streamlining is shaping the body or adopting a posture to reduce drag by minimising frontal area and surface friction; it is particularly effective at high speeds because drag increases with velocity squared." Strength — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Strength General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Strength The ability to exert force against a resistance — a foundational fitness quality that comes in several forms. 📖 What it means Strength is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to exert force against a resistance . It underpins power and is essential across most sports, both for performance and injury prevention.

Strength comes in several forms: maximal strength (the greatest force in a single contraction), elastic/explosive strength (producing force quickly, linked to power), and strength endurance (sustaining or repeating contractions). The type a sport needs shapes how it is trained. Strength is developed mainly through resistance training , with the load and repetitions adjusted for the type of strength required, and is commonly measured by the one-repetition maximum (1RM) or with dynamometers. 🏅 Sporting examples Maximal strength A weightlifter needs maximal strength — the greatest possible force in a single lift. Explosive strength

A sprinter or jumper relies on explosive strength to produce force rapidly for a powerful start or take-off. Strength endurance A rower needs strength endurance to repeat powerful strokes throughout a race. ✍️ Using the term in context Define strength and distinguish its types: "Strength is the ability to exert force against a resistance; it includes maximal strength (single maximum force), explosive strength (force produced quickly) and strength endurance (repeated contractions), each trained with different loads and repetitions." Stress Fracture — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stress Fracture IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Stress Fracture A crack from cumulative loading — the bone fatigue injury that builds gradually from repetitive stress. 📖 What it means A stress fracture is a small crack in a bone caused by repetitive loading rather than a single acute impact. The bone's ability to repair micro-damage is outpaced by the rate at which new micro-damage accumulates.

Stress fractures are common in weight-bearing bones (such as the tibia, fibula and metatarsals) in endurance runners and jumping athletes. They are associated with sudden increases in training load, low bone density, nutritional deficiencies and RED-S . They typically present with localised pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest . Management involves rest and a gradual, phased return. They are a classic overuse injury and highlight the importance of progressive training load increases. 🏅 Sporting examples Runner A distance runner who rapidly increases mileage may develop a tibial stress fracture. Risk factors

Low bone density, insufficient calcium and vitamin D, and RED-S all increase stress fracture risk. Prevention Gradual load progression and maintaining bone density through diet and weight-bearing training reduce risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a stress fracture and its causes: "A stress fracture is a crack in a bone from cumulative repetitive loading outpacing bone repair; common in weight-bearing bones, it is associated with rapid load increases, low bone density and RED-S, managed with rest and gradual return." Stretch Reflex — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stretch Reflex IB Sport Science General Stretch Reflex The muscle's automatic resistance to rapid stretch — the reflex that stops it from being overstretched. 📖 What it means The stretch reflex is an involuntary contraction of a muscle triggered by rapid elongation . When a muscle is stretched quickly, muscle spindles detect the change and initiate a rapid reflex contraction to resist further stretch. It is a monosynaptic reflex (the signal goes directly from the muscle spindle via a sensory neurone to the motor neurone in the spinal cord, then back to the muscle) — one of the fastest reflexes in the body.

In sport, the stretch reflex is central to the stretch-shortening cycle and plyometrics: a rapid pre-stretch activates the stretch reflex, adding to the force of the subsequent contraction. However, it is also why ballistic stretching carries injury risk — rapid stretch triggers the reflex contraction, working against the stretch. 🏅 Sporting examples Plyometrics In a jump squat, the rapid descent stretches the quads and triggers the stretch reflex, adding to the upward drive. Injury protection The stretch reflex contracts a muscle against sudden overstretch, helping protect it. Ballistic risk

Ballistic stretching triggers the stretch reflex, which actively opposes the stretch — raising injury risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the stretch reflex and link to the stretch-shortening cycle: "The stretch reflex is the involuntary contraction triggered by rapid muscle elongation, detected by muscle spindles; it underpins the stretch-shortening cycle and plyometrics, but also explains why ballistic stretching risks injury." Distinguish it from autogenic inhibition. 🔗 Related terms Muscle Spindle Autogenic Inhibition Plyometrics Elastic Energy Ballistic Stretching Proprioceptor 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library

Stretch-Shortening Cycle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stretch-Shortening Cycle IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Stretch-Shortening Cycle The 'rebound' action behind jumping and bouncing. 📖 What it means The stretch-shortening cycle (SSC) has three phases: an eccentric phase in which the muscle-tendon unit is stretched, a very short amortisation phase, and a concentric phase in which it shortens. The muscle produces more force than from a standing start because the tendons store and return elastic energy and the stretch reflex adds extra activation. The amortisation phase must be short to use this effect.

Plyometric training aims to improve the SSC. Examples are depth jumps, bounding and countermovement jumps. 🏅 Sporting examples Countermovement jump The dip before the jump uses the SSC. Running Each ground contact stores and releases elastic energy. Plyometrics Box jumps train a fast stretch-to-shorten transition. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the three phases: "In the stretch-shortening cycle, an eccentric stretch stores elastic energy and triggers the stretch reflex, followed by a rapid concentric contraction." Say why a short amortisation phase matters. 🔗 Related terms Plyometric Training Elastic Energy Stretch Reflex Eccentric Contraction Concentric Contraction Power

Stride Length — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stride Length IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Stride Length How far you travel with each stride. 📖 What it means Stride length is the distance from the point where one foot lands to where it lands again (the same foot ). Step length is the distance from one foot landing to the other foot landing, so a stride is two steps. Speed = stride length × stride rate . Runners increase speed by lengthening the stride, quickening the stride rate, or both.

Stride length is affected by leg length, power, flexibility and fatigue. Over-striding, landing with the foot far in front of the body, increases braking forces. 🏅 Sporting examples Sprinting Elite sprinters have long strides of over 2 metres at top speed. Fatigue In the late stages of a race the stride shortens. Gait analysis A coach filming a runner measures stride length from video. ✍️ Using the term in context Use the speed equation: "Running speed is the product of stride length and stride rate, so a longer stride at the same rate gives a higher speed." Stroke Volume — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Stroke Volume IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Stroke Volume The amount of blood the heart ejects with each beat — the quiet driver behind cardiac output and endurance fitness. 📖 What it means Stroke volume (SV) is the volume of blood ejected from the left ventricle with each heartbeat , typically around 70 ml at rest. It is one of the two components of cardiac output ( Q = HR × SV ).

Stroke volume increases during exercise, largely because more blood returns to the heart ( increased venous return ), stretching the ventricle so it contracts more forcefully — as described by Starling's law . It tends to plateau at around 40–60% of maximal effort. The key adaptation to note is that endurance training increases stroke volume through cardiac hypertrophy: a larger, stronger ventricle fills and empties more completely. This raises maximal cardiac output and, at rest, lowers heart rate (bradycardia) because more blood is pumped per beat. 🏅 Sporting examples Distance running

An endurance runner's large stroke volume delivers plenty of blood per beat, giving both a high maximal cardiac output and a very low resting heart rate. Starling's law in action As venous return rises during exercise, the ventricle stretches and contracts more forcefully, increasing stroke volume. Training adaptation Months of endurance training enlarge the ventricle (hypertrophy), raising stroke volume both at rest and at maximal effort. ✍️ Using the term in context Link stroke volume to cardiac output, venous return and training:

"Stroke volume is the blood ejected per beat and a component of cardiac output; it rises during exercise as increased venous return stretches the ventricle (Starling's law), and endurance training raises it through cardiac hypertrophy." Submaximal Tests — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Submaximal Tests IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Submaximal Tests Tests that predict maximum fitness without a maximal effort. 📖 What it means Submaximal tests are done at less than maximum effort . They use measures such as heart rate at a fixed workload to predict values like VO2 max. They are safer, quicker and need less motivation than maximal tests, so they suit beginners, large groups and people with health risks. Examples are the Astrand cycle test, step tests, the Rockport walk test and the PWC-170.

They are less accurate than direct measurement because they rely on estimates, such as predicted maximum heart rate. 🏅 Sporting examples School A class completes a step test and heart rate recovery. Summation of Force — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Summation of Force IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Summation of Force Coordinating the body's segments in the right order to generate maximum force — the key to powerful throwing and striking. 📖 What it means Summation of force is the process of using multiple body segments (muscles and joints) in the correct sequence and timing to generate maximum force . The forces from each segment add together to produce a greater total force than any segment could alone.

For maximum effect, the segments must be used in the right order and timing — typically the larger, stronger body parts first, followed by the smaller, faster ones — and each should contribute at the moment the previous one has reached its peak, so their forces build on one another. This principle is central to powerful throwing, striking and kicking actions, where force is developed sequentially through the body (a 'kinetic chain') from the ground up, culminating in the hand, foot or implement. 🏅 Sporting examples Throwing In a javelin throw, force is summed sequentially from the legs, through the trunk rotation, to the arm and hand, each adding to the total for maximum release velocity.

Tennis serve A serve builds force from the legs and trunk up through the shoulder, arm and wrist, timed so each segment adds to the racket-head speed. Golf drive A powerful drive sums force from the ground up through the hips, trunk and arms into the clubhead. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the sequential, well-timed use of segments: "Summation of force involves using body segments in the correct sequence and timing — larger, stronger parts first, then smaller, faster ones — so their forces add together; this maximises force in throwing and striking actions." Reference the kinetic chain from the ground up. 🔗 Related terms

Super Setting (Training System) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Super Setting (Training System) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Super Setting (Training System) Two exercises back to back with no rest. 📖 What it means A superset involves performing two exercises in a row without rest . They usually work opposing muscle groups (agonist and antagonist), such as biceps curls then triceps extensions, so one muscle rests while the other works. It increases the training density , saves time and adds a conditioning effect. Because of the shortened recovery, loads may need to be slightly reduced.

It is commonly used in hypertrophy and muscular endurance training. Using supersets in the same muscle group (compound sets) is more demanding and is used by advanced lifters. 🏅 Sporting examples Upper body Bench press followed straight away by bent-over row. Time-saving A lifter completes a session in less time. Hypertrophy Biceps curl and triceps extension paired together. ✍️ Using the term in context Say why antagonists are paired: "In a superset, pairing opposing muscle groups lets one muscle recover while the other works, increasing training efficiency." Supercompensation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Supercompensation IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Supercompensation Why the body comes back stronger — the rebound above baseline that turns training stress and recovery into improvement. 📖 What it means Supercompensation is the process by which, after a training stress and a period of recovery, the body rebuilds itself to a level slightly higher than before . It is the mechanism behind fitness improvement.

Training temporarily fatigues the body and depletes its resources , causing a short-term dip in performance. During recovery, the body not only restores itself but overcompensates , adapting to a higher level to cope better with future stress — provided the recovery is adequate. The timing of the next training session matters : training again at the peak of supercompensation drives continued improvement, whereas training too soon (before recovery) risks overtraining, and leaving it too long lets the adaptation fade back to baseline. 🏅 Sporting examples Improvement cycle

After a hard session and proper recovery, an athlete's fitness rebounds slightly above its previous level — supercompensation — and repeating this builds fitness over time. Training too soon Training hard again before recovering from the last session prevents supercompensation and can lead toward overtraining. Periodisation Coaches structure hard and easy sessions using periodisation to time training with the supercompensation cycle. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the stress–recovery–overcompensation cycle:

"Supercompensation is the process by which the body, after a training stress and adequate recovery, rebuilds to a level slightly above baseline; timing the next session at this peak drives improvement, while training too soon risks overtraining." Supination — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Supination IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Supination Rotating palm-up — the opposite of pronation, used in pulling and racket actions. 📖 What it means Supination is the rotation of the forearm so the palm faces upward (or forward); in the context of the foot, it refers to the outward rolling of the sole on landing. It is the opposite of pronation. Forearm supination occurs at the radioulnar (pivot) joint , produced by the biceps brachii and supinator muscles. It is used in many pulling, lifting and racket actions where the palm faces upward.

In running gait analysis , supination (or underpronation) is the outward roll of the foot, which can also be associated with overuse injuries if excessive. Understanding both supination and pronation is important in gait and injury analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Forearm Turning a door handle upward or performing a pull-up grip involves supination of the forearm. Opposite of pronation Supination (palm up) is the opposite of pronation (palm down). Running gait Excessive supination in running can increase stress on the outer foot and lower leg. ✍️ Using the term in context Define supination and contrast with pronation:

Supplements and Substances — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Supplements and Substances IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Supplements and Substances What athletes take beyond food, and the risks involved. 📖 What it means Supplements include vitamins and minerals, protein powders, creatine, caffeine, beta-alanine, nitrate and sodium bicarbonate . A few have good evidence, but many do not. A food-first approach is usually recommended. Supplements can also be contaminated with banned substances , which can cause an inadvertent doping offence, so athletes should use products that are third-party tested.

Banned substances are listed by WADA and include anabolic agents, stimulants and some diuretics. Athletes are responsible for what they take (strict liability). 🏅 Sporting examples Evidence-based Caffeine and creatine have good support for certain performance. Sympathetic Nervous System — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Sympathetic Nervous System IB Sport Science General Sympathetic Nervous System Fight or flight — the division of the autonomic nervous system that mobilises the body for action. 📖 What it means The sympathetic nervous system is the division of the autonomic nervous system that prepares the body for physical activity, stress and 'fight or flight' . It works in opposition to the parasympathetic ('rest and digest') system.

Sympathetic activation increases heart rate and stroke volume, dilates bronchioles, redirects blood to the muscles, raises adrenaline and mobilises fuel . These responses prepare the body rapidly for physical demand. At the onset of exercise, or in anticipation of it, the sympathetic nervous system dominates — driving the anticipatory rise in heart rate, increasing ventilation and readying the body for action. The balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity governs resting and active heart rate. 🏅 Sporting examples Onset of exercise Sympathetic activation raises heart rate, increases blood flow to muscles and mobilises fuel as exercise begins. Anticipatory rise

The anticipatory rise in heart rate before a race is driven by sympathetic stimulation. Balance with parasympathetic At rest, parasympathetic tone slows the heart; the sympathetic system overrides this during exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the sympathetic nervous system and contrast with parasympathetic: "The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for fight or flight, increasing heart rate, dilating bronchioles and redirecting blood to muscles; it contrasts with the parasympathetic system, which promotes rest and recovery." Synergist — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Synergist IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Synergist The agonist's helper — a muscle that assists the prime mover in producing a movement. 📖 What it means A synergist is a muscle that assists the agonist in producing a movement , either by contributing to the force or by stabilising a nearby joint to allow efficient action. Synergists work alongside the agonist (prime mover), supporting its action. For example, in elbow flexion the brachialis and brachioradialis are synergists assisting the biceps brachii (agonist).

They are part of the team of muscles — agonist, antagonist, synergist and fixator — that together produce controlled, efficient movement. Identifying synergists is part of complete movement analysis, and they are important in rehabilitation where the agonist may be weak. 🏅 Sporting examples Elbow flexion The brachialis is a synergist in elbow flexion, assisting the biceps brachii to flex the elbow. Supporting the agonist Synergists contribute force or stabilise joints to allow the agonist to work more efficiently. Synovial Fluid — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Synovial Fluid IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Synovial Fluid The joint's lubricant — the viscous fluid that keeps bone ends gliding smoothly and nourishes the cartilage. 📖 What it means Synovial fluid is a lubricating fluid within synovial joints produced by the synovial membrane. It reduces friction between the articular cartilage surfaces and nourishes the cartilage, which has no blood supply.

It is viscous (thick) at rest but becomes less viscous when the joint is warmed up and moving — one reason warm-up improves joint mobility and reduces injury risk . It fills the joint cavity and provides the lubricated surface on which the bones move. Together with articular cartilage, the joint capsule, ligaments and bursae, synovial fluid is one of the defining features of a synovial (freely movable) joint . 🏅 Sporting examples Lubrication Synovial fluid reduces friction between the bone ends at the knee during running. Warm-up Synovial fluid becomes less viscous when a joint warms up, improving mobility. Nourishment

Articular cartilage, which has no blood supply, receives nutrients via synovial fluid. ✍️ Using the term in context Define synovial fluid and its functions: "Synovial fluid is the lubricating fluid in synovial joints, produced by the synovial membrane; it reduces friction between articular cartilage surfaces, nourishes the cartilage and becomes less viscous during warm-up." Synovial Joint — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Synovial Joint IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Synovial Joint The freely movable joints that produce almost all sporting movement — built for a wide range of motion. 📖 What it means A synovial joint is a freely movable joint , the type responsible for almost all the movement used in sport. Examples include the knee, elbow, shoulder and hip. Synovial joints share common features that allow smooth, protected movement: a joint capsule , synovial fluid (which lubricates the joint), articular (hyaline) cartilage (which cushions the bone ends), and ligaments (which stabilise the joint).

Synovial joints are classified by the movement they allow — for example hinge joints (elbow, knee) allow movement in one plane, while ball and socket joints (shoulder, hip) allow movement in all planes. Identifying the joint type is central to movement analysis. 🏅 Sporting examples Range of movement The shoulder, a synovial ball and socket joint, allows the wide range of arm movement used in throwing and swimming. Joint protection Synovial fluid and articular cartilage in the knee reduce friction and cushion impact during running and jumping. Analysis Analysing a kick starts by identifying the synovial joints involved — the hip and knee — and the movements they allow.

Systematic Error — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Systematic Error IB Sport Science General Systematic Error A consistent bias in measurement — a flaw that shifts all results in the same direction. 📖 What it means A systematic error is a consistent, repeatable error in measurement that shifts all results in the same direction — either always higher or always lower than the true value. Unlike random errors, systematic errors do not cancel out with repeated measurement.

Sources include miscalibrated instruments , flawed protocol (always measuring at the same incorrect point) or environmental conditions that consistently affect results. Because they are consistent, they can be hard to detect without comparing against a known standard. Systematic errors affect validity — the results are consistently wrong in the same direction. They cannot be reduced by averaging repeated measures (unlike random errors) and must be identified and corrected at source. 🏅 Sporting examples Miscalibration A miscalibrated scale that always reads 2 kg too high introduces a systematic error into body mass data. Protocol flaw

Always measuring skinfold thickness at a slightly wrong site introduces a systematic error. Validity Systematic errors affect validity — results are biased in one direction, not just scattered. ✍️ Using the term in context Define systematic error and contrast with random: "A systematic error is a consistent bias that shifts all measurements in the same direction; unlike random errors, it cannot be reduced by averaging and affects validity, so must be corrected at source." Contrast clearly with random error. 🔗 Related terms Random Error Validity Reliability of Data Controlled Variable Standardisation Mean 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub →

Systolic Blood Pressure — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Systolic Blood Pressure IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General BTEC Sport Systolic Blood Pressure The higher blood pressure number — the pressure in the arteries when the heart contracts. 📖 What it means Systolic blood pressure is the pressure in the arteries during ventricular contraction — the heart's pumping phase. It is the higher of the two numbers in a blood pressure reading.

It represents the peak arterial pressure generated with each heartbeat. In a reading such as 120/80, the 120 is the systolic pressure. It is used alongside diastolic pressure (the lower number, between beats) to assess cardiovascular health. During aerobic exercise , systolic pressure rises substantially — because cardiac output increases — while diastolic pressure typically stays fairly stable. Chronically elevated systolic pressure at rest is a key indicator and risk factor for cardiovascular disease. 🏅 Sporting examples The higher number In a reading of 120/80, the 120 is the systolic pressure — recorded during ventricular contraction. Exercise rise

During a run, systolic pressure rises as cardiac output increases; diastolic tends to stay stable. Health indicator A persistently high systolic reading is a marker of hypertension and cardiovascular risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Define systolic blood pressure and contrast with diastolic: "Systolic blood pressure is the arterial pressure during ventricular contraction — the higher number in a reading; it rises during exercise as cardiac output increases and is used with diastolic pressure to assess cardiovascular health." Tabata Protocol — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tabata Protocol General BTEC Sport Tabata Protocol Twenty seconds on, ten seconds off — the iconic HIIT format that packs an intense workout into four minutes. 📖 What it means The Tabata Protocol is a HIIT method alternating 20 seconds of maximal effort with 10 seconds of rest, for 8 rounds — totalling four minutes. It was developed by Dr Izumi Tabata and shown to be highly effective for both aerobic and anaerobic fitness.

The very short rest periods and maximal efforts create high metabolic stress, producing large aerobic and anaerobic adaptations in a short time. It is more time-efficient than many traditional steady-state methods. It is demanding and not suitable for all athletes, but is used widely in conditioning, sport and general fitness. Any exercise can use the Tabata format, though it is most commonly applied to whole-body, cyclical exercises. 🏅 Sporting examples Format Eight rounds of 20 seconds maximal cycling and 10 seconds rest complete a Tabata Protocol. Adaptations Tabata produces aerobic and anaerobic gains simultaneously, making it highly time-efficient. Versatile

The protocol can be applied to any exercise — sprints, burpees, rowing or cycling. ✍️ Using the term in context Define the Tabata Protocol and its effects: "The Tabata Protocol is 8 rounds of 20 seconds maximal effort and 10 seconds rest (4 minutes total); it produces both aerobic and anaerobic adaptations, is highly time-efficient, and is a well-known HIIT format." Tachycardia — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tachycardia IB Sport Science General Tachycardia An unusually fast heart rate at rest — either a normal physiological response or a sign worth investigating. 📖 What it means Tachycardia is an elevated heart rate above 100 beats per minute at rest . It is the opposite of bradycardia (low resting heart rate). It can be physiologically normal — for example, immediately before competition (the anticipatory rise) or during illness, fever or dehydration. It can also indicate overtraining, cardiac pathology or anxiety .

In sport, an unexpectedly high resting heart rate on a given morning is sometimes used as a monitoring tool — a consistently elevated value may signal overtraining, illness or insufficient recovery, prompting the coach to adjust training load. 🏅 Sporting examples Pre-competition A higher resting heart rate the morning before a major event is a mild tachycardia — the anticipatory effect. Overtraining signal A persistently elevated morning heart rate may indicate insufficient recovery or overtraining. Dehydration Dehydration reduces plasma volume and the heart compensates by beating faster — a form of tachycardia. ✍️ Using the term in context Define tachycardia and its causes in sport:

Talent Identification — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Talent Identification General BTEC Sport Talent Identification Spotting potential early — the process of identifying individuals with the characteristics to succeed at elite level. 📖 What it means Talent identification is the process of recognising individuals with the potential to succeed in a sport . It typically involves assessing physical, technical, psychological and sometimes genetic characteristics.

It relies on the assumption that certain characteristics predict future success, though the relationship between early identification and long-term elite performance is complex. Physical maturity, birth-date effects and opportunity can all confound identification at young ages. Talent identification connects to LTAD frameworks, talent development systems and national sporting programmes . It is most effective when combined with well-designed development pathways rather than early specialisation. 🏅 Sporting examples Early screening Sports programmes screen young athletes on speed, power and coordination to identify those with potential. Talent Pathway — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Talent Pathway AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Talent Pathway The route from potential to performance — the structured system that develops identified athletes toward excellence. 📖 What it means A talent pathway is the structured route through which promising athletes are developed from identification toward high-level performance . Well-designed pathways align with LTAD principles — providing age-appropriate training, developing broad skills before specialising, and building both physical and psychological foundations. They are typically managed by national governing bodies and supported by funding and specialist coaches. Talent pathways can be imperfect — they may miss late developers, contribute to early dropout or fail to account for individual differences. Tapering — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tapering IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Tapering Easing off before competition to arrive fresh and fast — the pre-event reduction in training that unlocks peak performance. 📖 What it means Tapering is a planned reduction in training volume in the days or weeks before an important competition , designed to allow the body to recover fully and arrive at the event fresh, while maintaining fitness.

The aim is to reduce accumulated fatigue and allow the body to reach the peak of supercompensation — shedding tiredness so that the fitness built in training can be fully expressed. Typically, training volume is cut significantly while intensity is largely maintained , so fitness is preserved even as fatigue falls. Tapering is a key part of periodisation , used within the competition phase to ensure the athlete peaks at the right time . Too long or too severe a taper can cause detraining; too short a taper leaves residual fatigue. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance events

A marathon runner reduces their training volume in the final week or two before the race to arrive fresh while keeping some intensity. Swimming Swimmers taper before major meets, cutting volume so they peak with reduced fatigue and full fitness for their races. Peaking Tapering within a periodised plan helps an athlete peak precisely for a target competition. ✍️ Using the term in context Define tapering and its purpose within periodisation: "Tapering is a planned reduction in training volume before a key competition, cutting fatigue while maintaining fitness (usually by preserving intensity), so the athlete peaks fresh; it is part of periodisation and linked to supercompensation."
