Task Cohesion — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Task Cohesion IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Task Cohesion Working together toward the goal — the team's sense of unity around its sporting task. 📖 What it means Task cohesion is the degree to which members of a team work together effectively to achieve their shared sporting goal . It is one of two dimensions of group cohesion, alongside social cohesion. A team high in task cohesion is well-coordinated, committed to the collective performance goal and effective at combining individual contributions . Even teams whose members don't socialise closely can be high in task cohesion.

Research suggests task cohesion is more strongly linked to performance than social cohesion in sport. Coaches develop it through clear roles, shared goals, effective communication and reviewing collective performance. 🏅 Sporting examples High task cohesion A team that executes its set plays efficiently, with clear roles and good communication, shows high task cohesion. Vs social cohesion A team may have strong task cohesion (working well together) even if members don't socialise much off the pitch. Tecumseh Step Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tecumseh Step Test IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Tecumseh Step Test A fitness test of aerobic fitness. 📖 What it means The Tecumseh Step Test is a submaximal step test in which the participant steps for a set time and the recovery heart rate is used to estimate aerobic fitness. Protocol: The person steps on and off a low step at a steady rate for three minutes, and heart rate is measured in the minute after stopping.

Interpreting results: A lower recovery heart rate means better aerobic fitness. It is a safe, low-cost test suited to large groups and less fit people. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A community group is tested before starting an exercise programme. Training use Results are repeated after 12 weeks to track progress. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures:

Tempo Runs — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tempo Runs IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Tempo Runs Steady, comfortably hard runs that raise your threshold. 📖 What it means A tempo run is a sustained effort at a 'comfortably hard' pace , around the lactate threshold , typically for about 20 to 40 minutes after a warm-up. The runner can speak only in short phrases. Training at this intensity improves the body's ability to clear and buffer lactate and raises the pace that can be held aerobically. It also helps with pace judgement .

It can be run as one continuous block or as long intervals with short recoveries (cruise intervals). It should be balanced with easy running to avoid fatigue. 🏅 Sporting examples 10 km runner A 25-minute tempo run once a week. Marathon Longer tempo blocks at marathon-related pace. Tendinitis — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tendinitis IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Tendinitis An inflamed tendon — overuse causing pain, stiffness and reduced function at a key force-transfer point. 📖 What it means Tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon , usually caused by overuse, resulting in pain, stiffness and tenderness. Common sites include the Achilles tendon, patellar tendon and rotator cuff .

It results from the tendon being subjected to repetitive loading that exceeds its capacity to recover . Contributing factors include sudden load increases, poor technique, inadequate warm-up and muscle imbalances. (The term tendinopathy is increasingly preferred, as inflammation may not always be the primary pathology.) Management involves relative rest, load management, eccentric exercise and progressive return . Prevention focuses on gradual loading, strength and flexibility work. 🏅 Sporting examples Achilles A runner who rapidly increases mileage may develop Achilles tendinitis — pain above the heel. Patellar

Jumper's knee (patellar tendinitis) is common in basketball and volleyball players. Eccentric loading Eccentric heel drops are a key rehabilitation exercise for Achilles tendinopathy. ✍️ Using the term in context Define tendinitis and note the preferred term: "Tendinitis is inflammation of a tendon from repetitive overloading, causing pain and stiffness; common sites include the Achilles and patellar tendon, and it is managed with rest, load modification and eccentric exercise." Tendon Sheath — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tendon Sheath IB Sport Science General Tendon Sheath A slippery sleeve around a tendon — the protective sheath that lets tendons glide smoothly past other structures. 📖 What it means A tendon sheath is a protective, fluid-filled covering surrounding certain tendons that reduces friction as the tendon moves. It is lined with a synovial-like membrane that produces lubricating fluid. Tendon sheaths are found mainly around tendons that must slide over bones or past other structures — such as those of the fingers, wrist and ankle . They allow the tendon to glide smoothly during movement.

Inflammation of a tendon sheath is called tenosynovitis , which can be caused by overuse or repetitive strain, producing pain and restricted movement. It is an injury relevant to sports involving repetitive wrist and hand movements. 🏅 Sporting examples Finger tendons The tendon sheaths in the fingers allow the long flexor tendons to glide smoothly over the joints. Wrist Tendons crossing the wrist have sheaths that reduce friction during repeated wrist movements. Tenosynovitis Inflammation of a tendon sheath (tenosynovitis) can cause pain and stiffness in the wrist. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a tendon sheath and its function:

Tendon — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tendon IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General Tendon The cable between muscle and bone — dense, strong connective tissue that transfers contractile force. 📖 What it means A tendon is a fibrous connective tissue that connects muscle to bone . When a muscle contracts, the force is transmitted through its tendon to the bone, producing movement.

Tendons are strong, relatively inelastic and low in vascularity (limited blood supply). Their strength allows them to transmit large forces; their limited vascularity means they heal slowly when injured. The largest tendon in the body is the Achilles tendon , connecting the calf to the heel. Tendons can also store and release elastic energy via the stretch-shortening cycle, contributing to efficient, powerful movement. They can adapt to training loads over time, but this adaptation is slower than muscle adaptation. 🏅 Sporting examples Force transfer The patellar tendon transmits the force of the quadriceps to the tibia, extending the knee. Achilles

The Achilles tendon is the largest tendon, connecting the calf muscles to the heel. Elastic energy The Achilles tendon stores elastic energy during landing and releases it in push-off. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a tendon and its functions: "A tendon is fibrous connective tissue connecting muscle to bone, transmitting contractile force; tendons are strong and low in vascularity (slow to heal), can store elastic energy, and the Achilles is the largest example." Testosterone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Testosterone IB Sport Science General Testosterone An anabolic hormone driving muscle growth and performance — and a banned substance when synthetically misused. 📖 What it means Testosterone is a hormone (anabolic steroid) that promotes muscle protein synthesis, bone density, red blood cell production and development of male characteristics . It is produced by the testes in males and in smaller amounts by the ovaries and adrenal glands in females.

It is the main anabolic hormone in the body, driving muscle hypertrophy and strength development in response to training. Testosterone levels naturally vary with age, sex and training status. Synthetic testosterone and testosterone-like compounds ( anabolic steroids ) are banned in sport because they give an unfair advantage by accelerating muscle growth. Misuse carries significant health risks including cardiovascular, hormonal and psychological effects. 🏅 Sporting examples Muscle building Testosterone drives muscle protein synthesis, which is why resistance training raises testosterone and aids hypertrophy. Sex differences

Higher testosterone levels in males partly explain differences in muscle mass between sexes. Doping Synthetic testosterone is a banned anabolic substance, classified as doping in sport. ✍️ Using the term in context Define testosterone and link to doping: "Testosterone is an anabolic steroid hormone that promotes muscle protein synthesis, bone density and red blood cell production; it drives hypertrophy in response to training, and synthetic forms are banned in sport as they give unfair advantage." Thermoreceptor — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Thermoreceptor IB Sport Science General Thermoreceptor A temperature detector — the sensory receptors that tell the brain how hot or cold conditions are. 📖 What it means A thermoreceptor is a sensory receptor that detects changes in temperature and contributes to the body's thermoregulatory response. They are found in the skin and within the body (including the hypothalamus).

Skin thermoreceptors detect external temperature changes and send signals to the hypothalamus , which acts as the body's thermostat. Core thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect internal temperature. Together, they trigger the appropriate thermoregulatory response — sweating, vasodilation, vasoconstriction or shivering. Thermoreceptors are part of the negative feedback loop that maintains body temperature during exercise. Understanding them links to thermoregulation, homeostasis and the physiological responses to exercising in hot or cold environments. 🏅 Sporting examples Skin detection Skin thermoreceptors detect the heat of the sun and signal the hypothalamus to initiate cooling.

Core temperature Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect when core temperature rises and trigger sweating. Feedback loop Thermoreceptors are the 'receptors' in the thermoregulatory negative feedback loop. ✍️ Using the term in context Define thermoreceptors and their role: "Thermoreceptors are sensory receptors detecting temperature changes, found in the skin and hypothalamus; they initiate thermoregulatory responses such as sweating or vasoconstriction by signalling the hypothalamus, acting as the receptor in a negative feedback loop." Thermoregulation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Thermoregulation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Thermoregulation How the body keeps its temperature stable — a form of homeostasis that becomes critical during exercise and in the heat. 📖 What it means Thermoregulation is the process by which the body maintains its core temperature within a narrow, safe range , despite heat produced by exercise or changes in the environment. It is a form of homeostasis.

During exercise, working muscles produce large amounts of heat , which must be lost to prevent core temperature rising dangerously. The body loses heat through sweating (evaporation), and by redirecting blood flow to the skin (radiation and convection) ; these are controlled by negative feedback. Thermoregulation has important performance and safety implications : heavy sweating causes fluid loss and can lead to dehydration and cardiovascular drift, while a failure to lose heat adequately — especially in hot, humid conditions — risks heat illness. Acclimatisation and a good hydration strategy help the body cope. 🏅 Sporting examples Cooling in exercise

During a hard run, sweating and increased skin blood flow help lose the heat generated by the muscles, keeping core temperature safe. Hot conditions In hot, humid competition, thermoregulation is harder because sweat evaporates less easily, raising the risk of overheating. Trade-off Redirecting blood to the skin for cooling can compete with the muscles' demand for blood, contributing to cardiovascular drift. ✍️ Using the term in context Define thermoregulation and name the heat-loss mechanisms:

Third-Class Lever — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Third-Class Lever IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Third-Class Lever The body's most common lever — the arrangement that sacrifices force for speed and range of movement. 📖 What it means A third-class lever is one in which the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load . This is by far the most common lever arrangement in the human body . Because the effort arm is shorter than the load arm, a third-class lever does not give a mechanical advantage for force — instead it favours speed and range of movement , allowing the end of the limb to move quickly through a large range.

The classic example is flexion at the elbow by the biceps : the elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps (effort) attaches between it and the load (the forearm and any weight in the hand). This design suits the fast, wide movements used in throwing, kicking and striking. 🏅 Sporting examples Biceps curl A biceps curl uses a third-class lever — the effort (biceps) lies between the fulcrum (elbow) and the load — favouring speed and range over force. Kicking The leg acts as a third-class lever in a kick, allowing the foot to move quickly through a large range. Speed and range The body's many third-class levers sacrifice force for the speed and range useful in sporting movements.

✍️ Using the term in context State the arrangement and what it favours: "In a third-class lever the effort lies between the fulcrum and the load; it is the most common lever in the body and favours speed and range of movement rather than force, as in elbow flexion by the biceps." Thought Stopping — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Thought Stopping BTEC Sport General Thought Stopping Interrupting negative thoughts. 📖 What it means Thought stopping is a cognitive technique for interrupting unhelpful thoughts . The athlete notices the negative thought and uses a trigger, such as the word 'stop' , a snap of the fingers or a visual cue, to break it. They then replace it with a positive or neutral thought, such as a focus cue like 'smooth and strong'. It works best with practice. It is often used with positive self-talk, imagery and routines . It does not remove thoughts completely but helps the athlete control their response.

🏅 Sporting examples Missed shot A player stops 'I always miss' and refocuses on the next ball. Race A runner interrupts doubts at halfway. Training Practised in everyday situations to build the habit. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the steps: "Thought stopping involves recognising a negative thought, interrupting it with a cue word, and replacing it with a positive focus." Tidal Volume — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Tidal Volume IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Tidal Volume The volume of air in a normal breath — a basic respiratory measure that rises sharply during exercise. 📖 What it means Tidal volume is the volume of air breathed in or out of the lungs in a single normal breath . At rest it is around 500 ml. It is one of the two components of minute ventilation (tidal volume × breathing frequency). During exercise, tidal volume increases substantially as breathing becomes deeper, helping to move much more air per minute to meet the demand for oxygen and the removal of carbon dioxide.

The rise in tidal volume is one of the body's key acute responses to exercise. Early in exercise, the increase in ventilation comes mainly from increased tidal volume; at higher intensities, increased breathing frequency contributes more. 🏅 Sporting examples Exercise response As a runner increases their pace, their tidal volume rises as they breathe more deeply, moving far more air per breath. Rest to exercise Tidal volume increases several-fold from its resting value of around 500 ml during hard exercise. Ventilation component Together with breathing frequency, the rise in tidal volume drives the large increase in minute ventilation during exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define tidal volume and its role in minute ventilation: "Tidal volume is the volume of air moved in a single normal breath, around 500 ml at rest; it is a component of minute ventilation and increases substantially during exercise as breathing deepens to meet oxygen demand." Torque — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Torque IB Sport Science General Torque The turning effect of a force — the rotational equivalent of force, and the cause of all angular motion. 📖 What it means Torque (also called a moment of force ) is the turning effect produced when a force is applied at a distance from an axis of rotation . It is what causes a body to rotate. The size of a torque depends on the size of the force and the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of the force (the moment arm): torque = force × moment arm. Applying a force further from the axis, or a larger force, produces a greater turning effect.

Torque is central to generating and controlling rotation in sport — producing the spin on a diver or gymnast, the rotation of a limb about a joint, or the turning of an implement. Muscles create torque about joints to produce movement. 🏅 Sporting examples Generating spin A diver generates rotation at take-off by applying force off-centre, creating a torque that starts them spinning. Moment arm Applying force further from a joint increases the torque — the basis of how levers and limb positioning affect rotation. Muscle action Muscles produce torque about joints; the biceps creates a turning effect about the elbow to flex the arm. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define torque and the factors that determine it: "Torque is the turning effect of a force applied at a distance from an axis, equal to force multiplied by the perpendicular moment arm; it causes angular motion, and muscles generate torque about joints to produce movement." Total Lung Capacity (TLC) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Total Lung Capacity (TLC) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Total Lung Capacity (TLC) The most air the lungs can contain. 📖 What it means Total lung capacity (TLC) is the volume of air in the lungs at the end of a maximal inhalation . It equals vital capacity + residual volume , or the sum of all four lung volumes. Typical values are about 6 litres in a young adult male and about 4–5 litres in a female, varying with size, age and sex. Training has little effect on TLC; it is mainly set by body size and the size of the chest. 🏅 Sporting examples Spirometry

A person's TLC is calculated from vital capacity plus a measure of residual volume. Size A taller athlete generally has a larger TLC. Lung disease TLC can fall in restrictive conditions that stop the lungs expanding fully. ✍️ Using the term in context Give the equation: "Total lung capacity is the volume of air in the lungs after maximal inspiration, equal to vital capacity plus residual volume." Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) One number that sums up an athlete's mood state. 📖 What it means Total mood disturbance (TMD) is the overall score calculated from the Profile of Mood States (POMS) . It is found by adding the scores for tension, depression, anger, fatigue and confusion and subtracting vigour . A higher TMD indicates a more negative mood. TMD is used to monitor responses to training, and a rising score can warn of overtraining or inadequate recovery. 🏅 Sporting examples Monitoring A coach tracks TMD weekly during a heavy training block. Total Quality Recovery (TQR) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Total Quality Recovery (TQR) BTEC Sport General Total Quality Recovery (TQR) A rating scale for how recovered an athlete feels. 📖 What it means Total quality recovery (TQR) is a scale (6 to 20, similar to the Borg RPE scale) on which athletes rate how well recovered they feel , with higher numbers meaning better recovery. Training Principle — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Training Principle General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Training Principle The scientific rules of effective training — the guidelines that ensure training actually works. 📖 What it means Training principles are scientific guidelines for designing effective training programmes . They ensure training is structured in a way that drives adaptation safely and effectively.

Core principles include specificity (training matches the demands of the activity), progressive overload (load increases gradually), reversibility (adaptations are lost without training), individualisation (programmes are tailored to the individual) and recovery (adaptation happens during rest). Applying these principles in combination is what separates well-designed training from unstructured activity. They underpin the FITT principle, periodisation and programme design. 🏅 Sporting examples Specificity A swimmer focuses training on water-based activity (specificity) rather than general fitness. Progressive overload

Gradually increasing weight in resistance training drives continued strength adaptation. Recovery Training too frequently without recovery prevents adaptation — recovery is a principle, not an optional extra. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the core training principles: "Training principles are the scientific guidelines for effective programme design, including specificity, progressive overload, reversibility, individualisation and recovery; applying them ensures training drives adaptation safely." Link them to FITT, periodisation and programme design. 🔗 Related terms Specificity Principle of Progression Reversibility Individualisation FITT Principle Periodisation 🎓 Where this appears

Training Zones — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Training Zones IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Training Zones Intensity bands that tell an athlete how hard to train for a given aim. 📖 What it means Training zones divide exercise intensity into ranges , most often based on percentage of maximum heart rate , heart rate reserve, power or perceived exertion. A common five-zone model runs from very light recovery work in zone 1, through aerobic base in zones 2 and 3, to threshold in zone 4 and maximal efforts in zone 5.

Each zone drives different adaptations, so zones help athletes plan and balance their training. The exact zone boundaries differ between models and individuals. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance base A cyclist spends most hours in zone 2 to build aerobic fitness. Interval session A runner works in zone 5 for short repetitions with recovery. Recovery A swimmer uses zone 1 for a low-intensity recovery session. ✍️ Using the term in context Tie zone to purpose: "Training in zone 2 develops aerobic capacity and fat oxidation, while zone 5 targets VO2 max and anaerobic capacity." Trait Anxiety — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Trait Anxiety IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Trait Anxiety A stable tendency to feel anxious — the enduring personality characteristic behind how much nervousness a performer typically feels. 📖 What it means Trait anxiety is a stable, enduring personality characteristic — a general predisposition to perceive situations as threatening and to respond with anxiety . It is part of who a performer is, relatively consistent across time and situations.

It contrasts with state anxiety , which is the temporary, situation-specific anxiety felt in a particular moment. A performer with high trait anxiety tends to experience higher state anxiety in a given competitive situation than a performer low in trait anxiety. Understanding a performer's trait anxiety helps a coach anticipate how they are likely to respond to pressure and tailor anxiety-management support accordingly. Competitive trait anxiety is commonly measured by the SCAT questionnaire. 🏅 Sporting examples Predicting response A performer high in trait anxiety is likely to feel greater state anxiety before a big match, so a coach prepares extra support. Trait vs state

Trait anxiety is a stable tendency; state anxiety is the actual nervousness felt in a specific moment, which trait anxiety influences. Measurement Competitive trait anxiety is measured with the SCAT, identifying performers generally prone to competition anxiety. ✍️ Using the term in context Define trait anxiety and contrast it with state anxiety: "Trait anxiety is a stable personality predisposition to perceive situations as threatening and respond with anxiety; performers high in trait anxiety tend to experience higher situation-specific state anxiety, and it is measured by the SCAT." Trait Theory — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Trait Theory IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Trait Theory Personality as stable inner characteristics. 📖 What it means Trait theory proposes that personality consists of stable, enduring characteristics (traits) that are largely inherited and that make behaviour consistent across situations. Examples include introversion and extroversion , described by Eysenck. It suggests that personality can predict the sports someone prefers, with extroverts choosing team or high-arousal sports and introverts choosing individual or low-arousal sports. It can be measured with questionnaires.

It is criticised because behaviour changes with the situation and research shows weak links between traits and sporting success. The interactionist view is generally preferred. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sport An extrovert chooses rugby. Individual sport An introvert prefers long-distance running. Limitation The same person behaves differently in different contexts. ✍️ Using the term in context State the claim and the criticism: "Trait theory argues personality is stable and predicts behaviour, but it ignores the influence of the situation." Transfer of Learning — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Transfer of Learning AS Level / Cambridge General Transfer of Learning How learning one skill influences another — the effect coaches exploit to build skills efficiently and avoid interference. 📖 What it means Transfer of learning is the influence that the learning or performance of one skill has on the learning or performance of another . It can be positive, negative or effectively neutral.

Positive transfer occurs when one skill aids another (they share useful elements); negative transfer occurs when one skill hinders another (they are similar but require different responses); and there are further types such as bilateral transfer (from one side of the body to the other). Coaches use transfer deliberately: they maximise positive transfer by teaching fundamental skills and highlighting similarities, and minimise negative transfer by making learners aware of differences and structuring practice carefully. Making practice resemble the game promotes positive transfer to competition. 🏅 Sporting examples Positive transfer

The overarm throw transfers positively to the tennis serve, because the two actions share a similar movement pattern. Negative transfer A tennis player's firm-wristed habit can transfer negatively to the wristy action of squash. Bilateral transfer A skill learned with the dominant hand can transfer to the non-dominant hand — bilateral transfer. ✍️ Using the term in context Define transfer and name its types, with a coaching implication: "Transfer of learning is the effect of one skill on another; positive transfer aids learning, negative transfer hinders it, and coaches maximise the positive and minimise the negative by teaching fundamentals and highlighting similarities and differences."

Transverse Plane — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Transverse Plane IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Transverse Plane One of the three planes of movement — the horizontal divide between top and bottom, in which rotational movements occur. 📖 What it means The transverse plane is an imaginary horizontal plane that divides the body into top (superior) and bottom (inferior) halves . Movements in this plane are rotational . The main movements in the transverse plane are rotation — such as the trunk rotating, or the arm rotating medially and laterally — which occur about a vertical (longitudinal) axis running head to toe.

The transverse plane is one of the three planes of movement , alongside the sagittal and frontal planes. Rotational sporting actions — a golf swing, a discus turn, a spin — occur predominantly in the transverse plane. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf swing The rotation of the trunk during a golf swing occurs in the transverse plane about a vertical axis. Discus A discus thrower's spinning turn is a transverse-plane movement, rotating about the long axis of the body. Trapezius — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Trapezius IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Trapezius The large upper-back muscle — moving, elevating and stabilising the scapula across many sporting actions. 📖 What it means The trapezius is a large, broad muscle running from the back of the skull and spine to the shoulder blade (scapula) and clavicle . It has three functional parts: upper, middle and lower fibres, each capable of different actions.

Its main actions include elevation (shrugging) and retraction of the scapula (pulling the shoulders back), supporting the shoulder blade during arm movements, and stabilising the scapula during loaded upper-limb actions. It also assists head and neck movements. The trapezius is important in throwing, pulling, rowing and swimming actions, and its health and strength are relevant to posture and shoulder stability. Treadmill VO2 Max Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Treadmill VO2 Max Test IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Treadmill VO2 Max Test A fitness test of aerobic power (VO2 max). 📖 What it means The Treadmill VO2 Max Test is a laboratory test in which the athlete runs on a treadmill at increasing speed or gradient while expired gas is analysed to measure VO2 max directly. Protocol: The athlete wears a mask connected to a gas analyser. Speed or incline increases every few minutes until exhaustion. Oxygen uptake levels off or peaks at VO2 max.

Trigger Points — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Trigger Points IB Sport Science BTEC Sport General Trigger Points Painful tight spots in muscle that can refer pain elsewhere. 📖 What it means A trigger point is a small, tender, tight area in a muscle or its fascia. Pressing it can cause local pain and sometimes referred pain felt away from the spot. They are often linked to overuse, poor posture, stress or sudden overload. They are sometimes called muscle knots . Treatments include massage, stretching, foam rolling and dry needling. The exact cause of trigger points is still debated. 🏅 Sporting examples Desk posture

Tight trapezius trigger points can cause tension headaches. Runner A tender spot in the calf is treated with massage and stretching. Self-massage An athlete uses a ball against the wall to press a tender spot in the glutes. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe both effects: "A trigger point is a tender, tight spot within a muscle that causes local pain and may refer pain to other regions." Triglyceride — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Triglyceride IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Triglyceride The storage form of fat — the molecule in adipose tissue broken down to release fatty acids for energy. 📖 What it means A triglyceride is the storage form of fat in adipose tissue , consisting of a glycerol backbone with three fatty acid chains. It is the main form in which dietary fat is stored and the primary energy reserve of the body.

During exercise, particularly at lower intensities, the enzyme lipase breaks triglycerides down (lipolysis) into glycerol and free fatty acids, which are released into the blood and taken up by the muscles for aerobic energy production. Triglycerides are energy-dense — providing more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate. Understanding them is central to explaining fat metabolism, fuel utilisation and the energy contributions of different macronutrients . 🏅 Sporting examples Fat storage Triglycerides in adipose tissue are the body's main long-term energy reserve. Lipolysis

During a long, steady run, lipase breaks down triglycerides into fatty acids, which the muscles use aerobically. Energy density Fat (stored as triglycerides) provides more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate. ✍️ Using the term in context Define triglyceride and link to fat metabolism: "A triglyceride is the storage form of fat in adipose tissue; during exercise, lipase breaks it down (lipolysis) into glycerol and free fatty acids for aerobic energy production, and it is more energy-dense than carbohydrate." Triple Jump — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Triple Jump BTEC Sport General Triple Jump A hop, step and jump for distance. 📖 What it means The triple jump follows a sprint run-up with three consecutive phases: the hop (take-off and land on the same foot), the step (land on the opposite foot) and the jump (land in the sand on both feet). The athlete must carry horizontal speed through each phase while absorbing large ground reaction forces , often several times body weight, so strength, elasticity and rhythm are vital. A balance of phase distances is important.

Training uses plyometrics, bounding and strength work , and careful management of load to avoid injury to the knees, Achilles tendons and feet. 🏅 Sporting examples Phases Elite jumpers use a balanced hop-step-jump ratio. Training Bounding drills build elastic strength. Injury The high landing forces need careful progression. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the phases: "The triple jump consists of the hop, step and jump, requiring the athlete to maintain horizontal velocity through each landing." Troponin and Tropomyosin — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Troponin and Tropomyosin IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Troponin and Tropomyosin The proteins that switch muscle contraction on and off. 📖 What it means Tropomyosin is a thread-like protein lying along the actin filament. At rest it covers the binding sites for myosin, so contraction cannot occur. Troponin is a smaller protein attached to tropomyosin. When calcium ions are released, they bind to troponin, which changes shape and moves tropomyosin aside , exposing the sites.

Myosin heads can then attach to actin and the contraction cycle begins. When calcium levels fall, troponin returns to its original shape and tropomyosin covers the sites again. 🏅 Sporting examples Muscle contraction Calcium binding to troponin starts the process. Relaxation Calcium is removed so the sites are blocked again. Cardiac muscle Troponin levels in blood are used to diagnose heart damage. ✍️ Using the term in context Link to calcium: "Calcium binds to troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the myosin binding sites on actin." Type 2 Diabetes — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Type 2 Diabetes BTEC Sport General Type 2 Diabetes Impaired blood glucose control — a condition strongly linked to inactivity that physical activity can help prevent and manage. 📖 What it means Type 2 diabetes is a metabolic condition in which the body cannot regulate blood glucose effectively , either because cells become resistant to insulin or because insufficient insulin is produced. Blood glucose remains elevated.

It is strongly associated with physical inactivity, obesity and poor diet , making it largely preventable and manageable through lifestyle change. Unlike type 1, it is not an autoimmune condition and is typically adult-onset. Regular physical activity is one of the most effective strategies for both preventing and managing type 2 diabetes — it improves insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake in the muscles, helping control blood glucose. This is a key health benefit of active lifestyles. 🏅 Sporting examples Lifestyle link Type 2 diabetes is strongly associated with inactivity, obesity and poor diet — all modifiable risk factors. Exercise benefit

Regular aerobic exercise improves insulin sensitivity, helping manage blood glucose in type 2 diabetes. Prevention Meeting physical activity guidelines significantly reduces the risk of developing type 2 diabetes. ✍️ Using the term in context Define type 2 diabetes and the role of exercise: "Type 2 diabetes is impaired blood glucose control due to insulin resistance, strongly linked to inactivity and obesity; regular physical activity improves insulin sensitivity and glucose control, making it a key prevention and management strategy." Undulating Periodisation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Undulating Periodisation IB Sport Science General Undulating Periodisation Variation built into every week — a periodisation model that changes training variables frequently to drive constant adaptation. 📖 What it means Undulating periodisation (daily or weekly undulating periodisation) is a model that varies training variables such as volume and intensity frequently — even within a week — rather than maintaining the same emphasis for a whole block.

It contrasts with linear periodisation (progressively increasing intensity over a long phase) and block periodisation (concentrating on a few qualities in dedicated blocks). Undulating periodisation keeps the training stimulus varied, which some research suggests maintains motivation and prevents accommodation. It is well suited to multiple-goal training (e.g. developing both strength and endurance in the same week) and is increasingly popular in strength and conditioning, particularly with experienced athletes. 🏅 Sporting examples Week variation Monday is a strength session (high intensity, low volume), Wednesday is power, Friday is hypertrophy — undulating across the week.

Preventing accommodation Varying the stimulus prevents the body adapting too readily to a single repeated stimulus. Advanced athletes Experienced athletes often benefit from the varied stimulus of undulating periodisation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define undulating periodisation and contrast with linear: "Undulating periodisation varies training variables such as intensity and volume frequently within a week or month, contrasting with linear or block periodisation; it prevents accommodation to a single stimulus and suits multiple-goal training." Unilateral Exercises — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Unilateral Exercises IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Unilateral Exercises Exercises that work one arm or leg at a time. 📖 What it means Unilateral exercises train one limb at a time , for example lunges, split squats, step-ups, single-leg deadlifts and one-arm dumbbell rows. Use of Ice in Injury Treatment — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Use of Ice in Injury Treatment BTEC Sport General Use of Ice in Injury Treatment Using cold on injuries, and its limits. 📖 What it means Cold therapy (cryotherapy) is applied to acute soft-tissue injuries, such as sprains and strains, to reduce pain and swelling in the first hours. It causes vasoconstriction and numbs the nerves. Ice should be wrapped in a cloth, never applied directly to the skin, and used for about 10 to 20 minutes at a time to avoid ice burns. It is traditionally part of RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation).

Newer guidance stresses early protection followed by gentle movement and gradual loading , and notes that ice may slow healing if overused. People with circulation problems should avoid it. 🏅 Sporting examples Ankle sprain A cold pack for 15 minutes with compression. Contact sport An ice pack is used on a bruised thigh. Safety Always put a cloth between ice and the skin. ✍️ Using the term in context Give timing and caution: "Ice can reduce pain and swelling in acute injuries when applied for 10 to 20 minutes through a cloth, but prolonged use can damage the skin." Vagal Tone — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vagal Tone IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Vagal Tone A marker of how strongly the parasympathetic system is slowing the heart. 📖 What it means The vagus nerve is the main nerve of the parasympathetic nervous system. Vagal tone describes its ongoing activity, which acts as a brake on the heart by slowing the rate set by the sinoatrial node. High vagal tone is associated with a lower resting heart rate, faster heart rate recovery after exercise and greater heart rate variability. Endurance training tends to increase vagal tone, which is one reason trained athletes often have a low resting heart rate.

🏅 Sporting examples Endurance athlete A trained runner's resting heart rate of about 45 bpm partly reflects high vagal tone. Recovery A fast fall in heart rate after a hard effort suggests good vagal reactivation. Monitoring A drop in heart rate variability can indicate reduced vagal activity and incomplete recovery. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the nerve and its effect: "Increased vagal tone means greater parasympathetic activity, which slows the sinoatrial node and lowers resting heart rate." Vagal tone is not measured directly in sport; heart rate and heart rate variability are used as indirect indicators. 🔗 Related terms

Validity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Validity General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Validity Whether a test measures what it claims to — one of the two essential qualities of any worthwhile fitness test. 📖 What it means Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it is intended to measure . A valid fitness test genuinely assesses the specific component of fitness it claims to, in a way relevant to the performer.

For a test to be valid it should be appropriate and relevant — for example, using a running-based test to assess a runner's endurance is more valid than a cycling test, because it better reflects the demands of their sport (an aspect sometimes called specificity or ecological validity). Validity is distinct from reliability (consistency of results). A test can be reliable but not valid — giving consistent results while not measuring the intended quality. A good fitness test must be both valid and reliable , so that its results are meaningful and dependable. 🏅 Sporting examples Relevant test

Using the Bleep Test to assess a games player's aerobic fitness is reasonably valid because its stop-start format reflects their sport. Specificity A running-based endurance test is more valid for a runner than a cycling test, as it better matches their sport's demands. Valid vs reliable A test could give very consistent results (reliable) yet not actually measure the intended component of fitness (not valid). ✍️ Using the term in context Define validity and distinguish it from reliability:

"Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it claims to; it is distinct from reliability, and a good fitness test must be both valid and reliable, with a valid test being appropriate and relevant to the performer's sport." Variable Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Variable Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Variable Practice Practising a skill in many different situations — the practice structure that builds adaptable, transferable open skills. 📖 What it means Variable practice is a practice structure in which a skill is rehearsed in a range of different situations and conditions , rather than repeated identically. The performer experiences many variations of the skill.

It is best suited to open skills , which must be adapted to a constantly changing environment. By practising in varied conditions, the performer builds a rich schema — a set of adaptable rules — that lets them respond to new, unpredictable situations in competition. It contrasts with fixed practice , which repeats a skill in the same conditions and suits closed skills. Variable practice develops adaptability and transfer , and is strongly supported by schema theory. 🏅 Sporting examples Open skills A footballer practises passing from many angles, distances and under different pressures — variable practice building an adaptable skill. Schema building

By experiencing many variations of a throw, a player develops a rich schema that lets them adapt to a throw they have never made before. Contrast A closed skill such as a free throw is better suited to fixed practice, which grooves a consistent action. ✍️ Using the term in context Match variable practice to open skills and link to schema theory: "Variable practice rehearses a skill in many different situations, suiting open skills; by building a rich schema of adaptable rules, it develops the ability to respond to new situations, and is supported by schema theory." Vascular Shunt — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vascular Shunt IB Sport Science General Vascular Shunt The mechanism that redirects blood to where it's needed during exercise — opening vessels to the muscles, narrowing them elsewhere. 📖 What it means The vascular shunt mechanism is the process by which blood flow is redistributed during exercise — increased to the active muscles and decreased to less active organs . It ensures the working muscles get the oxygen and nutrients they need.

It works through two opposing actions on the blood vessels: vasodilation (widening) of the vessels supplying the working muscles increases flow to them, while vasoconstriction (narrowing) of the vessels supplying inactive areas, such as the gut, reduces flow there. The vascular shunt is controlled by the nervous system and local chemical changes at the muscles. It allows a much greater proportion of cardiac output to be directed to the muscles during exercise, and is the basis of blood redistribution. 🏅 Sporting examples Redirecting blood During a run, the vascular shunt increases blood flow to the leg muscles and reduces it to the digestive system. Vasodilation and vasoconstriction

Vessels to the working muscles vasodilate while those to inactive organs vasoconstrict, shunting blood to where it is needed. After a meal Exercising soon after a large meal can feel uncomfortable because the vascular shunt diverts blood away from digestion toward the muscles. ✍️ Using the term in context Name the two opposing processes and their purpose: "The vascular shunt mechanism redistributes blood during exercise through vasodilation of vessels to the active muscles and vasoconstriction of vessels to inactive organs, increasing oxygen delivery to where it is needed." Link it to blood redistribution and the control by the nervous system and local factors. 🔗 Related terms

Vasoconstriction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vasoconstriction IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Vasoconstriction Blood vessels narrowing — the mechanism that reduces flow to inactive areas and raises blood pressure. 📖 What it means Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of blood vessel diameter , reducing the flow of blood through the vessel. It is produced by contraction of the smooth muscle in the vessel wall.

During exercise, vasoconstriction of vessels supplying inactive areas (such as the gut) redirects blood to the working muscles as part of the vascular shunt mechanism . It is also used in thermoregulation — constricting skin vessels in the cold to conserve heat. Vasoconstriction raises resistance to flow and therefore increases blood pressure . It is one of the two opposing processes (with vasodilation) used to control blood distribution. 🏅 Sporting examples Vascular shunt During exercise, vasoconstriction of gut vessels diverts blood to the muscles. Cold response In cold conditions, skin vessels vasoconstrict to reduce heat loss and conserve core temperature. Blood pressure

Vasoconstriction raises peripheral resistance and blood pressure. ✍️ Using the term in context Define vasoconstriction and its roles: "Vasoconstriction is the narrowing of blood vessel diameter by smooth muscle contraction, reducing flow and raising resistance; during exercise it diverts blood from inactive areas to the muscles, and in cold conditions conserves heat." Vasodilation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vasodilation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Vasodilation Blood vessels widening — the mechanism that increases flow to muscles during exercise and heat. 📖 What it means Vasodilation is the widening of blood vessel diameter , increasing blood flow through the vessel. It is a key part of the vascular shunt mechanism . Vasodilation of skin vessels also increases heat loss during exercise or in hot conditions.

By lowering resistance to flow , vasodilation can also help to reduce blood pressure. Vealey's Model of Sports Confidence — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vealey's Model of Sports Confidence IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Vealey's Model of Sports Confidence How confidence builds and affects performance. 📖 What it means Vealey's model explains how sports confidence influences performance. Trait sport confidence (SC-trait) and competitive orientation interact with the objective sport situation (for example, a final) to create state sport confidence (SC-state) . State confidence leads to behaviour , which gives a performance result . The result and the athlete's subjective outcome (how they judge it) feed back to future confidence.

For coaches, the model shows how to build confidence by emphasising personal goals and success , not just winning and losing. 🏅 Sporting examples Final An athlete with high trait confidence has high state confidence. Vector Quantity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vector Quantity IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Vector Quantity A quantity with both size and direction — the other half of the fundamental biomechanics distinction with scalars. 📖 What it means A vector quantity is a quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction . To describe it fully, you must state both how much and which way. Common vector quantities in sport biomechanics include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum . For example, a force of '200 newtons directed forward' specifies both magnitude and direction.

Vectors contrast with scalar quantities , which have magnitude only (such as distance, speed and mass). Because direction matters, vectors can be added together (as arrows) to find a resultant — essential for analysing the combined effect of forces acting on an athlete. 🏅 Sporting examples Force The ground reaction force on a sprinter is a vector — it has both a size and a direction, which together determine the resulting motion. Velocity A projectile's release velocity is a vector; its direction (angle) as well as its magnitude affects the distance travelled. Resultant Two forces acting on a body can be added as vectors to find their combined (resultant) effect. ✍️ Using the term in context

Vein — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vein IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Vein The return route for blood — low-pressure vessels carrying deoxygenated blood back to the heart. 📖 What it means A vein is a blood vessel that carries blood from the body's tissues back toward the heart . Most veins carry deoxygenated blood (the pulmonary veins, from the lungs, are the exception). Veins have thinner, less muscular walls than arteries because they operate at lower pressure. They contain one-way valves that prevent backflow, ensuring blood moves only toward the heart. This low-pressure system is aided by the skeletal muscle and respiratory pumps.

The largest veins are the vena cavae — the superior and inferior — which return deoxygenated blood from the upper and lower body to the right atrium. Veins can also act as blood reservoirs , holding a large fraction of total blood volume. 🏅 Sporting examples Return route Veins return deoxygenated blood from the muscles and organs to the heart. Valves One-way valves in veins ensure blood flows toward the heart, not backward. Vena cava The inferior vena cava returns blood from the lower body to the right atrium. ✍️ Using the term in context Define a vein and contrast with an artery:

"A vein carries blood toward the heart, operating at low pressure with thin walls and one-way valves to prevent backflow; most carry deoxygenated blood, the pulmonary veins being the exception." Velocity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Velocity IB Sport Science General Velocity Speed with a direction — the vector quantity that describes how fast and which way a body is moving. 📖 What it means Velocity is the rate of change of displacement — how fast a body changes its position in a given direction. Because it includes direction, it is a vector quantity , unlike speed, which is a scalar. It is calculated as velocity = displacement ÷ time , measured in metres per second. The key difference from speed is the inclusion of direction: a runner can have a high speed but, if they change direction, a different velocity.

Velocity is fundamental to biomechanical analysis — it is used to calculate acceleration (the rate of change of velocity) and momentum (mass × velocity), and the release velocity of a projectile is a key factor in how far it travels. 🏅 Sporting examples Release velocity The velocity at which a shot or javelin is released is a major factor in the distance it travels. Speed vs velocity A runner completing a lap may have a high average speed but a low average velocity, because their displacement is small. Sprinting A sprinter's changing velocity over the race — rising rapidly then levelling off — describes both how fast and in which direction they move. ✍️ Using the term in context

Define velocity as a vector and contrast with speed: "Velocity is the rate of change of displacement in a given direction, a vector quantity, calculated as displacement divided by time; unlike speed, it includes direction, and it underpins calculations of acceleration and momentum." Venoconstriction — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Venoconstriction IB Sport Science General Venoconstriction Veins tightening to push blood forward — a mechanism that raises venous return during exercise. 📖 What it means Venoconstriction is the narrowing of veins that increases venous return of blood to the heart by reducing the venous reservoir. When veins constrict, they squeeze more blood forward toward the heart. It is controlled by the sympathetic nervous system and contributes to maintaining or increasing venous return during exercise — one of the mechanisms alongside the skeletal muscle and respiratory pumps.

Venoconstriction reduces the amount of blood 'pooling' in the veins, ensuring more returns to the heart with each beat. This supports stroke volume and cardiac output during exercise. 🏅 Sporting examples Increasing return Venoconstriction during exercise reduces venous pooling and pushes more blood toward the heart. Sympathetic control The sympathetic nervous system triggers venoconstriction as part of the exercise cardiovascular response. Cardiac support By boosting venous return, venoconstriction helps maintain stroke volume during exercise. ✍️ Using the term in context Define venoconstriction and its role:

"Venoconstriction is the narrowing of veins that reduces venous pooling and increases venous return; controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, it supports stroke volume and cardiac output during exercise." Venous Return — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Venous Return IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Venous Return The blood coming back to the heart — the often-overlooked driver of stroke volume and cardiac output. 📖 What it means Venous return is the volume of blood returning to the heart through the veins . It is important because, by Starling's law, the amount of blood returning to the heart directly affects how much is pumped out — greater venous return leads to a greater stroke volume.

Because the veins are low-pressure vessels, the body uses several mechanisms to aid venous return , especially during exercise: the skeletal muscle pump (contracting muscles squeeze the veins), the respiratory pump (breathing changes pressures in the chest), venoconstriction , and valves in the veins that prevent backflow. During exercise these mechanisms increase venous return , which raises stroke volume and cardiac output to meet demand. A sudden stop after hard exercise can reduce venous return sharply, causing blood pooling and dizziness — which is why an active cool down is used. 🏅 Sporting examples Muscle pump

During running, the rhythmic contraction of the leg muscles squeezes the veins, boosting venous return to the heart. Starling's law link Increased venous return stretches the ventricle more, so it contracts more forcefully, raising stroke volume. Cool down Stopping abruptly after exercise reduces venous return and can cause blood pooling and dizziness, which an active cool down prevents. ✍️ Using the term in context Define venous return and link it to stroke volume via Starling's law:

"Venous return is the volume of blood returning to the heart through the veins; by Starling's law it directly affects stroke volume, and is aided during exercise by the skeletal muscle pump, the respiratory pump, venoconstriction and venous valves." Ventilation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Ventilation IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Ventilation Moving air in and out of the lungs — the mechanical breathing process that drives gas exchange. 📖 What it means Ventilation is the mechanical process of moving air into and out of the lungs . It is the first step in the respiratory chain, bringing fresh oxygen into the lungs and removing carbon dioxide. It is measured as minute ventilation (VE) = tidal volume × breathing rate . During exercise, both components increase dramatically, raising total ventilation to meet the greater demand for oxygen and CO₂ removal.

Ventilation is not the same as gas exchange (which occurs at the alveoli). Effective ventilation is necessary for gas exchange but does not directly determine it — exchange depends on the diffusion gradient and capillary surface area too. 🏅 Sporting examples Breathing in and out Ventilation is the mechanical act of breathing — moving air into and out of the lungs. Exercise response During a sprint, ventilation rises sharply as both tidal volume and breathing rate increase. Distinct from exchange Ventilation moves air to the alveoli; gas exchange is the diffusion of gases across the alveolar membrane. ✍️ Using the term in context Define ventilation and distinguish from gas exchange:

"Ventilation is the mechanical process of breathing air in and out, measured as minute ventilation (tidal volume × breathing rate); it provides the air needed for gas exchange but is distinct from the diffusion process at the alveoli." Vertical Jump Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vertical Jump Test General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge Vertical Jump Test A simple, standard field test of explosive leg power — how high you can jump from standing. 📖 What it means The Vertical Jump Test (such as the Sargent Jump) is a field test that measures explosive leg power . The performer reaches up to mark their standing reach, then jumps as high as possible and marks the highest point; the difference between the two heights is the score.

It is simple, quick and cheap , needing only a wall and chalk (or a jump mat), and can test many people rapidly — making it popular in schools and clubs for assessing power . Its results can be compared against normative data or an athlete's previous scores to monitor power over time. As with all field tests, reliability depends on standardised technique and procedure, and it specifically measures lower-body power rather than power elsewhere in the body. 🏅 Sporting examples Power sports A basketball or volleyball coach uses the Vertical Jump Test to assess and monitor players' explosive leg power. Monitoring

Repeating the test across a training block shows whether power training is improving a performer's jump height. Comparison Results are compared against normative tables to rate a performer's leg power for age and sex. ✍️ Using the term in context State what it measures and evaluate it: "The Vertical Jump Test measures explosive leg power from the difference between standing reach and jump height; it is simple, quick and cheap, reliable when standardised, but assesses only lower-body power." Visual Imagery — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Visual Imagery IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Visual Imagery The mental movie of performance — using vivid visualisation to rehearse skills, build confidence and prepare to compete. 📖 What it means Visual imagery is a mental rehearsal technique where athletes mentally simulate sport performance , creating a vivid mental 'movie' of executing skills or competing successfully.

It can be used in internal mode (seeing through the athlete's own eyes) or external mode (watching oneself as if from a camera). Both modes can be effective, though internal imagery more closely replicates the actual sensory experience. Visual imagery improves performance by strengthening neural pathways, building confidence, rehearsing decision-making and managing arousal . It is most effective when vivid, controllable and practised regularly alongside physical training. 🏅 Sporting examples Skill rehearsal A diver mentally runs through the whole dive before stepping on the board — visual imagery. Confidence

Imagining a successful penalty kick builds confidence and pre-activates the relevant neural pathways. Internal vs external Internal imagery (seeing the kick from behind the eyes) typically produces a stronger preparation effect. ✍️ Using the term in context Define visual imagery and its modes: "Visual imagery is a mental rehearsal technique in which an athlete vividly imagines performing; used in internal (own viewpoint) or external (observer viewpoint) modes, it strengthens neural pathways, builds confidence and aids arousal control." Note it should accompany, not replace, physical practice. 🔗 Related terms Imagery Mental Rehearsal Self-Confidence Attentional Focus Arousal Self-Talk

Vital Capacity — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vital Capacity IB Sport Science General Vital Capacity The most air you can move in one breath — the maximum volume from a full inhalation to a full exhalation. 📖 What it means Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation — the greatest amount of air a person can move in a single breath. It represents the usable capacity of the lungs.

It is made up of the tidal volume plus the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes (the extra air that can be forcibly breathed in and out beyond a normal breath). It does not include the residual volume, the air that always remains in the lungs. Vital capacity gives an indication of lung function and size . Although endurance training has only a limited effect on it, a large vital capacity supports the high ventilation rates needed in endurance sport, and it is one of several lung volumes used to describe respiratory function. 🏅 Sporting examples Lung function

A large vital capacity indicates the lungs can move a large volume of air in a single breath, supporting high ventilation during exercise. Components Vital capacity combines tidal volume with the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes. Endurance sport Endurance athletes often have large vital capacities, though training has only a limited effect on this measure. ✍️ Using the term in context Define vital capacity and what it comprises: "Vital capacity is the maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation, made up of the tidal volume plus the inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes; it indicates lung function but is only modestly affected by training."

Vitamin D — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vitamin D IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Vitamin D The 'sunshine vitamin' needed for bone health. 📖 What it means Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin . The body makes it when the skin is exposed to ultraviolet (UVB) sunlight , and it is also found in oily fish, egg yolk and fortified foods . It helps the gut absorb calcium and phosphorus , so it is essential for bone health , and it also supports muscle function and the immune system. Deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

Low levels are common, particularly for people who spend little time outdoors, wear covering clothing or have darker skin. Supplements may be recommended after testing. 🏅 Sporting examples Winter training Less sunshine can lower vitamin D. Indoor athletes Gym and pool athletes may have low levels. Bone health Adequate vitamin D reduces the risk of stress fractures. ✍️ Using the term in context Link source and function: "Vitamin D from sunlight and diet helps absorb calcium for strong bones, and deficiency can increase the risk of stress fractures." Vitamins — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Vitamins IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Vitamins Organic micronutrients in tiny but vital amounts — regulating the processes that keep athletes performing and healthy. 📖 What it means Vitamins are organic micronutrients required in small amounts for normal metabolic function . They do not provide energy but are essential cofactors for countless metabolic reactions.

They are divided into fat-soluble (A, D, E, K — stored in body fat) and water-soluble (B vitamins and C — not stored, so needed regularly). Key vitamins for athletes include vitamin D (bone health and immunity), the B vitamins (energy metabolism) and vitamin C (immune function and collagen). Most athletes can meet their vitamin needs through a varied, balanced diet . Deficiency in key vitamins can impair performance and health, but excess supplementation of fat-soluble vitamins can be toxic. 🏅 Sporting examples Vitamin D Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption and bone health — a key vitamin for athletic performance. B vitamins

B vitamins are cofactors in energy metabolism, supporting the aerobic production of ATP. Diet first A varied diet of whole foods is the best source of vitamins; supplements are only necessary where genuine deficiency exists. ✍️ Using the term in context Define vitamins and give sport-relevant examples: "Vitamins are organic micronutrients needed in small amounts for metabolic function; fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B, C), key examples for athletes include vitamin D for bone health and B vitamins for energy metabolism." VO2 Max from a 1.5 Mile Run Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › VO2 Max from a 1.5 Mile Run Test IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport VO2 Max from a 1.5 Mile Run Test A fitness test of aerobic fitness. 📖 What it means The VO2 Max from a 1.5 Mile Run Test is a field test in which the athlete runs 1.5 miles (2.4 km) as fast as possible and the finishing time is used to estimate VO2 max. Protocol: The athlete runs 1.5 miles on a track or flat surface, and the time in minutes is recorded. A widely used equation is VO2 max = 483 ÷ time (minutes) + 3.5.

Interpreting results: A faster time gives a higher estimated VO2 max. The test depends on pacing and motivation, and is less accurate than lab testing. Training use Used in schools and the military as a simple fitness screen. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context

VO₂ Max — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › VO₂ Max IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport General VO₂ Max The single best physiological measure of aerobic fitness — the maximum rate at which the body can use oxygen. 📖 What it means VO₂ max is the maximum volume of oxygen a person can take in, transport and use per minute during maximal exercise . It is the standard measure of aerobic capacity and one of the best single predictors of endurance potential.

It reflects the combined effectiveness of the respiratory, cardiovascular and muscular systems in delivering and using oxygen. It is usually expressed relative to body mass (millilitres of oxygen per kilogram per minute) so that athletes of different sizes can be compared. VO₂ max is improved through endurance training (via adaptations such as increased stroke volume, capillary density and mitochondria), though it is also partly genetically limited . It can be measured directly in a laboratory with a gas analyser, or estimated from field tests such as the Bleep or Cooper Test. 🏅 Sporting examples Endurance athletes

Elite endurance athletes have very high VO₂ max values, reflecting an exceptional ability to deliver and use oxygen. Relative expression Expressing VO₂ max per kilogram of body mass allows a light runner and a heavier rower to be fairly compared. Measuring it VO₂ max is measured directly with a gas analyser in a lab, or estimated in the field from the Bleep Test or Cooper Test. ✍️ Using the term in context Define VO₂ max and note how it's improved and measured:

Volume (training) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Volume (training) General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Volume (training) The total amount of work done — one of the key variables manipulated in programme design. 📖 What it means Training volume is the total amount of training performed , typically expressed as total sets × reps × load in resistance training, or as distance, time or session count in endurance training. Volume is one of the key variables — alongside intensity and frequency — manipulated in programme design. Higher volume provides a greater stimulus for adaptation, but must be balanced with adequate recovery .

In periodisation , volume is typically high in the preparation phase (building fitness) and reduced during the competition phase and taper (shedding fatigue). Wall Squat Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Wall Squat Test BTEC Sport General Wall Squat Test A fitness test of leg muscular endurance. 📖 What it means The Wall Squat Test is a muscular endurance test in which the athlete holds a sitting position against a wall with the thighs parallel to the floor for as long as possible. Protocol: The athlete leans against the wall with hips and knees at about 90 degrees. The time is recorded until they can no longer hold the position.

Interpreting results: A longer time shows better isometric endurance of the quadriceps and glutes. It needs no equipment, so it is easy to use in class. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A student holds the position for 90 seconds. Training use Used to track leg conditioning. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures:

Warm Up — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Warm Up General BTEC Sport AS Level / Cambridge IB Sport Science Warm Up Preparing the body and mind for exercise — the pre-session routine that boosts performance and reduces injury risk. 📖 What it means A warm up is a period of preparatory activity performed before the main exercise or competition , designed to ready the body and mind for the demands to come and to reduce the risk of injury.

A warm up produces several beneficial effects: it raises heart rate and blood flow to the muscles, increases muscle temperature (improving flexibility and the speed of contraction), enhances oxygen delivery, and prepares the performer mentally . A raised muscle temperature is thought to reduce injury risk. A typical warm up progresses through phases: a gentle pulse-raiser , mobility and stretching (often dynamic), and sport-specific activities that rehearse the movements and skills of the activity, gradually increasing in intensity. 🏅 Sporting examples Team sports Before a match, players do a pulse-raiser, dynamic stretches and ball drills, progressively preparing body and mind for the game.

Sprinting A sprinter's warm up includes drills and build-up runs to raise muscle temperature and rehearse the sprinting action before racing. Injury prevention Raising muscle temperature and mobilising the joints in a warm up is thought to reduce the risk of muscle strains. ✍️ Using the term in context List the benefits and the typical phases of a warm up: "A warm up prepares the body and mind for exercise, raising heart rate, blood flow and muscle temperature to improve performance and reduce injury risk; it typically progresses through a pulse-raiser, mobility and stretching, and sport-specific activities." Water Intoxication — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Water Intoxication IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge BTEC Sport Water Intoxication The danger of drinking too much water. 📖 What it means Water intoxication , or exercise-associated hyponatraemia , happens when blood sodium is diluted by excess fluid intake, so cells swell, including brain cells. Symptoms include headache, nausea, confusion, swelling of hands and feet , and in severe cases seizures. It is a medical emergency. It most often occurs in long endurance events when athletes drink more than they sweat , so guidance is to drink to thirst and include sodium in long events. 🏅 Sporting examples

Marathon A slow runner over-drinks at every water station and develops hyponatraemia. Ultra event Athletes take electrolyte tablets to maintain sodium. Guidance Drinking to thirst reduces the risk. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the mechanism: "Drinking more than is lost in sweat dilutes blood sodium, which causes hyponatraemia and can lead to confusion and seizures." Water — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Water IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Water The foundation of everything physiological — the most critical and most underrated nutrient in sport. 📖 What it means Water is an essential component of all body fluids , critical for thermoregulation, transport, metabolic reactions and joint lubrication. It makes up roughly 60% of body mass. Even small losses through sweating during exercise — as little as 1–2% of body mass — can impair performance by reducing plasma volume, impairing thermoregulation and causing fatigue. Severe dehydration is dangerous.

Maintaining adequate hydration before, during and after exercise is one of the simplest and most effective performance and health strategies. The amount needed depends on sweat rate, environment, exercise intensity and duration. 🏅 Sporting examples Plasma volume Losing water through sweat reduces plasma volume, increasing blood viscosity and heart rate. 1-2% impairment Even a 2% reduction in body mass from dehydration is enough to measurably impair endurance performance. Hydration strategy Drinking before, during and after exercise helps maintain plasma volume and thermoregulation. ✍️ Using the term in context Define water's role and the risk of dehydration:

Wave Summation — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Wave Summation IB Sport Science General Wave Summation Firing faster to produce more force — the way repeated stimuli to a motor unit add up to greater tension. 📖 What it means Wave summation (temporal summation) is the increase in muscle force produced when successive stimuli arrive before the previous contraction has fully relaxed . Repeated stimuli build on each other, increasing total tension.

At low firing rates, a muscle fibre produces individual 'twitches' that relax between stimuli. As the firing rate increases, twitches begin to fuse — first into incomplete tetanus (partial summation) and at high rates into complete tetanus (maximum sustained tension). Wave summation works alongside spatial summation (recruiting more motor units) to allow the nervous system to grade muscle force smoothly from very light to very heavy efforts. 🏅 Sporting examples Increasing rate As the CNS fires a motor unit faster, individual twitches summate into greater force. Tetanus At high firing rates, twitches fuse into sustained maximum tension — tetanus. Combined summation

In practice, both wave summation (faster firing) and spatial summation (more units) occur together. ✍️ Using the term in context Define wave summation and contrast with spatial: "Wave summation is the increase in force from firing a motor unit so rapidly that successive twitches overlap and build on each other; alongside spatial summation (more motor units), it allows smooth grading of force from light to maximal effort." Place it as temporal summation in the force-gradation system. 🔗 Related terms Spatial Summation Motor Unit All-or-None Law Muscle Fibre Recruitment Tetanus Strength 🎓 Where this appears IB Sport Science Explore the course hub → ← Back to the full A–Z Library
