Weight — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Weight IB Sport Science General Weight The force of gravity on a body — distinct from mass, it is a force with a direction. 📖 What it means Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body , calculated as W = mg (mass × gravitational acceleration). It is a vector quantity , acting downward toward the centre of the Earth. It differs from mass (the amount of matter in a body, a scalar, measured in kilograms), though the two terms are often confused in everyday language. Weight is measured in newtons and varies with gravitational field strength, whereas mass does not.

In sport biomechanics, weight is one of the forces acting on a body (downward), balanced by other forces (such as ground reaction force when standing). It features in free body diagrams and Newton's law analyses. 🏅 Sporting examples Downward force The weight of an athlete acts downward; the ground reaction force acts upward, producing equilibrium when standing. Mass vs weight An athlete's mass is 80 kg; their weight is 80 × 9.81 ≈ 785 N — a force, not a mass. Weiner's Attribution Model — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Weiner's Attribution Model IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge Weiner's Attribution Model How people explain their wins and losses. 📖 What it means Attribution theory is about the reasons people give for success or failure. Weiner's model classifies them on two dimensions: locus of causality (internal or external) and stability (stable or unstable). Controllability was added later. For example, effort is internal and unstable, ability internal and stable, task difficulty external and stable, and luck external and unstable.

Attributing success to internal, stable causes, and failure to unstable causes (such as effort), supports confidence and persistence. Attribution retraining helps athletes who blame stable factors. 🏅 Sporting examples Win 'I won because I trained hard' (internal, unstable). Loss 'The referee was unfair' (external). Retraining A coach helps a player see that effort can change results. ✍️ Using the term in context Place attributions in the grid: "Weiner's model places luck as an external, unstable cause and ability as an internal, stable cause." Wellbeing — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Wellbeing BTEC Sport General AS Level / Cambridge Wellbeing Feeling good and functioning well — a holistic state that physical activity is one of the best tools to build and maintain. 📖 What it means Wellbeing is a holistic state of physical, mental and social health and satisfaction . It is more than the absence of illness — it encompasses positive physical function, positive emotions, meaningful relationships and a sense of purpose .

Physical activity is one of the most evidence-based contributors to wellbeing — it improves mood, reduces anxiety and depression, builds self-esteem, enhances social connection and maintains physical health . Wellbeing is central to the aims of PE and sport participation, and is a reason sporting programmes are valued beyond athletic performance. It underpins physical literacy, health promotion and the 'whole person' approach to sport. 🏅 Sporting examples Mental health Regular physical activity reduces symptoms of anxiety and depression, supporting mental wellbeing. Whole-Part-Whole Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Whole-Part-Whole Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Whole-Part-Whole Practice A best-of-both practice method — try the whole skill, drill the tricky part, then reassemble it. 📖 What it means Whole–part–whole practice is a method that combines whole and part practice . The performer first attempts the whole skill to get a feel for it, then practises a specific weak part in isolation, before returning to perform the whole skill again with the improved part integrated.

It aims to capture the advantages of both approaches : the whole phases preserve the skill's overall flow, timing and feel, while the part phase allows a difficult or weak element to be focused on and improved without the demands of the full skill. It is useful when a skill is largely sound but has a specific weakness , and for skills that have identifiable parts but also need their overall flow maintained. It is a flexible, widely-used coaching approach. 🏅 Sporting examples Swimming A swimmer performs the whole stroke, isolates and drills a weak breathing action, then reintegrates it into the whole stroke. Tennis serve

A player tries the whole serve, works separately on a faulty ball toss, then performs the full serve again with the improved toss. Targeting a weakness Whole–part–whole suits a skill that is mostly sound but has one specific element that needs focused work. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the three phases and the benefit: "Whole–part–whole practice combines both methods: the performer attempts the whole skill, isolates and practises a weak part, then performs the whole skill again; this preserves overall flow while allowing a specific element to be improved." Whole Practice — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Whole Practice AS Level / Cambridge General Whole Practice Practising a skill in its entirety — the method that preserves the flow and feel of skills best learned as one piece. 📖 What it means Whole practice is a method in which a skill is practised in its entirety, as a single unit , rather than being broken into parts. The performer rehearses the complete action from start to finish.

It is best suited to skills that are simple, rapid, or 'highly organised' — whose parts are closely interlinked and difficult to separate without disrupting the skill's timing and flow. Practising such skills whole preserves their fluency, timing and feel . It contrasts with part practice (breaking a skill into components) and combinations such as whole–part–whole . Whole practice suits many discrete skills and more experienced learners, whereas complex or dangerous skills may be better broken down. 🏅 Sporting examples Golf swing A golf swing is best learned by whole practice — its parts are so interlinked that breaking it up would disrupt the timing and flow. Cycling

A continuous, highly-organised skill such as cycling is practised as a whole rather than in separate parts. Contrast A complex swimming stroke, by contrast, might be broken into parts (part practice) before being combined. ✍️ Using the term in context Match whole practice to highly-organised skills and contrast with part practice: "Whole practice rehearses a skill in its entirety, suiting simple, rapid or highly-organised skills whose parts are hard to separate, as it preserves timing and flow; complex or dangerous skills may instead suit part practice." Wingate Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Wingate Test IB Sport Science General BTEC Sport Wingate Test The hardest 30 seconds on a bike — the gold-standard test of anaerobic power and capacity. 📖 What it means The Wingate Test is a maximal sprint cycling test measuring anaerobic power and capacity . The performer cycles all-out for 30 seconds against a set resistance, typically on a cycle ergometer. It yields three key measures: peak power (the highest power in the first few seconds, reflecting ATP-PC system), mean power (anaerobic capacity) and the fatigue index (percentage drop from peak to minimum, reflecting anaerobic endurance).

The Wingate Test is widely used in sport science research and performance assessment. It is maximal and demanding, producing a complete picture of an athlete's anaerobic profile. 🏅 Sporting examples Peak power The first few seconds of the Wingate sprint produce peak power — a measure of the ATP-PC system. Fatigue index The drop from peak to minimum power gives the fatigue index — how well power is sustained. Research standard The Wingate Test is the most widely used measure of anaerobic power in sport science. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the Wingate Test and its measures:

Work — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Work IB Sport Science General Work Force times distance — the mechanical measure of energy transferred when something moves. 📖 What it means In biomechanics, work is the product of force and displacement in the direction of the force , measured in joules (J). The equation is W = F × d . Work is done when a force causes a body to move through a distance. If there is no movement, no work is done — regardless of how much force is applied. For example, pushing against a wall with no resulting movement performs no mechanical work.

Work connects to power (work done per unit time: P = W/t) and energy — doing work transfers energy. In sport, maximising work done in the shortest time (power) or over the greatest distance (efficiency) is often the performance goal. 🏅 Sporting examples Lifting Lifting a 50 kg bar 1 m does work: W = (50 × 9.81) × 1 ≈ 490 J. No movement, no work Holding a heavy weight stationary does no mechanical work, despite muscular effort. Power link Doing the same work faster requires greater power. ✍️ Using the term in context Define work and state the equation:

X-ray — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › X-ray General BTEC Sport X-ray Seeing through to the bone — the go-to imaging tool for detecting fractures and skeletal injury. 📖 What it means An X-ray is an imaging technique using electromagnetic radiation to view dense structures, particularly bone . The X-rays pass through soft tissue more easily than bone, creating an image that reveals the skeleton. In sport medicine, X-rays are used primarily to detect fractures, dislocations and bone abnormalities . They are quick, widely available and effective for bone but provide limited information about soft-tissue injuries (muscles, ligaments and cartilage require MRI).

They are a key diagnostic tool in the assessment of acute bone injuries and form part of the decision-making process after pitch-side assessment. Radiation dose is low but not zero, so X-rays are used when clinically indicated. 🏅 Sporting examples Fracture detection An X-ray of a suspected broken bone quickly confirms whether a fracture is present. Dislocation An X-ray confirms a shoulder dislocation and its severity. Limitation X-rays reveal bone well but do not image ligament or muscle tears — MRI is needed for soft tissue. ✍️ Using the term in context Define X-ray and its use in sport:

Yerkes-Dodson Law — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Yerkes-Dodson Law IB Sport Science AS Level / Cambridge General Yerkes-Dodson Law The original basis of the inverted-U — the principle that there is an optimal level of arousal for performance. 📖 What it means The Yerkes–Dodson law is the principle, dating from early psychology, that performance improves with arousal up to an optimal point, beyond which further arousal impairs performance . It is the origin of the inverted-U relationship between arousal and performance.

A key refinement of the law is that the optimal level of arousal depends on the difficulty or complexity of the task : performance of simple tasks benefits from higher arousal, while complex or difficult tasks are performed best at lower arousal. In sport, this maps onto the inverted-U hypothesis — gross, simple skills have a higher optimal arousal level than fine, complex skills. The law provides the theoretical foundation for understanding how to help performers reach their optimal arousal for a given task. 🏅 Sporting examples Simple task A simple, powerful task such as a maximal lift is performed best at high arousal, in line with the Yerkes–Dodson law. Complex task

A complex, precise task such as a golf putt is performed best at lower arousal, as the law predicts for difficult tasks. Foundation The Yerkes–Dodson law underpins the inverted-U hypothesis widely used in sport psychology. ✍️ Using the term in context State the optimal-arousal principle and the task-difficulty refinement: "The Yerkes–Dodson law states that performance improves with arousal up to an optimal point, then declines, and that the optimal level is higher for simple tasks than for complex ones — the foundation of the inverted-U hypothesis." Zero Transfer — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Zero Transfer AS Level / Cambridge General Zero Transfer When one skill has no effect on another — the neutral case in the transfer of learning. 📖 What it means Zero transfer is a situation where a previously learned skill has no effect — positive or negative — on the learning of a new skill. The two skills are unrelated enough that learning one neither helps nor hinders the other. It is one of three possible outcomes when a previously learned skill meets a new one, alongside positive transfer (aids learning) and negative transfer (hinders learning).

Understanding zero transfer matters for coaching: it means time spent on one skill will not help with an unrelated one, so coaches focus effort on transfers that are positive and manage those that are negative. Skills that are biomechanically and cognitively unrelated tend to show zero transfer. 🏅 Sporting examples Unrelated skills Learning to swim has zero transfer to playing the piano — the skills are biomechanically and cognitively unrelated. Coaching implication Zero transfer means practice time on one skill won't aid an unrelated skill, so targeting is important. Three outcomes Transfer can be positive (helps), negative (hinders) or zero (no effect). ✍️ Using the term in context

Define zero transfer as one of three transfer outcomes: "Zero transfer occurs when a previously learned skill has no effect on learning a new one; it is one of three transfer outcomes alongside positive and negative transfer, and typically occurs between biomechanically and cognitively unrelated skills." Zig-Zag Test — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Zig-Zag Test BTEC Sport General Zig-Zag Test A fitness test of agility and change of direction. 📖 What it means The Zig-Zag Test is an agility test in which the athlete runs through a zig-zag course of cones, changing direction at each, as fast as possible. Protocol: Cones are set out in a zig-zag pattern. The athlete runs through the course, and the time to complete it is recorded.

Interpreting results: A faster time shows better agility and balance. Compare the same course layout on the same surface. Results are most useful when the same protocol, equipment, surface and conditions are used each time, and when they are compared with normative data or the athlete's own earlier scores. 🏅 Sporting examples Testing session A basketball player is timed through the course. Training use Used in talent identification. Good practice Standardise the warm-up, equipment and time of day so that repeat tests can be compared fairly. ✍️ Using the term in context Describe the test and what it measures:

"The Zig-Zag Test assesses agility and change of direction; the result is compared with normative data or earlier scores to judge fitness or progress." Zone of Optimal Functioning (ZOF) — Sport Science A–Z | Simply Sport Science Home › A–Z Library › Zone of Optimal Functioning (ZOF) IB Sport Science General Zone of Optimal Functioning (ZOF) The idea that each athlete has their own best arousal range — a more individualised take on arousal and performance. 📖 What it means The Zone of Optimal Functioning (ZOF) is a theory proposing that each performer has an individual range (or 'zone') of arousal or anxiety within which they perform best — and that this zone differs from person to person.

It refines the inverted-U hypothesis in two important ways: it suggests the optimal is a band or zone rather than a single point , and — crucially — that the ideal level of arousal is individual . One athlete may perform best when highly aroused, another when relatively calm. The practical implication is that arousal management should be personalised : a coach helps each athlete identify and reach their own optimal zone, rather than applying a single 'ideal' arousal level to everyone. It was developed particularly in relation to pre-competition anxiety. 🏅 Sporting examples Individual differences

One netball player performs best feeling calm, while a teammate performs best highly fired up — each has a different zone of optimal functioning. Personalised management A coach helps each athlete recognise their own optimal arousal zone and use strategies to reach it before competing. Zone not a point The ZOF frames the optimal as a range within which performance is best, rather than a single precise level. ✍️ Using the term in context Explain the individual, zone-based refinement of the inverted-U:

"The Zone of Optimal Functioning proposes that each performer has an individual band of arousal within which they perform best; it refines the inverted-U hypothesis by making the optimal a personalised zone rather than a single universal point."
